The distinguishing test: configure the import/storage URL to an internal or cloud-metadata address on a staging instance and confirm the server refuses the fetch - a platform that issues the request and returns the response is exploitable for SSRF / internal pivot, regardless of authentication posture.
new_control_requirements.evidence: https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-pc6f-259w-w3j6

CVE-2024-37060.name: MLflow Recipe Deserialization Remote Code Execution

attack_vector.description: A maliciously crafted MLflow Recipe (1.27.0-2.14.1) runs arbitrary code when executed, because it is reconstructed through unsafe deserialization.
attack_vector.privileges_required: low-to-none (upload to a registry the victim uses; victim must load/run the artifact - UI:R)
attack_vector.complexity: low
attack_vector.ai_factor: The abused surface is MLflow, an MLOps / model-registry platform. The lesson: an MLflow model artifact or Recipe is executable code - loading an untrusted one is code execution, so there is no patch, only provenance verification and sandboxed loading. One of the Protect AI / HiddenLayer model-flavor deserialization findings.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: Flaw remediation cannot patch this - loading an untrusted model is inherently code execution; the control is artifact provenance + sandboxing.

NIST-800-53-SI-10.gap: No input validation distinguishes a benign model artifact from a deserialization payload before MLflow loads it.

ALL-AI-PIPELINE-INTEGRITY.gap: No framework treats an MLflow model artifact / Recipe as untrusted executable code requiring provenance verification and sandboxed loading.

compliance_exposure_score.basis: MLflow model registries are shared across teams on trusted-collaborator assumptions; model artifacts are loaded without provenance verification or sandboxing, and no patch exists because the format is inherently executable.

new_control_requirements.name: UNTRUSTED-MODEL-ARTIFACT-LOADING
new_control_requirements.description: Treat ML model artifacts as untrusted code: never load .keras / pickle-based models from untrusted sources, verify provenance, prefer safe formats (e.g. safetensors), and load untrusted models only in a sandboxed, network-isolated, least-privilege environment. Upgrade Keras to the fixed release (>= 3.8.0 for CVE-2025-1550; past 3.10.0 for the CVE-2025-8747 safe_mode bypass) and do not rely on safe_mode alone — it was bypassable. The distinguishing test: load an attacker-crafted .keras archive with safe_mode enabled on a sandboxed instance and confirm no code executes.
new_control_requirements.evidence: https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2025-1550

CVE-2025-27520.name: BentoML serde.py Insecure Deserialization Unauthenticated Remote Code Execution

attack_vector.description: BentoML 1.3.4 through 1.4.2 reconstructs an attacker-supplied serialized object in serde.py from a request without validation, giving any unauthenticated user remote code execution - the same insecure-deserialization class that 1.2.5 fixed, recurring on the serde.py path.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none (unauthenticated)
attack_vector.complexity: low
attack_vector.ai_factor: The abused surface is BentoML, a model-serving / inference framework. The lesson: a model server must never reconstruct an untrusted serialized object from a request - the same inference-path deserialization class as the ShadowMQ / vLLM entries, here on the HTTP serving API, and it recurred in BentoML after the first fix.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: Flaw remediation closed one deserialization path (1.2.5) but the class recurred (serde.py, fixed 1.4.3) - the fix did not generalize to all request-deserialization sinks.

NIST-800-53-SI-10.gap: No input validation distinguishes a safe payload from a deserialization-gadget object at the model-serving endpoint.

ALL-AI-PIPELINE-INTEGRITY.gap: No framework treats a model-serving framework's request-deserialization path as a privileged execution surface.

compliance_exposure_score.basis: Model-serving frameworks are deployed for inference throughput on trusted-network assumptions; their request-deserialization paths are not treated as untrusted-input boundaries.

new_control_requirements.name: AI-INFERENCE-IPC-DESERIALIZATION-SAFETY
new_control_requirements.description: AI inference engines must use a safe serializer (e.g. JSON) for IPC/socket communication, never deserialize untrusted serialized objects, authenticate socket peers, and isolate the channel on a trusted network segment. Because the insecure primitive spread by code reuse, the control must be applied across every inference engine in the estate, not one at a time. Apply the project fix (NVIDIA TensorRT-LLM), and for vLLM keep the legacy V0 engine disabled. The distinguishing test: send a crafted serialized object to the inference engine's socket from an unauthorized peer on a staging instance and confirm it is rejected, not deserialized.
new_control_requirements.evidence: https://nvidia.custhelp.com/app/answers/detail/a_id/5648

CVE-2023-6038.name: H2O-3 REST API Unauthenticated Local File Inclusion (Arbitrary File Read)

attack_vector.description: H2O-3's REST API exposes a file-import path with no authorization check, so an unauthenticated remote attacker reads arbitrary files on the host with the H2O-3 process's permissions (Local File Inclusion).
attack_vector.privileges_required: none (unauthenticated)
attack_vector.complexity: low
attack_vector.ai_factor: The abused surface is H2O-3, an open-source ML/AutoML platform. The lesson: an ML platform's control plane is a privileged surface - its REST API must authenticate every endpoint; a 'trusted environment' deployment assumption is not a control.

NIST-800-53-IA-2.gap: The H2O-3 REST API does not authenticate callers before serving a file-import path; 'trusted environment' is assumed, not enforced.

NIST-800-53-SC-7.gap: Boundary protection does not treat the unauthenticated ML-platform REST API as an exposed surface.

ALL-AI-PIPELINE-INTEGRITY.gap: No framework requires authenticating every endpoint of an ML platform's control plane / REST API.

compliance_exposure_score.basis: H2O-3 is deployed for data-science productivity on trusted-network assumptions; its dashboard / REST API is frequently exposed without authentication, and the vendor ships no fix (trusted-environment-by-design).

new_control_requirements.name: AI-COMPUTE-CONTROL-PLANE-AUTHENTICATION
new_control_requirements.description: An AI compute framework's job/control API must authenticate every caller; 'deploy only on a trusted network' is an assumption, not a control, and must not substitute for authentication. Enable Ray token authentication (2.52.0+), never expose the dashboard / Job Submission API to untrusted networks, front it with an authenticating proxy, and treat any internet-exposed cluster as compromised (rotate model artifacts and cloud credentials). The distinguishing test: from the public internet, attempt to reach the Ray dashboard (default 8265) and submit a job unauthenticated on a staging cluster; it must be refused.
new_control_requirements.evidence: https://atlas.mitre.org/studies/AML.CS0023

CVE-2024-24591.name: ClearML Client SDK Dataset Path Traversal Arbitrary File Write

attack_vector.description: ClearML's client SDK writes dataset entries without path containment on retrieval, so a maliciously uploaded dataset with absolute / ../ entries writes files to arbitrary locations on the retrieving user's system (escalating to code execution by overwriting startup/config files).
attack_vector.privileges_required: low-to-none (upload access to a shared project; victim must retrieve the artifact - UI:R)
attack_vector.complexity: low
attack_vector.ai_factor: The abused surface is the MLOps / experiment-tracking layer that moves artifacts and datasets between data scientists. The lesson: an MLOps platform is a supply-chain channel - uploaded artifacts are untrusted code/file payloads and must never be auto-deserialized or extracted without containment.

NIST-800-53-SI-10.gap: No path validation is applied to dataset entries before the MLOps SDK extracts them.

NIST-800-53-CM-7.gap: Least-functionality is not enforced: dataset extraction writes entries without containing them to the cache directory.

ALL-AI-PIPELINE-INTEGRITY.gap: No framework treats an MLOps platform's uploaded datasets as an untrusted file-write surface.

compliance_exposure_score.basis: MLOps platforms are deployed for collaboration on trusted-team assumptions; their artifact/dataset retrieval paths are not treated as untrusted-content boundaries.

new_control_requirements.name: MLOPS-EXPERIMENT-ARTIFACT-TRUST-BOUNDARY
new_control_requirements.description: An MLOps / experiment-tracking platform (ClearML, and the class: Weights & Biases, MLflow artifact stores, model registries) must treat every uploaded artifact and dataset as untrusted third-party content, because these platforms move artifacts between collaborators automatically. On retrieval the client SDK must NOT reconstruct artifacts through an unsafe object-deserialization routine (use a safe loader / explicit schema, or sandbox the deserialization), and must constrain dataset extraction to a contained directory (reject absolute and ../ traversal entries). Run the SDK least-privilege and only pull from trusted projects. The distinguishing test: upload an artifact carrying a deserialization-gadget payload and a dataset with a ../ entry to a staging project, retrieve them from a separate client, and confirm neither runs code nor writes outside the cache directory - a 'secured MLOps' posture that still auto-deserializes or extracts uploaded content without containment is exposed.
new_control_requirements.evidence: https://hiddenlayer.com/innovation-hub/not-so-clear-how-mlops-solutions-can-muddy-the-waters-of-your-supply-chain/

CVE-2026-33017.name: Langflow Public Flow-Build Endpoint Unauthenticated Remote Code Execution

attack_vector.description: After the CVE-2025-3248 fix, Langflow's public flow execution surface remained exploitable: the unauthenticated /api/v1/build_public_tmp/{flow_id}/flow endpoint runs flow-supplied Python through an unsandboxed dynamic-execution sink, giving remote code execution again; fixed in 1.9.0.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none (unauthenticated public endpoint)
attack_vector.complexity: low
attack_vector.ai_factor: The abused surface is a widely deployed visual LLM app/agent builder. The lesson: an LLM app builder's flow endpoints are code-execution surfaces, so every one must authenticate and sandbox - and the fix must cover the whole class of endpoints, not the single route that was reported (the Langflow pattern recurred on a new endpoint after the first KEV-listed fix).

NIST-800-53-AC-3.gap: A second public flow endpoint reaches a code-execution sink without authentication - the access-control gap recurred on a new route after the first fix.

NIST-800-53-CM-7.gap: Least-functionality is not enforced: a public endpoint runs flow-supplied code through a dynamic-execution sink without sandboxing.

ALL-AI-PIPELINE-INTEGRITY.gap: No framework requires enumerating EVERY flow validate/build/run endpoint of an LLM app builder as an execution surface - so the same class recurred on a new endpoint.

compliance_exposure_score.basis: LLM app builders are stood up for rapid prototyping on trusted-network assumptions and exposed without authentication; their flow endpoints are not treated as code-execution surfaces.

new_control_requirements.name: AI-APP-BUILDER-EXECUTION-ENDPOINT-AUTH-AND-SANDBOX
new_control_requirements.description: A visual LLM app/agent builder (Langflow, Flowise, and similar) must authenticate every endpoint that can reach a code-execution path - validate-code, flow-build, flow-run, public-flow endpoints - and must never run flow-supplied or request-supplied code through a compile-and-run / dynamic-evaluation path with host privileges. Place the builder behind authenticated access control, never expose it to untrusted networks, and sandbox any code the platform executes on a user's behalf (no filesystem/network/process access beyond the flow's intent). The distinguishing test: send an unauthenticated request to each flow validate/build/run endpoint on a staging instance with a payload that attempts a non-flow action (a shell or network call) and confirm it is refused before any code runs - paper 'AI platform' policies that leave a public endpoint wired to a code-execution sink still permit unauthenticated RCE.
new_control_requirements.evidence: https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-vwmf-pq79-vjvx

CVE-2024-12366.name: PandasAI Prompt Injection to Remote Code Execution

attack_vector.description: PandasAI's chat interface turns a natural-language question into Python and runs it against DataFrames; it does not separate analytical input from injected instructions, so prompt injection generates and executes arbitrary Python, escaping the intended sandbox (RCE).
attack_vector.privileges_required: none (unauthenticated, no user interaction)
attack_vector.complexity: low
attack_vector.ai_factor: The flaw is intrinsic to the AI pipeline: the agent's purpose is to turn natural language into executed code, so prompt injection is the exploit primitive. The lesson - LLM-generated code is attacker-controllable code and must be sandboxed, never run with host privileges.

NIST-800-53-SI-3.gap: Malicious-code protection does not treat an LLM agent's generate-and-run-code path as a code-execution channel.

NIST-800-53-CM-7.gap: Least-functionality is not enforced - the code-execution / visualization path is on by default rather than sandboxed or disabled for untrusted input.

ALL-PROMPT-INJECTION-ACCESS-CONTROL.gap: No framework requires that prompt-injectable natural-language input be denied a path to code execution in NL-to-code/SQL agents.

compliance_exposure_score.basis: NL-to-code/SQL agents are adopted for analyst productivity and run model-generated code by design; their codegen path is rarely sandboxed and the natural-language input is not treated as untrusted.

new_control_requirements.name: AI-NL-TO-CODE-AGENT-EXECUTION-ISOLATION
new_control_requirements.description: An LLM data-analysis agent that generates and executes code or SQL from natural language (text-to-SQL, text-to-Python, charting agents) must treat BOTH the natural-language question and any analyzed data as untrusted, prompt-injectable input, and must never run model-generated code with host or network privileges. Disable code-execution/visualization paths by default for untrusted input, run generated code only in a hardened sandbox (no filesystem/network/process access beyond the dataset), enforce least functionality, and validate or constrain the generated artifact before execution. The distinguishing test: send an analytical question containing an injected instruction to emit non-analytical code (e.g. a shell/file/network call) on a staging agent and confirm the agent refuses to execute it - paper 'AI security' policies that do not sandbox the generate-and-run path still permit RCE.
new_control_requirements.evidence: https://www.kb.cert.org/vuls/id/148244

CVE-2025-67818.name: Weaviate Backup Restore ZipSlip Path Traversal

attack_vector.description: Weaviate OSS does not constrain backup entry paths on restore, so a write-capable attacker uses absolute / ../ paths to escape the restore root (CWE-22 ZipSlip) and create or overwrite arbitrary host files.
attack_vector.privileges_required: data-write access (NVD PR:H)
attack_vector.complexity: low
attack_vector.ai_factor: The abused surface is a widely used vector database - the RAG persistence layer that stores embeddings and source data behind LLM applications. The lesson: vector databases are sensitive, RCE-bearing data stores; their file/archive-handling paths must be containment-checked.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: Does not track the vector database (RAG persistence layer) as managed, RCE-bearing software.

NIST-800-53-SI-10.gap: Path validation is not applied to backup entry paths on restore.

ALL-AI-PIPELINE-INTEGRITY.gap: No framework treats the vector database as a sensitive RAG store whose backup/file paths must be containment-checked.

compliance_exposure_score.basis: Vector databases are deployed as convenience RAG infrastructure on trusted-network assumptions; their request and backup paths are not hardened.

new_control_requirements.name: AI-RUNTIME-API-PATH-TRAVERSAL-VALIDATION
new_control_requirements.description: An AI application's file/path-bearing inputs - including archive (backup) entry paths on extraction - must be canonicalized and constrained to the intended directory before any write (reject absolute paths and ../ traversal / ZipSlip). Upgrade Weaviate OSS to the fixed release on your maintained branch (1.30.20 / 1.31.19 / 1.32.16 / 1.33.4), restrict who can insert data or trigger restores, and run least-privilege. This is the same path-traversal class as the Ollama / AnythingLLM entries. The distinguishing test: restore a backup containing a ../ entry on a staging instance and confirm it is rejected, not written outside the restore root.
new_control_requirements.evidence: https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-7v39-2hx7-7c43

CVE-2026-26190.name: Milvus Port 9091 Missing Authentication / Weak Default Token

attack_vector.description: Milvus (CWE-306 missing authentication on port 9091 with weak default tokens) lets an unauthenticated network attacker reach the vector database's operations and data, bypassing authentication.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none (NVD/CNA AV:N / PR:N) - unauthenticated
attack_vector.complexity: low (AC:L)
attack_vector.ai_factor: The abused surface is the vector database - the RAG persistence layer that stores embeddings and the source documents (often PII) behind LLM applications. The lesson: vector databases are sensitive data stores, not caches; every API/management port (including metrics ports like 9091) must authenticate, default tokens must be replaced, and the DB must not be network-exposed. An auth bypass here exposes RAG data and enables retrieval poisoning.

NIST-800-53-IA-2.gap: Authentication is not enforced on the vector database's API/management surface.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: Does not track the vector database (RAG persistence layer) as managed, auth-bypass-bearing software.

ALL-AI-PIPELINE-INTEGRITY.gap: No framework treats the vector database as a sensitive RAG data store whose API/management ports must authenticate.

compliance_exposure_score.basis: Vector databases are deployed as convenience RAG infrastructure on trusted-network assumptions, often with default tokens and exposed management ports.

new_control_requirements.name: VECTOR-DB-AUTHENTICATION-ENFORCEMENT
new_control_requirements.description: A vector database storing RAG embeddings and source data must enforce authentication on every API and management/metrics port (including ports like Milvus 9091), reject forged/missing auth, replace default tokens, and never be exposed to untrusted networks. Upgrade Milvus to a patched release (2.5.27 / 2.6.10). The distinguishing test: from an unauthenticated client, attempt forged-header access to the Proxy and direct access to the metrics/management port on a staging instance and confirm both are refused.
new_control_requirements.evidence: https://github.com/milvus-io/milvus/security/advisories/GHSA-7ppg-37fh-vcr6

CVE-2024-4889.name: BerriAI LiteLLM Config Code Injection via UI_LOGO_PATH / KMS

attack_vector.description: BerriAI LiteLLM (CWE-94 code injection via the secret-management config path) on the LLM proxy/gateway lets admin-influenced config reach a dynamic-evaluation path and execute code on the credential-bearing proxy.
attack_vector.privileges_required: admin-level config influence (NVD PR:H)
attack_vector.complexity: low (NVD AC:L)
attack_vector.ai_factor: The abused surface is the LLM proxy/gateway - the shared chokepoint that holds provider API keys for many models and teams. The lesson: an LLM gateway is a high-value credential store, so its request and config planes must be isolated from the secrets (allow-list egress, no dynamic evaluation of config), or a single SSRF / config flaw becomes mass key theft or proxy RCE. CVE-2024-6587 was the SSRF link of a Pwn2Own full-chain RCE against LiteLLM.

NIST-800-53-IA-2.gap: Authenticator (API key) management does not isolate the gateway's stored provider keys from request-controlled egress.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: Does not track the LLM proxy/gateway as managed, credential-bearing software.

ALL-AI-PIPELINE-INTEGRITY.gap: No framework treats the LLM gateway as a high-value credential store whose request/config plane must be isolated from the secrets.

compliance_exposure_score.basis: LLM gateways concentrate provider keys but are deployed as convenience infrastructure; their request/config planes are not isolated from the credential store.

new_control_requirements.name: AI-GATEWAY-CREDENTIAL-STORE-ISOLATION
new_control_requirements.description: The LLM proxy/gateway must isolate its stored provider credentials from request- and config-controlled flows: allow-list permitted provider endpoints (reject attacker-supplied api_base), never forward stored keys to unvalidated destinations, disable dynamic evaluation of configuration, and keep the admin/config surface off untrusted networks. Upgrade BerriAI LiteLLM to a patched release (1.44.16+). The distinguishing test: send a /chat/completions request with an attacker api_base, and an admin config with a remote UI_LOGO_PATH, to a staging gateway and confirm no key egress and no code execution.
new_control_requirements.evidence: https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-423v-966v-frxg

CVE-2023-44467.name: LangChain-Experimental PALChain dunder-import Code Execution (CVE-2023-36258 bypass)

attack_vector.description: A LangChain experimental chain (CWE-94 prompt-generated Python with an incomplete builtin denylist) turns prompt-influenced input into executed Python, so prompt injection becomes arbitrary code execution in the LLM application.
attack_vector.privileges_required: control of the input prompt to the LLM application (NVD AV:N)
attack_vector.complexity: low-to-moderate (steer the chain's generated/evaluated code via the prompt)
attack_vector.ai_factor: This is an AI-native attack surface: the LLM-application prompt is the injection vector, and chains that execute generated code (PALChain, VectorSQLDatabaseChain, LLMMathChain) convert prompt injection into RCE. The CVE-2023-36258 -> CVE-2023-44467 sequence shows denylisting builtins is an incomplete fix; code generated under attacker influence must be sandboxed or not executed at all.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: Does not track LLM-orchestration libraries' code-executing chains as RCE-bearing software, nor that builtin denylists are an incomplete fix.

NIST-800-53-SI-10.gap: Input validation does not cover prompt-influenced strings an LLM chain turns into executable code.

ALL-PROMPT-INJECTION-ACCESS-CONTROL.gap: No framework treats prompt-influenced input to a code-executing LLM chain as untrusted code; prompt injection becomes arbitrary code execution.

compliance_exposure_score.basis: LLM apps wire in code-executing chains for convenience and trust the prompt; denylist-based mitigations are assumed sufficient despite documented bypasses.

new_control_requirements.name: LLM-CHAIN-GENERATED-CODE-EXECUTION-CONTROL
new_control_requirements.description: LLM chains/agents that execute generated or prompt-influenced code (PALChain, VectorSQLDatabaseChain, LLMMathChain, Python/Pandas agents) must sandbox execution in an isolated, least-privilege, network-restricted environment or disable code execution entirely; builtin/function denylists are insufficient (the CVE-2023-36258 fix was bypassed via the dunder-import builtin in CVE-2023-44467). Upgrade langchain-experimental to 0.0.306 or later, and never expose a code-executing chain to untrusted prompts. The distinguishing test: send a prompt-injection payload that requests code execution to a staging chain and confirm it is sandboxed/refused, not run in-process.
new_control_requirements.evidence: https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-gjjr-63x4-v8cq

CVE-2025-22224.name: VMware ESXi/Workstation VMCI TOCTOU → VMX Host Code Execution

attack_vector.description: Local administrative privilege on a guest VM exploits a TOCTOU race in VMCI (Virtual Machine Communication Interface), leading to OOB write in the VMX host process — VM escape to hypervisor. Huntress PDB-path evidence ('2024_02_19' folder) suggests the exploit chain pre-dated disclosure by ~12 months. Used in ransomware operations per CISA February 2026 follow-up.
attack_vector.privileges_required: local guest-admin in a VM on the host
attack_vector.complexity: moderate (TOCTOU race; in-wild PoC predates disclosure)
attack_vector.ai_factor: Not AI-discovered. Microsoft Threat Intelligence Center disclosure; no AI tool credit.

NIST-800-53-SC-39.gap: Hypervisor isolation control assumes guest-to-host boundary is intact; TOCTOU race breaks it.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.21.gap: Network segregation assumed at the virtualization layer; VM-escape sidesteps.

NIS2-Art21-business-continuity.gap: Hypervisor compromise blast radius covers all tenants on the host.

FedRAMP-SC-7.gap: Boundary protection assumes hypervisor as trust anchor.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: 4h KEV-listing mitigation SLA on the hypervisor estate.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2025-22224 — KEV-listed 2025-03-04; ransomware-confirmed in-wild use.

new_control_requirements.name: HYPERVISOR-VM-ESCAPE-TENANCY-ASSUMPTION
new_control_requirements.description: Multi-tenant virtualization must treat any guest-admin as a hypervisor adversary; KEV-listed hypervisor CVEs trigger 24h SLA regardless of tenancy.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2025-22224 — ~12 months of pre-disclosure in-wild use blew through every tenancy assumption.

compliance_exposure_score.basis: Hypervisor patch cadence is structurally slow due to maintenance-window scheduling; ransomware operators target the window directly.

CVE-2025-22225.name: VMware ESXi Arbitrary Kernel Write (VM-escape chain, ransomware-active)

attack_vector.description: Arbitrary kernel-write primitive inside the VMX process used to write to ESXi kernel memory and execute as the hypervisor. Chained with CVE-2025-22224 (TOCTOU) and CVE-2025-22226 (memory leak) for full VM-escape → hypervisor-management access.
attack_vector.privileges_required: code execution inside the VMX process (typically from CVE-2025-22224 chain step)
attack_vector.complexity: moderate (chain component; ransomware-confirmed)
attack_vector.ai_factor: Not AI-discovered. Microsoft Threat Intelligence Center co-disclosure; no AI tool credit.

NIST-800-53-SC-39.gap: Same hypervisor-isolation gap as CVE-2025-22224; ransomware-confirmed.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.21.gap: Network segregation assumed at the virtualization layer; chain breaks it.

DORA-Art10.gap: ICT third-party concentration risk realised at the hypervisor layer.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: 4h KEV-listing mitigation SLA; same VMSA-2025-0004 cluster as CVE-2025-22224.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2025-22225 — KEV-listed 2025-03-04; CISA Feb 2026 follow-up confirmed ransomware exploitation.

new_control_requirements.name: HYPERVISOR-VM-ESCAPE-TENANCY-ASSUMPTION
new_control_requirements.description: Same hypervisor tenancy posture as CVE-2025-22224.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2025-22225 — chain component in the same ransomware-confirmed exploitation cluster.

compliance_exposure_score.basis: Same hypervisor patch-cadence gap as CVE-2025-22224.

CVE-2025-22226.name: VMware ESXi HGFS Memory Leak (VM-escape chain helper)

attack_vector.description: HGFS (Host Guest File System) memory leak provides the heap-address oracle used to weaponise CVE-2025-22224 + CVE-2025-22225. Local guest-admin reads VMX-process memory via the leak primitive and supplies heap addresses for the TOCTOU + arbitrary-write CVEs in the same chain. Broadcom characterised as 'observed in attacks'.
attack_vector.privileges_required: local guest-admin
attack_vector.complexity: low (information-disclosure read primitive)
attack_vector.ai_factor: Not AI-discovered. Microsoft Threat Intelligence Center co-disclosure; no AI tool credit.

NIST-800-53-SC-28.gap: Memory-protection control assumes process isolation; leak escapes.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.24.gap: In-transit / at-rest crypto irrelevant to in-memory disclosure.

FedRAMP-SC-4.gap: Information in shared resources — direct violation.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: 4h KEV-listing mitigation SLA; same VMSA-2025-0004 cluster.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2025-22226 — KEV-listed 2025-03-04; the heap-address oracle that makes the chain reliable.

new_control_requirements.name: HYPERVISOR-VM-ESCAPE-TENANCY-ASSUMPTION
new_control_requirements.description: Same hypervisor tenancy posture as CVE-2025-22224.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2025-22226 — without this leak the rest of the chain is unreliable; chain-component classification still triggers the tenancy-assumption control.

compliance_exposure_score.basis: Memory-leak-class CVEs on hypervisors are commonly downgraded by operator patch programs; chain-context elevates them.

MAL-2024-PYPI-ULTRALYTICS-XMRIG.name: ultralytics PyPI Compromise → XMRig Cryptominer (60M-download AI library)

attack_vector.description: GitHub Actions script-injection in the ultralytics build pipeline allowed openimbot to inject a post-install downloader after code review. new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: A hosting fleet running cPanel & WHM or WP2 must be driven to the fixed release on a KEV-tied clock measured in hours, and applied fleet-wide rather than server-by-server on a rolling window. The bypass needs no credentials and targets the login flow itself, while the panel is by design internet-reachable so tenants can log in — so an unpatched host is a fully exposed control-plane takeover for the entire time it waits, and a rolling schedule simply means the last host in the queue stays open longest. Because no live-patch primitive is registered for this entry, the fix is a vendor update requiring a service restart or reboot, so that restart has to be pre-authorized against the KEV clock instead of deferred to the next tenant-notified maintenance slot. Hosts that cannot be updated inside the SLA must have their panel and WHM listeners restricted to operator networks and be booked as unremediated.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Packet: CISA KEV-listed 2026-04-30 with active_exploitation=confirmed; RWEP 83, CVSS 9.1, poc_available=true. The vector states WebPros cPanel & WHM (WebHost Manager) and WP2 (WordPress Squared) contain an authentication bypass vulnerability in the login flow that allows unauthenticated remote attackers to gain unauthorized access to the control panel (CWE-306, missing authentication for a critical function). patch_available=true, live_patch_available=false, and live_patch_notes state the vendor patch typically requires service restart or system reboot per the KEV requiredAction.

new_control_requirements.name: PERIMETER-COMPROMISE-REBUILD-NOT-PATCH
new_control_requirements.description: A panel host that was internet-reachable while unpatched must go through compromise assessment and credential rotation rather than patch-and-continue. Because the bypass hands an unauthenticated caller the control panel itself, the attacker inherits the panel's own legitimate capabilities — creating accounts and API tokens, rewriting mail and DNS records, writing files into tenant document roots, installing cron persistence — and none of that is removed by the update. The default response is configuration export, rebuild or restore of the panel host from known-good state, rotation of every tenant, reseller and API credential the panel issued, and an audit of accounts, cron entries and tenant webroots created since the KEV listing date. Anti-malware scanning is not the test here: the artifacts left behind are ordinary panel objects and ordinary web content, not malware signatures.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Packet: CISA KEV-listed 2026-04-30 with active_exploitation=confirmed, poc_available=true and RWEP 83, so an exposed unpatched host is an exploitation opportunity rather than a hypothetical. The vector states the authentication bypass in the login flow allows unauthenticated remote attackers to gain unauthorized access to the control panel of WebPros cPanel & WHM and WP2 — the attacker operates as a panel principal rather than through a memory-corruption payload (CWE-306). patch_available=true with live_patch_available=false; the packet's remediation is a vendor patch requiring service restart or system reboot, which closes the entry path but makes no statement about actions already taken through it.

new_control_requirements.name: FLEET-CONTROL-PLANE-ADMIN-PRIVILEGE-TIER
new_control_requirements.description: WHM is the fleet control plane for every tenant site, mailbox, database and DNS zone on the host, and this flaw is the argument for making its administration a distinct privilege tier instead of the same login surface at a higher permission level. The WHM root and reseller surface should be reachable only from a PAM jumphost or operator network, behind FIDO2 step-up and just-in-time elevation with a separate identity from tenant accounts, so that a defect in the login flow does not present the whole hosting estate to an anonymous internet caller. Splitting the surfaces also bounds the damage where the tenant-facing cPanel login has to stay internet-exposed for customers: that side gets patched under the KEV clock, while the administrative plane is never an unauthenticated caller's first hop in the first place.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Packet: CWE-306, missing authentication for a critical function — the vector records an authentication bypass in the login flow of WebPros cPanel & WHM (WebHost Manager) and WP2 (WordPress Squared) allowing unauthenticated remote attackers to gain unauthorized access to the control panel. CISA KEV-listed 2026-04-30, active_exploitation=confirmed, CVSS 9.1, RWEP 83, poc_available=true. The citing gaps recorded for this entry include NIST-800-53-AC-6 (Least Privilege) and UK-CAF-B2 (Identity and access control), both of which the packet marks as insufficient here.

new_control_requirements.name: PERIMETER-COMPROMISE-REBUILD-NOT-PATCH
new_control_requirements.description: Upgrading the ScreenConnect server to the fixed build removes the traversal but not what the traversal already wrote. CVE-2024-1708 is an arbitrary file-write primitive: chained with the companion authentication bypass it plants a web shell in a ScreenConnect-served directory, and that file is application content rather than product code, so the vendor update leaves it in place and running. Any ScreenConnect instance that was reachable from an untrusted network on a vulnerable build must therefore be handled as compromised rather than as remediated: export the configuration, session history and extension inventory for forensics, rebuild the host from known-good media, reinstall at the fixed version, and rotate everything the server held or brokered — the relay/agent join material, the ScreenConnect administrative and integrated-identity accounts, and any credential a technician entered through a remote session during the exposure window. Deleting the one web shell that was found and then patching is not equivalent, because the same write primitive places files anywhere the service account can reach, and the read half of the traversal means configuration secrets on the host should be assumed disclosed.
new_control_requirements.evidence: ConnectWise ScreenConnect, CISA KEV-listed 2026-04-28 with confirmed in-the-wild exploitation and a public PoC available. The attack-vector record states the path traversal (CWE-22) lets an attacker write or read files outside the intended directory and was used with the companion authentication bypass to drop a web shell — i.e. attacker-planted files persist independently of the vendor patch. RWEP 83 against CVSS 7.5: the gap between the two is exactly the post-exploitation persistence that a base score for an information-disclosure-shaped traversal does not carry.

new_control_requirements.name: FLEET-COMPROMISE-IR-PLAYBOOK
new_control_requirements.description: ScreenConnect is a fleet control plane, not an ordinary web application: its access agents run with service-level privilege on every managed endpoint and execute what the server tells them to. An incident-response plan scoped to 'the ScreenConnect host' therefore has the wrong blast radius, because a web shell reached through this traversal gives the attacker the same command channel into the managed estate that the legitimate operator has. The playbook must be written and rehearsed before the event and must cover: revocation and re-issue of the relay/agent trust material so existing agent installations cannot be driven by attacker-held server identity; an audit of session, command and file-transfer history plus any extension or extension directory added since the exposure window opened; quarantine criteria for endpoints that received a session or a queued command during that window; and rotation of every credential used through a remote session, including the customer-side administrative accounts a technician authenticated with. Recovery timing must assume the ScreenConnect server itself is unavailable during the response, since it is the system being rebuilt.
new_control_requirements.evidence: ConnectWise ScreenConnect path traversal, CISA KEV-listed 2026-04-28, active exploitation confirmed, public PoC available, RWEP 83. The traversal was used with the companion authentication bypass to drop a web shell on the server that brokers remote sessions to managed endpoints, which places every endpoint reachable from that server inside the incident scope rather than outside it.

new_control_requirements.description: For a DIR-823X the KEV clock has to terminate in a verified per-unit outcome, because the failure mode of consumer-router patching is not a missed deadline, it is an open-ended 'awaiting firmware' state that never resolves. new_control_requirements.name: ENDPOINT-MGMT-DEPLOYMENT-CHANNEL-INTEGRITY
new_control_requirements.description: The primitive in this CVE is an arbitrary write anywhere on the filesystem as the SimpleHelp server user — so the exposed asset is not just the web root but every file that remote-support server holds and hands out: session and client artifacts, technician-facing downloads, service configuration and any script the server executes. Treat that content as a privileged distribution channel rather than as application data: file-integrity-monitor the SimpleHelp installation and every directory it serves artifacts from, alert on writes that do not correspond to a sanctioned administrator action or a vendor update, and hold the support server to KEV-priority patching as a management-plane asset. This is the control that still has value after the patch lands, because the fix closes the zip-slip write path but removes nothing already written through it — an attacker file placed before remediation survives the upgrade, and neither signature-based anti-malware nor authentication logging will surface a bespoke artifact dropped through a legitimate upload endpoint.
new_control_requirements.evidence: The catalog vector states the flaw lets an actor 'upload arbitrary files anywhere on the file system by uploading a crafted zip file (i.e. zip slip)' and thereby 'execute arbitrary code on the host in the context of the SimpleHelp server user'; the attack_vector locates the flaw 'on the remote-support server'. KEV-listed 2026-04-24 with active_exploitation 'confirmed' and poc_available true, RWEP 83. The gaps this entry already cites include CIS Controls v8 10.1 (Deploy and Maintain Anti-Malware Software) and UK CAF C1 (Security monitoring) — neither detects an attacker-written artifact that carries no malware signature and arrives over an authenticated upload path.

attack_vector.description: a missing-authorization flaw (CWE-862) letting a low-privileged or unauthenticated attacker reach privileged functionality on the remote-support server. CISA KEV-listed 2026-04-24 with confirmed in-the-wild exploitation.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none (the flaw is reachable by an unauthenticated attacker on the platform's public interface)
attack_vector.complexity: low — KEV-listed, actively exploited; treat as weaponized
attack_vector.ai_factor: No AI involvement documented in discovery or weaponization.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Apply the SimpleHelp security update; hunt for web shells, rotate credentials and secrets, and review downstream managed/integrated systems — management platforms reach the whole estate, so treat compromise as fleet-wide.
prevention.adequacy: Patch is necessary but insufficient alone — web shells, stolen credentials, and pushed tasking survive the patch and require explicit cleanup across managed systems.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Monitoring on the SimpleHelp: exploit-shaped requests, new web-shell files, unexpected process execution, administrative actions without a matching session, and anomalous jobs/scripts pushed to managed endpoints.
detection.adequacy: Necessary to catch resident persistence and downstream tasking after patching.

response.what_would_have_worked: Patch immediately, hunt and remove web shells, rotate all platform and integration credentials, and audit every action the platform pushed to managed systems during the exposure window; assume downstream compromise.
response.adequacy: Mandatory; a management-platform compromise can re-establish itself through the very systems it administers, so downstream review is non-negotiable.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: The 30-day flaw-remediation SLA is far longer than the observed exploitation window for a KEV-listed, unauthenticated IT-management/enterprise platform RCE; these are mass-exploited within days, and RMM/ITSM/endpoint-management compromise reaches the entire managed estate.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: 'Appropriate timescales' is undefined; the standard 30-day reading is unsafe for an actively-exploited, internet-facing management platform whose compromise is fleet-wide.

NIS2-Art21-network-security.gap: Treats management platforms as essential-function infrastructure but lacks a CISA-KEV-style compressed remediation SLA, and does not require the web-shell-hunt / credential-rotation / downstream-review cleanup these RCEs need given their managed-estate reach.

PCI-DSS-4.0-6.3.3.gap: The 30-day critical-patch window is exploitation acceptance for an internet-facing management platform that can administer systems in or adjacent to the CDE.

compliance_exposure_score.basis: Internet-facing SimpleHelp is run by audited organizations on a standard patch SLA and is mass-exploited within days; the required web-shell hunt, credential rotation, and downstream-estate review are rarely part of the documented patch procedure, and the management reach amplifies the blast radius.

new_control_requirements.name: FLEET-CONTROL-PLANE-ADMIN-PRIVILEGE-TIER
new_control_requirements.description: SimpleHelp is a remote-support control plane, so its server admin role reaches every machine the technician population supports — the technician tier and the server-admin tier are not two shades of the same application user. This CVE collapses the distance between them: the entry records that low-privileged technicians can create API keys with excessive permissions and use those keys to escalate to the server admin role. Server administration of SimpleHelp needs to be classified as its own privilege tier — identity separate from every other admin role, jumphost-only access with hardware-key step-up, just-in-time elevation with approval — and the technician surface must not be able to mint or hold API keys at all. A framework that enumerates one admin role for this product attests accurately while the technician surface remains the real path into it.
new_control_requirements.evidence: SimpleHelp missing authorization (CWE-862), CVSS 8.8, RWEP 83. The entry states low-privileged technicians can create API keys with excessive permissions and that these keys can be used to escalate privileges to the server admin role, on a remote-support server. CISA KEV-listed 2026-04-24 with active_exploitation=confirmed and poc_available=true.

new_control_requirements.name: FLEET-COMPROMISE-IR-PLAYBOOK
new_control_requirements.description: The escalation product here is a durable credential rather than a session: an API key minted through the missing-authorization flaw still carries server-admin power after the vendor fix is installed. The playbook for this CVE therefore has to enumerate and revoke every API key issued on the SimpleHelp server across the exposure window, audit technician accounts and role assignments for keys they should never have been able to create, and treat every endpoint reached through the server during that window as requiring credential rotation and review — a remote-support server is a path into the machines it supports, so its compromise fans outward rather than stopping at the appliance. Patching closes the minting path and leaves already-minted keys valid, which is precisely the state an audit reading only installed version would score as clean.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Missing authorization (CWE-862) on a remote-support server; the entry records that the API keys created through the flaw can be used to escalate to the server admin role. active_exploitation=confirmed, poc_available=true, CISA KEV-listed 2026-04-24, RWEP 83, CVSS 8.8.

new_control_requirements.description: SimpleHelp entered CISA KEV on 2026-04-24 with confirmed exploitation and a public PoC and a vendor fix exists, so this runs on the KEV clock rather than a quarterly application-patch cycle. new_control_requirements.name: DEVICE-MANAGEMENT-GATEWAY-CONFIG-ENDPOINT-AUTH-INPUT-NEUTRALIZATION
new_control_requirements.description: Catalyst SD-WAN Manager is the management plane the packet names, and the defect sits on its API interface: improper file handling lets an uploaded file drive a privileged API into overwriting arbitrary files on the system, ending in vmanage user privileges. Bound to this product, the control means every file-accepting API endpoint on SD-WAN Manager authorizes its caller before the upload is processed at all, and normalizes and validates the destination path before the privileged write executes, so a caller-supplied name cannot select which file gets overwritten; and no SD-WAN Manager instance is left with that API interface reachable from a segment with no operational need to reach it. The packet's own summary describes the path as reachable by an unauthenticated attacker, which is why the endpoint's own authorization decision — not the surrounding account model — is the only thing standing between an untrusted caller and a privileged file write. This is also why the cited least-privilege gap does not close this path: the attacker never holds a vManage operator account, so per-account privilege scoping is never consulted and an AC-6 attestation passes cleanly while the path stays open. Distinguishing test: on a staging SD-WAN Manager, send each file-accepting API endpoint an unauthenticated upload whose destination path resolves outside the intended upload directory, and confirm it is refused before anything is written. Precondition: the endpoint-side authorization and path validation are properties the vendor update establishes — this control states what to verify, it does not implement it. Until that update and its restart land, restricting which segments can reach the API interface bounds who can send the upload but leaves the endpoint fully exploitable to anything inside the permitted segment, and it is unavailable where the API interface must stay reachable for normal operation.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Packet vector: 'Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN Manager contains an incorrect use of privileged APIs vulnerability due to improper file handling on the API interface of an affected system. An attacker could exploit this vulnerability by uploading a malicious file on the local file system. A successful exploit could allow the attacker to overwrite arbitrary files on the affected system and gain vmanage user privileges.' Packet attack_vector: 'an incorrect use of privileged APIs (CWE-648) reachable by an unauthenticated attacker, enabling privileged actions on the management plane.' Citing gaps record NIST-800-53-AC-6 (Least Privilege) against this entry. patch_available true; live_patch_available false.

Applied to this product, the control means treating the SD-WAN Manager installation as privileged content rather than as application data: file-integrity-monitor the installation and the directories its API writes into, and alert on any write that does not correspond to a sanctioned administrator action or a vendor update. This is the control that still has value after the update lands, because the fix closes the write path but removes nothing already written through it — a file overwritten or planted before remediation survives the upgrade and the restart. With exploitation confirmed and a public exploit recorded in the packet, an instance whose API interface was reachable before remediation needs forensic triage of what was written rather than being closed on the patch. Where no such baseline exists, the honest position is that the overwritten set is unknown and the instance is a rebuild candidate, not a patched-and-cleared one.

new_control_requirements.name: ENTERPRISE-ERP-MANAGEMENT-FUNCTION-AUTHENTICATION

new_control_requirements.name: FLEET-CONTROL-PLANE-ADMIN-PRIVILEGE-TIER
new_control_requirements.description: This flaw's entire precondition is a low-privileged local account on the SD-WAN Manager appliance: the packet has an authenticated, local attacker reading a credential file for the DCA user from the filesystem and thereby gaining DCA privileges. Bound here, privilege tiering means the appliance carries no general-purpose local accounts at all — every operator who can obtain shell or filesystem-level access on vManage sits in a distinct tier above application and network admins, reached only through a PAM jumphost with FIDO2 step-up, just-in-time elevation, an identity used for nothing else, and per-session attribution. State the precondition honestly rather than claiming the surface is removed: this shrinks the population that can reach the credential file, it does not make the stored password unrecoverable. Any principal that does obtain low-privileged local access on the appliance — through an operational account, a support process, or any other local-access defect on the same host — still recovers the DCA credential, and the control has no effect at all on a credential that was already read. The cited least-privilege and identity-and-access-control gaps are recorded here because the escalation runs from one local account to another via a file read, so an attestation that vManage roles are least-privileged passes cleanly while the recoverable credential file sits on disk. Distinguishing test: from a deliberately low-privileged local account on a staging appliance, attempt to read the DCA credential file and confirm the account cannot exist in the first place under the tiering policy.

new_control_requirements.name: FLEET-COMPROMISE-IR-PLAYBOOK
new_control_requirements.description: A recoverable-format password disclosure is not closed by the code fix: the update changes how the DCA credential is stored, but a password an attacker has already read stays valid until it is changed. With the packet recording confirmed in-the-wild exploitation from the 2026-04-20 KEV listing on a controller whose own filesystem held the credential, the response half of this control is the load-bearing half — rotate the DCA credential and any other credential recoverable from the appliance filesystem as part of the update rather than as a follow-up ticket, audit what that account was used for across the exposure window, and invalidate device-trust state established through the controller where the account's use cannot be accounted for. Two preconditions decide whether the rotation is worth anything. It has to happen after the fixed build is running: rotating first simply writes a fresh password back into the recoverable format, leaving the operator with a rotation record and an unchanged exposure. new_control_requirements.name: ENTERPRISE-ERP-MANAGEMENT-FUNCTION-AUTHENTICATION
new_control_requirements.description: KACE SMA takes an authentication decision in front of an endpoint-management console, and this CVE is that decision failing open: the packet has an attacker impersonating legitimate users without valid credentials, reaching functionality behind the gate without ever presenting an account. The precondition on the segmentation half must be stated rather than implied — it bounds who can reach the bypass, not whether the bypass works. A request originating from a permitted management segment, from an already-compromised administrator workstation, or from access obtained before the restriction was applied still reaches it, so segmentation buys time until the appliance is restarted onto the fixed build and never substitutes for that restart. new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: A vendor patch for this Office document-parsing flaw exists and the CVE identifier dates to 2009, yet CISA added it to KEV on 2026-04-14 on the strength of current in-the-wild exploitation. Any remediation queue that sorts or ages by CVE publication date, by 'newly disclosed' status, or by scanner first-seen date buries a CVE-2009 entry beneath every current-quarter finding and it never reaches a patch window, which is exactly why the long-tail estate is still being exploited. The KEV listing date must start the clock instead of the CVE year: on 2026-04-14 every Office installation in the estate is re-evaluated against the fixed build inside the KEV SLA, and any Office build that cannot reach it is cut off from untrusted documents rather than risk-accepted by age. The distinguishing test: query the vulnerability queue for KEV-listed CVEs older than ten years and confirm they carry the same due date as a current-quarter KEV entry — a program whose SLA derives from disclosure age reports 'no overdue criticals' while an actively exploited 2009 Office flaw sits unremediated on the frozen estate.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Packet: CVE-2009-0238, Microsoft Office Remote Code Execution, CWE-94 code injection in Office document parsing, exploitable by an attacker-controlled document for code execution in the Office process. CISA KEV-listed 2026-04-14, active_exploitation confirmed, CVSS 9.8, RWEP 77, poc_available true, patch_available true — the residual exposure is the long-tail unpatched estate, not an absent fix.

new_control_requirements.name: DOWNLOAD-PROVENANCE-ENFORCEMENT
new_control_requirements.description: Exploitation here requires the victim to open an attacker-supplied Office document, so on an estate that has not yet reached the fixed build the delivery path is the only enforceable control. Require Mark-of-the-Web on every Office file arriving by mail, web download, or untrusted file share, and require MOTW-tagged documents to open in Protected View — an isolated, reduced-privilege render — instead of the full parsing path that carries the CWE-94 sink at the user's own process privilege. Provenance must survive the container: files extracted from an archive, mounted from an ISO or VHD, or renamed must inherit the tag rather than lose it, and 'Enable Editing' on externally sourced documents must be blocked by policy rather than left to the user. The distinguishing test: mail a MOTW-tagged spreadsheet nested inside a ZIP to a managed workstation, extract it, and confirm the extracted file still opens in Protected View — a user-application-hardening attestation that covers only macro and ActiveX/OLE settings still lets a provenance-stripped document reach the vulnerable parser with full user privileges.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Packet attack vector: an attacker-controlled document reaching Microsoft Office's parser for code execution in the Office process (CWE-94). poc_available true and CISA-confirmed in-the-wild exploitation at the 2026-04-14 KEV listing. AU-Essential-8-App-Hardening (user application hardening) and NIST-800-53-AC-6 (least privilege) are both already recorded as insufficient controls citing this CVE.

new_control_requirements.description: Put the on-premises SharePoint Server farm on a clock that starts at the 2026-04-14 KEV listing rather than on the routine monthly server-patch ring. The remediation the packet actually records is the vendor patch with no live-patch path, and it notes the fix typically requires a service restart or system reboot per the KEV requiredAction. For a farm that means the SLA is met only when every web front-end and application server has been restarted onto the fixed build: a farm where the update is staged but the services were never recycled is unremediated, and must not be reported as patched-per-SLA. Where the restart cannot be completed inside the window, the deferral is a documented exposure with a time-bound action item, not a compensating control.

new_control_requirements.name: DOWNLOAD-PROVENANCE-ENFORCEMENT
new_control_requirements.description: The sink on this entry is reached only when a user opens an attacker-controlled document that causes VBA to resolve a library from a path the attacker controls, so on any workstation not yet on the fixed and restarted build the ingress path is the surface an operator can actually enforce. Require the untrusted-origin mark on every VBA-bearing Office document arriving by mail, web download or untrusted file share, and require marked documents to open in an isolated reduced-privilege render instead of the full load path that resolves the hijacked library at the user's own privilege. The mark has to be applied at the ingress boundary and survive the container the document travels in — extraction from an archive, mount of an ISO or VHD, rename — because a search-order hijack needs the substitute library to sit in a directory the opening process searches, which is typically the same container that carried the document; a provenance scheme that tags the document but not its sibling files leaves the payload sitting where the loader will find it. Precondition: this constrains delivery only, and it holds only where the mark is applied and preserved. A document reaching the user over an internal share, a sync client or any channel that strips the tag, or a policy that lets the user click through to full editing, restores the vulnerable path in one step; and once an attacker already has write access to a searched directory on the host, provenance enforcement contributes nothing. Those cases close only with the vendor fix, and there is no live-patch tool for this entry, with the fix typically requiring a service restart or system reboot — so hosts that have taken the update but not restarted must be counted as exposed rather than remediated.

AU-Essential-8-App-Hardening (User application hardening) and NIST-800-53-AC-6 (Least Privilege) are both recorded as citing gaps against this entry.

new_control_requirements.name: PERIMETER-COMPROMISE-REBUILD-NOT-PATCH
new_control_requirements.description: Exchange Server is internet-facing by construction and this CWE-502 sink yields code execution on the mail server itself. A vendor patch exists and the CVE identifier dates to the 2023 cycle, while the KEV listing is 2026-04-13 — so an estate installing the fixed cumulative/security update in response to that listing is patching a host that stayed reachable and exploitable throughout the interval, with a public PoC in circulation. Treat any Exchange server that ran a vulnerable build during confirmed in-the-wild exploitation as compromised until proven otherwise: alongside patching, hunt the OWA/ECP virtual directories and the Exchange install tree for web shells and unexpected .aspx/.dll drops, export and diff transport rules, mailbox permissions, and journaling configuration against last known-good, and rotate the machine account, Exchange service accounts, and every credential that authenticated through the server during the exposure window. Patch-in-place restores the build number and leaves a resident implant and any stolen credential fully operative. The distinguishing test: open a closed Exchange remediation ticket and look for a post-patch persistence sweep and a credential-rotation record — a 'patched within SLA' closure carrying neither is paper remediation of a service that was already being exploited.

new_control_requirements.name: OWA-PER-REQUEST-SIEM-INGESTION
new_control_requirements.description: A serialized object arriving in a request body or header is inert to file-based anti-malware — nothing is written to disk before the gadget chain runs inside the Exchange worker process — and it travels over a session that authentication logging records as ordinary, so the endpoint AV control credited for this server never had anything to detect. Ship Exchange's per-request IIS/OWA/ECP access logs (URI stem and query, method, request size, status, user agent, source address, responding backend) to a SIEM outside the Exchange trust zone with at least 90-day retention, and alert on POSTs to Autodiscover, ECP, and PowerShell endpoints with anomalous body sizes or from unexpected sources. Retention depth is the load-bearing part here: the KEV listing landed 2026-04-13 on a CVE from the 2023 cycle, so an investigation opened at patch time must be able to reach back into an exposure window that long. The distinguishing test: pick a date months before the current remediation and try to retrieve the full request line for a single OWA POST from the SIEM — if only the authentication event survives, the deserialization request that established the foothold is unrecoverable.

new_control_requirements.name: SECURITY-TOOL-INTEGRITY-VERIFICATION
new_control_requirements.description: Put the FortiClient EMS server itself inside vulnerability-management scope at the SLA of the most privileged software in the estate, instead of wherever 'endpoint security product' falls in the OS-versus-application patch split. The exploited surface is the management server operators deploy in order to secure endpoints, and the flaw is reachable by an unauthenticated caller sending crafted requests — so the EMS build level is itself a security control, not an operations detail. Audits must establish the deployed EMS build from the server rather than from the console's own status view, and must include the trust-anchor-inversion test: send an unauthenticated crafted request to the EMS request handlers on a staging instance and confirm it is refused before any code or command runs. Remediation is a scheduled EMS outage: the entry registers no live-patch path and the vendor patch requires a service restart or reboot, so the security console is offline during its own fix and that window must be planned on the KEV clock rather than deferred to the routine cycle.

CISA KEV-listed 2026-04-06, active_exploitation: confirmed, CVSS 8.8, RWEP 77, poc_available: true. patch_available: true with live_patch_available: false; live_patch_notes records 'No live-patch tool registered for this entry at bulk-import time. Vendor patch typically requires service restart or system reboot per the KEV requiredAction.'

new_control_requirements.name: ENDPOINT-MGMT-DEPLOYMENT-CHANNEL-INTEGRITY
new_control_requirements.description: Treat the EMS-to-FortiClient agent channel as a privileged supply-chain control plane for the duration of this exposure. Unauthenticated code or command execution on the EMS server hands an attacker the system that distributes configuration and software to every managed endpoint, so the blast radius is the agent fleet rather than one server: integrity-monitor the deployment artifacts and any key material the server holds, and alert on agent pushes and policy changes that do not correspond to a sanctioned admin action. Because the fix requires taking EMS down for a service restart, that monitoring has to span the outage and continue after it — restarting the server applies the patch but does not by itself evict anything placed through the flaw beforehand, and with exploitation confirmed in the wild an internet-reachable EMS instance is a forensic question, not a hypothetical. The distinguishing test: replay the deployment-artifact and key-table integrity baseline after the patch restart and confirm it matches the pre-exposure baseline.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Packet: improper access control (CWE-284) 'allowing an unauthenticated attacker to access functions or data beyond authorization', with the KEV description recording that it 'may allow an unauthenticated attacker to execute unauthorized code or commands via crafted requests'. CISA KEV-listed 2026-04-06, active_exploitation: confirmed, CVSS 8.8, RWEP 77, poc_available: true. live_patch_available: false and the vendor patch requires a service restart or system reboot per the KEV requiredAction.

new_control_requirements.name: FLEET-CONTROL-PLANE-ADMIN-PRIVILEGE-TIER
new_control_requirements.description: Classify FortiClient EMS as a fleet control plane and confine its reachability on that basis: the EMS console and its request handlers should be reachable only through a privileged administrative path (PAM jumphost or a dedicated admin segment), with EMS administration held as an identity separate from general IT or application admin roles and elevated just-in-time. Against this CVE the tier's operative benefit is reachability rather than authentication strength — the flaw is exercised pre-authentication via crafted requests, so any deployment that leaves the EMS request surface reachable from general user networks or the internet gives the attacker the entire path no matter how the EMS credentials are governed. Frameworks that enumerate a single 'admin' tier do not distinguish the server that governs every endpoint agent from an application administrator, which is why this network-position requirement has to be stated as its own control. The distinguishing test: from a general user subnet, attempt to reach the EMS request handlers and confirm the connection is refused at the network boundary before authentication is ever reached.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Packet: FortiClient EMS is exploited by 'an unauthenticated attacker to execute unauthorized code or commands via crafted requests' (CWE-284, improper access control). CISA KEV-listed 2026-04-06, active_exploitation: confirmed, CVSS 8.8, RWEP 77, poc_available: true. No live-patch tool is registered for this entry and the vendor patch requires a service restart or system reboot per the KEV requiredAction, so the exposure persists until an EMS restart window can be taken.

CVE-2026-3502.name: TrueConf Client Download of Code Without Integrity Check Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: the TrueConf client downloads code/updates without verifying their integrity (CWE-494), letting an attacker who can influence the download channel (a hijacked update endpoint or machine-in-the-middle) substitute malicious code that runs on the client. CISA KEV-listed 2026-04-02 with confirmed in-the-wild exploitation.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none (the attacker influences the download/update channel or the shipped artifact; no authentication to the victim is required)
attack_vector.complexity: low — KEV-listed, actively exploited; treat as weaponized
attack_vector.ai_factor: No AI involvement documented in discovery or weaponization.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Enforce cryptographic integrity verification on all downloaded code and updates (code signing with signature verification, Sigstore/in-toto, TLS-pinned update channels); for the embedded-malicious-code case, verify build provenance (SLSA) and pin/verify the tool's release artifacts before use.
prevention.adequacy: Signature and provenance verification is the definitive control; the flaw exists precisely because it was absent or unenforced — patching the version does not retroactively restore trust in artifacts already installed.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Monitoring for unexpected code/DLLs loaded by the TrueConf client, updates fetched over unauthenticated channels, and anomalous outbound connections or process execution from the tool.
detection.adequacy: Necessary because supply-chain substitution is silent — the tool runs as expected while the embedded/substituted code executes alongside it.

response.what_would_have_worked: Pull the affected version, reinstall from a verified-signed release, rotate any credentials the compromised process could reach, and audit every host where the tool ran — a compromised updater or scanner has broad reach.
response.adequacy: Mandatory; supply-chain compromise propagates through every host that ran the tainted code, so response is environment-wide, not host-local.

NIST-800-53-SR-11.gap: Component authenticity / anti-counterfeit is named, but verification is not enforced at install/update time — these products fetched or shipped code without a verified signature, so the control is paper unless signed-artifact verification (Sigstore/in-toto) is mandated at the download step.

NIST-SSDF-800-218-PS.2.gap: The SSDF calls for protecting release integrity and providing provenance, but downstream consumers had no enforced way to verify it; without signed releases plus provenance a consumer cannot detect substitution or embedded malicious code.

SLSA-build-provenance.gap: SLSA build provenance and signed releases would let a consumer detect tampering or substitution; absent enforced verification at the download/update step the trust gap remains open.

EU-CRA-secure-update.gap: The EU Cyber Resilience Act requires secure update mechanisms and shipping without known exploitable defects; an unauthenticated download path or embedded malicious code violates the secure-update and integrity expectations.

compliance_exposure_score.basis: Software-distribution and update integrity is widely assumed rather than verified; audited organizations that install vendor updates or run security tooling without enforcing signature/provenance verification are exposed to substitution and embedded-malicious-code attacks — and a compromised updater or scanner reaches every host it touches.

new_control_requirements.name: INDEPENDENT-INTEGRITY-VERIFICATION-OF-SIGNED-VENDOR-INSTALLERS
new_control_requirements.description: TrueConf Client fetches update code without verifying its integrity, so nothing on the client side distinguishes the vendor's build from one substituted by an attacker who has gained influence over the delivery path. The operator response is to stop letting the in-app updater be the trust decision: pull TrueConf Client builds through managed software distribution, verify each build against an integrity source independent of the download itself — vendor-published per-release hashes obtained over a separate channel, or a behavioural baseline of the installed binaries — and only then push it to endpoints. This is the harder form of the control's premise: the original lesson was that a valid signature is not proof of integrity, whereas here the client performs no verification step at all, so an out-of-band check is the only thing standing between a tampered payload and execution in the updating process's context.
new_control_requirements.evidence: This is a "download of code without integrity check vulnerability" (CWE-494) in which "An attacker who is able to influence the update delivery path can substitute a tampered update payload. If the payload is executed or installed by the updater, this may result in arbitrary code execution in the context of the updating process or user," and identifies the delivery-path influence as "a hijacked update endpoint or machine-in-the-middle." CISA KEV-listed 2026-04-02 with active_exploitation confirmed, poc_available true, CVSS 8.8, RWEP 77.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: The KEV clock here governs a client fleet rather than a single server: every endpoint running TrueConf Client is independently exploitable by whoever can influence its update fetch, so the fixed client has to reach all of them on the KEV window rather than on the ordinary endpoint-software refresh cycle. Two facts make the rollout a scheduled fleet action rather than a background update — the packet registers no live-patch tool for this entry, and the vendor patch typically requires a service restart or system reboot per the KEV requiredAction. Until the fixed build is present on a given endpoint, the interim posture is to keep that endpoint's updater off networks where the delivery path can be influenced, because the vulnerable client will accept whatever the channel returns.

Vendor patch typically requires service restart or system reboot per the KEV requiredAction." The exploitation precondition per the packet is an attacker who "can influence the download channel (a hijacked update endpoint or machine-in-the-middle)." CVSS 8.8, RWEP 77, CWE-494.
