attack_vector.description: The attacker emails a .tar (or .cpio/.rpm) archive to any address the Zimbra server accepts. amavis automatically submits the attachment for malware inspection and shells out to GNU cpio, which honours the archive's symlink and absolute-path entries because of the unfixed 2015 cpio flaw CVE-2015-1197, writing outside the extraction directory. Public tooling plants a JSP web shell under the Jetty-served Zimbra web directories — the Metasploit module drops a randomly named 4-10 character .jsp under /opt/zimbra/jetty_base/webapps/zimbra/ and polls the URL until it answers — yielding command execution as the zimbra service account and access to every mailbox on the host.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none — PR:N and UI:N; sending mail to any address the server accepts is the entire trigger, because amavis extracts the attachment without operator involvement
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L, but distribution-dependent as well as version-dependent: Ubuntu carries pax as a Zimbra prerequisite and amavis prefers it, while RHEL/CentOS 7 and later dropped pax from the default install, leaving the vulnerable GNU cpio path in place. The Metasploit module landed 2022-10-07, three days before the vendor patch, collapsing the skill floor to point-and-shoot; EPSS sits around 0.955
attack_vector.ai_factor: Not AI-discovered — this surfaced through in-the-wild compromise rather than research: Zimbra forum operators reported compromised servers in September 2022, Rapid7 published its analysis on 2022-10-06 while the flaw was still unpatched, and Kaspersky counted roughly 876 servers already compromised before a CVE identifier existed. No AI tooling is credited by Zimbra, Rapid7 or Kaspersky.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Apply Zimbra Collaboration 9.0.0 Patch 27 or 8.8.15 Patch 34 (published 2022-10-10), which drops the cpio dependency and makes pax a Zimbra prerequisite. Before the patch existed, the effective control was Zimbra's own workaround — install the distribution's pax package and restart Zimbra, after which amavis prefers pax over cpio.
prevention.adequacy: The patch closes the extraction path but does not evict an existing shell, so remediation on any exposed host is incomplete without hunting and removing JSP files under /opt/zimbra/jetty/webapps/zimbra/public and /opt/zimbra/jetty_base/webapps/zimbra/. The pax workaround was the only control available during the September 2022 mass-exploitation window and remains worth applying wherever patch state is uncertain.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Alert on amavis producing writes outside its extraction directory, on any .jsp appearing in a Jetty-served Zimbra directory, and on those URLs being fetched over HTTPS shortly after an inbound archive attachment. The named shells Kaspersky recovered — .error.jsp, ResourcesVerificaton.jsp, ResourceVerificaton.jsp, ZimletCore.jsp, searchx.jsp, seachx.jsp — are direct file-integrity indicators.
detection.adequacy: File-integrity monitoring on the web-served directories is high-fidelity here because those paths should never receive new files from the mail pipeline. It arrives after the write, though — the attacker has code execution as the zimbra account by the time the shell is fetched.

response.what_would_have_worked: Patch or install pax, remove every JSP web shell from the Zimbra web directories, rotate mailbox and service credentials, and treat all mail data on the host as exfiltrated given the zimbra account's access to every mailbox.
response.adequacy: Kaspersky recorded a blanket wave against effectively every vulnerable server in Central Asia from 2022-09-30, so an unpatched internet-facing ZCS host from that period should be treated as compromised rather than merely vulnerable, with the full mailbox corpus in scope for breach assessment.

NIST-800-53-SI-3.gap: SI-3 requires malicious-code protection at system entry points, and here that protection was the entry point — amavis invoked GNU cpio to unpack inbound attachments for antivirus scanning, so a traversing archive gave the sender an arbitrary write as the zimbra user out of the scanner itself. Nothing in SI-3 asks whether the scanning pipeline's own extractors are sandboxed or safe on untrusted input.

NIS2-Art21-supply-chain.gap: Art.21 supply-chain measures scope direct suppliers and service providers, but exploitability was decided by a transitive OS component — GNU cpio still carrying CVE-2015-1197 — reached through amavis. Both Zimbra's supplier assurance and the operator's would show conformant while a RHEL/CentOS 7+ host with cpio and no pax stayed one email away from remote code execution.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: B4 secure configuration assumes platform components run with least function, yet ZCS extracted untrusted archives as the zimbra user, which also owns /opt/zimbra/jetty/webapps/zimbra/public — writable by the extractor and served by Jetty at the same moment. One traversal therefore produced a live executable endpoint with no second exploitation stage required.

AU-Essential-8-App-Hardening.gap: User application hardening targets browsers, Office macros and PDF readers on workstations and says nothing about a server-side Jetty instance executing attacker-written JSP out of a public/ directory, which is the entire exploitation path. The shells simply ran because their URLs were requested.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: A.8.8 schedules technical-vulnerability work by rated severity, but roughly 876 servers were compromised before this had a CVE identifier and the KEV due date of 2022-11-10 falls a month after the 2022-10-10 patch. An entity on a risk-rated cadence had no artefact to prioritise during the September waves; only the non-version-based workaround changed the outcome in that window.

new_control_requirements.name: SECURITY-TOOL-INTEGRITY-VERIFICATION
new_control_requirements.description: Security tools (AV/AM, EDR, vulnerability scanners) must be treated as in-scope of vulnerability management with the same SLAs as other privileged software. Definition-update channels must use TLS with certificate pinning. Compliance audits must include a trust-anchor-inversion test: deliver a crafted input to the security tool in a sandbox and confirm rejection.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2022-41352 makes the malicious-code protection the entry point: amavis invoked GNU cpio to unpack inbound mail attachments for antivirus scanning, so an archive with a traversing entry gave any sender an arbitrary write as the zimbra user out of the scanner itself. The trust-anchor-inversion test — deliver a crafted archive to the scanning pipeline in a sandbox and confirm rejection — is the only audit step that treats the scanner's own extractor as attack surface.

new_control_requirements.name: TIER-3-DEPENDENCY-INVENTORY
new_control_requirements.description: Supply chain inventory must extend to tier-3 dependencies (dependencies of dependencies of direct dependencies). SBOM coverage for libsystemd-class transitive dependencies cannot be omitted under SR-3.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2022-41352's exploitability was decided by a transitive OS-level component — GNU cpio still carrying the 2015 symlink flaw CVE-2015-1197 — reached through amavis, not by Zimbra code. A RHEL/CentOS 7+ host with cpio and no pax was one email from remote code execution while both Zimbra's supplier assurance and the operator's own showed conformant, because neither inventory reached the extractor binary.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2022-41352 had roughly 876 servers compromised before it carried a CVE identifier, and the KEV due date of 2022-11-10 falls a month after the 2022-10-10 patch, so a risk-rated cadence had no artefact to schedule during the September mass-exploitation waves. The only thing that changed the outcome was a non-version-based compensating control — install pax so amavis stops calling cpio — which is exactly what a KEV clock that accepts documented compensating controls records as remediation.

attack_vector.description: An unprivileged local user calls unshare(CLONE_NEWUSER|CLONE_NEWNS) to obtain CAP_SYS_ADMIN inside a new user namespace, then mounts an overlayfs — possible only because Ubuntu carries a downstream patch marking overlayfs FS_USERNS_MOUNT. Setting the security.capability extended attribute granting CAP_SETUID on a copy of a chosen binary in the overlay's upper directory causes the copy-up to write that xattr through to the underlying filesystem without the kernel validating it against the namespace's uid mapping. Executing the resulting file from the init namespace yields full root. The Shikitega Linux loader used exactly this as a second stage, pairing it with CVE-2021-4034 before installing crontab persistence and an XMRig miner.
attack_vector.privileges_required: low — PR:L; any unprivileged local account that can reach clone(CLONE_NEWUSER), which is the Ubuntu default
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L and deterministic: no race window, no memory corruption and no infoleak requirement. The published exploit is a few hundred lines of C that works first try, so it functions as a reliable second stage after any low-privilege foothold. The binding constraint is distribution rather than version — upstream kernels refuse unprivileged overlayfs mounts, which is why EPSS sits near 0.49 rather than at the top of the range
attack_vector.ai_factor: Not AI-discovered — reported by an independent researcher through the SSD Secure Disclosure programme, with Ubuntu shipping USN-4917-1 on 2021-04-15 and the upstream check landing in Linux 5.11. No AI-assisted discovery is claimed by SSD, Canonical or the kernel maintainers, and weaponisation followed the disclosure by more than a year.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Apply Canonical Livepatch LSN-0076-1, which carries this fix for the 4.4, 4.15 and 5.4 generic, lowlatency, aws, azure, gcp, gke, gkeop and oem flavours across Ubuntu 14.04 through 20.04 with no reboot; otherwise take USN-4917-1 kernels (4.4.0-209.241, 4.15.0-142.146, 5.4.0-72.80, 5.8.0-50.56) or any upstream kernel from 5.11 onward. Where neither can be applied, disable unprivileged user namespaces with kernel.unprivileged_userns_clone=0 or user.max_user_namespaces=0.
prevention.adequacy: Unusually good for a kernel LPE: the live-patch path closes it without downtime, and the sysctl removes the exploit's entry primitive outright for hosts that cannot be patched at all. The failure mode is organisational — the USN path requires a reboot, which is the step that slips longest on long-uptime Linux fleets, and nothing routes operators toward the livepatch as the faster option.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Alert on an unprivileged process calling unshare(CLONE_NEWUSER|CLONE_NEWNS) and immediately mounting overlayfs with attacker-controlled lower/upper/work directories, on setxattr of security.capability inside an overlay upper directory, and on getcap -r finding capability xattrs on files in user-writable paths outside the distribution's expected set.
detection.adequacy: The syscall sequence is distinctive and cheap to instrument, but the whole chain completes in milliseconds, so this detects a successful escalation rather than preventing one. The stronger downstream signals are Shikitega's own artefacts — crontab entries for both the user and root, a /var/tmp/vm.lock flock guard and an XMRig download.

response.what_would_have_worked: Livepatch or reboot into a fixed kernel, set the userns sysctl as a standing control, audit for stray security.capability xattrs, remove crontab persistence for both the compromised user and root, and investigate the initial low-privilege foothold that preceded the escalation.
response.adequacy: Because this is always a second stage, response that stops at the root shell misses the point — the question worth answering is how the unprivileged foothold was obtained, since the same loader also carried a second escalation path.

NIST-800-53-AC-6.gap: Least privilege is voided by a distribution build choice rather than an account policy: Ubuntu's downstream FS_USERNS_MOUNT patch lets any unprivileged user mount an overlay inside a user namespace, and the missing capability validation attaches CAP_SETUID to a binary that then runs privileged in the init namespace. No role assignment, sudoers restriction or privileged-account review constrains a user who can reach clone(CLONE_NEWUSER).

NIS2-Art21-patch-management.gap: Art.21 assumes a maintenance-window cadence, and the USN-4917-1 kernels need a reboot — the step long-uptime Linux fleets defer hardest. The article gives no credit for the control that closes this without downtime, Canonical Livepatch LSN-0076-1, so an entity can be cadence-compliant on paper, months behind on reboots, and exploitable throughout.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: B4 hardening baselines are written against upstream behaviour, and upstream Linux refuses unprivileged overlayfs mounts outright — the exposure exists only because Ubuntu re-enables them. A configuration standard reading 'currently supported kernel, CIS-hardened' still ships the exploit primitive, because nothing in B4 asks whether the distribution re-enabled a mount type upstream forbids.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: Patch urgency under Essential Eight derives from internet-facing exposure, and this is a local escalation on hosts with no network-reachable surface, so it sorts to the bottom of every queue. That ranking is inverted for a second-stage bug — Shikitega paired it with CVE-2021-4034 immediately after gaining a foothold, which is what earned the KEV listing.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.9.gap: A.8.9 would have neutralised this by baselining kernel.unprivileged_userns_clone=0 or user.max_user_namespaces=0, but the control only requires configurations to be defined, monitored and reviewed and names no such setting. A fully conformant Ubuntu baseline leaves unprivileged user namespaces enabled by default and the overlayfs primitive reachable.

new_control_requirements.name: LIVE-PATCH-CAPABILITY
new_control_requirements.description: For any system that processes production workloads and cannot tolerate unplanned reboots: live kernel patching capability (kpatch, livepatch, kGraft, or equivalent) must be deployed and tested quarterly.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2021-3493 is one of the rare kernel LPEs with a true no-reboot fix: Canonical Livepatch LSN-0076-1 carries it for the 4.4, 4.15 and 5.4 flavours across Ubuntu 14.04 through 20.04, while the USN-4917-1 path requires the reboot that long-uptime Linux fleets defer hardest. Without a deployed and tested livepatch capability an entity stays cadence-compliant on paper, months behind on reboots, and exploitable throughout.

new_control_requirements.name: CONTAINER-HOST-NAMESPACE-ESCAPE-HARDENING
new_control_requirements.description: Container hosts must treat the kernel - not the namespace boundary - as the last line of defense against a confined workload. Patch host kernels to the fixed release for each maintained series (with reboot) or apply a vendor live-kernel-patch, and layer compensating controls that block cgroups/namespace escapes even on an unpatched kernel: confine every container with AppArmor or SELinux and a seccomp profile, drop CAP_SYS_ADMIN, and disable unprivileged user namespaces where workloads do not need them. The distinguishing test: from inside a representative container on a staging host, attempt the release_agent escape (create user+cgroup namespaces, mount cgroupfs, write a payload path to release_agent, trigger cgroup release) and confirm it is refused before any code runs as root - a fleet that passes image-scan and RBAC audits but permits this on an unpatched, unconfined host still allows container-to-host root.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2021-3493 exists only because Ubuntu's downstream FS_USERNS_MOUNT patch lets an unprivileged user mount an overlay inside a user namespace that upstream Linux refuses outright, and the missing capability validation then attaches CAP_SETUID to a binary that runs privileged in the init namespace. The documented interim mitigation is this control's namespace clause exactly — kernel.unprivileged_userns_clone=0 or user.max_user_namespaces=0 — which removes the clone(CLONE_NEWUSER) primitive that no role assignment, sudoers restriction or CIS-hardened baseline constrains.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2021-3493 is a local escalation on hosts with no network-reachable surface, so exposure-driven patch ranking sorts it to the bottom of every queue — inverted for a second-stage bug that the Shikitega loader paired with CVE-2021-4034 immediately after gaining a foothold. The 2022-10-20 KEV listing is the override that re-ranks it, and it accepts the userns sysctl as a documented compensating control where neither livepatch nor reboot is available.

CVE-2022-40684.name: Fortinet Multiple Products Authentication Bypass Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: A single unauthenticated request to the FortiOS / FortiProxy / FortiSwitchManager management interface carrying Forwarded: for="[127.0.0.1]:8000";by="[127.0.0.1]:9000"; (or an equivalent X-Forwarded-For) together with User-Agent: Report Runner — or Node.js — makes the REST API set the connection's client_ip to 127.0.0.1 and treat the caller as a trusted local process. PUT /api/v2/cmdb/system/admin/admin then succeeds without authentication, and public tooling writes an attacker RSA key into the admin account's ssh-public-key1 field and logs in over SSH as admin for full device control. Fortinet also observed configuration exfiltration and creation of a super_admin account named fortigate-tech-support.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none — PR:N and UI:N; two attacker-set headers on one HTTP(S) request are the entire precondition, and the request never enters the authentication path
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L; no memory corruption and no timing dependency, which is why EPSS sits at roughly 0.9998. The only real barrier is exposure rather than skill: a device whose administrative interface is confined to a management network is not reachable, but with a Nuclei template and a Metasploit module public since October 2022, internet-wide opportunistic scanning is the baseline expectation for any exposed device
attack_vector.ai_factor: Not AI-discovered — Fortinet's PSIRT advisory FG-IR-22-377 records the discovery as External and names no credited reporter, and the public exploit chain was reconstructed by Horizon3.ai from the patched firmware three days after disclosure. No AI tooling is credited by Fortinet or by Horizon3.ai.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Upgrade per FG-IR-22-377 — FortiOS 7.2.2+ and 7.0.7+ (7.0.5 B8001+ for the FG6000F and 7000E/F series), FortiProxy 7.2.1+ and 7.0.7+, FortiSwitchManager 7.2.1+ and 7.0.1+ — with the device reboot the firmware upgrade requires. Where the upgrade cannot be scheduled immediately, disable the HTTP/HTTPS administrative interface or restrict it to known source addresses with a local-in policy.
prevention.adequacy: The firmware fix is complete for the bypass but not for the incident: upgrading does not remove an implanted super_admin account or an injected SSH key, so any device that was internet-exposed before the upgrade must have its administrative configuration reconciled afterwards. The source-restriction workaround is the stronger standing control, since it removes reachability rather than one bug.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Alert on unauthenticated requests to the management interface carrying a Forwarded or X-Forwarded-For header claiming 127.0.0.1 with User-Agent Report Runner or Node.js, on PUT/GET against /api/v2/cmdb/system/admin/admin with no preceding successful admin login, and on device log entries containing user=Local_Process_Access — Fortinet's own published artefact for this chain.
detection.adequacy: user=Local_Process_Access is a near-zero-false-positive indicator and the header combination is trivially matchable at the edge, but both require that management-plane logs are shipped off-device — an attacker with full admin can edit what remains locally. Configuration-drift comparison catches the persistence artefacts independently.

response.what_would_have_worked: Upgrade, then audit the full device configuration against a known-good baseline: delete any super_admin the operator did not create (fortigate-tech-support being the observed name), clear unexpected ssh-public-key1 values, rotate every credential and pre-shared key held on the device, and reissue certificates on the assumption the configuration was exfiltrated.
response.adequacy: Configuration exfiltration is the part that outlives remediation — VPN pre-shared keys, local accounts and routing detail taken during the exposure window remain valid after the firmware upgrade unless explicitly rotated. CISA records ransomware use against this CVE, so an exposed unpatched device should be handled as an intrusion, not a finding.

NIST-800-53-IA-2.gap: IA-2 requires unique identification and authentication before access is granted, but the FortiOS API decided a request came from a trusted internal process using two attacker-supplied fields. No IA-2 mechanism is even consulted on a request that never enters the authentication path, so admin MFA, password policy and lockout are bypassed rather than defeated.

NIS2-Art21-network-security.gap: Art.21 treats the perimeter firewall as a control providing assurance rather than as an asset with its own internet-exposed management plane. Here the administrative HTTPS interface was the preauth entry point, and CISA records ransomware use — the device enforcing segmentation for everything behind it was the first thing taken over.

UK-CAF-B2.gap: B2 is evidenced through privileged-account management — named admins, MFA coverage, session logging, periodic review — and all of it stays green while the attacker adds a super_admin and pushes an SSH key into the admin's ssh-public-key1 field. The account inventory B2 asks for is precisely the artefact the attack modifies, and nothing requires reconciling it against the device's own configuration history.

AU-ISM-1546.gap: The ISM patch clock starts at vendor release, but Fortinet shipped fixed builds on 2022-10-03 and published FG-IR-22-377 only on 2022-10-10 after a confidential customer notice. An operator tracking public advisories lost the first week outright, and Horizon3's PoC plus a Nuclei template and Metasploit module arrived from 2022-10-13 — the compliant patch window opened after mass scanning had begun.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.22.gap: A.8.22 network segregation is exactly what Fortinet's workaround asks for, but the control is written for segregating user, service and system networks — not for confining the management plane of the segmentation device itself. An A.8.22-conformant design routinely leaves the FortiGate administrative interface reachable from the untrusted side, which is the exposure this CVE monetises.

new_control_requirements.name: PERIMETER-DEVICE-ZERODAY-SLA-TIER
new_control_requirements.description: Compliance frameworks must define a distinct patch SLA tier for pre-auth RCE on perimeter-trust-boundary devices (firewalls, VPN concentrators, WAFs, edge load-balancers). Tier requirement: vendor-mitigation deployed within 4 hours of KEV listing OR isolation of the vulnerable interface; standard 14/30-day SLAs do not apply because the device IS the trust boundary.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2022-40684 let an unauthenticated request reach the FortiGate / FortiProxy / FortiSwitchManager administrative interface via a Forwarded header claiming 127.0.0.1 and a Report Runner User-Agent, taking over the device that enforces segmentation for everything behind it. Fortinet shipped fixed builds on 2022-10-03 but published FG-IR-22-377 only on 2022-10-10 and Horizon3's PoC landed 2022-10-13, so a routine appliance-patch window opened after mass scanning had begun — the alternative tier requirement, isolating the management interface with a local-in policy, was the only control available in that gap.

new_control_requirements.name: PERIMETER-COMPROMISE-REBUILD-NOT-PATCH
new_control_requirements.description: Pre-rehearsed IR runbook for any perimeter device that suffers a pre-auth RCE CVE in active exploitation MUST default to config-exfil + rebuild + credential rotation, not patch-in-place. Patch-in-place leaves attacker-installed implants intact.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2022-40684 leaves persistence the firmware upgrade does not touch: an implanted super_admin (observed as fortigate-tech-support) and an SSH public key pushed into the admin's ssh-public-key1 field, with the exfiltrated configuration's VPN pre-shared keys and local accounts still valid afterwards. CISA records ransomware use, so an exposed unpatched device needs baseline reconciliation, credential rotation and certificate reissue rather than a patch-and-close.

new_control_requirements.name: FIREWALL-EGRESS-TELEMETRY-SEPARATE-TRUST-ZONE
new_control_requirements.description: Firewall and other perimeter-trust-boundary devices must forward syslog, threat logs, and authentication logs to a SIEM hosted in a separate trust zone (different management plane, different credentials, different authentication path). Telemetry stored on the compromised device is destroyed by the attacker; telemetry on a separate-trust-zone collector survives.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2022-40684 gives the attacker full administrative control of the device that holds its own logs and account inventory, so Fortinet's near-zero-false-positive artefact (log entries carrying user=Local_Process_Access) and the privileged-account evidence that named-admin reviews depend on are only trustworthy if the management-plane logs were already shipped to a collector the attacker cannot edit.

CVE-2022-41033.name: Microsoft Windows COM+ Event System Service Privilege Escalation Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: Code already running as a standard user drives the SYSTEM-hosted COM+ Event System Service over local COM through the IEventSubscription / IEventSystem interfaces. InMemoryRegRow::PutPropertyBag in es.dll does not validate the vt field of the PROPVARIANT structures it stores, and CAPROPVARIANT is structurally aliased with BLOB, so a fake VT_UNKNOWN variant can be smuggled inside a VT_BLOB byte buffer. The COM runtime never checks the embedded pointer because it lives inside the blob's data; when the variant is added to the property bag, PropVariantCopy dereferences it to reach the vtable and calls IUnknown::AddRef — a call through an attacker-chosen pointer inside a SYSTEM service. The October 2022 patch adds a ValidatePropertyBag routine that checks variant types and sizes first.
attack_vector.privileges_required: low — PR:L; the attacker must already be executing code as a low-privileged local user, with no user interaction (UI:N)
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L, and the trigger is deterministic rather than racy. Reliability of the full SYSTEM chain still depends on shaping memory at a known address, and no weaponised public exploit surfaced; Project Zero's C++ demonstrates the primitive rather than shipping a turnkey escalation, so the constraint is exploit-engineering effort, not trigger reliability
attack_vector.ai_factor: Not AI-discovered — Microsoft's October 2022 CVRF credits the report to 'Anonymous' and flags the issue Exploited: Yes with Publicly Disclosed: No. Google Project Zero tracks it in its in-the-wild 0-day set and published the root-cause analysis afterwards. No party credits AI-assisted discovery or exploit development, and the anonymous acknowledgement means the discovery method is not publicly attributable beyond that.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Install the October 11, 2022 Windows update for the affected SKU and reboot — KB5018427 (Win11 22H2), KB5018418 (Win11 21H2), KB5018410 (Win10 20H2/21H1/21H2), KB5018419 (Win10 1809 / Server 2019), KB5018421 (Server 2022), KB5018411 (Win10 1607 / Server 2016), KB5018425 (Win10 1507), KB5018474/KB5018476 (8.1, RT 8.1, Server 2012 R2) and KB5018457/KB5018478 (Server 2012).
prevention.adequacy: Complete where the update is obtainable — but on Windows 7 SP1, Server 2008 SP2 and Server 2008 R2 SP1 the fix ships only in ESU-gated packages (KB5018454/KB5018479, KB5018450/KB5018446), so estates on those out-of-support SKUs without a paid Extended Security Update subscription have no route to a patched state at all. Those hosts can only attack the precondition: eliminate low-privilege local code-execution footholds and restrict standard-user COM reachability to the service. No live-patch or hotpatch path applies to any affected SKU.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Hunt for a standard-user process creating a COM+ event subscription and writing a property bag containing a malformed PROPVARIANT, for SYSTEM process creation or token use originating from a session whose interactive user holds no administrative rights, and for repeated crashes and restarts of the EventSystem service (svchost.exe -k netsvcs -p -s EventSystem) with access violations inside es.dll.
detection.adequacy: Weak by necessity: Microsoft published no IoCs and issued no detection content, so these signals are derived from Project Zero's root-cause analysis rather than from an intrusion report. The es.dll crash pattern only appears on failed attempts — a working chain produces no such artefact.

response.what_would_have_worked: Patch and reboot, then investigate the foothold that preceded the escalation — this is always a second-stage bug, so a SYSTEM compromise here means an earlier initial-access vector went undetected. On ESU-less legacy SKUs, isolate or retire the host rather than accepting a permanently unremediable escalation.
response.adequacy: Response is the weakest link in this chain because there is nothing specific to hunt for. MSRC marked it Exploitation Detected at release, so on an affected unpatched estate the honest posture is to assume any unexplained SYSTEM activity from a standard-user session may be this bug.

NIST-800-53-AC-6.gap: Running users as standard users is Microsoft's own standing compensating advice for elevation-of-privilege bugs, and that is exactly the boundary this deletes: low-privileged code drives a SYSTEM-hosted service over local COM and lands SYSTEM. AC-6 governs what a principal is authorised to do and has no answer for a type confusion inside a service acting on that principal's request.

NIS2-Art21-patch-management.gap: The fix exists only inside the October 11, 2022 cumulative update, and on Windows 7 SP1 / Server 2008 SP2 / Server 2008 R2 estates it is ESU-gated. An entity running those SKUs without a paid subscription cannot reach a patched state at all, and Art.21's cadence language has no vocabulary for a vulnerability whose remediation is commercially unavailable.

UK-CAF-C1.gap: C1 presumes the operator has indicators to hunt for. Microsoft credited an anonymous reporter, published no IoCs and marked the bug Exploited: Yes with Publicly Disclosed: No, leaving only indirect local signals. A C1 attestation that monitoring is in place says nothing about whether this specific escalation is visible, because no vendor detection content was ever issued.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: Every severity input here reads routine — Microsoft rated it Important rather than Critical, CVSS 7.8, EPSS around 0.018 — while MSRC's 'Exploitation Detected' assessment and the 2022-11-01 KEV due date say the opposite. Maturity measured as a percentage of endpoints patched within a window cannot surface that inversion because it never re-ranks by exploited status.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: A score-driven evaluation puts a local 7.8 with sub-2% EPSS behind every internet-facing critical, while this one was already the escalation half of a live intrusion chain across 40 product entries from Windows 7 SP1 to Server 2022. The control's own prioritisation inputs are what mis-rank it; only treating the exploited flag as an override reorders it correctly, and A.8.8 does not require that.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2022-41033 reads routine on every prioritisation input — Microsoft rated it Important rather than Critical, CVSS is 7.8 and EPSS around 0.018 — while MSRC marked it Exploitation Detected at release and CISA set a 2022-11-01 due date. Only treating the KEV/exploited flag as an override reorders the escalation half of a live intrusion chain ahead of the internet-facing critical queue that score-driven scheduling produces.

new_control_requirements.name: EOL-ASSET-DECOMMISSION
new_control_requirements.description: Network-reachable end-of-life devices with no vendor patch path must be isolated and decommissioned within a bounded window; mandatory compensating segmentation applies until removal since no remediation exists.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2022-41033's fix reaches Windows 7 SP1, Server 2008 SP2 and Server 2008 R2 SP1 only through ESU-gated packages (KB5018454/KB5018479, KB5018450/KB5018446), so an estate without a paid Extended Security Update subscription cannot reach a patched state at all and no live-patch or hotpatch path exists for any affected SKU. Those hosts carry a permanently unremediable SYSTEM escalation, which makes isolation and retirement on a bounded clock the only honest remediation.

CVE-2022-41082.name: Microsoft Exchange Server Remote Code Execution Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: An attacker holding any valid mailbox credential uses the CVE-2022-41040 SSRF against the Autodiscover endpoint — an autodiscover/autodiscover.json request containing an @ plus a backend path such as .../powershell — to reach the Exchange PowerShell Remoting backend, which is normally admin-only. A crafted serialized object is then deserialized by that backend (CWE-502), giving code execution in the Exchange worker process. Operators observed Chopper/Antsword web shells dropped for persistence, followed by Active Directory reconnaissance and data exfiltration. After Microsoft's URL Rewrite mitigation blocked the original SSRF pattern, the same deserialization sink was reached through CVE-2022-41080 instead — the OWASSRF chain used by Play ransomware.
attack_vector.privileges_required: low — PR:L and AV:A; any valid mailbox credential with no administrative role and no privileged group membership is the entire authentication requirement before the SSRF stage
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L once a credential exists, and fully automated: the Metasploit module drives the whole chain against Exchange Server 2019. Not exploitable on its own, which is why the vector is AV:A/PR:L and the score lands at 8.0 rather than 9.8 — but the reachability problem was solved twice over, first by CVE-2022-41040 and then by CVE-2022-41080. EPSS sits around 0.9997 and CISA records ransomware use
attack_vector.ai_factor: Not AI-discovered — found during live incident response: GTSC's SOC identified the chain in early August 2022 while investigating an attack on a customer's Exchange infrastructure and reported it privately through ZDI as ZDI-CAN-18333 and ZDI-CAN-18802 roughly three weeks before public disclosure. No AI tooling is credited by GTSC, ZDI or Microsoft.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Install the November 8, 2022 Exchange Server security update KB5019758, covering Exchange Server 2013 CU23, 2016 CU22 and CU23, and 2019 CU11 and CU12, with the service restart it requires. Exchange Online is not affected.
prevention.adequacy: There was nothing to install for forty days. Between Microsoft's 2022-09-29 acknowledgement and the November update the only vendor control was a URL Rewrite rule, delivered manually or through the Exchange Emergency Mitigation Service — a pattern Microsoft revised twice after researchers bypassed it, and which the OWASSRF chain sidestepped entirely by substituting a different SSRF. The mitigation must not be recorded as equivalent to the patch, and hosts exposed during that window need web-shell hunting under the Exchange web directories in addition to the update.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Query IIS logs for autodiscover.json requests containing an @ together with a backend path such as powershell — Microsoft's published hunting pattern — alert on w3wp.exe spawning cmd.exe or powershell.exe, and act on Defender detections Exploit:Script/ExchgProxyRequest.A/.B/.C, Backdoor:ASP/Webshell.Y, Backdoor:JS/SimChocexShell.A!dha and Trojan:Win32/IISExchgSpawnCMD.A.
detection.adequacy: This was the only control that could act during the mitigation-only window, and the IIS log query is precise. The signature half is routinely silenced in practice: antivirus exclusions over Exchange directories are a common deployment convention and suppress every Defender detection listed above, so the exclusions have to be reviewed before the detections can be trusted.

response.what_would_have_worked: Apply KB5019758, hunt and remove Chopper/Antsword web shells from the Exchange web directories, review and remove Exchange-directory AV exclusions, rotate mailbox credentials and any service accounts reachable from the Exchange host, and assess Active Directory for the reconnaissance and exfiltration that followed the shell.
response.adequacy: Patching does not evict an existing shell, and the observed post-exploitation is domain-wide rather than mail-only. An internet-facing unpatched on-prem Exchange from that period should be treated as compromised rather than merely vulnerable — and under NIS2 the compromise of an entity's own mail infrastructure starts the Art.23 early-warning clock.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: SI-2 had nothing to install for forty days: Microsoft acknowledged the zero-day on 2022-09-29 and shipped KB5019758 only on November 8, 2022. The interim control was a URL Rewrite rule Microsoft revised twice after bypasses, and the OWASSRF chain reached the same deserialization sink through a different SSRF — so any SI-2 programme that recorded 'vendor mitigation applied' as remediated was wrong for the entire window.

NIS2-Art21-vulnerability-handling.gap: Art.21 treats applying vendor guidance as discharge of the duty, but the guidance was mitigation-not-patch, was publicly bypassed, and protected the entity's own mail infrastructure — the same estate whose compromise starts the Art.23 24-hour clock. Nothing in the article obliges re-testing a mitigation after the vendor revises its pattern, which is the step that separated the compromised from the unaffected in October 2022.

UK-CAF-B2.gap: B2 lets an organisation evidence governed access while every ordinary mailbox credential remains a working exploitation prerequisite. This is PR:L — one phished user password, no admin role and no privileged group membership, is the whole authentication requirement before the SSRF stage hands over the PowerShell backend and code execution on the server.

AU-Essential-8-MFA.gap: MFA is scoped to users of internet-facing services, but at lower maturity levels legacy and basic authentication paths on OWA and Autodiscover stay reachable — precisely the low-privilege authentication this chain consumes. MFA on the administrative portal, the usual evidence produced for this control, sits entirely outside the path the exploit takes.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.16.gap: A.8.16 was the only control that could act during the mitigation-only window, and it is written generically while the detections that worked were specific — the autodiscover.json-plus-@-plus-powershell IIS pattern, w3wp.exe spawning cmd.exe, and four named Defender signatures. An attestation that logs are collected and reviewed implies none of those queries exist, and Exchange-directory AV exclusions silently suppress the signature-based half.

new_control_requirements.name: MITIGATION-ACTIVE-PATCH-PENDING-VERDICT-CLASS
new_control_requirements.description: Compliance verdicts must distinguish three states: (a) binary patch deployed (vulnerability eliminated), (b) vendor-mitigation rule active, no binary patch (residual risk: any defect in the mitigation rule reopens the vulnerability), (c) no mitigation, no patch (full exposure). Audit reports must surface (b) as a distinct compensating-control state with an associated time-bound action item, not as a 'patched per SLA' outcome.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2022-41082 had nothing to install for forty days — Microsoft acknowledged the zero-day on 2022-09-29 and shipped KB5019758 only on November 8, 2022 — and the interim URL Rewrite rule was revised twice after researchers bypassed it, while the OWASSRF chain reached the same deserialization sink through CVE-2022-41080 instead. Any programme that recorded 'vendor mitigation applied' as remediated held a false verdict for the entire window.

new_control_requirements.name: VENDOR-PUSH-MITIGATION-OPT-IN-PRE-DISCLOSURE
new_control_requirements.description: For vendors offering push-mitigation services (Microsoft EEMS, Palo Alto Threat Prevention auto-update, etc.), opt-in must be enabled BEFORE the next disclosure event, not in response to it. Compliance frameworks must require operators to enable available vendor-push-mitigation services as a baseline control — opt-in late means the mitigation rule arrives after exploitation, not before.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2022-41082's only pre-patch control was a URL Rewrite pattern delivered either by hand or through the Exchange Emergency Mitigation Service, and Microsoft revised that pattern twice after public bypasses. Operators who had not already enabled the push service had to notice each revision and reapply it manually, which is precisely the step that separated the compromised from the unaffected during October 2022.

new_control_requirements.name: OWA-PER-REQUEST-SIEM-INGESTION
new_control_requirements.description: Exchange OWA per-request access logs (not just authentication events) must be forwarded to an external SIEM with at least 90-day retention. Authentication-only logging misses XSS-stage telemetry — the malicious request flows over an already-authenticated session.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2022-41082 needs only one ordinary mailbox credential (PR:L), so exploitation flows over an already-authenticated session and the detections that actually worked were per-request: IIS entries where an autodiscover.json request contains @ together with powershell, and w3wp.exe spawning cmd.exe. Authentication-event-only ingestion never carries those records, and the Defender signature half is silently suppressed by the Exchange-directory AV exclusions common in these deployments.

CVE-2022-41091.name: Microsoft Windows Mark of the Web (MOTW) Security Feature Bypass Vulnerability (CVE-2022-41091)

attack_vector.description: The payload — a .lnk, .js, .hta or macro-enabled document — is packed inside a container (ISO, IMG, VHD/VHDX, ZIP, 7z or CAB) and mailed or downloaded, so the container itself receives the Zone.Identifier alternate data stream. On mount or extraction Windows fails to propagate that stream to the inner file, so SmartScreen, Office Protected View and the macro-from-internet block all see an apparently local file and stay silent while the payload runs with the user's token. The offensive packer PackMyPayload automates the whole step in one command and names this CVE as its ZIP MOTW-strip mode.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none — PR:N; the attacker needs no account or foothold on the target, only that the recipient opens the mailed or downloaded container (UI:R)
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L; packing a payload into a container is a single command with no race, no memory corruption and no reliability tuning, and the required user interaction is simply opening an attachment, which is the premise of the delivery chain
attack_vector.ai_factor: Not AI-discovered — MSRC's acknowledgement API records no external finder and the report is attributed to a Microsoft MSRC engineer; the 2022 Mark-of-the-Web research was manual container-format differential testing, mounting and extracting archives to see whether the Zone.Identifier stream survived.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Apply the 8 November 2022 cumulative updates — KB5019959 (Windows 10 20H2-22H2), KB5019980 (Windows 11 22H2), KB5019961 (Windows 11 21H2), KB5019966 (1809/Server 2019), KB5019964 (1607/Server 2016), KB5019970 (1507), KB5019081 (Server 2022) — or, on Windows Server 2022 Datacenter: Azure Edition, the reboot-free hotpatch KB5019080.
prevention.adequacy: Patching is the entirety of prevention: no policy or configuration can force the provenance marker onto container contents on an unpatched build. It is also almost entirely reboot-bearing — the hotpatch stream covers one server SKU while the real exposure is overwhelmingly client-side mail delivery.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Enumerate the Zone.Identifier stream (dir /R, Get-Item -Stream *) on files extracted from internet-sourced containers, and alert on process creation whose image path sits on a mounted virtual-disk volume backed by a downloaded .iso or .img rather than under Downloads.
detection.adequacy: The defining artefact is an absence — the missing alternate data stream — which no signature engine looks for, and by the time it is observable the payload has already launched with no prompt shown to the user.

response.what_would_have_worked: Retro-hunt mail archives and Explorer MountPoints2 / jump-list residue for container attachments delivered before the fix landed, and treat any container-delivered execution on an unpatched host as a successful loader run rather than a blocked one.
response.adequacy: Response here is reconstruction after the fact; the bypass leaves no file-content indicator, so the only durable outcome is patching plus assuming the delivered payload executed.

NIST-800-53-SI-3.gap: Every SI-3 layer that would have caught the payload — SmartScreen reputation, Office Protected View, the macro-from-internet block — reads the same Zone.Identifier stream, so removing it at container-mount time blinds all of them simultaneously while an SI-3 assessment verifying AV currency and SmartScreen policy still returns fully compliant.

NIS2-Art21-network-security.gap: ISO, IMG and VHD attachments are legitimate business formats that mail gateways pass by policy, and the payload only becomes dangerous after the operating system declines to tag it — a failure that occurs downstream of every gateway and endpoint measure Art.21 contemplates.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: The platform protective features B4 asks about were configured and enabled; the defect was in Windows' own propagation of the marker they depend on, so B4 configuration sampling evidences a green control on a machine that is completely bypassable. The only honest B4 test is launching a payload from a downloaded container and checking a warning actually appears.

AU-Essential-8-App-Hardening.gap: User application hardening and the companion Office macro control are scored on policy state, and both policies are evaluated against the Mark-of-the-Web tag; stripping the tag before the policy is consulted lets a Maturity Level 3 estate open a container-delivered macro document fully enabled with no measurement that would catch it.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.7.gap: A.8.7 assumes its layers — detection software, user awareness, attachment handling — fail independently, but a single alternate-data-stream defect disables the reputation check and the user-visible warning at once, and no A.8.7 review item asks whether the platform still marks downloaded content.

new_control_requirements.name: DOWNLOAD-PROVENANCE-ENFORCEMENT
new_control_requirements.description: Enforce Mark-of-the-Web / content-provenance on all internet-sourced files and block execution of provenance-stripped shortcuts, installers, and script hosts regardless of a reputation service verdict, which attackers bypass by design.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2022-41091 is the provenance marker failing at its source: Windows declined to write the Zone.Identifier stream to files mounted or extracted from an internet-sourced ISO, IMG, VHD or ZIP, so SmartScreen, Office Protected View and the macro-from-internet block all read an apparently local file and stayed silent while a ransomware loader ran. Microsoft published no configuration workaround, so enforcing provenance on internet-sourced content and blocking execution of provenance-stripped shortcuts and script hosts is the only control that survives the missing marker.

new_control_requirements.name: ARCHIVE-CONTENT-TYPE-PROVENANCE
new_control_requirements.description: Archive and document handlers must dispatch rendering/execution on the content-verified file type rather than the displayed name or extension, and must propagate Mark-of-the-Web to every extracted file.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2022-41091 is specifically a container-handler defect: the downloaded container did receive the Zone.Identifier stream and the mount/extract step failed to propagate it to the inner .lnk, .js, .hta or macro-enabled document, a step the offensive packer PackMyPayload automates as its named ZIP MOTW-strip mode. Requiring the archive handler to propagate Mark-of-the-Web to every extracted file is exactly the behaviour Windows omitted.

new_control_requirements.name: PROTECTION-MECHANISM-FAILURE-CLASS-REGRESSION
new_control_requirements.description: Detonation chambers, EDR rules, and AppLocker/WDAC policies covering protection-mechanism classes (MOTW, SmartScreen, AMSI, ASR, WDAC, Driver Block Rules) must include class-level regression testing executed on every patch deployment, not just one-off bypass-CVE remediation. The test battery for class-X must include all historic class-X bypass primitives — incomplete patches re-introduce risk that one-off testing does not detect.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2022-41091 is a MOTW/SmartScreen protection-mechanism bypass that was KEV-listed with ransomware campaign use recorded, and its defining artefact is an absence — a missing alternate data stream — which no configuration review or signature engine observes. The only test that distinguishes a configured protective feature from an effective one is launching a payload from a downloaded container and confirming a warning actually appears, run as a class-level battery on every patch deployment.

CVE-2022-41073.name: Microsoft Windows Print Spooler Privilege Escalation Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: A standard user starts printfilterpipelinesvc.exe (a SYSTEM-integrity local service), creates an object-manager symbolic link that remaps the C: drive inside their own DOS device map, then triggers a print job. The DLL load itself is protected by OBJ_IGNORE_IMPERSONATED_DEVICEMAP so the legitimate PrintConfig.dll loads, but CSRSS then builds the activation context without ignoring impersonation — reading the attacker's copy of the WinSxS manifest, edited to add a dependentAssembly pointing at an attacker-controlled path, which loads attacker DLLs into the SYSTEM process. The 'Print Spooler' title names the exploited path; the root cause is privileged code resolving files through an impersonated device map.
attack_vector.privileges_required: low — PR:L; an ordinary local standard-user account suffices, and printfilterpipelinesvc.exe is startable by that account on any Windows install with printing present
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L; no race, no heap grooming and no memory-corruption reliability work, only a symbolic link and a print job. Project Zero assesses the in-the-wild actor built it from the CVE-2022-29104 proof of concept already sitting on VirusTotal in July 2022, four months before Microsoft detected the use.
attack_vector.ai_factor: Not AI-discovered — MSRC credits its own Threat Intelligence Center, which surfaced the bug from in-the-wild telemetry rather than code review or fuzzing, and the attacker side is variant reuse from a leaked PoC, the opposite of machine-assisted novelty.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Apply the 8 November 2022 updates (KB5019959, KB5019980, KB5019961, KB5019966, KB5019964, KB5019970, KB5019081, plus the 2012/2008-era rollup and security-only packages), then the December 2022 and January 2023 updates that add and finally enable the broader CSRSS OBJ_IGNORE_IMPERSONATED_DEVICEMAP mitigation.
prevention.adequacy: November alone broke the exploit but not the root cause — the broader CSRSS mitigation only arrived in December 2022 and was not enabled for printfilterpipelinesvc.exe until January 2023 — so a host patched to the KEV due date carried the device-map flaw for two more months. Disabling the Print Spooler is a partial compensating control that removes this path only.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Alert on a non-administrative process creating an object-manager symbolic link that remaps a drive root inside its own DOS device map immediately before a print job, and on csrss.exe or printfilterpipelinesvc.exe resolving side-by-side manifests from outside C:\Windows\WinSxS.
detection.adequacy: Both signals are visible in Process Monitor-class telemetry and absent from default Windows auditing. Worse, the CWE recorded for this CVE by NVD, the Microsoft CNA and KEV alike is CWE-787, so detection engineering built from the classification hunts for memory corruption that never occurs.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treat any host showing the symlink-then-print sequence as SYSTEM-compromised: rebuild, rotate local and cached credentials, and hunt the estate for the sibling primitives CVE-2022-29104 and CVE-2022-22047, which share the same root cause.
response.adequacy: Because SYSTEM was reached without touching memory, rebuilding is the only reliable eviction; scoping the incident to a single CVE misses the activation-context family the actor was drawing from.

NIST-800-53-AC-6.gap: The token was correct throughout — the attacker stayed a standard user and the service stayed SYSTEM. AC-6 models privileges, not namespaces, and here the privileged service resolved manifest paths through the user's DOS device map, so the low-privileged half of the operation decided which files SYSTEM read.

NIS2-Art21-vulnerability-handling.gap: Handling is downstream of vendor classification and the classification was misleading: triaging on 'Windows Print Spooler Elevation of Privilege' produces the post-PrintNightmare reflex of stopping the spooler service, which leaves the impersonated-device-map flaw reachable through any other privileged process that loads a DLL under impersonation.

UK-CAF-B2.gap: B2 assumes a privileged process acts under one coherent identity, but authority and identity split inside a single operation here and the lower-privileged half governed path resolution. No B2 evidence artefact — account inventories, privileged-access reviews, impersonation policy — records which identity resolves namespaces inside CSRSS.

AU-ISM-1546.gap: Evidence that the November 2022 update landed inside the ISM timeframe would be true and still insufficient, because Microsoft shipped the fix in three stages and the root-cause mitigation was not enabled for the exploited service until January 2023; 1546 has no concept of a symptom fix versus a root-cause fix.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.9.gap: The WinSxS baseline was never modified and its permissions held. Substitution happened one layer down, at path resolution, so baseline hashing, drift detection and CIS-benchmark scanning all inspect the correct manifest on disk while a different file is the one actually read.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2022-41073 was KEV-listed on 2022-11-08 with a 2022-12-09 due date and ransomware campaign use recorded, and Project Zero assesses the in-the-wild actor built it from the CVE-2022-29104 proof of concept already sitting on VirusTotal in July 2022 — four months before Microsoft detected the use. A month-long remediation window on a standard-user-to-SYSTEM primitive with a public sibling PoC is exploitation acceptance.

new_control_requirements.name: BUG-FAMILY-MITIGATION-PERSISTENCE
new_control_requirements.description: When a CVE patch lands, retain the pre-patch compensating controls (module blacklists, sysctl restrictions) until the patched code has soaked for a stated review period. Patches for one bug in a primitive class can introduce sibling bugs in the same class; the original compensating control may still apply to the sibling.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2022-41073's November 2022 update reverted impersonation around the winspool.drv LoadLibraryExW call and broke the exploit, but the broader CSRSS OBJ_IGNORE_IMPERSONATED_DEVICEMAP mitigation only shipped in December 2022 and was not enabled for printfilterpipelinesvc.exe until January 2023 — so the Print Spooler disable used as a pre-patch compensating control still applied to the unfixed device-map root cause for two months after the host was recorded as patched.

new_control_requirements.name: INCOMPLETE-PATCH-SEQUENCE-SEVERITY-MULTIPLIER
new_control_requirements.description: Vulnerability-management programs must apply a severity multiplier when a CVE is the Nth in an incomplete-patch sequence on the same primitive (third MOTW bypass, second AMSI bypass, etc.). Framework controls treating each CVE as discrete obscure the structural defect; the Nth CVE in a sequence implies that future bypasses on the same primitive are likely.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2022-41073 shares the impersonated-DOS-device-map primitive with CVE-2022-29104 and CVE-2022-22047, and Microsoft's three-stage fix is itself the incomplete-patch signature. Triaged discretely on the misleading 'Windows Print Spooler Elevation of Privilege' title, it reads as a spooler bug to be answered by stopping the service — which leaves the primitive reachable through any other privileged process that loads a DLL under impersonation.

CVE-2022-41125.name: Microsoft Windows CNG Key Isolation Service Privilege Escalation Vulnerability (CVE-2022-41125)

attack_vector.description: A low-privileged local process reaches the CNG key isolation service — hosted inside lsass.exe, which Microsoft documents as the key isolation process — through the key storage router's LRPC channel, and triggers an out-of-bounds write that yields SYSTEM. Microsoft published one FAQ sentence and no root cause, so the corrupted structure is not in the public record; what is established is that the code running at SYSTEM sits inside the very process whose purpose is holding long-lived asymmetric private keys outside application memory.
attack_vector.privileges_required: low — PR:L; an ordinary local account is enough, and the LRPC surface into the key isolation process is reachable from a standard-user context by design
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L per the vendor vector, though the practical barrier is unknowable from primary sources: Microsoft named no affected function, Project Zero published no root-cause analysis for this CVE despite publishing them for two siblings from the same release, and no exploit code has ever surfaced
attack_vector.ai_factor: Not AI-discovered — MSRC credits MSTIC and MSRC themselves as finders, i.e. discovery from Microsoft's own in-the-wild telemetry followed by internal analysis. No external research effort of any kind exists for this CVE, which is why the AI question can be answered with confidence rather than left unknown.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Apply the 8 November 2022 updates (KB5019959, KB5019980, KB5019961, KB5019966, KB5019964, KB5019970, KB5019081, KB5020023/KB5020010, KB5020009/KB5020003), or the KB5019080 hotpatch on Windows Server 2022 Datacenter: Azure Edition, and pair the patch with rotation triage for long-lived private keys held in the Microsoft software KSP on any host suspected of compromise.
prevention.adequacy: Microsoft published no workaround or mitigation, so patching is the whole of prevention — but it is not the whole of remediation, because code that executed at SYSTEM inside the LSA process was adjacent to the very keys the component exists to isolate, and a patch does not un-expose a key.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Watch for anomalous LRPC calls into the ncrypt.dll key-storage-router path from low-privileged processes, and for lsass.exe faults, Windows Error Reporting records or crash dumps naming keyiso, ncrypt or bcrypt shortly before a privilege escalation.
detection.adequacy: There is no signature option at all — no sample, no hash, no command line, no network artefact — so detection reduces to LSA-process integrity telemetry, and a failed out-of-bounds write crashing lsass is the most reliable indicator available.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treat SYSTEM execution inside the LSA process as key compromise: rotate code-signing, S/MIME, DPAPI-NG and IIS/ADFS certificate keys held in the Microsoft software KSP on affected hosts, then rebuild.
response.adequacy: Rotation is the only defensible response given nobody can determine from the public record whether stored keys were reachable; patch-and-close leaves that question permanently open.

NIST-800-53-SC-28.gap: SC-28 evidence is normally 'private keys live in the platform key store and are non-exportable', a claim CNG key isolation exists to make true. An out-of-bounds write inside the isolation service attacks the boundary rather than the store, so the control statement stays literally satisfied while the property it asserts stops holding, and no SC-28 test separates the two.

DORA-Art-9.gap: Art.9 attestations for signing and transport keys routinely rest on OS-level isolation and non-exportability. This CVE placed SYSTEM execution inside the process enforcing that assumption, and with no published root cause a financial entity could neither verify nor honestly disclaim the control during the exposure window — only assert it.

UK-CAF-C1.gap: C1 expects detection coverage maintained against current threat intelligence, which is unachievable here: the CVE is KEV-listed as actively exploited yet has no published root cause, no exploit sample, no hash and no network indicator, so a C1 score derived from a threat-intel feed records coverage that cannot exist.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: Higher E8 maturity tightens the OS-patch window when a working exploit exists, and pipelines commonly read that from vendor exploit-maturity metadata — but MSRC's temporal vector carries E:U while the same record reports 'Exploitation Detected' and CISA listed it the day it shipped, so an automated decision scheduled a confirmed in-the-wild SYSTEM escalation as routine monthly patching.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.24.gap: A.8.24 asks process questions — is there a cryptography policy, are keys managed across generation, storage, archival and destruction — all of which could be answered correctly here. None asks whether the component performing the storage is memory-safe, so a full A.8.24 review during the exposure window would legitimately have concluded key custody was sound.

new_control_requirements.name: CRYPTO-SUBSYSTEM-CVE-DISCLOSURE
new_control_requirements.description: When a CVE affects a kernel cryptographic subsystem (IPsec, RxRPC, etc.), any compliance controls that rely on that subsystem must be documented as 'not a compensating control' until the CVE is patched. Risk assessments must note this explicitly.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2022-41125 places SYSTEM-level code execution inside the CNG key isolation service hosted in lsass.exe — the component whose stated purpose is keeping long-lived private keys out of application process memory — so every key-custody attestation resting on 'keys are held in the Microsoft software KSP and are non-exportable' stops holding while the control statement stays literally true. Microsoft published no root cause, so the reliance must be documented as void until the November 2022 update lands and keys are triaged for rotation.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2022-41125 shipped with MSRC's temporal vector reading E:U (exploit code unproven) while the same MSRC record set the exploitability index to 'Exploitation Detected' and CISA added it to KEV the day it shipped, so any patch clock driven by vendor exploit-maturity metadata scheduled a confirmed in-the-wild SYSTEM escalation as routine monthly work. Microsoft published no workaround or mitigation, so a clock keyed to the KEV listing is the only trigger that fires correctly.

CVE-2022-41128.name: Microsoft Windows Scripting Languages Remote Code Execution Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: An Office document — in the observed APT37 campaign one referencing the 29 October 2022 Itaewon crowd crush — fetches a remote RTF template, which pulls remote HTML that Office renders through the Internet Explorer engine in-process. Inside jscript9.dll, GlobOpt::OptArraySrc type-checks a variable at function entry and then assumes the type is invariant; forcing JIT compilation of a function that reassigns an Int32Array variable to an Object under a conditional makes later array writes land at an attacker-chosen address. The chain then overwrites array lengths for relative read/write, leaks jscript9.dll vtable pointers to defeat ASLR, repoints a DataView buffer, and calls VirtualProtect through a fake string vtable to bypass Control Flow Guard — reaching user-level code execution with no second bug, because Office is not sandboxed by default.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none — PR:N; the attacker needs no account or foothold, only that a targeted user opens the document (UI:R), an interaction the lure engineered around a national tragedy three days after it happened
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L; Project Zero published the JIT trigger verbatim and MSRC's own temporal vector for this November 2022 Windows CVE carries E:F (functional exploit code), not E:U
attack_vector.ai_factor: Not AI-discovered — Google TAG's Benoît Sevens and Clément Lecigne recovered in-the-wild Office documents and reversed the JScript9 JIT path by hand, comparing it to the closely similar CVE-2021-34480; manual variant analysis on a 31 October report to 8 November patch timeline, with no AI tooling credited by Google, Microsoft or any third party.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Apply the 8 November 2022 updates (KB5019959, KB5019980, KB5019961, KB5019966, KB5019964, KB5019970, KB5019081, and for the legacy SKUs KB5020023/KB5020010, KB5020009/KB5020003, KB5020000/KB5020013 plus the IE cumulative KB5019958), AND cut Office's route to the engine — disable remote-template and RTF loading, block outbound template fetches, enforce Protected View.
prevention.adequacy: Patching alone is incomplete in two directions. The MSHTML/Trident platform and jscript9.dll remain shipped on patched systems as a supported compatibility component, so Office can still reach the engine for the next variant; and for Windows 7 SP1, 8.1, Server 2008 R2 SP1 and Server 2012/2012 R2 the fix arrived through Monthly Rollup, Security Only and IE Cumulative channels that are now ended or ESU-gated, leaving decommissioning or isolation as the only compliant path on those hosts.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Alert on winword.exe or another Office host issuing an outbound HTTP(S) request for a remote RTF template immediately after a document opens, and on mshtml.dll plus jscript9.dll loading inside an Office process followed by a VirtualProtect call through a corrupted vtable and child-process creation.
detection.adequacy: The remote-template fetch is the earliest observable event because the delivered document is clean and carries no file-based indicator until after exploitation — but monitoring baselines almost never enumerate Office applications as HTTP clients, so the signal exists and is routinely not collected.

response.what_would_have_worked: Block the TAG-published template and C2 domains (word-template[.]net, openxmlformat[.]org, ms-office[.]services, ms-offices[.]com, template-openxml[.]com), hunt the five published document hashes and the RTF template hash across mail and endpoint stores, and rebuild any host that fetched a template.
response.adequacy: Indicator-based response closes this specific APT37 campaign and nothing beyond it, since both the JScript9 engine and the Office remote-template delivery mechanism survive the patch intact.

NIST-800-53-CM-7.gap: 'Internet Explorer is retired' is the answer most CM-7 inventories give and it is a false answer — the IE11 desktop app was retired in June 2022 and disabled in February 2023, but the MSHTML/Trident platform and jscript9.dll remain shipped and supported for legacy compatibility, and the exploit never launched a browser at all.

NIS2-Art21-patch-management.gap: Art.21 frames patching as a cadence obligation that presumes a patch remains obtainable; for the Windows 7, 8.1, Server 2008 R2 and Server 2012/2012 R2 population the servicing channels that carried this fix are ended or ESU-gated, so on those hosts the duty can only be discharged by decommissioning or isolation — an outcome the article's cadence framing does not contemplate.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: B4 expects supported software protected against known exploitation, but this CVE straddles both sides at once: it hit fully supported Windows 10, 11 and Server 2022 alongside Windows 7 and Server 2008 R2, and even on current builds the retired-application inventory and the loaded-module reality disagree.

AU-Essential-8-App-Hardening.gap: E8 explicitly requires IE11 to be disabled or removed and scores it by policy state, but the chain never invoked the browser — Office fetched the remote template and rendered attacker HTML through the engine inside its own process — so an estate assessed at Maturity Level 3 for this control was fully exploitable.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.16.gap: The only pre-execution event available to monitor is an Office process making an outbound HTTP request for a remote template; full A.8.16 evidence of log coverage, retention and review would still have produced no alert, because remote-template fetches by winword.exe are in nobody's anomaly baseline.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2022-41128 was already being used by APT37 when Google TAG reported it on 31 October 2022; Microsoft shipped the fix on 8 November and CISA listed it the same day with a 2022-12-09 due date. The delivered Office document is clean and carries no file-based indicator until after exploitation, so nothing before the patch reduces exposure and the remediation clock is the only lever that shortens it.

new_control_requirements.name: EOL-ASSET-DECOMMISSION
new_control_requirements.description: Network-reachable end-of-life devices with no vendor patch path must be isolated and decommissioned within a bounded window; mandatory compensating segmentation applies until removal since no remediation exists.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2022-41128's fix reached Windows 7 SP1, 8.1, RT 8.1, Server 2008 R2 SP1 and Server 2012/2012 R2 only through Monthly Rollup, Security Only and IE Cumulative channels (KB5020000/KB5020013, KB5020023/KB5020010, KB5020009/KB5020003, KB5019958) that are now ended or ESU-gated. On that population the patch obligation cannot be discharged at all, so bounded-window isolation and decommissioning is the only remaining remediation.

CVE-2021-25337.name: Samsung Mobile Devices Improper Access Control Vulnerability (CVE-2021-25337)

attack_vector.description: Any untrusted app calls ContentResolver.insert() on content://com.sec.android.semclipboardprovider with Android's special '_data' column set to an arbitrary path, then openFileDescriptor(uri, 'w') — and system_server, which hosts Samsung's SemClipboardProvider and declares it android:exported='true' with no android:permission at all, opens the file and returns a writable descriptor. In the recovered in-the-wild chain the primitive is used four separate times: to drop a stage-2 ELF into /data/system/users/0/, to rewrite SamsungTTSSettings.xml on both candidate paths so the privileged SamsungTTS app System.load()s an attacker library, and to obtain a descriptor to the DPU driver for the next stage.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none — PR:N; no Android permission is requested and no root is needed, only that an untrusted_app-context process runs on the device (the CVSS UI:R is satisfied by installing or launching that app)
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L; the trigger is six lines of ordinary Android SDK code with no memory corruption, no race and no special permission, published in full by Project Zero
attack_vector.ai_factor: Not AI-discovered — Google TAG recovered a partial in-the-wild chain it assesses belonged to a commercial surveillance vendor, and Project Zero's own view is the bug was likely found by code auditing or static analysis of an exported provider's manifest declaration. No party claims AI tooling.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Move handsets to Samsung SMR Mar-2021 Release 1 or later (SVE-2021-19527), which adds a system-UID caller check on insert(), update() and delete(); enforce a minimum security-patch level by MDM and block sideloaded installs on devices that cannot reach that build.
prevention.adequacy: The SMR fix is complete and was later strengthened structurally — SemClipboardProvider was moved out of system_server into the Samsung Keyboard app, which does not run as the system UID — but delivery is carrier-staggered and reboot-bearing, Google Play system updates do not cover OEM system_server code, and handsets past their SMR support window (the S10/A50/A51 class the sample targeted) never receive it and can only be replaced.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Alert on any untrusted_app calling the semclipboardprovider with a '_data' path outside the clipboard image store, on system_server-attributed writes under /data/system/users/0/, and on modification of the SMT_LATEST_INSTALLED_ENGINE_PATH key in SamsungTTSSettings.xml.
detection.adequacy: Every one of these is inspectable on an imaged device and on essentially no managed handset in normal operation — Android exposes no fleet-wide hook for provider-call telemetry, and because TAG never recovered the delivering app there is no app-level indicator to hunt.

response.what_would_have_worked: Correlate the three chained CVEs on one device timeline rather than triaging them separately, image the handset for the SamsungTTS settings write and the stage-2 ELF, and replace devices past their SMR window.
response.adequacy: For a commercial-surveillance chain that reached the kernel, retiring the handset is the only defensible eviction; a patch applied afterwards does not undo system_app or kernel-level persistence already established.

NIST-800-53-AC-3.gap: Android's reference monitor worked exactly as configured and correctly permitted everyone, because Samsung declared the provider exported with no permission attribute; SELinux stayed enforcing and system_server performed the writes legitimately. AC-3 evidence for a mobile fleet is MDM policy, lock and encryption state — it never includes reading the handset vendor's framework manifest.

NIS2-Art21-supply-chain.gap: The vulnerable component is OEM code injected into system_server rather than AOSP, and no supplier-assurance questionnaire enumerates a handset vendor's framework-level additions; an entity can execute the Art.21 supplier process completely and still carry an exported system_server provider it has never been told exists.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: Platform separation never broke — a single missing caller check let one untrusted app use system_server as a file-writing proxy four times without defeating SELinux, Linux permissions or the app sandbox — so a B4 hardening review finds every protective feature enabled and enforcing while the escalation runs straight through them.

AU-ISM-1808.gap: 1808 is written around software an entity procures and can hold a supplier to; handset firmware inverts that, with the OEM injecting privileged code into the OS and the fix arriving through a carrier-gated SMR that stops entirely at end of support, so for the affected device generation the outcome cannot be achieved at all — only accepted, or the fleet replaced.

ISO-27001-2022-A.5.15.gap: The access rule that failed was one missing android:permission attribute authored by the handset vendor and shipped in firmware, invisible to every artefact the ISMS holds. Compounding it, Samsung as CNA scored this 4.4 with low confidentiality and integrity impact where NVD scored 7.1 with C:H/I:H, so a register inheriting the vendor score deprioritised a primitive that carried a surveillance vendor to the kernel.

new_control_requirements.name: MOBILE-OS-MINIMUM-PATCH-LEVEL-ENFORCEMENT
new_control_requirements.description: Managed mobile fleets must enforce a minimum OS security-patch level as a condition of access to organizational data, not merely report it. For Android, the MDM/EMM must read the device security-patch level and block or quarantine devices below the patch level that fixes a KEV-listed Framework flaw (here, 2026-06-01), and constrain installation of untrusted/side-loaded apps on devices that cannot yet update - since the privilege escalation is driven by locally running code. The distinguishing test: enroll a device pinned below 2026-06-01 and confirm the MDM policy denies it access to protected resources (rather than only recording the stale patch level on a dashboard) - paper 'mobile patching' policies that surface patch level without enforcing it leave exploitable devices in production.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2021-25337 is driven entirely by a locally installed untrusted app calling Samsung's exported SemClipboardProvider in system_server with no permission attribute, and the caller check that fixes it exists only in SMR Mar-2021 Release 1 or later — a carrier-staggered, reboot-bearing OEM update that Google Play system updates do not cover.
