new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Microsoft Word, Word Viewer and the Office Compatibility Pack are the affected products; MS09-027 fixed them on 2009-06-09 and CISA opened the KEV clock on 2022-06-08 with a 2022-06-22 due date, EPSS 0.63081 at the 99.129th percentile on 2026-08-13. The 'whichever is later' clause governs: patch availability predates KEV listing by thirteen years, so the clock runs from 2022-06-08, and on a legacy estate the verified mitigation deployable inside the window is the File Block registry policy MS09-027 documents, not the Office migration. The capability floor is zero — a Metasploit module for Word 2003 on Windows XP has been public since April 2011, filed at the aggregator under the sibling id CVE-2009-0565 — so a KEV clock keyed on this CVE alone never surfaces it.

new_control_requirements.name: ARCHIVE-CONTENT-TYPE-PROVENANCE
new_control_requirements.description: For this CVE the requirement is that Word's Protected View decision be taken from verified provenance of the file — established outside the document — rather than from metadata that travels with the document and that an attacker controls, and that the untrusted-origin marking survive whatever container the document is delivered in so the handler still sees it as externally sourced. The operator-side expression of the control: the mail gateway and file-share boundary apply and preserve the untrusted-origin marking themselves, so the sandbox decision does not depend on the application deriving it from attacker-supplied input. The distinguishing test: deliver an externally-sourced document through each ingress path and confirm it reaches Word marked untrusted, instead of confirming only that Protected View is enabled in policy.
new_control_requirements.evidence: This is a Word document-delivery CVE and the control names the right decision point: MS09-027 gives the mail-attachment and hosted-file scenarios as the two delivery paths, and opening the file is the whole interaction. State the precondition honestly for the affected set — Word 2002 and Word 2003 have no Protected View, so on those builds only the gateway-side provenance marking and the File Block policy are deliverable, and the sandbox half arrives with Word 2010 or later. Where Protected View does exist, gateway-applied provenance is what makes it fire on a document extracted from an archive rather than downloaded directly.

CVE-2009-1862.name: Adobe Acrobat and Reader, Flash Player Unspecified Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: One Flash runtime, two carriers. A crafted Flash application corrupts memory in the runtime and yields code execution: delivered either as a .swf rendered by the browser plugin, or as a Flash object embedded in a PDF that Reader and Acrobat 9.x render through authplay.dll. Code runs in the browser or reader process at the user's privilege. Blocking one carrier leaves the other fully exploitable.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none — PR:N; the attacker supplies a file or a web page
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L; no race, no leak, no foothold. The packet's UI:R reflects the reader path where a user opens a document; the browser path needs only a page visit. Adobe characterised the observed activity as limited targeted attacks against Reader 9 on Windows, which is what per-build tuning rather than commodity exploitation looks like.
attack_vector.ai_factor: None, and the discovery direction is the point: Adobe published APSA09-03 in response to attacks already underway, so the flaw surfaced from adversary telemetry rather than from research disclosure. No researcher is credited from a primary source, and no AI tooling or AI-branded research arm appears on either side.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: During the 2009-07-22 to 2009-07-30 window, denying access to authplay.dll to close the reader path and removing or blocking the Flash browser plugin to close the other. Afterwards, Reader/Acrobat 9.1.3 plus the APSB09-10 Flash update — and, from 2020-12-31, removing Flash Player outright rather than patching it.
prevention.adequacy: The DLL-denial mitigation is unusually precise — a single named component — but it removes Flash rendering inside PDFs, which breaks any workflow that depended on it, and it must be re-applied after a Reader repair or reinstall. The patch is complete for the defect and does not survive the product's end of life.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Alerting on authplay.dll being loaded by Reader or Acrobat on hosts where Flash-in-PDF has no business role, and on browser or reader processes spawning children after rendering .swf content.
detection.adequacy: The DLL-load signal is genuinely useful because it detects exposure rather than exploitation, so it fires before anything goes wrong — but it needs module-load telemetry, which is less commonly collected than process creation. Against limited targeted attacks, payload signatures are behind by construction.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treating a confirmed render as targeted intrusion rather than commodity infection: rebuild the endpoint, rotate the user's credentials, and review what that user had access to, since the observed activity was targeted rather than opportunistic.
response.adequacy: Correct escalation and rarely applied, because the alert that starts it usually reads as a browser crash. Scoping is also hard: with two delivery paths, establishing which one was used changes which artefacts to look for.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: SI-2's unit of action is a released fix, so a perfect programme was fully exposed for the nine days between the 2009-07-22 advisory and the 2009-07-30 update; and it does not distinguish the reader carrier from the browser carrier.

NIST-800-53-CM-7.gap: Removing the Flash plugin and denying authplay.dll closes both paths, but neither a DLL inside a document reader nor a near-universal browser plugin was ever enumerated as an unnecessary function.

NIS2-Art21-patch-management.gap: Structurally cannot report Flash Player, for which patching stopped being a category on 2020-12-31 and the correct action is disconnection.

EU-CRA-Art13.gap: Manufacturer vulnerability-handling and support-period duties are exactly the frame for a runtime embedded as a component in a second product on a separate update track — and did not exist in 2009, leaving operators unaware Reader carried its own Flash runtime.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: A patched fleet that still renders embedded Flash evidences secure configuration; B4 never requires justifying a general-purpose media runtime inside a document reader.

UK-CAF-B5.gap: Resilience framing is about maintaining function, so a system that still requires Flash content can be evidenced as resilient while depending on an unfixable runtime.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: Flash copies redistributed inside OS images and third-party installers escape the application inventory the rating is computed from, and the remove-unsupported half is not sampled.

AU-Essential-8-App-Hardening.gap: Blocking Flash content closes the browser path and says nothing about Reader rendering an embedded Flash object through its own bundled runtime.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: The control's process language does not distinguish an advisory with confirmed exploitation and no patch from a routine vulnerability record, so both go through the same workflow.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.7.gap: Anti-malware and awareness do not touch a legitimate runtime rendering attacker-supplied content, and bespoke payloads in targeted attacks defeat signature coverage by construction.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Adobe Reader and Acrobat 9.x through 9.1.2 and Adobe Flash Player through 9.0.159.0 / 10.0.22.87 are the affected products; APSA09-03 landed 2009-07-22 with exploitation already underway, the fixes landed 2009-07-30 and 2009-07-31, and CISA opened the KEV clock on 2022-06-08 with a 2022-06-22 due date. EPSS is 0.25006 at the 97.721st percentile on 2026-08-13. The compensating-control arm is what makes the 4-hour window achievable here: denying access to authplay.dll and pulling the Flash plugin are both deployable immediately, where the binary patch did not exist for another eight days — and for Flash Player today, end-of-life since 2020-12-31, removal is the only verified mitigation there is.

new_control_requirements.name: MITIGATION-ACTIVE-PATCH-PENDING-VERDICT-CLASS
new_control_requirements.description: Compliance verdicts must distinguish three states: (a) binary patch deployed (vulnerability eliminated), (b) vendor-mitigation rule active, no binary patch (residual risk: any defect in the mitigation rule reopens the vulnerability), (c) no mitigation, no patch (full exposure). Audit reports must surface (b) as a distinct compensating-control state with an associated time-bound action item, not as a 'patched per SLA' outcome.
new_control_requirements.evidence: This CVE spent nine days in exactly state (b), and the dates are in the record: Adobe's APSA09-03 was published 2009-07-22 reporting limited targeted attacks against Reader 9 on Windows, and the binary updates — Flash Player on 2009-07-30, Reader/Acrobat 9.1.3 on 2009-07-31 — did not exist until after. The available posture in between was denying access to authplay.dll, which removes the reader path but leaves Flash-in-PDF workflows broken and is silently undone by a Reader repair or reinstall. Every property the control names applies: a mitigation whose defect reopens the flaw, needing a time-bound action item rather than a 'patched' verdict. Flash Player has since moved permanently into a fourth position the control's three states do not cover — end-of-life on 2020-12-31, so state (a) is unreachable and disconnection is the terminal answer.

CVE-2009-3953.name: Adobe Acrobat and Reader Universal 3D Remote Code Execution Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: A PDF carries a /3D annotation referencing a U3D stream. Adobe's U3D implementation parses the stream's CLODProgressiveMeshDeclaration block and trusts a count field in it as an array bound; a crafted value drives writes past the end of the array. The public exploit precedes the trigger with a two-stage heap spray so the out-of-bounds writes land on data it controls, giving execution in the reader process at the user's privilege.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none — PR:N; the attacker supplies a PDF and needs nothing on the target
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L for reachability: no authentication, no race, no info leak. Reliability is a different matter and required the heap engineering the module performs; the same module records Reader 8.1.2 and 9.1.0 as working targets and 8.1.3 as not, so build drift moves exploitability without moving vulnerability.
attack_vector.ai_factor: None. Manual binary-format research on a 3D mesh parser in 2009; no discovery credit was recoverable from the vendor bulletin, and the exploitation side is credited in the Metasploit module to Felipe Andres Manzano and jduck. No AI tooling and no AI-branded research arm.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Disabling 3D and multimedia content in the Reader/Acrobat trust manager, which removes the U3D parser from the reachable path, plus reaching 9.3 / 8.2 / 7.1.4 across all three serviced lines and both the Reader and Acrobat update tracks. Disabling JavaScript additionally breaks the heap spray the published exploit depends on.
prevention.adequacy: Disabling 3D content is close to free for most estates — few workflows render U3D in a PDF — which makes it the strongest available control, and it also covers the sibling defect CVE-2009-2994 in the same parser. The patch is complete for this defect but has to be landed on up to six distinct update paths, and all three lines are now unsupported.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Gateway inspection flagging PDFs that carry a /3D annotation with a /U3D stream at all — an exposure signal rather than an exploit signature — and process-lineage alerting on AcroRd32.exe spawning children.
detection.adequacy: Flagging U3D presence works because legitimate 3D-bearing PDFs are rare in most estates, so the false-positive cost is low; where CAD or engineering workflows do use them, the signal collapses. Process lineage fires only after execution.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treating a confirmed open as a user-context compromise — rebuild the endpoint, rotate that user's credentials, sweep for the same document elsewhere — and disabling 3D content fleet-wide as the immediate containment step rather than waiting for the upgrade.
response.adequacy: The fleet-wide setting change is the part that actually contains, since it is deployable in hours where the upgrade across three lines is not. Endpoint rebuild is correct and, with a public Metasploit module, the payload is operator-chosen, so absence of a known-malware signature proves nothing.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: Three serviced lines times two products times unmanaged per-user copies means the remediation record can read complete while an Acrobat 8.1.x install still parses U3D; and all three fixed versions are now on unsupported lines.

NIST-800-53-CM-7.gap: Disabling 3D and multimedia content removes the parser from the reachable path, but a media sub-parser inside a document reader is never enumerated as an unnecessary function.

NIS2-Art21-vulnerability-management.gap: Tracking is met; reachability is not. With a public module since 2010 and EPSS 0.83855, exposure is decided by whether any uninventoried pre-fix copy survives.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: A patched fleet with 3D content enabled evidences secure configuration while leaving the U3D parser reachable for the next defect in it — and NVD records a prior distinct one, CVE-2009-2994.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: Scores from inventoried applications, so an unmanaged Reader 8.1.x copy — the exact build the public module names as a working target — is not a finding.

AU-Essential-8-App-Hardening.gap: PDF settings are in scope, but the trust-manager 3D/multimedia toggle and the JavaScript toggle that breaks the published spray are not the artefacts assessed.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: No trigger reopens a closed evaluation when a public weaponized module appears later, and eight CVEs in one bulletin against one component is not read as a signal about the component.

ISO-27001-2022-A.5.7.gap: Threat intelligence is evidenced as feed consumption, not structural inference; nothing requires concluding from a second distinct defect in one parser that the parser should be disabled rather than patched again.

The distinguishing test: after the managed update lands, enumerate the Acrobat and Reader installs on the estate and confirm none still report a pre-fix version — an estate that patches the inventoried Reader while a second Acrobat track keeps the old build still opens crafted PDFs into the sink, with a flaw-remediation attestation that reads clean. Precondition: this reaches only copies the inventory can see and the operator can update; an unmanaged per-user install is remediated by removing it, not by recording it as patched. The packet registers no live-patch path, so each copy carries the service restart or system reboot the vendor fix requires, and a copy updated but not restarted is not yet remediated.
new_control_requirements.evidence: This entry is the hardest version of the parity problem in the batch: APSB10-02 fixes three concurrently-serviced lines — 9.3, 8.2 on Windows and macOS, and 7.1.4 — and Reader and Acrobat each have their own track within every line, so the estate has up to six distinct pre-fix versions to enumerate rather than one. The public Metasploit module names Reader 8.1.2 as a working target specifically, which is the older-line build an inventory scoped to the current major version never sees. Restart nuance for this product: no host reboot, but Reader/Acrobat and any browser hosting the plugin must be relaunched before the fixed parser is in use.

new_control_requirements.name: INCOMPLETE-PATCH-SEQUENCE-SEVERITY-MULTIPLIER
new_control_requirements.description: Vulnerability-management programs must apply a severity multiplier when a CVE is the Nth in an incomplete-patch sequence on the same primitive (third MOTW bypass, second AMSI bypass, etc.). Framework controls treating each CVE as discrete obscure the structural defect; the Nth CVE in a sequence implies that future bypasses on the same primitive are likely.
new_control_requirements.evidence: NVD states the relationship explicitly for this entry: CVE-2009-3953 is recorded as a different vulnerability than CVE-2009-2994, both in Adobe's U3D implementation inside Reader and Acrobat, within a single release cycle — the second distinct memory-safety defect found in one 3D mesh parser. APSB10-02 then bundled eight CVEs on 2010-01-12. Treating each as discrete is what produced the observed outcome: operators patched twice and left the U3D parser enabled, when the structural read is that a rarely-used media sub-parser generating repeat defects should be disabled in the trust manager rather than serviced again. The multiplier is what would have moved the response from 'apply APSB10-02' to 'turn off 3D content'.

CVE-2009-4324.name: Adobe Acrobat and Reader Use-After-Free Vulnerability (CVE-2009-4324)

attack_vector.description: A PDF's embedded JavaScript calls Doc.media.newPlayer; Multimedia.api frees an object and keeps using the pointer. The same script sprays the heap so the freed allocation is reclaimed with attacker data, and execution lands in the context of whoever opened the file. Delivery was spearphished attachments during the December 2009 window and remains any path that gets a PDF in front of Reader or Acrobat.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none — PR:N; the attacker needs no account on the target, only a document the victim opens. Impact is bounded by the user's own rights, which on a 2009-era workstation was frequently local administrator.
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L; no race, no info leak, no second bug. The real constraint is UI:R (the victim must open the file) and that Acrobat JavaScript is enabled, which is the default.
attack_vector.ai_factor: None. The flaw was found and used by attackers in 2009 and became public through sample analysis; no research arm — AI-branded or otherwise — is credited. Nothing about the discovery or the weaponization involved automated analysis.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Disabling Acrobat JavaScript across the estate, which Adobe named in APSA09-07 and which removes the trigger entirely, held until the 9.3 / 8.2 builds could be deployed to both the Reader and the Acrobat tracks.
prevention.adequacy: It is complete against this specific path and nothing more. Disabling AcroJS does not touch the font, image or rendering parsers in the same products, so it is a stopgap for one CVE rather than a posture. It also breaks legitimate interactive forms, which is why estates that set it in December 2009 quietly reverted it.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Alerting on AcroRd32.exe or Acrobat.exe as the parent of any process, and on repeated Reader crashes concentrated on a single document. Both survive obfuscation because they are effects of the exploit rather than features of the file.
detection.adequacy: Parent-child alerting fires after code is already running, so it bounds dwell time rather than preventing compromise. Content inspection of the PDF was weaker still in 2009: the samples carried the script inside ZLib-compressed streams, so a scanner that did not decompress object streams saw nothing to match.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treating any workstation that opened a suspect PDF during the exposure window as compromised — credential rotation for accounts used on it and a rebuild — rather than closing the ticket when Reader reported the fixed build.
response.adequacy: This is the step most often skipped, because the patch record is the artifact an auditor asks for. Updating Reader removes the path and removes nothing the attacker left behind, and the update does not take effect in an already-running Reader process at all.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: Nominally met by any patch-management programme, but SI-2 assumes a live vendor update stream. For Reader/Acrobat 8.x and 9.x there is none, so a compliant assessment finds nothing to apply while a host running 9.2 stays exploitable, and per-user installs outside the inventory are never assessed at all.

NIST-800-53-CM-7.gap: Least-functionality baselines enumerate applications, not the scripting engines inside them. Adobe's own pre-patch mitigation — disabling Acrobat JavaScript — sits below the level CM-7 evidence is collected at, so the attestation passes with AcroJS enabled everywhere.

NIS2-Art21-patch-management.gap: The obligation is satisfied by applying the vendor update, and the vendor update here lands on 9.3 or 8.2 — builds that stopped receiving fixes long ago. Article 21 as written has no retirement leg, so 'patched' and 'unsupported' can be true at the same time.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: B4 evidence for desktop software is patch currency against a version Adobe no longer supports, and the CAF asset register rarely descends to a document-handling feature on every workstation. The one setting that closes the path — AcroJS disabled — is not in the evidence pack.

AU-Essential-8-App-Hardening.gap: PDF-reader hardening is explicitly in scope, but an assessor can mark it met without disabling the reader's JavaScript engine. Since the exploit is a JavaScript call into Multimedia.api, the control is recorded and the path is untouched.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: A.8.8 has no timing tier for exploit availability. Ranking by the 7.8 base score puts this below CVSS 9.x items that have no public exploit, while this one has had a Metasploit module and Exploit-DB 16503 since 2009 and sits at EPSS 0.81933 (99.621st percentile).

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Adobe Reader and Acrobat 8.x/9.x are the product identity here, and the ordinary patch SLA produces the wrong answer for them: the vendor update exists (9.3 / 8.2) but lands on an unsupported line, so the compensating-control branch of this control is the one that has to fire. CISA gave 14 days (KEV 2022-06-08, due 2022-06-22) on a flaw exploited in the wild since December 2009 with an Exploit-DB entry (16503) and a Metasploit module the whole time; the 2026 EPSS pair is 0.81933 at the 99.621st percentile. Disabling Acrobat JavaScript is the documented compensating control and can be pushed in hours, which is why this control's mitigation-or-patch framing is the one that fits.

new_control_requirements.name: MITIGATION-ACTIVE-PATCH-PENDING-VERDICT-CLASS
new_control_requirements.description: Compliance verdicts must distinguish three states: (a) binary patch deployed (vulnerability eliminated), (b) vendor-mitigation rule active, no binary patch (residual risk: any defect in the mitigation rule reopens the vulnerability), (c) no mitigation, no patch (full exposure). Audit reports must surface (b) as a distinct compensating-control state with an associated time-bound action item, not as a 'patched per SLA' outcome.
new_control_requirements.evidence: An Adobe Reader or Acrobat host with AcroJS disabled is in state (b), not state (a): the CWE-416 defect in Multimedia.api is untouched and returns the moment a user re-enables JavaScript for a form, or the moment a build is restored from an image predating the setting. Estates that set the APSA09-07 mitigation in the December 2009 window and reverted it when interactive forms broke are exactly the failure this state class exists to make visible. Recording those hosts as 'patched per SLA' is how a twelve-year-old KEV entry survives to a 2022-06-08 listing.

CVE-2010-0738.name: Red Hat JBoss Authentication Bypass Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: The jmx-console deployment descriptor scopes its JBossAdmin role check to the GET and POST verbs it enumerates. A HEAD request is therefore dispatched to the default GET handler with no authorization decision, exposing the whole MBean tree at /jmx-console/HtmlAdaptor. The attacker invokes MainDeployer or the BeanShell deployer, deploys a WAR, and thereafter interacts with the web shell rather than the console.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none — PR:N; the attacker needs only network reachability to the console path. No JBoss account exists or is checked at any point in the chain.
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L; a logic gap in a deployment descriptor with no timing, memory-layout or information-leak dependency. The real constraint is reachability, and internet-wide scanning for these paths is exactly how the SamSam operators selected targets.
attack_vector.ai_factor: None. Published by Minded Security (Giorgio Fedon) on 2010-04-30 from reading the security-constraint, with acknowledgement to Christian Papathanasiou of Trustwave SpiderLabs. No tooling-assisted discovery and no AI-branded research arm involved.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Removing the <http-method> elements from the jmx-console security-constraint so the deny applies to every verb — deployable in minutes without waiting for an erratum, and the only fix available for the end-of-life community JBoss AS 4.0.x line — combined with restricting /jmx-console to a management segment.
prevention.adequacy: Complete against this path. Its limit is discovery, not efficacy: the estates SamSam hit in 2016 could not apply it because nobody knew the JBoss instance was there, embedded inside a departmental or third-party application. The edit also has to survive a redeploy of the console, which restores the shipped descriptor.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Alerting on any request to /jmx-console with a method other than GET or POST, and on any file appearing under the JBoss deploy/ directory outside a change window. Both are cheap and near-zero-noise on a production application server.
detection.adequacy: The verb rule catches the bypass at the moment it is attempted, but only if the web tier logs the method and forwards logs off the host — and the outcome of this bug is code execution on the host doing the logging. The deploy-directory rule survives that, because it is a filesystem change a separate integrity monitor can see.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treating a JBoss instance exposed during the window as compromised rather than patchable: inventory the deploy directory against a known-good manifest, rebuild the instance, and rotate every credential the application held — datasource passwords, keystore material, service accounts — before restoring service.
response.adequacy: This is the step the ransomware outcome makes non-optional and the one an erratum-based remediation record hides. RHSA-2010:0379 closes the verb gap and removes nothing already deployed through it; a WAR dropped before the fix survives the upgrade and keeps serving.

NIST-800-53-AC-3.gap: The console declares a JBossAdmin role requirement, so AC-3 evidence is genuine — and it is true only for the two verbs the descriptor enumerates. AC-3 has no concept of a method-scoped access decision, so the attestation and the unauthenticated MainDeployer invocation are both accurate at the same time.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: The erratum existed from April 2010 and the SamSam campaign ran in 2016. The failure is population coverage: an embedded or forgotten JBossAS is not on the asset inventory SI-2 measures against, so it is never counted as unremediated.

NIST-800-53-SC-7.gap: Publishing the application port is a deliberate, documented SC-7 decision — and it publishes /jmx-console with it, because both are served from the same listener. SC-7 is not assessed at URI-path granularity, which is the granularity this defect lives at.

NIS2-Art21-patch-management.gap: Satisfiable by applying RHSA-2010:0379, which says nothing about the community JBoss AS 4.0.x line that never received an erratum, or about a JBossAS the entity does not know it is running inside a third-party product.

NIS2-Art21-network-security.gap: Segment-level network-security documentation legitimately covers a published web application. It does not drive the finer requirement — restricting an administrative URI path on a shared listener — which is what internet-wide scanning for /jmx-console actually defeated.

UK-CAF-B2.gap: B2 examines the identity and role model protecting privileged interfaces. Here the account model is bypassed rather than abused: no JBoss identity is presented and none is checked, so a complete B2 assessment inspects a mechanism the exploit never touches.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: The control assumes an enumerated application with an available vendor patch. Community JBoss AS 4.0.x has neither, and the configuration edit that fixes it is not a patch in the control's terms, so a compliant estate can still be running the defective descriptor.

ISO-27001-2022-A.5.15.gap: The deployment descriptor is itself a documented access-control rule restricting the console to administrators — a complete A.5.15 artefact. A.5.15 has no test separating a stated rule from its enforcement, and the enforcement here is method-scoped.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: Prioritising by the 5.3 base score buries an unauthenticated code-execution path on an internet-facing server that carries a Metasploit module, an Nmap NSE script, Exploit-DB 16319, a KEV ransomware flag and EPSS 0.79415 at the 99.567th percentile.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: JBoss EAP and every Red Hat product embedding the same jmx-console are the identity here, and this is the KEV entry that shows why the 'documented compensating controls' branch cannot be optional: the community JBoss AS 4.0.x line has no erratum at all, so a patch-only SLA leaves it permanently non-compliant while the descriptor edit could close it the same afternoon. CISA gave 21 days (added 2022-05-25, due 2022-06-15) on a flaw with an April 2010 erratum, knownRansomwareCampaignUse Known, and EPSS 0.79415 at the 99.567th percentile; the SamSam operators reached internet-facing instances six years after the fix shipped.

new_control_requirements.name: CONFIGURATION-SIDE-LIVE-PATCH-INVENTORY
new_control_requirements.description: For any web-fabric vulnerability with a configuration-side mitigation path: that path must be inventoried, tested, and deployable independent of the vendor-patch path. Operators cannot wait for nginx 1.30.1+ if a named-capture refactor mitigates immediately.
new_control_requirements.evidence: This JBoss flaw is entirely configuration-side: removing the <http-method> elements from the jmx-console security-constraint restores deny-all across every verb, which is Red Hat's own guidance in solution 30744 and the only remedy available for community JBoss AS 4.0.x, where RHSA-2010:0379 does not apply. Treating that edit as an inventoried, tested artefact — held in configuration management and reapplied after any console redeploy — is what lets an operator close the path without an EAP upgrade window, and it is also what would have covered the embedded JBossAS instances the SamSam campaign found in 2016.

attack_vector.description: An applet defines an untrusted class that subclasses a trusted one without overriding the method the privilege check inspects. The JRE's stack walk attributes the frame to the trusted declaring class, so a chain through Statement.invoke() reaches privileged APIs and turns off the sandbox. Delivery is a page load — the applet runs on visit, from a compromised site or an ad slot, and the payload is an executable inside the JAR or fetched from a URL the exploit carries.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none — PR:N; the attacker needs no account and no prior foothold. Code lands with the rights of the user running the browser.
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L; a security-model flaw with no memory-layout dependency, so one applet works unchanged across Windows, macOS and Linux and across every JRE build in range. The only precondition is a browser with the Java plugin enabled.
attack_vector.ai_factor: None. Sami Koivu found it by reasoning about the JVM's stack-walking privilege check and reported it through ZDI (ZDI-10-056, reported 2009-11-24, public 2010-04-05). No automated discovery, and no research arm with an AI brand is involved.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Removing or disabling the browser Java plugin estate-wide. That ends the applet path outright and does not depend on knowing the JRE version, which matters because application-bundled runtimes are the ones the inventory misses. Where applets were genuinely required, restricting them to an allowlist of internal sites.
prevention.adequacy: Complete against this delivery path and against the whole applet class that followed it. Its limit is that a vendor application which bundles and re-registers a JRE can restore the plugin at its next upgrade, so this needs periodic verification rather than a one-time change.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Alerting on java.exe or javaw.exe as the parent of any process, and on JAR fetches from hosts unrelated to the page being browsed. Both are effects of the exploit rather than properties of the applet, so obfuscating the JAR does not evade them.
detection.adequacy: It fires after the sandbox is already gone, so it bounds dwell time rather than preventing execution. Static inspection of the JAR is weak here: the classes involved are ordinary library types, so there is no malformed structure to match on — the maliciousness is in the inheritance relationship, not in the bytes.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treating a workstation that loaded a hostile applet as having run attacker code as the logged-on user: rotate the credentials that user held and rebuild, rather than recording the JRE update as closure.
response.adequacy: The JRE update is the artefact an audit asks for and it removes nothing the loader already dropped. It also does not take effect in a browser that is still running, so a host can report the fixed JRE and keep executing the vulnerable plugin until the browser is restarted.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: Remediation is measured against a software inventory that application-bundled and embedded JREs do not appear in, so a host recorded as patched can carry a second, older runtime. SI-2 also has no faster tier for a platform-independent exploit that needs no offsets.

NIST-800-53-CM-7.gap: The control that actually closes this — removing the browser Java plugin — sits below CM-7's evidence level. A plugin registered by an approved runtime into an approved browser is neither an installed program nor a network service, so the baseline never reaches it.

NIS2-Art21-patch-management.gap: For the 5.0 and 1.4.2 lines on Windows and Linux the fix existed only on the paid Java for Business track, the free Java SE releases being Solaris-Component-Use-Only against already-EOSL lines. The article has no leg that forces buying the entitlement or retiring the runtime, so compliance with the update obligation and continued exposure are simultaneously true.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: B4 evidence is patch currency against a supported version, which for two of the three affected lines existed on Windows and Linux only inside a paid Java for Business entitlement, and B4 does not frame the browser as an execution surface for untrusted code, which is the question that mattered.

AU-Essential-8-App-Hardening.gap: Blocking Java from the internet in browsers is explicitly in scope, which makes this the closest fit in the set — but the control is markable from a policy statement, and an application-bundled JRE that re-registers its plugin on upgrade silently restores the path.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: No tier for exploit maturity. A base-score-driven queue treats this like any other 9.8, when a deterministic cross-platform applet exploit with a Metasploit module since 2010 and EPSS 0.96319 (99.876th percentile) calls for plugin removal today rather than scheduling.

ISO-27001-2022-A.5.7.gap: Threat-intelligence intake keyed to advisory feeds sees this once, on 2010-04-05. The operationally decisive events — adoption into browser exploit kits, then the 2022-05-25 KEV listing — arrive through different channels that an A.5.7 programme built on vendor advisories does not subscribe to.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Oracle Java SE and Java for Business are the product identity, and this entry is the one in the batch where the control's 'documented compensating controls' branch carries part of the estate on its own: Oracle's March 2010 CPU fixed the 5.0 and 1.4.2 lines on the free Java SE track for Solaris Component Use Only, putting the Windows and Linux fix for those lines behind a paid Java for Business entitlement, so a host on 5.0 Update 23 without that contract cannot deploy a patch inside any SLA and is closed by removing the browser plugin instead. CISA allowed 21 days (added 2022-05-25, due 2022-06-15) on a flaw disclosed 2010-04-05 with a Metasploit module, Exploit-DB 16297, a Microsoft-tracked in-the-wild family, and EPSS 0.96319 at the 99.876th percentile.

new_control_requirements.name: MITIGATION-ACTIVE-PATCH-PENDING-VERDICT-CLASS
new_control_requirements.description: Compliance verdicts must distinguish three states: (a) binary patch deployed (vulnerability eliminated), (b) vendor-mitigation rule active, no binary patch (residual risk: any defect in the mitigation rule reopens the vulnerability), (c) no mitigation, no patch (full exposure). Audit reports must surface (b) as a distinct compensating-control state with an associated time-bound action item, not as a 'patched per SLA' outcome.
new_control_requirements.evidence: A workstation whose browser Java plugin is disabled but whose JRE is still 6 Update 18 is in state (b): the privilege-check defect is untouched and returns the moment a vendor application re-registers the plugin at upgrade, or a user restores it to reach a legacy internal applet. Because the Windows and Linux fix for the 5.0 and 1.4.2 lines shipped only on the paid Java for Business track, a large share of the affected population could not leave state (b) by patching on the free track at all, and recording those hosts as 'patched per SLA' is what allowed the flaw to remain the highest-volume Java exploit in browser kits years after 2010-04-05.

new_control_requirements.name: CVE-REGRESSION-WATCHER
new_control_requirements.description: Threat-intake pipelines must surface PoC announcements that reference historical CVE IDs (CVE-YYYY-NNN where YYYY <= current_year - 2) as candidate silent-regression cases. The historical-CVE-in-PoC-text class would have caught MiniPlasma's re-regression at T+0 — the original CVE-2020-17103 is cited in every news writeup but no advisory feed surfaces 'CVE-2020 references appearing in 2026 PoCs'.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2010-0840 is the historical-CVE-in-current-tooling case exactly: disclosed 2010-04-05, then repeatedly named in exploit-kit composition reporting and in Microsoft's Exploit:Java/CVE-2010-0840 detection family long after every advisory feed had moved on, and finally KEV-listed on 2022-05-25 — twelve years after the fix. An intake rule keyed on historical CVE identifiers appearing in current exploit tooling and detection-family names is what turns EPSS 0.96319 at the 99.876th percentile into an action item before a regulator's clock does.

CVE-2010-1297.name: Adobe Flash Player Memory Corruption Vulnerability (CVE-2010-1297)

attack_vector.description: Malformed use of the AVM2 newfunction instruction inside a DoABC tag leaves the ActionScript virtual machine working with an invalid pointer; a prior heap spray decides what that pointer reaches and turns the fault into execution. The same runtime ships as authplay.dll inside Reader and Acrobat, so the payload works as a web page or as an SWF inside a PDF.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none — PR:N in effect; the attacker needs no account, only that the target renders their SWF. Code runs with the rights of the user running the browser or the PDF reader.
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L; the trigger is deterministic and the delivery is a page visit or an opened document. The version-sensitive part is the payload stage: the public module's DEP bypass uses a hardcoded syscall number and is unreliable across Windows versions.
attack_vector.ai_factor: None. Discovery is attributed to no one — an attacker-found zero-day surfaced from June 2010 samples, with the Metasploit module recording discovery as unknown. No research arm, AI-branded or otherwise, is credited.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Removing Flash Player from browsers and, separately, deleting or renaming authplay.dll under every Reader and Acrobat install so PDFs stop rendering SWF at all. The second half is the one estates skipped, and it is the half that covers the delivery path the public exploit actually used.
prevention.framework_requiring_it: CISA BOD 22-01 (KEV remediation, added 2022-06-08, due 2022-06-22; required action: the impacted product is end-of-life and should be disconnected if still in use)
prevention.adequacy: Complete against this path and durable — it is the same action Flash's 2020 end-of-life eventually forced anyway. Its limit is enumeration: authplay.dll lives inside a product the inventory records as 'Adobe Reader', so finding every copy is an inventory problem before it is a configuration one.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Alerting on authplay.dll being loaded by a Reader or Acrobat process, and on Reader or plugin-container processes becoming the parent of any process. Both are cheap, and the first doubles as an exposure sweep because it identifies which installs still carry the runtime.
detection.adequacy: Content inspection is the weak leg here: the trigger is ordinary ActionScript bytecode with an unusual instruction usage, not a malformed file structure, so a gateway that validates SWF and PDF structure sees nothing wrong. The process-level signals fire only after execution has already occurred.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treating a host that rendered hostile SWF during the window as having run attacker code as the logged-on user — credential rotation and rebuild — and sweeping the whole estate for embedded Flash runtimes rather than closing on the Flash Player version alone.
response.adequacy: The sweep is the part that has lasting value. Closing the incident on 'Flash Player updated' is the specific mistake this CVE punishes, because the copy inside Reader is on a different update track and is untouched by it.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: Remediation is tracked per installed product, and the vulnerable code on most affected hosts is a DLL inside Reader rather than an installed product. Evidence that Flash Player was removed is genuine and leaves the defect reachable. SI-2 also has no branch for an end-of-life product whose correct disposition is removal.

NIST-800-53-SR-3.gap: No bill of materials exists for a runtime the vendor embedded inside its own other product, so nothing in an SR-3 assessment connects a Flash advisory to the PDF estate. Reader is one line in the inventory and carries two independently-versioned remediation obligations.

NIST-800-53-CM-7.gap: The action that closes the PDF path — removing authplay.dll — is a change to a file inside an approved application, which is below the level CM-7 baselines enumerate. A complete attestation coexists with every Reader install rendering attacker-supplied SWF.

NIS2-Art21-patch-management.gap: Applying the 2010 update satisfies the wording indefinitely. For a product Adobe ended in 2020 and CISA says to disconnect, the update leg gives the wrong answer and Article 21 supplies no retirement leg to correct it.

NIS2-Art21-supply-chain.gap: Supplier-level assurance for Adobe is fully achievable and says nothing about a second runtime embedded inside an Adobe product. The obligation has no component granularity, which is the granularity this defect is at.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: Patch-currency evidence is meaningless for an end-of-life product where no current version exists, and B4 does not descend to component level, so the authplay.dll copy inside Reader never appears in the assessment.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: Flash Player is explicitly named in scope and the control's unit is the application, so removing Flash Player marks it compliant while Reader and Acrobat keep their own copy of the same runtime on a separate track.

AU-Essential-8-App-Hardening.gap: Blocking Flash in browsers and hardening PDF readers are assessed as separate items, and closing only the browser half leaves the PDF-delivered SWF path open. The specific action — removing authplay.dll — is not in the control's evidence vocabulary.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: A.8.8 does not prompt the cross-product evaluation this needs — whether an advisory for Flash Player implies exposure in Reader — and base-score ranking under-prioritises a flaw whose public exploit code (Exploit-DB 16614 and 16687) arrived at the same time as the in-the-wild attacks, at EPSS 0.82365 and the 99.632nd percentile.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Adobe Flash Player, Adobe AIR and the authplay.dll runtime inside Adobe Reader and Acrobat are the identity here, and this is the KEV entry whose required action is not 'apply updates per vendor instructions' but that the product is end-of-life and should be disconnected — so the compensating-control branch of this control is the operative one. CISA gave 14 days (added 2022-06-08, due 2022-06-22) on a flaw exploited in the wild in June 2010 with public exploit code available from the same moment per CERT/CC VU#486225, at EPSS 0.82365 and the 99.632nd percentile. Deleting or renaming authplay.dll is deployable inside the SLA window; a Reader upgrade across an unsupported product line is not.

new_control_requirements.name: TIER-3-DEPENDENCY-INVENTORY
new_control_requirements.description: Supply chain inventory must extend to tier-3 dependencies (dependencies of dependencies of direct dependencies). SBOM coverage for libsystemd-class transitive dependencies cannot be omitted under SR-3.
new_control_requirements.evidence: This CVE is the desktop-software instance of exactly that gap: the AVM2 runtime is a component inside Adobe Reader and Acrobat, shipped as authplay.dll on its own version track, and CERT/CC additionally placed an affected Flash runtime inside Photoshop CS3, Photoshop Lightroom, Freehand MX and Fireworks. An inventory that records 'Adobe Reader 9.3.2' and stops there cannot answer whether the estate is exposed to a Flash Player advisory, which is why removing Flash Player from browsers was widely taken as remediation and was not. The requirement this control states — inventory to the embedded-component level, not the installed-product level — is what turns a Flash advisory into an actionable list of Reader, Acrobat, Photoshop and Fireworks installs.

new_control_requirements.name: MITIGATION-ACTIVE-PATCH-PENDING-VERDICT-CLASS
new_control_requirements.description: Compliance verdicts must distinguish three states: (a) binary patch deployed (vulnerability eliminated), (b) vendor-mitigation rule active, no binary patch (residual risk: any defect in the mitigation rule reopens the vulnerability), (c) no mitigation, no patch (full exposure). Audit reports must surface (b) as a distinct compensating-control state with an associated time-bound action item, not as a 'patched per SLA' outcome.
new_control_requirements.evidence: A Reader or Acrobat install with authplay.dll deleted is in state (b): the AVM2 defect is untouched and the mitigation is a file rename that a product repair, a reinstall or an image restore silently undoes. Because Flash Player itself is end-of-life with no supported build to reach, a large part of this population can never reach state (a) at all and must be tracked as compensating-control-with-a-removal-deadline. Recording those hosts as 'patched per SLA' is how a June 2010 flaw with public exploit code stayed in service long enough to need a 2022-06-08 KEV listing.

CVE-2010-1428.name: Red Hat JBoss Information Disclosure Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: The web-console deployment descriptor scopes its role check to the GET and POST verbs it enumerates, so any other verb reaches the default GET handler unauthenticated. That returns ServerInfo.jsp with JVM, OS and deployment detail, and exposes /web-console/Invoker — the MBean invocation endpoint that JexBoss treats as one of four interchangeable ways into a JBoss server.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none — PR:N; network reachability to the console path is the whole requirement, and no JBoss identity is presented or checked at any point.
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L; a single request with a non-standard verb. No timing, no memory layout, no information leak needed first. The binding constraint is reachability, which internet-wide scanning removes.
attack_vector.ai_factor: None. Human analysis of JBossAS deployment descriptors published by Minded Security (Giorgio Fedon) on 2010-04-30, with acknowledgement to Christian Papathanasiou of Trustwave SpiderLabs. No automated discovery and no AI-branded research arm.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Undeploying the web-console outright on instances that do not use it — the cheapest and most complete action — or removing the <http-method> elements from its security-constraint so the deny applies to every verb, combined with restricting the path to a management segment.
prevention.adequacy: Undeployment is complete; the descriptor edit is complete for this path but has to survive a console redeploy, which restores the shipped file. Neither helps on an instance nobody knows exists, which was the actual failure mode in the 2016 campaign — the defect was fixable from April 2010 and the exposed servers were ones their owners had lost track of.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Alerting on any request to /web-console with a method other than GET or POST, and on file appearances under the JBoss deploy/ directory outside a change window. The second catches the escalation even when the disclosure request itself was not logged.
detection.adequacy: The verb rule depends on the web tier recording the request method and shipping logs off the host — and the endpoint this bypass exposes leads to code execution on the host doing the logging. The deploy-directory rule survives that because a separate integrity monitor observes it.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treating a JBoss instance exposed during the window as compromised rather than patchable: compare the deploy directory against a known-good manifest, rebuild, and rotate every credential the application held — datasource passwords, keystore material, service accounts — before restoring service.
response.adequacy: The ransomware history makes this non-optional and the erratum record hides it. RHSA-2010:0376 closes the verb gap and removes nothing already deployed through the Invoker endpoint; a WAR dropped before the fix survives the upgrade and keeps serving.

NIST-800-53-AC-3.gap: The console declares a role requirement and AC-3 evidence reflects that truthfully — for GET and POST only. AC-3 has no concept of a method-scoped access decision, so the attestation and an unauthenticated ServerInfo.jsp response are simultaneously accurate.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: The erratum shipped in April 2010; the exposed servers in 2016 were ones absent from the asset register. SI-2 measures remediation coverage across a known inventory, and an embedded JBossAS is not in it.

NIST-800-53-SC-7.gap: Publishing the application listener is a documented SC-7 decision that publishes /web-console with it. SC-7 is not assessed per URI path, which is where this exposure lives, and JexBoss selects targets by scanning for exactly these paths.

NIS2-Art21-patch-management.gap: Applying the erratum satisfies the obligation and covers neither community JBoss AS 4.0.x, which never received one, nor an embedded JBossAS the entity does not know it runs.

NIS2-Art21-network-security.gap: Segment-level measures legitimately cover a published web application. The obligation never prompts the finer action — restricting or undeploying an administrative path on a shared listener — which is the cheapest complete fix available here.

UK-CAF-B2.gap: B2 inspects the identity and role model guarding privileged interfaces. Here no identity is presented and none is checked, so the assessment examines a mechanism the exploit bypasses rather than abuses.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: The control assumes an enumerated application with an available vendor patch; community JBoss AS 4.0.x has neither, and the descriptor edit that fixes it is not a patch in the control's own terms.

ISO-27001-2022-A.5.15.gap: The deployment descriptor is a complete documented access-control rule. A.5.15 has no test separating a stated rule from its enforcement, and the enforcement here is verb-scoped.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: Ranking by the 7.5 base score classifies this as disclosure, when the same bypass exposes /web-console/Invoker — an invocation surface, with a Metasploit scanner module, a live JexBoss vector, EPSS 0.62308 (99.109th percentile) and a KEV ransomware flag behind it.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: JBoss EAP and the products embedding the same JBossAS web-console are the identity, and the compensating-control branch is load-bearing because community JBoss AS 4.0.x has no erratum to install — undeploying the console or editing its security-constraint is the only route to closure there, and both fit inside the SLA window where an EAP upgrade does not. CISA allowed 21 days (added 2022-05-25, due 2022-06-15) on a flaw with an April 2010 erratum (RHSA-2010:0376 / RHSA-2010:0379), knownRansomwareCampaignUse Known, and EPSS 0.62308 at the 99.109th percentile; the SamSam operators reached internet-facing instances six years after the fix shipped.

new_control_requirements.name: CONFIGURATION-SIDE-LIVE-PATCH-INVENTORY
new_control_requirements.description: For any web-fabric vulnerability with a configuration-side mitigation path: that path must be inventoried, tested, and deployable independent of the vendor-patch path. Operators cannot wait for nginx 1.30.1+ if a named-capture refactor mitigates immediately.
new_control_requirements.evidence: The whole remedy for this JBoss defect is configuration: undeploy /web-console where it is unused, or remove the <http-method> elements from its security-constraint so deny-all covers every verb, which is Red Hat's own guidance in solution 30744 and the only remedy available for community JBoss AS 4.0.x where RHSA-2010:0376 does not apply. Holding that artefact in configuration management — tested, and reapplied after any console redeploy restores the shipped descriptor — is what closes the path without an EAP upgrade window, and it is the only measure that would have covered the embedded JBossAS instances JexBoss found in 2016.

attack_vector.description: A crafted PowerPoint 95 document is opened in PowerPoint 2002 or 2003. The legacy converter that handles that format — PP7X32.DLL in the Office10\Xlators directory on PowerPoint 2002 — parses it past a fixed-size buffer, and execution lands with the opening user's rights. Delivery is a mail attachment or a link to a hosted file; the format, not the transport, is the distinguishing feature.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none — PR:N; the attacker needs no account. Impact is bounded by the opening user's rights, and Microsoft notes explicitly that users with fewer rights are less affected.
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L for the parse. The binding constraints are UI:R and format: the user must open the file, and on PowerPoint 2003 SP3 the file-block policy blocks PowerPoint 95 documents by default, which is why Microsoft rated the same flaw Moderate there and Important on PowerPoint 2002.
attack_vector.ai_factor: None. Reported by Alin Rad Pop of Secunia Research through coordinated disclosure — manual file-format analysis by a named researcher at an outside firm, with no tooling pipeline described and no AI-branded research arm involved.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Blocking the PowerPoint 95 format estate-wide through the Office file-block policy, which is the default on PowerPoint 2003 SP3 and is not on PowerPoint 2002, plus the MS10-088 update. On PowerPoint 2002 hosts that could not take the update immediately, denying access to PP7X32.DLL with the cacls/icacls commands Microsoft published.
prevention.adequacy: Format blocking is complete against this path and costs nothing operationally, because no current business process authors PowerPoint 95 files. Its weakness is durability: it is a policy setting and an ACL, both restorable by an Office repair, a reinstall, or an administrator relaxing the block for one legacy file and never re-tightening it.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Flagging .ppt attachments whose content is the PowerPoint 95 format at the mail gateway, and alerting on POWERPNT.EXE as the parent of any process. The format check is nearly free and has an extremely low false-positive rate against modern mail flow.
detection.adequacy: There is no public exploit code and therefore no community signature set to draw on, so content detection here has to be structural — the legacy format itself is the anomaly — rather than signature-based. Microsoft's own Exploit:Win32/CVE-2010-2572.A coverage exists but is vendor-internal telemetry, not something an operator can implement from.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treating a workstation that opened a PowerPoint 95 attachment during the exposure window as having potentially run attacker code as the logged-on user — rotate that user's credentials and rebuild — rather than closing on the KB installation record.
response.adequacy: The update record is what an audit asks for and it removes nothing already dropped. It is also conditional on a restart: MS10-088 states the update requires one when the files it replaces are in use, so a host that installed the KB with PowerPoint open and deferred the restart is recorded as patched and is not.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: The update has existed since 2010-11-09, so an assessment on a host running PowerPoint 2002 finds it applied and no further vendor artefact — while the whole Office release has been out of support for years. SI-2 also does not cover standalone PowerPoint installs and unused suite components the update mechanism services independently.

NIST-800-53-CM-7.gap: The vulnerable code is a converter for a 1995 file format that no current process produces — the archetypal unnecessary function. CM-7 baselines stop at 'Office: approved' and never reach which format converters may run, which is why Microsoft had to publish the fix as a manual cacls command.

NIS2-Art21-patch-management.gap: Applying KB2413272 satisfies the wording permanently, on an Office release that is out of support and receives no fixes for anything found since. The obligation has no leg that prompts the migration decision.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: Patch-currency evidence is meaningless for Office XP and Office 2003, and B4 does not descend to the file-format level — so the assessment never asks whether PowerPoint 95 documents can be opened, which is the setting that separates Microsoft's Important and Moderate ratings for this same flaw.

AU-Essential-8-App-Hardening.gap: Office hardening evidence centres on macros, ActiveX and OLE. Legacy-format blocking — the mitigating factor Microsoft credits for the lower rating on PowerPoint 2003 SP3 — is not what an assessor collects, so a thoroughly macro-hardened estate can still open a crafted PowerPoint 95 attachment straight into the vulnerable converter.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: Base-score ranking schedules a 7.8 rather than prompting the cheap evaluation that closes the path outright — whether the legacy format is blocked by policy. EPSS 0.62598 at the 99.117th percentile is unusually high for a client-side bug with no public exploit code, which reflects the format's persistence in mail flow rather than exploit availability.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.9.gap: Both things that decide exposure — the KB 938810 file-block policy and the ACL on PP7X32.DLL — are configuration items outside a standard desktop baseline, so there is nothing for A.8.9 to review, and their reversal by an Office repair or reinstall produces no drift event that either A.8.9 or the patch record would surface.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Microsoft PowerPoint 2002 SP3 and 2003 SP3 are the identity, and this is a case where the compensating-control branch is faster and more durable than the binary patch: MS10-088 (KB2413272 / KB2413304) requires a restart wherever the replaced files are in use, while the Office file-block policy for PowerPoint 95 files and the PP7X32.DLL ACL are group-policy-and-script deployable inside the SLA window. CISA gave 14 days (added 2022-06-08, due 2022-06-22) on a flaw patched 2010-11-09 whose exploitation began after the bulletin, with Microsoft tracking in-the-wild samples as Exploit:Win32/CVE-2010-2572.A and EPSS at 0.62598 (99.117th percentile).

new_control_requirements.name: MITIGATION-ACTIVE-PATCH-PENDING-VERDICT-CLASS
new_control_requirements.description: Compliance verdicts must distinguish three states: (a) binary patch deployed (vulnerability eliminated), (b) vendor-mitigation rule active, no binary patch (residual risk: any defect in the mitigation rule reopens the vulnerability), (c) no mitigation, no patch (full exposure). Audit reports must surface (b) as a distinct compensating-control state with an associated time-bound action item, not as a 'patched per SLA' outcome.
new_control_requirements.evidence: A PowerPoint 2003 SP3 host protected only by the KB 938810 file-block default, or a PowerPoint 2002 host protected only by the cacls deny on PP7X32.DLL, is in state (b): the missing bound in the legacy parser is untouched and the mitigation is a policy setting or a file ACL that an Office repair, a reinstall, or one administrator relaxing the block for a legacy deck reverses without any event the patch record shows. Microsoft's own severity split for this CVE — Important on PowerPoint 2002, Moderate on 2003 SP3 — is a vendor rating that depends entirely on a mitigation being active, which is exactly the state this control requires to be surfaced separately rather than recorded as patched.

CVE-2010-2883.name: Adobe Acrobat and Reader Stack-Based Buffer Overflow Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: A PDF embeds a TrueType font whose SING table uniqueName field is longer than the fixed-size stack buffer CoolType.dll copies it into. Rendering the document overwrites the stack frame; the public chain then loads icucnv36.dll via an AcroForm and returns through its gadgets to defeat DEP. Delivery is an emailed or downloaded PDF, and no scripting is required to reach the parser.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none in the attacker's hands — the CVSS PR:L reflects that the document is opened by an already-logged-on user, not that the attacker holds an account. Code runs with that user's rights.
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L to trigger. The engineering cost sits in the DEP bypass, which depends on a specific non-relocated module being loaded, so the public chain is tied to particular Reader builds (tested on 8.2.4 and 9.3.4).
attack_vector.ai_factor: None. Surfaced from an in-the-wild sample in September 2010, with Adobe crediting Mila Parkour of contagiodump.blogspot.com for working with them on it. The original finder is unknown, and no research arm — AI-branded or otherwise — is credited with discovery.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Rendering untrusted PDFs in an isolated viewer, or stripping and blocking PDFs carrying embedded fonts at the mail gateway, during the window between APSA10-02 on 2010-09-08 and the 9.4 / 8.2.5 builds — then enumerating every Reader and Acrobat track and confirming each reached the fixed build.
prevention.adequacy: Containment worked where detection could not, because the artefact is structurally valid. Neither measure was a supported Adobe workaround, so operators had to devise them, and the reflexive Reader control of the period — disabling Acrobat JavaScript — was useless here since the font path is reached by rendering.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Alerting on AcroRd32.exe or Acrobat.exe as the parent of any process, on icucnv36.dll loading into a Reader process, and on Reader crashes whose faulting module is CoolType.dll. The icucnv36.dll signal is unusually specific because the public chain has to force that load.
detection.adequacy: All three fire at or after execution, so they bound dwell time rather than prevent compromise. Content inspection is the weak leg: a valid PDF containing a valid TrueType font with a long string field offers nothing structural to reject, which is why signature-based anti-malware provided no cover during the September 2010 window.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treating any workstation that opened a suspect PDF during the exposure window as having run attacker code as the logged-on user — credential rotation and rebuild — and sweeping every Acrobat and Reader install on the estate rather than closing on the one the inventory records.
response.adequacy: The multi-track sweep is the part with lasting value, because Reader and Acrobat update independently and per-user installs do not update at all. Closing on the managed Reader package's version is the specific mistake this product pair punishes.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: There is no live vendor stream for Reader/Acrobat 8.x and 9.x, so an assessment on a host running 9.3.4 finds nothing to apply and closes clean; per-user installs are outside the inventory the control measures against entirely.

NIST-800-53-SI-3.gap: The artefact is a valid PDF containing a valid TrueType font with a long field, and the exploitation stage is a ROP chain from a signed Adobe module. Signature-based protection had nothing to key on, so complete SI-3 coverage and successful exploitation were simultaneously true through September 2010.

NIST-800-53-CM-7.gap: The measures that helped — blocking embedded-font PDFs at the gateway, isolating the renderer for untrusted documents — sit below the level CM-7 baselines enumerate. Worse, the hardening step CM-7 evidence usually does capture for Reader, disabling Acrobat JavaScript, does not touch this path at all.

NIS2-Art21-patch-management.gap: Applying the update lands on 9.4 or 8.2.5, both out of support. The obligation is also silent on the September 2010 window between APSA10-02 and a fix — exactly when the flaw was being used — because an update-only obligation has nothing to require when no update exists.

NIS2-Art21-vulnerability-handling.gap: Having a defined handling process satisfies the obligation without forcing the distinction that matters: whether a host is fixed in binary or is running under a gateway or isolation control that a policy change reverses. A pre-patch mitigation recorded as remediation and never revisited after 9.4 shipped is a compliant process over an unremediated estate.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: Evidence is patch currency against an unsupported build, and the asset register does not descend to a font engine shared by two products on separate update tracks — which is the granularity that decides whether a workstation is exposed.

AU-Essential-8-App-Hardening.gap: PDF-reader hardening is in scope and the actions assessors collect — disabling JavaScript, blocking advertisements — are inert against a defect reached by rendering. The attestation is fully evidenced and the path is untouched.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.7.gap: Deployed anti-malware with current definitions satisfies A.8.7 and delivered nothing during the exposure window against a structurally valid document. The control frames malware protection as detection and offers no containment alternative, which was the only measure that worked here.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: No tier for exploit maturity: the 7.3 base score is the lowest of the three Adobe entries here, while this one has had a Metasploit module and Exploit-DB 16619 since autumn 2010 and sits at EPSS 0.82485, the 99.635th percentile.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Adobe Reader and Acrobat 8.x/9.x are the identity, and the flaw's own history is the argument for the compensating-control branch: Adobe published APSA10-02 on 2010-09-08 reporting active exploitation with no fix available, so for that window the only route to closure was gateway blocking or isolated rendering rather than a patch. Today the same branch is needed for the opposite reason — the fixed builds 9.4 and 8.2.5 are unsupported, so 'apply the vendor update' does not produce a remediated host. CISA allowed 14 days (added 2022-06-08, due 2022-06-22) on a flaw with a Metasploit module and Exploit-DB 16619 since 2010 and EPSS 0.82485 at the 99.635th percentile.

new_control_requirements.name: MITIGATION-ACTIVE-PATCH-PENDING-VERDICT-CLASS
new_control_requirements.description: Compliance verdicts must distinguish three states: (a) binary patch deployed (vulnerability eliminated), (b) vendor-mitigation rule active, no binary patch (residual risk: any defect in the mitigation rule reopens the vulnerability), (c) no mitigation, no patch (full exposure). Audit reports must surface (b) as a distinct compensating-control state with an associated time-bound action item, not as a 'patched per SLA' outcome.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Every Reader and Acrobat host during the 2010-09-08 window was in state (b) at best — protected, if at all, by a gateway rule stripping embedded-font PDFs or by isolated rendering, with the missing bound in CoolType.dll untouched. The specific trap this control exists for is visible on this CVE: an estate that recorded 'Acrobat JavaScript disabled' as its Reader mitigation was in state (c) and believed it was in state (b), because that setting does not reach a parser invoked by rendering. Time-bounding state (b) with an action item is what forces the follow-through to 9.4 or 8.2.5 and then off the unsupported line entirely.

attack_vector.description: A spreadsheet arrives by mail with a Flash object embedded in it. Opening it hands attacker-controlled ActionScript to the AVM2 verifier, which lets through bytecode whose JIT output reads and executes uninitialized memory the attacker has already sprayed. Code runs as the user. The same runtime is reachable from a web page through the plugin, from an AIR application, and from a PDF through authplay.dll.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none - PR:N; the attacker needs no account and no foothold, only that the target open the document or load the page
attack_vector.complexity: low - AC:L in the CVSS vector, but reliability is the real constraint: the exploit depends on a heap spray landing where the uninitialized reference points, and DEP defeats the public module
attack_vector.ai_factor: None. This was found by whoever was on the receiving end of the March 2011 attacks; no researcher credit resolved from a primary source and no automated-discovery claim exists. 2011 predates the AI-assisted discovery tooling that shows up in later entries.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Removing the Flash runtime from hosts with no business need for it - all three instances: the browser plugin, the AIR runtime, and authplay.dll inside Adobe Reader and Acrobat. For hosts that needed Flash, opening mailed Office documents in an isolated, reduced-privilege view rather than the full parsing path.
prevention.adequacy: Removal is complete but was politically hard in 2011 and is trivial now; the honest limit is scope. Every plugin-focused hardening standard of the era, Essential Eight user application hardening included, would have left the Reader and AIR copies running. BOD 22-01 arrives eleven years after the fact and only tells federal agencies to disconnect a product that should already be gone.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Alerting on Office and PDF processes spawning children or making outbound connections, and treating repeated Flash-container or AcroRd32 access-violation crashes as a hunt trigger rather than a support ticket.
detection.adequacy: Both are post-exploitation signals: they fire after code is already running as the user. The pre-execution signal - an embedded SWF stream in a mailed spreadsheet - is cheap to look for at the mail gateway and was not standard practice in 2011.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treating any host that opened one of these documents as compromised rather than as patched, rotating the credentials that were live in that user session, and inventorying every Flash-bearing product rather than only browsers.
response.adequacy: Sound but late. The exploit runs at user privilege, so the blast radius is whatever that user could reach; a patch record closes the vulnerability ticket without answering that question.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: Nominally met by any organisation that installed Flash Player 10.2.153.1 in March 2011, and unanswerable after the 2020-12-31 end of life, when there is no update to install and the control still reports clean.

NIST-800-53-CM-7.gap: Least functionality would have removed the exposure, but the standard evidence - a browser plugin inventory - misses the same runtime inside Adobe Reader/Acrobat as authplay.dll and inside AIR applications.

NIS2-Art21-patch-management.gap: The obligation presumes an available patch. For a seven-day zero-day window and then a permanently end-of-life product, only removal discharges it, which the control text does not say.

EU-CRA-Art13.gap: Flash Player left the market before CRA manufacturer duties applied, so there is no support period, no coordinated vulnerability handling and no upstream to escalate to - the operator holds all of the residual risk.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: Documented vulnerability management and current builds were both true during the March 2011 attack window; B4 evidence does not test whether the system can be made to parse attacker-supplied active content at all.

AU-Essential-8-App-Hardening.gap: The mitigation names Flash in web browsers. The observed delivery was a spreadsheet, and the runtime also ships inside Adobe Reader and Acrobat, so browser-scoped hardening leaves two live paths.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: Maturity is measured from patch availability, so the zero-day window scores green, and an end-of-life product with no patch stream scores green or not-applicable while still running.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: Identification works on the Flash version string but not on the embedded copy inside Reader and Acrobat, and the action the control contemplates - patching - does not exist for this product any more.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.7.gap: Anti-malware deployment is the usual compensating evidence and is defeated by a structural exploit in a document whose payload changes per campaign.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Adobe Flash Player CVE-2011-0609 is the case where the SLA clock has to accept a compensating control rather than a patch. Adobe disclosed active attacks on 2011-03-14 and shipped 10.2.153.1, AIR 2.6 and Reader/Acrobat 9.4.3 only in the week of 2011-03-21; CISA then listed it on 2022-06-08 with a 2022-06-22 due date and a required action of disconnection, not update. The control's own wording - patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls - is what makes it usable in both windows, where a patch-only SLA has nothing to measure. EPSS still puts this at 0.66821 (99.227th percentile) on 2026-08-13, fifteen years after the fix, because residual Flash installs remain a live target.

new_control_requirements.name: EOL-ASSET-DECOMMISSION
new_control_requirements.description: This entry is the case the control exists for, and both halves are on record. patch_available is true — a fixed build carrying this JavaScriptCore fix exists — and the vector itself states that the impacted product could be end-of-life and/or end-of-service and that users should discontinue product utilization. Those facts together define the requirement: on a unit whose hardware can still take an Apple security update, reaching the fixed build is an interim state; on a unit that can no longer take one, the terminal state is removal or replacement, because that device is exposed not only to this code-execution flaw but to everything found in that engine since its last build. Scope to what the packet names — macOS, iOS, tvOS, Safari and watchOS — and inventory those. The packet ties the CWE-94 sink to JavaScriptCore in those products and gives no mapping into other vendors' browsers or other software that embeds a web engine, so treating every renderer in the estate as an instance of this CVE manufactures findings and replacement work against software no evidence implicates.
