In operational terms: enumerate every macOS, iOS, tvOS, watchOS and Safari install that renders untrusted web content, record for each whether its hardware can still receive a build carrying the fix, put those on the interim clock against the 2025-10-20 KEV listing, and put the rest on a dated replacement schedule — a risk acceptance with no removal date leaves a KEV-listed flaw with a public PoC and confirmed exploitation in service indefinitely. Precondition on the interim half: live_patch_available is false and the vendor patch typically requires a service restart or system reboot per the KEV requiredAction, so a device that downloaded the update but has not restarted still runs the vulnerable code and is not remediated. And because exploitation is confirmed and delivery is attacker-controlled web content, a device that rendered untrusted content while exposed belongs on the incident path rather than being closed on the patch record.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Applied here to Adobe Flash Player, Adobe AIR and the authplay.dll copy inside Adobe Reader and Acrobat. Both halves the control describes are present: fixed builds exist (Flash Player 10.2.153.1, AIR 2.6, Reader/Acrobat 9.4.3, 2011-03-21) and the product line is dead - Adobe stopped supporting Flash Player on 2020-12-31, blocked Flash content in the player on 2021-01-12, and tells users to uninstall. CISA's KEV entry of 2022-06-08 states the required action as disconnection rather than update. So reaching a patched Flash build is not an end state for any of the three product families; enumerating every install that can render Flash - browsers, AIR applications, and Reader/Acrobat 9.x and 10.0.x - and putting each on a dated removal schedule is. A risk acceptance with no removal date leaves a KEV-listed flaw with public Metasploit and Exploit-DB code (EDB-17027) in service indefinitely, and the runtime does not restart-and-remediate: an updated host that never closed its browser or PDF reader is still executing the old code.

CVE-2011-2462.name: Adobe Reader and Acrobat Universal 3D Memory Corruption Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: A PDF carrying crafted Universal 3D data corrupts memory inside Reader's and Acrobat's 3D component; JavaScript in the same document sprays the heap so the corrupted pointer lands in attacker data, and code runs as the user who opened the file. Delivery is ordinary - mail attachment or download - and the target does nothing unusual.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none - PR:N; no account, no foothold, no network position, only that someone opens the document
attack_vector.complexity: low - AC:L; 3D rendering is on by default in the affected builds and the spray ships inside the same file, so no separate info leak or second bug is needed
attack_vector.ai_factor: None. Found by Lockheed Martin's CIRT and the Defense Security Information Exchange in traffic aimed at the defence industrial base and reported to Adobe; no tooling claim, automated or otherwise, appears in the record.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Disabling 3D rendering in Reader and Acrobat estate-wide - the U3D parser is unreachable without it - and inventorying Acrobat separately from Reader so both update tracks reach the fixed build.
prevention.adequacy: Disabling 3D is a complete defence against this specific parser and costs a feature almost nobody in a corporate estate uses; it was available from the 2011-12-06 advisory onwards, weeks before the X line was patched. Its limit is that it is a per-application setting an operator has to push and verify, and it does nothing about the next parser in the same product.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Mail-gateway inspection for PDFs that pair a 3D annotation with document-level JavaScript, and endpoint alerting on Reader or Acrobat spawning children.
detection.adequacy: The document-shape check is a genuine pre-execution signal and cheap; the endpoint signal fires only after code is already running as the user. Neither would have caught a variant that dropped the scripted spray in favour of a different grooming technique.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treating a workstation that opened one of the December 2011 documents as compromised - collecting the PDF, checking for child processes and persistence, rotating that user's credentials - rather than closing the ticket on the 9.4.7 upgrade.
response.adequacy: Correct but reactive, and it depends on knowing which documents were opened, which most estates could not answer in 2011 and many still cannot.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: Counting installed updates against one Adobe package closes the finding while the second product line - Acrobat, or the X line waiting for 2012-01-10 - stays on the vulnerable build.

NIST-800-53-SC-44.gap: A detonation chamber running a patched Reader answers a different question from the one the estate needs answered, and reports clean on a document that would still work on 9.4.6.

NIS2-Art21-patch-management.gap: Satisfied by deploying the December and January updates; silent on the interim window when disabling 3D rendering was the only available action.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: Evidence is about the patch process, not about which parsers untrusted documents can reach, so an estate scores well while every workstation renders arbitrary U3D content.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: Measured from availability per product, so a staggered vendor fix - 9.x on 2011-12-16, X on 2012-01-10 - scores on time in both cases while one line sits unpatched for 25 days.

AU-Essential-8-App-Hardening.gap: The mitigation covers browsers, macros and Flash; the hardening that mattered here, disabling PDF 3D rendering, is not in it.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: Passes on process while unmanaged per-user Acrobat installs, which the inventory never enumerated, stay on 9.4.6.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.7.gap: Signature-based protection against a targeted, structurally-triggered document exploit with a per-campaign payload is the weakest claim in the pack.

new_control_requirements.name: EMBEDDED-MEDIA-PARSER-LIBRARY-INVENTORY-AND-PATCH-PARITY
new_control_requirements.description: The packet names the affected product as Adobe Acrobat and Reader, which on a real estate is never one install: Reader and Acrobat ship as separate products on separate update tracks, and per-user copies land outside managed software distribution. The control here means enumerating every installed Acrobat and Reader copy across those tracks and confirming each reports the fixed build, rather than closing the flaw-remediation ticket when the single inventoried Reader package updates. Scope it to those products: the packet ties the CWE-1321 sink to Acrobat and Reader and provides no mapping from the vulnerable code into other PDF-handling software, so instructing operators to treat every PDF-capable binary in the estate as an instance of this CVE manufactures findings and removal work against renderers no evidence implicates. Widen the inventory only where a verified source identifies another product carrying the same component. The distinguishing test: after the managed update lands, enumerate the Acrobat and Reader installs on the estate and confirm none still report a pre-fix version — an estate that patches the inventoried Reader while a second Acrobat track keeps the old build still opens crafted PDFs into the sink, with a flaw-remediation attestation that reads clean. Precondition: this reaches only copies the inventory can see and the operator can update; an unmanaged per-user install is remediated by removing it, not by recording it as patched. The packet registers no live-patch path, so each copy carries the service restart or system reboot the vendor fix requires, and a copy updated but not restarted is not yet remediated.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Adobe Reader and Acrobat are exactly the split this control describes, and CVE-2011-2462 made the cost visible: Adobe fixed Reader and Acrobat 9.4.7 for Windows on 2011-12-16 but did not ship Reader X and Acrobat X 10.1.2 or the 9.x Linux Reader until 2012-01-10, so an estate that closed the ticket on the December package left its X-line installs exploitable for another 25 days while the vulnerability was under active targeted attack per Adobe's APSA11-04. Public exploit code (Exploit-DB 18366) landed 2012-01-14, four days after the last fix, and EPSS still rates this 0.86563 at the 99.721st percentile on 2026-08-13 because unmanaged Reader and Acrobat copies persist. The parity test is per-product and per-track, not per-package.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: The Adobe Reader and Acrobat U3D flaw shows why this control's mitigation clause carries the weight rather than its patch clause. Adobe's advisory APSA11-04 landed 2011-12-06 with attacks already running; the Windows 9.x fix came 2011-12-16 and the X-line fix 2012-01-10. For those windows the only verified mitigation was disabling 3D rendering, which is a documented compensating control the SLA accepts and a patch-only SLA cannot record. CISA listed the CVE on 2022-06-08 with a 2022-06-22 due date and a required action of applying vendor updates.

CVE-2012-0151.name: Microsoft Windows Authenticode Signature Verification Remote Code Execution Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: Windows verifies a signed executable over less than the whole file. An attacker adds code to a genuinely signed binary in a region the digest does not cover; Windows still reports it as validly signed by the original publisher, and everything downstream - the user, allowlisting, reputation scoring, an updater that trusts the signature - treats it as the vendor's own software.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none - PR:N; the attacker needs no account on the target, only a signed binary to modify and a delivery path
attack_vector.complexity: low - AC:L; deterministic, no race and no memory-corruption reliability problem, though the CVSS UI:R is real: something has to run the file
attack_vector.ai_factor: None. Reported by Robert Zacek and Igor Glucksmann of Avast Software, worked through with Microsoft over several months - manual analysis of how signed binaries are validated, with no automated-discovery claim in the record.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Deploying KB2653956 with the required restart, and pairing publisher-based application control with hash-based rules for the binaries that matter so a valid signature is never the only thing standing between a file and execution.
prevention.adequacy: The update fixes this CVE and nothing more. The class survived it: CVE-2013-3900 revisited the same boundary in 2013, and its stricter check is still shipped disabled by default, so a fully patched modern host is not automatically covered against the variant.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Comparing signed binaries against publisher-published hashes rather than trusting the signature verdict, and treating a signed binary that behaves unlike its publisher's software as a first-class alert.
detection.adequacy: Effective but only where an independent hash source exists, which is a small subset of installed software. Behavioural detection catches the payload rather than the trust failure, so it fires after execution.

response.what_would_have_worked: On finding a tampered signed binary, quarantining every host that received it from the same distribution path and treating the path itself - the update channel, the file share, the software repository - as compromised rather than the single file.
response.adequacy: Right instinct, hard to scope: the attraction of this technique is that the file looks legitimate everywhere it lands, so the population that ran it usually has to be reconstructed from distribution logs rather than from detections.

NIST-800-53-SR-11.gap: Component authenticity delegates to the exact mechanism this CVE breaks: a valid Authenticode result on a file carrying appended attacker content.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: Closed by KB2653956, with no way to record that the successor fix for the same code path is installed but disabled by default.

NIST-800-53-SI-3.gap: Products that reduce inspection for validly signed binaries turn the control into a delivery aid for this specific defect.

NIS2-Art21-supply-chain.gap: Supplier assurance evidenced as 'vendor software is digitally signed' is exactly the assurance the affected Windows builds could not enforce.

NIS2-Art21-vulnerability-handling.gap: Per-CVE closure hides the sequence: April 2012 here, December 2013 for the padding variant, with the current mitigation still opt-in.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: A fully patched fleet evidences secure configuration while the successor hardening value is never set.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: Maturity is measured on update currency and cannot see a shipped-but-disabled verification change.

AU-Essential-8-App-Hardening.gap: Hardening limits what runs after the trust decision; this bug corrupts the trust decision itself.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.7.gap: Signature and reputation tooling both key on the publisher identity the bug preserves intact.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: Complete on patch tracking while the durable exposure is an unset configuration value rather than a missing update.

new_control_requirements.name: INCOMPLETE-PATCH-SEQUENCE-SEVERITY-MULTIPLIER
new_control_requirements.description: Vulnerability-management programs must apply a severity multiplier when a CVE is the Nth in an incomplete-patch sequence on the same primitive (third MOTW bypass, second AMSI bypass, etc.). Framework controls treating each CVE as discrete obscure the structural defect; the Nth CVE in a sequence implies that future bypasses on the same primitive are likely.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Windows Authenticode signature validation is a documented sequence on one primitive, and CVE-2012-0151 is the entry that starts it: MS12-024 on 2012-04-10 fixed digest validation over PE files, and twenty months later CVE-2013-3900 (MS13-098, advisory 2915720) reopened the same boundary through certificate padding, with a fix Microsoft ships disabled by default because enabling it breaks genuine installers. A programme scoring these as two discrete Windows CVEs records both as patched; a programme applying the multiplier records that the estate's signature-trust decisions are structurally unreliable and that the second fix is inert unless EnableCertPaddingCheck is set. EPSS rates CVE-2012-0151 at 0.83534, 99.659th percentile, on 2026-08-13.

new_control_requirements.name: PROTECTION-MECHANISM-FAILURE-CLASS-REGRESSION
new_control_requirements.description: Detonation chambers, EDR rules, and AppLocker/WDAC policies covering protection-mechanism classes (MOTW, SmartScreen, AMSI, ASR, WDAC, Driver Block Rules) must include class-level regression testing executed on every patch deployment, not just one-off bypass-CVE remediation. The test battery for class-X must include all historic class-X bypass primitives — incomplete patches re-introduce risk that one-off testing does not detect.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Authenticode signature validation is the protection-mechanism class here, and every allowlisting and reputation control in a Windows estate is downstream of it. CVE-2012-0151 shows what a one-off test misses: Microsoft recorded no mitigating factors and no workarounds, Avast found the appended-content technique already in legitimate use by vendors avoiding re-signing, and the class returned in CVE-2013-3900 with an opt-in fix. The regression battery this control asks for - present a signed binary with content appended past the digested region, and a padded-certificate variant, against the estate's application-control policy on every patch cycle - is what distinguishes a WDAC or AppLocker policy that actually rejects tampered publisher-signed files from one that is merely deployed.

CVE-2012-0754.name: Adobe Flash Player Memory Corruption Vulnerability (CVE-2012-0754)

attack_vector.description: A Flash object loads an MP4 whose copyright atom carries more data than the parser's buffer, overflowing it; a JavaScript heap spray puts shellcode where the corrupted control flow lands, and code runs as the user. The public exploit delivers it as a web page; the real campaign delivered it as a Word attachment with the Flash object embedded, so the media was fetched by Word rather than by a browser.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none - PR:N; no credentials and no foothold, just a rendered page or an opened document
attack_vector.complexity: high - AC:H; the overflow needs a successful heap spray and target-appropriate offsets, which is why the public module ships per-target variants rather than one path
attack_vector.ai_factor: None. Manual research by Alexander Gavrun, submitted through the Zero Day Initiative, which received it on 2011-10-21 and published ZDI-12-047 on 2012-03-22. ZDI's current TrendAI branding postdates the finding by more than a decade and is not evidence of AI-assisted discovery.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Applying APSB12-03 inside the sixteen days between the fix and the first observed attacks, and blocking Office applications from instantiating Flash objects so the document delivery path did not exist at all.
prevention.adequacy: The patch is complete for this bug and useless for the next one; the object-embedding block is the durable half, because it removes a whole delivery class rather than one defect. Neither was required by anything in 2012 - BOD 22-01 arrives a decade later and, for a product Adobe ended in 2020, its answer is disconnection rather than either.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Alerting on an Office process making an outbound HTTP request for media, and detonating attachments in an environment that fails a document for fetching remote content rather than merely rendering it.
detection.adequacy: The callback is a genuine pre-execution signal and survives payload changes, which signature matching does not. It depends on egress being observable per process - on an estate where all HTTP leaves through one proxy identity, the Word-fetching-media shape is invisible.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treating the recipients of the document as a population rather than the detections as a list: pulling the attachment from mail stores, checking every recipient host for child processes and persistence, and rotating what those users could reach.
response.adequacy: Workable because the delivery was mail, which leaves a recipient list. It says nothing about the browser path, where there is no equivalent record of who loaded the page.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: Compliant monthly patching and a sixteen-day n-day interval put a fully-compliant estate inside the exploitation window.

NIST-800-53-SC-44.gap: Detonation configured for executables and macros treats an embedded object fetching remote media as rendering rather than as a callback worth failing.

NIST-800-53-CM-7.gap: Read as an inventory of installed software rather than as which components an application may load, so Office keeps its ability to host the Flash control.

NIS2-Art21-patch-management.gap: No urgency proportional to observed exploitation; a documented 30-day cycle is compliant and exploitable on the same date.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: Evidences plugin currency but not whether Word may host a Flash object that fetches remote media - the setting that decided the outcome.

AU-Essential-8-App-Hardening.gap: Flash hardening and Office object-embedding controls are separate maturity items, and the campaign used the gap between them.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: The two-week maturity target and the observed sixteen-day n-day interval are the same length, so compliance and exposure coincide.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: The treatment plan records the update and not the delivery-path control that actually held during the gap.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.7.gap: First-seen targeted document, structural exploit, per-campaign payload - the case signature-based protection is worst at.

new_control_requirements.name: DOWNLOAD-PROVENANCE-ENFORCEMENT
new_control_requirements.description: Exploitation here requires the victim to open an attacker-supplied Office document, so on an estate that has not yet reached the fixed build the delivery path is the only enforceable control. Require Mark-of-the-Web on every Office file arriving by mail, web download, or untrusted file share, and require MOTW-tagged documents to open in Protected View — an isolated, reduced-privilege render — instead of the full parsing path that carries the CWE-94 sink at the user's own process privilege. Provenance must survive the container: files extracted from an archive, mounted from an ISO or VHD, or renamed must inherit the tag rather than lose it, and 'Enable Editing' on externally sourced documents must be blocked by policy rather than left to the user. The distinguishing test: mail a MOTW-tagged spreadsheet nested inside a ZIP to a managed workstation, extract it, and confirm the extracted file still opens in Protected View — a user-application-hardening attestation that covers only macro and ActiveX/OLE settings still lets a provenance-stripped document reach the vulnerable parser with full user privileges.
new_control_requirements.evidence: The in-the-wild campaign against Adobe Flash Player CVE-2012-0754, found 2012-03-02, was a Word document ('Iran's Oil and Nuclear Situation.doc') with an embedded Flash object that fetched the malicious MP4 - so the vulnerable Flash MP4 parser was reached through Office, sixteen days after Adobe shipped 10.3.183.15 and 11.1.102.62 on 2012-02-15. Provenance enforcement is the control that covers that interval on an estate that has not yet updated, because a document opened in an isolated reduced-privilege render does not instantiate the embedded object at the user's own privilege. The same enforcement is the durable answer for the residual population: Flash Player has been end-of-life since 2020-12-31, so for any host that still has the runtime there is no fixed build left to reach, only the delivery path to close.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Adobe Flash Player CVE-2012-0754 is the n-day case this SLA is calibrated for. Adobe shipped the fix on 2012-02-15; the malicious-document campaign was found on 2012-03-02 and public Metasploit code followed on 2012-03-08. Sixteen days separated availability from exploitation, so any cadence measured in weeks lost the race while remaining compliant, and a four-hour clock from patch availability is the only one that closes it. CISA listed the CVE on 2022-06-08 with a 2022-06-22 due date; EPSS still rates it 0.9203 at the 99.811th percentile on 2026-08-13.

CVE-2012-0767.name: Adobe Flash Player Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: The victim follows a mailed link. The page loads a crafted SWF, and Flash executes attacker script in another site's origin rather than the attacker's, so the attacker can read and act inside whatever sessions that user already holds - webmail, internal applications, anything cookie-authenticated. Nothing is written to disk and no process is spawned; the damage is entirely within the user's existing authority.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none - PR:N; the attacker holds no credentials, and borrows the victim's
attack_vector.complexity: low - AC:L; no memory corruption, no spray, no target-specific offsets, so it works first time wherever the affected runtime loads
attack_vector.ai_factor: None. Reported by Google to Adobe, per the APSB12-03 acknowledgements - human research by a browser vendor's security team on a runtime it also shipped.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Not running the Flash plugin in browsers that have no business need for it - the only control that covers the pre-patch window, since Adobe records the attacks as already running at release - and then applying APSB12-03 everywhere it was still needed.
prevention.adequacy: Removing Flash is complete and was the only pre-patch defence; the patch itself was available on 2012-02-15 but arrived after exploitation had started. Neither addresses the sessions already acted on, and BOD 22-01's answer - disconnect an end-of-life product - only reaches the residual population a decade later.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Monitoring authenticated applications for state changes that arrive without a matching authentication event: new forwarding rules, changed recovery contacts, permission grants inside an existing session.
detection.adequacy: This is the only detection that sees a UXSS at all, and most estates do not have it because their monitoring is anchored on logins. It is also blind to pure reads - an attacker who only exfiltrates mail contents through the victim's own session leaves no state change to alert on.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treating a confirmed UXSS exposure as a session-integrity incident: invalidating sessions for affected users, reviewing account settings for attacker-made changes, and rotating anything the browser session could have retrieved.
response.adequacy: Necessary and rarely done, because the vulnerability record closes on a plugin version. Session invalidation is also only as good as the applications' support for it, which in 2012 was thin.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: Measured per host while the impact is per session - an open browser keeps the vulnerable runtime after the update is recorded as deployed.

NIST-800-53-CM-7.gap: Scoped to installed software rather than to whether a browser may run plugin-hosted content from arbitrary origins.

NIS2-Art21-patch-management.gap: Discharged by the February 2012 update and silent on the residual case, where the vendor has withdrawn the product and only removal remains.

EU-CRA-Art13.gap: Flash left the market before CRA manufacturer duties applied; no support period, no vulnerability handling, no upstream to escalate to.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: Plugin currency is evidenced; whether the browser may run arbitrary-origin active content is not.

AU-Essential-8-App-Hardening.gap: Would have neutralised the CVE in browsers, but is written about browsers while the runtime is embeddable in other applications.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: The clock starts at vendor availability, so a zero-day exploited before 2012-02-15 is invisible to the maturity measure.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: Closes on plugin version and never asks which authenticated sessions could have been acted on during exposure.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.16.gap: Monitoring anchored on authentication events cannot see an attack that creates none - the session already exists and the actions come from the user's own browser.

new_control_requirements.name: BROWSER-MANAGED-UPDATE-NO-DEFERRAL
new_control_requirements.description: Enterprise update rings must not defer security-channel browser updates beyond 24h.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Adobe Flash Player was a browser-delivered runtime and this CVE was already being exploited in targeted attacks when APSB12-03 shipped on 2012-02-15, so every day of deferral on the browser and its plugin channel was a day of live exposure to a same-origin bypass against users' authenticated sessions. The control also names the failure mode that survives deployment: Flash updates take effect only when the browser process restarts, and the sessions a UXSS monetises live in browsers that are never closed, so a 24-hour ring has to include a forced relaunch rather than only a package push. CISA listed the CVE on 2022-06-08 with a 2022-06-22 due date.

new_control_requirements.name: EOL-ASSET-DECOMMISSION
new_control_requirements.description: This entry is the case the control exists for, and both halves hold here. patch_available is true — a fixed build carrying this JavaScriptCore fix exists — and the vector itself states that the impacted product could be end-of-life and/or end-of-service and that users should discontinue product utilization. Those facts together define the requirement: on a unit whose hardware can still take an Apple security update, reaching the fixed build is an interim state; on a unit that can no longer take one, the terminal state is removal or replacement, because that device is exposed not only to this code-execution flaw but to everything found in that engine since its last build. Scope to what the packet names — macOS, iOS, tvOS, Safari and watchOS — and inventory those. The packet ties the CWE-94 sink to JavaScriptCore in those products and gives no mapping into other vendors' browsers or other software that embeds a web engine, so treating every renderer in the estate as an instance of this CVE manufactures findings and replacement work against software no evidence implicates. In operational terms: enumerate every macOS, iOS, tvOS, watchOS and Safari install that renders untrusted web content, record for each whether its hardware can still receive a build carrying the fix, put those on the interim clock against the 2025-10-20 KEV listing, and put the rest on a dated replacement schedule — a risk acceptance with no removal date leaves a KEV-listed flaw with a public PoC and confirmed exploitation in service indefinitely. Precondition on the interim half: live_patch_available is false and the vendor patch typically requires a service restart or system reboot per the KEV requiredAction, so a device that downloaded the update but has not restarted still runs the vulnerable code and is not remediated. And because exploitation is confirmed and delivery is attacker-controlled web content, a device that rendered untrusted content while exposed belongs on the incident path rather than being closed on the patch record.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Applied to Adobe Flash Player, where both halves hold in the same shape: a fixed build exists (10.3.183.15 and 11.1.102.62, 2012-02-15) and the product line is dead - Adobe ended support on 2020-12-31, blocked Flash content in the player on 2021-01-12, and instructs users to uninstall, while CISA's KEV entry of 2022-06-08 states the required action as disconnection rather than update. Reaching a patched Flash build is therefore an interim state only; the terminal state is removing the runtime from every browser and every application that embeds it, because a host that still renders Flash content is exposed not just to this same-origin bypass but to everything found in that runtime since its last build. Delivery here was attacker-controlled web content reached from a mailed link, so a user who followed one while exposed belongs on the session-integrity incident path rather than being closed out on the plugin version.

attack_vector.description: A page the victim loads instantiates an ActiveX control that Oracle's WebCenter Forms Recognition Designer registered on their workstation, then calls its save method with a path of the attacker's choosing. The control writes where it is told, so the attacker creates or overwrites a file anywhere the user can write and takes execution from there. The server tier is never touched.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none - PR:N; no Forms Recognition account and no network position, only that a workstation with the Designer installed loads the page
attack_vector.complexity: low - AC:L; a file write with a caller-supplied path, with no memory corruption and no version-specific offsets, though the victim must have the Designer installed for any of it to be reachable
attack_vector.ai_factor: None. Found by Andrea Micalizzi (rgod) through manual review of the product's COM surface and submitted to the Zero Day Initiative in October and November 2011; the programme's current TrendAI branding is a later corporate name, not a discovery method.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Not installing the Designer on workstations that only consume capture results, and kill-bitting the Sssplt30 and CroScPlt CLSIDs everywhere else so a web page cannot instantiate them - both available without waiting for Oracle, and both surviving the fact that the underlying release is out of support.
prevention.adequacy: The kill bit is decisive for the browser path and costs nothing on hosts that do not script the control; removing the Designer is decisive outright. Neither addresses the twin CVE-2012-1709 unless both controls are covered, and neither is what a middleware patching process is built to do - which is why the workstation population is where this finding survives.

detection.what_would_have_worked: File-integrity and autostart monitoring on Designer workstations, plus alerting when a browser process loads a line-of-business COM control.
detection.adequacy: File writes are the primitive, so file-level monitoring sees the attack at its first step rather than after payload execution - genuinely early. It depends on knowing which workstations have the Designer, which is exactly the inventory question this CVE exposes as unanswered.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treating a Designer workstation with an unexplained file write as a compromise of that user's context: reviewing autostart locations and application load paths for planted binaries, and rebuilding rather than deleting the artefact.
response.adequacy: Proportionate, but the KEV entry's ransomware flag raises the stakes without giving responders anything to hunt for: CISA marks the CVE as ransomware-associated while no public report names the operation or publishes indicators, so response has to be driven by host evidence rather than by threat intelligence.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: Runs against the server inventory while the vulnerable code is a client-side ActiveX control on Designer workstations.

NIST-800-53-CM-7.gap: Evidenced as an installed-software list rather than as a per-component decision about what a browser may instantiate.

NIST-800-53-SI-10.gap: Written for systems the organisation builds; for purchased middleware it collapses into trusting vendor validation that was absent across two controls at once.

NIS2-Art21-patch-management.gap: Satisfiable in 2012, when Oracle Forms Recognition 10gR3 sat inside Premier Support, and not satisfiable forward today - Premier Support ended December 2016 with no Extended tier, so the line is on Sustaining Support and gets no new security fixes; migration rather than patching is the compliant act.

NIS2-Art21-supply-chain.gap: An unsupported vendor component with client-side code on user workstations is rarely captured by supplier assurance aimed at the server contract.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: Server-oriented hardening evidence never reaches the workstation configuration that actually decides exposure.

AU-Essential-8-App-Hardening.gap: Oriented at Flash, ads and Java rather than at a vendor's own scriptable line-of-business controls.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: Cannot express that the patch must reach a workstation population the middleware patching process does not own.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: Designer workstations are registered as endpoints, not as instances of the affected Fusion Middleware component, so the vulnerability and the asset never join up.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.9.gap: Baselines cover OS settings and rarely enumerate third-party COM registrations, leaving the kill-bit decision outside the audited configuration.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Oracle WebCenter Forms Recognition in Fusion Middleware 10.1.3.5 is the case where the SLA's compensating-control clause does the work, because the patch route is compromised twice over: Oracle's fix is patch 13882540 from the April 2012 CPU (released 2012-04-17), and Oracle Forms Recognition 10gR3 (10.1.3.x) left Premier Support in December 2016 with no Extended tier and now sits on Sustaining Support, which ships no new security fixes, so an estate still running it cannot reach a currently-supported build inside any SLA. The clause that can be met in hours is the documented compensating control - kill-bitting the Sssplt30 and CroScPlt CLSIDs, or removing the Designer from workstations that do not author layouts. CISA listed the CVE on 2022-05-25 with a 2022-06-15 due date and flags it ransomware-associated, which is the reason a four-hour clock rather than a quarterly middleware window is the right unit here.

new_control_requirements.name: EOL-ASSET-DECOMMISSION
new_control_requirements.description: This entry is the case the control exists for, and both halves hold. patch_available is true — a fixed build carrying this JavaScriptCore fix exists — and the vector itself states that the impacted product could be end-of-life and/or end-of-service and that users should discontinue product utilization. Those facts together define the requirement: on a unit whose hardware can still take an Apple security update, reaching the fixed build is an interim state; on a unit that can no longer take one, the terminal state is removal or replacement, because that device is exposed not only to this code-execution flaw but to everything found in that engine since its last build. Scope to what the packet names — macOS, iOS, tvOS, Safari and watchOS — and inventory those. The packet ties the CWE-94 sink to JavaScriptCore in those products and gives no mapping into other vendors' browsers or other software that embeds a web engine, so treating every renderer in the estate as an instance of this CVE manufactures findings and replacement work against software no evidence implicates. In operational terms: enumerate every macOS, iOS, tvOS, watchOS and Safari install that renders untrusted web content, record for each whether its hardware can still receive a build carrying the fix, put those on the interim clock against the 2025-10-20 KEV listing, and put the rest on a dated replacement schedule — a risk acceptance with no removal date leaves a KEV-listed flaw with a public PoC and confirmed exploitation in service indefinitely. Precondition on the interim half: live_patch_available is false and the vendor patch typically requires a service restart or system reboot per the KEV requiredAction, so a device that downloaded the update but has not restarted still runs the vulnerable code and is not remediated. And because exploitation is confirmed and delivery is attacker-controlled web content, a device that rendered untrusted content while exposed belongs on the incident path rather than being closed on the patch record.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Applied to Oracle WebCenter Forms Recognition on Fusion Middleware 10.1.3.5, where both halves the control describes hold: a fixed build exists (Oracle patch 13882540, April 2012 CPU, released 2012-04-17) and the release line is past its supported life, since Oracle Forms Recognition 10gR3 (10.1.3.x) - GA February 2011 - left Premier Support in December 2016, has no Extended Support tier available, and now carries only indefinite Sustaining Support, which delivers no new security fixes. Applying 13882540 is therefore an interim state; the terminal state is migration to a supported Forms Recognition release or retirement of the component, because a 10.1.3.5 install carries not only this caller-controlled file write but everything found in that release since its last patch. The inventory this control demands is unusually specific here: it is the Designer workstations with Sssplt30.ocx and CroScPlt.dll registered, not the server tier, and each needs either a dated migration or removal of the Designer. A risk acceptance with no removal date leaves a CVE that CISA listed on 2022-05-25 and flagged ransomware-associated in service indefinitely.

CVE-2012-1889.name: Microsoft XML Core Services Memory Corruption Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: A page asks MSXML for the definition of a node that was never initialised. MSXML follows the uninitialised memory as if it were an object, the attacker has already sprayed that address from JavaScript, and execution transfers to their code inside the browser at the user's privilege. Nothing is downloaded and nothing is opened - visiting the page is the whole interaction.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none - PR:N; no credentials, no foothold, no prior access to the network
attack_vector.complexity: low - AC:L; the public module ships DEP-aware ROP chains for Vista and Windows 7 with IE8/IE9 and a plain spray for XP, so the exploit generalised across the fleet rather than needing per-victim work
attack_vector.ai_factor: None. Credited by Microsoft to the Google Security Team and Qihoo 360 Security Center - human analysis, consistent with a bug surfaced from live attack traffic rather than from an automated pipeline.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Enabling Microsoft's own interim mitigation from advisory 2719615 on 2012-06-12 - the Fix it, the MSXML 5.0 kill bits and Active Scripting set to prompt - and then deploying MS12-043 for every MSXML version present, including the MSXML 5.0 that Office installed.
prevention.adequacy: The interim controls were sufficient against the public exploit and were available four weeks before the patch, which is the whole point: they were opt-in, so only estates that had already decided to consume vendor pre-patch mitigations got them. The patch is complete but arrives as four separate component updates with different restart requirements, so partial deployment is easy and looks finished.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Proxy or endpoint inspection for pages that instantiate the MSXML CLSID together with large repeated JavaScript allocations, and alerting on the browser spawning children.
detection.adequacy: The CLSID-plus-spray shape is a real pre-execution signal and was published with the module, so defenders could build it the same week. It is evadable by obfuscating the script, and it does nothing for the Office-delivered MSXML 5.0 path if inspection is scoped to browser traffic.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treating hosts that visited a flagged page as compromised at user privilege, checking for persistence and rotating that user's credentials, then verifying MSXML version by version rather than accepting a single patch record.
response.adequacy: The verification half is the part usually skipped, and it is where this CVE hides: a machine can be fully patched for MSXML 3.0 and 6.0 through Windows Update and still carry an unpatched MSXML 5.0 that came with Office.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: Reports clean through the four weeks between the advisory and MS12-043, and cannot represent a fix that ships as four component updates with different restart requirements.

NIST-800-53-SI-3.gap: Weak against a scripted drive-by with a public, modifiable module, and it does nothing to stop the vulnerable component being reachable.

NIST-800-53-CM-7.gap: Treated as an application inventory rather than as a decision about which COM components web content may instantiate, so the kill bits stayed unset.

NIS2-Art21-patch-management.gap: Unsatisfiable for four weeks, with no place to record the vendor interim mitigation that was available from 2012-06-12.

NIS2-Art21-vulnerability-handling.gap: A binary patched/unpatched verdict records an estate running the vendor Fix it identically to one that did nothing.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: Evidence built on patch currency and OS baselines does not enumerate ActiveX compatibility flags or zone scripting policy, which is where the pre-patch defence lived.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: The clock starts at 2012-07-10, so four weeks of public-exploit exposure are outside the measurement, and Office-delivered MSXML 5.0 falls on the applications side of the split.

AU-Essential-8-App-Hardening.gap: Written about Flash, ads and Java rather than an in-box Microsoft XML component, so maturity here implies nothing about the MSXML kill bits.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: An asset register of operating systems cannot answer which hosts carry MSXML 5.0 because Office or Word Viewer installed it.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.7.gap: A page-delivered exploit that writes nothing to disk before executing, with public code circulating for three weeks before the patch.

new_control_requirements.name: VENDOR-PUSH-MITIGATION-OPT-IN-PRE-DISCLOSURE
new_control_requirements.description: For vendors offering push-mitigation services (Microsoft EEMS, Palo Alto Threat Prevention auto-update, etc.), opt-in must be enabled BEFORE the next disclosure event, not in response to it. Compliance frameworks must require operators to enable available vendor-push-mitigation services as a baseline control — opt-in late means the mitigation rule arrives after exploitation, not before.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Microsoft published Security Advisory 2719615 for the MSXML uninitialised-memory flaw on 2012-06-12 carrying a Fix it that altered msxml3.dll, msxml4.dll and msxml6.dll behaviour whenever Internet Explorer loaded, plus kill bits for the MSXML 5.0 controls - and did not ship MS12-043 until 2012-07-10. Public Metasploit code (Exploit-DB 19186) appeared on 2012-06-16, four days after the advisory. An organisation that already consumed Microsoft's interim mitigations as a standing practice was defended from day one of that four-week window; one that treated the advisory as reading material was exposed to a commodity exploit for three weeks. That is the difference this control encodes, and it is why the decision has to be made before the disclosure rather than during it.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Microsoft XML Core Services CVE-2012-1889 is the case the SLA's or-clause exists for: for four weeks there was no patch at all, only Microsoft's advisory 2719615 Fix it, the MSXML 5.0 kill bits and Active Scripting restrictions - all documented compensating controls the SLA accepts and a patch-only clock cannot record. Once MS12-043 shipped on 2012-07-10, the four-hour clock from availability is what the exposure demanded, because public exploit code had been circulating since 2012-06-16. CISA listed the CVE on 2022-06-08 with a 2022-06-22 due date, and EPSS still rates it 0.83638 at the 99.663rd percentile on 2026-08-13.

attack_vector.description: A crafted page mass-allocates DOM objects, references them all through execCommand("selectAll"), and frees the CMshtmlEd object while the command is still in flight. mshtml.dll re-enters CMshtmlEd::Exec() on the freed memory, which the attacker has already reclaimed with a heap spray, and the dispatch runs attacker-supplied code with the browsing user's rights.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none — PR:N. The attacker needs no account and no prior foothold; the whole precondition is that the victim loads a page in an affected Internet Explorer build.
attack_vector.complexity: high — AC:H. The free-and-reuse fires reliably, but code execution on a DEP/ASLR host needs a non-relocated module to build the ROP chain from, which is why the public exploit is target-conditional (msvcrt.dll on XP SP3/IE8; JRE 1.6.x's MSVCR71.dll on Vista and Windows 7).
attack_vector.ai_factor: None. The bug was recovered from an attacker's staging server by a researcher who was already watching that infrastructure for a previous Java zero-day, then reversed into a framework module by hand; MS12-063's Acknowledgments record a parallel coordinated report from an anonymous researcher working with TippingPoint's Zero Day Initiative, with Mitre also thanked. No AI-assisted discovery, triage or exploit generation is claimed by any party involved.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Removing Internet Explorer from the estate, not merely displacing it as the default browser — the vulnerable renderer is mshtml.dll and stays loadable through embedded WebBrowser controls after users have moved to another browser.
prevention.adequacy: Removal is the only durable answer now that the product line is retired, but it is often blocked by a legacy application that requires the legacy engine. Where that is true, the honest state is a compensating control — no outbound web access from the host — rather than a remediation.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Network IDS coverage for the execCommand use-after-free pattern (Snort 24210/24212) combined with process-lineage alerting on any child process spawned by a browser or a WebBrowser-control host.
detection.adequacy: Signature coverage arrived after the exploit was already public and only matches the known variant; the process-lineage half is the durable signal, because whatever the exploit looks like on the wire, the outcome is still an unexpected child process under the renderer.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treating a confirmed hit as a host compromise rather than a browser incident: the original chain dropped a Poison Ivy RAT, so credential rotation for anything used on that host and a rebuild are the correct actions, not just applying the update.
response.adequacy: Effective only if the exploit attempt was detected at all; the delivery is a single page load and leaves nothing on disk beyond the payload, so response depends entirely on the detection layer above it.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: Nominally met by applying every published Internet Explorer update. The control cannot express that no further updates exist for IE 6-9 and that the last one was years ago, so an unpatchable browser reports the same as a current one.

NIST-800-53-CM-7.gap: Least functionality is assessed against approved applications, not against loadable rendering engines. Moving users to a supported browser satisfies the control while mshtml.dll stays reachable through embedded WebBrowser controls.

NIS2-Art21-patch-management.gap: A monthly patch cadence conforms to Article 21 and still absorbs an out-of-band emergency update — MS12-063 shipped seven days after the exploit was found live — into the next scheduled cycle.

NIS2-Art21-vulnerability-handling.gap: The handling process presumes a supplier who can issue a fix. For a withdrawn product the only valid output is decommissioning, and a process that parks the finding as 'awaiting vendor fix' holds it open forever.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: Secure configuration and vulnerability management can both be evidenced on a host carrying Internet Explorer, because the component shipped with the OS and its last available update has been applied. B4 does not surface that the component is unmaintained.

AU-Essential-8-App-Hardening.gap: The control's browser measures target plug-ins and ads. This exploit uses no plug-in — it is plain DOM manipulation in the browser's own renderer — so a clean hardening attestation says nothing about it.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: A two-week or one-month application-patching window is both too slow for an out-of-band release under live exploitation and inapplicable to a browser that no longer receives patches, where removal is the required action.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: Vulnerability information is obtained and exposure is evaluated, but the evaluation does not have to record whether the affected component still has a supplier — so a KEV-listed flaw in an unmaintained renderer audits the same as a patched supported product.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Internet Explorer 6-9 carry this use-after-free with EPSS 0.81716 (99.6th percentile) and a public Metasploit module and Exploit-DB entry that have been available since September 2012. CISA listed it on 2022-06-08 with a 2022-06-22 due date; because the product line is retired, the 'documented compensating controls' branch of this control is the only one an operator can actually satisfy on a surviving IE 6-9 host, and it forces that decision onto the clock instead of leaving the host in an indefinite 'no patch available' state.

new_control_requirements.name: MITIGATION-ACTIVE-PATCH-PENDING-VERDICT-CLASS
new_control_requirements.description: Compliance verdicts must distinguish three states: (a) binary patch deployed (vulnerability eliminated), (b) vendor-mitigation rule active, no binary patch (residual risk: any defect in the mitigation rule reopens the vulnerability), (c) no mitigation, no patch (full exposure). Audit reports must surface (b) as a distinct compensating-control state with an associated time-bound action item, not as a 'patched per SLA' outcome.
new_control_requirements.evidence: This CVE produced state (b) twice for the same product. In September 2012, Microsoft advisory 2757760 carried the only vendor remediation until MS12-063 shipped out of band on 2012-09-21 — EMET configuration from the advisory's publication on 2012-09-17, then the Fix it shim added in revision V1.2 on 2012-09-19. In 2026 it recurs permanently: an IE 6-9 host that cannot be removed is running on compensating controls with no binary fix ahead of it, because the browser line ended with IE11's retirement on 2022-06-15. A report that renders either state as 'patched per SLA' hides the residual risk that the shim or the network restriction is the only thing holding.

new_control_requirements.name: BROWSER-MANAGED-UPDATE-NO-DEFERRAL
new_control_requirements.description: Enterprise update rings must not defer security-channel browser updates beyond 24h.
new_control_requirements.evidence: MS12-063 was an out-of-band Internet Explorer cumulative update released 2012-09-21, one week after the exploit was recovered live from an attacker's staging server on 2012-09-14 and days after a working Metasploit module existed. Any update ring that treated browser updates as part of the normal monthly rollup left every IE 6-9 host exposed for that entire window to a bug with EPSS 0.81716 and a public exploit, which is exactly the deferral this control forbids.

CVE-2012-5054.name: Adobe Flash Player Integer Overflow Vulnerability (CVE-2012-5054)

attack_vector.description: Malformed arguments to Matrix3D.copyRawDataTo overflow the size computation that guards the copy, so the bounds check passes on a wrapped value and the copy writes past the destination allocation. The trigger is an ActionScript API, so the same script that overflows the buffer also grooms the heap it corrupts, and the corrupted allocation is turned into execution inside the Flash runtime at the browsing user's rights.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none — PR:N. No account and no foothold; the attacker needs only content that instantiates the SWF.
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L with UI:R. The user has to load the content, but that is the plug-in's normal operation on any web page, malvertising slot, or Office document with an embedded Flash object. Nothing about the primitive requires a race, an information leak, or a prior compromise.
attack_vector.ai_factor: None claimed and none plausible. The bug was fixed in a scheduled 2012 Adobe bulletin; the reporter credit could not be retrieved because adobe.com did not serve APSB12-19 during this review, so attribution is recorded as unknown rather than guessed.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Removing the Flash runtime from every channel it installed through, rather than disabling it in the browser: the plug-in, the ActiveX control, the Chrome-bundled build, the standalone projector, and the AIR runtime that embeds it.
prevention.framework_requiring_it: CISA BOD 22-01 (KEV remediation, added 2022-06-08; required action is disconnection, the product being end-of-life)
prevention.adequacy: Complete when it is complete — but Flash's multiple install channels are why removal projects reported success over surviving copies. The distinguishing check is an inventory sweep for the runtime binaries themselves, not a browser policy audit.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Alerting on abnormal termination of the Flash host process correlated with the page that was loading, plus process-lineage alerting on any executable spawned by a browser or Office process that had just loaded the runtime.
detection.adequacy: Both signals are reactive and only fire on unreliable exploitation or on a successful payload drop. A working exploit against a matched build produces neither a crash nor necessarily an immediate child process.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treating a confirmed hit as a workstation compromise — rebuild plus rotation of credentials used on the host — rather than as a plug-in update task, since the primitive yields code execution as the browsing user.
response.adequacy: Depends entirely on detection having fired. With no public exploit artefact to signature and no named campaign report for this CVE, the realistic trigger is the payload's behaviour, not the exploit.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: No outstanding vendor update exists for a product whose vendor left in 2020, so the control produces no finding on a host still running the vulnerable runtime. It also tolerates a fixed build on disk with an unrestarted browser still executing the old code.

NIST-800-53-CM-7.gap: Application baselines enumerate applications, not runtimes. Four install channels for one vulnerable runtime read as zero unapproved applications.

NIS2-Art21-patch-management.gap: Patch management reports 'nothing outstanding' where CISA's required action is disconnection. The framework has no state for a product that cannot be patched because the supplier has gone.

NIS2-Art21-supply-chain.gap: The supplier record for this runtime is stale in both directions: Adobe exited the Flash line, and the AIR runtime that embeds the same code moved to HARMAN — a supplier the original assessment never covered.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: A final released build with no outstanding updates evidences secure configuration and vulnerability management. B4 does not require the assessor to record that 'final' means abandoned.

AU-Essential-8-App-Hardening.gap: The control names Flash and requires browsers not to process it, which is right — but it is scoped to the browser, leaving the standalone projector, embedded SWF in Office and PDF, and the AIR runtime outside a passing attestation.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: The patch window is satisfied vacuously when no vendor update exists, so the control is clean on a host CISA told operators to disconnect.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: The clause permits documented risk acceptance without a removal date, converting a disconnect-now KEV entry into an indefinitely open acceptance.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Adobe Flash Player entered KEV for this integer overflow on 2022-06-08 with a 2022-06-22 due date and a required action that says to disconnect the product rather than patch it, because Adobe ended support on 2020-12-31. EPSS is 0.21194 at the 97.4th percentile. The control's 'documented compensating controls' branch is what an operator can actually execute here, and putting it on a clock is what stops a surviving Flash install from sitting in an untracked 'no patch available' bucket.

new_control_requirements.name: BROWSER-MANAGED-UPDATE-NO-DEFERRAL
new_control_requirements.description: Enterprise update rings must not defer security-channel browser updates beyond 24h.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Flash Player's fixed builds for this CVE — 11.4.402.265 on Windows and macOS, 11.2.202.238 on Linux — reached most estates through the browser's own update channel, including the Chrome-bundled PPAPI build where the runtime ships inside the browser release. Deferring that channel deferred the Flash fix with it, and because the runtime update takes effect only when the browser process relaunches, a deferred restart extended the exposure past the recorded patch date.

attack_vector.description: A crafted Silverlight application passes an attacker-chosen pointer into System.Windows.Browser.ScriptObject.Initialize(), which does not validate it. The resulting double dereference is an arbitrary read/write primitive available to untrusted code inside the plug-in; the public exploit chains it with a WriteableBitmap flaw to leak mscorlib.ni.dll's base address, build a ROP chain past DEP and ASLR, and execute code as the browsing user.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none — PR:N. The victim only has to load a page that instantiates the XAP; there is no account, foothold or prior compromise in the path.
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L. NVD's rescoring reads AV:L/UI:R, which understates delivery: Microsoft rated MS13-022 Critical for a straightforward drive-by. The real constraints are that the Silverlight 5 plug-in is installed and enabled below build 5.1.20125.0, and that the exploit knows the target's module layout — which the published exploit solves with the paired information leak.
attack_vector.ai_factor: None. Found and reported by James Forshaw of Context Information Security under coordinated disclosure and credited by name in MS13-022; the exploit that reached the kits was hand-written and published to Packet Storm.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Removing the Silverlight plug-in from every host that does not run a Silverlight application, and where one host must keep it, kill-bitting the ActiveX CLSID and deleting the MozillaPlugins registration everywhere else.
prevention.adequacy: Decisive, and it survives the fact that Silverlight went end-of-support on 2021-10-12 — but it is blocked wherever one legacy internal application still needs the plug-in, which is the usual reason it is still installed at all.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Alerting on XAP retrieval by hosts that have no business reason to run Silverlight applications, joined to process-lineage alerting for executables spawned by a browser.
detection.adequacy: Effective against the exploit-kit pattern, where the XAP is served from a landing page the host was redirected to and has never used before. It gives nothing against a targeted delivery from a site the user visits legitimately.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treating a hit as a workstation compromise with ransomware exposure: KEV records ransomware campaign use as Known for this CVE, and Angler was a primary ransomware delivery kit in the period it carried this exploit.
response.adequacy: Only as fast as the detection above; by the time the ransomware stage is visible the response is recovery rather than containment, which is why the backup and isolation posture matters more than the exploit signature.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: Patch-time compliance in March 2013 says nothing about the November 2013 exploit publication that made this a mass-market attack, and SI-2 evidence of build 5.1.20125.0 is compatible with an unrestarted browser still running the old plug-in.

NIST-800-53-CM-7.gap: Approved-application baselines do not enumerate per-browser plug-in registrations, so removing the Silverlight application entry can leave the ActiveX CLSID and the MozillaPlugins key able to instantiate the runtime.

NIS2-Art21-patch-management.gap: A conforming patch window closed this in March 2013 and never reopened it when working exploit code was published eight months later, which is the event that changed the risk.

NIS2-Art21-vulnerability-handling.gap: Handling processes fire on advisory feeds, not on exploit publications. Microsoft states there was no known exploitation at bulletin time; the transition to exploit-kit use came from a Packet Storm release nothing in the process watches.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: A final-build plug-in with no outstanding updates evidences the outcome. B4 does not require the assessment to state that Silverlight went end-of-support on 2021-10-12.

AU-Essential-8-App-Hardening.gap: The control's enumerated browser targets are Flash, ads and Java. Silverlight is not named, so a passing attestation can coexist with the plug-in enabled — and Cisco's Angler analysis has Silverlight as one of the two exploits actually delivered from the landing page, so the plug-in the control omits is the one that lands.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: Measures time since vendor release, not time since exploit publication, and is vacuously satisfied now that no further Silverlight update will ship.

ISO-27001-2022-A.5.7.gap: Threat intelligence may be collected without being joined back to the closed vulnerability register, so the November 2013 exploit-kit reporting arrives without reopening the finding on hosts that skipped MS13-022.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: Documented risk acceptance is an allowed 'appropriate measure' and carries no removal date, which is how an end-of-support plug-in kept for one legacy application stays in service indefinitely.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Silverlight's fixed build 5.1.20125.0 has existed since 2013-03-12, yet CISA still listed this CVE on 2022-05-25 with a 2022-06-15 due date and ransomware use marked Known — the population that matters is the tail that never took MS13-022, and EPSS 0.81868 (99.6th percentile) reflects a fully public exploit. Because Silverlight went end-of-support on 2021-10-12, the control's compensating-controls branch (kill-bit the CLSID, remove the MozillaPlugins registration, or remove the plug-in) is the enforceable outcome and this puts it on a clock.

new_control_requirements.name: MITIGATION-ACTIVE-PATCH-PENDING-VERDICT-CLASS
new_control_requirements.description: Compliance verdicts must distinguish three states: (a) binary patch deployed (vulnerability eliminated), (b) vendor-mitigation rule active, no binary patch (residual risk: any defect in the mitigation rule reopens the vulnerability), (c) no mitigation, no patch (full exposure). Audit reports must surface (b) as a distinct compensating-control state with an associated time-bound action item, not as a 'patched per SLA' outcome.
new_control_requirements.evidence: MS13-022 shipped two named workarounds for hosts that could not take the update — the ActiveX kill bit on CLSID {DFEAF541-F3E1-4C24-ACAC-99C30715084A} and deletion of HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SOFTWARE\MozillaPlugins\@Microsoft.com/NpCtrl,version=1.0 — and since Silverlight's 2021-10-12 end of support those workarounds are permanent rather than interim on any host that still needs the plug-in. A report that records those hosts as 'patched per SLA' hides that a single registry restore, an application reinstall or a re-imaged workstation reopens the vulnerability.

new_control_requirements.name: BROWSER-MANAGED-UPDATE-NO-DEFERRAL
new_control_requirements.description: Enterprise update rings must not defer security-channel browser updates beyond 24h.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Silverlight reached most estates through the browser update path and its own auto-updater, and MS13-022 states no host restart is required — which is precisely why deferral is invisible here: the update lands, the ring reports success, and the plug-in in the running browser process is still the pre-5.1.20125.0 build until the browser relaunches. Eight months of deferral separated the 2013-03-12 fix from Angler's adoption of the public exploit in November 2013.

CVE-2013-0422.name: Oracle JRE Remote Code Execution Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: An unsigned applet calls the public JmxMBeanServer.getMBeanInstantiator() to obtain the private MBeanInstantiator, uses its findClass() to retrieve restricted Class references, and separately drives the new reflection API recursively so that getCallerClass() misreports the caller and MethodHandles.Lookup.checkSecurityManager passes. With a privileged class handle in hand it disables the SecurityManager and executes arbitrary code as the browsing user, outside the sandbox.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none — PR:N, and UI:N in the CVSS vector. The applet loads and runs on page load; the Java security-level prompt introduced in 7u10 was the only user-visible barrier and the in-the-wild exploit ran under default settings.
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L. Pure Java: no memory corruption, no heap grooming, no ASLR or DEP to defeat, and no per-build offsets, so one applet works across Windows, macOS and Linux. The version boundary was the only real constraint, and NVD records that even that was disputed for 7u11.
attack_vector.ai_factor: None. The bug reached the world as live exploit-kit traffic and was reversed by human malware researchers — AlienVault Labs and Kafeine — before Oracle's own alert. No AI-assisted discovery, triage or weaponization is claimed.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Removing the Java browser plug-in and Web Start integration from endpoints, keeping the JRE only where a local application needs it — the action US-CERT recommended in VU#625617 while no patch existed.
prevention.adequacy: This is the only control that held during the three days between live exploitation and Oracle's 7u11, and it is the only one that survived the disputed completeness of that fix. Its limit is organisational, not technical: it breaks the internal application that was the reason Java was installed.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Process-lineage alerting on java.exe or javaw.exe spawned by a browser and then spawning anything else, joined to network alerting on a JAR fetch immediately followed by an executable fetch from the same origin.
detection.adequacy: Robust because it keys on the outcome rather than the exploit — the escape has to leave the JVM to be useful. It fires only after the sandbox has already been broken, so it bounds damage rather than preventing it.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treating any confirmed applet escape as a full workstation compromise with ransomware exposure — KEV marks ransomware campaign use Known for this CVE and Blackhole was the delivery kit — meaning rebuild and credential rotation, not a JRE update.
response.adequacy: Correct but late. The payload stage is what most estates actually detected, by which point the escape had already succeeded and the response is recovery.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: The exploit ran against a fully current 7u10 with no update to install, and the 7u11 fix that followed was publicly disputed. SI-2 records installation, not whether the primitive was actually removed.

NIST-800-53-CM-7.gap: Approved-software lists approve Java for a line-of-business application and never separately govern whether the browser plug-in and Web Start integration are registered — which is the entire attack surface.

NIS2-Art21-patch-management.gap: A conforming programme reported compliance before, during and after the exploitation window, because there was nothing outstanding to apply on 2013-01-10 and 7u11 satisfied it three days later.

NIS2-Art21-vulnerability-handling.gap: Intake keyed to advisory feeds learned of this from public malware analysis, days after exploitation began and years before the 2022-05-25 KEV listing made it an obligation.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: A supported, current runtime and a documented patch process evidence the outcome. B4 does not ask whether browser and Web Start integration are enabled on hosts that never run browser-delivered Java.

AU-Essential-8-App-Hardening.gap: It names the right target — browsers must not process Java from the internet — but is browser-scoped, leaving Java Web Start via .jnlp and plug-in re-registration after a JRE reinstall outside the attestation.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: The clock starts at vendor release, and on 2013-01-10 there was no release; it also cannot express that an in-window 7u11 host stayed exposed to the sibling JMX escape until 7u13.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: Permits risk acceptance in place of the measure that worked (removing the plug-in) with no requirement to date the retirement of the application dependency that forced the acceptance.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Oracle Java SE 7 through Update 10 carries this sandbox escape at CVSS 9.8 with EPSS 0.97612 (99.9th percentile) — effectively the top of the corpus — and CISA listed it on 2022-05-25 with a 2022-06-15 due date and ransomware use marked Known. The control's compensating-controls branch is what mattered in the real window: the exploit was live on 2013-01-10 and Oracle's 7u11 did not exist until 2013-01-13, so removing the browser plug-in per US-CERT VU#625617 was the only deployable mitigation, and this control makes that a timed action rather than a discretionary one.

new_control_requirements.name: INCOMPLETE-PATCH-SEQUENCE-SEVERITY-MULTIPLIER
new_control_requirements.description: Vulnerability-management programs must apply a severity multiplier when a CVE is the Nth in an incomplete-patch sequence on the same primitive (third MOTW bypass, second AMSI bypass, etc.). Framework controls treating each CVE as discrete obscure the structural defect; the Nth CVE in a sequence implies that future bypasses on the same primitive are likely.
new_control_requirements.evidence: This is the CVE that makes the case. NVD itself records that a reliable third party claimed the findClass/MBeanInstantiator vector was not fixed in Java 7 Update 11, and the JMX sandbox-escape primitive recurred immediately as CVE-2013-0431 (Security Explorations Issue 52, fixed in 7u13) and again as the reflection type-confusion escape CVE-2013-2423 (fixed in 7u21). An estate that treated each as a discrete patch ticket kept re-closing the same structural defect three times in four months while the Java plug-in stayed enabled.

attack_vector.description: The JMX Introspector reflectively invokes a java.lang.reflect.Method without the package access check the sandbox relies on, so untrusted applet code can call into restricted internal classes through the introspection path, disable the SecurityManager, and execute as the browsing user. The public exploit also defeats the Java 7 Update 10 security-level prompt, so the unsigned applet runs with no warning shown.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none — PR:N. No account, no foothold. NVD calls it user-assisted; in practice the assistance required is loading a page, because the exploit removes the approval dialog.
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L. Pure Java with no memory corruption or platform-specific stage. The CVSS 5.3 with C:L reflects Oracle's sandbox-bypass framing rather than the observed outcome, which is code execution — read EPSS 0.89987 at the 99.8th percentile and the Known ransomware flag instead.
attack_vector.ai_factor: None. Found by manual analysis of the Java class libraries at Security Explorations and reported to Oracle on 2013-01-18 as Issue 52 of SE-2012-01. Their published papers describe the reasoning; nothing about it is automated discovery.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Unregistering the Java browser plug-in and Web Start integration as an enforced configuration, rather than relying on the Java security-level prompt — which this exploit deliberately suppresses.
prevention.adequacy: Complete against this and against the sibling escapes in 7u11 and 7u21, which is the point: it removes the surface rather than the individual bug. It is blocked wherever an internal application still delivers Java through a browser, and it does nothing for Java run locally.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Alerting when an unsigned remote applet executes without the Java security prompt appearing, and on any process spawned by java.exe or javaw.exe under a browser.
detection.adequacy: The missing-prompt signal is specific and cheap but requires that the prompt's expected behaviour is baselined in the first place; the process-lineage half is the reliable one, and it fires only after the escape has already happened.

response.what_would_have_worked: Handling a confirmed escape as a workstation compromise with ransomware exposure, given KEV's Known ransomware flag and Blackhole's role delivering ransomware in February 2013 — rebuild plus credential rotation, not a JRE update.
response.adequacy: Correct but downstream. Updating the JRE closes the path for the future and removes nothing the attacker already placed on the host.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: An estate current on 7u11 — the fix for the previous JMX escape — was fully exposed to this one and still evidenced clean flaw remediation until 7u13 shipped on 2013-02-01.

NIST-800-53-CM-7.gap: Least functionality implemented as the Java security-level prompt provided nothing here: the public exploit bypasses that prompt so the unsigned applet runs silently.

NIS2-Art21-patch-management.gap: Conformity is measured as distance from the vendor's latest release, so the same subsystem being repaired in 7u11, 7u13 and 7u21 reads as three separate satisfied cycles.

NIS2-Art21-vulnerability-handling.gap: The research papers and the exploit-kit analysis were both public before an advisory-feed-driven handling process would have registered anything, missing the two-week window between disclosure and commodity exploitation.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: A supported runtime under an operating patch process evidences the outcome, both for a 7u11 estate in January 2013 and for a Java 7 estate today that has had no public update since April 2015.

AU-Essential-8-App-Hardening.gap: Right target, incomplete scope: the browser-side Java block does not cover Java Web Start from a .jnlp file and does not survive a JRE reinstall that re-registers the plug-in.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: The window opens at vendor release, so it covers none of the 2013-01-18 to 2013-02-01 exposure and is vacuously satisfied on a Java 7 estate with no further updates coming.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: Per-CVE closure records three tidy findings across 7u11, 7u13 and 7u21 and never surfaces the structural conclusion that the plug-in surface should be removed rather than repeatedly patched.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
