new_control_requirements.evidence: Oracle Java SE 7 through Update 11 and OpenJDK 7 carry this JMX sandbox escape with EPSS 0.89987 (99.8th percentile) and a public Metasploit module that also suppresses the Java warning prompt. CISA listed it on 2022-05-25 with a 2022-06-15 due date and ransomware use marked Known. Java 7 has had no public updates since April 2015, so on a surviving Java 7 host the only branch of this control that can be satisfied is documented compensating controls — unregistering the plug-in — and this puts that on a clock instead of leaving it as an open risk acceptance.

new_control_requirements.name: INCOMPLETE-PATCH-SEQUENCE-SEVERITY-MULTIPLIER
new_control_requirements.description: Vulnerability-management programs must apply a severity multiplier when a CVE is the Nth in an incomplete-patch sequence on the same primitive (third MOTW bypass, second AMSI bypass, etc.). Framework controls treating each CVE as discrete obscure the structural defect; the Nth CVE in a sequence implies that future bypasses on the same primitive are likely.
new_control_requirements.evidence: This is the second JMX sandbox escape in the Java 7 plug-in inside one month: CVE-2013-0422 was fixed in 7u11 on 2013-01-13, Security Explorations reported Issue 52 on 2013-01-18, and 7u13 landed on 2013-02-01 — followed by the reflection type-confusion escape CVE-2013-2423 in 7u21. Multiplying severity on the second occurrence would have converted a routine JRE patch ticket into the decision that actually mattered, which was removing the browser plug-in rather than waiting for the third repair.

new_control_requirements.name: PROTECTION-MECHANISM-FAILURE-CLASS-REGRESSION
new_control_requirements.description: Detonation chambers, EDR rules, and AppLocker/WDAC policies covering protection-mechanism classes (MOTW, SmartScreen, AMSI, ASR, WDAC, Driver Block Rules) must include class-level regression testing executed on every patch deployment, not just one-off bypass-CVE remediation. The test battery for class-X must include all historic class-X bypass primitives — incomplete patches re-introduce risk that one-off testing does not detect.
new_control_requirements.evidence: NVD assigns this CVE CWE-693, protection mechanism failure, and the mechanism that failed is the one an operator was relying on: the public exploit defeats the Java 7 Update 10 security-level prompt so an unsigned applet runs with no warning. A control programme that verified 'the Java prompt appears for unsigned applets' once, at 7u10 deployment, and never re-tested it against each subsequent JRE update, was reporting a protection that had already been bypassed in the wild by February 2013.

attack_vector.description: A crafted PNG carried in or referenced by an Office document drives the shared Office 2003 image-processing component into an allocation that does not match the data written into it, corrupting memory past the buffer and yielding code execution as the user who opened the file. Office for Mac 2011 carries the same defect. Where Outlook 2003 is configured with Word as the email reader, previewing the message is enough.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none — PR:N. The attacker holds no account on the target; the exploit runs with whatever rights the opening user has, which is why an administrative user turns this into full host control.
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L with UI:R. No race, no leak, no foothold. The binding constraint is the target population: only Office 2003 SP3 and Office for Mac 2011 are affected, with 2007, 2010, 2013 and the viewers explicitly out of scope, so the exploit is only useful against a specific legacy estate.
attack_vector.ai_factor: None. Reported through coordinated disclosure by Andrew Lyons and Neel Mehta of Google Inc, credited by name in MS13-051 — a defender-side analysis of observed targeted attacks, not automated discovery.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Migrating off Office 2003 and Office for Mac 2011 — both terminal product lines — so that documents from outside the organisation are parsed by a suite that still receives fixes and has a sandboxed render mode.
prevention.adequacy: Decisive and the only durable option, but it is a migration project rather than a patch. In the interim MS13-051's own workarounds are what an operator holds: refusing externally-sourced Office files, and on Mac disassociating the binary Office formats in LaunchServices — which stops automatic opening but not a user who opens the file from inside the application.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Process-lineage alerting on any child process spawned by an Office application, plus mail-gateway extraction of embedded image streams from binary Office attachments rather than signature scanning alone.
detection.adequacy: The lineage signal is the reliable half and fires only post-exploitation. Gateway extraction is preventive but depends on the gateway understanding legacy binary Office containers, which is exactly the format an estate on Office 2003 is still receiving.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treating a hit as targeted intrusion rather than commodity malware: Microsoft recorded targeted attacks and the reporters were Google's security team, so the appropriate response is host rebuild, credential rotation and a hunt for lateral movement.
response.adequacy: Under-triggered in practice. A single crafted document leaves little on disk beyond the payload, so response depends on the detection layer above and on someone classifying the event as targeted rather than closing it as a blocked attachment.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: The June 2013 update satisfies the control, but an installed update with Word still running keeps the old parser resident, and an Office 2003 host today generates no finding at all because no further update exists.

NIST-800-53-CM-7.gap: Restricting which Office applications are approved does not reduce the surface, because the vulnerable PNG handling is a shared Office 2003 component reached from all of them; the one setting that matters — Word as the Outlook 2003 email reader — is not in any standard baseline.

NIS2-Art21-patch-management.gap: The process closes on the 2013 update and never escalates an end-of-support productivity suite that still parses external documents into a decommissioning obligation.

NIS2-Art21-incident-handling.gap: Governs what happens after detection. A targeted crafted-document intrusion against a legacy suite is precisely the case where detection does not happen, and the control does not require the capability that would produce it.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: 'Patched to the latest available level' is evidenced identically by a fully patched Office 2003 host and a supported suite, because B4 does not require the assessment to state that 'latest available' has meant nothing since 2014.

AU-Essential-8-App-Hardening.gap: The control's Office measures target macros and OLE. This exploit uses neither, and the affected products predate Protected View, so a passing attestation covers the exact configuration the exploit needs.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: Would have driven the 2013 update out in-window, then goes vacuous on an unsupported suite; its version-based measurement also cannot see an update installed while the application kept running.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: Permits an undated risk acceptance in place of migration, which is how a suite past end of support keeps opening externally-sourced documents years after the appropriate measure became replacement.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Microsoft Office 2003 SP3 and Office for Mac 2011 carry this PNG-handling overflow at EPSS 0.81877 (99.6th percentile), Microsoft confirmed targeted attacks at MS13-051's publication on 2013-06-11, and CISA listed it on 2022-06-08 with a 2022-06-22 due date. Both product lines are past end of support (2014-04-08 and 2017-10-10), so on a surviving host the deployable branch of this control is documented compensating controls — MS13-051's refuse-untrusted-documents and LaunchServices disassociation workarounds — held on a clock until migration completes.

new_control_requirements.name: MITIGATION-ACTIVE-PATCH-PENDING-VERDICT-CLASS
new_control_requirements.description: Compliance verdicts must distinguish three states: (a) binary patch deployed (vulnerability eliminated), (b) vendor-mitigation rule active, no binary patch (residual risk: any defect in the mitigation rule reopens the vulnerability), (c) no mitigation, no patch (full exposure). Audit reports must surface (b) as a distinct compensating-control state with an associated time-bound action item, not as a 'patched per SLA' outcome.
new_control_requirements.evidence: MS13-051 shipped named workarounds alongside the binary update, and on Office for Mac 2011 one of them is explicitly fragile: Microsoft states the LaunchServices disassociation must be re-applied whenever that database is cleaned, because cleaning it resets the values from the application's info.plist. A host running on that workaround is state (b) — one database rebuild away from full exposure — and recording it as 'patched per SLA' hides exactly that. The same applies to any Office 2003 host held on the do-not-open-untrusted-documents workaround because update 2817421 could not be deployed.

attack_vector.description: Untrusted code reaches the reflection path with weak access control on final fields of static classes, bypasses the permission check via MethodHandles, and writes a value of the wrong type into a public final field — the type confusion NVD records as demonstrated with integer and double fields — to overwrite the security manager reference and disable confinement. The applet then runs as the browsing user. The public exploit delivers through a crafted JNLP file via the Java Web Start ActiveX control on Internet Explorer, skipping click-to-play.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none — PR:N, UI:N in the CVSS vector. No account, no foothold, and with the JNLP delivery path no approval click either.
attack_vector.complexity: high per CVSS — AC:H — but that value comes from Oracle's 'unknown vectors related to HotSpot' CPU wording, not from the exploit. The public module is pure Java with no memory corruption, no heap grooming and no per-build offsets, and EPSS 0.85333 at the 99.7th percentile is the better guide to how reachable this actually is.
attack_vector.ai_factor: None. The finding came from an outside researcher reading the reflection implementation and publishing the account NVD cites; Oracle's CPU credits researchers for the release rather than per CVE, so the attribution is stated at that level rather than asserted more precisely than the sources support.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Removing the Java browser plug-in AND the Java Web Start integration and .jnlp association together, since the published exploit routes around an applet-only block by delivering through Web Start.
prevention.adequacy: Complete only if all three registrations go. This is the control most often half-implemented on Java estates, because the applet block is the visible one and the .jnlp association is the one nobody inventories.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Alerting on javaws.exe launched from browser-delivered content and on any process spawned by java.exe or javaw.exe under a browser, plus baselining that the Java security prompt is expected and alarming when it does not appear.
detection.adequacy: The javaws.exe signal is unusually specific to this exploit's delivery choice and cheap to collect; the process-lineage half is general but fires only after the sandbox has already gone.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treating a confirmed escape as a workstation compromise — rebuild and credential rotation — rather than as a JRE patch task, since the primitive yields full user-context execution regardless of the 3.7 CVSS.
response.adequacy: Correct, and the severity mismatch is the practical obstacle: an incident triaged against a 3.7 score is unlikely to be escalated to rebuild, which is exactly how this CVE's real impact got under-weighted.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: Met by deploying 7u21, but CVSS-driven prioritisation deprioritised a 3.7 entry with a public exploit that disables the security manager, and a scan reporting the newest JRE passes while a superseded 7u17 stays registered on the same host.

NIST-800-53-CM-7.gap: Blocking applets in the browser leaves the Java Web Start ActiveX control and the .jnlp association intact — the delivery path the public exploit uses specifically to skip click-to-play.

NIS2-Art21-patch-management.gap: Severity-tiered patching schedules this behind higher-scored items because Oracle's CPU wording produced a low score, while a working public exploit existed within days of the April 2013 release.

NIS2-Art21-vulnerability-handling.gap: Triage that reads the vendor advisory alone never sees the mechanism: Oracle described unknown HotSpot vectors affecting integrity and never commented on the researcher's security-manager-disabling account, which NVD had to append.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: A supported runtime under a patch process evidences the outcome without requiring the assessment to record that Java 7 has had no public update since April 2015, or that Web Start and the .jnlp association are still registered.

AU-Essential-8-App-Hardening.gap: The measure governs browsers processing Java; the exploit delivers through a JNLP file handled by the Java Web Start ActiveX control, outside that scope, so the attestation and the working chain coexist.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: Drives 7u21 out in-window and expresses nothing about the superseded JRE left installed, the bypassable click-to-play prompt, or migration being the terminal action for a Java 7 estate.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: Evaluation of exposure is not required to reconcile a vendor severity summary against exploit availability or EPSS, so a 3.7 score produced a low-priority finding for a one-page-load sandbox escape.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: This is the entry where a KEV-driven clock beats a severity-driven one outright. Oracle Java SE 7 through Update 17 and OpenJDK 7 carry a sandbox escape whose public Metasploit module disables the security manager and ships a JNLP click-to-play bypass, at EPSS 0.85333 (99.7th percentile) — while NVD's CVSS reads 3.7 because Oracle's April 2013 CPU described it only as affecting integrity via unknown HotSpot vectors. CISA listed it on 2022-05-25 with a 2022-06-15 due date; keying remediation to that listing rather than to the score is what gets 7u21 (or, today, migration off Java 7) deployed at all.

new_control_requirements.name: INCOMPLETE-PATCH-SEQUENCE-SEVERITY-MULTIPLIER
new_control_requirements.description: Vulnerability-management programs must apply a severity multiplier when a CVE is the Nth in an incomplete-patch sequence on the same primitive (third MOTW bypass, second AMSI bypass, etc.). Framework controls treating each CVE as discrete obscure the structural defect; the Nth CVE in a sequence implies that future bypasses on the same primitive are likely.
new_control_requirements.evidence: This is the third Java 7 sandbox escape in four months to reach CISA KEV — CVE-2013-0422 fixed in 7u11 on 2013-01-13, CVE-2013-0431 fixed in 7u13 on 2013-02-01, and this one fixed in 7u21 in April 2013 — all defeating the same confinement boundary through the reflection and access-check surface. The multiplier is what converts the third repair into the structural decision the sequence was pointing at: unregister the plug-in and Web Start rather than wait for the fourth.

new_control_requirements.name: PROTECTION-MECHANISM-FAILURE-CLASS-REGRESSION
new_control_requirements.description: Detonation chambers, EDR rules, and AppLocker/WDAC policies covering protection-mechanism classes (MOTW, SmartScreen, AMSI, ASR, WDAC, Driver Block Rules) must include class-level regression testing executed on every patch deployment, not just one-off bypass-CVE remediation. The test battery for class-X must include all historic class-X bypass primitives — incomplete patches re-introduce risk that one-off testing does not detect.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Two protection mechanisms failed together on this CVE and neither failure is visible without class-level regression testing. The security manager itself is overwritten by the type confusion, and the click-to-play prompt an operator would point to as a compensating control is bypassed by the module's crafted JNLP through the Java Web Start ActiveX control — the same warning-bypass class Immunity analysed in April 2013. Re-testing 'does an unsigned remote applet or Web Start application still prompt?' on every JRE deployment is what surfaces that; testing it once at 7u10 does not.

attack_vector.description: An attacker-supplied Silverlight application makes the runtime access an element through an unvalidated pointer and hands back a live address, from which the exploit derives the mscorlib.ni.dll base. It steals no user data worth having - what it steals is the layout of the address space, which is what makes the memory-corruption bug it is paired with land every time instead of once in a while.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none - PR:N; the attacker needs no account, only that the target loads a page while the Silverlight 5 plugin is installed and enabled
attack_vector.complexity: low - AC:L; deterministic disclosure, no heap grooming and no race. UI:R is real but is satisfied by ordinary browsing, and in the observed campaign by a malicious advertisement rather than a click on a link
attack_vector.ai_factor: None. Found by an independent researcher, Vitaliy Toropov, through manual analysis, and weaponised by exploit-kit authors by hand a year later. No AI-branded tooling appears anywhere in the discovery or the weaponisation record.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Removing the Silverlight plugin from any host without a documented application dependency, and blocking plugin content from ad-network origins on the ones that keep it. Where the plugin had to stay, MS13-087 (5.1.20913.0) plus a browser restart closed the leak.
prevention.adequacy: BOD 22-01 arrived nine years after the patch and seven months after Silverlight itself went unsupported - by then its only meaningful instruction is the one CISA actually gave, disconnect the product. As a control for the 2014 exposure window it is retrospective and did nothing.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Proxy and DNS telemetry on .xap retrievals from non-application origins, and endpoint alerting on browser processes spawning children. The Talos-documented campaign left a dropped DLL and two listening ports, which is a far better detection surface than the leak itself.
detection.adequacy: Partial by construction. The information disclosure produces no observable artefact - it is a read inside the browser process - so detection can only ever catch the stage after it, by which point code is already running as the user.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treating any host that loaded a malvertising-delivered .xap as executed-upon rather than exposed: credential rotation for the logged-on user and a rebuild, since the chain ends in user-context code execution.
response.adequacy: Sound but rarely triggered, because the leak stage generates no alert and the exploit kit's payload was the only thing most estates ever saw.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: The control is met by a monthly patch cycle that treats an Important-rated information disclosure as routine, and by a pipeline that cannot see a self-updating plugin. Both are true of an SI-2 assessment that passes.

NIST-800-53-CM-7.gap: Least functionality is assessed at build time; nothing in CM-7 forces a re-review when a browser plugin's business case expires, so the plugin survives long after the applications that needed it.

NIS2-Art21-patch-management.gap: Patching obligations presuppose a vendor. Since 2021-10-12 there is no Silverlight patch to apply, so the clause is trivially satisfied while the runtime stays in service.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: An estate on the final Silverlight build evidences B4 cleanly. B4 does not ask whether a retired browser plugin should still be installed, which is the only remediation left.

AU-Essential-8-App-Hardening.gap: Hardening evidence is usually written against Flash, Java and ads; Silverlight rarely appears in the same enumeration, so the plugin stayed enabled on estates rated compliant.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: 5.1.20913.0 is permanently current because it is permanently final - the maturity model reads that as compliant rather than as an unsupported component.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: The vulnerability process only sees software the asset register lists, and a per-user self-updating plugin is routinely absent from it, so this CVE never reaches the register at all.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Microsoft Silverlight is the case where the mitigation clause matters more than the patch clause. CISA listed this on 2022-05-25 with a 2022-06-15 due date and told operators to disconnect the product because it is end-of-life - eight months after Silverlight support ended on 2021-10-12 and nine years after MS13-087 shipped 5.1.20913.0. An SLA that only recognises patch deployment records this entry as closed the moment a host reports the final build; an SLA that recognises documented compensating controls forces the actual answer, which is uninstalling the runtime. EPSS 0.6961 at the 99.3rd percentile (2026-08-13) says packaged exploit code for the chain is still in circulation.

new_control_requirements.name: BROWSER-MANAGED-UPDATE-NO-DEFERRAL
new_control_requirements.description: Enterprise update rings must not defer security-channel browser updates beyond 24h.
new_control_requirements.evidence: The exposure window for this Silverlight flaw was six months wide: MS13-087 shipped 5.1.20913.0 on 2013-10-08 with no in-the-wild use, and Angler was running the chain in malvertising from 2014-04-23. Silverlight updated through its own auto-updater rather than the managed browser channel, so estates that deferred or never enrolled the plugin carried the leak through that whole window while the browsers around it were current. The control has to name the browser's plugin runtimes, not just the browser binary, or the component that actually gets exploited is the one outside the ring.

CVE-2013-3993.name: IBM InfoSphere BigInsights Invalid Input Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: An authenticated user hands a BigInsights API a file or directory parameter containing traversal sequences. The platform builds a path from it without normalising, and reads or acts on a file outside the intended directory using the service account's rights. The account that starts the attack is ordinary; the reach it acquires is the platform's.
attack_vector.privileges_required: low - PR:L; any authenticated cluster account will do, which on an analytics platform is a large population and often includes service and batch identities
attack_vector.complexity: low - AC:L; no exploit engineering, no race, no memory corruption. The difficulty is knowing which parameter to send, and that has never been published
attack_vector.ai_factor: None recorded on either side. No finder is named in the vendor bulletin and no automated discovery is claimed; the exploitation record is a KEV listing with a ransomware-use flag and no technical reporting behind it.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Levelling the cluster to 2.1.0.3 or above per IBM swg21677445 while the product was supported, and - now that it is not - retiring the platform. Between those two, confining the console and API to an operator segment removes the population that can authenticate at all.
prevention.adequacy: BOD 22-01 gives the right instruction and no timetable an operator can meet: disconnecting an analytics platform is a migration project, not a 20-day patch action, and the directive offers no interim state for a cluster that cannot be turned off by the due date.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Filesystem auditing on the BigInsights service account for reads outside its own directories, and API access logging retained long enough to show traversal probing against file parameters.
detection.adequacy: Workable but usually absent: analytics clusters are noisy file readers by design, so the rule needs a tight allowlist of the service account's legitimate paths or it produces nothing usable.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treating a confirmed traversal as credential exposure for the whole cluster - rotating keytabs, service-account passwords and any secret stored in Hadoop configuration - because the primitive returns files, and on this platform the files are credentials.
response.adequacy: Correct in scope but rarely rehearsed; CISA's ransomware-use flag on this entry means the realistic follow-on is not data theft alone but staged encryption, which needs the fleet playbook rather than a cluster one.

NIST-800-53-SI-10.gap: Input-validation assurance stops at the boundary of code the organisation writes; the unvalidated parameter is in purchased platform code that no SI-10 assessment inspects.

NIST-800-53-AC-6.gap: The privilege abused is the BigInsights service account's, reached through a legitimate low-privilege user session - account-scoped least-privilege reviews never look at it.

NIS2-Art21-vulnerability-management.gap: A withdrawn product emits no advisories, so a conformant vulnerability process has nothing to consume and the exposure persists untouched.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: A cluster at its final fix level evidences B4 as maintained; B4 does not force the question of whether an unsupported analytics platform should remain in service.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: With no vendor updates left, the control scores at maturity permanently while the KEV-listed, ransomware-associated flaw stays exploitable.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.28.gap: Secure coding applies to in-house development only, so a traversal defect in vendor code falls outside the control entirely and no supplier control picks it up.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: The register only carries what a feed reports; an end-of-life product goes silent, and the 2022-05-25 KEV entry was the first signal most operators received.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: For InfoSphere BigInsights the only clause of this SLA that can be satisfied is the compensating-controls clause. CISA listed the CVE on 2022-05-25 with a 2022-06-15 due date, flagged known ransomware campaign use, and instructed disconnection because the product is end-of-life - a patch SLA alone has nowhere to land, since the last fix (2.1.0.3) predates the listing by years. Writing the documented compensating control instead - console and API confined to an operator segment, cluster credentials and keytabs rotated, a dated migration off the platform - is what turns an unactionable KEV entry into a tracked one.

new_control_requirements.name: MITIGATION-ACTIVE-PATCH-PENDING-VERDICT-CLASS
new_control_requirements.description: Compliance verdicts must distinguish three states: (a) binary patch deployed (vulnerability eliminated), (b) vendor-mitigation rule active, no binary patch (residual risk: any defect in the mitigation rule reopens the vulnerability), (c) no mitigation, no patch (full exposure). Audit reports must surface (b) as a distinct compensating-control state with an associated time-bound action item, not as a 'patched per SLA' outcome.
new_control_requirements.evidence: A BigInsights cluster sitting at 2.1.0.3 on an end-of-life platform is reported today as state (a) - patched, closed - when it is really state (b) at best: network confinement of the console and API is holding, and nothing else is. The distinction matters more here than on a maintained product, because state (b) on BigInsights has no exit through patching at all; the time-bound action item the control demands is the migration date. CISA's ransomware-use flag on this entry is the reason an indefinite (b) is not an acceptable resting place.

CVE-2013-7331.name: Microsoft Internet Explorer Information Disclosure Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: A page hands the XMLDOM control XML that references a local path, a UNC share or an intranet address, and reads the parser's error code to learn whether the target exists. Repeated across a supplied list it produces an inventory of installed software - in the documented cases, which endpoint-security product is running - and of reachable internal hosts, before any exploit is attempted.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none - PR:N; an untrusted web page is sufficient, and in the documented cases it was a compromised legitimate site rather than one the victim chose to visit
attack_vector.complexity: low - AC:L; ordinary script, no memory corruption and no chaining requirement. The only real constraint is that the attacker must know which paths to test
attack_vector.ai_factor: None. Published by an independent researcher in April 2013 through manual analysis of parser error behaviour, and implemented in Metasploit by hand. The reconnaissance the bug provides is the kind of target profiling now often automated, but nothing in this CVE's history involved AI tooling.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Blocking ActiveX in the internet zone, or removing Internet Explorer from hosts that do not need it - both close the oracle without a patch, which mattered because the technique was public seventeen months before MS14-052 shipped. After September 2014, KB2977629 plus a reboot.
prevention.adequacy: Adequate once a patch existed and useless before it: Microsoft explicitly identified no workarounds for this vulnerability, so between April 2013 and September 2014 the only real control was not exposing Internet Explorer to untrusted pages.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Proxy inspection for res:// references in page content and for compact result POSTs following a burst of parse failures, plus alerting when a landing page serves different content to different clients.
detection.adequacy: Weak in practice. The whole exchange happens inside a normal page load with no file writes and no process creation, so unless the proxy inspects content there is nothing on the endpoint to catch.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treating a confirmed fingerprinting hit as pre-exploitation on that host - reviewing what was served next, and assuming the attacker chose a payload to evade the specific security product they found.
response.adequacy: Rarely acted on, because an information-disclosure alert with no payload reads as noise. The FireEye and Bromium cases show the same primitive preceding two different chains, which is the argument for escalating it rather than closing it.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: The control's clock starts at patch release, so the seventeen months between public disclosure in April 2013 and MS14-052 are invisible to it.

NIST-800-53-CM-7.gap: Least functionality is evidenced against installed software, not against object models a web page can instantiate, so ActiveX access survives a clean assessment.

NIS2-Art21-patch-management.gap: Priority follows impact metrics, which rank a reconnaissance oracle far below the exploits it enables - so it is queued behind everything it precedes.

UK-CAF-C1.gap: Monitoring can be effective and still be enumerated in advance; C1 does not ask whether the estate can tell when its defences are being fingerprinted.

AU-Essential-8-App-Hardening.gap: Hardening evidence usually covers Flash, ads and Java; ActiveX object instantiation is not enumerated, so the oracle stays reachable at full maturity.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: CVSS 6.5 with low confidentiality impact never reaches the expedited path, while EPSS 0.58023 (99.0th percentile) reflects framework-packaged exploit code - the control does not require both to be read together.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: This Internet Explorer flaw is why the SLA has to accept documented compensating controls as a terminal state, not only patches: Microsoft published no workaround, the technique was public from April 2013, and the fix did not arrive until MS14-052 in September 2014 - so for seventeen months the only satisfiable clause was blocking ActiveX in the internet zone or removing IE from hosts that did not need it. When the patch did land it required a system restart, meaning an SLA that stops at deployed rather than restarted still reports a vulnerable host as closed. CISA listed it on 2022-05-25 with a 2022-06-15 due date.

new_control_requirements.name: BROWSER-MANAGED-UPDATE-NO-DEFERRAL
new_control_requirements.description: Enterprise update rings must not defer security-channel browser updates beyond 24h.
new_control_requirements.evidence: MS14-052 is a cumulative Internet Explorer update, so this flaw is fixed only by taking the browser's whole security-channel roll-up - and it is a reboot-required one, which is the deferral that actually happens on managed estates. A ring that holds IE cumulative updates for a validation window leaves a publicly documented, actively exploited fingerprinting oracle live on every workstation for the length of that window, and the Metasploit implementation of it has been publicly available since 2014-09-09. Measure completion by installed build after restart, not by approved in the console.

CVE-2014-0546.name: Adobe Reader and Acrobat Sandbox Bypass Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: A document defeats the reader's own sandbox. Code that the design confines to a low-privilege renderer ends up running natively with the logged-on user's rights, so the containment that justified opening untrusted PDFs at all stops being a boundary. The specific primitive has never been published - the operator-relevant fact is that document content alone was sufficient.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none - PR:N in the retrofit scoring; in reality the attacker needs code already running inside the sandbox, which is supplied by a second defect in the same document rather than by any account
attack_vector.complexity: low - AC:L as scored, but the honest constraint is the chain: a renderer-side bug to get inside, this bug to get out, and a user who opens the file. That combination kept it in limited, isolated attacks
attack_vector.ai_factor: None. Found by a vendor research team analysing in-the-wild samples - the bug was discovered because it was already being used, not through fuzzing or automated analysis, and no AI tooling is claimed.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Taking APSB14-19 on the day it shipped, on every Reader and Acrobat track including per-user installs, and restarting the applications afterwards. Structurally: opening externally sourced PDFs in a reader other than the one under active attack, or in an isolated environment.
prevention.adequacy: The patch is the answer, and the KEV clock arrived nearly eight years after it. The residual limit is inventory, not deployment: the directive says patch, and the copies that stay vulnerable are the ones nothing knows about.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Process-lineage alerting on the reader spawning children or writing outside its sandbox directories, and egress monitoring on the reader process.
detection.adequacy: This is the only workable detection surface, because the escape leaves no network artefact of its own - but the same alert fires on legitimate document-services features, so it needs tuning per estate before it is usable.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treating a confirmed escape as user-context code execution: credential rotation for the logged-on user, and a rebuild rather than a clean-up, since the attacker held the user's full rights at that point.
response.adequacy: Correct but hard to trigger, because the visible artefact is a child process rather than an exploit, and the reader crashing beforehand is routinely dismissed as instability.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: Remediation is measured against an inventory that misses the second product track and per-user installs, so a clean SI-2 report coexists with unpatched copies on the same workstations.

NIST-800-53-SC-39.gap: Process isolation is evidenced as present and enabled; nothing in the control tests whether the boundary survives hostile input, which is exactly what failed here.

NIS2-Art21-patch-management.gap: The obligation is cadence-shaped, and this fix arrived out of band on 2014-08-12 under active exploitation - a compliant monthly window still leaves weeks of exposure.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: An estate at the fixed builds passes B4 while running product lines that ended support in 2015 and 2017, on software that opens untrusted attachments daily.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: The 48-hour clock is right and applies only to inventoried applications; the unmanaged second track is where the exposure survives the deadline.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: Prioritising on the 9.8 retrofit misreads a chained sandbox escape as a standalone remote code execution, spending expedited capacity in the wrong place in the chain.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Adobe released the fix for this Reader and Acrobat sandbox bypass out of band on 2014-08-12, having found an exploit already in use in limited, isolated attacks against Windows users - the whichever-is-later clause is what makes that release, not the much later 2022-05-25 KEV listing, the start of the clock. Verified mitigation is the operative word for this product: the patched binary at 10.1.11 or 11.0.08 does not take effect until every Reader and Acrobat process relaunches, so a deployment record without a relaunch check reports a still-vulnerable workstation as remediated.

new_control_requirements.name: PROTECTION-MECHANISM-FAILURE-CLASS-REGRESSION
new_control_requirements.description: Detonation chambers, EDR rules, and AppLocker/WDAC policies covering protection-mechanism classes (MOTW, SmartScreen, AMSI, ASR, WDAC, Driver Block Rules) must include class-level regression testing executed on every patch deployment, not just one-off bypass-CVE remediation. The test battery for class-X must include all historic class-X bypass primitives — incomplete patches re-introduce risk that one-off testing does not detect.
new_control_requirements.evidence: The Adobe Reader sandbox is a protection-mechanism class and this CVE is a bypass of it - one of a sequence, since Reader's protected mode has been escaped repeatedly since it shipped with version X. Because the primitive was never published, an estate cannot test for this specific bypass; what it can do is keep a battery of the historic Reader sandbox-escape behaviours - renderer process spawning children, writing outside its sandbox directories, opening network connections - and re-run it on the detonation chamber and the EDR ruleset every time the reader is updated. That is the only way an operator learns that the boundary has stopped holding when the vendor cannot say how it was crossed.

CVE-2014-2817.name: Microsoft Internet Explorer Privilege Escalation Vulnerability (CVE-2014-2817)

attack_vector.description: A page reaches a path where Internet Explorer does not validate permissions, and script that the sandbox should have held at low integrity runs at the user's own integrity level instead. It is the hinge of a two-bug chain: the partner defect gets code into the tab, this one gets it out, and only then does anything the user cares about become reachable.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none - PR:N; no account is needed, only that the target loads attacker-controlled content, which in a web-based attack includes a compromised legitimate site or a hosted advertisement
attack_vector.complexity: low - AC:L; no grooming or race is described. The real cost is holding a second exploit for the same browser version, which is why this was in the hands of an attacker rather than in an exploit kit
attack_vector.ai_factor: None. Reported by a named human researcher, James Forshaw of Context Information Security, from manual analysis of the browser's permission model; the parallel in-the-wild use has no published tooling of any kind.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: MS14-051 (KB2976627) with the restart taken, and - because Microsoft published no workaround - removing Internet Explorer from hosts that did not need it. Running interactive sessions as a standard user caps the value of the escape at that user's own data.
prevention.adequacy: Adequate once installed and restarted, and the restart is the gap: the directive is satisfied by installation records, while the flaw survives until reboot. The KEV clock also arrived almost eight years after the fix, so it disciplined nobody during the exposure.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Integrity-level-aware endpoint telemetry - alerting when an Internet Explorer tab process writes outside its low-integrity locations or spawns an unexpected child - correlated with browser crashes on the same host.
detection.adequacy: Genuinely the right signal and rarely collected. Most estates monitor process creation but not the integrity level of the writer, which is precisely the distinction this bug erases.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treating a confirmed escape as user-context compromise: rotate the logged-on user's credentials and any token cached in that session, and rebuild rather than remediate, since the attacker held the user's full rights.
response.adequacy: Correct in scope, but under-triggered - an elevation-of-privilege finding with no payload reads as low severity, and the payload in this chain belongs to the partner CVE.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: Ranking by standalone impact queues the escape stage below the memory-corruption bugs it enables, which inverts the actual dependency.

NIST-800-53-AC-6.gap: Least privilege determines the blast radius of the escape but is assessed against administrative accounts, not against which integrity level a browser tab lands in.

NIS2-Art21-patch-management.gap: The cadence makes no distinction for a flaw the vendor records as already exploited and not publicly disclosed - the case where out-of-cycle deployment is warranted.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: No workaround exists to harden toward, and an installed-but-not-restarted host reports as compliant while remaining exploitable.

AU-Essential-8-App-Hardening.gap: Browser hardening addresses delivery, not the integrity boundary this bug crosses; full maturity leaves the escape untouched.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: Compliance is measured on installation, and the deferred restart is where a compliant fleet stays vulnerable.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: Each CVE is scored discretely, so a portable escape stage spanning IE 6 through 11 is not weighted for the other flaws in the same bulletin it makes usable.

new_control_requirements.name: BROWSER-MANAGED-UPDATE-NO-DEFERRAL
new_control_requirements.description: Enterprise update rings must not defer security-channel browser updates beyond 24h.
new_control_requirements.evidence: MS14-051 shipped this fix inside the August 2014 Internet Explorer cumulative update, with Microsoft recording the flaw as already exploited in the wild and not publicly disclosed - the exact profile that a validation-window deferral is worst for. The update also requires a system restart, so the ring's completion criterion has to be installed-and-restarted: an estate that reports KB2976627 deployed but has not rebooted its workstations is still handing a medium-integrity escape to any chain that lands code in an Internet Explorer tab.

new_control_requirements.name: PROTECTION-MECHANISM-FAILURE-CLASS-REGRESSION
new_control_requirements.description: Detonation chambers, EDR rules, and AppLocker/WDAC policies covering protection-mechanism classes (MOTW, SmartScreen, AMSI, ASR, WDAC, Driver Block Rules) must include class-level regression testing executed on every patch deployment, not just one-off bypass-CVE remediation. The test battery for class-X must include all historic class-X bypass primitives — incomplete patches re-introduce risk that one-off testing does not detect.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Internet Explorer's Protected Mode integrity boundary is a protection-mechanism class, and MS14-051 patched two bypasses of it in one bulletin - CVE-2014-2817 and CVE-2014-2819 - which is the signature of a class defect rather than an isolated bug. The regression battery an operator can actually maintain is behavioural: after each browser update, confirm the detonation chamber and the EDR ruleset still flag a tab process writing outside its low-integrity locations or spawning an unexpected child. Testing only for the specific CVE is impossible here anyway, since the exploited code was never published.

attack_vector.description: An unprivileged local process asks the kernel to requeue a futex waiter onto the same futex it is already waiting on. The kernel's priority-inheritance bookkeeping is left describing a state that does not exist, and the process turns that inconsistency into writes to kernel memory and then into root credentials for itself. No file is dropped, no privileged binary runs, nothing crosses the network.
attack_vector.privileges_required: low - PR:L; any local execution context will do, including an unprivileged service account or an ordinary installed application on Android
attack_vector.complexity: low - AC:L; deterministic, no race and no preceding information leak. The only per-target work is offsets, which is why published exploits name specific distributions and handsets
attack_vector.ai_factor: None. Discovery credited to an individual researcher and weaponisation to geohot's towelroot, both manual. What is notable is the speed from disclosure to consumer-grade tooling - weeks - which is the dynamic AI-assisted exploit development now reproduces on other bug classes.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: The distribution kernel update followed by a reboot - the reboot is the control, not the package. Where a reboot could not be scheduled, a pre-existing live-patching capability (kpatch, livepatch, Ksplice) is the only substitute, and it has to be deployed before the disclosure to be available during it.
prevention.adequacy: Adequate on managed Linux and unavailable on the Android and embedded side, where no fixed build was ever published for most affected devices - there the directive's only satisfiable reading is retirement.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Host audit or eBPF rules on the requeue-with-priority-inheritance futex operation where both addresses match, paired with alerting on any process acquiring root credentials without a setuid or sudo event in its lineage.
detection.adequacy: High-fidelity - the trigger is essentially never legitimate - but it requires host telemetry already collected and shipped off-host before the attempt. On shared multi-user hosts, the population most exposed, that telemetry is least often present.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treating a confirmed escalation as full host compromise: rebuild rather than remediate, and rotate every credential, key and token that was resident on or reachable from the host, because root was held.
response.adequacy: Correct and expensive. The bug leaves no artefact of its own, so the trigger for this response is usually the attacker's later, noisier activity rather than the escalation itself.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: Installed package version is the wrong measurement for a kernel flaw; the running kernel is what is exploitable, and SI-2 has no pending-reboot state.

NIST-800-53-SI-4.gap: The exploit produces no network, file or process artefact, so monitoring evidenced through network and log collection sees nothing.

NIS2-Art21-availability.gap: Remediation requires a reboot the availability commitment discourages, and Article 21 provides no rule for which obligation yields.

NIS2-Art21-patch-management.gap: Distribution kernels were fixed on 2014-06-05; the Android and embedded population had no fixed build to apply, so no compliant patching action exists for it.

UK-CAF-C1.gap: Monitoring assessed as effective can still be blind to an in-process privilege transition driven entirely by syscalls.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: Maturity is scored on installed kernel version, which diverges from the running kernel exactly where long-uptime hosts are concerned.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: A local-access 7.8 sorts below remote flaws, while a published Exploit-DB entry, a Metasploit module and a consumer rooting app make this one of the most exploitable items in any 2014-era queue.

new_control_requirements.name: LIVE-PATCH-CAPABILITY
new_control_requirements.description: For any system that processes production workloads and cannot tolerate unplanned reboots: live kernel patching capability (kpatch, livepatch, kGraft, or equivalent) must be deployed and tested quarterly.
new_control_requirements.evidence: This futex flaw is the archetype the control exists for: the fix is a kernel change, USN-2235-1 states that a reboot is required after the standard update, and no live patch is recorded for the CVE. The hosts carrying the most risk - shared build, application and jump servers where unprivileged local execution is normal - are the same hosts whose availability commitments push the reboot out, so without a live-patching capability already deployed and exercised the organisation has to choose between an unpatched kernel and an unplanned outage. Deployed beforehand, this class is remediable without the outage; deployed afterwards, it is useless for the incident at hand.

new_control_requirements.name: KERNEL-EXPLOITATION-DETECTION
new_control_requirements.description: Deploy auditd or eBPF-based monitoring rules for kernel privilege escalation indicators. Alert within 60 seconds of detection.
new_control_requirements.evidence: For CVE-2014-3153 the detectable event is unusually crisp: a requeue-with-priority-inheritance futex operation whose source and destination addresses are equal, which the fixed kernel rejects outright and which no legitimate program issues. Pair it with the outcome - a process holding root credentials with no setuid execution, su or sudo in its lineage - because the escalation happens inside an existing process and creates no privileged binary to alert on. Nothing else will see it: the exploit touches no file and no socket, so file-integrity monitoring, network detection and signature-based endpoint tooling have no artefact to match. The precondition is that host audit or eBPF telemetry is already being collected and shipped off-host, which on shared multi-user Linux is exactly where it is least often enabled.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Canonical shipped fixed kernels across every supported Ubuntu release on 2014-06-05, roughly a month after disclosure and while towelroot was putting a working exploit in consumer hands - so for this CVE the patch-availability arm of the SLA, not the 2022-05-25 KEV listing, is the clock that mattered. Verified is the operative word: verification for a kernel flaw means the running kernel, not the installed package, so the SLA is met by a host at 3.13.0-29.53 that has rebooted and is not met by one that has merely installed it. For Android and embedded devices with no fixed build, the only satisfiable arm is documented compensating controls plus a dated retirement.

CVE-2014-4077.name: Microsoft IME Japanese Privilege Escalation Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: Code confined inside a document reader's sandbox writes a dictionary file, and the Japanese IME's dictionary component loads it without adequately constraining where it came from. The load happens outside the sandbox, so the attacker's code ends up running with the logged-on user's rights. The sandbox is not broken from the inside - it is walked around, through an operating-system component the sandboxed application is allowed to talk to.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none as scored - PR:N; but Microsoft's own mitigating factor is that the attacker must have authenticated write access to the system, so in practice this is reached from code already running inside a sandboxed application
attack_vector.complexity: low - AC:L once the file can be written; UI:R is satisfied by opening the crafted document. The narrow part is the target population, not the technique: only Microsoft IME for Japanese is affected
attack_vector.ai_factor: None. Privately reported through coordinated disclosure with no finder named and no tooling described; the in-the-wild use was limited and never publicly analysed in technical detail.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Removing Microsoft IME (Japanese) from hosts with no Japanese-language requirement - that deletes the component the escape depends on. Where it is needed, KB2991963 and KB2889913 with a restart. Microsoft's EMET attack-surface-reduction rule blocking IMJP*.DIC from IMJPDCT.EXE was the interim control, and EMET reached end of life in July 2018.
prevention.adequacy: The patch closes it, but the directive cannot make an organisation look for a component it does not know is installed - and every affected platform is now out of support, so the compliant end state is migration rather than patching.

detection.what_would_have_worked: File-write monitoring on IME dictionary paths, and alerting when a sandboxed reader process writes to them or when IMJPDCT.EXE loads a dictionary from outside its installation directory.
detection.adequacy: Precise where it is deployed and almost never deployed: monitoring rules are written for well-known persistence and execution paths, and an IME dictionary directory is on nobody's list until a bulletin puts it there.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treating a confirmed escape as user-context code execution on the host - rotating the logged-on user's credentials and rebuilding - and reviewing the delivering document rather than only the escape.
response.adequacy: Correct but rarely reached, because the escape produces no distinctive artefact of its own; what surfaces is whatever the attacker did afterwards with the user's rights.

NIST-800-53-CM-7.gap: Least functionality reviews enumerate services and applications, not optional OS components like an IME, so the component that carries the flaw is never in scope.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: A Moderate-rated update on an unrecognised component stays in the backlog even under a compliant remediation process - while the same bulletin reports limited attacks in progress.

NIS2-Art21-patch-management.gap: The update is offered to systems that are not vulnerable, so deployment telemetry cannot identify which hosts were actually exposed or whether removal was the better answer.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: The vulnerable component arrives with the base image rather than through a configuration decision, so it is inherited estate-wide and invisible to the assurance record.

AU-Essential-8-App-Hardening.gap: Hardening baselines constrain macro, ActiveX and OLE inside the document application; the escape route runs into an OS input component no baseline covers.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: Optional OS features are not enumerated as software, so a CVE scoped to Microsoft IME (Japanese) never matches anything on the register.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.9.gap: Approved-configuration baselines do not enumerate language and input components, so no control point ever asks whether a Japanese IME belongs on the estate at all.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Microsoft shipped MS14-078 (KB2991963 for Windows, KB2889913 for the Office 2007 IME) on 2014-11-11 while stating it was aware of limited attacks already exploiting the flaw, and rated it only Moderate - so a severity-driven queue never reaches it and the SLA has to be triggered by the exploitation status instead. The documented-compensating-controls arm carries real weight for this CVE, because the strongest available action is not the patch: removing Microsoft IME (Japanese) from hosts with no Japanese-language requirement deletes the component the sandbox escape depends on. CISA listed it on 2022-05-25, by which time every affected platform was already out of support.

new_control_requirements.name: PROTECTION-MECHANISM-FAILURE-CLASS-REGRESSION
new_control_requirements.description: Detonation chambers, EDR rules, and AppLocker/WDAC policies covering protection-mechanism classes (MOTW, SmartScreen, AMSI, ASR, WDAC, Driver Block Rules) must include class-level regression testing executed on every patch deployment, not just one-off bypass-CVE remediation. The test battery for class-X must include all historic class-X bypass primitives — incomplete patches re-introduce risk that one-off testing does not detect.
new_control_requirements.evidence: The document-reader sandbox is the protection-mechanism class here, and this CVE shows how the class is defeated in practice: not by breaking the sandbox but by reaching an operating-system component outside it - IMJPDCT.EXE loading an attacker-written IMJP*.DIC. Microsoft's own remedy was an attack-surface-reduction rule on that exact module pattern, which is a class-level test an operator can keep: after each reader or OS update, confirm that a sandboxed renderer still cannot write into and trigger a load from OS component directories. Testing only for this CVE is impossible anyway, since no exploit was published; testing the class is not.

CVE-2014-4123.name: Microsoft Internet Explorer Privilege Escalation Vulnerability (CVE-2014-4123)

attack_vector.description: A page the victim visits drives Internet Explorer through an operation whose permissions the browser does not properly validate, and code confined to the low-integrity sandbox ends up executing at medium integrity with the user's own rights. It is the escape half of a two-bug chain: a separate memory-corruption flaw puts the attacker inside the tab, and this one gets them out of it.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none — PR:N; the attacker holds no account on the target and needs only to get the user's browser onto content they control
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L; the escape is a permission-validation logic failure with no race or heap groom, but real use requires a paired renderer RCE first, which is how Microsoft describes it being exploited
attack_vector.ai_factor: None. MS14-056 credits James Forshaw of Context Information Security — a human researcher at a consultancy, working the IE broker surface by hand in 2014. No AI-assisted discovery or weaponisation is claimed by any source.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Installing MS14-056 (KB2987107) and rebooting, on the October 2014 release day, across every host running Internet Explorer 7-11 — and, structurally, removing Internet Explorer from the estate so the broker surface is not present at all.
prevention.adequacy: Partial. The patch closes this instance, but Microsoft published no workaround for the pre-patch window, and MS14-056 fixed a second elevation-of-privilege bug (CVE-2014-4124) in the same broker area on the same day — evidence that patching one instance leaves the class. Only retiring the browser removes the surface.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Process-lineage telemetry that alerts when a low-integrity Internet Explorer tab process becomes the parent of a medium-integrity process, correlated with the browsing session that preceded it.
detection.adequacy: Weak on its own. The escape produces one process transition inside a legitimate browsing session and no file-system or network artefact of its own; without the parent-child integrity-level pairing, the follow-on activity looks like ordinary user-launched software.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treating any host that browsed attacker-controlled content while unpatched as user-context compromised: rotate the browsing user's credentials, audit user-writable persistence, and rebuild rather than close the ticket on the patch.
response.adequacy: Necessary but bounded. The escape lands at medium integrity, not SYSTEM, so the blast radius is the user's own data and credentials — which on a workstation is usually enough to continue the intrusion, and the patch removes none of what was already placed.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: Flaw remediation is driven off Microsoft's Important/EoP rating, which is a rating of this bug alone and not of the chain it completes, so the escape is scheduled behind the Critical RCEs it is paired with.

NIST-800-53-SC-39.gap: Protected Mode satisfies the process-isolation requirement on paper while a permission-validation gap inside the broker path lets low-integrity content act at medium integrity; the control is never tested against escape primitives.

NIS2-Art21-patch-management.gap: A monthly cadence measured against Patch Tuesday leaves the exploited window open, and for the affected Internet Explorer builds there is no longer a vendor patch to measure against at all.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: B4 evidence covers build hardening and patch baselines; this defect is inside the browser's own privilege boundary, with no configuration lever and no Microsoft-published workaround to attest to.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: The patch-applications control measures deployment against an available vendor update and reports maturity, not the fact that the only durable outcome for an unsupported browser is removal.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: Technical vulnerability management prioritises from the vendor severity, which classes this as a privilege bug that 'does not allow arbitrary code to be run' — accurate in isolation and misleading about the chain, and blind to the KEV clock.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Microsoft's own MS14-056 disclosure table marked this Internet Explorer 7-11 elevation-of-privilege flaw as already exploited on release day, 2014-10-14, and CISA later listed it in KEV on 2022-05-25 with a 2022-06-15 due date. There is no workaround published for it, so the 4-hour clock has exactly one action behind it — install KB2987107 and reboot — and on hosts where Internet Explorer is unsupported, the only verified mitigation left is removing the browser. EPSS 0.47259 (98.731st percentile, 2026-08-13) shows the exposure is still live on whatever population never took either step.

new_control_requirements.name: BROWSER-MANAGED-UPDATE-NO-DEFERRAL
new_control_requirements.description: Enterprise update rings must not defer security-channel browser updates beyond 24h.
new_control_requirements.evidence: The fix for this flaw arrived as an Internet Explorer cumulative update (MS14-056 / KB2987107) carrying fourteen CVEs, which is exactly the kind of package a testing ring holds back for application-compatibility validation — while Microsoft was recording active exploitation of CVE-2014-4123. Applied here the control means the browser's security channel is not subject to the general OS deferral window, and that the ring's exit criterion is the reboot completing, since MS14-056 requires a restart for the update to take effect. For an estate that still runs Internet Explorer 7-11 with no vendor channel remaining, the control converts to the same deadline against browser removal.

CVE-2014-4148.name: Microsoft Windows Remote Code Execution Vulnerability (CVE-2014-4148)

attack_vector.description: An attacker emails a document — or serves a page — carrying a malformed embedded TrueType font. Windows parses that font inside win32k.sys in kernel mode, and the malformed data drives the parser into running the attacker's code at ring 0. The user takes one ordinary action, opening the file, and the machine is fully compromised with no second bug needed.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none — PR:N; the attacker needs no account and no foothold, only for the font to reach the parser
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L; the attacker fully controls the font file and the kernel parses it on open; MS14-058 lists 32-bit and 64-bit Windows alike as affected and no retrievable source narrows the in-the-wild attacks to one architecture
attack_vector.ai_factor: None. FireEye analysts recovered the exploit from a live targeted attack and worked with Microsoft on the fix, per MS14-058's acknowledgements. No AI-assisted discovery or exploit development is claimed anywhere in the reporting.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Deploying MS14-058 / KB3000061 and completing the reboot across the fleet, with Microsoft's t2embed.dll deny-access workaround applied in the interim on hosts that could not restart immediately.
prevention.adequacy: Good but conditional. The patch fully removes the defect — but only after restart, and the workaround that covers the gap costs embedded-font rendering, so it has to be decided and tested before the next font-parser bulletin rather than during it.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Treating win32k bugchecks and Office-spawned child processes on user workstations as security signals and correlating them with the document that was opened, plus mail-gateway inspection of documents carrying embedded font resources.
detection.adequacy: Limited. A successful kernel exploit leaves little in user-mode telemetry, and code running at ring 0 can suppress what a host agent reports; the honest value is catching the failed attempts and the delivery, not the successful run.

response.what_would_have_worked: Rebuilding any host believed to have opened a weaponised font while unpatched, rather than patching in place, and rotating every credential that host held.
response.adequacy: The only defensible option for a kernel-mode compromise. The patch replaces the driver; it does not evict a rootkit or a driver installed by code that already held ring 0, so patch-in-place closes the entry route and leaves the occupant.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: Remediation is measured at installation, not at the restart that actually loads the fixed win32k.sys, and the monthly cycle covers a bulletin Microsoft already knew was under attack.

NIST-800-53-CM-7.gap: Least-functionality baselines enumerate software and services, never in-kernel parsers reachable from documents, so embedded-font support is never disabled in advance despite a vendor-tested way to do it.

NIS2-Art21-vulnerability-handling.gap: The handling process starts at advisory ingestion, and this vulnerability became known only because an incident responder recovered it from a live attack — the operator-visible signal arrived with the patch.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: Build-level secure-configuration and patch evidence says nothing about whether the reboot happened or whether documents from outside can reach the font parser at all.

AU-Essential-8-App-Hardening.gap: Application hardening targets browser plugins and Office macro settings; a document with an embedded font needs neither, and the vulnerable parser is not in the application being hardened.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: The OS-patching maturity metric counts installed updates on supported platforms, not restart state, and offers no compliant answer for the end-of-life Windows releases in the affected list.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: The kernel-driver framing of the bulletin steers the risk assessment towards servers, while the actual delivery path was an emailed Office attachment to end-user workstations.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: MS14-058 shipped on 2014-10-14 with Microsoft already recording limited attacks against this win32k TrueType parser, and CISA listed it in KEV on 2022-05-25 with a 2022-06-15 due date. For this Windows defect the control's 'verified' qualifier is the load-bearing word: KB3000061 does not take effect until the host restarts, so verification means comparing the running win32k.sys against the fixed build rather than reading 'installed' from the update console. Where the restart cannot be taken inside the window, the documented compensating control exists and is specific — Microsoft's t2embed.dll deny-access commands — and it costs embedded-font rendering, so it belongs in the runbook before the next bulletin.

new_control_requirements.name: MITIGATION-ACTIVE-PATCH-PENDING-VERDICT-CLASS
new_control_requirements.description: Compliance verdicts must distinguish three states: (a) binary patch deployed (vulnerability eliminated), (b) vendor-mitigation rule active, no binary patch (residual risk: any defect in the mitigation rule reopens the vulnerability), (c) no mitigation, no patch (full exposure). Audit reports must surface (b) as a distinct compensating-control state with an associated time-bound action item, not as a 'patched per SLA' outcome.
new_control_requirements.evidence: This CVE produces exactly the three states the control names, and an estate running MS14-058 will hold hosts in all of them at once: patched and rebooted, running Microsoft's t2embed.dll deny-access workaround with KB3000061 not yet applied or not yet restarted, and untouched. The middle state is a real reduction in exposure and also a functional regression — Microsoft states applications relying on embedded fonts fail to display properly — so recording it as 'patched per SLA' both overstates the security position and hides a service-impact item that someone will silently revert. A fourth trap sits inside state (a): KB3000061 installed without the required reboot is still full exposure and must not be reported as remediated.

new_control_requirements.name: DOWNLOAD-PROVENANCE-ENFORCEMENT
new_control_requirements.description: Exploitation here requires the victim to open an attacker-supplied Office document, so on an estate that has not yet reached the fixed build the delivery path is the only enforceable control. Require Mark-of-the-Web on every Office file arriving by mail, web download, or untrusted file share, and require MOTW-tagged documents to open in Protected View — an isolated, reduced-privilege render — instead of the full parsing path that carries the CWE-94 sink at the user's own process privilege. Provenance must survive the container: files extracted from an archive, mounted from an ISO or VHD, or renamed must inherit the tag rather than lose it, and 'Enable Editing' on externally sourced documents must be blocked by policy rather than left to the user. The distinguishing test: mail a MOTW-tagged spreadsheet nested inside a ZIP to a managed workstation, extract it, and confirm the extracted file still opens in Protected View — a user-application-hardening attestation that covers only macro and ActiveX/OLE settings still lets a provenance-stripped document reach the vulnerable parser with full user privileges.
new_control_requirements.evidence: The in-the-wild attack FireEye reported to Microsoft delivered this exact CWE-94 sink through content carrying a malicious TrueType font, with Qualys' 2014-10-14 analysis naming an Office document as an exploit vector — so on the unpatched Windows population the provenance of the incoming document is the only lever an operator holds. The control's own caveat is sharper here than usual: the font is parsed by win32k.sys in the kernel, so the reduced-privilege render is a delivery-path control and not a containment boundary for this bug, and it must be paired with KB3000061 plus the reboot rather than treated as sufficient. Its value is that it bounds who can get a weaponised font in front of the parser during the window before that reboot lands.

CVE-2014-8439.name: Adobe Flash Player Dereferenced Pointer Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: A page loads a crafted SWF; Flash Player dereferences a pointer into memory it no longer owns, and with the heap arranged by the attacker that dereference becomes execution of attacker code inside the plugin process. Angler, Astrum and Nuclear delivered it as a commodity drive-by, so the victim's only action was visiting a page carrying a malicious advert.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none — PR:N; no account, no foothold, delivery is whatever page the user happens to load
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L; exploit-kit authors re-weaponised it within about a week of Adobe's incomplete October fix, and it was reliable enough for three separate kits to ship it
attack_vector.ai_factor: None. Kafeine identified continued exploitation by watching Angler, and Timo Hirvonen of F-Secure reverse-engineered the sample and established that the root cause was still present. Human sample analysis, on both the attacker's and the defender's side.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Not having Flash Player on user workstations at all — uninstalled, or at minimum click-to-play gated — which removes every exploit-kit Flash CVE simultaneously rather than one at a time. Failing that, the APSB14-26 update of 2014-11-25 with all browser processes restarted.
prevention.framework_requiring_it: CISA BOD 22-01 (KEV remediation, added 2022-05-25, due 2022-06-15; requiredAction: the impacted product is end-of-life and should be disconnected if still in use)
prevention.adequacy: Removal is complete and permanent; patching was neither. The 2014-10-14 release left the root cause in place, so for roughly six weeks an estate could be fully patched and fully exploitable at the same time.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Watching for the operational signal rather than the version number: repeated plugin-process crashes, and web-proxy evidence of landing-page-to-SWF-to-binary chains on rotating domains.
detection.adequacy: This was the only defence that could have caught the post-October window, because the version check passed on hosts that were still being compromised. It depends on someone treating browser crash telemetry as a security feed.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treating a host that ran an exploit-kit SWF as compromised at user level — rotate the user's credentials, hunt the second-stage binary, rebuild — rather than closing on the Flash update.
response.adequacy: Necessary. Exploit kits drop a second stage immediately; the runtime update removes the entry route and nothing that arrived through it.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: The control records deployment of the vendor fix, and the 2014-10-14 fix did not fix it; there is no compliance state for 'patched against an incomplete patch', and none at all for an end-of-life runtime.

NIST-800-53-CM-7.gap: Least-functionality inventories treat a browser plugin as part of the browser, so Flash is never surfaced as a separately removable component that could have closed the whole class.

NIS2-Art21-patch-management.gap: The obligation ends at applying the vendor release; the exposed window here opened because the vendor release was insufficient and closed only when an outside researcher forced a second one.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: B4 evidence rests on running supported, updated software — a state that was exploitable between October and late November 2014 and is unattainable for Flash Player at all after 2020-12-31.

AU-Essential-8-App-Hardening.gap: The requirement is right and the verification is thin: attestations cover the managed browser's policy and miss second browsers, portable builds and packaged AIR applications carrying the same runtime.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: Vulnerability management fed by advisories and scanners reported the estate remediated on 2014-10-14 and had no mechanism to re-open the finding while exploitation continued.

ISO-27001-2022-A.5.7.gap: The signal that would have re-opened the finding — an exploit kit still succeeding against patched clients — lives in operational threat intelligence, which most implementations of this control do not ingest at that granularity.

new_control_requirements.name: INCOMPLETE-PATCH-SEQUENCE-SEVERITY-MULTIPLIER
new_control_requirements.description: Vulnerability-management programs must apply a severity multiplier when a CVE is the Nth in an incomplete-patch sequence on the same primitive (third MOTW bypass, second AMSI bypass, etc.). Framework controls treating each CVE as discrete obscure the structural defect; the Nth CVE in a sequence implies that future bypasses on the same primitive are likely.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Adobe Flash Player is the clearest case of this pattern in the corpus: the 2014-10-14 APSB14-22 release hardened the symptom, Angler was exploiting the same root cause again within about a week, Astrum and Nuclear followed, and only the out-of-band APSB14-26 on 2014-11-25 shipped the real fix (Flash 15.0.0.239 / 13.0.0.258 / 11.2.202.424, AIR 15.0.0.293, AIR SDK 15.0.0.302). Applied to this product the control means an incomplete-fix signal on Flash raises the priority of the whole runtime rather than of one CVE id, and it points at the conclusion the estate eventually reached anyway — that a component drawing repeated incomplete fixes should be removed, which is what CISA's KEV requiredAction states outright.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
