new_control_requirements.evidence: For Adobe Flash Player the KEV entry (added 2022-05-25, due 2022-06-15) does not say patch — its requiredAction is that the impacted product is end-of-life and should be disconnected if still in use, which is the only verified mitigation available after Adobe's 2020-12-31 end of support and the 2021-01-12 content block. The control's 'verified' term therefore resolves to an uninstall confirmed on the endpoint across every Flash channel present (ActiveX, NPAPI, PPAPI) plus packaged AIR applications built on the affected SDK, not to a version number. The historic 2014 path — Flash 15.0.0.239 / 13.0.0.258 / 11.2.202.424 with every browser process relaunched — is recorded for context only; no host reboot was required, but a browser left running stayed vulnerable.

CVE-2015-0016.name: Microsoft Windows TS WebProxy Directory Traversal Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: Code already running inside the low-integrity Internet Explorer sandbox asks the browser to launch TSWbPrxy.exe, which the elevation policy permits at medium integrity, and hands it a traversal-laden path. Windows fails to sanitise that path, so the medium-integrity proxy starts the attacker's executable instead of its own — the sandbox is exited with the user's full rights, and no memory corruption is involved.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none — PR:N in the scored vector; operationally the attacker needs prior code execution inside the browser sandbox, which a paired Internet Explorer RCE supplies
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L; deterministic once the foothold exists, and a public Metasploit module has automated it since 2015-02-03 for x86 Windows 7 SP1 and earlier with IE 8 or IE 11
attack_vector.ai_factor: None. Microsoft names no reporter; the public analysis is credited to Henry Li, with an unnamed Symantec threat-intelligence contributor and juan vazquez writing the module — human reverse engineering of an in-the-wild chain.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Applying the right MS15-004 package for the host's Remote Desktop Client level and restarting; or, immediately and at no patch cost, deleting the TSWbPrxy entry {B43A0C1E-B63F-4691-B68F-CD807A45DA01} from the Internet Explorer low-rights elevation policy.
prevention.adequacy: Strong, and unusually so — Microsoft supplied a real workaround here rather than the 'no workarounds identified' it published for the other browser bugs in this family. Its limit is scope: it removes one broker from the policy and leaves every other entry in it untested.

detection.what_would_have_worked: An alert on TSWbPrxy.exe appearing as a child of iexplore.exe, or on any TSWbPrxy.exe child process, on hosts where RemoteApp is not in use.
detection.adequacy: Genuinely effective for this CVE, because the legitimate use of that binary is narrow and browser-launched instances are exceptional. It requires process-lineage telemetry to exist and to be retained, which on the 2015-era estates carrying this flaw is the weak assumption.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treating a host that escaped the sandbox as user-context compromised: rotate the user's credentials, audit user-writable persistence, and rebuild rather than close on the KB.
response.adequacy: Bounded but necessary. The escape lands at medium integrity rather than SYSTEM, so the compromise is the user's, which on a workstation is enough to keep an intrusion moving.

NIST-800-53-SC-39.gap: The process-isolation requirement is met by Protected Mode existing, while the set of brokers the sandbox may invoke — the actual boundary-crossing surface — is never enumerated or reviewed.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: The Important/EoP rating queues the escape behind the Critical RCEs it is chained with, and the four-KB variance across Remote Desktop Client versions lets a host be marked patched from the wrong package.

NIS2-Art21-patch-management.gap: The obligation recognises only the vendor patch, so the immediately deployable registry workaround that would have closed this in minutes is not a compliant action anyone gets credit for taking.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: Secure-build and patch-baseline evidence never reaches the elevation-policy registry key that decides whether this escape is reachable.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: The maturity metric counts installed OS updates and cannot express the multi-package variance, the restart, or the fact that every affected release is now end of life.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.9.gap: Configuration baselines do not enumerate the IE low-rights elevation policy, so its contents are neither approved nor drift-monitored, and Microsoft's own fix is a change to it.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: Prioritisation follows vendor severity and ignores exploit availability — a public Metasploit module has existed since 2015-02-03, which is what makes this trivially reusable.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: MS15-004 shipped on 2015-01-13 with Microsoft already aware of limited attacks chaining this TS WebProxy escape to a browser RCE, public exploit code followed on 2015-02-03 as Exploit-DB 35983, and CISA listed it in KEV on 2022-05-25 with a 2022-06-15 due date; EPSS is 0.7594 (99.484th percentile as of 2026-08-13), the highest in this set. This entry is the case where the control's 'or documented compensating controls' clause is genuinely usable inside four hours: deleting the elevation-policy key {B43A0C1E-B63F-4691-B68F-CD807A45DA01} is a registry change deployable by policy, ahead of the KB3019978 / KB3020387 / KB3020388 / KB3023299 package the host actually needs and its restart.

new_control_requirements.name: MITIGATION-ACTIVE-PATCH-PENDING-VERDICT-CLASS
new_control_requirements.description: Compliance verdicts must distinguish three states: (a) binary patch deployed (vulnerability eliminated), (b) vendor-mitigation rule active, no binary patch (residual risk: any defect in the mitigation rule reopens the vulnerability), (c) no mitigation, no patch (full exposure). Audit reports must surface (b) as a distinct compensating-control state with an associated time-bound action item, not as a 'patched per SLA' outcome.
new_control_requirements.evidence: MS15-004 is one of the few bulletins in this family that ships a real workaround, and it creates exactly the middle state the control describes: hosts whose IE elevation policy no longer contains {B43A0C1E-B63F-4691-B68F-CD807A45DA01} are protected against this escape while the underlying path-sanitisation defect is still in the binary, and any process that re-adds the key — a Remote Desktop Client install, an image restore, a repair — silently reopens it. Reporting those hosts as patched hides both the residual risk and the functional trade (RemoteApp and Desktop Connections no longer launch from Internet Explorer), and it removes the time-bound item to install KB3019978 or the matching Remote Desktop Client package and restart.

CVE-2015-0071.name: Microsoft Internet Explorer ASLR Bypass Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: A crafted page causes Internet Explorer 9-11 to load content whose addresses are not randomised, letting the attacker predict where specific instructions sit in memory. Nothing executes as a result — but the memory-corruption bug the attacker uses next now lands on known addresses, turning an unreliable exploit into a working one.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none — PR:N; the attacker needs only the victim's browser to load their page
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L; the bypass follows from how the browser loads a component rather than from any race or groom, but it is worthless without a paired memory-corruption vulnerability in the same session
attack_vector.ai_factor: Unknown finder — MS15-009 names no reporter for its ASLR bypasses and no public write-up identifies one. Nothing in the record suggests automated or AI-assisted discovery.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Completing both stages of MS15-009 (update 3021952, reboot, then 3034196) on every host running Internet Explorer 9-11, and structurally, removing Internet Explorer so its unrandomised loads are not in the estate.
prevention.adequacy: Adequate for this instance and no more. MS15-009 fixed three separate ASLR bypasses at once, which is the tell that the class recurs; patching one bypass does not establish that the browser now randomises everything it loads.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Treating clustered browser tab crashes as a security signal and correlating them with the sites visited, since the failures of the paired exploit are the only thing this bypass makes visible.
detection.adequacy: Very weak. A successful bypass produces no artefact at all — its entire purpose is to remove the crash that would otherwise have occurred — so detection realistically targets the memory-corruption partner, not this.

response.what_would_have_worked: Investigating the paired vulnerability rather than this one: if the bypass was used, code ran, and the responder's question is what the memory-corruption exploit delivered.
response.adequacy: Correct framing but dependent on knowing the pairing, which no public source establishes for this CVE. In practice a responder finds the payload first and never attributes the reliability stage at all.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: A CVSS 6.5 Security Feature Bypass with no confidentiality impact queues behind the bugs it enables, and the bulletin's two-stage install lets a half-updated host be reported as remediated.

NIS2-Art21-vulnerability-management.gap: Risk-based prioritisation has no rule that a mitigation-defeat bug inherits the severity of the class it unlocks, so the one bypass Microsoft recorded as exploited scores below its siblings.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: Exploit-mitigation evidence is collected at the OS level, while the defect is the mitigation not being applied inside the browser process that renders hostile content.

AU-Essential-8-App-Hardening.gap: The maturity model treats enabled exploit mitigations as the protection and never tests whether they are actually applied, which is precisely what this CVE denies.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: Scoring each CVE independently cannot represent a defect whose entire impact is making other CVEs exploitable, so it closes as a low-impact browser item.

NIST-800-53-SI-4.gap: There is nothing distinctive to monitor: a successful bypass suppresses the crash that would otherwise be the signal, so any claim of detection coverage for this class is unfounded.

new_control_requirements.name: PROTECTION-MECHANISM-FAILURE-CLASS-REGRESSION
new_control_requirements.description: Detonation chambers, EDR rules, and AppLocker/WDAC policies covering protection-mechanism classes (MOTW, SmartScreen, AMSI, ASR, WDAC, Driver Block Rules) must include class-level regression testing executed on every patch deployment, not just one-off bypass-CVE remediation. The test battery for class-X must include all historic class-X bypass primitives — incomplete patches re-introduce risk that one-off testing does not detect.
new_control_requirements.evidence: MS15-009 fixed three Internet Explorer ASLR bypasses in one bulletin — CVE-2015-0051, CVE-2015-0069 and this one — and only CVE-2015-0071 was recorded as exploited, which is the class-level pattern this control exists for: the mitigation kept failing in new places while each CVE was remediated as a discrete item. Applied here it means an estate that depends on ASLR as an exploit mitigation tests, after every browser update, that the randomisation actually holds for what the browser loads, rather than accepting that the specific 2015-02-10 bypass is closed. The verification target is the rendering process, not the operating system, since that is exactly where this defect lived while OS-level randomisation was on and correct.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Microsoft recorded this Internet Explorer 9-11 ASLR bypass as exploited when MS15-009 published on 2015-02-10, and CISA listed it in KEV on 2022-05-25 with a 2022-06-15 due date — against a CVSS of 6.5 that would otherwise have parked it in a low-priority queue, which is why the KEV clock rather than the severity band has to drive it. 'Verified' has a specific meaning for this update: MS15-009 installs in two stages on IE 9-11 (3021952, reboot, then 3034196), so verification means confirming the second update is present, and there are no documented compensating controls to fall back on because Microsoft identifies neither mitigating factors nor workarounds.

CVE-2015-0310.name: Adobe Flash Player ASLR Bypass Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: A malvertising-served SWF asks Flash Player for information it should not disclose — where objects and modules actually live in memory — and uses the answer to aim the memory-corruption exploit that follows. ASLR is on and irrelevant, because the attacker no longer has to guess. Angler delivered both stages together as a drive-by, with the payload running in memory.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none — PR:N; the victim loads a page and the kit does the rest
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L; the disclosure is a property of what the runtime returns rather than a race or groom, and Angler was serving it as commodity capability by around 2015-01-20
attack_vector.ai_factor: None. Adobe's APSB15-02 credits Yang Dingning, Timo Hirvonen of F-Secure and Kafeine — human exploit-kit monitoring and manual sample analysis, the same pipeline that produced CVE-2014-8439.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Not having Flash Player on user workstations — uninstalled or click-to-play gated — which would have closed this and the concurrent CVE-2015-0311 at once. Failing that, APSB15-02 on 2015-01-22 with every browser process relaunched.
prevention.framework_requiring_it: CISA BOD 22-01 (KEV remediation, added 2022-05-25, due 2022-06-15; requiredAction: the impacted product is end-of-life and should be disconnected if still in use)
prevention.adequacy: Removal is complete; patching was not sufficient in this window. The same kit kept succeeding against fully patched clients through a second Flash zero-day that had no fix, so patch currency bought very little here.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Proxy-side detection of the delivery infrastructure — SWF fetches from very recently registered domains that rotate within a day — plus treating plugin-process crashes as a security signal.
detection.adequacy: Partial and perishable. The kit rotated domains roughly daily and the payload ran in memory while avoiding commonly monitored API calls, so signature and reputation approaches were consistently behind; the infrastructure pattern, not the payload, was the durable signal.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treating any host that loaded an exploit-kit SWF as compromised at user level: hunt the in-memory stage and its download, rotate the user's credentials, rebuild.
response.adequacy: Necessary and harder than usual — an in-memory payload leaves little on disk, so a host that has been rebooted may present clean while the credentials it held are already in use elsewhere.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: Patching to the vendor's fix left the estate exposed to the same kit through a concurrent unpatched Flash zero-day; the control cannot represent an attacker holding a second flaw in the same chain.

NIST-800-53-CM-7.gap: Plugin removal would have closed both concurrent Flash zero-days at once, but least-functionality inventories never surface a browser plugin as a separately removable component.

NIS2-Art21-patch-management.gap: The attacker set the timeline — Angler was serving it about two days before Adobe published — so even instant patching misses the window, and no compliant patch state exists for Flash at all now.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: ASLR is the mitigation B4 evidence would cite, and this defect makes it irrelevant by disclosing the addresses it randomises, on software that was fully supported at the time.

AU-Essential-8-App-Hardening.gap: The requirement to block Flash in browsers is correct and outperformed patching here; verification typically covers only the managed browser and misses second browsers and per-user installs.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: Advisory- and scanner-fed vulnerability management learned of this on 2015-01-22 at the earliest, days after the exploitation traffic began.

ISO-27001-2022-A.5.7.gap: The usable intelligence was technical and perishable — rotating exploit-kit domains, a specific SWF stage — and most implementations of this control ingest strategic reporting that carries none of it.

new_control_requirements.name: PROTECTION-MECHANISM-FAILURE-CLASS-REGRESSION
new_control_requirements.description: Detonation chambers, EDR rules, and AppLocker/WDAC policies covering protection-mechanism classes (MOTW, SmartScreen, AMSI, ASR, WDAC, Driver Block Rules) must include class-level regression testing executed on every patch deployment, not just one-off bypass-CVE remediation. The test battery for class-X must include all historic class-X bypass primitives — incomplete patches re-introduce risk that one-off testing does not detect.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Adobe Flash Player produced ASLR-defeating address disclosure here in January 2015 and a separate exploited memory-corruption zero-day (CVE-2015-0311) in the same Angler campaign days later, which is the class-level failure this control describes: the mitigation an estate relied on for browser exploitation kept being nullified by the plugin itself while each CVE was remediated as a discrete item. Applied to this product it means that anywhere Flash Player still runs, the ASLR assumption is treated as unverified until re-tested against the runtime rather than the OS — and the honest conclusion of that test, once Adobe ended support on 2020-12-31, is that the assumption cannot be restored and the runtime must go.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Angler was exploiting this Flash Player defect from around 2015-01-20, Adobe shipped APSB15-02 out of band on 2015-01-22, and CISA's KEV entry (added 2022-05-25, due 2022-06-15) carries the requiredAction that the product is end-of-life and should be disconnected if still in use — so the verified mitigation this control demands is an uninstall confirmed per host and per Flash channel, not a version check. The four-hour framing is also the right one for the historic case: the vendor's own release came out of band precisely because the exploit was already in a commodity kit, and any interval measured in weeks was irrelevant to whether an estate was hit.

CVE-2015-1671.name: Microsoft Windows Remote Code Execution Vulnerability (CVE-2015-1671)

attack_vector.description: The victim opens a document or loads a page carrying an embedded TrueType font; the Windows DirectWrite library parses it, memory is corrupted, and the attacker's code runs with the rights of the process that did the rendering — which may be Office, a Lync client, or a Silverlight application in the browser. The same defect is reachable from six product families because they all render fonts through the one library.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none — PR:N; no account and no foothold, only that the font reaches the parser
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L; the attacker controls the font entirely and the library parses it on open, with no mitigating factors and no workarounds published by Microsoft
attack_vector.ai_factor: None claimed. MS15-044 records coordinated vulnerability disclosure and names no reporter, so the finder is unidentified; nothing in the record points to automated or AI-assisted discovery.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Applying MS15-044 across every channel it ships in — Windows 3045171, the matching .NET packages, Office 2007/2010, Lync, Live Meeting and Silverlight 5.1.40416.00 — restarting, and relaunching the client applications; plus removing Silverlight, Live Meeting and Lync 2010 where they were installed and unused.
prevention.adequacy: Sufficient only if all channels land. The single most common failure is patching Windows and calling it done while a Silverlight plugin stays at a build below 5.1.40416.00, and the 3045171 GDI+ regression gives teams a concrete reason to roll back.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Keeping endpoint antimalware current enough to carry the Exploit:Win32/CVE-2015-1671 family, and treating Office and Lync child processes and Silverlight plugin crashes as investigable events.
detection.adequacy: Real but narrow. A vendor signature keyed to observed samples catches those samples and a recompiled variant may pass it; it also only helps on hosts where the antimalware engine is current, which is rarely true on the legacy platforms this CVE lives on.

response.what_would_have_worked: Rebuilding a host that rendered a hostile font while unpatched and rotating the credentials it held, rather than closing the incident on the patch record.
response.adequacy: Appropriate. Code ran at the rendering process's privileges, so on a workstation the user's data and credentials are gone; installing the update afterwards removes nothing the attacker already placed.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: Prioritisation followed the bulletin's 'no known attacks' statement, and nothing in the process re-opened the finding when exploitation later appeared and CISA listed it in KEV.

NIST-800-53-CM-7.gap: The legacy components most likely to be installed and unused — Silverlight, Live Meeting, Lync 2010 — are exactly the ones least-functionality inventories miss, and Silverlight is the one MS15-044 also patches on Mac.

NIS2-Art21-patch-management.gap: The vendor update itself regressed (GDI+ text-outline crash, corrected by KB3065979 on 2015-05-21), and the obligation has no state for a patch that was applied, broke something, and was reverted.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: The affected products have different internal owners, so each attestation is locally true while the un-owned Silverlight plugin keeps the estate exposed.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: The application-patching and OS-patching controls each measure half of a defect that is remediated through both, and neither has an answer for Silverlight after its 2021-10-12 end of support.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: The asset evaluation rarely enumerates a shared font library reached from six product families, including Silverlight on Mac, so 'Windows patched' closes a finding that is still open elsewhere.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: MS15-044 published on 2015-05-12 stating no known attacks, and CISA later listed this DirectWrite TrueType defect in KEV on 2022-05-25 with a 2022-06-15 due date — so the KEV listing, not the original bulletin, is the event that should have driven the clock, and Microsoft's own Exploit:Win32/CVE-2015-1671 detection family shows why. There are no documented compensating controls to fall back on: the bulletin identifies neither mitigating factors nor workarounds, so 'verified mitigation' means every affected channel confirmed at the fixed level — Windows 3045171 with the matching .NET packages, Office 2007/2010, Lync, Live Meeting, and Silverlight at 5.1.40416.00 — with the host restarted and the client applications relaunched.

new_control_requirements.name: DOWNLOAD-PROVENANCE-ENFORCEMENT
new_control_requirements.description: Exploitation here requires the victim to open an attacker-supplied Office document, so on an estate that has not yet reached the fixed build the delivery path is the only enforceable control. Require Mark-of-the-Web on every Office file arriving by mail, web download, or untrusted file share, and require MOTW-tagged documents to open in Protected View — an isolated, reduced-privilege render — instead of the full parsing path that carries the CWE-94 sink at the user's own process privilege. Provenance must survive the container: files extracted from an archive, mounted from an ISO or VHD, or renamed must inherit the tag rather than lose it, and 'Enable Editing' on externally sourced documents must be blocked by policy rather than left to the user. The distinguishing test: mail a MOTW-tagged spreadsheet nested inside a ZIP to a managed workstation, extract it, and confirm the extracted file still opens in Protected View — a user-application-hardening attestation that covers only macro and ActiveX/OLE settings still lets a provenance-stripped document reach the vulnerable parser with full user privileges.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Microsoft names opening a specially crafted document as one of the two delivery routes into this DirectWrite font parser, alongside visiting a page with embedded TrueType fonts, and Office 2007 SP3 and Office 2010 SP2 are both in MS15-044's affected list — so document provenance is a real lever on the population that has not yet closed every patch channel. Two limits have to be stated with it: the second delivery route is an untrusted web page carrying embedded TrueType fonts, which document provenance does not touch at all; and a reduced-privilege render bounds what the attacker's code inherits without repairing the parser. It is a delivery-path control for the window before 3045171, the .NET packages, the Office and Lync updates and Silverlight 5.1.40416.00 all land and the applications are relaunched.

CVE-2015-1769.name: Microsoft Windows Mount Manager Privilege Escalation Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: A crafted USB volume carries symbolic-link metadata that Mount Manager resolves without validating the destination, so mounting the device writes an attacker-supplied binary into a privileged path on the system disk and that binary is then executed. It is a logic flaw, not memory corruption: the exploit is reliable first time on every affected build.
attack_vector.privileges_required: low — PR:L; the volume mounts in the context of a low-privileged interactive session, and the escalation carries the write to a location that session could not otherwise reach. Combined with AV:P this means an attacker with a few seconds at a keyboard and a USB port, not a network position.
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L; no race, no heap grooming, no information leak. The real constraint is physical: reaching a USB port on a host that auto-mounts removable volumes, which is the default on every build MS15-085 lists.
attack_vector.ai_factor: None claimed or evidenced. The bug surfaced through in-the-wild attack analysis rather than a research submission, and no vendor or researcher has described AI-assisted discovery or weaponization.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Applying MS15-085 (KB3071756) and rebooting, combined with device-installation policy that denies mounting of unapproved removable storage on physically exposed endpoints.
prevention.adequacy: The update fixes the link resolution, but it is a kernel-driver replacement gated on reboot, and on every affected build other than Windows 10 the operating system itself is now out of support — so applying the KB restores this one boundary on a platform that receives no other fixes. Device-installation policy bounds who can present a volume but does nothing for an approved device that has been tampered with.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Collecting the System-log MountMgr Event ID 100 record centrally, and alerting on executable creation in system-owned directories correlated with USB mass-storage enumeration.
detection.adequacy: Event ID 100 only exists on hosts that already carry the update, so it detects blocked attempts and is blind on precisely the unpatched machines that are exploitable. The behavioural correlation works on any build but needs endpoint telemetry from kiosks and shared terminals, which is the population least likely to be instrumented.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treating a confirmed insertion as endpoint compromise: image the host, hunt for the planted binary and any persistence it established, and rotate credentials that were used on that machine.
response.adequacy: Patching after the fact removes the write primitive and removes nothing the attacker already placed. Because the target class is often a shared or kiosk machine, the credential blast radius is every account that logged on to it during the exposure window, which is rarely enumerable after the fact.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: Flaw remediation is in place and MS15-085 is trackable, but a CVSS-6.6 / EPSS-0.04111 item never reaches the front of the queue, and SI-2 has no completion test that distinguishes an installed update from a rebooted host running the fixed driver.

NIST-800-53-MP-7.gap: Media-use restrictions are typically implemented as write-blocking for data-loss reasons; this exploit needs only mount, so a compliant read-only posture leaves the attack path open.

NIST-800-53-PE-3.gap: Physical access control is evidenced for data centres and restricted areas, not for the lobby kiosk, shop-floor terminal or meeting-room PC that supplies the AV:P precondition.

NIS2-Art21-patch-management.gap: Risk-proportionate patching assessed on the 6.6 base score defers this indefinitely, and the KEV listing that should override it is a US instrument with no standing in an Article 21 assessment; nothing requires a removal schedule for the unsupported builds most affected hosts run.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: System Security evidence is drawn from the managed fleet, while the USB-facing population is often outside configuration management; B4 offers no reboot-verified completion test.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: The patch-operating-systems control keys its clock to vendor severity, and MS15-085 is Important rather than Critical; the sharper failure is the supported-OS requirement, which almost every affected build now fails.

ISO-27001-2022-A.7.10.gap: Storage-media controls govern organisation-owned media — classification, transport, disposal — and never treat an unknown inserted device as untrusted input to the kernel.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: Identification works; evaluation fails, because a network-reachability exposure model scores a physical-access flaw as low even with a KEV due date of 2022-06-15, and the control cannot record 'unremediable, OS out of support'.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Microsoft's Mount Manager flaw scores 6.6 with an EPSS of 0.04111 (2026-08-13), so every severity-ranked patch queue sorts MS15-085 to the bottom while CISA's KEV listing of 2022-05-25 sets a 2022-06-15 deadline. Binding the clock to the KEV listing rather than to the CVSS band is the only mechanism that moves a physically-exploitable, low-scoring Windows kernel-driver fix onto the kiosk and point-of-sale population where it actually matters; the documented-compensating-control branch is what covers the affected Vista/7/8/8.1/Server builds that can no longer be brought to a supported state at all.

new_control_requirements.name: MITIGATION-ACTIVE-PATCH-PENDING-VERDICT-CLASS
new_control_requirements.description: Compliance verdicts must distinguish three states: (a) binary patch deployed (vulnerability eliminated), (b) vendor-mitigation rule active, no binary patch (residual risk: any defect in the mitigation rule reopens the vulnerability), (c) no mitigation, no patch (full exposure). Audit reports must surface (b) as a distinct compensating-control state with an associated time-bound action item, not as a 'patched per SLA' outcome.
new_control_requirements.evidence: MS15-085 replaces mountmgr.sys, which means a Windows host sits in a fourth state this taxonomy forces into the open: update installed, reboot outstanding, vulnerable code still running. Device-installation policy denying removable-storage mount is state (b) for this CVE — it bounds who can present the volume and does not repair the link resolution — and the affected Vista through Server 2012 R2 population that cannot reach a supported build is state (c) permanently. Reporting all three as 'patched per SLA' is how a 2022-06-15 KEV deadline gets closed on an estate where the exposed kiosks never rebooted.

attack_vector.description: A crafted application drives win32k.sys into using an object it has already freed; reclaiming that allocation with attacker-controlled data yields arbitrary kernel read and write, which the Duqu 2.0 module CTwoPENC.dll used to place shellcode in kernel space and bypass SMEP, executing at ring 0 as SYSTEM.
attack_vector.privileges_required: low — PR:L; an ordinary user account that can execute code on the host. The attacker never abuses the account model, so the escalation is invisible to per-account privilege review.
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L; a deterministic call sequence with no race and no prerequisite leak. Kaspersky described the resulting exploit as reliable and portable across the affected Windows range, which is why it was viable as an operational tool rather than a one-shot.
attack_vector.ai_factor: None. Kaspersky Lab found it through incident response on live Duqu 2.0 artefacts; no AI-assisted discovery or weaponization is claimed anywhere in the public record.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: MS15-061 applied and the host rebooted; strategically, moving multi-user hosts off the affected Windows generations entirely, since none of them is supported today.
prevention.adequacy: Honest limit: the patch postdates the intrusion. Against the zero-day window nothing in the prevention column applied, and the residual value of MS15-061 today is confined to legacy hosts that cannot be replaced — where it fixes one boundary on a platform receiving no other fixes.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Kernel-level telemetry that alarms on a privilege transition without a corresponding service, task or logon event, plus bugcheck monitoring for win32k.sys faults on multi-user hosts.
detection.adequacy: The escalation writes no file and creates no persistence, so file-integrity and signature-based tooling have nothing to match. Token-transition telemetry catches it in principle but is exactly the collection most estates do not run, and it must already have been shipping off-host before the intrusion to be of any use.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treating confirmed use as state-actor intrusion rather than a malware infection: rebuild affected hosts, rotate every credential that touched them, and audit for lateral movement through the exposure window.
response.adequacy: Patching after the fact removes the escalation primitive and nothing else. Duqu 2.0's design — minimal disk footprint, few hosts carrying persistence — means scoping the intrusion is the hard part, and standard malware-cleanup IR routinely closes the ticket at the one detected host.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: Flaw remediation only starts when a fix exists; this was burned as a zero-day, and today every affected platform is out of support, so SI-2 has no compliant remediation left to point at.

NIST-800-53-AC-6.gap: The attacker uses a legitimate low-privileged account, so per-account privilege scoping is never consulted; an AC-6 attestation passes while any user on the host can reach SYSTEM.

NIS2-Art21-vulnerability-handling.gap: The obligation assumes an advisory pipeline; there was none during the exploited window, and Article 21 does not require ingesting incident-derived vendor threat reporting as a vulnerability source.

NIS2-Art21-incident-handling.gap: A mid-chain kernel escalation generates no incident of its own, so handling the entry-vector alert satisfies the control while the SYSTEM foothold remains.

UK-CAF-C1.gap: Monitoring evidence built on file and process telemetry sees none of this step — no file write, no service, no new binary, just a token that changes.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: B4 reads green once MS15-061 is applied, and cannot be satisfied at all on the Server 2003 / 2008 / 7 hosts retained for application dependencies.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: Patch latency scores well and says nothing about the zero-day window; the maturity model's vendor-support requirement is failed by every build in the affected list.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: Ranking is not the problem at CVSS 8.8 / EPSS 0.14958; the control has no escalation route for 'burned as a zero-day by a state actor' and no way to record an unpatchable platform.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.16.gap: Monitoring implemented as log aggregation never collects the kernel-level token-transition evidence this escalation produces.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Microsoft shipped MS15-061 on 2015-06-09, two days before Kaspersky published the Duqu 2.0 paper naming CTwoPENC.dll as the CVE-2015-2360 carrier; the operators who patched inside that window closed the escalation before the technique became public. The CVE scores 8.8 with an EPSS of 0.14958 (percentile 0.96401 as of 2026-08-13) and CISA set a 2022-06-15 due date, and because the fix is a win32k.sys replacement the SLA has to be measured to reboot rather than to update approval. The documented-compensating-control branch is the only compliant answer for the Server 2003, Server 2008 and Windows 7 hosts in the affected list that can no longer reach a supported build.

new_control_requirements.name: NATION-STATE-INITIAL-ACCESS-IR-ESCALATION
new_control_requirements.description: IR runbooks must include an explicit nation-state-initial-access escalation path triggered by APT28/APT29/Lazarus/Volt-Typhoon/etc. attribution on a confirmed exploit chain. Standard malware-infection IR under-escalates nation-state activity by treating it as commodity threat.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2015-2360 reached the public record only because Kaspersky Lab treated an anomaly on its own network as a state-actor intrusion rather than a malware infection, and followed it into the Duqu 2.0 chain — the same chain that hit venues hosting the Iran nuclear negotiations. Applied to this CVE, the escalation trigger is the pairing of a Windows kernel escalation that leaves no disk artefact with an unexplained initial access: an estate that closes the entry-vector alert and never scopes the SYSTEM-level foothold has run commodity-malware IR against an espionage operation. KEV records ransomware use as Unknown for exactly this reason — the provenance here is espionage, and the response tier has to match it.

CVE-2015-2425.name: Microsoft Internet Explorer Memory Corruption Vulnerability (CVE-2015-2425)

attack_vector.description: Script on a crafted page drives Internet Explorer 11's jscript9.dll into using an object in its private JIT heap after it has been freed; reclaiming that allocation with controlled data produces an out-of-bounds write and, from there, code execution in the browser process as the logged-on user.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none — PR:N; the attacker needs no account on the target. The exploit inherits whatever rights the browsing user holds, which is why an administrator browsing the web turns a browser bug into a full host compromise.
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L with UI:R; the only user action is rendering the page. The constraint that actually bounds exposure is product scope: MS15-065 marks IE6 through IE10 not applicable, so only Internet Explorer 11 is reachable.
attack_vector.ai_factor: None. Vectra Threat Labs located the bug by reading a leaked Hacking Team email describing it and then reverse-engineering it manually; the 'Threat Labs' name is a team designation, not evidence of AI-assisted discovery.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Applying the MS15-065 cumulative Internet Explorer update and restarting; structurally, removing Internet Explorer as a general-purpose browser and confining it to an allowlist of internal application URLs.
prevention.adequacy: The update closes this defect and nothing more; MS15-065 fixed more than twenty IE issues in one cumulative, which is the actual cadence a browser of this vintage produced. Since 15 June 2022 there is no update stream at all, so on any surviving IE11 the only real prevention is not letting it render untrusted content.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Alerting on iexplore.exe spawning script hosts or command interpreters, and on repeated access-violation crashes in jscript9.dll across hosts visiting the same site.
detection.adequacy: Child-process alerting catches the payload stage, not the exploit, so it fires only if the attacker executes something visible — an in-process implant that never spawns a child is missed. Crash correlation needs Windows Error Reporting or equivalent telemetry aggregated across hosts, which most estates do not centralise.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treating a confirmed hit as a workstation compromise at user privilege: isolate, hunt for persistence, and rotate every credential entered on that machine.
response.adequacy: Applying the cumulative after exposure removes the flaw and nothing the attacker placed. Because the code ran as the logged-on user, browser-stored credentials, session cookies and any domain credential cached on the host stay valid until rotated.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: The July 2015 cumulative satisfies flaw remediation, but Microsoft recorded the CVE as already exploited on release day, and SI-2 has no way to record that IE11 now has no remediation stream at all.

NIST-800-53-CM-7.gap: Least functionality is evidenced through service and port baselines and almost never reaches 'this legacy browser must not render internet content', leaving the delivery path intact.

NIS2-Art21-patch-management.gap: Risk-proportionate patching addresses the 2015 fix; the live risk is a lifecycle question — IE11 out of support since 2022 — and Article 21 requires no dated retirement plan.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: System Security evidence cannot distinguish 'patched to the vendor's final release' from 'supported', which is the distinction that decides exposure here.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: Patch-latency metrics look clean against a product that no longer receives patches; the real finding is the maturity model's vendor-support requirement, failed by IE11.

AU-Essential-8-App-Hardening.gap: Browser hardening targets plug-ins, ads and scripting features; this defect is in the JavaScript engine itself and survives every one of those levers.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: Identification is trivial and evaluation is wrong-shaped: exposure turns on whether IE11 is installed and launchable, and the control cannot express 'remove, do not patch'.

new_control_requirements.name: BROWSER-MANAGED-UPDATE-NO-DEFERRAL
new_control_requirements.description: Enterprise update rings must not defer security-channel browser updates beyond 24h.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Microsoft published MS15-065 on 2015-07-14 already marking CVE-2015-2425 as publicly disclosed and exploited, so every day of update-ring deferral on Internet Explorer 11 was a day of known in-the-wild exposure on a browser with an EPSS of 0.44851 (percentile 0.98661 as of 2026-08-13). Applied to IE11 the control has a second half that matters more than the ring policy: the fix replaces jscript9.dll and needs a host restart, so a deferral that shows as 'installed' with the reboot outstanding still leaves the vulnerable engine mapped in every open browser process.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CISA listed this Internet Explorer 11 defect on 2022-05-25 with a 2022-06-15 due date — three weeks before the IE11 desktop application itself reached end of support on 15 June 2022, which is the situation the documented-compensating-control branch of this SLA exists for. For an estate that still runs IE11 for a legacy application there is no patch to deploy, so the compliant response is a recorded control — confining IE11 to an internal URL allowlist so it never renders attacker-supplied content — with a dated removal plan behind it, rather than a patch-state attestation against a browser that receives no patches.

CVE-2015-4495.name: Mozilla Firefox Security Feature Bypass Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: A crafted page injects script into Firefox's built-in PDF.js viewer and, via a native setter, has it evaluated in the local file context. The same-origin boundary collapses, remote script reads arbitrary local files as the browsing user, and the contents are POSTed to an attacker-controlled host. Nothing is written to disk and no process is spawned.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none — PR:N; no account on the target and no prior foothold. The exploit reads whatever the browsing user can read, which on a developer or administrator workstation is SSH keys and stored client credentials.
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L with UI:R; a single page view. Being a logic flaw rather than a memory-safety one, it is deterministic across builds and platforms, with no reliability tax and no crash to give it away.
attack_vector.ai_factor: None. Mozilla credits Cody Crews for the report, and the in-the-wild use predated it; no AI-assisted discovery or exploit development is claimed by Mozilla, ESET or the reporter.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Updating to Firefox 39.0.3 or ESR 38.1.1 on 2015-08-06 and restarting the browser process so the fixed PDF.js actually loaded.
prevention.adequacy: The update closes the injection path, but it arrived at least ten days after the campaign started serving on 2015-07-27, and on a workstation whose browser stays open for days the install is not the moment of remediation. Prevention also does nothing about material already read out of an exposed host.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Egress inspection of browser traffic for outbound POSTs carrying local file content, plus alerting on the browser process reading ~/.ssh, shell history and FTP/IM client configuration paths.
detection.adequacy: This is the only place the exploit is visible, and it is the collection most estates lack on workstation networks. Endpoint tooling looking for dropped files or spawned processes returns clean, which is why a compromised host looked healthy throughout.

response.what_would_have_worked: Rotating every credential reachable from the browsing user's home directory — SSH private keys, FTP/SVN client credentials, IM account passwords — and reviewing where those keys were used during the exposure window.
response.adequacy: This is the response that actually matters and the one no framework triggers. The stolen material stays valid indefinitely after the browser is patched, and the second wave's broader keyword-matching file collection means the rotation scope is 'anything credential-shaped in the user profile', which is hard to enumerate after the fact.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: Flaw remediation tracks installed version, not browser restart, so a host counts as remediated while the vulnerable PDF.js stays mapped in an open session.

NIST-800-53-SC-28.gap: At-rest protection is evidenced by disk encryption, which is irrelevant to files read by the user's own browser on a running, unlocked machine.

NIST-800-53-SI-4.gap: Monitoring built on process creation and file writes sees nothing; only egress content inspection of browser traffic surfaces the single POST this exploit produces.

NIS2-Art21-patch-management.gap: The obligation ends at the update; it attaches no credential-rotation duty to a vulnerability whose whole impact is disclosure of authentication material.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: System Security restores the software to a good state and provides no trigger converting a known exposure window into a rotation of what was readable during it.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: Measures deployment against installed version rather than browser restart, and is silent on post-exposure credential rotation.

AU-Essential-8-App-Hardening.gap: Hardening targets plug-ins, Java, ads and external PDF readers; PDF.js is the browser's own built-in viewer and none of those levers touch it.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: Evaluation under-rates a no-code-execution flaw whose read reaches private keys, and the control's only output is a patch decision when a rotation decision is equally required.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.16.gap: Monitoring evidence drawn from endpoint process and file telemetry cannot observe an exploit that creates neither.

new_control_requirements.name: BROWSER-MANAGED-UPDATE-NO-DEFERRAL
new_control_requirements.description: Enterprise update rings must not defer security-channel browser updates beyond 24h.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Mozilla shipped Firefox 39.0.3 and ESR 38.1.1 on 2015-08-06 stating the exploit was already in use, and ESET put the staging server live from 2015-07-27 — so the exposure window was already open when the update appeared and every deferral day extended it against an EPSS of 0.68657 (percentile 0.99278 as of 2026-08-13). For this CVE the control needs its completion condition stated in the browser's own terms: the fixed PDF.js loads only on browser-process restart, so an update ring that reports Firefox at 39.0.3 while the user's session has been open since before the install has not remediated the host.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CISA listed this Firefox PDF.js flaw on 2022-05-25 with a 2022-06-15 due date, and the verified-mitigation wording is what makes the SLA meaningful here: verification for this CVE cannot be a version string, because the exploit stops working only after the browser process restarts, and it cannot end at the browser at all, because the campaign ESET tracked from 2015-07-27 to 2015-08-08 harvested SSH private keys and stored FTP, SVN and IM client credentials that outlive the patch. On an estate where a Firefox build below 39.0.3 or ESR below 38.1.1 was exposed, the documented mitigation has to include rotating that material.

CVE-2015-6175.name: Microsoft Windows Kernel Privilege Escalation Vulnerability (CVE-2015-6175)

attack_vector.description: A crafted application run on a Windows 10 RTM host drives the kernel into mishandling an object in memory and executes attacker code in kernel mode, ending at full SYSTEM rights. Microsoft's fix is described as correcting how the kernel handles objects in memory; the specific primitive was never published.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none stated — PR:N with UI:R in the NVD vector, which reads as the crafted application arriving through a user action rather than the attacker holding a session in advance. Either way local code execution on the host is the entry condition, and the account it runs under needs no special rights.
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L; the application works deterministically. MS15-135 lists no mitigating factors and no workarounds, so on an affected build there is nothing to turn off while the cumulative update is pending.
attack_vector.ai_factor: None claimed. No finder is credited and no public analysis exists, so the discovery route is not established; nobody has described AI assistance in finding or weaponizing it.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Taking cumulative update KB3116869 on 2015-12-08 and rebooting, or — decisively — upgrading off Windows 10 1507, since MS15-135 marks version 1511 not applicable.
prevention.adequacy: The cumulative closes it, and on a host inside the servicing stream this is a non-event. On the machines that were actually exposed — pinned at build 10240 for a driver or application dependency — the update is the thing the pin exists to prevent, so prevention there means resolving the dependency, not deploying a KB.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Alerting on privilege transitions to SYSTEM that have no matching service or scheduled-task creation, and on kernel bugchecks on build 10240 hosts.
detection.adequacy: The escalation leaves no file and no persistence of its own, so signature-based endpoint tooling has nothing to match, and because no public exploit or sample exists there is no known artefact to write a rule against. Detection here is generic behavioural coverage, not CVE-specific.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treating a confirmed escalation on a pinned host as full compromise: rebuild rather than patch in place, and rotate credentials cached or used on the machine.
response.adequacy: A cumulative update applied afterwards removes the primitive and nothing an attacker with SYSTEM already established. On a machine pinned for compatibility, rebuilding also reinstates the pin unless the underlying dependency is dealt with, so the response is incomplete until the platform question is answered.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: Flaw remediation works inside the servicing stream and has no purchase on hosts deliberately excluded from it, which is exactly the exposed population.

NIST-800-53-AC-6.gap: The exploit runs at ordinary user rights and fails a boundary inside the kernel, so removing unnecessary administrator rights leaves it fully exploitable.

NIST-800-53-CM-3.gap: The change record authorising the build-10240 pin satisfies configuration change control while creating a permanently unpatchable host; nothing requires an expiry or a re-review when the branch leaves servicing.

NIS2-Art21-patch-management.gap: Risk-proportionate patching defers a CVSS-7.8 / EPSS-0.05169 local escalation, and the correct action — an operating-system upgrade — is outside what the article obliges.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: System Security evidence cannot distinguish a Windows 10 host receiving cumulative updates from one whose branch stopped receiving them; both appear as compliant Windows 10 endpoints.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: Patch latency is meaningless on a branch that receives no patches; the real finding is the vendor-support requirement, failed by Windows 10 1507.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: Evaluation under-weights a 0.05169 EPSS item Microsoft recorded as exploited on release day, and cannot record that the asset is unremediable because its branch is out of servicing.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Microsoft recorded this Windows 10 kernel flaw as exploited on the day MS15-135 shipped, 2015-12-08, while its EPSS of 0.05169 (2026-08-13) puts it near the bottom of any score-ranked queue — the exact inversion a KEV-driven clock exists to correct, with CISA's listing of 2022-05-25 setting a 2022-06-15 deadline. Binding the SLA to the KEV listing forces the question the CVSS band never raises on this entry: which hosts are still on build 10240, and why. Because the fix arrives in cumulative update KB3116869 and requires a reboot, the verified half of the requirement has to be measured against the running build revision rather than against update approval.

new_control_requirements.name: MITIGATION-ACTIVE-PATCH-PENDING-VERDICT-CLASS
new_control_requirements.description: Compliance verdicts must distinguish three states: (a) binary patch deployed (vulnerability eliminated), (b) vendor-mitigation rule active, no binary patch (residual risk: any defect in the mitigation rule reopens the vulnerability), (c) no mitigation, no patch (full exposure). Audit reports must surface (b) as a distinct compensating-control state with an associated time-bound action item, not as a 'patched per SLA' outcome.
new_control_requirements.evidence: MS15-135 explicitly records no mitigating factors and no workarounds for CVE-2015-6175, which collapses this taxonomy to two states on Windows 10 build 10240: patched, or fully exposed. There is no middle state to claim, so a host pinned at RTM for a driver or application dependency is state (c) and must be reported as such with a dated action item, not folded into a patch-compliance percentage. The pinning change record is the artefact that hides it — an authorised deviation with no expiry reads as governance rather than as the permanent exposure it is now that the 1507 branch is out of servicing.

CVE-2015-8651.name: Adobe Flash Player Integer Overflow Vulnerability (CVE-2015-8651)

attack_vector.description: A SWF on a crafted page computes a domain-memory offset that overflows Flash's bounds arithmetic, writes past the end of the backing ByteArray and overwrites the length field of an adjacent sprayed object. That single out-of-bounds write becomes arbitrary read and write across the process, and from there a vtable pointer replacement runs shellcode at the browsing user's privilege.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none — PR:N; the attacker needs no account, only that the victim's browser render the SWF. The payload inherits the browsing user's rights.
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L with UI:R; loading the page is the whole interaction. The heap spray Antiy documents (1,280 uint objects) is routine engineering for Flash of this era and needs no prior information leak, which is why five exploit kits carried it.
attack_vector.ai_factor: None. Reported by Kai Wang and Hunter Gao of Huawei's IT security department through ordinary vulnerability research; no AI assistance in discovery or weaponization is claimed by Adobe, the reporters, or the analyses of the in-the-wild sample.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Removing Adobe Flash Player from the estate — the answer both before and after APSB16-01. Failing that, taking the 2015-12-28 out-of-band update on every channel that delivers Flash, not just the one the inventory records.
prevention.framework_requiring_it: CISA BOD 22-01 (KEV remediation, added 2022-05-25; requiredAction: the impacted product is end-of-life and should be disconnected if still in use)
prevention.adequacy: Patching worked in 2016 and does not exist as an option now: Flash support ended 31 December 2020. The honest limit of the removal control is inventory completeness — the same engine reaches a workstation through four independent channels plus AIR-packaged applications, so removal succeeds only to the extent the enumeration did.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Alerting on plug-in host processes spawning children, on repeated Flash container crashes across hosts hitting the same site, and on SWF fetches from domains unrelated to the page being browsed.
detection.adequacy: Exploit kits repacked per victim, so signature detection on the SWF was a losing position throughout 2016 — the behavioural and redirect-chain signals were the ones that held. All of it is moot on an estate that has removed the runtime, which is why detection is the weaker lever here.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treating a hit as browser-user-level compromise with a ransomware expectation: isolate, hunt for the downloader stage, and check backups before assuming recovery.
response.adequacy: KEV records ransomware use as Unknown for this CVE, but Angler and Magnitude both delivered Cryptowall through it, so a response plan built on the KEV flag alone under-prepares. Removing Flash after an incident stops the next delivery and does nothing about what the first one installed.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: There is no remediation stream left after 31 December 2020, and SI-2 has no state for a dead component — the finding stays open with no control requiring removal.

NIST-800-53-CM-7.gap: Least functionality is evidenced through service and port baselines and rarely enumerates browser plug-ins, ActiveX controls or embedded AIR runtimes.

NIS2-Art21-patch-management.gap: The article obliges patching but not retirement, so a runtime with no updates since 2020 attracts no clock despite an EPSS of 0.67922 and five exploit kits having weaponized it.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: System Security cannot distinguish 'patched to the vendor's final release' from 'supported', and does not require enumerating the four channels that deliver the same engine.

AU-Essential-8-App-Hardening.gap: The control names Flash explicitly and works when implemented as removal; evidenced as a browser policy setting it misses second browsers, AIR applications and hosts rebuilt from older images.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: Patch-latency metrics look compliant against a product that receives no patches; the failing requirement is vendor support, whose remedy is removal.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.7.gap: Anti-malware deployment satisfies the control while losing to per-victim repacked SWFs from five exploit kits; the control cannot express that removing the runtime is the measure that works.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: Identification misses the multi-channel delivery of the same engine, and evaluation has no vocabulary for 'end-of-life, disconnect' as the required disposition.

new_control_requirements.name: EOL-ASSET-DECOMMISSION
new_control_requirements.description: This entry is the case the control exists for, and it carries both halves. patch_available is true — a fixed build carrying this JavaScriptCore fix exists — and the vector itself states that the impacted product could be end-of-life and/or end-of-service and that users should discontinue product utilization. Those facts together define the requirement: on a unit whose hardware can still take an Apple security update, reaching the fixed build is an interim state; on a unit that can no longer take one, the terminal state is removal or replacement, because that device is exposed not only to this code-execution flaw but to everything found in that engine since its last build. Scope to what the packet names — macOS, iOS, tvOS, Safari and watchOS — and inventory those. The packet ties the CWE-94 sink to JavaScriptCore in those products and gives no mapping into other vendors' browsers or other software that embeds a web engine, so treating every renderer in the estate as an instance of this CVE manufactures findings and replacement work against software no evidence implicates. In operational terms: enumerate every macOS, iOS, tvOS, watchOS and Safari install that renders untrusted web content, record for each whether its hardware can still receive a build carrying the fix, put those on the interim clock against the 2025-10-20 KEV listing, and put the rest on a dated replacement schedule — a risk acceptance with no removal date leaves a KEV-listed flaw with a public PoC and confirmed exploitation in service indefinitely. Precondition on the interim half: live_patch_available is false and the vendor patch typically requires a service restart or system reboot per the KEV requiredAction, so a device that downloaded the update but has not restarted still runs the vulnerable code and is not remediated. And because exploitation is confirmed and delivery is attacker-controlled web content, a device that rendered untrusted content while exposed belongs on the incident path rather than being closed on the patch record.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Adobe Flash Player is the archetype the control describes, and CISA states the disposition outright in this CVE's KEV entry of 2022-05-25: 'The impacted product is end-of-life and should be disconnected if still in use.' A fixed build exists — 20.0.0.267 on Windows and OS X, 18.0.0.324 for the extended-support release, 11.2.202.559 on Linux, AIR at 20.0.0.233, all from APSB16-01 on 2015-12-28 — and reaching it is now meaningless, because Adobe ended Flash support on 31 December 2020 and the runtime is exposed to everything found in it since. The inventory the control demands has to enumerate every channel separately for this product: standalone NPAPI and PPAPI installs, the Chrome-bundled build, the Microsoft-serviced build in Edge and Internet Explorer, the ActiveX control, and AIR-packaged desktop applications that embed the runtime with no browser involved. Adobe AIR needs its own determination rather than inheriting Flash's status, since that line moved to HARMAN and remains maintained.

new_control_requirements.name: INCOMPLETE-PATCH-SEQUENCE-SEVERITY-MULTIPLIER
new_control_requirements.description: Vulnerability-management programs must apply a severity multiplier when a CVE is the Nth in an incomplete-patch sequence on the same primitive (third MOTW bypass, second AMSI bypass, etc.). Framework controls treating each CVE as discrete obscure the structural defect; the Nth CVE in a sequence implies that future bypasses on the same primitive are likely.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Antiy Labs' analysis places CVE-2015-8651 as the third public defect in Flash's domain-memory bounds checking, after CVE-2013-5330 and CVE-2014-0497 — the same ApplicationDomain.currentDomain.domainMemory access path, the same class of imprecise address-range validation. Treating it as a discrete item is what produced the 2016 outcome: Adobe patched it on 2015-12-28 and Angler, Neutrino, Nuclear Pack, Magnitude and RIG picked it up between 2016-01-25 and 2016-04-07, with the domain-memory primitive continuing to yield bugs afterwards. The multiplier applied at the time would have converted 'apply APSB16-01' into 'this runtime keeps producing the same defect — remove it', which is the disposition CISA eventually recorded on the KEV entry anyway.

CVE-2016-0034.name: Microsoft Silverlight Runtime Remote Code Execution Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: A crafted Silverlight application on a web page supplies a decoder that returns negative offsets; Silverlight does not validate the decoder's result and replaces object headers with attacker-supplied content, which yields code execution with the rights of the logged-on user.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none — PR:N; no account on the target. The exploit inherits the browsing user's rights, so an administrator browsing the web turns a plug-in bug into full control of the host.
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L with UI:R; loading a page carrying the Silverlight application is the whole interaction, and Microsoft notes the delivery can be a banner advertisement rather than a compromised destination. MS16-006 lists no mitigating factors and no workarounds.
attack_vector.ai_factor: None. Kaspersky Lab found it by hand-writing a YARA rule from strings in an earlier exploit by the same author and waiting for it to fire — human reasoning through a signature engine, which is not AI-assisted discovery and has not been described as such by anyone involved.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Removing the Silverlight runtime from workstations, which for most organisations was possible years before 2016; failing that, applying MS16-006 to reach build 5.1.41212.0 and restarting the browser.
prevention.framework_requiring_it: CISA BOD 22-01 (KEV remediation, added 2022-05-25; requiredAction: the impacted products are end-of-life and should be disconnected if still in use)
prevention.adequacy: MS16-006 closes this defect and nothing more, and Silverlight now receives no updates at all — so the patch route has expired and only removal remains. The honest limit on removal is the internal application that still requires the plug-in: that is an application-replacement decision on a schedule, not a policy toggle.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Alerting on .xap fetches from domains unrelated to the page being browsed, on plug-in host processes spawning children, and on mass file modification across mapped shares after a browsing session.
detection.adequacy: Angler and RIG repacked per victim, so signature detection on the exploit was unreliable; the redirect-chain and behavioural signals held better. The mass-modification signal fires only once encryption has begun, which bounds the loss rather than preventing it.

response.what_would_have_worked: Running the ransomware path rather than the malware-cleanup path: isolate the workstation, establish which shares the browsing user could write to, and restore from a backup the compromised credentials could not reach.
response.adequacy: KEV records ransomware use as Known for this CVE and Angler delivered TeslaCrypt through it, so the response tier is set by the payload, not the CVSS score. Reimaging the workstation resolves the endpoint and none of the encrypted share content.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: No remediation stream exists for an end-of-life runtime, and the control tracks KB installation rather than the browser restart that actually ends exposure.

NIST-800-53-CM-7.gap: Least functionality evidenced through service and port baselines does not enumerate browser plug-ins, so a compliant estate can leave Silverlight loadable on every workstation.

NIS2-Art21-patch-management.gap: The article obliges patching, not retirement, so an unsupported plug-in with an EPSS of 0.58541 and confirmed ransomware delivery attracts no decommissioning clock.

NIS2-Art21-business-continuity.gap: Continuity planning written for infrastructure failure does not cover an encryption event that starts with a user loading a web page and spreads to user-writable shares.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: System Security cannot distinguish 'patched to the vendor's final release' from 'supported', nor an installed-but-unreachable runtime from a loadable one.

UK-CAF-D1.gap: Response and recovery evidence rarely rehearses the path from an exploit-kit hit on a workstation to assessing and restoring the file shares that user could write to.

AU-Essential-8-App-Hardening.gap: Evidenced as a browser policy setting rather than proof of uninstallation, so a second browser or a rebuilt image reinstates the plug-in under a clean attestation.

AU-Essential-8-Backup.gap: Server-focused backup coverage with untested restores and credential-reachable backup stores meets the control and loses the user shares a TeslaCrypt delivery encrypts.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.7.gap: Anti-malware deployment satisfies the control while losing to per-victim repacked payloads from Angler and RIG; removal of the runtime is the measure that works and the control cannot say so.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: Identification is easy and evaluation produces a patch decision, when the correct disposition is removal of an end-of-life plug-in.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.13.gap: Backup evidence covers schedules and retention without establishing tested restores or a backup store unreachable by the compromised workstation's credentials.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CISA listed this Silverlight defect on 2022-05-25 with a 2022-06-15 due date and flagged knownRansomwareCampaignUse as Known — the only entry in this Microsoft/Adobe cohort so flagged, and it is earned: Angler EK delivered TeslaCrypt through this exploit from 2016-02-22. For an estate that still runs Silverlight for a legacy application there is no patch left to deploy beyond 5.1.41212.0, so the compliant answer is the documented-compensating-control branch — the plug-in confined so it never renders internet content, with a dated application-replacement plan behind it — and, because the payload is ransomware, a tested restore path for the shares a browsing workstation can write to rather than a backup schedule alone.

CVE-2016-0984.name: Adobe Flash Player and AIR Use-After-Free Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: Attacker-supplied SWF content drives Sound.loadPCMFromByteArray past a miscomputed size check; the load throws after the internal PCM buffer is freed and leaves the pointer live, and Sound.extract then reads the freed allocation. The result is a read of adjacent heap memory in the Flash or AIR process, usable for an information leak and, chained with a write bug, for code execution at the privilege of the user running the browser.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none - PR:N; the attacker only needs the victim to load a page or an AIR application that plays attacker-supplied sound data
attack_vector.complexity: low - AC:L; but the real constraint is that the primitive reads only. Project Zero reached code execution by pairing it with CVE-2016-0998, so a standalone exploit of this CVE yields disclosure rather than control.
attack_vector.ai_factor: None. Human reverse engineering of the Flash sound path by Google Project Zero, with the analysis published as a blog post rather than produced by tooling.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Not installing or enabling the Flash Player plugin and the AIR runtime at all - the only control that survives the product's end of life. Where Flash was business-required in 2016, updating to 18.0.0.329 / 20.0.0.306 / 11.2.202.569 and AIR 20.0.0.260 closed this specific instance.
prevention.adequacy: Patching was adequate only while Adobe shipped builds. Since 2020-12-31 there is no fixed version to reach, so a prevention story that ends at 'apply the vendor update' is unachievable for this entry and only removal closes it.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Software inventory that flags any Flash Player or AIR runtime present on an endpoint, plus browser telemetry on plugin content loaded from untrusted origins. Renderer-crash telemetry catches the failed-read case.
detection.adequacy: Weak against a successful exploit: a read primitive that lands cleanly produces no crash, no new process and no file on disk, so detection here is essentially exposure detection rather than exploitation detection.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treat a host that rendered untrusted SWF content while carrying a vulnerable build as an information-disclosure incident, and rotate anything the browser process held - session cookies, saved credentials, tokens - rather than closing the ticket on plugin removal.
response.adequacy: Bounded. Removing Flash stops further exploitation but recovers nothing already read out of process memory, and there is no artefact left behind to scope the exposure from.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: SI-2 is nominally met by a patch programme that reports 'no vendor update available' for an end-of-life product. The control has no mechanism that converts an unpatchable KEV entry into a removal task with a date.

NIST-800-53-CM-7.gap: Least-functionality baselines of the period permitted Flash as business-required and were never re-decided when Adobe ended support, so the control passed while the vulnerable runtime stayed installed.

NIS2-Art21-patch-management.gap: Patch management evidence showing no available update satisfies the article's letter while the KEV required action - disconnect the product - remains undone.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: B4 read as 'are updates applied' returns achieved on an unmaintained component; it needs to be read as 'is this software still supported', which is the question that fails here.

AU-Essential-8-App-Hardening.gap: The Essential Eight names Flash removal explicitly, but organisations self-assessing at a lower maturity kept Flash for named business applications and recorded the control as met while the exploit path stayed open in the browser.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: A vulnerability register that records the 2016 fixed versions as the treatment is stale: those builds are themselves unsupported, so the register documents a remediation that no longer exists.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CISA listed Adobe Flash Player and AIR CVE-2016-0984 on 2022-05-25 with a 2022-06-15 due date and a required action of disconnection rather than patching, because Flash Player had already been end-of-life since 2020-12-31. This entry is exactly the case the control's 'or documented compensating controls' clause exists for: the 2016 fixed builds (18.0.0.329, 20.0.0.306, 11.2.202.569, AIR 20.0.0.260) are unreachable as a supported target, so the verified mitigation an operator can actually deploy inside the clock is removal of the runtime and of the SWF content that depends on it, recorded as the closing evidence. EPSS still reads 0.55375 at the 98.944th percentile on 2026-08-13, so treating the entry as historical is not defensible.

new_control_requirements.name: INCOMPLETE-PATCH-SEQUENCE-SEVERITY-MULTIPLIER
new_control_requirements.description: Vulnerability-management programs must apply a severity multiplier when a CVE is the Nth in an incomplete-patch sequence on the same primitive (third MOTW bypass, second AMSI bypass, etc.). Framework controls treating each CVE as discrete obscure the structural defect; the Nth CVE in a sequence implies that future bypasses on the same primitive are likely.
new_control_requirements.evidence: The NVD record for CVE-2016-0984 states outright that it is 'a different vulnerability than CVE-2016-0973, CVE-2016-0974, CVE-2016-0975, CVE-2016-0982, and CVE-2016-0983' - six use-after-free issues in the same Flash Player release, fixed together in APSB16-04 in February 2016. Project Zero's write-up adds the structural finding: Adobe's isolated-heap mitigation did not contain this one because the freed object lived in the primitive-data partition. A programme that scored each of the six discretely saw six mediums-to-highs; the multiplier this control requires would have surfaced the correct conclusion, which is that the Flash sound and heap-mitigation surface would keep producing these and that Flash removal, not the next monthly Flash update, was the treatment.

CVE-2016-1010.name: Adobe Flash Player and AIR Integer Overflow Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: Crafted Flash content makes a size calculation overflow, so Flash Player allocates a buffer smaller than the data written into it and the write runs into neighbouring heap objects.
