new_control_requirements.evidence: CISA listed CVE-2022-30333 on 2022-08-09 with ransomware use Known and a 2022-08-30 due date, pointing operators at the RARLAB 6.12 release; RarLab had been notified on 2022-05-04. The 'documented compensating controls' branch matters for this component because the fastest deployable mitigation on a mail server is removing or replacing the unrar binary the attachment scanner invokes, which needs no vendor package and no restart since the extractor is exec'd per message.

new_control_requirements.name: TIER-3-DEPENDENCY-INVENTORY
new_control_requirements.description: Supply chain inventory must extend to tier-3 dependencies (dependencies of dependencies of direct dependencies). SBOM coverage for libsystemd-class transitive dependencies cannot be omitted under SR-3.
new_control_requirements.evidence: The chain on the affected estates is Zimbra invoking Amavis invoking RARLAB's unrar — the operator procured one product and inherited a third-party extractor that processes attacker-controlled bytes from every inbound message. RARLAB published no advisory, so nothing propagated up the chain, and the fixed level is expressed as UnRAR 6.12 binary / 6.1.7 source, a version string no mail-platform inventory carries. Inventory that reaches the extractor is the difference between having something to patch on 2022-08-09 and having nothing in the queue.

CVE-2022-34713.name: Microsoft Windows Support Diagnostic Tool (MSDT) Remote Code Execution Vulnerability (CVE-2022-34713)

attack_vector.description: A crafted .diagcab causes the Windows troubleshooting stack to copy a diagnostic package directory from an attacker-controlled network file system before verifying its signature. The file system returns names containing ..\..\, the copy honours them, and an executable lands in the user's Startup folder to run at next logon.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none — PR:N; the attacker holds no account and the payload runs as the user who opened the file
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L with UI:R; the temp path the copy targets is deterministic, so reliability is high, and the real work is getting the victim to open a file that reaches an attacker-controlled WebDAV or SMB share
attack_vector.ai_factor: Manual reverse engineering of sdiageng.dll by an independent researcher, published in January 2020 with working Perl PoC code and a Dockerised rogue WebDAV server. No AI-assisted discovery is claimed for either the original primitive or the 2022 variant.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Denying outbound WebDAV and SMB to untrusted destinations and removing the .diagcab handler association — both available since the 2020 publication — then installing the August 2022 cumulative update and confirming every host restarted onto it.
prevention.adequacy: BOD 22-01 arrives two and a half years after working exploit code was public. For the whole interval there was no CVE, no advisory and no directive, so the only operators protected were those who hardened against a technique rather than against an identifier.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Alerting on writes into a user's Startup folder that do not originate from an installer or management agent, correlated with outbound WebDAV from the same host.
detection.adequacy: Reliable, because a legitimate Startup-folder write from the diagnostic stack does not occur. It fires after the traversal has already succeeded — this is containment before the next logon, not prevention.

response.what_would_have_worked: On a host that opened a .diagcab from an untrusted source, treating the Startup folder as an execution list to audit and reviewing what ran at the following logon, rather than closing the case on the patch record.
response.adequacy: Cheap and effective for a single suspected host, and useless at fleet scale without the process and file-write telemetry above having been collected beforehand.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: SI-2 governs applying vendor fixes and offers nothing for the two and a half years between the 2020-01-15 public PoC and Microsoft's 2022-08-04 decision to issue one.

NIST-800-53-CM-7.gap: Least-functionality baselines cover services, ports and software, not file-type handler associations or outbound WebDAV reachability — the two dispensable preconditions this exploit needs.

NIST-800-53-SI-3.gap: Anti-malware is handed a cabinet file and a write performed by a trusted Windows component; its first decision point comes after the payload is already positioned to run.

NIS2-Art21-patch-management.gap: Cadence is adequate; completion is evidenced from console approval rather than each host's running build, which is precisely where a reboot-gated fix is over-reported as done.

NIS2-Art21-vulnerability-handling.gap: A publicly exploitable defect with no CVE and no vendor advisory produces no record in a feed-driven handling process, so the exposure was invisible for two and a half years.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: A fully compliant, fully patched July 2022 workstation build still opened .diagcab files and could mount an external WebDAV share.

AU-Essential-8-App-Hardening.gap: The control is written around browsers, Office, PDF and Java; a .diagcab handled by a Windows diagnostic component is outside every clause of it.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: The one-month workstation window puts the compliant deadline in September 2022 for a flaw with public exploit code since 2020 and confirmed exploitation before the KEV listing.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.7.gap: Every binary in the chain up to the Startup-folder write is signed by Microsoft, so malware protection is never presented with something to reject in time.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: Feed-driven vulnerability management had no CVE and no advisory to consume between January 2020 and August 2022, so the entire pre-CVE exposure window is unassessed by design.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Microsoft's record for CVE-2022-34713 carries Exploitation Detected: Yes with a functional-exploit temporal vector (E:F/RL:O/RC:C), and CISA listed it on 2022-08-09 with a 2022-08-30 due date. Because the August 2022 cumulative update is reboot-gated on a Windows workstation fleet, the control's compensating-controls branch is what an operator can actually complete inside four hours — blocking .diagcab at the mail and web boundary and denying outbound WebDAV and SMB — while the restart is driven across the estate.

new_control_requirements.name: INCOMPLETE-PATCH-SEQUENCE-SEVERITY-MULTIPLIER
new_control_requirements.description: Vulnerability-management programs must apply a severity multiplier when a CVE is the Nth in an incomplete-patch sequence on the same primitive (third MOTW bypass, second AMSI bypass, etc.). Framework controls treating each CVE as discrete obscure the structural defect; the Nth CVE in a sequence implies that future bypasses on the same primitive are likely.
new_control_requirements.evidence: This is the second exploited Windows diagnostic-tool flaw of 2022 after Follina (CVE-2022-30190) in May, and Rapid7 records Microsoft describing it as a variant of the DogWalk issue that was reported on 2019-12-22, declined, and published with working code on 2020-01-15. Scored as a discrete CVSS 7.8 workstation item it sits behind higher-scored monthly entries; scored as the second exploited defect in the same component within one quarter, with a two-year-old public PoC, it is the item to expedite — and it predicts that further defects in the same diagnostic stack are likely rather than exceptional.

CVE-2022-37042.name: Synacor Zimbra Collaboration Suite (ZCS) Authentication Bypass Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: The mailbox-import servlet computes an authentication failure and forgets to return, so it rejects the caller in the HTTP response and extracts the submitted archive anyway. Paired with the unfixed relative-path handling, one unauthenticated POST plants a JSP in the web root of a server holding every mailbox in the organisation.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none — PR:N; the incomplete fix for CVE-2022-27925 removed the administrator precondition entirely
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L, UI:N; a single POST, with the operationally significant twist that a successful exploit returns 401, so error-response monitoring reads the attack as a blocked login
attack_vector.ai_factor: Identified by Volexity Threat Research during incident response on compromised servers, then published with detection guidance and reference file lists. No AI-assisted discovery is claimed.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Reaching 8.8.15 Patch 33 or 9.0.0 Patch 26 as soon as it shipped in late July 2022, and — for the preceding month when no fix existed — restricting the /service/extension/backup/ path at the reverse proxy so it could not be reached from the internet.
prevention.adequacy: The directive's 2022-09-01 due date lands six weeks after mass exploitation began at the end of June. The proxy restriction is the only measure available during the window with no patch, and no framework required it.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Alerting on POSTs to /service/extension/backup/mboximport that return 40x, and diffing the deployed JSP set against the vendor's default list for the installed release.
detection.adequacy: Both work, and both invert normal practice: a 401 has to be read as success rather than as a blocked attempt, and the JSP baseline only became available when Volexity published it on 2022-08-10.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treating any internet-facing ZCS instance that ran below Patch 33 / Patch 26 during summer 2022 as compromised — exporting configuration, rebuilding, and rotating mailbox, admin and service credentials rather than upgrading in place.
response.adequacy: The only response that removes the implant, and the most expensive one available, since it takes the organisation's mail down. That cost is why most operators upgraded in place and left the webshell resident.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: The first vendor fix was incomplete, and SI-2 has no mechanism for reopening a closed finding when a patch turns out to be partial — the asset read as remediated throughout the exploitation window.

NIST-800-53-AC-3.gap: The access decision is computed and then not enforced, so every artefact an assessor examines — including the 401 in the log — is evidence the control works while unauthenticated callers write to disk.

NIST-800-53-SI-4.gap: Monitoring treats 401 as a blocked attempt; here it is the signature of a completed upload, so tuning either buries the event in brute-force noise or suppresses it.

NIS2-Art21-patch-management.gap: For roughly a month of the exploitation window no patch existed, so a programme measured on patch currency reports no failing for the period in which the compromises occurred.

NIS2-Art21-incident-handling.gap: Detection required a vendor default-JSP baseline that did not exist publicly until 2022-08-10, so a compliant process had nothing to trigger on.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: Running a supported line with vendor patches applied was true of exposed Network Edition estates in June 2022, and a deployment that needs mailbox import cannot drop the licensed backup extension that serves mboximport, so B4 offers no remaining lever short of re-platforming to Open Source Edition.

UK-CAF-D1.gap: Mail-platform response plans are written for availability events, not for treating the mail server as attacker-controlled infrastructure whose secrets must be assumed read.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: Adequate against the late-July release, useless for the preceding month, and never applied at internet-facing speed by estates that classified ZCS as an internal mail server.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: The vendor's advisory is a patch announcement with no exploitation context, so a good-faith A.8.8 response schedules routine maintenance instead of incident response.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.16.gap: Mail-platform monitoring covers mail flow, authentication and availability; the signals here are web-endpoint access patterns and web-root filesystem drift, which are out of scope.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2022-37042 is a PR:N, CVSS 9.8 pre-authentication code-execution path into Zimbra ZCS 8.8.15 and 9.0.0, listed by CISA on 2022-08-11 with ransomware use Known and EPSS 0.91893 (99.809th percentile as of 2026-08-13). The control's compensating-controls branch is what covers the month between exploitation starting at the end of June 2022 and the 8.8.15P33 / 9.0.0P26 fix arriving in late July — blocking /service/extension/backup/ at the reverse proxy is deployable in minutes and needs no vendor release.

new_control_requirements.name: PERIMETER-COMPROMISE-REBUILD-NOT-PATCH
new_control_requirements.description: Pre-rehearsed IR runbook for any perimeter device that suffers a pre-auth RCE CVE in active exploitation MUST default to config-exfil + rebuild + credential rotation, not patch-in-place. Patch-in-place leaves attacker-installed implants intact.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Volexity counted over 1,000 internet-facing Zimbra ZCS instances already carrying webshells when it published on 2022-08-10, with exploitation dating to the end of June — before 8.8.15 Patch 33 and 9.0.0 Patch 26 existed. Upgrading to those levels closes the servlet and leaves every JSP written beforehand in place on a host that holds the organisation's entire mail store, which is why an exposed ZCS instance belongs on the config-export, rebuild and credential-rotation path rather than the patch path.

CVE-2026-20349.name: Cisco Secure Firewall Adaptive Security Appliance (ASA) and Secure Firewall Threat Defense (FTD) Heap Inspection Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: One crafted HTTP request to the Remote Access SSL VPN service hits a path where errors are not checked adequately, and the firewall reloads. The service must answer unauthenticated internet clients to do its job, so there is no access-control layer in front of the defect and no workaround the vendor can offer short of the fixed build.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none — PR:N; the target service is designed to answer arbitrary internet clients before any authentication takes place
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L, UI:N; a single request with no race, no groom and no prior foothold, gated only by whether the device carries one of the advisory's three vulnerable configurations — SSL VPN, IKEv2 remote access with client services, or Zero Trust Network Access on FTD
attack_vector.ai_factor: Credited by Cisco to Valerio Brussani (@val_brux, harmonyguard.cloud) together with Cisco internal security testing. The researcher's security-company affiliation is branding, not evidence of AI-assisted discovery, and the advisory attributes no automated analysis.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Taking the per-train hotfix named in cisco-sa-asaftd-vpn-dos-dzv4mQFF and reloading each unit, sequenced across HA members, inside the three-day BOD 26-04 window that opened on 2026-08-11 and closed on 2026-08-14.
prevention.adequacy: It is the only measure that works — Cisco states there are no workarounds — and it demands a reload of the device every remote worker connects through, inside three days. The requiredAction's alternative, discontinuing use of the product, is the honest fallback for a unit that cannot take the change.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Off-box syslog to a collector in a separate trust zone, so the reload event and the HTTP traffic that preceded it survive the restart and can be correlated rather than lost with the process.
detection.framework_requiring_it: CISA BOD 26-04 Forensics Triage Requirements (cited in the KEV requiredAction)
detection.adequacy: This is what makes the difference between reporting an availability incident and evidencing an exploitation attempt, and it only helps if it was already in place — telemetry cannot be collected retrospectively from a device that has restarted.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treating repeated unscheduled reloads on a VPN-enabled ASA or FTD as attack rather than instability: preserving the crashinfo from disk0:, escalating to Cisco TAC, and prioritising that unit's hotfix ahead of the rest of the fleet.
response.adequacy: Correct and bounded. Its limit is that this CVE's impact is availability only — there is no confidentiality or integrity effect to hunt for — so the response is restoring and patching the device, not an intrusion investigation, unless other findings say otherwise.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: Cycle-based remediation cannot meet a three-day clock, and per-train hotfix builds defeat a process that compares an installed version against one published fixed release.

NIST-800-53-SC-5.gap: DoS protection is built around volume; one request crashes the process, so every rate threshold sits above the traffic needed and never engages.

NIST-800-53-SC-7.gap: The vulnerable interface must answer arbitrary internet clients to function, and there is nothing left to place in front of the outermost perimeter device.

NIST-800-53-SI-4.gap: The device that would have logged the request is the device that reloaded, so on-box telemetry is lost exactly when CISA's forensics triage requirement needs it.

NIS2-Art21-patch-management.gap: Article 21's own change-control expectation is structurally slower than the three-day window, because the fix requires a reload of the asset terminating every remote session.

NIS2-Art21-availability.gap: Read conventionally, the availability duty argues for deferring the reload — which is the availability risk, since an unauthenticated attacker is already reloading the device at will.

NIS2-Art21-business-continuity.gap: The HA pair both members share the defect, so failover converts one outage into a flapping pair rather than providing continuity.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: Every affected train is current, supported software; no staleness or misconfiguration exists for a B4 assessment to find on a remotely crashable device.

UK-CAF-B5.gap: Resilience is assessed as redundancy topology, not as diversity, so an estate passes while both redundant units carry the identical crash.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: The two-week internet-facing window is four times longer than BOD 26-04 allowed; no maturity level closes the gap.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: EPSS 0.00874 at the 55.75th percentile on a four-day-old CVE is a lag artefact, and a risk-weighted queue that trusts it ranks a vendor-confirmed exploited perimeter flaw mid-list.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.16.gap: An unscheduled reload is indistinguishable from a fault without off-box correlation, so the event is recorded as instability and closed.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.21.gap: The control assumes a network service can be secured by adjusting its security features; Cisco states there are no workarounds, so only the software build changes the outcome.

new_control_requirements.name: PERIMETER-DEVICE-ZERODAY-SLA-TIER
new_control_requirements.description: Compliance frameworks must define a distinct patch SLA tier for pre-auth RCE on perimeter-trust-boundary devices (firewalls, VPN concentrators, WAFs, edge load-balancers). Tier requirement: vendor-mitigation deployed within 4 hours of KEV listing OR isolation of the vulnerable interface; standard 14/30-day SLAs do not apply because the device IS the trust boundary.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Cisco Secure Firewall ASA and FTD are the trust boundary this tier exists for, and CISA's own clock agrees with it — three days from the 2026-08-11 listing to the 2026-08-14 due date under BOD 26-04, against the two weeks an Essential Eight internet-facing window allows. The tier as written names pre-auth RCE and this defect is an unauthenticated denial of service, which is exactly the gap: with S:C and A:H the device stops forwarding for everyone, so the perimeter fails whether the attacker is running code on it or reloading it, and an SLA tier keyed on impact class rather than on the device's role lets this one fall back to the ordinary 14-day queue. The tier's alternative branch — isolation of the vulnerable interface — is the honest fallback here, since Cisco publishes no workaround and disabling the vulnerable configuration in service (webvpn, IKEv2 client-services, or FTD zero-trust) is the only operator-side lever.

new_control_requirements.name: FIREWALL-EGRESS-TELEMETRY-SEPARATE-TRUST-ZONE
new_control_requirements.description: Firewall and other perimeter-trust-boundary devices must forward syslog, threat logs, and authentication logs to a SIEM hosted in a separate trust zone (different management plane, different credentials, different authentication path). Telemetry stored on the compromised device is destroyed by the attacker; telemetry on a separate-trust-zone collector survives.
new_control_requirements.evidence: This CVE destroys its own evidence by design: the exploit reloads the ASA or FTD, so buffered syslog and the record of the HTTP request that caused it go with the restart, leaving crashinfo on disk0: and nothing about the traffic. CISA's requiredAction for the 2026-08-11 listing cites its Forensics Triage Requirements alongside the patch, and an operator can only satisfy that if the device was already exporting to a collector outside its own trust zone before the reload. Retrofitting it after the first crash produces nothing about the crash that prompted it.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CISA listed CVE-2026-20349 on 2026-08-11 with a 2026-08-14 due date under BOD 26-04 and Cisco confirmed PSIRT awareness of active exploitation the same month; as of 2026-08-15 that due date has passed. The four-hour requirement is what forces the per-train hotfix (ASA 9.20.4.235, 9.24.1.221; FTD 7.0.9.1-1, 10.0.0.1-2) and its reload onto an emergency change rather than the next maintenance window — the only alternative Cisco leaves open, since the advisory states there are no workarounds, is removing the vulnerable configuration itself — webvpn enable, crypto ikev2 client-services, or zero-trust enable on FTD.

CVE-2026-68820.name: Microsoft Windows Ancillary Function Driver for WinSock Use-After-Free Vulnerability (CVE-2026-68820)

attack_vector.description: A local user runs a crafted program that races concurrent overlapped socket I/O in afd.sys so a kernel object is freed while a dangling reference survives; reclaiming the freed allocation with controlled data converts the stale pointer into a kernel write and elevates the process to SYSTEM.
attack_vector.privileges_required: low — PR:L; the attacker must already run code as an ordinary local user, so this is a second-stage escalation rather than initial access.
attack_vector.complexity: high — AC:H; success depends on winning a narrow free/use race, which the exploit achieves by looping the socket operation and pool-grooming the freed slot.
attack_vector.ai_factor: Human vulnerability research by Check Point (Moshe Marelus, David Driker). No AI-assisted discovery is indicated, and Check Point's brand is not an AI-tooling signal.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Install the August 2026 cumulative update for the exact SKU and reboot every affected host onto the fixed build on the KEV clock that opened 2026-08-11, prioritising RDS/session and shared-workstation hosts where authorized local users are numerous.
prevention.adequacy: Fully removes the vulnerable code, but only after the reboot lands — a host that installed the update without rebooting still runs vulnerable afd.sys, and the reboot is the step most often deferred on session hosts.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Kernel-behaviour telemetry (auditd-equivalent EDR) alerting on a SYSTEM process spawned from a standard-user session and on afd.sys bugcheck clusters on hosts with local code-execution.
detection.adequacy: Detection fires after the escalation and cannot prevent it; the race leaves little artifact beyond the resulting privilege transition, so telemetry must already be collected and shipped off-host.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treat a confirmed SYSTEM escalation on an exposed host as a chained-intrusion event: isolate the host, rotate credentials that were valid on it, and review for the initial-access flaw this LPE was paired with.
response.adequacy: Response contains blast radius but does not undo the escalation; by the time SYSTEM is held the attacker may already have persisted.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: Monthly-rollup flaw-remediation cadence and console 'approved/downloaded' state do not meet the 2026-08-25 KEV due date, and 'downloaded' is not remediated until the reboot lands.

NIST-800-53-AC-6.gap: Least privilege is nominally met yet irrelevant — the attacker is already an authorized local user and the escalation happens in kernel mode.

NIS2-Art21-patch-management.gap: No expedited clock for an actively-exploited OS component; standard maintenance-window patching is nominally compliant while the path stays open.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: Patch-deployment records satisfy B4 without confirming the reboot onto the fixed build, missing unrebooted residual exposure.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: The maturity target measures install state via patch tooling and does not enforce the reboot that this fix requires to take effect.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: The SLA is left to the organization's risk assessment; filing this at the CVSS 7.0 band ignores the KEV listing and detected exploitation.

new_control_requirements.name: ACTIVELY-EXPLOITED-OS-LPE-REMEDIATION-WINDOW-ENFORCEMENT
new_control_requirements.description: The packet's vector places this in Windows Remote Desktop Services and describes an authorized attacker elevating privileges locally (CWE-269) — the account is already legitimate, so no account model is being abused; a privilege boundary inside the service is failing. For this CVE the control means the Windows update carrying the fix is driven across every affected host on the KEV clock that opened 2026-02-10 rather than folded into the next monthly rollup, with completion measured by each host's installed build against the fixed build for its SKU rather than by 'approved' or 'downloaded' in the management console. Hosts running the Remote Desktop Services role are the population to enumerate first, because a machine where many non-administrative users hold interactive sessions is a machine where the precondition this flaw needs — an already-authorized local user — is the normal operating state rather than an anomaly. There is a vendor patch with no live-patch path, and the fix typically requires a service restart or system reboot, so a host that has taken the update but not restarted still carries the vulnerable code and must be counted as exposed; on a session host that restart is also the step most likely to be deferred, because taking it evicts logged-on users, and a deferral recorded as 'patched' is the specific way this remediation goes wrong. The control's second half is the load-bearing one here: since the attacker is already authorized, tightening account privilege does not contain the escalation, which is exactly why the least-privilege and identity-and-access controls cited on this entry can pass their attestations while the flaw stays fully exploitable. Priority follows the packet rather than the CVSS band: a public PoC, confirmed exploitation, and the packet's own note that LPEs of this class are routinely paired with an initial-access flaw by ransomware operators make this the containment step for a chain, not a standalone endpoint item.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2026-68820 is an afd.sys use-after-free that elevates an already-authorized local user to SYSTEM, KEV-listed 2026-08-11 with a 2026-08-25 due date and Microsoft's Exploitation Detected flag. The fix (e.g. KB5121003 to build 10.0.26200.9168) has no live-patch path and requires a reboot; RDS and shared-workstation hosts, where many non-admin users hold interactive logons, are exactly where the 'already-authorized local user' precondition is normal, and where the reboot is most often deferred.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2026-68820 was added to CISA KEV on 2026-08-11 with a 2026-08-25 due date and detected in-the-wild exploitation. With no live-patch path, verified mitigation means the August 2026 cumulative update installed and the host rebooted onto the fixed build — the KEV-priority clock this control enforces, rather than the CVSS 7.0 'important' band an ordinary program would file it under.

attack_vector.description: An unauthenticated POST to /api/session/reset_password carries a JSON object where a scalar token is expected; Metabase feeds it into its HoneySQL query builder, so the object becomes attacker-chosen SQL against core_user/core_session. The attacker forges an admin session (or reads superuser rows), then acts as administrator to steal connected-database credentials and export data.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none — PR:N; the endpoint is pre-authentication and requires no account.
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L; one HTTP request, no race, no foothold, no user interaction. The only precondition is network reachability of the instance.
attack_vector.ai_factor: Found in the wild as a zero-day by Metabase and researched by humans (GHSA credit to perivamsi). No AI-assisted discovery indicated.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Upgrade to the fixed release on the affected train (v58.24 / v59.21 / v60.17 / v61.11 / v62.9 / v63.5) and restart the service on the KEV clock that opened 2026-08-11 (due 2026-08-14); where immediate upgrade was impossible, block /api/session/reset_password at the network edge.
prevention.adequacy: The upgrade closes the injection, but on a confirmed-exploited instance it does not evict attacker-created access — forged sessions, API keys, and stolen database credentials survive it, so session clearing and credential rotation are required alongside.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Ingress/application logging that alerts on POST /api/session/reset_password with a JSON-object (non-string) token, on the 400-then-200 /api/user/current pattern, and on new admin accounts or API keys.
detection.adequacy: Detects exploitation but only if reset_password request bodies and per-request access logs are captured; authentication-only logging misses it because the forged session presents as a valid admin.

response.what_would_have_worked: Post-upgrade: clear core_session, revoke unrecognized API keys, audit administrators, rotate every connected-database credential Metabase stored, and review warehouse query history for the exposure window.
response.adequacy: Necessary to undo an admin-level compromise; credentials read before rotation stay valid until rotated, and exported data cannot be recalled.

NIST-800-53-SI-10.gap: Input validation resting on a WAF or app-layer checks does not verify the HoneySQL builder parameterizes a non-string reset token on the pre-auth path.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: Normal application-patch cadence cannot meet a three-day KEV due date, and patching without session/credential rotation leaves attacker access intact.

NIS2-Art21-patch-management.gap: No expedited clock for a CVSS 10.0 pre-auth flaw under active exploitation on an internet-facing service; standard schedule is nominally compliant while credentials remain exfiltratable.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: Patch records satisfy B4 without secure-development verification of the query path or rotation of the stored database credentials the instance held.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: Measures install state, not the post-compromise cleanup — forged sessions, API keys, and stolen credentials outlive the upgrade.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.28.gap: Secure-coding attestation that never sends a non-string token to the reset endpoint passes while the object-to-SQL injection stays open.

new_control_requirements.name: DB-ABSTRACTION-LAYER-PARAMETERIZATION-VERIFICATION
new_control_requirements.description: Parameterization must be verified at the database abstraction layer / query builder, not assumed from application-layer input validation or a perimeter WAF. For Drupal, apply SA-CORE-2026-004 (10.4.10 / 10.5.10 / 10.6.9 / 11.1.10 / 11.2.12 / 11.3.10), prioritize PostgreSQL-backed sites, and meet the CISA KEV due date 2026-05-27. The distinguishing test: send a JSON:API request with a SQL metacharacter in a filter condition against a staging instance and confirm the query builder parameterizes rather than concatenates it.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2026-72898 is exactly a query-builder parameterization failure: Metabase passed a caller-supplied JSON object (token / user-id) into HoneySQL on the unauthenticated /api/session/reset_password path, so {"select":{"raw":...}} became live SQL against core_session. The distinguishing test applies directly — send a non-string token ({"select":1}) to a staging instance and confirm rejection rather than a HoneySQL error. Fixed in v58.24 / v59.21 / v60.17 / v61.11 / v62.9 / v63.5; KEV-listed 2026-08-11, due 2026-08-14.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2026-72898 carries an unusually short KEV due date — added 2026-08-11, due 2026-08-14 — for a CVSS 10.0 pre-auth injection under confirmed exploitation with public Nuclei and GitHub PoCs and EPSS 0.104 (95.3rd percentile). Verified mitigation is the upgrade to the fixed train and service restart, or blocking /api/session/reset_password at the edge as the documented compensating control — the KEV-priority clock this control enforces.

CVE-2007-3010.name: Alcatel OmniPCX Enterprise Remote Code Execution Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: An unauthenticated HTTP GET to the OmniPCX Enterprise web management interface reaches masterCGI's ping action, whose 'user' parameter is passed to a shell without metacharacter filtering. A semicolon and a second command run on the call server as the web server account, giving the attacker a foothold on the telephony control plane along with the dial plan, trunk credentials and voicemail stores held there.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none — PR:N; the ping action is reachable before any authentication decision, so no OXE operator account, session or token is involved at any point
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L; a single GET with a shell metacharacter, no race and no memory work. The real constraint is reachability of the management interface, and the practical one is that the httpd process terminates spawned interactive shells after the HTTP 200, so payloads run as one-shot commands
attack_vector.ai_factor: None. RedTeam Pentesting found this by reading a CGI ping feature during a 2007 penetration test; no research arm, AI-branded or otherwise, is involved in the discovery record.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Confining the Unified Maintenance Tool web interface to a voice-management segment reachable only from named administration hosts, and migrating the call server off R7.1 to a release carrying the metacharacter filtering.
prevention.adequacy: Segmentation bounds who can send the GET but does not repair masterCGI: anything inside the permitted segment still executes commands, and a compromised administrator workstation satisfies the precondition in full. The migration is the only closure, and it costs a telephony outage.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Web-request logging on the OXE management interface forwarded off the appliance, alerting on shell metacharacters in the masterCGI user parameter, plus process-execution telemetry on the call server for shell children of the web account.
detection.adequacy: PBX appliances are routinely outside the logging estate — nobody ships call-server web logs to the SIEM — so this is a capability that has to be built before it can fire. It also detects rather than prevents: by the time the metacharacter appears in a log line the command has already run.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treating a confirmed hit as a control-plane compromise: rebuild the call server from a known-good image rather than patching in place, rotate trunk and administrative credentials, and review the dial plan for injected call-forwarding or toll-fraud routes.
response.adequacy: Rebuilding an in-service PBX is a scheduled outage that competes with the migration it is supposed to precede, and toll-fraud routes injected into a dial plan are hard to spot without a known-good configuration to compare against.

NIST-800-53-SC-7.gap: An organisation running an OXE can evidence SC-7 with a perimeter firewall and still leave masterCGI answering every host on the corporate LAN, because voice administration is treated as an internal function that needs broad reachability. The control never asks whether a 2007-vintage appliance with no authentication on a maintenance endpoint belongs inside the same boundary as user workstations, which is the only question that changes the exposure.

NIST-800-53-SI-10.gap: SI-10 is met by the organisation's own development and integration practice, and the unvalidated sink here is inside a vendor CGI binary the operator cannot inspect, modify or test. An assessor confirming input-validation standards for in-house systems produces a clean SI-10 finding while the 'user' parameter on the OXE keeps reaching a shell unfiltered, because the control has no expression that reaches closed appliance firmware.

NIS2-Annex-I-Telecom.gap: NIS2 places electronic communications services in scope and requires proportionate risk management, but the risk here has no proportionate treatment: R7.1 and earlier receive no fix, so the sectoral obligation resolves to replacing the telephony platform. A risk register entry accepting the exposure until the next refresh cycle satisfies the paperwork and leaves an unauthenticated command-execution path on the call server for years.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: CAF B4 outcomes are assessed against a secure build standard and the accounts that administer it, both of which an OXE deployment can meet. Neither reaches CVE-2007-3010, because the ping action authorises nobody: the endpoint is exposed in the vendor's default configuration and the hardening the assessment examines happens on a layer the attacker never touches.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: Essential Eight maturity levels count days from vendor patch release, and for the affected OXE line there is no release to count from — the 2007 fix went into then-supported versions only. The model's only available answer for an unsupported asset is an exception, so an estate can hold a Maturity Level 2 rating on patching while the KEV-listed call server sits permanently outside the measurement.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.9.gap: A.8.9 is satisfied by an approved and enforced configuration baseline for the OXE, and every setting in such a baseline leaves the defect intact, because masterCGI's ping handler behaves this way by design in R7.1 and earlier. The only configuration variable that changes the outcome is which networks may reach the Unified Maintenance Tool, and nothing in A.8.9 forces that question onto a voice appliance's baseline.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: The Alcatel OmniPCX Enterprise Communication Server has no patch an R7.1 operator can deploy — the 2007 fix went into then-supported releases only — so this control's 'documented compensating controls' branch is the operative one and it has a clock: CISA listed the CVE on 2022-04-15 with a 2022-05-06 due date, and the compensating control (removing the Unified Maintenance Tool from any network an untrusted host can reach) is deployable in hours where the platform migration is not. EPSS 0.97407 at 2026-08-16 and a Nuclei template carrying a Shodan fingerprint mean the reachability decision, not the migration schedule, is what stands between the call server and a mass scan.

new_control_requirements.name: MITIGATION-ACTIVE-PATCH-PENDING-VERDICT-CLASS
new_control_requirements.description: Compliance verdicts must distinguish three states: (a) binary patch deployed (vulnerability eliminated), (b) vendor-mitigation rule active, no binary patch (residual risk: any defect in the mitigation rule reopens the vulnerability), (c) no mitigation, no patch (full exposure). Audit reports must surface (b) as a distinct compensating-control state with an associated time-bound action item, not as a 'patched per SLA' outcome.
new_control_requirements.evidence: An OXE on R7.1 can only ever be in state (b) or (c): there is no binary patch for that line, so an estate that has segmented the Unified Maintenance Tool holds an active compensating control and one that has not holds full exposure to a one-GET command injection with EPSS 0.97407. Recording either as 'patched' against the 2022-05-06 KEV due date destroys the distinction that matters, because state (b) reopens the moment a routing change, a jump-host compromise, or a remote-maintenance exception puts an untrusted host back inside the permitted segment — and it carries an action item the migration to a supported OmniPCX Enterprise release is supposed to close.

attack_vector.description: An unauthenticated peer completes an ordinary TLS or DTLS handshake and sends a heartbeat request whose declared payload length far exceeds the bytes actually supplied. OpenSSL copies the response using the declared length, returning up to 64KB of adjacent process memory. The read is repeatable, invisible to application logging, and yields whatever the process was holding: session tokens, credentials in flight, decrypted request bodies, and sometimes the private key.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none — PR:N; no client certificate, no account and no prior access are needed, only the ability to complete a handshake with the listener
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L; a single malformed record with no race and no chaining. The only real limit is what happens to sit in the heap on each read, which the attacker addresses by repeating the request rather than by engineering anything
attack_vector.ai_factor: None. Two independent human discoveries weeks apart — Neel Mehta of Google Security per the OpenSSL advisory, and the Codenomicon team who named it — from reading and testing the heartbeat extension.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Upgrading every OpenSSL instance to 1.0.1g or a backported distribution package, restarting every process linked against it, and — for anything that could not be upgraded — rebuilding with -DOPENSSL_NO_HEARTBEATS to remove the code path.
prevention.adequacy: Complete for the defect and incomplete for the incident. The upgrade stops further reads; it does not invalidate a token, key or credential already taken, and on vendor appliances it is unavailable until the vendor ships a rebuilt image — which is where the first confirmed exploitation landed.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Network IDS signatures for over-length heartbeat responses on every TLS listener, correlated against VPN and application session logs for a single session appearing from two distant source addresses within seconds.
detection.adequacy: This is the one control that demonstrably worked: the IDS fired over 17,000 times during the Mandiant case. It only mattered because someone correlated it with VPN logs — the alerts alone had been firing against an unpatched device without producing a response.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treating every exposed service as having leaked: regenerate keys, reissue and revoke certificates, invalidate all sessions, and rotate every credential that transited the service during the exposure window.
response.adequacy: Necessary and rarely completed. The exposure window for most estates ran from 2012 to whenever the process actually restarted, which makes the credential-rotation scope enormous — and the material that leaked is indistinguishable, after the fact, from material that did not.

NIST-800-53-SC-8.gap: Transmission confidentiality was never violated: the TLS session did exactly what SC-8 requires while the endpoint terminating it handed out the plaintext and the key from its own heap. An assessor can verify current protocol versions, cipher suites and certificate validity on a 1.0.1f listener and produce a fully compliant SC-8 finding on a service that is leaking 64KB per request to anyone who asks.

NIST-800-53-SR-3.gap: Supply chain controls were exercised against contracted suppliers, and the affected component arrived as a transitive dependency inside appliance firmware and distribution packages that no supplier agreement enumerates. In April 2014 an organisation with a complete SR-3 programme still could not produce the list of its devices linking OpenSSL 1.0.1 through 1.0.1f, which is the only artefact the response actually needed.

NIS2-Art21-vulnerability-handling.gap: The article's vulnerability handling measures treat remediation as one act, and here it is three: upgrade the library, restart every linked process, then rotate every secret that was exposed. An entity that patched packages on 2014-04-08 and stopped there can evidence Article 21 handling in full while its listeners run the old code in memory and the session tokens read out of them remain valid.

UK-CAF-B2.gap: B2's identity and access outcomes were fully met on the concentrator Mandiant investigated — users authenticated, privileged access was managed, and the attacker still walked in. Lifting a live session token out of heap memory sidesteps the access decision rather than defeating it, so the evidence B2 collects is intact and irrelevant, and the control set has no outcome covering the lifetime or binding of the token issued after authentication.

AU-Essential-8-MFA.gap: This is the documented case of Essential Eight MFA maturity being met and bypassed in the same intrusion: the second factor was presented correctly by the legitimate user, and the attacker replayed the resulting session token read from the VPN concentrator's memory. Maturity levels describe which users and services require MFA and by what method; nothing in them binds the resulting session to a device or address, which is the property that would have stopped this.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.24.gap: An organisation with an approved cryptographic policy, an algorithm standard and a documented key-management lifecycle satisfies A.8.24 while running OpenSSL 1.0.1f. The control governs how keys are generated, stored and destroyed, not whether a running service can be induced to read one out of its own heap — and it offers no trigger for the decision this CVE forces, which is to rotate a key on the possibility of compromise with no evidence either way.

new_control_requirements.name: TIER-3-DEPENDENCY-INVENTORY
new_control_requirements.description: Supply chain inventory must extend to tier-3 dependencies (dependencies of dependencies of direct dependencies). SBOM coverage for libsystemd-class transitive dependencies cannot be omitted under SR-3.
new_control_requirements.evidence: OpenSSL is the archetype this control exists for: no organisation procured it, and in April 2014 the operative question was which appliances, packages and firmware images linked 1.0.1 through 1.0.1f. Mandiant's confirmed case landed on an SSL VPN concentrator — a vendor-delivered image whose bundled OpenSSL was invisible to the operator's package inventory and unpatchable without a vendor rebuild. A transitive-dependency inventory that reaches into appliance firmware is what turns the CISA KEV listing of 2022-05-04 into an actionable target list instead of a search.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: OpenSSL 1.0.1g shipped on 2014-04-07, the same day as the advisory, and Mandiant recorded successful exploitation of an SSL VPN concentrator beginning 2014-04-08 — the exposure window for a real intrusion was one day wide, which is what a four-hour SLA is calibrated for. Applied to this CVE the SLA has to be measured against the live listener rather than the package database, because patch_required_reboot is false and an upgraded-but-unrestarted daemon keeps serving the vulnerable handler; and the documented-compensating-control branch is what covers the appliance population, where -DOPENSSL_NO_HEARTBEATS or taking the listener off untrusted networks is available while a vendor image is not.

attack_vector.description: A page loaded in Internet Explorer 9 or 10 mutates the document from an onpropertychange handler on a script element, causing the browser to keep using a CMarkup object after it has been freed. The exploit converts that into a one-byte write at a chosen address and uses a loaded Flash SWF to arrange the heap and defeat ASLR and DEP, running code as the browsing user. In the observed campaign the page was reached through an iframe injected into a legitimate site the victim already visited.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none — PR:N; the attacker needs no account and no prior access on the target, only for the browser to render their content
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L, with UI:R; the trigger is deterministic script, and the difficulty lived in the ASLR and DEP bypass, which the attacker solved once by requiring Flash Player to be present rather than by winning anything at runtime
attack_vector.ai_factor: None. Recovered by FireEye's incident responders from an exploit already running in a watering-hole compromise, and independently reported by Liu Long of Qihoo; both are human analysis of live attacker code.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Applying MS14-012 and restarting; before it existed, enabling the KB 2925418 'MSHTML Shim Workaround' Fix it, or setting Internet and Local intranet zones to High, and removing Flash Player to break the bypass the exploit depended on.
prevention.adequacy: The update closes it and needs a restart that on a workstation fleet is routinely deferred. The pre-patch measures were interim and costly: the shim blocked only this vector, zone hardening breaks working sites, and removing Flash defeated the observed chain without removing the defect.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Process-lineage telemetry on iexplore.exe child processes and file writes, plus web-proxy alerting on a known-good site suddenly serving an iframe to an unrelated host alongside a SWF.
detection.adequacy: Both fire after code has already executed in the browser, and the proxy signal has a high false-positive rate on any site carrying third-party advertising. The strategic web compromise is designed precisely so that domain reputation says nothing useful.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treating a hit as a targeted-intrusion foothold rather than a commodity infection: isolate the host, hunt for the second stage, and rotate the credentials the browsing user held.
response.adequacy: Appropriate to Operation SnowMan's actual targeting, and it depends on the first-stage detection above having fired at all. An estate that finds only the payload weeks later is doing malware cleanup on what was a nation-state initial-access event.

NIST-800-53-SI-3.gap: Malicious code protection was deployed, current, and blind to this. The exploit arrived as script and a Flash object from vfw.org, a site with every reputational signal in its favour, and the memory corruption completed inside the browser process before any file touched disk for a scanner to inspect. SI-3 evidence is about coverage and definition currency, neither of which changes the outcome for an in-memory browser use-after-free delivered from a trusted domain.

NIS2-Art21-patch-management.gap: The whole exposure that mattered fell outside what patch management can express: FireEye found the exploit in use on 2014-02-11 and MS14-012 shipped on 2014-03-11, so for four weeks the correct action was Microsoft's Fix it shim from Advisory 2934088. An entity that deployed that shim across its fleet and one that did nothing produce the same patch-management record, because neither has a patch to report against.

UK-CAF-C1.gap: Monitoring outcomes were achievable and still gave nothing on the first stage. The request is TLS to a legitimate host, the exploitation never leaves the browser process, and the earliest observable is whatever the payload does afterwards — so a CAF C1 assessment that evidences full network and endpoint telemetry coverage is describing visibility that begins only after the compromise it was meant to catch.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: Essential Eight counts application patching against installed applications, and the vulnerable component here is the MSHTML engine rather than the browser a user launches. An estate that standardised on another browser and retired Internet Explorer from its application list still carries the engine behind any embedded WebBrowser control, and the maturity assessment records a browser risk that has been removed from the report rather than from the machines.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: Timely vulnerability information was available — Advisory 2934088 was published on 2014-02-19, three weeks before the fix — so A.8.8's awareness requirement was met throughout. The control is silent on the decision that determined exposure, which was whether to accept the functional cost of blocking Active Scripting or deploying the MSHTML shim while a targeted campaign was running, and an organisation that documented the risk and chose neither is fully compliant.

new_control_requirements.name: BROWSER-MANAGED-UPDATE-NO-DEFERRAL
new_control_requirements.description: Enterprise update rings must not defer security-channel browser updates beyond 24h.
new_control_requirements.evidence: MS14-012 shipped on 2014-03-11 against an Internet Explorer 10 zero-day that FireEye had already observed being served from vfw.org a month earlier, and the bulletin's own reference tables require a system restart on every affected SKU — so on this CVE the no-deferral requirement has to bind the restart, not just the download, because an IE host with the update staged and the reboot deferred still loads the pre-update MSHTML. The control also has to reach past iexplore.exe: the same platform update is what fixes every application embedding the WebBrowser control, and those are the installs an update ring scoped to 'the browser' never counts.

new_control_requirements.name: VENDOR-PUSH-MITIGATION-OPT-IN-PRE-DISCLOSURE
new_control_requirements.description: For vendors offering push-mitigation services (Microsoft EEMS, Palo Alto Threat Prevention auto-update, etc.), opt-in must be enabled BEFORE the next disclosure event, not in response to it. Compliance frameworks must require operators to enable available vendor-push-mitigation services as a baseline control — opt-in late means the mitigation rule arrives after exploitation, not before.
new_control_requirements.evidence: This CVE is the case the control describes: Microsoft published Security Advisory 2934088 with the KB 2925418 'MSHTML Shim Workaround' Fix it on 2014-02-19, three weeks before MS14-012, and it blocked the CVE-2014-0322 attack vector outright. An organisation with a standing mechanism to take vendor interim mitigations was protected for those three weeks; one that had to evaluate, approve and pilot the shim from scratch was still deciding when the patch arrived. The shim is also the only layer that touched this — malicious code protection had no artefact to match, because the exploit ran in-process from a legitimate domain.

CVE-2014-0780.name: InduSoft Web Studio NTWebServer Directory Traversal Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: An unauthenticated web request to NTWebServer escapes the document root and returns an arbitrary readable file. Pointed at the loaded project's .APP file it returns the HMI/SCADA application's administrative passwords, and the attacker then configures the application through its own legitimate interface to execute code — so the compromise completes as authorised product use on an engineering or HMI node.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none — PR:N; the traversal is served before any authentication decision, and the credential the attacker ends up holding is the one the read returned
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L; one HTTP request with a traversal sequence. The binding precondition is that NTWebServer is running, which the vendor says it should not be in production, and the second stage depends on the recovered .APP password being live and reused
attack_vector.ai_factor: None. Found by researcher John Leitch and reported through the Zero Day Initiative to ICS-CERT; a coordinated human disclosure with no automated tooling claimed.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Removing or disabling NTWebServer on every production node per the vendor's own guidance, and where it must remain, upgrading to v7.1 + SP2 + Patch 4 and restricting the listener to the engineering segment.
prevention.adequacy: Removal is complete and free of the outage the patch costs, which makes it the better answer for most sites. Restricting the listener bounds who can send the request but leaves it fully exploitable to anything already inside the engineering segment, including a contractor laptop.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Web-request logging from NTWebServer forwarded off the node with alerting on traversal sequences and on any request naming a .APP file, plus file-access auditing on the project directory.
detection.adequacy: HMI nodes are rarely inside the logging estate, and the read itself is a single well-formed HTTP request that leaves no crash, no new process and no disk artefact. Detection here has to be built in advance against a request shape, because there is nothing else to see.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treating a confirmed read as disclosure of the project's administrative credential: rotate the .APP passwords across every cell that shared them, and compare project logic and user configuration against a known-good copy.
response.adequacy: Necessary, because upgrading the component does not invalidate a password that already left the site. The comparison step is the harder half — an OT site without a maintained known-good project copy has no way to establish whether the logic it is running is the logic it approved.

NIST-800-82r3.gap: The ICS guidance directs effort at control-network segmentation and industrial protocol exposure, and neither is involved: the attacker reads a project file over HTTP from an engineering-side component and then operates the HMI as its own administrator. A site can hold thorough 800-82r3 conformance and still lose control of the process, because every action after the .APP read is indistinguishable from legitimate engineering work.

NIS2-Art21-vulnerability-management.gap: Applying v7.1 SP2 Patch 4 satisfies the article's vulnerability management measures and leaves a demonstration web server running on a production HMI node in a sector NIS2 covers. The vendor's guidance — that NTWebServer is for demonstration and training and does not belong in production — is the stronger remediation and the article has no requirement that reaches it, so the compliant outcome is weaker than the vendor's own advice.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: B4 measures conformance to the operator's secure build standard, and an HMI standard that includes NTWebServer because the InduSoft installer places it there is conformed to exactly. The assessment has no mechanism for asking whether a component the vendor labels demonstration-and-training-only should be in the standard at all, which is the only decision that removes this exposure without an outage.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: The patch that fixes this stops the NTWebServer process and takes the HMI runtime down with it, so the Essential Eight timeframe collides with production scheduling rather than with an administrative delay. The model's only escape is an exception, and OT sites carry those indefinitely — so the maturity rating stays intact while a KEV-listed unauthenticated credential read stays live on the node that runs the plant.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.22.gap: Network segregation is evidenced at the IT/OT boundary, and this defect is served to whatever is already inside it. A site with tested separation between the business network and the plant network still exposes the traversal to every device on the plant side — engineering workstations, contractor laptops, jump hosts — and A.8.22 as written does not push segregation down to the point where an HMI node's web listener is unreachable from a general plant segment.

new_control_requirements.name: MITIGATION-ACTIVE-PATCH-PENDING-VERDICT-CLASS
new_control_requirements.description: Compliance verdicts must distinguish three states: (a) binary patch deployed (vulnerability eliminated), (b) vendor-mitigation rule active, no binary patch (residual risk: any defect in the mitigation rule reopens the vulnerability), (c) no mitigation, no patch (full exposure). Audit reports must surface (b) as a distinct compensating-control state with an associated time-bound action item, not as a 'patched per SLA' outcome.
new_control_requirements.evidence: On an InduSoft Web Studio node the three states are genuinely different and routinely collapsed. Upgrading to v7.1 + SP2 + Patch 4 is state (a) but costs an HMI runtime outage; disabling NTWebServer per the vendor's demonstration-and-training-only guidance, or confining its listener to the engineering segment, is state (b) and is available immediately; and a node running the bundled server unrestricted at a pre-Patch-4 level is state (c), one unauthenticated request from the project's administrative password. Recording the segment restriction as 'patched' against the 2022-05-06 KEV due date hides that it reopens the moment a contractor laptop or a routing change puts an untrusted host back on the permitted side.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: InduSoft published the fixed level years before CISA listed this on 2022-04-15, so for an HMI estate the SLA clock started at the listing and the 2022-05-06 due date has long passed. The control matters on this product precisely because the patch is expensive and the documented compensating control is not: disabling NTWebServer on nodes that never needed it — the vendor's own position — is a same-day action that removes the path entirely, where the service-pack upgrade waits on a production window. Applying the SLA forces that choice to be made and dated rather than deferred into an open OT patching exception at a site in a sector where the recovered .APP credential controls a physical process.

attack_vector.description: A crafted application run by any logged-on user drives win32k.sys, through TrackPopupMenu window-message handling, into dereferencing a pointer the attacker has arranged to be NULL. Where user mode may map the NULL page, the attacker plants a crafted object at address zero and redirects the kernel's dereference into their own code, ending with SYSTEM privileges on the host — the escalation step that turns a single compromised user account into control of the machine.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none — PR:N in the CVSS vector, which is misleading in isolation: the attacker needs a valid local logon or an already-authenticated user willing to run the application, but no administrative or special rights beyond that
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L; deterministic on the affected platforms with no race and no information leak needed. The one variable is the platform: NULL page mapping is disabled by default from Windows 8 onward, which breaks the published technique without removing the defect
attack_vector.ai_factor: None. Recovered by CrowdStrike incident responders from live intrusion data during an engagement that began in the spring of 2014, and independently credited to FireEye by Microsoft; both are human threat-intelligence work on attacker binaries.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Applying MS14-058 (KB 3000061) and taking the restart on every affected host, prioritising terminal servers and multi-user workstations, and constraining who may log on interactively and execute arbitrary binaries.
prevention.adequacy: The update closes it; the restart is what makes the update real, and on a session host that restart is the step that gets deferred. Microsoft identified no workaround, so the interim posture is only about narrowing the population that can attempt it — which does not contain an attacker who already holds a user account.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Token-integrity and process-lineage telemetry that alarms when a process started under a standard user account acquires a SYSTEM token without a corresponding service or elevation event, correlated with local administrative account creation.
detection.adequacy: This is the only layer with anything to see, because the exploit compiles nothing, loads no driver, crashes nothing and touches no file. It also requires that telemetry to have been collected and shipped off-host before the attempt — on the multi-user servers most exposed to this, it usually is not.

response.what_would_have_worked: Escalating a confirmed hit as targeted-actor activity rather than commodity malware: isolate the host, hunt for the web shell and the lateral movement that CrowdStrike saw paired with it, and rotate every credential the host held or that authenticated through it.
response.adequacy: Correct for what this exploit was actually used for, and dependent on the escalation having been noticed at all. An estate that treats the SYSTEM-level artefact as an isolated infection closes the ticket and leaves the intrusion in place.

NIST-800-53-AC-6.gap: Least privilege was the design assumption this exploit was built to void. Because the attacker starts from a legitimate non-administrative logon and reaches SYSTEM through a kernel driver, the privilege model is never queried and an AC-6 assessment showing standard users everywhere, minimal administrative accounts and enforced separation of duties describes a control that is simultaneously fully implemented and fully bypassed on every unpatched host.

NIST-800-53-SI-4.gap: Monitoring under SI-4 is calibrated to network, authentication and file-level events, and the escalation generates none: no driver load, no crash, no new binary on disk beyond the one the user ran, and no authentication at all. What surfaced it was endpoint detection on one 64-bit Windows Server 2008 R2 host inside an engagement already running against the actor, roughly five months after the exploit binary's May 2014 build date — which is the honest measure of what compliant monitoring sees: the web shell and the lateral movement afterwards, never the step that produced them.

NIS2-Art21-incident-handling.gap: Incident handling procedures cannot start without a detected incident, and this class of flaw is deliberately the quietest link in an intrusion chain. An entity can hold tested, documented Article 21 handling arrangements that were never invoked, because a local escalation to SYSTEM raised nothing to invoke them with — and by the time the noisier stages surface, the exposure window measured from the 2022-05-04 KEV listing has already been open for the whole intrusion.

UK-CAF-B2.gap: B2 outcomes are about who may access what and how that access is authenticated, reviewed and constrained, and every one of them can be met on a host where any standard user can become SYSTEM by running a program. The failing boundary is inside win32k.sys, so the identity and access evidence a CAF assessment collects is truthful and entirely disconnected from whether the privilege separation it describes actually holds.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: MS14-058 requires a system restart on every affected SKU, and Essential Eight patch maturity is scored on deployment within a timeframe rather than on the host running the fixed driver. A terminal server whose users cannot be evicted keeps the vulnerable win32k.sys mapped indefinitely while showing as patched, so the estate's maturity level and its actual exposure diverge exactly where the exploit's precondition — many interactive users on one machine — is strongest.

ISO-27001-2022-A.5.15.gap: A.5.15 requires an access control policy established and enforced on the basis of business and security requirements, and this CVE makes enforcement optional from the attacker's side. Rights allocated by role, reviewed periodically and separated between duties are all demonstrable, and none of it survives a user-mode program that replaces its own token in kernel memory — the policy is intact as a document and void as a boundary.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: MS14-058 shipped 2014-10-14 against a Windows kernel flaw CrowdStrike had already watched HURRICANE PANDA use against infrastructure companies — the exploit binary's own build timestamp of 2014-05-03 puts in-the-wild use at least five months ahead of the bulletin — and CISA listed it on 2022-05-04 with a 2022-05-25 due date. On this CVE the SLA has to be measured against the installed win32k.sys build after the restart, because the bulletin requires a reboot on every affected SKU and a host that took KB 3000061 without one still runs the vulnerable driver. Microsoft published no workaround, so the compensating-control branch has almost nothing to offer — which makes the deployment-and-restart clock the whole control, and terminal servers the population to run it against first.

new_control_requirements.name: NATION-STATE-INITIAL-ACCESS-IR-ESCALATION
new_control_requirements.description: IR runbooks must include an explicit nation-state-initial-access escalation path triggered by APT28/APT29/Lazarus/Volt-Typhoon/etc. attribution on a confirmed exploit chain. Standard malware-infection IR under-escalates nation-state activity by treating it as commodity threat.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CrowdStrike attributed this exploit to the China-nexus actor it tracks as HURRICANE PANDA, an adversary it says it had been engaging daily since the spring of 2014 and which it describes as targeting infrastructure companies and using the ChinaChopper web shell as its common initial foothold, and Microsoft separately credited FireEye on the same CVE — two threat-intelligence firms finding one privilege escalation inside targeted intrusions. An estate that recovers the Metasploit-equivalent artefact from a terminal server and closes it as an endpoint infection has under-escalated the exact activity this exploit was built for. The runbook has to trigger on the escalation step, not on the payload, because on this CVE the escalation is the quiet part and the noisy part comes afterwards.

CVE-2014-9163.name: Adobe Flash Player Stack-Based Buffer Overflow Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: A crafted SWF, delivered as web content, an advertisement, or Flash embedded in an Office document, overruns a stack buffer while Adobe Flash Player parses it. Code then executes in whichever process hosts the player — a browser tab or the Office application — with the logged-on user's rights, from which the attacker proceeds as that user. The victim's only action is opening content they had reason to open.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none — PR:N; no account and no prior foothold on the target, only that the content reaches an application hosting the Flash runtime
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L with UI:R; no preconditions beyond the user opening the content, though exploiting a 2014-era stack overflow reliably still required a DEP and ASLR bypass, which fits the targeted use Adobe reported rather than mass exploit-kit delivery
attack_vector.ai_factor: Unknown and not guessed at. Adobe's acknowledgements for this CVE could not be resolved and no finder is named in any source that could be opened; nothing in the record points to AI involvement in either discovery or weaponisation.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Removing Adobe Flash Player from every update path on the host, which is CISA's own required action for this entry; failing that, bringing each of the four paths to its fixed level and restarting the hosting process.
prevention.adequacy: Removal is complete and is the only durable answer, because the product has been end of life since 2020-12-31. Version-based remediation is partial by construction: no host reboot is involved, so an updated-but-unrestarted browser or Office process keeps the vulnerable player mapped.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Process-lineage telemetry alarming on browser-tab and Office child processes and executable writes, plus mail and gateway inspection surfacing externally sourced Office documents that embed Flash content.
detection.adequacy: Both fire after the overflow has already executed code, and the document-inspection half only helps for the Office delivery path — content arriving through a browser or an advertisement slot produces nothing to inspect before the player parses it.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treating a hit as a user-context compromise: isolate the host, rotate the credentials that user held, and remove the player rather than updating it, since the KEV action for this product is disconnection.
response.adequacy: Sound, and it depends on the first-stage detection having fired. The removal step is what stops the same host being exploited by the next Flash defect, of which there were many after December 2014 — updating the plugin closes this CVE and keeps the surface.

NIST-800-53-CM-7.gap: Least functionality is exactly the right control and it is implemented as a baseline with an exception process, which is how Flash Player survived on estates for years after this fix. An organisation that documented a business justification for the plugin, obtained approval and recorded it in the baseline is fully CM-7 compliant, and the compliant outcome is the plugin still being installed on hosts where CISA's own required action is that it be disconnected.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: Flaw remediation is only as good as the inventory beneath it, and this product presents four independently versioned copies per machine — ActiveX, NPAPI, Pepper and the Office-embedded path. An SI-2 report showing Flash Player at 16.0.0.235 is truthful about one of them and silent about the other three, so a machine can be recorded as remediated while a copy below 15.0.0.246 still parses whatever SWF a crafted document supplies.

EU-CRA-Art13.gap: The CRA's manufacturer obligations run for a declared support period and Adobe's ended when Flash Player reached end of life on 2020-12-31, with content blocked from 2021-01-12. An operator still running the player therefore holds software with no manufacturer vulnerability-handling obligation attached, and the regulation gives them nothing to invoke — it governs how a supported product is maintained and is silent on a product whose support has stopped while installations have not.

UK-CAF-A1.gap: Governance outcomes are met by identifiable ownership, an articulated risk appetite and a maintained register, and all three are compatible with Flash Player remaining installed for a legacy application. The mechanism that keeps a KEV-listed end-of-life plugin in service is a properly minuted risk acceptance with no removal date, and A1 assesses whether the acceptance was made correctly rather than whether the exposure was ever closed.

AU-Essential-8-App-Hardening.gap: This is the Essential Eight control that names Flash explicitly, and the gap is scope rather than intent. Browser hardening that blocks or removes the plugin from web browsers leaves the Office-embedded path fully live, so an estate holding a maturity rating on user application hardening can still deliver a crafted SWF to the vulnerable player through a document — the control was implemented as written and the delivery path it does not cover is the one Office documents use.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: The control's process ends at a treatment decision, and the treatment decision that keeps an end-of-life Flash Player installed is as compliant as the one that removes it. An ISMS can evidence that it received the vulnerability information, assessed exposure across its estate and recorded the outcome, without A.8.8 ever forcing the question CISA's required action forces — whether a product Adobe stopped supporting on 2020-12-31 belongs on the machine at all.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: This is the entry where the KEV action is not a patch: CISA listed Adobe Flash Player's stack overflow on 2022-04-13 with a 2022-05-04 due date and stated that the impacted product is end-of-life and should be disconnected if still in use. Applying the SLA to that action means the four-hour clock runs on removing the player from every update path on the host — ActiveX, NPAPI, Pepper and Office-embedded — rather than on reaching 16.0.0.235, which is exactly the least-functionality and user-application-hardening action those gaps describe. The SLA is what converts a standing risk acceptance on a plugin Adobe stopped supporting on 2020-12-31 into a dated removal.

new_control_requirements.name: BROWSER-MANAGED-UPDATE-NO-DEFERRAL
