new_control_requirements.description: Enterprise update rings must not defer security-channel browser updates beyond 24h.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Flash Player of this era was distributed through the browsers themselves — bundled with Chrome as a Pepper build, delivered to Internet Explorer as an ActiveX control — so the update ring that governs browser currency is the one that decided whether a host reached 16.0.0.235, 15.0.0.246, 13.0.0.259 or Linux 11.2.202.425 after Adobe's December 2014 release. Applied here the control has to bind the process restart as well as the download, because patch_required_reboot is false and an open browser or Office application keeps the pre-update player mapped; and the ring must enumerate the plugin paths separately, since a machine's lowest Flash version is the one that matters and a single inventory entry hides it.

CVE-2015-0311.name: Adobe Flash Player Remote Code Execution Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: A malicious advertisement loads a SWF that calls ByteArray.uncompress() on a broken zlib stream. Flash frees the array's buffer on the failed inflate but keeps the object usable, and the attacker reads and writes through the dangling allocation until a sprayed Vector's length field is corrupted, giving arbitrary memory access inside the browser and then code execution as the logged-on user.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none — PR:N; the attacker holds no account on the target and needs nothing from the victim beyond loading a page that carries the ad
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L; the memory-corruption work is non-trivial but was solved once by the exploit-kit author and shipped as a landing page. The only real constraint is that the victim runs Flash outside Chrome's Pepper sandbox, which described most of the installed base in January 2015.
attack_vector.ai_factor: None claimed and none evidenced. Discovery was manual traffic analysis by an independent researcher tracking Angler; the weaponisation was human exploit-kit development that predated the vendor advisory.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Removing the Flash runtime, or blocking Flash content in browsers, before the disclosure. Where the plugin had to stay, click-to-play so a SWF from an ad slot never auto-executed, plus running the browser under a per-tab sandbox.
prevention.framework_requiring_it: CISA BOD 22-01 (KEV remediation, added 2022-04-13; required action: disconnect the end-of-life product)
prevention.adequacy: Blocking Flash content genuinely closes this path, and it is the one control that was already written down in 2015 as an Essential Eight application-hardening requirement. Its limit is scope: policy usually covers the standalone plugin, while the Flash engines bundled inside Internet Explorer 10/11 and Chrome, and any standalone SWF player, sat outside that policy and still parsed the same content.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Alerting on a browser or plugin process creating or injecting into explorer.exe, and on outbound impression traffic from a host with no user at the keyboard — the observable half of the Bedep ad-fraud stage.
detection.adequacy: This detects the payload, not the exploit. Everything up to and including code execution happens inside one browser process against a freed heap chunk, leaving nothing on disk to match, so detection bounds dwell time rather than preventing compromise. Antivirus coverage of the Angler landing SWFs was poor at the time because the kit re-encoded per delivery.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treating a confirmed hit as a credential-exposure event for the logged-on user, since Bedep is a loader and the ad-fraud module observed in this campaign is only one of the payloads it can pull.
response.adequacy: Reimaging the workstation removes the loader but not what the loader already fetched or exfiltrated during its residency, and the campaign's rotating infrastructure means indicator-based scoping understates the affected population. Response was also structurally late here: the exploit was in Angler before Adobe had an advisory to respond to.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: The organisation can evidence flaw remediation, but the clock SI-2 measures did not start until Adobe published 16.0.0.296 on 2015-01-24, two days after Kafeine found the exploit already live in Angler. During those two days a compliant SI-2 programme has nothing to do and reports nothing wrong. The control is equally blind to the split update surface: Flash inside Internet Explorer 10/11 and Chrome moved on the browser vendors' tracks, so patching the Adobe runtime produced a clean SI-2 record while vulnerable copies of the same engine kept rendering ad content.

NIS2-Art21-patch-management.gap: Article 21 is written for a product with a maintainer. Adobe stopped supporting Flash Player on 2020-12-31 and blocked Flash content from running on 2021-01-12, so an operator running it today has no patch to apply and can close the obligation with a risk acceptance. That acceptance leaves a CVSS 9.8, PR:N, UI:N code-execution path whose exploit is a Metasploit module in service, and nothing in the patch-management wording escalates an unmaintained runtime into the removal decision it actually requires.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: A B4 assessment is satisfied by a securely configured, maintained system, and a host reporting Flash 16.0.0.296 in 2015 met that bar. What B4 never asks is whether the SWF parser needs to be present on the host at all, which is the only question that resolves this CVE in 2026. Estates routinely hold a positive B4 outcome while a dead browser plugin stays registered on engineering workstations, kiosk terminals and legacy line-of-business viewers that no browser policy covers.

AU-Essential-8-App-Hardening.gap: Blocking Flash content in web browsers is an explicit Maturity Level One application-hardening requirement, and it is the single control that would have neutralised this campaign outright — the Angler landing page had nothing to execute without a Flash host. The gap is how the control is evidenced: a maturity assessment reads a browser policy setting, while this CVE was reachable through Internet Explorer 10/11's and Chrome's internally bundled Flash engines and through standalone SWF players outside any browser policy. Attesting the policy is not the same as demonstrating the parser is unreachable.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: A.8.8 gets the identification step right — the 2026-08-16 EPSS pair of 0.8582 at the 0.99711 percentile is precisely the signal the control expects to surface — and then routes the finding into a risk evaluation with no defined outcome for software that has no vendor, no fixed version and a public Metasploit module. Because Flash's end-of-life arrived five years after the fix and eleven years before this review, the evaluate-and-treat loop terminates in an open-ended acceptance rather than a dated removal, which is how a 2015 KEV entry survives a decade of clean A.8.8 audits.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Adobe Flash Player carried this defect from an unknown date until 16.0.0.296 reached auto-update clients on 2015-01-24, two days after Kafeine found Angler already exploiting it and after APSA15-01 had been published with no fix. CISA listed it on 2022-04-13 with a 2022-05-04 due date and an unusual required action — disconnect the end-of-life product — which is exactly the 'documented compensating control' branch of this SLA rather than the patch branch. The 2026-08-16 EPSS pair of 0.8582 at the 0.99711 percentile shows the exploitation pressure has not decayed, so the four-hour clock still has meaning for any estate that finds a Flash runtime today.

new_control_requirements.name: MITIGATION-ACTIVE-PATCH-PENDING-VERDICT-CLASS
new_control_requirements.description: Compliance verdicts must distinguish three states: (a) binary patch deployed (vulnerability eliminated), (b) vendor-mitigation rule active, no binary patch (residual risk: any defect in the mitigation rule reopens the vulnerability), (c) no mitigation, no patch (full exposure). Audit reports must surface (b) as a distinct compensating-control state with an associated time-bound action item, not as a 'patched per SLA' outcome.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Adobe's APSA15-01 of 2015-01-22 named CVE-2015-0311 in Flash Player 16.0.0.287 and earlier and offered no fix — every Flash-bearing host in the estate was in state (c) for two days while Angler dropped Bedep, and the only lever available was disabling the plugin, which is state (b). A vulnerability register that carries a single patched/unpatched flag records nothing at all during that window. The same three-state distinction is what separates an honest 2026 verdict on Flash from a false one: with the runtime unsupported since 2020-12-31 there is no state (a) available, so browser-side blocking is a state (b) holding measure and removal is the only closure.

attack_vector.description: A malicious ad delivers a SWF that maps a ByteArray as domainMemory, then frees it from a separate ActionScript Worker while the main thread still addresses it directly. Reads and writes then hit freed heap; sprayed Vector objects reoccupy it, one length field is corrupted, and the attacker has arbitrary memory access inside the browser and code execution as the logged-on user.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none — PR:N; the victim holds no relationship with the attacker and supplies no credential, only a page view on a mainstream video site
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L; the cross-thread race is real but was solved once by the kit author and shipped in a working kit whose hits Trend Micro was already counting on 2015-01-14. The genuine constraint is version, not skill — and the two authorities differ on where it sits: Adobe withdrew 11.x from APSA15-02 saying 11.x and earlier lack the affected functionality, while NVD and Adobe's own APSB15-04 keep Linux 11.2.202.440 and earlier in scope.
attack_vector.ai_factor: None. Adobe credits Elia Florio and Dave Weston of Microsoft and Peter Pi of Trend Micro — human reverse-engineering of samples captured from the live malvertising chain. No 'AI' branding appears anywhere in this disclosure chain, and no automated discovery is claimed.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Not having a Flash runtime on the host, or holding browsers at click-to-play so an ad slot could not auto-execute a SWF. Failing that, an ad-blocking or ad-network-filtering control at the browser or proxy, since the delivery path was entirely third-party ad infrastructure.
prevention.framework_requiring_it: CISA BOD 22-01 (KEV remediation, added 2022-04-13; required action: disconnect the end-of-life product)
prevention.adequacy: Removing Flash closes it completely, and click-to-play closes it for practical purposes because the exploit needed to run unprompted from an ad frame. Ad filtering is weaker than it sounds here — the chain hung off dailymotion.com, a mainstream publisher, and reached the victim through third-party advertising infrastructure rather than a known-bad destination, so a reputation-based filter had no signal to act on.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Flagging SWF content that combines ActionScript Workers with domainMemory assignment at a web proxy or content-inspection tier, since that pair is the exploit precondition and is rare in advertising creatives.
detection.adequacy: This is a narrow, high-signal check but it depends on being able to inspect the SWF at all, and the kit served it once per client from a single-use host over a short-lived path. It also assumes decrypted inspection of third-party ad traffic, which many estates do not perform. Detection here shortens dwell time; it does not stop the process-internal corruption.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treating any confirmed hit as browser-session compromise for the logged-on user — session cookie invalidation, credential reset, and review of anything the browser had authenticated to during the exposure window.
response.adequacy: Scoping is the weak point. The documented exploitation window opens on 2015-01-14, when Trend Micro began monitoring the campaign, and the advisory only lands on 2015-02-02, so a response scoped from the advisory date misses about three weeks of exposure. The delivery chain was already down when Trend Micro published, so proxy-log hunting for the one known URL finds a fraction of the affected population.

NIST-800-53-CM-7.gap: Least functionality is the control that would actually have prevented this, by removing a SWF parser nobody needed from workstations that render untrusted web content. It fails on granularity and on inventory: a browser plugin registered by a browser update does not appear in the application inventory a CM-7 baseline compares against, and the abused surface here is finer still — the Worker plus domainMemory feature pair inside the plugin, which no baseline in the field expresses. An estate can hold a clean CM-7 assessment with the vulnerable parser fully reachable.

NIS2-Art21-vulnerability-handling.gap: The handling duty is triggered by disclosure, and disclosure lagged exploitation by about three weeks: Trend Micro says it was monitoring this attack from 2015-01-14 and saw the hit spike around 2015-01-27, while Adobe published APSA15-02 on 2015-02-02. For that whole period an entity with a fully conformant handling process received nothing, evaluated nothing, and had users compromised through dailymotion.com ad slots. Article 21 defines no obligation that fires on third-party exploitation evidence in the absence of a vendor advisory.

UK-CAF-C1.gap: Security monitoring is nominally in place and structurally blind to this chain. The compromise runs to completion inside a single browser process against freed heap, delivered by a legitimate ad network to a legitimate publisher, producing no anomalous authentication, no new listening service and no unusual destination until the payload stage. A C1 outcome assessed on network and identity telemetry is honestly earned and gives the defender nothing to alert on while the exploit is landing.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: Patch applications measures from vendor release, and 16.0.0.305 was released on 2015-02-04 with the Linux 11.2.202.442 build following in APSB15-04 on 2015-02-05, so an estate can report full compliance across the three weeks from 2015-01-14 in which Trend Micro was already recording hits against this exploit. The control also assumes one update channel per product, whereas the same Flash engine reached a single Windows host through Adobe's auto-update, Internet Explorer 10/11's bundled copy and Chrome's Pepper Flash — three tracks, of which a 'Flash patched' attestation typically evidences one.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.7.gap: Anti-malware protection was deployed across the whole 2015-01-14 to 2015-02-05 exploitation-to-fix window and did not stop this. The delivered artefact was a SWF served from a short-lived host at hxxp://www.retilio.com/skillt.swf; Trend Micro's SWF_EXPLOIT.MJST signature exists only after the sample was captured, and the exploit reached code execution without writing to disk. A.8.7 evidence describes coverage and update currency, neither of which speaks to a memory-corruption chain that runs entirely inside the browser process.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Adobe Flash Player 16.0.0.296 and earlier carried this Worker/domainMemory use-after-free while an exploit kit served it through dailymotion.com ad slots, a campaign Trend Micro was already monitoring on 2015-01-14; the fix, 16.0.0.305, only reached auto-update clients on 2015-02-04 with manual download the day after and the Linux 11.2.202.442 build in APSB15-04 on 2015-02-05. CISA listed the CVE on 2022-04-13 with a 2022-05-04 due date and a required action of disconnecting the product, which is the documented-compensating-control branch of this SLA rather than the patch branch. The 2026-08-16 EPSS pair of 0.95683 at the 0.99866 percentile puts it in the top 0.2% of scored CVEs, so the four-hour clock is the correct posture for any Flash runtime still found on an estate.

new_control_requirements.name: VENDOR-PUSH-MITIGATION-OPT-IN-PRE-DISCLOSURE
new_control_requirements.description: For vendors offering push-mitigation services (Microsoft EEMS, Palo Alto Threat Prevention auto-update, etc.), opt-in must be enabled BEFORE the next disclosure event, not in response to it. Compliance frameworks must require operators to enable available vendor-push-mitigation services as a baseline control — opt-in late means the mitigation rule arrives after exploitation, not before.
new_control_requirements.evidence: This CVE is the clearest possible demonstration on Flash Player. Adobe states in APSA15-02 that users who had enabled auto-update for the desktop runtime began receiving 16.0.0.305 on 2015-02-04, with the manual download expected 2015-02-05 and distribution partners' browser-bundled builds later still. The opt-in decision therefore had to have been taken before the advisory to be worth anything: an estate that enabled auto-update in response to the 2015-02-02 advisory gained nothing over one that did not. The same asymmetry applied a fortnight earlier on CVE-2015-0311, where auto-update clients got 16.0.0.296 on 2015-01-24 and manual downloaders waited until the following week.

CVE-2015-2502.name: Microsoft Internet Explorer Memory Corruption Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: An attacker who has compromised a site the target population already visits injects an iframe that redirects the browser to exploit content. Internet Explorer mishandles an object in memory while rendering it, the resulting out-of-bounds write is steered into code execution in the browser process, and the payload — PlugX in the observed campaign — is installed with the logged-on user's rights.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none — PR:N; the attacker needs no account on the target and no prior foothold, only control of content the browser will render
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L with UI:R; the user must load the page, and the campaign removed that friction by compromising a legitimate site rather than sending a lure. Microsoft recorded no mitigating factors and no workarounds; server SKUs get partial relief only from Enhanced Security Configuration being on by default.
attack_vector.ai_factor: None claimed. Microsoft published no named discovery credit and marked the flaw exploited before public disclosure; the subsequent reporting from Heimdal Security and Symantec attributes the campaign, not the bug's discovery, and no automated-discovery claim appears anywhere in the record.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Applying MS15-093 in the out-of-band window with the KB3078071 prerequisite in the right order and the restart taken, and running Internet Explorer without administrative rights so the PlugX install ran as a limited user.
prevention.adequacy: The patch is complete and the fix is real, but the timing was hostile — an out-of-band release on 2015-08-18 with exploitation already under way, and a reboot requirement on the terminal servers Microsoft names as most at risk, which are precisely the hosts where restarts get deferred. Running without admin rights limits the damage without preventing the browser-process compromise or the user-scope implant.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Alerting on Internet Explorer spawning a child process or writing an executable, and on any browser redirect from a trusted site to a bare IPv4 address — the two observable steps in this chain that do not depend on a signature.
detection.adequacy: Behavioural rules of that shape would have fired; signature-based detection would not, and did not — Heimdal Security recorded low antivirus detection rates for both the exploit and the payload. The redirect-to-bare-IP heuristic is noisy in estates that use content-delivery infrastructure heavily, so it needs tuning rather than deployment as-is.

response.what_would_have_worked: Retrospective proxy-log hunting for the compromised host and java.html, plus credential rotation for any user whose browser retrieved it, since PlugX is a full remote-access trojan with a six-month-old command-and-control history at EhostIDC.
response.adequacy: The response is right and the scoping input is missing: nobody published the start date of the compromise of the church website, so the correct hunting window is unknown and most proxy retention will not cover it. An implant with the dwell time this campaign allowed also makes host reimaging a floor rather than a resolution — anything the implant collected stays valid until rotated.

NIST-800-53-SI-4.gap: Monitoring is deployed and structurally cannot see this. Users requested a site their organisation had every reason to permit, and the malicious element was an injected iframe to 115.144.107.55 serving java.html — no anomalous account, no anomalous destination category, no volume signal. The first alertable behaviour is the PlugX implant beaconing, which is post-compromise, and Heimdal Security's observation that antivirus detection rates for both the exploit and the payload were low is a direct measurement of how little SI-4 telemetry there was to work with.

NIS2-Art21-incident-handling.gap: The handling process is in place and starts too late. Microsoft's out-of-band MS15-093 landed on 2015-08-18 already flagging the flaw as exploited, and the watering-hole reporting followed on 2015-08-19, so an Article 21 process begins after the exposure window closed rather than during it. Scoping then requires answering which staff visited one specific Hong Kong church website across an unknown period, which typical 30-to-90-day web-proxy retention cannot support.

UK-CAF-D1.gap: Response and recovery plans exist, are exercised, and depend on the incident being recognised — which is the step this CVE removes. The outcome was a PlugX implant delivered through a trusted page on a browser Microsoft names as most exposed on workstations and terminal servers, with low antivirus detection at the time. D1 evidence covers plans and roles; it does not test whether the organisation can establish that a trusted site served an exploit iframe during a window that ended before any indicator was published.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: The control is correct and its assumptions were violated three ways at once. MS15-093 shipped out of band on 2015-08-18, outside the monthly cadence estates schedule around; the bulletin makes KB3078071 of 2015-08-11 a hard prerequisite on Windows 7, Server 2008 R2, Windows 8.1, Server 2012 R2 and Windows RT 8.1, with degraded functionality if the order is wrong; and the update requires a restart, so a host marked patched in the console but not rebooted is still running vulnerable browser code. None of those three conditions appears in a maturity-level attestation.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.16.gap: Monitoring activities looks for anomalies, and this attack produced one HTTP redirect from a legitimate site to 115.144.107.55 followed by a fetch of java.html — statistically indistinguishable from ordinary third-party content loading. A.8.16 evidence is normally log coverage and alert-rule inventory, neither of which surfaces that sequence. The first genuinely anomalous artefact is implant traffic to infrastructure at EhostIDC that Heimdal Security had already tied to six months of prior PlugX activity, which is a threat-intelligence match rather than a monitoring outcome.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Microsoft released MS15-093 for Internet Explorer 7 through 11 out of band on 2015-08-18, marking CVE-2015-2502 exploited but not publicly disclosed, and the Evangelical Lutheran Church of Hong Kong watering hole delivering PlugX was reported one day later. CISA listed the CVE on 2022-04-13 with a 2022-05-04 due date. Applied here the SLA is specifically about the reboot and the prerequisite: KB3078071 of 2015-08-11 must precede KB3087985, and the restart must be taken, so 'verified mitigation' means an installed build plus a completed restart rather than a console status. The 2026-08-16 EPSS pair of 0.38705 at the 0.98454 percentile keeps this in the top two percent of exploitation likelihood.

new_control_requirements.name: NATION-STATE-INITIAL-ACCESS-IR-ESCALATION
new_control_requirements.description: IR runbooks must include an explicit nation-state-initial-access escalation path triggered by APT28/APT29/Lazarus/Volt-Typhoon/etc. attribution on a confirmed exploit chain. Standard malware-infection IR under-escalates nation-state activity by treating it as commodity threat.
new_control_requirements.evidence: The payload delivered through this Internet Explorer flaw was PlugX, also tracked as Korplug — a remote-access trojan associated with Chinese-linked espionage rather than commodity crime — and Heimdal Security reported the command-and-control server, hosted at the Korean hosting company EhostIDC, had already featured in APT activity involving PlugX over the preceding six months. A watering hole placed on the website of the Evangelical Lutheran Church of Hong Kong is target selection, not opportunistic infection. Handling that as a routine malware clean-up sets the wrong scope: the correct response is credential rotation and retrospective hunting across everyone who visited the compromised site, on an exposure window whose start date was never published.

CVE-2015-3113.name: Adobe Flash Player Heap-Based Buffer Overflow Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: A crafted FLV declares a Nellymoser audio DataSize the decoder does not validate, so decoding writes past the end of a heap buffer. The exploit corrupts neighbouring vector metadata for arbitrary read/write, uses it to locate modules despite ASLR, builds a ROP chain to get past DEP, and runs its payload as the user hosting the Flash runtime.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none — PR:N; the attacker holds no account and needs only for the target to load the media
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L and UI:N for the primitive itself, though the campaign added its own friction by routing victims through phishing links to compromised servers that served the SWF selectively. The exploit defeats ASLR and DEP in one payload, which is engineering, not chance.
attack_vector.ai_factor: None. FireEye's managed-detection team found it in live intrusion activity and Unit 42's follow-up was manual exploit and malware analysis; neither claims automated discovery, and no 'AI'-branded research arm appears in the chain.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Not having a Flash runtime capable of decoding FLV audio on the host at all. Where it had to remain, moving to 18.0.0.194 on the day APSB15-14 published, and treating the earlier CVE-2015-3043 remediation as void rather than as coverage.
prevention.framework_requiring_it: CISA BOD 22-01 (KEV remediation, added 2022-04-13; required action: disconnect the end-of-life product)
prevention.adequacy: Removal closes it. Patching closes this instance and demonstrably not the class — the same decoder path had already been fixed in April 2015 and was exploitable again by June, so an estate that patched twice bought three months. Browser hardening alone is incomplete because the parser is reachable from non-browser Flash hosts that render FLV.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Hunting for the payload rather than the exploit: the Pirpi.2015 configuration file at %APPDATA%\vcl.tmp or %TEMP%\vcl.tmp, and outbound HTTP GETs carrying oversized opaque Cookie values.
detection.adequacy: Both are durable indicators and both are post-exploitation. The exploit stage leaves nothing but a possible crash, and the campaign's servers served benign content selectively, so retrospective retrieval of the malicious SWF often fails — which also means indicator sets built from one victim understate the population.

response.what_would_have_worked: Escalating on the attribution rather than the artefact: APT3 with a zero-day and a 25-command backdoor carried over almost unchanged from its 2014 build is a targeted-intrusion response, with credential rotation and lateral-movement review, not an endpoint clean-up.
response.adequacy: Correct in shape, expensive to scope. The phishing was deliberately generic, so mail-side hunting has weak selectors, and Pirpi's command breadth means the operator's activity after installation is not bounded by anything visible on the compromised host. Reimaging is necessary and does not resolve what was taken.

NIST-800-218-SSDF-PW.7.1.gap: Code review was performed and the defect came back anyway. Adobe fixed the same Nellymoser root cause in April 2015 as CVE-2015-3043, and by June the identical exploit worked again — the Metasploit module ships one payload citing both CVE ids for exactly that reason. PW.7.1 requires review of changes but not a regression test that replays each fixed memory-safety proof of concept against the new build, so its evidence trail cannot distinguish a fix that held from one a later refactor in the same audio path silently undid.

NIS2-Art21-vulnerability-management.gap: The process ran correctly twice and hid the thing worth knowing. CVE-2015-3043 was opened and closed in April 2015 on a fixed Flash build; CVE-2015-3113 opened in June against the same decoder with no recorded relationship between the two entries. Article 21 requires the process, not the linkage, so the register shows two well-handled items rather than one primitive that defeated remediation twice — which is the signal that would have argued for removing the runtime rather than patching it again.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: A B4 statement built on browser build levels is satisfied by a host reporting Flash 18.0.0.194, and it was. The exposure it misses is that the vulnerable code is a media decoder, not a script engine: standalone Flash projectors, e-learning packages and embedded players all render FLV audio and sit outside a browser-scoped assessment. FireEye's delivery path — a link in generic phishing mail to a compromised web server — needs exactly one such host still carrying the decoder.

AU-Essential-8-App-Hardening.gap: Blocking Flash content in browsers meets Maturity Level One and does close the documented delivery path for this campaign. It does not close the defect's real surface, because a Nellymoser overflow triggers on FLV media and is reachable from any Flash host that plays it, browser or otherwise. Attesting the browser policy therefore leaves the FLV parsing surface intact in e-learning and embedded players — the places where end-of-life Flash survives longest on real estates.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.28.gap: Secure coding is attested from standards, training and tooling, all of which a vendor that reintroduced the same heap overflow within three months would pass. The specific, testable requirement it lacks: retain the proof of concept for every fixed memory-safety defect and re-run it against every subsequent release of that component. Without that gate, nothing in A.8.28's evidence separates a codebase where the CVE-2015-3043 fix held from one where the June build handed the same exploit back to APT3.

new_control_requirements.name: INCOMPLETE-PATCH-SEQUENCE-SEVERITY-MULTIPLIER
new_control_requirements.description: Vulnerability-management programs must apply a severity multiplier when a CVE is the Nth in an incomplete-patch sequence on the same primitive (third MOTW bypass, second AMSI bypass, etc.). Framework controls treating each CVE as discrete obscure the structural defect; the Nth CVE in a sequence implies that future bypasses on the same primitive are likely.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Adobe Flash Player's Nellymoser FLV audio decoder is the primitive and this is its second CVE in ten weeks: CVE-2015-3043 was fixed by APSB15-06 on 2015-04-14 and CVE-2015-3113 shipped as a zero-day used by APT3 on 2015-06-23, with the Metasploit module adobe_flash_nellymoser_bof stating in its own description that one exploit works against both because 3113 is a regression to the same root cause. An estate that scored 3113 on its CVSS 9.8 alone treated it as a new item; scoring it as the second failure of the same decoder would have moved the decision from 'patch to 18.0.0.194' to 'remove the runtime', which is where it ended up anyway once Adobe stopped supporting Flash on 2020-12-31.

new_control_requirements.name: NATION-STATE-INITIAL-ACCESS-IR-ESCALATION
new_control_requirements.description: IR runbooks must include an explicit nation-state-initial-access escalation path triggered by APT28/APT29/Lazarus/Volt-Typhoon/etc. attribution on a confirmed exploit chain. Standard malware-infection IR under-escalates nation-state activity by treating it as commodity threat.
new_control_requirements.evidence: FireEye published this Flash zero-day on 2015-06-23 as Operation Clandestine Wolf and attributed it to APT3, with Unit 42 tracking the same intrusion set as UPS and the payload as Pirpi.2015 — a backdoor whose 25-command loop (values 1-17, 32-38 and 49, covering domain and DC enumeration, netstat, file upload and DLL loading) differs from the group's 2014 build in only two commands, keeping its configuration at %APPDATA%\vcl.tmp or %TEMP%\vcl.tmp and beaconing over HTTP GET with encrypted data in Cookie headers. An actor holding an unpublished Flash zero-day and a full-featured backdoor is not a commodity infection, and treating a %TEMP%\vcl.tmp hit as an endpoint clean-up sets the wrong scope; the correct response is credential rotation and lateral-movement review across everything the compromised identity reached.

attack_vector.description: A page delivers a SWF that sets DisplayObject.opaqueBackground to an object whose valueOf() the attacker controls. Flash calls that callback inside the setter, the callback frees the object's backing storage, and the setter continues on the dangling pointer. Sprayed Vector objects take the freed chunk, one length field is overwritten, and the attacker reads and writes process memory freely before executing code as the logged-on user.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none — PR:N; no account, no prior access, nothing asked of the victim but a page load
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L; the valueOf callback lets the attacker choose the moment of the free rather than win a race, and the engineered exploit came out of a surveillance vendor's archive already working, so kit operators inherited reliability they did not have to build.
attack_vector.ai_factor: None. The exploit was written by a commercial surveillance vendor and became public through a breach; the analysts who triaged the archive, FireEye among them, did manual reverse engineering. No AI-assisted discovery or weaponisation is claimed by any party.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Having no Flash runtime, or disabling the plugin the day the archive leaked — before Adobe had anything to ship. Click-to-play would have blunted the drive-by delivery that exploit kits used.
prevention.framework_requiring_it: CISA BOD 22-01 (KEV remediation, added 2022-04-13; required action: disconnect the end-of-life product)
prevention.adequacy: Disabling the plugin is the only control that existed during the interval that mattered, since the exploit was public and in kits before APSB15-18 shipped on 2015-07-14. Its limits are coverage rather than efficacy: the browser-bundled Flash engines and embedded runtimes in kiosk and signage estates are not governed by the browser policy an organisation would point to as evidence.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Content-side inspection for SWF that assigns opaqueBackground from an object with an overridden valueOf(), and for the Vector heap-spray pattern the public exploit uses to reoccupy the freed chunk.
detection.adequacy: Both constructs are specific enough to be low-noise, and both require the ability to inspect SWF in transit, which fails against kits that serve once per client over TLS from short-lived hosts. Detection here reduces dwell time after the fact; it does not interrupt a corruption chain that completes inside the plugin process.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treating any confirmed hit as full compromise of the browser session and the local user context — session invalidation, credential rotation, and review of everything the browser had authenticated to during the window between the leak and the patch.
response.adequacy: Scoping is unusually hard because the leak-to-kit interval was days and the kits rotated infrastructure per campaign, so indicator-based hunting recovers a fraction of the exposed population. Reimaging removes the payload of the day and not what a loader fetched before it, which for kit-delivered compromises is frequently unknown.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: The remediation clock starts at patch availability and the exploit beat the patch: working code left the Hacking Team archive and reached commodity kits before Adobe published APSB15-18 on 2015-07-14, so a conformant SI-2 programme has nothing to record during the window when the estate is most exposed. SI-2 evidence also collapses the two fixed builds this CVE has — 18.0.0.209 on the mainline and 13.0.0.309 on extended support — into one 'Flash current' assertion that does not show which target was applied to which host.

DORA-Art-9.gap: Protection and prevention obligations reduce ICT attack surface through policy, tooling and segmentation, none of which reaches a memory-corruption chain completing inside a single browser process on a workstation. Article 9 also presumes a supported product with a vendor security lifecycle to lean on, and Flash has had none since Adobe stopped supporting it on 2020-12-31 and blocked content execution on 2021-01-12 — a financial entity discharging Article 9 against this CVE today is documenting compensating controls around a runtime with no maintainer, not preventing anything.

UK-CAF-C1.gap: Monitoring is in place and produced nothing usable during the days between the leak and the bulletin. The estate-side events were a browser fetching a SWF from a malvertising or compromised host and, on success, whatever the kit's payload did next — no authentication anomaly, no new listening service, no unusual destination category. A C1 assessment based on log coverage and alert-rule inventory reads identically on an exploited host and a clean one right up to the post-exploitation stage.

AU-Essential-8-App-Hardening.gap: Blocking Flash content in browsers is the Maturity Level One requirement and, uniquely on this entry, it was the only effective control while the exploit was public and unpatched. That raises the evidence bar rather than lowering it: an attestation citing a browser policy does not reach the Flash engines Internet Explorer 10/11 and Chrome carried internally, nor standalone projectors, nor embedded runtimes in kiosk and signage fleets. In July 2015 the gap between an attested policy and a demonstrated absent runtime was the gap between compromised and not.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.9.gap: Configuration management is the control that should make this exposure countable and routinely does not, because browser plugins evade baselines: they arrive with browser updates, enable per user profile, and exist in three separate copies on one Windows host — the Adobe runtime, Internet Explorer's bundled build and Chrome's Pepper Flash. A.8.9 evidence covers operating-system and application baselines, so an organisation can hold documented, enforced configurations and still be unable to state how many loadable ActionScript 3 engines it owns.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: For Adobe Flash Player this CVE is the case where the SLA's 'documented compensating controls' branch is the only one that existed: working exploit code was public from the Hacking Team archive and folded into exploit kits before Adobe shipped 18.0.0.209 and 13.0.0.309 on 2015-07-14, with the Metasploit module published 2015-07-13, a day ahead of the bulletin. CISA listed the CVE on 2022-04-13 with a 2022-05-04 due date and a required action of disconnecting the end-of-life product. The 2026-08-16 EPSS pair of 0.93688 at the 0.99834 percentile shows the exploitation likelihood has not decayed in eleven years.

new_control_requirements.name: BROWSER-MANAGED-UPDATE-NO-DEFERRAL
new_control_requirements.description: Enterprise update rings must not defer security-channel browser updates beyond 24h.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Flash for this CVE was not one update but three tracks on the same Windows host: Adobe's own runtime moving to 18.0.0.209 or 13.0.0.309 per APSB15-18, Internet Explorer 10/11's bundled Flash, and Chrome's Pepper Flash — with the Linux Chrome build carrying its own version range up to 18.0.0.204 in the affected list. An update ring that deferred the browser channel therefore left a vulnerable engine on a host whose Adobe runtime was already current, and the deferral window here had to be measured against exploit kits that adopted the leaked exploit within days rather than against a monthly cycle.

attack_vector.description: A crafted SWF passes an object with an attacker-controlled valueOf() into a BitmapData method. Flash calls that override to coerce the argument, the callback frees or moves the BitmapData's backing buffer, and the method carries on using the stale pointer. Reoccupying the freed chunk and corrupting length metadata gives arbitrary read and write in the Flash process, then code execution as the user running it.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none — PR:N; no account and nothing asked of the victim except that the content be rendered
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L; the free is triggered from a callback the runtime must invoke — a valueOf override reached through BitmapData.paletteMap that calls BitmapData.dispose() — so the primitive is deterministic rather than a race. The practical constraint in 2015 was code access: Trend Micro published a proof-of-concept and named no exploit kit for this CVE, so anyone outside the leaked archive had to build the corruption chain rather than run someone else's.
attack_vector.ai_factor: None. Trend Micro and the independent researcher slipstream/RoL found it by analysing the leaked Hacking Team archive; the underlying exploit was written by a commercial surveillance vendor. No automated or AI-assisted discovery is claimed by any party in this chain.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Removing the Flash runtime, browser and non-browser alike, or moving to 18.0.0.209 / 13.0.0.309 when APSB15-18 published on 2015-07-14 and restarting the hosting process.
prevention.framework_requiring_it: CISA BOD 22-01 (KEV remediation, added 2022-04-13; required action: disconnect the end-of-life product)
prevention.adequacy: The patch is complete for this defect and the coverage problem is where the runtime lives. Kiosk, signage, e-learning and HMI hosts embed Flash with no update channel and no browser policy, so an estate that patched every browser could still hold vulnerable engines — and those are the hosts most likely to still hold them in 2026, with no vendor left to supply a fix.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Content inspection for SWF passing a valueOf-overriding object into BitmapData methods, plus alerting on Flash host processes that crash repeatedly or spawn children after rendering.
detection.adequacy: The construct-level check is specific and cheap where SWF can be inspected in transit; it is unavailable on kiosk and signage estates that pull content over TLS from a vendor endpoint nobody proxies. Crash-and-spawn alerting is post-exploitation. Vendor detection did appear immediately — Trend Micro shipped Deep Security DPI rule 1006859 for this CVE with its 2015-07-11 write-up — but that is a licensed product control on the hosts that carry it, not a signature an unlicensed estate inherits.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treating the host as compromised at user scope and rebuilding it, and — because the affected population skews to appliances — verifying the content source itself rather than only the endpoint.
response.adequacy: Response guidance here is generic because no named campaign for this CVE was located: KEV records in-the-wild use, while the 2015 reporting goes no further than a proof-of-concept under monitoring. That leaves an organisation with no indicator set to hunt against, so response has to be driven from exposure — which Flash-bearing hosts existed, and what content they rendered — rather than from detection.

NIST-800-53-SC-44.gap: Detonation chambers answer exactly the question this CVE poses — is this SWF hostile — and are almost never aimed at the delivery path it uses. Deployments detonate email attachments and downloaded files; a BitmapData use-after-free triggered by a valueOf override arrives as inline rendered content fetched by a browser or an appliance's content client, never becomes a file the user opened, and therefore never enters the chamber. An accurate SC-44 attestation can cover none of this vulnerability's surface.

EU-CRA-Art13.gap: The manufacturer obligations the Cyber Resilience Act imposes — security updates across the support period, vulnerability handling, documented security properties — are precisely what an operator of a Flash-bearing product needs and cannot obtain. Article 13 postdates the 2015-07-14 fix entirely and binds products being placed on the market, not a runtime whose vendor ended support on 2020-12-31. The lag is concrete: an embedded signage unit shipping Flash today would owe an operator updates, while the identical unit shipped a decade ago owes nothing and carries the same CVE.

UK-CAF-A1.gap: Governance processes, roles and accountability are in place and produce no removal date. A1 does not require a dated retirement plan for a product with no maintainer, so a CVSS 9.8 flaw with a KEV listing of 2022-04-13 and a 2026-08-16 EPSS pair of 0.18493 at the 0.96995 percentile — inside the top four percent — is exactly the profile that gets recorded as a tolerated risk with an annual review rather than a decommissioning schedule.

AU-Essential-8-App-Hardening.gap: Blocking Flash content in web browsers satisfies Maturity Level One and, for this CVE, secures the half of the estate least likely to still be affected. The hosts that plausibly still run a vulnerable ActionScript 3 engine in 2026 are kiosk terminals, digital signage, e-learning players and industrial HMI panels with an embedded runtime — never governed by a browser policy, never reached by a browser update channel, and invisible to an assessment evidenced from browser configuration.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: The control identifies the vulnerability correctly and then prioritises it on an absence. In July 2015 its sibling CVE-2015-5122 had a Metasploit module within days, while for this one Trend Micro published a proof-of-concept and said only that it was monitoring for attacks that might employ it — no named kit, no named campaign — so a risk-based A.8.8 evaluation reasonably ranked it lower and deferred it. Nothing in the control forces a re-read when the basis of the deferral is 'nothing observed yet', which is how a deferred item survives long enough for its product's vendor to disappear underneath it.

new_control_requirements.name: BROWSER-MANAGED-UPDATE-NO-DEFERRAL
new_control_requirements.description: Enterprise update rings must not defer security-channel browser updates beyond 24h.
new_control_requirements.evidence: APSB15-18 fixed this BitmapData use-after-free on 2015-07-14 by moving Adobe Flash Player to 18.0.0.209, or 13.0.0.309 on the extended-support line, but the same engine reached a Windows host through three channels — Adobe's runtime, Internet Explorer 10/11's bundled Flash, and Chrome's Pepper Flash, with the Linux Chrome build carrying its own range up to 18.0.0.204. A deferred browser ring therefore keeps a vulnerable engine resident on a host whose Adobe runtime already reports the fixed build, and because the fix loads only on process restart, a browser left running across the update is not remediated either.

new_control_requirements.name: MITIGATION-ACTIVE-PATCH-PENDING-VERDICT-CLASS
new_control_requirements.description: Compliance verdicts must distinguish three states: (a) binary patch deployed (vulnerability eliminated), (b) vendor-mitigation rule active, no binary patch (residual risk: any defect in the mitigation rule reopens the vulnerability), (c) no mitigation, no patch (full exposure). Audit reports must surface (b) as a distinct compensating-control state with an associated time-bound action item, not as a 'patched per SLA' outcome.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Between Adobe naming this BitmapData flaw in APSA15-04 on 2015-07-10 — an advisory that offered no fix, only the expectation of updates 'during the week of July 12, 2015' — and the APSB15-18 bulletin of 2015-07-14, every Flash-bearing host sat in state (c): no patch and, for anything outside a browser, not even a plugin toggle to reach state (b). Eleven years later the same three-state test gives the only honest verdict available: with Adobe support ended on 2020-12-31 and content execution blocked from 2021-01-12, state (a) no longer exists for this product, so browser-side blocking is a state (b) holding measure carrying a time-bound action and removal is the only closure. A register with a single patched/unpatched flag cannot express either situation.

CVE-2016-0162.name: Microsoft Internet Explorer Information Disclosure Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: Crafted JavaScript in a page rendered by Internet Explorer 9-11 learns whether a named local file exists, because the browser returns more about a failed resource load than it should. An attacker enumerates hundreds of paths to inventory security products, hypervisors, debuggers and packet-capture tools, then decides whether the visitor is worth exploiting — serving the real chain only to hosts that look unmonitored.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none — PR:N; the attacker needs no account and reads nothing but the presence or absence of paths the script names
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L with UI:R; the user must load the page in Internet Explorer and nothing else is required. Microsoft identified no mitigating factors and no workarounds. Server SKUs get partial relief only from Enhanced Security Configuration being enabled by default, which is why the same flaw rates Moderate on clients and Low on servers.
attack_vector.ai_factor: None. No discovery credit was published, the bulletin records the flaw as exploited before public disclosure, and the named public analysis — ESET on Stegano, Proofpoint on AdGholas — documents attacker use rather than discovery. No AI-branded research arm appears anywhere in the record.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Installing Internet Explorer cumulative update 4014661 or a later rollup and restarting — not the April 2016 MS16-037 release alone — and removing Internet Explorer from hosts that do not need it, including the embedded WebBrowser-control surfaces.
prevention.adequacy: The second-round update closes it; the first-round one demonstrably did not, which is the whole lesson of this entry. Removal is stronger and harder, because the IE engine survives inside line-of-business applications long after the browser icon is gone, and those surfaces are the ones an inventory built from installed browsers will miss.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Alerting on script that issues a burst of local-path probes, and treating an analyst or sandbox host that receives only benign content from a suspect ad chain as a positive evasion signal rather than a clean result.
detection.adequacy: The enumeration is the loudest thing this attack does and it is still quiet: no process is created, no file is written, nothing leaves the browser. The harder problem is inverted — Stegano used this flaw precisely so that instrumented hosts saw nothing, so an estate that samples ad traffic on analysis machines is being shown the benign branch by design.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treating a confirmed probe as the first stage of a chain and hunting forward on the same host for the exploit and payload that would have followed had the machine looked unmonitored.
response.adequacy: This is right in principle and thin in evidence: the probe leaves no host artefact, so response is driven from network or proxy records if they exist at the necessary granularity. On an ordinary user's workstation the probe succeeded, the chain proceeded, and the only recoverable evidence is whatever the later stages left — which is why the reconnaissance stage is worth patching rather than only detecting.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: Remediation evidence for this CVE is a KB record against a CVE identifier, and Microsoft closed this identifier twice: MS16-037 on 2016-04-12, then a V2.0 revision on 2017-04-11 announcing Internet Explorer cumulative update 4014661, which Microsoft says adds to the original release to comprehensively address CVE-2016-0162. An estate that installed the first round marked the item remediated and stayed exposed for a further year, with SI-2 reporting green throughout because nothing in the control reopens a closed identifier when the vendor revises its own fix.

NIS2-Art21-vulnerability-handling.gap: The handling process treats an advisory as an event with an outcome, and this CVE arrived as one bulletin number carrying two fixes a year apart. An entity that ingested MS16-037 in April 2016, remediated and closed has fully conformant records and an unpatched estate until it separately picks up the 2017-04-11 revision — which arrives as a bulletin revision rather than a new advisory and therefore never re-enters most intake pipelines. Article 21 requires the process to exist; it does not require re-ingestion of revised advisories against already-closed items.

UK-CAF-C1.gap: Monitoring is present and this flaw was used specifically to route around it. The Stegano script enumerated packet-capture, sandboxing and virtualization software, security products and graphics and security drivers, and aborted before the landing page when it found any — so a monitored host observes reconnaissance and no attack while an ordinary workstation observes both. A C1 assessment that draws confidence from telemetry collected on analysis-capable systems is being shown the benign branch on purpose, which inverts the coverage it believes it has.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: The control measures cadence and this CVE fails on completeness: an estate that applied MS16-037 within its window in April 2016 answers the maturity question correctly and remains exposed until Internet Explorer cumulative update 4014661 lands in April 2017. The Security Only versus Monthly Rollup split introduced later in 2016 sharpens it further — 4014661 is the Security Only package against rollups 4015549, 4015550 and 4015551 — so which package an estate consumes decides whether the second round arrived at all, and neither distinction is visible in a maturity attestation.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: Scored on its own metrics this is a CVSS 4.3 information disclosure with no integrity or availability impact and a 2026-08-16 EPSS pair of 0.22088 at the 0.97461 percentile — a profile that loses every prioritisation contest it enters. Its actual severity is positional: it is the gate a malvertising chain uses to decide whether to fire, so its real impact is the impact of the payload that follows a successful probe. A.8.8 provides no mechanism for scoring a vulnerability by its role in a chain rather than by its own impact metrics, which is why this one sat unpatched behind higher-scoring items.

new_control_requirements.name: INCOMPLETE-PATCH-SEQUENCE-SEVERITY-MULTIPLIER
new_control_requirements.description: Vulnerability-management programs must apply a severity multiplier when a CVE is the Nth in an incomplete-patch sequence on the same primitive (third MOTW bypass, second AMSI bypass, etc.). Framework controls treating each CVE as discrete obscure the structural defect; the Nth CVE in a sequence implies that future bypasses on the same primitive are likely.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Microsoft's own bulletin carries the incomplete-patch admission for this one. MS16-037 shipped on 2016-04-12 for Internet Explorer 9, 10 and 11, and the V2.0 revision of 2017-04-11 announces cumulative update 4014661 with the statement that it adds to the original release to comprehensively address CVE-2016-0162 and that customers should install it to be fully protected. That is one CVE identifier requiring two vendor fixes twelve months apart, on a flaw Microsoft had already marked as exploited. An estate that had applied the severity multiplier to the second round would have retested rather than trusting a remediation record it had closed a year earlier.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CISA listed this Internet Explorer information-disclosure flaw on 2022-05-24 with a 2022-06-14 due date, six years after MS16-037 and five after the 4014661 cumulative update that Microsoft says comprehensively addresses it. On this entry the operative word in the control is 'verified': a KB record showing MS16-037 is not verification, because Microsoft revised that bulletin to add a second update, and an installed-but-not-restarted host is not remediated either. Verification here means the browser build on the host is at or above the 4014661 level with a restart taken, on every Internet Explorer and embedded WebBrowser-control surface in the estate.

CVE-2016-3298.name: Microsoft Internet Explorer Messaging API Information Disclosure Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: A page rendered in Internet Explorer calls into the Microsoft Internet Messaging API in a way the API mishandles, and the response differs according to whether a named path exists on the victim's disk. Repeat the call across a path list and the browser reports the endpoint's software inventory to the attacker. Malvertising operators read that inventory as a go/no-go signal, aborting the chain on any machine that looked like a research host.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none — PR:N; the attacker needs no account, no prior foothold and no credential, only the ability to place content in front of an Internet Explorer render, which a syndicated advertising slot provides
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L with UI:R; the only precondition is that the victim loads a page in Internet Explorer on an affected Windows build, and the exploit is deterministic, with no race, no heap grooming and no information leak needed first
attack_vector.ai_factor: None. Proofpoint's Will Metcalf and Kafeine found it by analysing live malvertising traffic in April 2016. No AI-assisted discovery is claimed by any party, and no vendor research arm involved here carries an AI brand that could be mistaken for one.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Removing Internet Explorer from the path that renders syndicated advertising — a different default browser, or a policy that confines IE to a named intranet allowlist — would have denied the oracle its render context regardless of patch state, which matters because the bug ran unpatched from at least April to October 2016.
prevention.adequacy: BOD 22-01 arrived 2022-05-24, more than five years after the October 2016 fix, so as a prevention control it enforced hygiene on residual legacy hosts rather than defending anyone during the exploitation window. Browser confinement is real but partial: it moves the ad-rendering risk to whichever engine replaces IE and does nothing for a line-of-business application that pins Internet Explorer.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Retaining served ad-slot HTML and JavaScript for review and comparing what analysis VMs receive against what ordinary endpoints receive on the same ad network. The divergence — clean content to the sandbox, redirect chains to the users — is the observable, and it is visible without ever seeing the exploit itself.
detection.adequacy: Weak on its own. The filter's success looks exactly like a quiet day: no payload, no alert, no artefact on disk. Detection here needs a deliberate comparison across two populations, and an estate with only one detonation environment has nothing to compare against.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treating a confirmed fingerprinting stage as evidence the analysis estate itself is burned — rebuilding detonation images with different tooling footprints and file associations, rather than closing the ticket once the browser is patched.
response.adequacy: Rebuilding an analysis image restores the ability to see the next campaign but recovers nothing already missed, and it is a running cost, not a fix: the operators re-fingerprint. It also does nothing for the user endpoints that passed the filter and took the payload.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: The control is met by evidence of a deployed vendor patch, and on Windows Vista SP2 and Server 2008 SP2 that evidence can be honest and still wrong, because Microsoft requires both the MS16-118 IE cumulative update and KB3193515 from MS16-126 to close CVE-2016-3298. One-KB-per-CVE tracking marks the host remediated. SI-2 also offers no disposition for an affected product that no longer receives patches at all, which is now the state of Internet Explorer and every Windows build in the affected list.

NIS2-Art21-vulnerability-handling.gap: Handling processes consume disclosure feeds, and this defect produced no feed entry between its first observed use in GooNky chains in April 2016 and the October 11, 2016 bulletin — Microsoft's own table records it as exploited but not publicly disclosed. An organisation running a fully compliant Article 21 process was blind for that entire period, and by the time CISA created a due date on 2022-05-24 the compliant action had changed from patching to retiring the browser.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: A B4 configuration baseline of this era hardened the operating system and left the advertising path alone, so every managed endpoint remained configured to execute attacker-supplied JavaScript on ordinary sites. Enhanced Security Configuration, the one control Microsoft names, applies to server SKUs and only to sites outside Trusted Sites, while the CVE-2016-3298 oracle ran against client endpoints. Passing B4 and being profiled by an ad slot were entirely compatible states.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: Maturity is scored in days from vendor release, which cannot express the two-package requirement Microsoft imposed on Vista and Server 2008 for this CVE, and cannot express the position an operator is in today. Internet Explorer and every affected Windows version are unsupported, so the correct answer is a removal date rather than a patch window, and the Essential Eight patch rung has no field for one — a fleet of unsupported hosts can report full maturity by patching what remains patchable.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: The register records CVSS 6.5 information disclosure and treats the exposure as bounded. What the bug actually delivered was reconnaissance against the defender: an arbitrary-path existence oracle used to recognise analyst and sandbox machines and route the payload elsewhere. A.8.8 never prompts the follow-up question of whether the organisation's own detection estate has been fingerprinted, so the control can be fully evidenced while the analysis capability it protects is being deliberately starved of samples.

new_control_requirements.name: BROWSER-MANAGED-UPDATE-NO-DEFERRAL
new_control_requirements.description: Enterprise update rings must not defer security-channel browser updates beyond 24h.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Microsoft shipped the Internet Explorer fix for CVE-2016-3298 on 2016-10-11 across ten distinct cumulative packages (KB3191492 through KB3194798), and on Windows Vista SP2 and Server 2008 SP2 also required KB3193515 from MS16-126. Any deferral ring that held the October IE cumulative update left the arbitrary-path file-existence oracle live on the exact endpoints AdGholas and Neutrino EK were profiling, and Microsoft's own bulletin marked the CVE as exploited at release.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CISA listed CVE-2016-3298 on 2022-05-24 with a 2022-06-14 due date, against a Microsoft Internet Explorer and Internet Messaging API defect whose patch had existed since 2016-10-11. On a 2022 estate the only mitigation that verifies is removal of Internet Explorer from the ad-rendering path, because the affected Windows builds were already out of support — which is precisely why the control's 'documented compensating controls' branch, not its patch branch, is the one that applies here.

CVE-2016-3351.name: Microsoft Internet Explorer and Edge Information Disclosure Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: Script in an ordinary web page asks Internet Explorer or Edge which file extensions are associated with installed applications, and the browser answers. The operator reads the answer as an identity check: analysis tooling registers extensions that consumer machines never carry, so the presence of .py, .pcap, .saz or .har associations marks the host as a research environment and the chain is terminated before any exploit is served.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none — PR:N; the attacker holds no account and needs no foothold, only an ad slot or a compromised page that will render script to the victim's browser
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L with UI:R; the browser returns the answer directly and repeatably, and the only user action required is loading a page, which the malvertising delivery path supplies without the victim choosing anything
attack_vector.ai_factor: None. Proofpoint and Trend Micro analysts identified the check by watching how the Ec-Centre and AdGholas chains behaved differently under dynamic analysis. No AI-assisted discovery is claimed, and no AI-branded research arm is involved in the attribution.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Applying both September 2016 bulletins — MS16-104 for Internet Explorer and MS16-105 for Edge — removes the association oracle outright. Before 2016-09-13 the only real prevention was not rendering syndicated advertising in an affected browser, since Microsoft published no workaround and no mitigating factor for this CVE.
prevention.adequacy: Patching ends this specific oracle and nothing more. Malvertising operators had other selection signals and, per Proofpoint, had been performing this class of check since January 2014; removing one primitive shifts the operator to the next. BOD 22-01's clock also started 2022-05-24, nearly six years after the fix, so it disciplined leftovers rather than the campaign.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Hardening the analysis estate so it is not recognisable — analysis images whose shell associations match a consumer build, and a comparison of ad-network responses served to instrumented versus uninstrumented endpoints.
detection.adequacy: This restores visibility rather than preventing anything, and it degrades: once the operator has a new discriminator the images need rebuilding again. It is also expensive to sustain, because the tooling that makes an analysis host useful is the same tooling that makes it identifiable.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treating a confirmed selection stage as a reason to hunt on the endpoints that were not filtered out, since those are the population that received whatever the chain delivered — in this lineage, Angler Exploit Kit payloads including Reveton ransomware.
response.adequacy: The hunt is retrospective and its scope is unknowable from the defender's side: the filter ran client-side, so there is no server-side log of which endpoints passed. Response can only work from what the payload left behind, which is why the KEV record's ransomware flag is the practical trigger rather than the information-disclosure CVE itself.

NIST-800-53-SI-3.gap: Malicious-code protection acts on content that arrives, and this CVE's entire function is to ensure content does not arrive at the inspecting host. The probe reads shell associations for Python, Wireshark, Fiddler, HTTPWatch and Charles and terminates the chain when it finds them, so the better-instrumented an endpoint is, the more reliably it is excluded from the sample set. SI-3 imposes no requirement that the inspection environment be indistinguishable from a user endpoint, which is the property that actually decides the outcome here.

DORA-Art10.gap: Article 10 detection mechanisms watch for anomalous activity on the entity's own assets, and the anomaly here is that nothing happens: a client-side capability probe followed by a redirect leaves no process, no file and no authentication event. Recognising it requires cross-population comparison of what an ad network serves to different endpoint classes, a signal that exists off the asset entirely. Compliance and blindness are fully compatible states for this defect.

UK-CAF-C1.gap: C1 monitoring is nominally in place and is precisely what the technique targets. The extension set Proofpoint documented is a portrait of a monitored, instrumented workstation, so the organisation's investment in monitoring tooling is what supplies the discriminator. Increasing C1 maturity on an unhardened analysis image makes the host more identifiable, not less, which inverts the usual assumption that more monitoring yields more coverage.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: Maturity here is a patch interval counted per bulletin, and the 2016-09-13 fix arrived in two of them — MS16-104 (KB3183038) for Internet Explorer and MS16-105 (KB3183043) for Microsoft Edge. Those two map to a single installed package on Windows 10, the September cumulative KB3185611 / KB3185614 / KB3189866, and on Windows 7, 8.1 and the 2008 through 2012 R2 servers only the MS16-104 half applies because there is no Edge on those platforms. The verification query is therefore different per platform family, and a fleet-wide percentage hides which query was actually run. The rung likewise has no way to record that both engines are now retired and the remaining action is browser replacement.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.7.gap: A.8.7 is defeated without being engaged. No malware is delivered by this CVE; it decides who will receive malware later, and Proofpoint traces the same discriminator back to January 2014 feeding Angler Exploit Kit chains that delivered Reveton ransomware — which is why the KEV record carries a ransomware flag on an information-disclosure bug. Complete anti-malware coverage leaves the selection stage untouched, and the payloads it filters for change faster than the filter does.

new_control_requirements.name: BROWSER-MANAGED-UPDATE-NO-DEFERRAL
new_control_requirements.description: Enterprise update rings must not defer security-channel browser updates beyond 24h.
new_control_requirements.evidence: The Microsoft Internet Explorer and Edge fix for CVE-2016-3351 landed 2016-09-13 in two bulletins — MS16-104 (KB3183038) for Internet Explorer and MS16-105 (KB3183043) for Microsoft Edge — delivered as the package KB3185319 on Windows 7 through Server 2012 R2 and as the single Windows 10 cumulative KB3185611 / KB3185614 / KB3189866. Microsoft recorded the CVE as exploited at release with no workaround and no mitigating factor, so a ring that deferred the September package on either platform family left the shell-association oracle answering for AdGholas, which Proofpoint dates to February 2016, and for GooNky from April 2016.

new_control_requirements.name: PROTECTION-MECHANISM-FAILURE-CLASS-REGRESSION
new_control_requirements.description: Detonation chambers, EDR rules, and AppLocker/WDAC policies covering protection-mechanism classes (MOTW, SmartScreen, AMSI, ASR, WDAC, Driver Block Rules) must include class-level regression testing executed on every patch deployment, not just one-off bypass-CVE remediation. The test battery for class-X must include all historic class-X bypass primitives — incomplete patches re-introduce risk that one-off testing does not detect.
new_control_requirements.evidence: This CVE is a detonation-chamber failure rather than a browser failure: Proofpoint published the exact discriminator used against Internet Explorer and Edge — .py, .pcap and .saz as the associations that must be absent, widened in the Ec-Centre variant to .303, .cap, .hwl, .har, .halog, .chls, .py, .bfr and .pcap with .303 recorded as a negative marker held for comparison, .doc, .mkv, .torrent and .skype as the associations that must be present, and a separate .html check confirming Internet Explorer was the default browser — and traced the technique to January 2014, well before the 2016-09-13 patch. A chamber tested only against the current bypass keeps the same recognisable footprint for the next one.

attack_vector.description: An unauthenticated request carrying a crafted path reaches VTScada's legacy WAP listener on 9201/TCP. The path handling indexes outside the intended buffer, the read runs past the allocation, and the component crashes. It does not restart itself, so the alarm-notification and mobile-monitoring function stays down until someone relaunches it by hand on the operator station.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none — PR:N; ZDI states outright that authentication is not required, and the WAP parser acts on the request before any VTScada account or role is consulted
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L with UI:N; no race, no grooming and no victim interaction, and ICS-CERT assesses that an attacker with low skill could exploit it. The only genuine constraint is reachability of a listener that is off by default and needs the optional Alarm Notification licence
attack_vector.ai_factor: None. An anonymous researcher submitted it to Zero Day Initiative on 2016-02-18. ZDI's current TrendAI branding is a Trend Micro marketing name and is not evidence of AI-assisted discovery on a 2016 submission.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Disabling the WAP port — Trihedral's own stated interim action for current WAP users — removes the listener and with it the entire attack path, and costs nothing on the many sites that migrated mobile access to the Mobile Internet Client in 2013 or the Anywhere Client in 2016 and never turned WAP off.
prevention.adequacy: Complete for this CVE and honest about its limits: it is a feature disablement, not a repair, so a site that genuinely still needs WAP monitoring gets nothing from it and must upgrade to 11.2.02 and migrate the function. BOD 22-01's clock opened 2022-04-15, nearly six years after the 2016-06-07 advisory, so it enforced cleanup of long-lived installations rather than a timely response.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Alerting on the VTScada WAP component exiting, rather than on the host or the SCADA application as a whole, plus flow monitoring for inbound connections to 9201/TCP from outside the engineering segment.
detection.adequacy: Process-exit alerting catches the crash after the function is already lost, which on an alarm-notification path is exactly the window that matters. Flow monitoring on 9201/TCP is the earlier signal but only helps where the segment boundary is instrumented, and many VTScada sites sit on flat plant networks where no such boundary exists.

response.what_would_have_worked: A runbook that treats loss of the WAP component as a security event rather than a software fault, because the failure mode ICS-CERT documents — no automatic return — makes an unexplained manual relaunch the single most likely artefact of exploitation.
response.adequacy: This produces awareness, not containment: nothing stops the next packet, and repeated crashes can be driven at will until the port is closed or the upgrade lands. It also depends on the operator distinguishing this crash from ordinary instability on an aging Windows SCADA station, which without the 9201/TCP correlation is guesswork.

NIST-800-82r3.gap: An OT asset inventory built to 800-82r3 records the VTScada host, its version and its network position, and none of those three fields determine exposure. What determines it is whether the optional Alarm Notification licence is installed and whether the WAP port was explicitly enabled, because the default installation is not vulnerable and Trihedral states only a small fraction of the installed base uses the feature. The guidance produces a complete inventory of hosts that mostly are not exposed and does not isolate the few that are.

NIS2-Art21-availability.gap: Availability planning assumes a crashed service returns, whether by supervisor, watchdog or failover. ICS-CERT records the opposite for this defect: the server does not come back without being manually relaunched. A single unauthenticated packet to 9201/TCP therefore produces an outage bounded only by how quickly a person reaches the operator station, and for the water, energy and transport operators in NIS2 scope that is a loss of the alarm-notification path rather than a restartable component.

UK-CAF-B5.gap: B5 resilience assessments reason about the SCADA application's accounts, roles and redundancy, and the WAP parser sits entirely upstream of all of it — ZDI states authentication is not required, so the request is processed before any of those controls are consulted. ICS-CERT's mitigation advice is correspondingly network-only: keep control systems off the internet, firewall them, isolate them from the business network. Where the site is flat, B5 can be evidenced in full while 9201/TCP answers anything on the plant.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: The remediation is not a patch and does not behave like one. Trihedral removed the WAP code in 11.2 rather than repairing it, so there is no fixed WAP server to move to and a site still using WAP monitoring must migrate the function to the Mobile Internet Client or Anywhere Client. The rung equally cannot record the vendor's own interim instruction, disabling the WAP port through Trihedral support, which fully removes the exposure while leaving the installed version unchanged and therefore non-compliant on paper.
