ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: Jenkins delivers vulnerability information twice over — a published advisory and a warning inside the controller's own update centre — so A.8.8's intake requirement is met without effort. The failure mode is partial treatment: the 2019-03-06 advisory carried this Script Security defect and the sibling Pipeline: Groovy defect together, and an operator who updated one plugin holds a closed record over a controller still reachable through the other.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.28.gap: The defect is a design assumption, not a coding slip: the sandbox intercepts operations at execution time, so anything the Groovy runtime evaluates during parsing, compilation or instantiation was never in scope for it. Secure-coding review looks for injection sinks and unsafe deserialisation, not for whether a security control's interception point covers every phase of a language's own lifecycle — which is why this sandbox produced bypasses across several advisories rather than one.

OWASP-CICD-SEC-3.gap: The dependency-chain category names exactly this asset class, and organisations still inventory the libraries their builds consume far more carefully than the plugins their build system runs on. Script Security is not an install someone chose — it arrives as a dependency of the Pipeline plugins — so it appears in no application SBOM and no procurement record, and its version currency is visible only inside the controller's own plugin manager.

new_control_requirements.name: FLEET-CONTROL-PLANE-ADMIN-PRIVILEGE-TIER
new_control_requirements.description: Administrators of fleet-control-plane systems (MDM/UEM, EDR consoles, identity providers, container orchestrators, configuration management) must be classified as a distinct privilege tier above application admins, with: PAM-jumphost-only access, FIDO2 step-up per session, just-in-time elevation with approval workflow, separate identity from any other admin role, and dedicated PAW (privileged access workstation) hardware. Compliance frameworks must enumerate this tier explicitly rather than collapsing it into 'admin'.
new_control_requirements.evidence: A Jenkins controller holding the credentials store, agent connection secrets and API tokens for an entire build-and-deploy estate is a control plane in exactly this sense, and CVE-2019-1003029 shows why the tier has to cover read access and not only administrative access: Overall/Read was sufficient to execute code in that JVM, and the ACL-bypass gadget in public tooling against Jenkins core 2.137 and earlier removed even that. Treating the controller as a control-plane asset means no untrusted population reaches it at all — which is the only posture that survives the next Groovy sandbox bypass, given this plugin had already produced several before the 2019-03-06 advisory.

new_control_requirements.name: BUG-FAMILY-MITIGATION-PERSISTENCE
new_control_requirements.description: When a CVE patch lands, retain the pre-patch compensating controls (module blacklists, sysctl restrictions) until the patched code has soaked for a stated review period. Patches for one bug in a primitive class can introduce sibling bugs in the same class; the original compensating control may still apply to the sibling.
new_control_requirements.evidence: The Groovy sandbox in Jenkins Script Security is a primitive class that produced bypass after bypass, and this advisory itself shipped two at once — CVE-2019-1003029 in Script Security 1.53 and CVE-2019-1003030 in Pipeline: Groovy 2.63, the same weakness reached through a second plugin. An operator who removed the interim access restrictions after upgrading to 1.54 gave back the only protection that was not version-specific. The compensating controls here are concrete: withdraw blanket Overall/Read, keep the descriptor endpoints off untrusted networks, and hold both until the sandbox has gone a stated period without a further bypass.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Jenkins published Script Security 1.54 and Pipeline: Groovy 2.64 on 2019-03-06, CISA listed CVE-2019-1003029 on 2022-04-25 with a 2022-05-16 due date, and EPSS now stands at 0.73854 (99.434th percentile) with the CVE carried as a reference in a shipped Metasploit module. The four-hour clock has to be measured to a completed controller restart rather than to the plugin manager showing 1.54, because the running JVM keeps serving the old plugin code until it recycles — and the documented-compensating-control branch covers the interim on a busy instance, by withdrawing Overall/Read from untrusted users until the restart window arrives.

CVE-2019-1130.name: Microsoft Windows AppX Deployment Service Privilege Escalation Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: A local, non-admin user hard-links a path AppXSVC will act on to a protected system file and races the service; AppXSVC follows the link and performs its privileged file operation on the target, letting the user overwrite a SYSTEM-owned file and execute as SYSTEM.
attack_vector.privileges_required: low — PR:L; the attacker already has an interactive local logon and can run an arbitrary application.
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L, but a real timing race against AppXSVC; multi-core hosts make it reliable per the public weaponization.
attack_vector.ai_factor: None. Manual Windows-internals research by SandboxEscaper ('Polar Bear'); no AI tooling involved in discovery or weaponization.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Installing the July 2019 cumulative update (corrected AppXSVC hard-link handling) and rebooting every affected host.
prevention.adequacy: Fully effective once installed and restarted, but the reboot requirement is where remediation stalls on multi-user hosts, and end-of-support 8.1/2012 lines need migration rather than a patch.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Endpoint telemetry alerting on a non-admin process producing a SYSTEM-context child after an app-deployment action, and on hard links from user-writable paths to protected system files.
detection.adequacy: Detects the escalation after it fires; the race is brief and file-integrity tools that only scan on-disk state may miss the transient link swap.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treating a confirmed SYSTEM escalation on a host as full compromise: rebuild, rotate credentials that were used on the host, and hunt for the ransomware often paired with LPEs of this class.
response.adequacy: Necessary once escalation is confirmed, but response cannot undo a SYSTEM-level foothold already established.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: SI-2 is nominally satisfied by an approved July-2019 update, but this CVSS 7.8 AppXSVC LPE (KEV 2022-05-23, ransomware use) is only remediated once each host installs the fixed build and reboots; the control's 'approved/deployed' evidence does not prove the vulnerable service was replaced, so a downloaded-but-not-restarted host reads clean while staying exploitable.

NIST-800-53-AC-6.gap: AC-6 least privilege is in place for the account, yet it provides no protection here because AppXSVC itself performs the privileged write the attacker redirects via a hard link; a standard user reaches SYSTEM without ever holding elevated rights, so tightening account privilege leaves the CWE-59 path fully open.

NIS2-Art21-patch-management.gap: NIS2 Art.21 patch-management is met by having a documented cadence, but a monthly Patch-Tuesday rhythm does not deliver the compressed KEV clock (added 2022-05-23, due 2022-06-13) this ransomware-associated LPE warrants, so an essential entity stays conformant while the July-2019 AppXSVC fix waits behind the next window on exposed multi-user hosts.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: CAF B4 accepts a demonstrated patch process, but its security outcome is not achieved while hosts run pre-July-2019 AppXSVC; on shared and terminal-server hosts the mandated reboot is deferred to avoid dropping user sessions, so the race remains live under an assessment that reads as compliant.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: Essential Eight OS-patch maturity is scored from approval/deployment state, not installed-and-rebooted build, so a fleet can claim the OS-patching control while the July-2019 fix for this local ransomware-carrier LPE is pending a restart precisely on the multi-core hosts where the race is most reliable.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: A.8.8 is evidenced by vulnerability-scan output, but a scanner reading an 'approved update' or OS package version can mark a host remediated while AppXSVC still executes pre-fix code awaiting reboot; the control as run does not separate a July-2019-listed-but-not-restarted host from a truly patched one for CVE-2019-1130.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2019-1130 is a KEV-listed (2022-05-23, due 2022-06-13) ransomware-associated AppXSVC LPE (CVSS 7.8, EPSS 0.02284) whose July-2019 fix requires a per-host install and reboot; measuring remediation by installed-and-restarted build against the KEV clock, not by 'approved', is what closes it on Windows fleets.

new_control_requirements.name: INCOMPLETE-PATCH-SEQUENCE-SEVERITY-MULTIPLIER
new_control_requirements.description: Vulnerability-management programs must apply a severity multiplier when a CVE is the Nth in an incomplete-patch sequence on the same primitive (third MOTW bypass, second AMSI bypass, etc.). Framework controls treating each CVE as discrete obscure the structural defect; the Nth CVE in a sequence implies that future bypasses on the same primitive are likely.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2019-1130 is one of a repeated AppXSVC hard-link LPE sequence dropped by SandboxEscaper (the twin CVE-2019-1129 shipped the same July 2019 bulletin), so treating it as a discrete item understates that the same link-handling primitive kept yielding fresh bypasses and warrants class-level regression rather than one-off remediation.

CVE-2019-11707.name: Mozilla Firefox and Thunderbird Type Confusion Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: Attacker JavaScript installs an indexed accessor on an array prototype and calls Array.pop; IonMonkey mis-predicts the return type, producing a type confusion, OOB access and an arbitrary read/write in the Firefox content process — renderer RCE that is paired with a sandbox escape for full compromise.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none — PR:N; the attacker only needs the victim to load content.
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L; the confusion is deterministic once the prototype accessor is set, though UI:R means the victim must open the page or emailed link.
attack_vector.ai_factor: None in the human sense: reported by Samuel Groß using the Fuzzilli fuzzer (a coverage-guided fuzzer, not AI) and independently by Coinbase Security from the live attack.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Upgrading to Firefox 67.0.3 / ESR 60.7.1 / Thunderbird 60.7.2 and forcing a process relaunch across managed endpoints.
prevention.adequacy: Effective once the process actually restarts; the relaunch requirement is the practical gap on a browser users keep open for days.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Monitoring for firefox.exe spawning children or making unexpected egress right after a user opens an emailed link.
detection.adequacy: Post-execution signal; the renderer-stage primitive runs before disk artifacts appear, so pure AV/SI-3 is weak here.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treating a confirmed hit as targeted intrusion — isolate the host, rotate the user's credentials and session tokens, and notify the wider targeted set as Coinbase did.
response.adequacy: Contains spread but cannot undo renderer code execution already achieved.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: SI-2 marks Firefox patched once 67.0.3/ESR 60.7.1 is pushed, but this type-confusion RCE (KEV 2022-05-23, EPSS 0.37951) stays exploitable in any browser process that updated its files without relaunching, and SI-2 evidence keyed on installed version rather than running-process version does not surface that residency.

NIST-800-53-SI-3.gap: SI-3 is assumed met by endpoint AV, but the CVE-2019-11707 payload executed in the renderer before any file hit disk, and the macOS sample was only detected by chance via a 2016 XProtect signature; signature-based malicious-code protection gives no real coverage of this JIT-stage execution.

NIS2-Art21-patch-management.gap: NIS2 Art.21 is satisfied by a documented update process, but the bug was used in live spear-phishing against Coinbase staff during disclosure; a cadence that patches Firefox as routine application software rather than an actively-exploited endpoint priority leaves the emailed-link chain reachable while the entity stays conformant.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: CAF B4 accepts a functioning browser-update mechanism, but the outcome is not met while any ring runs Firefox below 67.0.3/ESR 60.7.1; because the fix needs a relaunch, pushing the update while users keep sessions open passes the process check yet leaves the type-confusion primitive live.

AU-Essential-8-App-Hardening.gap: Essential Eight application-hardening blocks Flash, Java, ads and Office macros, none of which is on this path: the exploit is pure JavaScript against IonMonkey, so a fully compliant browser-hardening posture does nothing to stop the crafted page or emailed link from reaching the vulnerable JIT.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: A.8.8 reporting keyed on installed Firefox version cannot distinguish a host relaunched into 67.0.3 from one that merely staged the update; since the running-process version is what determines exposure for a browser, the control as implemented can read remediated while the JIT bug is still resident.

new_control_requirements.name: BROWSER-MANAGED-UPDATE-NO-DEFERRAL
new_control_requirements.description: Enterprise update rings must not defer security-channel browser updates beyond 24h.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2019-11707 is a KEV-listed (2022-05-23, EPSS 0.37951) Firefox/ESR/Thunderbird JIT RCE actively used against Coinbase staff whose fix (67.0.3 / ESR 60.7.1 / 60.7.2) needs a prompt push and process relaunch; deferring the security channel is exactly what leaves the emailed-link chain reachable.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: As a KEV-listed browser RCE exploited in the wild, CVE-2019-11707 warrants the compressed KEV clock rather than a routine application-patch window; verified mitigation here means the fixed Firefox/ESR/Thunderbird build running after a relaunch, not merely staged.

CVE-2019-11708.name: Mozilla Firefox and Thunderbird Sandbox Escape Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: A compromised content process sends an under-vetted Prompt:Open IPC message to the non-sandboxed parent, which opens web content of the child's choosing outside the sandbox; chained with a renderer bug this turns content-process execution into full host code execution.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none — PR:N externally, but the escape presupposes prior renderer code execution.
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L, S:C, UI:N; once the child is controlled the malformed IPC message is simple to craft.
attack_vector.ai_factor: None. Identified and fixed by Mozilla engineers after Coinbase Security reported the live chain; no AI involvement.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Upgrading to Firefox 67.0.4 / ESR 60.7.2 / Thunderbird 60.7.2 (paired with the 67.0.3 renderer fix) and relaunching the process.
prevention.adequacy: Effective when both fixes are resident and the process restarts; patching only one point release leaves the chain intact.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Alerting on the parent Firefox process opening unsolicited content or dropping a binary, and on cross-tab frame-script injection.
detection.adequacy: Fires after the escape; the trusted IPC path gives little pre-execution signal.

response.what_would_have_worked: Full-host intrusion handling — isolate, rotate the user's credentials and tokens, and hunt persistent frame-script backdoors.
response.adequacy: Necessary once the sandbox is escaped, but cannot reverse parent-context execution.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: SI-2 is only partly effective if the fleet installs the CVE-2019-11707 renderer fix but not this escape fix; 67.0.4/ESR 60.7.2 shipped separately from 67.0.3, so an SI-2 record reading 'Firefox updated' without pinning the exact point release can leave a host that still completes the observed chain.

NIST-800-53-CM-7.gap: CM-7 relies on the browser sandbox to constrain a compromised renderer, but here the sandbox boundary itself fails: the parent honours a child-supplied Prompt:Open request, so least-functionality settings on plugins or features cannot touch the trusted IPC path that the escape abuses.

NIS2-Art21-patch-management.gap: NIS2 Art.21 met by a general cadence still misses that this is the escape stage of a live chain against exchange staff; without a requirement to reach the 67.0.4/ESR 60.7.2 build specifically, an essential entity stays conformant while the sandbox-escape half remains available to any paired renderer bug.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: CAF B4's outcome is unmet while any instance runs Firefox below 67.0.4/ESR 60.7.2; because the fix needs a relaunch and only bites alongside a renderer bug, a B4 review that checks 'a patch process exists' overlooks that both fixes must be resident and the process restarted.

AU-Essential-8-App-Hardening.gap: Essential Eight application-hardening has nothing to block here — no plugin, macro or content type is involved; the flaw is in the parent's vetting of an internal IPC message, so a fully hardened Firefox still permits a controlled child to escape via Prompt:Open.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: A.8.8 keyed on 'Firefox present and updated' cannot separate CVE-2019-11708 from CVE-2019-11707: a scan showing a June-2019 Firefox may read remediated while the host is patched for the renderer bug but not the escape (or the reverse), leaving the chain viable.

new_control_requirements.name: BROWSER-MANAGED-UPDATE-NO-DEFERRAL
new_control_requirements.description: Enterprise update rings must not defer security-channel browser updates beyond 24h.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2019-11708 is the KEV-listed (2022-05-23) sandbox-escape stage of a live Firefox chain against exchange staff; its fix (67.0.4 / ESR 60.7.2) shipped days after the paired renderer fix, so any deferral of the security channel risks a host patched for one half of the chain but not the other.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: As a CVSS 10 KEV-listed sandbox escape used in the wild, CVE-2019-11708 warrants the compressed KEV clock, and verified mitigation must confirm the 67.0.4/ESR 60.7.2 build is running after a relaunch rather than merely staged alongside the renderer fix.

attack_vector.description: A crafted page drives Chrome WebAudio (ConvolverNode) into a use-after-free, reclaiming the freed object with attacker data to gain a read/write primitive and renderer RCE; delivered from a watering-hole page needing only that the victim's Chrome load the script.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none — PR:N; the attacker only needs the victim to browse.
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L, UI:R; the trigger is deterministic script, with heap grooming to make the UAF reliable.
attack_vector.ai_factor: None. Found in the wild by Kaspersky (Kulaev, Ivanov) via detection telemetry; no AI involvement, and the weak Lazarus code overlap may be a false flag.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Updating Google Chrome to 78.0.3904.87 and every Chromium-based browser to a build with the WebAudio fix, then relaunching each.
prevention.adequacy: Effective per engine, but only if the whole Chromium fleet — not just branded Chrome — is patched and relaunched.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Watching for renderer crashes tied to WebAudio and for a trusted news site suddenly loading a remote profiling script.
detection.adequacy: Limited pre-compromise value against a watering hole delivering in-renderer code from a legitimate domain.

response.what_would_have_worked: Isolating affected hosts, rotating browser-session credentials, and hunting the WizardOpium second stage.
response.adequacy: Contains the intrusion but cannot reverse renderer code execution already achieved.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: SI-2 scoped to the Chrome package misses that the CWE-416 defect is in shared Blink WebAudio; patching Chrome to 78.0.3904.87 while Chromium-based Edge/Opera/Brave stay on pre-fix builds leaves the same UAF exploitable, so a branded-Chrome-only inventory under-scopes this KEV RCE.

NIST-800-53-SI-4.gap: SI-4 monitoring geared to known-bad domains and dropped files gives little warning here, because WizardOpium ran in-renderer from a compromised legitimate news portal; the malicious script arrives from a trusted site, so the compromise is under way before typical SI-4 signals fire.

NIS2-Art21-patch-management.gap: NIS2 Art.21 by cadence does not encode that this was a live zero-day (patched 2019-10-31, two days after Kaspersky's report) delivered by watering hole; an entity treating Chrome as routine patching and not enumerating its other Chromium browsers stays conformant while part of its browser estate remains exploitable.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: CAF B4 is unmet while any Chromium-based browser sits below the WebAudio fix; a review that checks only 'Chrome auto-updates' overlooks the Edge/Opera/Brave instances sharing the identical bug, and the required full relaunch is easily skipped on a background-updated browser.

AU-Essential-8-App-Hardening.gap: Essential Eight application-hardening blocks Flash, Java and ads, none of which is on this path: the exploit is script-driven WebAudio manipulation, so a hardened Chrome still parses the crafted page and reaches the use-after-free, leaving the hardening attestation green and the primitive reachable.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: A.8.8 keyed on installed Chrome version cannot confirm a relaunch into 78.0.3904.87, nor does a Chrome-only asset record surface the Chromium-derived browsers sharing the engine; the control as run can read remediated while a not-yet-restarted Chrome or an unpatched Edge still carries the flaw.

new_control_requirements.name: BROWSER-MANAGED-UPDATE-NO-DEFERRAL
new_control_requirements.description: Enterprise update rings must not defer security-channel browser updates beyond 24h.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2019-13720 was a live Chrome WebAudio zero-day (KEV 2022-05-23, EPSS 0.4914) patched in 78.0.3904.87 two days after report; the same CWE-416 lives in every Chromium-based browser, so no security-channel deferral across the browser estate is defensible and each engine must be relaunched onto the fix.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: As a KEV-listed browser zero-day exploited via watering hole, CVE-2019-13720 warrants the compressed KEV clock, and verified mitigation must confirm the fixed build (78.0.3904.87 for Chrome, the equivalent for each Chromium browser) is running after a relaunch, not merely downloaded.

CVE-2019-1385.name: Microsoft Windows AppX Deployment Extensions Privilege Escalation Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: A local non-admin user runs a crafted application that steers the AppX Deployment Extensions' privileged link/file resolution onto a protected system file, gaining access to system files and a path toward SYSTEM — a privilege-management flaw in the deployment path, not memory corruption.
attack_vector.privileges_required: low — PR:L; an interactive local logon and the ability to run an application.
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L; deterministic privilege mishandling, though the attacker must steer the extension's resolution to a chosen target.
attack_vector.ai_factor: None. Credited to human researchers and a ZDI-coordinated submission; THEORI is a research firm, not an AI-discovery signal.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Installing the November 2019 cumulative update (corrected AppX Deployment Extensions privilege management) and rebooting every affected host.
prevention.adequacy: Fully effective once installed and restarted; the reboot is where remediation stalls on multi-user hosts.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Alerting on AppX deployment activity that writes to or resolves protected system files on behalf of a non-admin user.
detection.adequacy: Detects abuse of the deployment path after it fires; benign AppX activity is common, so tuning is needed to avoid noise.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treating a confirmed escalation as host compromise: rebuild, rotate credentials used on the host, and hunt the ransomware often paired with such LPEs.
response.adequacy: Necessary once escalation is confirmed but cannot undo a SYSTEM-level foothold.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: SI-2 is nominally met by an approved November-2019 update, but this CVSS 7.8 AppX Deployment Extensions LPE (KEV 2022-05-23, ransomware use) is only remediated once each host installs the fixed build and reboots; approval/deployment evidence cannot prove the vulnerable privilege-management code was replaced, so a staged-but-not-restarted host reads clean while remaining exploitable.

NIST-800-53-AC-6.gap: AC-6 least privilege is in place, yet it offers no protection because the AppX Deployment Extensions themselves perform the privileged resolution the attacker steers; a standard user reaches protected system files without ever holding elevated rights, so tightening account privilege leaves the CWE-59 path fully open.

NIS2-Art21-patch-management.gap: NIS2 Art.21 is met by a documented cadence, but a monthly window does not deliver the compressed KEV clock (added 2022-05-23, due 2022-06-13) this ransomware-associated LPE warrants, so an essential entity stays conformant while the November-2019 AppX fix waits behind the next cycle on exposed multi-user hosts.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: CAF B4 accepts a demonstrated patch process, but its outcome is unmet while hosts run a pre-November-2019 AppX Deployment Extensions build; on shared and terminal hosts the mandated reboot is deferred to avoid dropping sessions, leaving the privilege-management flaw live under a compliant-looking assessment.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: Essential Eight OS-patch maturity is scored from approval/deployment state, not installed-and-rebooted build, so a fleet can claim the OS-patching control while the November-2019 fix for this local ransomware-carrier LPE is pending a restart on the multi-user hosts most exposed to a hostile interactive user.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: A.8.8 is evidenced by vulnerability-scan output, but a scanner reading an approved-update signal or OS package version can mark a host remediated while the AppX Deployment Extensions still execute pre-fix code awaiting reboot; the control as run does not separate a November-2019-listed-but-not-restarted host from a truly patched one for CVE-2019-1385.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2019-1385 is a KEV-listed (2022-05-23, due 2022-06-13) ransomware-associated AppX Deployment Extensions LPE (CVSS 7.8, EPSS 0.03625) whose November-2019 fix requires a per-host install and reboot; measuring remediation by installed-and-restarted build against the KEV clock, not by 'approved', is what closes it.

new_control_requirements.name: INCOMPLETE-PATCH-SEQUENCE-SEVERITY-MULTIPLIER
new_control_requirements.description: Vulnerability-management programs must apply a severity multiplier when a CVE is the Nth in an incomplete-patch sequence on the same primitive (third MOTW bypass, second AMSI bypass, etc.). Framework controls treating each CVE as discrete obscure the structural defect; the Nth CVE in a sequence implies that future bypasses on the same primitive are likely.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2019-1385 is another entry in the recurring Windows AppX deployment link-resolution LPE line (alongside the AppXSVC hard-link CVE-2019-1130/1129), so treating it as discrete understates that the AppX package-deployment privilege-management surface kept yielding fresh escalation bugs and warrants class-level regression rather than one-off fixes.

CVE-2019-16057.name: D-Link DNS-320 Remote Code Execution Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: One unauthenticated GET to /cgi-bin/login_mgr.cgi with a shell metacharacter in the 'port' parameter injects a command that runs on the DNS-320 with web-server privileges, giving remote command execution on the NAS with no credentials or interaction.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none — PR:N; the endpoint is pre-authentication.
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L; a single crafted HTTP request, reachability being the only precondition.
attack_vector.ai_factor: None. Disclosed by CyStack researchers in 2019 through manual analysis; no AI involvement.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Decommissioning the end-of-life DNS-320 and, until removed, isolating its ShareCenter web interface from all untrusted networks.
prevention.framework_requiring_it: CISA BOD 22-01 (KEV remediation, added 2022-04-15, due 2022-05-06 — required action: disconnect)
prevention.adequacy: Removal is fully effective and is the only durable control; isolation bounds exposure but a consumer NAS at a remote site is easily re-exposed via UPnP or a port-forward.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Alerting on GET requests to login_mgr.cgi carrying shell metacharacters in 'port', and on the NAS spawning shell processes or unexpected egress.
detection.adequacy: Useful where the device is behind monitored network paths, but an internet-exposed NAS often sits outside enterprise telemetry entirely.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treating any internet-exposed DNS-320 as already compromised: remove it, rebuild rather than trust its data, and rotate credentials that transited it.
response.adequacy: Necessary given routine automated exploitation, but cannot recover data integrity already lost on a compromised NAS.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: SI-2 cannot be satisfied here because there is no patch: the DNS-320 reached end of support on 2018-12-01 and D-Link ships no firmware for it, so an SI-2 program built on 'apply the vendor update' has nothing to apply and must record removal as closure — a state most SI-2 workflows do not represent, leaving the CVE open on the books.

NIST-800-53-SC-7.gap: SC-7 is the effective interim control but is often unmet in practice: the DNS-320 ShareCenter UI is frequently internet-reachable via UPnP or a router port-forward at remote/branch sites, and SC-7 as audited for a corporate perimeter rarely covers a consumer NAS, so the unauthenticated CWE-78 endpoint stays exposed.

NIS2-Art21-patch-management.gap: NIS2 Art.21 patch-management presumes a fixable asset, but this end-of-life NAS (KEV 2022-04-15, EPSS 0.87065) has no patch path; the real obligation is vulnerability-handling by retirement, and a patch-management control lacking an explicit end-of-life-removal state leaves the exposure open indefinitely under an otherwise-conformant programme.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: CAF B4 has no update to point at for the DNS-320, so its outcome is only reachable by removing the device; a B4 assessment that treats 'no patch available' as accepted risk without a dated decommission plan leaves an internet-scanned, actively-exploited unauthenticated RCE live on the network.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: Essential Eight patch-application assumes vendor patches exist to apply, which is impossible for this retired DNS-320; the maturity model has no lever for an end-of-life appliance, so scoring 'no patch available' as compliant never closes the CVSS 9.8 exposure — only retirement does.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: A.8.8 for this device resolves to its own 'no longer supported — remove' outcome rather than patching: a scan will flag DNS-320 firmware <= 2.05.B10 indefinitely because no fixed build exists, so an A.8.8 program without an enforced decommission action simply re-reports the same command-injection exposure each cycle.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2019-16057 is a KEV-listed (2022-04-15, due 2022-05-06) unauthenticated command-injection RCE (CVSS 9.8, EPSS 0.87065) on an end-of-life D-Link DNS-320 with no patch; here the verified mitigation the control permits is the documented compensating control of disconnection/isolation on the KEV clock, since no update exists to deploy.

new_control_requirements.name: PERIMETER-COMPROMISE-REBUILD-NOT-PATCH
new_control_requirements.description: Pre-rehearsed IR runbook for any perimeter device that suffers a pre-auth RCE CVE in active exploitation MUST default to config-exfil + rebuild + credential rotation, not patch-in-place. Patch-in-place leaves attacker-installed implants intact.
new_control_requirements.evidence: The DNS-320 is an internet-reachable, pre-auth RCE device under routine automated exploitation (EPSS 0.87065) with no patch to apply, so any exposed unit must be handled as already compromised: removed and rebuilt rather than trusted, with credentials that transited it rotated — exactly the rebuild-not-patch default this control encodes.

attack_vector.description: An attacker crafts a WhatsApp message so its link-preview is a javascript: URI masked behind an https prefix; on the victim's WhatsApp Desktop, clicking it runs script in the web.whatsapp.com origin (persistent XSS), a missing object-src CSP lets it pull a remote payload, and the Electron app turns that XSS into local file reads.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none — PR:N; the attacker only needs to message the victim.
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L, S:C, but UI:R: the victim must click the crafted link preview, and the vulnerable Desktop/iPhone version pairing must be present.
attack_vector.ai_factor: None. Manual research by Gal Weizman (PerimeterX / Human Security); no AI involvement.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Upgrading WhatsApp Desktop to 0.3.9309 (and the paired iPhone app to 2.20.10) and relaunching the client, enrolling the messaging app as managed software.
prevention.adequacy: Effective once both sides are current and the client relaunched; the practical gap is that consumer messaging apps often sit outside managed patching.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Flagging WhatsApp Desktop rendering javascript: URIs in previews, local file reads from the Electron process, and egress to unfamiliar payload domains.
detection.adequacy: Feasible only where the desktop app is within endpoint telemetry; the XSS runs inside an already-trusted app session.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treating a confirmed hit as data-disclosure: identify files readable from the user profile, rotate any secrets exposed, and review the paired phone.
response.adequacy: Contains disclosure but cannot recall data already read from the local file system.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: SI-2 for this CVE must track both WhatsApp Desktop reaching 0.3.9309 and the paired iPhone app reaching 2.20.10, since the pairing is the vulnerable condition; an SI-2 record inventorying only the desktop client can read remediated while a below-2.20.10 iPhone still enables the crafted link-preview path.

NIST-800-53-SI-10.gap: SI-10 input validation is precisely what failed: WhatsApp accepted a sender-crafted link-preview whose URI was a javascript: scheme behind an https prefix and shipped a CSP with no object-src directive, so a control assuming server-side validation covers rendered content never reached the preview crafted on the sending client and rendered in the victim's origin.

NIS2-Art21-patch-management.gap: NIS2 Art.21 endpoint patch-management often omits consumer messaging apps; an essential entity can be conformant for OS and browser patching while this KEV-listed client-side XSS-to-local-file-read stays unpatched on staff WhatsApp Desktop installs because the app was never enrolled as managed software.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: CAF B4 is undermined when a consumer messaging client sits outside the managed estate: the fix needs WhatsApp Desktop at 0.3.9309 and relaunched, but a B4 review centred on OS and enterprise-app patching usually has no visibility into whether staff desktop installs — or their paired phones — are current.

AU-Essential-8-App-Hardening.gap: Essential Eight application-hardening targets browsers and Office, not a standalone Electron messaging app; none of its levers touches a javascript: URI in a WhatsApp link preview or a missing object-src CSP, so a compliant hardening posture leaves this local-file-read path fully reachable.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: A.8.8 keyed on enterprise software inventory frequently does not enumerate WhatsApp Desktop or the paired mobile app, so a scan can report the endpoint remediated while a below-0.3.9309 desktop client with a below-2.20.10 iPhone still renders the crafted preview into the WhatsApp origin with local file-system reach.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2019-18426 is a KEV-listed (2022-05-23, EPSS 0.67859) WhatsApp Desktop XSS-to-local-file-read whose fix requires WhatsApp Desktop 0.3.9309 and the paired iPhone app 2.20.10; treating the messaging client as KEV-priority managed software, verified as relaunched onto the fixed build, is what closes it on staff endpoints.

CVE-2019-3568.name: WhatsApp VOIP Stack Buffer Overflow Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: A call to the target's number carrying crafted RTCP control packets overflows a fixed buffer in WhatsApp's native VOIP parser before the call is answered, giving code execution in the messaging app and, in the observed campaign, installation of the Pegasus implant.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none — PR:N; the attacker supplies only the target's phone number and reaches the parser through WhatsApp's own call signalling, with no account relationship, no prior message and no network position required.
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L; a single call sequence triggers the defect, and UI:N is literal: the target does not answer, tap or read anything. The real constraint is engineering a per-platform heap groom and payload, which is why the working exploit came from a commercial surveillance vendor.
attack_vector.ai_factor: None claimed by anyone. Discovery was operational detection of anomalous call traffic by WhatsApp's own security team in May 2019, and the subsequent public work (Check Point's patch diff) is manual reverse engineering of the shipped fix.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Reaching the fixed client build — 2.19.134 on Android, 2.19.51 on iOS, 2.19.44 for Business on Android — and, for the population plausibly inside a commercial-surveillance targeting set, not carrying the app on the device used for sensitive work at all.
prevention.adequacy: Inadequate as timing: the exploit was a zero-day, so no patch existed while the targeting ran, and the only thing that stopped it in the exposure window was Meta's server-side block on 10 May 2019. BOD 22-01 attached to this CVE in April 2022, nearly three years after the fixed builds shipped.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Handset-level forensic triage of targeted individuals — crash logs from the messaging app around inbound calls, and examination of device backups against a published implant indicator set.
detection.adequacy: Weak and retrospective. Nothing in the delivery path is visible to network or endpoint tooling an organization operates, and the implant's purpose is to remove its own traces; the targets in this campaign learned of it because WhatsApp and Citizen Lab told them.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treating a confirmed target as a full device compromise: replace the handset, rotate every credential and session that lived on it, and review the accounts and conversations reachable from it rather than closing on the app update.
response.adequacy: The app update stops re-exploitation but removes nothing an implant already established; for a targeted individual the mail, messaging and cloud sessions held on the handset are the actual loss, and they survive the patch.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: The control is nominally satisfied by an app store that auto-updates, but SI-2 produces no evidence: nothing records which WhatsApp build a given handset ran on a given date, so the organization cannot show when it crossed 2.19.134 or 2.19.51. A remediation programme driven by the 2022-04-19 KEV listing opens the item years after the 13 May 2019 client fix, and closes it on the assumption that auto-update already worked.

NIS2-Art21-patch-management.gap: The patching obligation attaches to systems on the entity's register, and a consumer messaging client is not on it, even in entities where WhatsApp is the channel used to convene incident calls. Nothing in an Article 21 patch plan would have surfaced the six fixed builds, and the control that actually protected unpatched handsets — Meta's server-side block of 10 May 2019 — was neither commissioned nor evidenced by any covered entity.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: B4 can be met in full on the managed estate while this component stays untouched, because there is no configuration that disables a pre-answer RTCP parser and the handset is frequently not the organization's to configure. The only B4-shaped lever is denying the app on devices used for sensitive work, which is a device-policy decision most organizations make in the opposite direction.

UK-CAF-C1.gap: Monitoring is nominally in place and structurally blind here. The exploit arrives inside Meta-relayed, end-to-end encrypted call signalling, executes on the handset and installs an implant designed to erase its own traces, so no C1-collected source carries a detectable event. Confirmation of targeting in this campaign came from the vendor and from Citizen Lab, not from any organization's own monitoring.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: An assessment can award maturity level three for patching applications while every handset runs a WhatsApp build below 2.19.134, because the control's enumerated application classes — browsers, office suites, email clients, PDF readers, security products — do not include a messaging client, and the maturity ladder is expressed in days-to-patch for classes the organization already inventories.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: A.8.8 fails at identification rather than at evaluation. Without an inventory that reaches installed app versions on personally-enrolled handsets, the fixed builds of 13 May 2019 cannot be compared against anything, and an audit sampling servers and managed workstations returns clean while the exploited component sits on the phones the executives carry.

ENISA-mobile-secure-baseline.gap: Every baseline item held: current OS, device encryption, official-store provenance, no side-loading. The compromise still succeeded because it came through a legitimate app's network parser on an unanswered call, which is a threat the baseline has no control for — it governs device posture, not the reachability of an application's protocol handler by an arbitrary caller.

new_control_requirements.name: MITIGATION-ACTIVE-PATCH-PENDING-VERDICT-CLASS
new_control_requirements.description: Compliance verdicts must distinguish three states: (a) binary patch deployed (vulnerability eliminated), (b) vendor-mitigation rule active, no binary patch (residual risk: any defect in the mitigation rule reopens the vulnerability), (c) no mitigation, no patch (full exposure). Audit reports must surface (b) as a distinct compensating-control state with an associated time-bound action item, not as a 'patched per SLA' outcome.
new_control_requirements.evidence: WhatsApp is the exact case: Meta blocked the attack server-side on 10 May 2019 and shipped client builds on 13 May 2019, so for three days every handset in the world sat in state (b) — protected only by a vendor-operated rule, with the vulnerable RTCP parser still executing locally. An operator asking 'are we exposed to CVE-2019-3568?' during that window would get a true answer of 'no, because Meta is filtering it', which is a different risk statement from 'no, because the code is fixed', and the distinction determines whether the handsets still need the 2.19.134 / 2.19.51 update.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: The KEV entry for Meta Platforms WhatsApp landed on 2022-04-19 with a 2022-05-10 due date, nearly three years after the 13 May 2019 client builds — so for this CVE the SLA's 'whichever is later' clause resolves to the KEV date and the only defensible action is a verified inventory statement that no handset runs below 2.19.134 (Android), 2.19.51 (iOS) or 2.19.44 (Business for Android). EPSS still reads 0.39166 at the 98.472nd percentile on 2026-08-16, so verification, not assumed auto-update, is the deliverable.

CVE-2019-3929.name: Crestron Multiple Products Command Injection Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: One unauthenticated HTTP POST to /cgi-bin/file_transfer.cgi with shell metacharacters in the dir parameter runs arbitrary commands as root on a wireless-presentation appliance sitting on the meeting-room network.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none — PR:N; no credential, no session and no prior interaction with the device. The CGI executes the injected command as root, so the attacker's privilege on the appliance is total from the first request.
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L; a single request, no race and no memory-corruption reliability problem. The only real constraint is a network path to the appliance's HTTP service, which in most estates exists from every user VLAN in the building.
attack_vector.ai_factor: None. Jacob Baines of Tenable Research found it by manually analysing a Crestron AM-100 and then matching the AWIND codebase across the other OEM badges; the disclosure claims no automated discovery.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Firmware at AM-100 1.7.1.7 / AM-101 2.8.0.27, wePresent WiPG-1000P 2.3.2.20 or WiPG-1600W 2.4.1.19, combined with placing the appliances on a segment no general user network can route to.
prevention.adequacy: Partial by construction. Six of the eleven affected product lines have no published fixed firmware, so for those units segmentation and replacement are the whole of prevention, and a presentation appliance whose purpose is to accept connections from visiting laptops cannot be isolated from the people it serves.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Web-log inspection on the appliance segment for POSTs to /cgi-bin/file_transfer.cgi, and egress monitoring for outbound connections originating from AV appliances.
detection.adequacy: Rarely available in practice: these devices ship no log forwarding worth the name, and their traffic is usually inside a segment nobody instruments. Egress from the AV VLAN is the more reliable signal, because a rooted presentation box has no legitimate reason to talk to arbitrary internet hosts.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treating an exposed unit as compromised: reflash, regenerate the web server certificate, rebuild configuration from a known-good baseline and rotate any credential the device held or that transited it.
response.adequacy: This is the vendor's own position rather than an inference — Crestron's release notes state Server.pem was compromised and required regeneration. Response is adequate only if it goes past the firmware version; an upgrade that inherits the old certificate and configuration leaves the attacker's material in place.

NIST-800-53-SC-7.gap: The control is implemented at the internet boundary and satisfied there, while the exploit only ever needed a path from a user VLAN to the appliance's web service inside the building. Because a presentation gateway exists to be reachable by whoever is in the room, the segment that would contain it is the one the device's function argues against, and SC-7 offers no way to express that tension.

NIST-800-53-CM-7.gap: Least functionality is met on paper because there is nothing extraneous left to disable — the management web server and its CGI set are what the appliance is. file_transfer.cgi cannot be removed on firmware at or below AM-100 1.6.0.2 or wePresent 2.3.0.10 without disabling administration entirely, so the control cannot reduce the surface that carries the injection.

NIS2-Art21-supply-chain.gap: Supplier assessments were run against Crestron, Barco, Extron and the rest individually, and every one of them can pass while the shared AWIND platform underneath carries the same injectable CGI. The failure is structural: the entity has no contractual or informational relationship with the party that wrote the vulnerable code, and six of the badges never produced a fixed firmware version to demand under the contract.

NIS2-Art21-incident-handling.gap: Handling procedures exist and would record this as remediated once firmware moved to 1.7.1.7 or 2.3.2.20. That verdict is wrong on any unit that was reachable during the exposure window, because the vendor states the flaw exposed the filesystem and compromised the web server certificate — the correct outcome is rebuild and key regeneration, which no version-based closure criterion will ever trigger.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: The control is not so much inadequate as unapplied: AV appliances are commissioned by facilities or an integrator and typically never enter the asset scope a B4 assessment is drawn against. With no owner holding the firmware version, the fixed levels published in 2019 are never compared to anything, and the assessment returns a result that simply does not cover the device.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: Maturity is measured against operating systems and the enumerated application classes, and a room appliance flashed by hand from a vendor download page belongs to neither. An organization can be assessed at maturity level three for application patching while a fleet of AM-100s sits years behind the firmware Crestron released on 2019-05-07, because nothing in the model asks the question.

ISO-27001-2022-A.5.21.gap: ICT supply-chain management is documented and exercised per supplier, which is exactly the frame that hides this defect: eleven products, nine brands, one codebase. Nothing in the supplier questionnaire, the contract or the advisory feed connects the Crestron AM-100 to the InFocus LiteShow4, so a compliant A.5.21 programme still cannot tell an operator which of its rooms share the flaw.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: Technical-vulnerability management runs, and cannot see this asset. No agent runs on the appliance, unauthenticated fingerprinting of its web UI generally cannot distinguish AM-100 1.6.0.2 from 1.7.1.7, and the eleven firmware strings NVD lists have no corresponding field in most CMDBs. The control is fully implemented for the estate it can enumerate, and this device is outside it.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: The Crestron/AWIND presentation platform went into KEV on 2022-04-15 with a 2022-05-06 due date, three years after Crestron's 2019-05-07 firmware and Barco's 2.3.2.20, and it still reads EPSS 0.98952 at the 99.926th percentile on 2026-08-16 — commodity scanning against a one-request unauthenticated root RCE does not decay. For the six badges with no published fixed firmware, the SLA's 'documented compensating controls' branch is the only one available and must name the segment the appliance was moved to and the date it is scheduled for replacement.

new_control_requirements.name: PERIMETER-COMPROMISE-REBUILD-NOT-PATCH
new_control_requirements.description: Pre-rehearsed IR runbook for any perimeter device that suffers a pre-auth RCE CVE in active exploitation MUST default to config-exfil + rebuild + credential rotation, not patch-in-place. Patch-in-place leaves attacker-installed implants intact.
new_control_requirements.evidence: The AM-100 is not a firewall, but it is an unmanaged appliance that answered a pre-auth root RCE from the user network, which puts it in the class this runbook governs, and Crestron itself supplies the proof that patch-in-place is insufficient: the AM-100 1.7.1.7 / AM-101 2.8.0.27 release notes state the flaw exposed the filesystem and the web server certificate and that Server.pem was compromised and required regeneration. Applied here the runbook means reflashing to 1.7.1.7, regenerating the certificate, rebuilding configuration from a known-good baseline and rotating any wireless or directory credential the unit held, rather than closing the item on a firmware version.

attack_vector.description: A page that gets two references to one ArrayBuffer through FileReader and frees one of them leaves script reading and writing freed heap memory, which the public exploit turns into shellcode execution inside the Chrome renderer.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none — PR:N; the attacker needs no account and no foothold, only that the target's browser render content they control, which an ad frame or a compromised third-party script satisfies.
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L, but with UI:R; the real constraint is heap grooming reliability, which the published exploit solves by reloading itself in a cross-origin iframe so site isolation hands each attempt a fresh renderer to brute-force.
attack_vector.ai_factor: None. Clement Lecigne of Google's Threat Analysis Group found it by analysing an attack already running against users; the later public exploits are hand-written, and no party claims automated discovery or automated weaponization.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Chrome relaunched onto 72.0.3626.121 or later, retiring Windows 7 32-bit hosts so the paired escalation had no target, and blocking third-party ad and script delivery so attacker-controlled content had fewer routes into the renderer.
prevention.adequacy: It was a zero-day, so prevention could not have run ahead of 1 March 2019 — but the window that mattered afterwards was the relaunch, not the download, and BOD 22-01 attached only in May 2022, by which time the exposure was historical for anyone still running a supported browser.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Renderer-crash telemetry correlated across the fleet, and alerting on any process spawned by a Chrome renderer.
detection.adequacy: Crash clustering is a real signal for a brute-forced use-after-free and almost nobody collects it centrally. Process-spawn alerting is the stronger control because it catches the sandbox escape rather than the renderer bug, but it fires only after code execution has already happened.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treating a host that showed a renderer-spawned child process as compromised at SYSTEM level, given the paired win32k.sys escalation, and rebuilding rather than clearing the browser profile.
response.adequacy: Adequate only if the response scopes to the chain rather than the browser. Clearing cache and profile addresses a renderer compromise and does nothing about a kernel-level escalation that already ran on a Windows 7 host.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: Flaw remediation looks exemplary for a browser that updates itself, and the metric it produces is the wrong one. Chrome installed 72.0.3626.121 within hours of the 1 March 2019 release on most fleets while the vulnerable Blink kept running in every session that had not been relaunched, and the console SI-2 evidence is drawn from records the install. Nothing in the control asks for the relaunched build.

NIS2-Art21-vulnerability-handling.gap: Handling procedures run off advisories, and Google deliberately published almost no technical detail so that users would update before exploitation spread. The consequence is that an entity's triage had nothing to assess, while working exploit code appeared publicly roughly ten weeks later in a GitHub repository and a Metasploit module. The process is compliant and paced to a clock the attacker was not using.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: Browser hardening under B4 is expressed as policy configuration — extensions, downloads, safe browsing — and none of it reaches a lifetime bug in the engine's own FileReader implementation. The control that actually contained this was the renderer sandbox, which held until a second, unrelated Windows defect broke it, and B4 has no way to record that its most effective control is itself a piece of software with its own CVEs.

AU-Essential-8-App-Hardening.gap: Every hardening measure the control names could be at maximum maturity and this exploit still runs, because it is ordinary JavaScript in an ordinary page rather than Flash, Java or an unwanted plugin. The single item with real effect here is blocking ads and untrusted third-party script, which narrows delivery — and it is also the item most commonly waived for business reasons.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: Web browsers are named in the control and would be patched under it, but the maturity ladder's tiers — 48 hours for internet-facing services, two weeks otherwise — have no slot for a browser defect already exploited in the wild on the day the fix ships. An organization patching Chrome inside two weeks of 1 March 2019 is at full maturity and was exposed for the entire period the exploit was in use.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: The technical-vulnerability register tracks Chrome by version and reports it green, while the two exposures that mattered are invisible at that granularity: whether the browser was actually relaunched onto 72.0.3626.121, and which Electron or embedded-Chromium applications on the same host still carry the pre-fix Blink on their own slower release train.

new_control_requirements.name: BROWSER-MANAGED-UPDATE-NO-DEFERRAL
new_control_requirements.description: Enterprise update rings must not defer security-channel browser updates beyond 24h.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Google released Chrome 72.0.3626.121 on 1 March 2019 for a defect already being exploited, and published exploit code — the Exodus Intelligence repository and the Metasploit module merged 2019-05-08 — followed within about ten weeks. Any enterprise ring that held the security-channel release for testing was holding a fleet in the exploited state, and because the vulnerable Blink persists in running processes, the control has to be written as relaunched-within-24h rather than installed-within-24h for this CVE.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Chrome Blink entered KEV on 2022-05-23 with a 2022-06-13 due date, and EPSS still reads 0.61537 at the 99.095th percentile on 2026-08-16 because the Exodus exploit and the Metasploit module remain obtainable. For this CVE the SLA's verification step is the load-bearing one: an estate must be able to show no Chrome process is running below 72.0.3626.121 and must extend the same check to Chromium-derived browsers and embedded runtimes, which the KEV product string 'Chrome Blink' does not name.

CVE-2019-7286.name: Apple Multiple Products Memory Corruption Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: Code already running on the device sends bundled XPC messages to cfprefsd whose handlers never fire the reply block, causing the daemon to release pointers it never retained; a heap spray then puts a fake Objective-C object in the freed slot and the next method call pivots into a ROP chain with the daemon's privileges.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none — PR:N in the CVSS vector, but read it with AV:L: the attacker needs no account or entitlement, and needs to already be executing code on the device, which in the observed chain was a Safari renderer compromised by a hacked website.
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L; there is no race and no info-leak prerequisite, only an XPC heap spray that has to land the fake object in the freed allocation. The genuine constraint is positional: this bug is only useful as a sandbox escape once something else is already running inside the sandbox.
attack_vector.ai_factor: None. Google TAG recovered live exploit chains from compromised websites and Project Zero reverse-engineered them by hand; the discovery route was sample analysis, and no automated or AI-assisted method is claimed by Apple or by the credited researchers.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: iOS at 12.1.4, Mojave at the 10.14.3 Supplemental Update, tvOS at 12.2 and watchOS at 5.2, each with the device restart completed, plus denying organizational data to any device below the fixed build for its platform.
prevention.adequacy: Prevention was unavailable while the chain was running — this was one of the two still-zero-day bugs in the collection — and afterwards it was unavailable for tvOS and watchOS for another six weeks. BOD 22-01 attached in May 2022, three years after every fixed build shipped.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Collecting and triaging cfprefsd crash reports from managed Apple devices, and treating daemon crashes on a device that rendered untrusted web content as an incident rather than as noise.
detection.adequacy: Real but rarely instrumented: the crash data exists on the device and almost no estate collects it centrally, and by design the successful exploitation path produces no crash at all — only the failed attempts do.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treating a device that visited one of the compromised sites during the window as fully compromised — replace or wipe and rebuild, and rotate every credential and session the device held.
response.adequacy: Correct but almost impossible to scope in practice: the campaign attacked visitors indiscriminately, the site list was not public at the time, and the implant's own persistence characteristics determine what survives a restart. Patching to 12.1.4 stops re-exploitation and settles nothing about what already ran.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: Flaw remediation is implemented and produces a single verdict for a CVE with four vendor release dates. Anchored on 7 February 2019 the control declares the estate remediated while no tvOS or watchOS fix yet exists; anchored on 27 March 2019 it silently grants the iPhones seven weeks they never had. Neither reading tells an operator which platform is still exposed today.

NIST-800-53-CM-7.gap: Restricting installation is a real control and reaches only one of the two delivery paths. It raises the bar against a malicious application arriving on the device, and it does nothing about the route actually used in this chain — a compromised Safari renderer reached by visiting a hacked site — nor does it evict an application that is already installed on a device suspected of running one.

NIS2-Art21-patch-management.gap: The measure binds to systems on the register, and the platforms that stayed vulnerable longest are the ones least likely to be on it: an Apple TV bought as boardroom AV equipment and a personally-owned Watch both carried this defect until late March 2019. Article 21 pressure therefore lands hardest on the phones Apple fixed first.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: Configuration management for the Apple estate is in place and has no setting that touches cfprefsd's XPC handling. The one usable B4 lever is making the fixed build an access condition rather than a dashboard row — denying mail, VPN and document access below 12.1.4 — and most estates implement it as reporting, which records the exposure without removing it.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: Operating-system patching is assessed for workstations and internet-facing services, so an organization at maturity level three patches its iPhones and Macs against the 7 February 2019 releases and never raises an item for tvOS or watchOS. The devices the model does not name are exactly the ones that waited until 25 and 27 March 2019 for the same fix.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: The register is populated and too coarse to answer the question. Evaluating this CVE requires per-platform build data — iOS 12.1.4, Mojave 10.14.3 Supplemental, tvOS 12.2, watchOS 5.2 — and a register carrying 'Apple device, current' cannot be compared against any of them. KEV's 'Multiple Products' string offers nothing to key on either.

ENISA-mobile-secure-baseline.gap: Every baseline item was satisfied on the devices this chain compromised: supported OS, encrypted storage, store-only applications, no side-loading. The compromise came through Safari rendering a hacked page and escalated through Apple's own framework, so the baseline's device-posture controls never had a decision to make about the privilege boundary that actually failed.

new_control_requirements.name: MOBILE-OS-MINIMUM-PATCH-LEVEL-ENFORCEMENT
new_control_requirements.description: The trigger is a malicious application causing unexpected changes in memory shared between processes, so for this entry the control's access-condition half is the load-bearing one: on any Apple device that cannot yet take the fixed build, the operator's remaining levers are constraining what code is allowed to run at all and withholding organizational data from the device until its build is at or above the fix. The fixed build must function as an access condition — mail, VPN and document access denied to a device below it — not as a row on a patch-compliance dashboard. The distinguishing test is to enrol a device pinned below the fixed build and confirm the policy actually denies it access to protected resources; an estate that surfaces the stale build on a report while the device keeps its access has recorded the exposure rather than removed it. Precondition: restricting untrusted or side-loaded application installation raises the bar for getting the attacker's application onto the device, but it does not evict an application already installed, and it does not cover one that arrived through the normal store channel. A device suspected of already running the malicious application belongs on the incident path, not the install-policy path. This is a holding measure for the window before the fixed build and its required restart land, not a substitute for them.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Apple's own impact line for this CVE is that an application may be able to gain elevated privileges, and the fixed builds are specific and staggered: iOS 12.1.4 and the macOS Mojave 10.14.3 Supplemental Update on 7 February 2019, tvOS 12.2 on 25 March 2019, watchOS 5.2 on 27 March 2019. That six-to-seven-week spread is precisely the window this control governs — Apple TVs and Watches could not take a fixed build at all while the phones already had one, so the only available lever on those units was withholding access and constraining what they could run. There is no live-patch path and a device restart is required, so a unit that downloaded the update and has not rebooted is still below the fix for enforcement purposes.

new_control_requirements.name: MOBILE-ENDPOINT-MDM-ENFORCED-KEV-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: iOS / iPadOS / macOS estates must enforce KEV-class updates within 24h via DDM; user-deferral disallowed.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Apple shipped iOS 12.1.4 out of band on 7 February 2019, seven days after Google reported the pair — an emergency release whose entire value is speed, and which a user-deferrable update policy converts back into a normal one. The control has to be extended past its stated scope for this CVE: the same Foundation fix reached tvOS 12.2 and watchOS 5.2 in late March 2019, so an enforcement policy covering only iOS, iPadOS and macOS leaves two of the four affected platforms with no enforced clock at all.

attack_vector.description: A process holding a send right to ProvInfoIOKitUserClient calls ucEncryptSUInfo with an oversized length field; the driver passes it straight to memmove and writes attacker data past the end of a kernel heap buffer, which the in-the-wild chain turned into arbitrary kernel read and write.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none — PR:N with AV:L; no entitlement or account is needed, but the calling process must be able to reach the user client, which the renderer sandbox denies and an installed application does not.
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L; the overflow size is attacker-chosen and the write is deterministic, with no race and no info-leak prerequisite. The real cost is positional: reaching the driver at all required chaining a separate sandbox escape, which is why this bug never appeared as a standalone exploit.
attack_vector.ai_factor: None. Google TAG recovered the chains from compromised websites and Project Zero reverse-engineered the driver by hand; no automated discovery, fuzzing harness or AI assistance is claimed by Apple or the credited researchers.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: iOS at 12.1.4 with the restart completed, and retiring handsets outside the iOS 12 hardware line rather than leaving them enrolled with organizational data.
prevention.adequacy: Unavailable while it mattered: this was still zero-day when TAG found the chains, and Apple's fix arrived seven days after the report. The residual value of prevention is entirely about hardware — devices that cannot reach iOS 12 stay exposed permanently, and no SLA changes that.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Collecting iOS analytics and panic logs from managed handsets and triaging IOKit-related kernel panics, particularly alongside daemon instability on the same device.
detection.adequacy: Weak by construction. A successful kernel compromise removes the device's ability to report on itself, so panic logs surface failed attempts and nothing else, and almost no estate collects that telemetry at all.

response.what_would_have_worked: Retiring or fully rebuilding any handset believed to have rendered content from the compromised sites, and rotating every credential, token and session the device held.
response.adequacy: Correct and largely unscopeable at the time — the campaign hit visitors indiscriminately and the site list was not public. Updating to 12.1.4 prevents re-exploitation and says nothing about what a kernel-privileged implant already took.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: The control drives the update and accepts the wrong evidence. iOS 12.1.4 shipped 7 February 2019, and an MDM console recording it as installed says nothing about whether the handset restarted onto it — which for a driver fix is the only state that matters. On a fleet where users defer restarts, SI-2 closure systematically overstates remediation.

NIST-800-53-SC-39.gap: Process isolation was enforced and did its job: the renderer sandbox denied web content the send right this driver needs, forcing the attacker to spend a second zero-day to get it. The control is nonetheless inadequate as an assurance statement, because it records isolation as a property while the isolation is itself software that failed in the same chain.

NIS2-Art21-vulnerability-management.gap: The process runs and had nothing to consume. Details were withheld from 7 February 2019 until Project Zero published in August 2019, so a covered entity's vulnerability management could record 'apply iOS 12.1.4' and could not assess residual risk, reachability or compensating options for handsets that had not yet taken the build.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: Device configuration is managed and offers no lever against an IOKit user client the operating system exposes by design. The only B4 action available before the reboot landed was to refuse organizational resources to handsets below 12.1.4, and that is an access-enforcement decision most estates render as a compliance report instead.

UK-CAF-C1.gap: Monitoring is implemented for the estate the organization can instrument, and an iOS handset is not in it. The exploit's endpoint is kernel read and write, after which the device's own reporting is untrustworthy; the only defender-visible artefact is a panic log from a failed attempt, held on-device and almost never collected.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: Operating-system patching would drive 12.1.4 and its tiers are measured in days from release. Apple published an emergency build seven days after a seven-day-deadline report on a bug already in a live chain, so even the strictest tier is slower than the threat was, and none of the tiers account for the user-controlled restart that gates the fix.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: Evaluation needs one data point — running iOS build against 12.1.4 — and the register frequently cannot supply it honestly. Enrolled handsets report; unenrolled personal devices reaching the same mail and document accounts do not appear at all, so the control's output describes the managed subset rather than the exposed population.

new_control_requirements.name: MOBILE-ENDPOINT-MDM-ENFORCED-KEV-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: iOS / iPadOS / macOS estates must enforce KEV-class updates within 24h via DDM; user-deferral disallowed.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Apple released iOS 12.1.4 out of band on 7 February 2019, seven days after Google reported this driver bug and its paired sandbox escape under a seven-day deadline. The fix is reboot-gated, so a user-deferrable policy converts an emergency build into a suggestion and leaves the vulnerable ProvInfoIOKitUserClient loaded indefinitely; the enforcement this control requires is what turns 'downloaded' into 'restarted onto 12.1.4', which is the only state that removes the flaw.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: The iOS IOKit entry went into KEV on 2022-05-23 with a 2022-06-13 due date, more than three years after iOS 12.1.4 shipped, so the SLA's deliverable for Apple iOS here is verification rather than deployment: a defensible statement that no enrolled handset is running below 12.1.4 and that devices outside the iOS 12 hardware line — which can never reach a fixed build — have been retired rather than risk-accepted. EPSS sits at 0.04551 on 2026-08-16, which argues for verification effort rather than emergency effort.

CVE-2019-8506.name: Apple Multiple Products Type Confusion Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: A page builds a regular-expression match array whose property is written with putDirect in violation of the structure's inferred type, then gets the JIT to trust that inference — turning a pointer into a readable double and a double into a writable pointer, which is arbitrary memory access from JavaScript.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none — PR:N; no account, no entitlement and no foothold. The attacker needs only that the target render content they control, which an advertisement frame or a compromised third-party script provides without any deliberate visit.
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L with UI:R; the confusable layout is produced by deterministic script rather than a race or a heap groom. The remaining work is the standard read/write-to-execution chain inside the WebContent sandbox, and a further bug to leave it.
attack_vector.ai_factor: None. Samuel Gross of Google Project Zero found it by auditing JavaScriptCore, and the public trigger on Exploit-DB comes from the Project Zero issue tracker; no automated discovery or AI-assisted analysis is claimed by Apple or by the researcher.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Reaching iOS and tvOS 12.2, watchOS 5.2, Safari 12.1, iTunes 12.9.4 for Windows and iCloud for Windows 7.11, and blocking untrusted third-party advertisement and script delivery to reduce the routes attacker-controlled content takes into the engine.
prevention.adequacy: Prevention is available and incomplete in one direction: patching Safari does not remove the engine from in-app web views or from the Windows components, and the KEV clock arrived in May 2022, three years after every fixed build shipped.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Collecting WebContent crash reports across the Apple estate and treating clusters of JavaScriptCore crashes tied to a single origin as an investigation trigger rather than as browser noise.
detection.adequacy: Genuinely useful for an unreliable trigger, which crashes far more often than it lands, and almost never implemented — crash reports on iOS stay on the device, and iTunes crashes on a Windows workstation are treated as an application-support ticket.

response.what_would_have_worked: Scoping response to the engine rather than the browser: identifying every product on the host that embeds the same JavaScriptCore, restarting or updating each, and treating credentials reachable from the compromised process as exposed.
response.adequacy: The sandbox limits what a renderer compromise reaches without a second bug, so the response bar is lower than for a kernel flaw — but only if the responder knows the engine also lives in iTunes, iCloud for Windows and every in-app web view, which is the part usually missed.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: The control produces one remediation record for six fixed builds and closes it on the largest population.
