detection.what_would_have_worked: Alerting on any request to the iControl REST surface carrying a Connection header that names X-F5-Auth-Token, and forwarding /var/log/audit off the appliance so root command execution is visible on a collector rather than only on the device the attacker now controls.
detection.adequacy: Detection here fires after root has been obtained, not before. It is still worth having because the audit log is the only record of which commands ran, and it is worthless if it stays on a compromised appliance where the attacker can rewrite it.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treating any reachable unexploited-but-exposed BIG-IP as compromised: exfiltrate the configuration, rebuild from a known-good baseline on a fixed release, and rotate every credential the appliance held, including the TLS keys it terminated and any monitor or SSO secrets in its configuration.
response.adequacy: Rebuild is the only response that removes an implant, and it is the most commonly skipped step because the appliance keeps passing traffic after the upgrade. Nothing in the KEV required action asks for it — 'apply updates per vendor instructions' is satisfied by a patch that leaves an attacker's account and startup script in place.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: An organisation running BIG-IP under a documented flaw-remediation programme was nominally compliant throughout May 2022 and still exposed. SI-2 sets a process for identifying and correcting flaws; it does not require the correction to outrun the public exploit, and here the interval from F5's 2022-05-04 advisory to weaponized code on Exploit-DB was eight days. The control is also silent on the case that matters most for the 12.1.x and 11.6.x branches, where the correct remediation is decommissioning a device the vendor will never fix rather than applying an update that does not exist.

NIST-800-53-IA-2.gap: Every BIG-IP in a mature estate satisfies IA-2 — unique administrator identities, no shared logins, multi-factor on the management console. That attestation is fully intact on an appliance being exploited, because the bypass never reaches the identity layer: the back end accepts the admin username on the strength of the reverse proxy's supposed decision, and the password supplied is arbitrary. Auditing identity strength on this asset measures a control the attack does not touch, which is why an identity-focused assessment gave no warning of a pre-authentication root path.

NIS2-Art21-patch-management.gap: Article 21 obliges essential and important entities to run vulnerability handling and patching proportionate to risk, and an operator with a 14-day critical tier can evidence that. Proportionality is left undefined, so nothing in the obligation forces a BIG-IP that fronts the estate's TLS termination into a shorter tier than an internal reporting server. Applied to this CVE, a compliant 14-day tier starting on 2022-05-04 puts remediation on 2022-05-18 — eight days after CISA listed the bug with ransomware campaign use already recorded.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: B4 is evidenced with hardened builds and restricted administrative interfaces, and F5's own hardening guidance for BIG-IP — management on a dedicated network, self-IP port lockdown — produces exactly that evidence. The outcome is achieved and the appliance is still exploitable, because the header-smuggling bypass behaves identically when the request comes from a permitted management host, which is where an attacker who has already phished an administrator's workstation sits. B4 also offers no assessment language for a device whose software branch has left vendor support entirely.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: The Essential Eight puts internet-facing services on a 48-hour clock at Maturity Level Two, which is the closest any of the frameworks assessed here comes to the real tempo of CVE-2022-1388. It still measures the wrong thing: compliance is recorded when the update is applied, and a BIG-IP only stops being vulnerable when it reboots into the new boot volume, which in an HA pair means a sequenced failover the operator may postpone. The model has no maturity level that can be reached at all on the 12.1.x and 11.6.x branches, where no update exists to apply.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: A.8.8 was met the moment F5's 2022-05-04 notification was received, logged and risk-assessed, and the control's own text asks for nothing faster. Its weakness on this entry is the asset model behind the assessment: it evaluates the BIG-IP as one system with one risk rating, when a rooted BIG-IP hands over the TLS private keys it terminates, the authentication decisions it enforces for applications behind it, and a routing position inside the network. The residual-risk figure an A.8.8 assessment produces for 'a load balancer' is not the consequence this CVE actually carries.

new_control_requirements.name: PERIMETER-DEVICE-ZERODAY-SLA-TIER
new_control_requirements.description: Compliance frameworks must define a distinct patch SLA tier for pre-auth RCE on perimeter-trust-boundary devices (firewalls, VPN concentrators, WAFs, edge load-balancers). Tier requirement: vendor-mitigation deployed within 4 hours of KEV listing OR isolation of the vulnerable interface; standard 14/30-day SLAs do not apply because the device IS the trust boundary.
new_control_requirements.evidence: F5 BIG-IP is the edge load balancer and WAF this tier exists for. F5 published K23605346 on 2022-05-04; public exploit code reached Exploit-DB as entry 50932 on 2022-05-12; CISA listed the CVE on 2022-05-10 with knownRansomwareCampaignUse recorded as Known and a due date of 2022-05-31. EPSS now stands at 0.99958 (0.99975 percentile, 2026-08-16). A 14-day or 30-day tier applied to this device would have completed remediation after the ransomware activity CISA recorded, which is precisely the failure the separate tier prevents.

new_control_requirements.name: PERIMETER-COMPROMISE-REBUILD-NOT-PATCH
new_control_requirements.description: Pre-rehearsed IR runbook for any perimeter device that suffers a pre-auth RCE CVE in active exploitation MUST default to config-exfil + rebuild + credential rotation, not patch-in-place. Patch-in-place leaves attacker-installed implants intact.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Exploitation of CVE-2022-1388 executes as root through /mgmt/tm/util/bash, so an attacker who reached a BIG-IP before the operator upgraded to 16.1.2.2, 15.1.5.1, 14.1.4.6 or 13.1.5 could add accounts, alter startup configuration and read the TLS keys the appliance terminates. Upgrading to a fixed build closes the header-smuggling path and removes none of that. With ransomware campaign use recorded at the 2022-05-10 KEV listing and mass scanning under way within days of the advisory, any F5 appliance whose iControl REST surface was reachable in that window is a rebuild candidate rather than a patch candidate.

CVE-2022-20821.name: Cisco IOS XR Open Port Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: A monitoring feature brings its own datastore. Turning on the IOS XR health check installs an RPM that starts Redis inside the NOSi container listening on TCP/6379 with authentication disabled, so anyone who can route to the router speaks to it directly — reading the health-check database, writing keys, and using Redis persistence commands to drop files into the container. The sandbox around that container is what keeps it out of the IOS XR host.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none — PR:N; the Redis instance requires no credential, so the connection itself is the authorization
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L; the constraint is not skill but configuration, since only 8000 Series routers on IOS XR 7.3.3 with the health check RPM active present the listener at all
attack_vector.ai_factor: None. Cisco attributes the finding to the resolution of a TAC support case, which is human support engineering rather than any automated discovery programme.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Removing the health check RPM on routers that were not actually consuming its output, or applying an infrastructure ACL denying TCP/6379 to the routers' own addresses — both of which Cisco publishes as workarounds and both of which land without waiting for IOS XR 7.3.4 or the 7.3.3 SMU.
prevention.adequacy: The iACL bounds who can reach the port and does not repair the missing authentication, so anything already inside the permitted segment still speaks to the Redis instance. RPM removal is the stronger answer and costs the operator the health check function on that router.

detection.what_would_have_worked: A recurring port sweep of the routers' own management and interface addresses, treating any listener not on the approved list — TCP/6379 in particular — as a finding, rather than relying on configuration review to describe what the device exposes.
detection.adequacy: This is the one control that would have found the exposure before Cisco's advisory, because the port is invisible in the running configuration. It detects the exposure rather than the abuse; distinguishing legitimate health-check traffic from an attacker's Redis session still needs flow records from the management segment.

response.what_would_have_worked: On a router whose 6379 was reachable, comparing the NOSi container filesystem against a known-good state and reinstalling the health check RPM rather than assuming the write primitive was unused, then completing the move to 7.3.4.
response.adequacy: Bounded by what the sandbox allows: Cisco is explicit that the attacker cannot reach the IOS XR host or its integrity from the container, so response scope is the container and the health-check data, not a full router rebuild. That bound is a vendor statement about the deployed configuration, not a proof.

NIST-800-53-CM-7.gap: CM-7 is satisfied on these routers by the ordinary evidence — an approved feature list, a reviewed running configuration, no unauthorised services enabled. The evidence is genuine and it misses this entirely, because the Redis listener is not a service anyone enabled; it is what the health check RPM starts when the approved monitoring feature is activated. A control assessed against declared configuration cannot see a port that the configuration never mentions, and on the 7.3.3 build that port answers with no authentication at all.

NIST-800-53-SC-7.gap: Boundary protection on a core router is documented and audited in terms of what the device filters for the networks it serves, and that documentation was intact while TCP/6379 answered on the router itself. The control's own remedy was available the whole time — Cisco's published workaround is an infrastructure ACL denying 6379 — so this is not a missing capability but a control aimed at the wrong side of the device. Until the advisory named the port, no SC-7 assessment had a reason to add that ACL line.

NIS2-Art21-network-security.gap: An essential entity operating this hardware can evidence Article 21 network security through segmentation, transit filtering and management-plane separation. None of that reaches an unauthenticated datastore the router hosts for its own monitoring: the obligation directs attention to traffic the router carries, while the exposure is a service the router runs. Cisco reported attempted exploitation in the wild in May 2022 against a listener that a compliant Article 21 programme had no prompt to enumerate.

UK-CAF-B5.gap: B5 is achieved on a well-engineered core network and stays achieved throughout this exposure, because nothing about CVE-2022-20821 threatens availability — Cisco scores it A:N and the router forwards normally while its health-check store is being read and written. The outcome's focus on keeping the service running is what makes it blind here: the loss is confidentiality and integrity of container-resident data on 8000 Series routers running 7.3.3, and a resilience assessment has no vocabulary for that.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: Essential Eight patching is written for operating systems and applications and is normally scoped away from network device software, so most estates can claim the mitigation while never applying it to IOS XR at all. Even applied generously it would drive the fleet toward 7.3.4 and miss the two faster remediations Cisco publishes, since removing the health check RPM and adding an iACL for TCP/6379 are neither of them patches. It also cannot express the SMU case, where 8000-7.3.3.CSCwb82689 shows as installed while the container carrying the fix has not been restarted.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.9.gap: Configuration management is met by proving the routers match an approved baseline, and they did — the health check function is a deliberate monitoring choice, not drift. The control's limit is what a baseline is understood to contain: a statement-level baseline records the feature and says nothing about the TCP/6379 listener the RPM starts. Extending the baseline to enumerate listening ports on 8000 Series devices is what turns this from an invisible side effect into an exposure someone has to justify.

new_control_requirements.name: IN-MEMORY-DATASTORE-MEMORY-DISCLOSURE-NETWORK-EXPOSURE-AUDIT
new_control_requirements.description: Quarterly inventory of Redis / KeyDB / Valkey direct-internet exposure.
new_control_requirements.evidence: The exposed asset in CVE-2022-20821 is literally a Redis instance — one the operator never deployed, started by the IOS XR health check RPM inside the NOSi container on Cisco 8000 Series routers running 7.3.3, listening on TCP/6379 with authentication disabled. An inventory of Redis exposure scoped to servers and containers the organisation deployed would not have listed it; scoping the same audit to every address the estate answers on, network devices included, is what surfaces it. Cisco reported attempted exploitation in May 2022 and CISA listed the CVE on 2022-05-23 with a 2022-06-13 due date.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: This entry is the case where the compensating-control half of the SLA is the operative half. Reaching IOS XR 7.3.4 across a service-provider core is a change-window exercise measured in weeks, but Cisco's two documented workarounds — removing the health check RPM, or an infrastructure ACL denying TCP/6379 — are configuration changes deployable within hours of the 2022-05-23 KEV listing, well inside the 2022-06-13 due date. Recording either as the verified mitigation is what lets the SLA be met honestly on hardware that cannot be upgraded on that clock.

attack_vector.description: A kernel media decoder that writes more than it measured. An application feeds AppleAVD a crafted stream, the extension writes past the end of its kernel buffer, and controlled corruption of kernel memory becomes execution at kernel privilege — at which point the sandbox that was supposed to contain the application and the code-signing that was supposed to vouch for it are both being enforced by code the attacker owns.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none — PR:N with UI:R; no elevated rights are needed, but the user has to run the attacker's application, which places delivery rather than privilege on the critical path
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L as scored, though a reliable kernel write-to-execution chain on current Apple kernels needs heap shaping and a route past pointer authentication, which is why no public exploit ever appeared
attack_vector.ai_factor: None recorded. The credit is to an anonymous researcher with no organisation named, and Apple publishes no detail about the discovery route; nothing here suggests automated or AI-assisted analysis.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Driving every Apple device to the fixed build and confirming the restart — macOS 12.3.1 or 11.6.6, iOS and iPadOS 15.4.1, tvOS 15.5, watchOS 8.6 — with the inventory extended to the Apple TV and Apple Watch population, not just the managed Macs and iPhones.
prevention.adequacy: Complete as a fix and incomplete as a programme: the tvOS and watchOS updates only landed on 2022-05-16, after the KEV due date, so devices on those platforms could not have been remediated inside the clock at all. Hardware too old for a fixed build has no compliant state short of replacement.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Treating a kernel panic on an Apple device as a security event rather than a stability one, and alarming when a managed device stops reporting to the management plane while still on the network.
detection.adequacy: Marginal. A successful exploit does not panic the device, and a kernel compromise can suppress the agent's own telemetry, so both signals are more likely to appear on failed attempts than on successful ones. Apple published no sample, so there is nothing to hunt for directly.

response.what_would_have_worked: Retiring rather than reimaging any device with credible evidence of exploitation, and rotating every credential, token and certificate that device held — the correct assumption after kernel code execution is that everything on the device left it.
response.adequacy: Right in principle and hard to trigger in practice, because the entry condition — evidence of exploitation — is what this CVE denies the operator. In the absence of evidence, the honest fallback is scoping by exposure window and by which devices ran unmanaged applications while below the fixed build.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: An organisation can hold a fully compliant flaw-remediation programme, patch every Mac to 12.3.1 and every iPhone to 15.4.1 inside the KEV window, and still leave the AppleAVD defect live on its Apple TVs and Apple Watches, because those devices are not in the inventory SI-2 is assessed against. The control has no mechanism that maps one CVE across five operating systems with different update mechanisms and different release dates — tvOS 15.5 and watchOS 8.6 did not ship until 2022-05-16, three weeks past CISA's due date.

NIST-800-53-SI-3.gap: Malicious code protection is deployed, current and reporting healthy on the very device this exploit takes. The delivery is an application the user runs and the outcome is kernel execution, so the agent ends up subordinate to the attacker — and because Apple never published the in-the-wild sample, there was never a signature to distribute in the first place. SI-3's evidence is agent coverage and definition currency, both of which stay green through a compromise the control cannot see or stop.

NIS2-Art21-incident-handling.gap: An essential entity with a rehearsed incident-handling capability, defined severity tiers and a notification clock can evidence Article 21 fully and still have no case to open on this CVE. Apple disclosed one sentence, no indicators and the hedge 'may have been actively exploited'; kernel code execution on iOS or watchOS produces no artefact the entity can collect. Compliance here measures the readiness of a process whose input — evidence that something happened — this vulnerability structurally withholds.

UK-CAF-C1.gap: C1 is achieved by a fleet that ships endpoint and network telemetry into a monitored SIEM with defined use cases, and that achievement is real. It is also irrelevant to a bug that executes below the level any of those sources can observe: iOS, iPadOS, tvOS and watchOS expose essentially no kernel telemetry to an operator, and on macOS the visible layer sits above the boundary AppleAVD failed at. The monitoring outcome is met against what Apple's platforms are willing to emit, which for this event is nothing at all.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: The mitigation is evidenced against operating systems on workstations and servers, so patching macOS to 12.3.1 satisfies it while the tvOS and watchOS devices carrying the identical AppleAVD extension fall outside the model's scope entirely. Even within scope it counts the update rather than the restart the kernel fix depends on, and on user-held iPhones the restart is precisely the deferred step. The staggered releases — 2022-03-31 for macOS Monterey, iOS and iPadOS, then 2022-05-16 for macOS Big Sur, tvOS and watchOS — do not fit a single patch window.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: Vulnerability information was obtained on 2022-03-31 and rated high, correctly, because Apple's own advisory carried the actively-exploited notice. The control then evaluates that vulnerability against the asset inventory, and the inventory is where this comes apart: laptops and phones are listed, the conference-room Apple TV and the watches paired to corporate iPhones are not. A CVE spanning five Apple operating systems is risk-assessed against two, and the residual exposure never appears on the risk register at all.

new_control_requirements.name: MOBILE-ENDPOINT-MDM-ENFORCED-KEV-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: iOS / iPadOS / macOS estates must enforce KEV-class updates within 24h via DDM; user-deferral disallowed.
new_control_requirements.evidence: The AppleAVD fix shipped simultaneously to macOS 12.3.1, iOS 15.4.1 and iPadOS 15.4.1 on 2022-03-31 with Apple's actively-exploited notice attached, and CISA listed the CVE on 2022-04-04 due 2022-04-25. Every one of those updates is inert until the device restarts, and on user-held iPhones and iPads the restart is the deferrable step — which makes enforced update and enforced restart, not download success, the only measurement that reflects whether the vulnerable kernel extension is still running. Extending the same enforcement to the tvOS 15.5 and watchOS 8.6 devices is what closes the population this CVE actually reached.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: This entry is where the SLA's 'or patch availability, whichever is later' clause does the work. CISA listed CVE-2022-22675 on 2022-04-04 with a due date of 2022-04-25, but Apple did not ship tvOS 15.5 and watchOS 8.6 until 2022-05-16, so no Apple TV or Apple Watch in the estate could have been remediated inside the KEV clock at all. Anchoring the obligation to per-platform patch availability produces an honest record for those devices instead of a blanket overdue status that no action could have cleared, and it forces the application-restriction holding measure to be documented as the mitigation in the meantime.

CVE-2022-22718.name: Microsoft Windows Print Spooler Privilege Escalation Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: A SYSTEM service that every ordinary user is entitled to talk to. The Print Spooler accepts printer, driver and port management from unprivileged callers by design, and one of those paths performs a privileged operation it should have refused for the caller, ending with code execution as SYSTEM. Microsoft never published which path, so the mechanism is known by its boundary rather than by its primitive.
attack_vector.privileges_required: low — PR:L; any authenticated interactive local session is sufficient, with no requirement for administrative rights, printer configuration or group membership
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L, and Microsoft's own assessment is 'Exploitation More Likely'. The Print Spooler starts by default on every SKU, so there is no configuration precondition to satisfy either
attack_vector.ai_factor: None. Microsoft acknowledges NSFOCUS TIANJI Lab via TianfuCup — human competitive exploit research against a live target. The word 'Lab' in that credit is an organisational name, not an indication of automated discovery.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Stopping and disabling the Print Spooler on every host with no printing role, which removes this CVE and the rest of the component's history in one action, and installing the February 2022 cumulative update with a reboot everywhere the service must keep running.
prevention.adequacy: Disabling the service is the only durable answer, and it is unavailable on print servers and on user workstations that print. On those hosts remediation is the patch alone, verified by installed build rather than by the console's approval state, since Microsoft marks every affected product restart-required.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Alerting on spoolsv.exe creating child processes or writing outside the spool tree, and on printer driver or port registration performed by non-administrative accounts.
detection.adequacy: These are class-level indicators for the component rather than signatures for this CVE, because Microsoft published no root cause. That makes them durable — they cover the next spooler escalation as readily as this one — and imprecise, since legitimate driver installation produces similar activity on print servers.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treating a spooler escalation on a multi-user host as a credential exposure: rotating the accounts whose sessions or cached credentials lived on the machine, and reviewing what was installed into the printer driver directories during the exposure window.
response.adequacy: Scoped correctly, but conditional on detection that most estates do not run against the spooler. With no public exploit and no vendor root cause, there is also no reference artefact to search for retrospectively — the response has to work from the driver directory contents and from process ancestry, if either was recorded.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: The programme worked as designed and produced the wrong answer. Microsoft's 2022-02-08 release rated this Important with exploitation unproven and no public disclosure, so a risk-ranked remediation queue placed it below that month's critical remote bugs — a defensible decision on the vendor's own data. SI-2 contains no trigger to revisit it when CISA listed the CVE on 2022-04-19 with a 2022-05-10 deadline, and to this day Microsoft's record still reports exploited: No, so the control's authoritative input never changed.

NIST-800-53-CM-7.gap: Least functionality is claimed across the estate on the strength of hardened role baselines, and those baselines almost universally leave the Print Spooler started because Windows ships it that way. The control is genuinely implemented and aimed one level too high: it asks whether unnecessary services are approved, and a default OS component reads as approved. The consequence is a SYSTEM-context service reachable by every interactive user on domain controllers, database servers and jump hosts that have never had a printer defined.

NIS2-Art21-patch-management.gap: An entity operating a defined, risk-proportionate patch cycle can evidence Article 21 compliance throughout this exposure, because every input it is required to weigh — vendor severity Important, exploitation not reported, exploit code unproven — pointed at routine handling. The obligation has no clause that reopens a proportionality judgement when a national catalog disagrees with the vendor, which is the entire situation from 2022-04-19 onward. Compliance and exposure ran in parallel for ten weeks without either being wrong on its own terms.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: B4 is evidenced with conformance to a recognised Windows hardening baseline, and estates that do this well can show it fleet-wide. The baselines themselves have historically left the Print Spooler running on server roles that never print, so the outcome is achieved on exactly the hosts where the strongest remediation was available and unused. B4 asks whether systems are configured securely against a standard; it does not ask whether the standard removed a service that produced PrintNightmare, SpoolFool and this CVE in under a year.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: Operating-system patching is one of the mitigations organisations evidence most reliably, and its one-month window for non-internet-facing systems made early March 2022 a compliant date for the 2022-02-08 update — comfortably ahead of CISA's 2022-05-10 due date. The compliance signal is nonetheless weak here: the mitigation records that the update was applied rather than that the host rebooted, and it awards nothing for disabling the spooler on non-printing roles, which is the action that would have remediated this CVE and its successors together.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.9.gap: Configuration management is fully in place: baselines are defined, conformance is monitored, and drift is investigated. Every affected host in this entry conforms, because the Print Spooler running is the baseline rather than a deviation from it. A.8.9 measures distance from an approved configuration and has nothing to say about whether that configuration is minimal, so the control passes on a Server Core domain controller that has never printed and is one interactive session away from a SYSTEM escalation.

new_control_requirements.name: INCOMPLETE-PATCH-SEQUENCE-SEVERITY-MULTIPLIER
new_control_requirements.description: Vulnerability-management programs must apply a severity multiplier when a CVE is the Nth in an incomplete-patch sequence on the same primitive (third MOTW bypass, second AMSI bypass, etc.). Framework controls treating each CVE as discrete obscure the structural defect; the Nth CVE in a sequence implies that future bypasses on the same primitive are likely.
new_control_requirements.evidence: The Windows Print Spooler is the clearest instance of the pattern this multiplier exists for: PrintNightmare, then SpoolFool as CVE-2022-21999 in the same 2022-02-08 release as this CVE, then several further elevation bugs in that single patch cycle. Rated discretely, CVE-2022-22718 is an Important 7.8 local escalation with no public exploit and Microsoft reporting exploitation unproven, and it sits low in a February queue. Rated as one more entry on a primitive that keeps failing, it triggers the durable action — disabling the spooler on non-printing roles — rather than another single patch, and its EPSS of 0.18464 at the 0.96991 percentile reflects the component's history rather than this bug's tooling.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Microsoft's record for CVE-2022-22718 reports exploited: No and publicly disclosed: No, with exploit-code maturity E:U, so no vendor-driven process would ever escalate this bug above routine handling. The 2022-04-19 KEV listing, ten weeks after the 2022-02-08 release, is the only signal that exists, and keying the SLA to it is what pulls a deferred February rollup back into scope before the 2022-05-10 due date. The control's compensating-control clause is unusually strong here, because stopping and disabling the Print Spooler on hosts with no printing role is a verified mitigation deployable in minutes.

CVE-2022-22947.name: VMware Spring Cloud Gateway Code Injection Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: A management endpoint that accepts route definitions, and a routing engine that treats those definitions as expressions to evaluate. An unauthenticated caller posts a route whose filter argument is a SpEL expression, asks the gateway to refresh, and the expression runs inside the gateway JVM with that process's privileges and network position. Deleting the route afterwards removes the definition while the code has already executed.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none — PR:N; the Gateway Actuator answers unauthenticated where it has been enabled and exposed, so no credential is involved at any point
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L; three HTTP requests with no race and no leak. The gating factor is deployment configuration rather than difficulty, since Spring Boot does not expose the gateway actuator unless someone chose to
attack_vector.ai_factor: None. Spring credits security researcher Wyatt Dahlenburg with a private disclosure ahead of the 2022-03-01 publication; the analysis is manual review of expression handling in route filters.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Setting management.endpoint.gateway.enabled to false, or putting Spring Security in front of the actuator, on every deployment that did not need route management exposed — and then upgrading the dependency to 3.1.1 or 3.0.7 and redeploying each service.
prevention.adequacy: The configuration workaround is genuinely sufficient here — with the endpoint disabled there is no path to the evaluator — and it lands in a redeploy rather than a rebuild. Its limit is discovery: an organisation has to know which of its own services embed the library before it can apply either fix, and the KEV vendor field of 'VMware' actively points that search in the wrong direction.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Alerting on any unauthenticated request to /actuator/gateway/routes or /actuator/gateway/refresh, and on the gateway JVM spawning a child process or resolving an unfamiliar external domain.
detection.adequacy: Strong for this CVE, because the exploit sequence is distinctive and appears in ordinary HTTP access logs the gateway already writes. It is weak against the aftermath: the public tooling loads a Godzilla web shell into memory, so post-exploitation traffic arrives on the gateway's own listener and looks like application traffic.

response.what_would_have_worked: Rebuilding any exposed gateway from a clean artefact rather than upgrading it in place, and rotating every credential the gateway process held for the services behind it — database, message broker and service-to-service tokens included.
response.adequacy: This is the step most often skipped because the upgrade appears to close the finding. An in-memory web shell leaves no file for a post-patch scan to find and dies with the JVM, so redeploying the container is both the remediation and the eviction — but only if the operator knows to treat it as eviction and rotates what the process could read.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: A flaw-remediation programme covering operating systems, appliances and vendor applications can be fully compliant and never see this CVE, because the vulnerable component is a Maven coordinate inside a first-party service rather than an inventoried system. Even where it is seen, the timing defeats an ordinary cycle: Spring published the fix on 2022-03-01 and Exploit-DB entry 50799 appeared on 2022-03-07. SI-2 also treats remediation as complete at update, whereas a dependency bump is inert until the service is rebuilt, redeployed and its JVM restarted.

NIST-800-53-CM-7.gap: Least functionality is attested at host and service granularity — ports, packages, running daemons — and every one of those attestations is accurate on a gateway that exposes /actuator/gateway/routes to the internet. The enabled function that matters is an actuator endpoint inside the application, turned on by a management exposure property during development and never revisited. CM-7 has no review step that enumerates the HTTP endpoints an application publishes, so the entire attack surface of this CVE sits outside what the control examines.

NIS2-Art21-vulnerability-management.gap: The obligation is met by a documented, risk-proportionate handling process, and such a process would have escalated a CVSS 10.0 unauthenticated remote code execution immediately — if it had known the component was in scope. Article 21 directs vulnerability handling at systems and at the supply chain, and Spring Cloud Gateway sits in neither category cleanly: it is a library that first-party developers pulled in, often transitively through a Spring Cloud release train. An entity can therefore be entirely compliant between 2022-03-01 and the 2022-05-16 KEV listing while never establishing that it was affected.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: B4 is achieved with hardened base images, controlled JVM and container configuration, and administrative access restricted to a management plane, and none of that changes state during this exploit. The reason is the endpoint's nature: /actuator/gateway/routes is served by the application on the same listener as normal traffic, so it is not an administrative interface B4 would recognise or restrict. A gateway hardened to the outcome's satisfaction still evaluates an unauthenticated caller's SpEL expression inside its own process.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: Application patching at Maturity Level Two demands 48 hours for internet-facing services, which is close to the tempo this CVE actually required given a public exploit within a week of the 2022-03-01 advisory. The mitigation still measures the wrong artefact for a library flaw: there is no vendor patch to install, only spring-cloud-gateway 3.1.1 or 3.0.7 in a build file, and a service whose manifest is updated but whose containers have not been rebuilt and restarted reports remediated while running the vulnerable code.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.21.gap: An organisation running an API gateway can evidence A.8.21 through documented service definitions, agreed security features and monitored network service levels, and that evidence is intact throughout this exposure. The control's outward orientation is the problem: it governs the services delivered and consumed across the gateway, not the gateway's own management endpoint published on the same port. Nothing in A.8.21 asks whether /actuator/gateway/routes requires authentication, and that endpoint is the whole of the vulnerability.

new_control_requirements.name: PERIMETER-COMPROMISE-REBUILD-NOT-PATCH
new_control_requirements.description: Pre-rehearsed IR runbook for any perimeter device that suffers a pre-auth RCE CVE in active exploitation MUST default to config-exfil + rebuild + credential rotation, not patch-in-place. Patch-in-place leaves attacker-installed implants intact.
new_control_requirements.evidence: A Spring Cloud Gateway instance is the perimeter for everything it routes to, and CVE-2022-22947 gives an unauthenticated caller code execution inside that process. The public tooling makes patch-in-place specifically inadequate: whwlsfb/cve-2022-22947-godzilla-memshell loads a Godzilla web shell into the running JVM, which leaves nothing on disk for a post-upgrade file scan to find. Bumping the dependency to 3.1.1 or 3.0.7 and restarting is therefore both the fix and the eviction — but only when the operator also rotates the downstream credentials the gateway process could read, on every instance exposed between the 2022-03-01 advisory and the 2022-05-16 KEV listing.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Rebuilding and redeploying every service that embeds spring-cloud-gateway cannot be done in four hours across a microservice estate, and this CVE is the case where the SLA's documented-compensating-control clause carries the load instead: Spring's own workaround — setting management.endpoint.gateway.enabled to false, or requiring authentication on the actuator through Spring Security — is a configuration change deployable inside the window and closes the path completely. CISA listed the CVE on 2022-05-16 due 2022-06-06, by which point Exploit-DB 50799 had been public for two months and a Metasploit module existed, so the interim mitigation was the difference between exposure and containment while the 3.1.1 and 3.0.7 rollout ran.

CVE-2022-22954.name: VMware Workspace ONE Access and Identity Manager Server-Side Template Injection Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: A single unauthenticated GET to the Workspace ONE Access catalog-portal carries a FreeMarker expression in deviceUdid or deviceType; the appliance evaluates it and runs the attacker's shell command as the horizon account, which owns the organisation's SSO configuration, master keys and directory credentials.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none — PR:N; the vulnerable path sits on the appliance's pre-authentication surface, so no account, token or session is needed and the appliance returns the same HTTP 400 body on success as on failure
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L; one request, no race, no memory grooming and no information leak. The practical constraint is only whether the catalog-portal path is reachable, and on an SSO appliance it is reachable by design.
attack_vector.ai_factor: Found by Steven Seeley (mr_me) of Qihoo 360 Vulnerability Research Institute through manual review of the appliance's template handling. The speed that mattered was on the offensive side and was human too: CISA records actors reverse-engineering the 2022-04-06 patch into a working exploit within 48 hours.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Applying the VMSA-2022-0011 patch from KB88099 within hours of 2022-04-06, or taking the catalog-portal off the internet until it landed, would have closed the path before the first observed compromise on 2022-04-12.
prevention.adequacy: The BOD due date was 2022-05-05, three weeks after actors were already exfiltrating appliance credentials, so meeting the directive on time was compatible with being fully compromised. The patch also removes only the injection path — it does not evict a webshell, does not rotate the master keys the actors collected, and does not restore the logs they deleted.

detection.what_would_have_worked: URL-decoding the appliance's greenbox_web.log and alerting on freemarker.template.utility.Execute, plus alerting on the horizon account spawning any shell utility, would have caught both observed actors at the first request.
detection.adequacy: Neither detection is available by default: the appliance's logs are local, and the string does not match unless the log is decoded first, which is precisely the step an operator who has not read the advisory will skip. Once the actor reaches root through CVE-2022-22960 the local logs are editable, so detection has value only if the telemetry has already left the appliance.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treating any internet-facing instance that ran unpatched after 2022-04-06 as compromised — rebuilding the appliance, rotating master keys and every credential it stored, and hunting the named webshell paths across the estate.
response.adequacy: This is what CISA explicitly recommended and what almost no compliance framework requires: the standard response to a patched vulnerability is to close the ticket. Rebuilding an SSO appliance also has a cost most organisations will not pay on suspicion alone, which is why the decision has to be pre-authorised in a runbook rather than argued during the incident.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: SI-2 is met by any programme that ingested VMSA-2022-0011 and scheduled the fix, and it will read as met even where the fix landed weeks after 2022-04-06. The control has no concept of an exploit-development interval, and here that interval was 48 hours from patch to working exploit, so a compliant remediation cadence still leaves the appliance owned. Nothing in SI-2 asks whether the master keys the horizon account held were rotated after remediation.

NIST-800-53-SC-7.gap: SC-7 is satisfied by placing Workspace ONE Access in a controlled DMZ with published ports, which is exactly the deployment the product requires. The attack arrives on the permitted port over the permitted protocol to a path the product publishes unauthenticated, so every boundary rule evaluates to allow. A boundary control cannot distinguish a catalog-portal request that carries a FreeMarker expression from one that does not.

NIS2-Art21-vulnerability-handling.gap: The Article 21 handling obligation is satisfied by the disclosure and listing chain that actually happened — vendor advisory 2022-04-06, KEV listing 2022-04-14, CISA IOC publication 2022-05-18. The obligation does not bound how quickly an operator must act inside that chain, and the compromises CISA investigated began on 2022-04-12, before the CVE was even listed. Handling that is timely by the regulation's standard is late by this CVE's.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: B4 assesses whether systems are securely configured and maintained, and a patched 21.08.0.1 appliance answers that in the affirmative today. The principle carries no state for an asset that was reachable and unpatched during a known exploitation window and is therefore suspect regardless of its current build. CISA's instruction to assume compromise on internet-facing instances has no expression in a B4 assessment, so an operator can be assessed as adequate while running a rebuilt-in-name-only identity appliance.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: Patch applications at maturity level three demands 48 hours for an internet-facing service with a working exploit, and this CVE produced that working exploit at roughly the 48-hour mark by reverse-engineering the fix. Completing patching exactly on the control's clock therefore coincides with the start of mass exploitation rather than preceding it. The control measures the installed version and cannot see that the appliance holding that version already handed out its master keys.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: A.8.8 is discharged by obtaining vulnerability information, evaluating exposure and taking action, all of which a competent ISMS did from VMSA-2022-0011. The clause treats the vendor fix as the close-out, which means an auditor sees a resolved item on an appliance that may still be serving horizon_all.jsp from its portal directory. There is no requirement in the clause to prove post-exposure key rotation, and on an SSO appliance the keys are the asset.

OWASP-Top-10-2021-A03.gap: An assurance programme built on A03 will show injection coverage through parameterised queries, output encoding and SAST gates on first-party code. None of those reach a FreeMarker sink compiled into a purchased identity appliance, where the operator has no source, no build and no ability to change the sink. A03 coverage is genuine and simply aimed at a different half of the estate than the one this CVE lives in.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: VMware shipped the Workspace ONE Access and vIDM fix on 2022-04-06 and CISA listed it on 2022-04-14 with a 2022-05-05 due date, but the compromises CISA investigated began on 2022-04-12 — before the listing and three weeks before the due date. A four-hour clock running from patch availability is the only cadence that beats an exploit reverse-engineered out of that same patch in 48 hours, and with EPSS at 0.99995 (99.988th percentile, 2026-08-16) this entry sits at the top of the scale for exactly that reason.

new_control_requirements.name: PERIMETER-COMPROMISE-REBUILD-NOT-PATCH
new_control_requirements.description: Pre-rehearsed IR runbook for any perimeter device that suffers a pre-auth RCE CVE in active exploitation MUST default to config-exfil + rebuild + credential rotation, not patch-in-place. Patch-in-place leaves attacker-installed implants intact.
new_control_requirements.evidence: This is a pre-authentication RCE on an internet-published VMware identity appliance under confirmed multi-actor exploitation, and CISA's own guidance in AA22-138B is to assume compromise on any internet-facing instance not patched immediately. The observed post-exploitation was webshell installation at three named paths plus exfiltration of the appliance's usernames, passwords and master keys, none of which the KB88099 patch removes or rotates — patch-in-place on this appliance preserves both the implant and the stolen key material.

new_control_requirements.name: MITIGATION-ACTIVE-PATCH-PENDING-VERDICT-CLASS
new_control_requirements.description: Compliance verdicts must distinguish three states: (a) binary patch deployed (vulnerability eliminated), (b) vendor-mitigation rule active, no binary patch (residual risk: any defect in the mitigation rule reopens the vulnerability), (c) no mitigation, no patch (full exposure). Audit reports must surface (b) as a distinct compensating-control state with an associated time-bound action item, not as a 'patched per SLA' outcome.
new_control_requirements.evidence: VMware published two separate articles for VMSA-2022-0011 — KB88099 for the fixed versions and KB88098 for the workaround — so a Workspace ONE Access estate in April 2022 genuinely contained appliances in all three states at once. An operator who applied the KB88098 workaround to a 21.08.0.1 appliance and recorded it as remediated has state (b) filed as state (a), and any gap in that workaround reopens a CVSS 9.8 pre-auth path on the SSO tier.

CVE-2022-22960.name: VMware Multiple Products Privilege Escalation Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: An attacker already running as the appliance's horizon service account writes into /opt/vmware/certproxy/bin/certproxyService.sh, then triggers it through a sudo-permitted support script — publishCaCert.hzn or gatherConfig.hzn — so the appliance runs the injected content as root and hands over the identity tier, including the ability to delete the evidence.
attack_vector.privileges_required: low — PR:L with AV:L; the attacker needs local code execution as horizon first, which in every case CISA documented came from chaining CVE-2022-22954 against the same appliance
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L; once the foothold exists the escalation is a file write plus a sudo call, with no race window, no grooming and no leak to defeat. The real constraint is obtaining the foothold, not performing the escalation.
attack_vector.ai_factor: Discovered by Steven Seeley (mr_me) of Qihoo 360 Vulnerability Research Institute by reviewing the shipped appliance's file permissions and sudo policy. Weaponisation was equally conventional: a Metasploit local module by jheysel-r7 and two public Python scripts that run the CVE-2022-22954 to CVE-2022-22960 chain end to end.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Patching both halves of VMSA-2022-0011 in the same change on 2022-04-06 — the escalation alongside the pre-auth RCE — rather than sequencing the local 7.8 behind the remote 9.8.
prevention.adequacy: The directive's 2022-05-06 due date fell more than three weeks after the observed 2022-04-12 chaining, and BOD 22-01 treats the two CVEs as independent items with independent clocks, which is exactly the framing that lets an operator close one and defer the other. The patch also cannot tell an operator whether certproxyService.sh was already written to before it landed.

detection.what_would_have_worked: File-integrity monitoring on /opt/vmware/certproxy/bin/certproxyService.sh and the /usr/local/horizon/scripts directory, with alerting on any sudo invocation of a .hzn script by uid 1001, shipped off the appliance in real time.
detection.adequacy: The window between the write and the sudo call is seconds, so an alert that lands anywhere other than an external collector is racing the root shell that will delete it. CISA's victims lost localhost_access, Horizon application and greenbox logs for the day of the intrusion, which is the practical demonstration that on-appliance detection does not survive this CVE.

response.what_would_have_worked: Rebuilding the appliance from a vendor image and rotating every secret it held — appliance master keys, directory bind accounts and any credential recoverable from /usr/local/horizon/conf — rather than patching in place.
response.adequacy: Nothing obliges this, and the cost of rebuilding the SSO tier makes it a decision that gets argued rather than executed unless it is pre-authorised. It is also the only response that addresses what the attacker actually took: CISA's samples archived passwords, master keys and firewall rules, and a patch changes none of those values.

NIST-800-53-AC-6.gap: The appliance already implements the least-privilege pattern AC-6 asks for by running its web tier as horizon rather than root, so the control reads as satisfied. The vendor's own sudoers entries for publishCaCert.hzn and gatherConfig.hzn then hand that unprivileged account a root path, and an AC-6 review scoped to operator-created accounts never inspects them. Least privilege that the product undoes internally is a control the operator cannot exercise.

NIST-800-53-AU-9.gap: AU-9 depends on the audit record being outside the reach of the account under investigation, and this CVE's entire yield is that account becoming root on the machine holding the record. CISA observed the deletion of localhost_access, Horizon application and greenbox logs for 2022-04-12 along with the .pem-overwrite cleanup of publishCaCert.hzn. On-appliance permissions cannot protect logs from a defect whose output is the privilege that overrides them.

NIS2-Art21-patch-management.gap: Patch management under Article 21 is satisfied by tracking VMSA-2022-0011 to closure, and it treats each CVE as an independently scheduled item. Because the local 7.8 scores lower than the remote 9.8 published in the same advisory, ordinary triage puts them in different windows — and the two were used together on 2022-04-12. The obligation has no notion of a documented chain whose links must be closed in one change.

UK-CAF-B2.gap: B2 governs identity and access control for the accounts the organisation issues and reviews, and this escalation uses none of them. The attacker holds a vendor-created service identity and traverses a vendor-authored sudo rule, so the recertification, joiner-mover-leaver and privileged-access evidence a B2 assessment collects is all true and all irrelevant. There is no B2 question that would surface a writable script reachable through sudo inside a purchased appliance image.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: Patch applications sets the clock and this CVE meets it, but the maturity model ranks by exposure and severity, which places a local AV:L/PR:L escalation behind the internet-facing CVSS 9.8 in the same advisory. Sequencing the two that way reproduces the exact appliance state the actors used on 2022-04-12. The control also ends at the version number and never asks whether certproxyService.sh matches the vendor image after the update.

ISO-27001-2022-A.5.15.gap: A.5.15 asks the organisation to define access-control rules from its own business and security requirements, and the rules that fail here were written by VMware and shipped inside the appliance image. A documented, approved access-control policy covering appliance administrators can be complete and correct while the horizon service account retains an undocumented sudo path to root. The clause has no mechanism for auditing rules the operator did not author and cannot change.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.15.gap: Logging under A.8.15 was in place and working — the appliance recorded the 2022-04-12 activity in localhost_access, the Horizon application logs and greenbox_web.log before the actor removed all three. Because the clause is satisfied by producing, storing and reviewing logs without requiring that storage be outside the monitored host, the entire trail sat inside the blast radius of the escalation. A review process pointed at a log the attacker has already rewritten reports a clean appliance.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: VMware shipped this fix with the rest of VMSA-2022-0011 on 2022-04-06 and CISA listed it on 2022-04-15 with a 2022-05-06 due date, while the chained exploitation CISA investigated occurred on 2022-04-12. A four-hour clock measured from patch availability is also what removes the sequencing failure specific to this entry, because it forbids treating the local 7.8 escalation as a later item than the 9.8 remote RCE published beside it on the same appliance.

new_control_requirements.name: FIREWALL-EGRESS-TELEMETRY-SEPARATE-TRUST-ZONE
new_control_requirements.description: Firewall and other perimeter-trust-boundary devices must forward syslog, threat logs, and authentication logs to a SIEM hosted in a separate trust zone (different management plane, different credentials, different authentication path). Telemetry stored on the compromised device is destroyed by the attacker; telemetry on a separate-trust-zone collector survives.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Workspace ONE Access is an internet-published trust-boundary asset in exactly the sense this control governs — it is the authentication decision point for the estate — and this CVE's output is root on it. CISA recorded the actor deleting localhost_access, Horizon application and greenbox logs for 2022-04-12 and overwriting publishCaCert.hzn with fd86ald0.pem to hide the escalation itself. Only appliance logs already forwarded to a collector with separate credentials would have survived, and greenbox_web.log is the specific artefact that had to be off-box to be readable afterwards.

CVE-2022-22965.name: Spring Framework JDK 9+ Remote Code Execution Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: An unauthenticated request names object properties that Spring's data binder walks, reaching the class loader through class.module.classLoader — a path the JDK 9 module system opened and Spring's denylist did not cover. On a WAR deployment under Tomcat that reaches the AccessLogValve, and reconfiguring the valve makes the access log itself into a JSP web shell in webapps/ROOT.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none — PR:N; data binding runs before any authorisation decision the controller would make, so any reachable endpoint that binds to a POJO is an entry point
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L for the request, but reachability is the real gate: JDK 9 or later, a standalone servlet container, WAR packaging, spring-webmvc or spring-webflux, and a writable webapps directory. The vendor names Tomcat, Payara and GlassFish as known vulnerable and other containers as possibly so. Spring Boot executable jars are not exploitable by the published chain, and the vendor still warns the underlying defect is more general than that chain.
attack_vector.ai_factor: Reported by codeplutos and meizjm3i of AntGroup FG Security Lab, with a secondary report from Praetorian — human analysis of an existing denylist against a newly available property path. Weaponisation was human and fast: public exploits and a Mirai campaign both appeared within about a week of the 2022-03-31 disclosure.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: A build-time component inventory of every deployed Java artefact, so that on 2022-03-31 the operator could list which WARs carried spring-webmvc below 5.3.18 and which of those ran on a standalone servlet container — Tomcat, Payara or GlassFish — under JDK 9 or later, then rebuild and redeploy those first.
prevention.adequacy: BOD 22-01 sets a 2022-04-25 due date and says nothing about how to find the affected artefacts, which was the entire difficulty. For applications supplied as prebuilt WARs the operator cannot remediate at all until the third party ships a rebuild, so the directive's clock runs against an action outside the operator's control.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Alerting on any request parameter whose name begins class. at the reverse proxy or WAF, and file-integrity monitoring on webapps/ROOT that flags a .jsp appearing outside a deployment.
detection.adequacy: The parameter-name signal is high fidelity and was published as a WAF denylist within days, so it is genuinely usable — but only in front of applications the operator knows are Spring, which is the same inventory problem the prevention side has. The webapps/ROOT check is reliable and late: by the time the JSP exists the attacker already has code execution and only needs one more request.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treating any Tomcat host with an unexplained JSP in webapps/ROOT as compromised — capturing the file, hunting for the /tmp download-and-chmod pattern, and rebuilding the host rather than deleting the shell.
response.adequacy: The observed Mirai payloads deleted themselves from disk after execution, so a host examined after the fact may show only the JSP and a running process. Removing the web shell and redeploying a fixed WAR leaves anything the attacker installed in the interim, and gives no account of what the Tomcat identity could reach on the internal network.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: SI-2 is satisfied by tracking the Spring advisory and recording corrective action, and the corrective action it envisages is installing a vendor update. Here it is a dependency bump to 5.3.18 or 5.2.20 followed by a rebuild and redeploy of every artefact, which stalls completely for any WAR whose build pipeline is gone or whose supplier never ships a rebuild. The control also accepts an updated manifest as evidence, while the vulnerable bytecode keeps serving until the container restarts.

NIST-800-53-SR-3.gap: SR-3 supply-chain controls are assessed against supplier agreements and acceptance processes, and Spring Framework entered nearly every affected estate transitively with no supplier to hold an agreement with. Complete SR-3 evidence for every contracted vendor is compatible with total ignorance of which deployed WARs contain spring-webmvc below 5.3.18. The control governs the relationship, not the component graph, and only the component graph answers this CVE.

NIS2-Art21-supply-chain.gap: The Article 21 supply-chain measure asks about the security of direct suppliers and the quality of their products and services, and produces supplier questionnaires and contractual security requirements. Spring is an upstream open-source project outside every such relationship, and the entity's exposure sat inside artefacts its suppliers built. Assessing suppliers does not enumerate what those suppliers embedded, so a fully compliant supply-chain measure leaves the operator unable to scope the 2022-03-31 disclosure.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: B4 evidence describes configuration baselines and update posture for systems the operator manages, and none of it records the conditions that make this CVE exploitable: WAR packaging, a standalone servlet container, JDK 9 or later, and a writable webapps directory. An operator assessed as adequate under B4 can still be unable to name which applications meet them, or which container each runs on — and the container matters, since Spring names Payara and GlassFish vulnerable alongside Tomcat. Worse, the principle offers nowhere to record the vendor's own caveat that the defect is more general than the published chain, so a Spring Boot fat-jar estate records itself as out of scope without testing that belief.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: Patch applications drives an aggressive clock once an exploit exists, and public exploits existed from 2022-03-31, so the maturity target here was measured in days. The control's unit of work is applying a vendor update to an application, and the work this CVE requires is a transitive dependency bump plus a rebuild plus a redeploy across the whole Java estate. For a prebuilt third-party WAR the operator has one real lever while waiting on the supplier — Spring's 2022-04-01 Mitigation Alternative, upgrading Tomcat to 10.0.20, 9.0.62 or 8.5.78 — and the mitigation as written has no way to credit a container upgrade as remediation of an application flaw, nor any equivalent to offer where the container is Payara or GlassFish.

ISO-27001-2022-A.5.21.gap: A.5.21 requires processes managing ICT supply-chain risk, implemented as supplier requirements, agreements and monitoring. Because Spring arrives transitively and free, there is no agreement into which a version requirement could have been written and no supplier to monitor. The clause is therefore fully satisfiable while producing none of the component-level inventory that scoping this CVE needed on 2022-03-31.

OWASP-Top-10-2021-A06.gap: A06 names vulnerable and outdated components as the risk and prescribes inventory plus continuous monitoring, which is the correct instruction. Its precondition is that the deployed artefacts have a readable bill of materials, and in the estates hurt by this CVE the deployed WARs had neither an inventory nor a reproducible build to derive one from. The guidance identifies the right control and offers nothing that works on an artefact whose composition was never captured.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Spring published 5.3.18 and 5.2.20 on 2022-03-31, CISA listed the CVE on 2022-04-04 with a 2022-04-25 due date, and Trend Micro observed Mirai being installed through it at the start of April 2022 — inside the directive's window. The control's explicit allowance for documented compensating controls is what makes it usable here, because the WAF denylist on class.* parameter names could be deployed in hours while the rebuild-and-redeploy of every affected WAR could not.

new_control_requirements.name: TIER-3-DEPENDENCY-INVENTORY
new_control_requirements.description: Supply chain inventory must extend to tier-3 dependencies (dependencies of dependencies of direct dependencies). SBOM coverage for libsystemd-class transitive dependencies cannot be omitted under SR-3.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Spring Framework is the Java-side instance of exactly this problem: on 2022-03-31 the question every operator had to answer was which deployed WARs carried spring-webmvc or spring-webflux below 5.3.18 or 5.2.20, and in most estates that framework was a transitive dependency of a vendor artefact rather than a chosen one. Without a component inventory reaching that depth an operator cannot scope the CVE, cannot tell which applications also meet the JDK 9 plus standalone-container plus WAR preconditions, and cannot prove remediation once the rebuild is done.

CVE-2022-23176.name: WatchGuard Firebox and XTM Privilege Escalation Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: A caller holding credentials for an unprivileged Firebox or XTM account reaches the appliance's management surface and receives a privileged management session instead of one scoped to the account's role, taking control of the device that terminates the organisation's VPNs and enforces its rule base.
attack_vector.privileges_required: low — PR:L; the attacker needs a working unprivileged appliance credential, not an administrative one, and the appliance grants the privilege the account does not hold
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L; no race and no memory corruption. The binding constraint is reachability: the exploit needs the management interface exposed, and AA22-054A states only devices reconfigured away from manufacturer defaults to open remote management externally were infected.
attack_vector.ai_factor: No finder is publicly credited — WGSA-2021-00004 carries no credit line and the MITRE record's credits array is empty. Exploitation is attributed by the vendor to Sandworm, a state intelligence service, and AA22-054A describes Cyclops Blink as a hand-built modular framework deployed since at least June 2019; nothing indicates AI involvement in either discovery or weaponisation.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Keeping the Fireware management interfaces unreachable from the internet — the manufacturer-default posture — so that no external caller could present an unprivileged credential to them, and upgrading to 12.7.2_U1 or the matching branch build once WatchGuard shipped it.
prevention.adequacy: The directive's clock started on 2022-04-11 with a 2022-05-02 due date, while WatchGuard had published the advisory on 2021-12-30 and Sandworm had been deploying Cyclops Blink since at least June 2019 — the compliance window opened years after the exposure. Restricting management access prevents this exploit and does nothing for a device already implanted, since the implant persists through firmware.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Forwarding Firebox authentication and management logs to an external collector and alerting on an unprivileged account performing configuration operations, plus alerting on any firmware change not tied to an administrator's change record.
detection.adequacy: Both signals are only usable if the telemetry already left the appliance, because a privileged management session controls what the device retains. Firmware-change alerting is the higher-value half given that Cyclops Blink installs as a firmware update, but very few estates baseline appliance firmware hashes, so the change looks like an ordinary vendor update.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treating any externally reachable Firebox as suspect and running WatchGuard's Cyclops Blink diagnostic and remediation procedure, then rotating every credential, certificate, pre-shared key and VPN secret the appliance held before returning it to service.
response.adequacy: This is expensive and disruptive on the device that carries the organisation's remote access, so it will not happen on suspicion unless the decision is pre-authorised. It is also the only response matched to the threat: an implant deployed as firmware survives reboot and survives an upgrade that does not follow the vendor's full procedure, and the appliance's stored secrets stay valid until rotated.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: SI-2 closes on the Fireware upgrade to 12.7.2_U1 or the branch equivalent, which is the correct action and an incomplete one. Because AA22-054A records Cyclops Blink installing itself as a firmware update to survive reboot, a device that was externally reachable before the fix can be current and still implanted, and SI-2 has no state that expresses that. It also has nothing to say about a hardware revision with no fixed build, where the remediation is replacement rather than an update.

NIST-800-53-SC-7.gap: SC-7 is assessed on what the boundary device permits through it, and the Firebox will be presented as the evidence that boundary protection exists. The reachability that mattered was inbound to the appliance's own management plane, which is a different question the control does not ask. An estate can hold a well-documented, well-tested SC-7 posture and still meet the precondition AA22-054A names for infection.

NIST-800-53-AU-9.gap: AU-9 protects audit information through permissions and separation on the system that generates it, and this CVE hands the attacker a privileged management session on exactly that system. With Cyclops Blink persisting as firmware and beaconing over individually keyed TLS, the record of appliance activity sits inside the adversary's control from the first session. Local retention satisfies the control and leaves an investigator with no independent account of what the device did.

NIS2-Art21-network-security.gap: An entity demonstrating this measure will point at the Firebox as the network-security control, which is precisely the inversion this CVE exploits — the appliance is the target, and a privileged session on it is a position on the trust boundary of everything behind it. The measure carries no requirement that the security appliance's own management plane be treated as a protected asset with restricted reachability. That gap is the specific condition the joint advisory identifies as making infection possible.

NIS2-Art21-incident-handling.gap: Incident handling is scoped to detecting, containing and recovering from a bounded event, and Cyclops Blink has been deployed to WatchGuard devices since at least June 2019 by a GRU-attributed actor. Containment for a firmware-resident implant means the vendor's full remediation procedure and wholesale secret rotation, not isolation and cleanup. The measure also has no escalation trigger that distinguishes a state-actor foothold on a perimeter device from a commodity infection, so it is handled at the wrong tier.

UK-CAF-D1.gap: D1 asks for response and recovery plans that are documented, tested and adequate for the systems in scope, and most such plans for a firewall describe failover and configuration restore. Neither addresses recovering an appliance a state actor implanted through the firmware update path, where the config restore may carry the compromise forward and every stored VPN secret must be treated as disclosed. A tested plan that ends at restoring the last known-good configuration satisfies D1 and reinstates the adversary's access.

AU-ISM-1546.gap: The control requires users to authenticate before being granted access, and every step of this attack complies: the caller presents a real Firebox credential and is authenticated. The defect is in what the appliance grants afterwards, mapping an unprivileged identity onto a privileged management session, which is an authorisation decision no authentication control inspects. Evidence that all Firebox accounts authenticate correctly is true and does not touch the flaw.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: Patching drives the Fireware upgrade and measures completion by installed version, which misreads this appliance family in two ways. A unit that has staged 12.7.2_U1 but not restarted is still executing the vulnerable build while reporting the fixed version, and a unit that was externally reachable beforehand may carry a firmware-resident implant the upgrade does not remove. The control also tends to be scoped to current T-series and M-series hardware, leaving T15, T35 and the legacy XTM line off the report entirely.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.22.gap: A.8.22 requires groups of services, users and information systems to be segregated on the network, and it is normally evidenced by the segmentation this very appliance enforces. The segregation that would have prevented this CVE is around the Firebox's own management interfaces, deciding which segments may reach them at all — a control rarely applied to the device performing the segregation. AA22-054A's finding that only externally reachable management interfaces were infected makes this the decisive control and the one the clause is least likely to direct at the appliance.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: WatchGuard published WGSA-2021-00004 with fixed Fireware builds on 2021-12-30 and CISA listed the CVE on 2022-04-11 with a 2022-05-02 due date, more than three months later, against an actor that had been deploying Cyclops Blink to these appliances since at least June 2019. The control's compensating-control clause is what makes it actionable on this device family, because restricting management access to trusted networks — WatchGuard's own interim guidance — can be done in minutes on every Firebox and XTM unit while firmware upgrades and their restarts are scheduled.

new_control_requirements.name: FIREWALL-EGRESS-TELEMETRY-SEPARATE-TRUST-ZONE
new_control_requirements.description: Firewall and other perimeter-trust-boundary devices must forward syslog, threat logs, and authentication logs to a SIEM hosted in a separate trust zone (different management plane, different credentials, different authentication path). Telemetry stored on the compromised device is destroyed by the attacker; telemetry on a separate-trust-zone collector survives.
new_control_requirements.evidence: This is a Firebox and XTM firewall and the CVE's whole output is a privileged management session on it, so every authentication event and configuration change relevant to detecting the abuse is generated on the device the attacker now controls. AA22-054A records Cyclops Blink persisting through a firmware update and beaconing over individually keyed TLS, meaning the exposure spans reboots and firmware changes — only appliance authentication and management logs already forwarded to a collector with separate credentials give an investigator any record of when an unprivileged account first received privileged rights.

new_control_requirements.name: NATION-STATE-INITIAL-ACCESS-IR-ESCALATION
new_control_requirements.description: IR runbooks must include an explicit nation-state-initial-access escalation path triggered by APT28/APT29/Lazarus/Volt-Typhoon/etc. attribution on a confirmed exploit chain. Standard malware-infection IR under-escalates nation-state activity by treating it as commodity threat.
new_control_requirements.evidence: WatchGuard's own advisory for this CVE attributes exploitation to Sandworm, which the NCSC, CISA, NSA and FBI attribute to the Russian GRU's Main Centre for Special Technologies in AA22-054A, and the payload is a modular implant deployed as a firmware update on the organisation's perimeter device. Handling that as a routine appliance-malware event produces a firmware upgrade and a closed ticket, whereas the attribution should force secret rotation across every VPN and certificate the Firebox held, the vendor's full diagnostic path, and an exposure window measured from June 2019 rather than from the 2022-04-11 KEV listing.

CVE-2022-24521.name: Microsoft Windows CLFS Driver Privilege Escalation Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: A standard user hands the Common Log File System driver a malformed Base Log File whose container metadata is trusted as an offset, corrupting the pContainer field into a controlled kernel write; the exploit grooms the pool with named-pipe attributes so the write lands where it wants, then steals the SYSTEM token and keeps executing as SYSTEM.
attack_vector.privileges_required: low — PR:L with AV:L; any local execution context will do, including an ordinary interactive session or a service account, and no group membership or user interaction is required
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L; the exploitation work is heap grooming rather than winning a race, which makes it repeatable rather than probabilistic. Public source targets specific builds, but the primitive spans every Windows SKU Microsoft was servicing in April 2022.
attack_vector.ai_factor: Credited by Microsoft to Adam Podlosky and Amir Bazine of CrowdStrike and to the National Security Agency — human reverse engineering of a driver already under attack, consistent with Microsoft recording the CVE as not publicly disclosed but exploited at publication. CrowdStrike's platform-level AI branding says nothing about how these researchers found this bug.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Installing the April 2022 cumulative update for each SKU and restarting the host, prioritised by whether non-administrative users hold interactive sessions on it, so that multi-user hosts reached the fixed build first.
prevention.adequacy: The directive's 2022-05-04 due date sits before Unit 42's early-May Cuba observations, so a compliant federal estate was ahead of that campaign — but only if the reboot happened, and BOD compliance is normally evidenced by update deployment rather than by running build.
