new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Rails shipped 3.2.18, 4.0.5 and 4.1.1 on 2014-05-06, so by the 2022-03-25 KEV listing and its 2022-04-15 due date the patch had been available for nearly eight years. This CVE also gives the control its cheapest possible compensating branch: the vendor's own routing workaround removes exposure with a one-line routes.rb change, which is deployable inside the four-hour window on estates where a framework upgrade is not.

attack_vector.description: A search engine ships with server-side scripting enabled by default and no authentication on its REST API. A search request carrying a script in its body is evaluated inside the engine's JVM with access to Java runtime facilities, so the request executes operating-system commands and returns their output as search results.
attack_vector.privileges_required: low — PR:L as scored, but no credential is defeated: Elasticsearch 1.x has no authentication, and the scoring reflects the vendor's position that the default is only a policy violation on a node not isolated in its own virtual machine.
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L; a single POST to /_search. The only real requirement is a network route to port 9200.
attack_vector.ai_factor: None. Public research on a documented scripting feature, credited in the Metasploit module to Alex Brasetvik and Bouke van der Bijl, with write-ups NVD tags as Exploit references.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Disabling dynamic scripting on the running nodes immediately, and upgrading to Elasticsearch 1.2.0 or later where it is off by default — plus Logstash 1.4.3 wherever the affected engine is embedded.
prevention.adequacy: The configuration change is genuinely immediate and does not wait for a cluster upgrade, which makes it the stronger half in the short term. It has to be applied per node and survives no rebuild — a node reimaged from an old template comes back with the vulnerable default, and the setting is invisible to any inventory keyed to product version.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Alerting whenever the Elasticsearch JVM spawns a child process, and inspecting search bodies for script elements originating outside the application's own query builders.
detection.adequacy: Process-spawn alerting on a search engine is close to zero-noise and catches execution regardless of the script language used, so it survives payload variation the body inspection would miss. It reports after code has already run, and it depends on host telemetry being collected from the data nodes themselves — where those hosts are exempted from endpoint agents, the rule has no input and the search-body inspection is all that remains.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treating a confirmed hit as compromise of the host and of everything the cluster indexed, then rebuilding the node and rotating any credential the Elasticsearch process could read.
response.adequacy: Upgrading past 1.2.0 removes the path and nothing else — it does not evict a persistence mechanism installed through it, and it does not revalue the indexed data already read out. Where the cluster held application logs, the exposure includes whatever those logs captured.

NIST-800-53-CM-7.gap: CM-7 evidence is generated by comparing systems to an approved baseline and investigating deviations. For Elasticsearch before 1.2.0 the exploitable state is the vendor default, so there is no deviation to investigate and no operator decision to review; the node is compliant with its own approved build while it evaluates attacker-supplied MVEL from an unauthenticated request.

NIST-800-53-SC-7.gap: Boundary protection was doing the entire job, which is the problem. Elastic's stated policy makes running the node in its own virtual machine the security assumption, so SC-7 is not defence in depth here but the sole control, and the moment any host inside the permitted segment is compromised, a fully SC-7-compliant architecture provides no barrier at all to code execution on the search tier.

NIS2-Art21-network-security.gap: Network-security measures are documented and implemented, and on this product they are load-bearing in a way the article does not anticipate. Elasticsearch 1.x authenticates nobody, so reachability is the entire access-control model and the network measure is not one layer among several — an entity that has fully implemented Article 21 network security has implemented the only thing standing between a routable client and command execution.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: The B4 assessment compares the deployment against a secure baseline, and no vendor-supplied hardened baseline exists for Elasticsearch 1.x — the scripting default is on, and turning it off is documented as a workaround. An assessor can verify the node matches its approved configuration, record B4 as adequate, and have verified only that the vulnerable default was faithfully reproduced.

AU-Essential-8-App-Hardening.gap: The control's scope is user applications processing untrusted content on endpoints, and every measure at every maturity level targets browsers, Office, PDF readers, Java and web advertising. A server-side datastore that compiles and runs MVEL and Java from request bodies is not in that scope, so the maturity rating can be at its highest while the estate's search tier executes untrusted code by design.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: Currency reporting against Elasticsearch 1.2.0 answers the question for clusters the operator installed. It does not answer it for Logstash 1.4.2, whose bundled Elasticsearch 1.1.1 is affected and whose remediation is Logstash 1.4.3 — a different product, a different version number, and a row that reads current on any patch dashboard scoped to installed applications.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.9.gap: Configuration management detects and corrects drift from a documented state. Because dynamic scripting was never enabled by an operator, no configuration record contains it, and the documented state and the exploitable state coincide exactly — so continuous configuration monitoring reports full conformance for as long as the node runs a pre-1.2.0 build, and the one setting worth monitoring is the one nobody wrote down.

new_control_requirements.name: DATABASE-SERVER-SIDE-SCRIPTING-DEFAULT-DENY
new_control_requirements.description: In-memory and document datastores must ship with server-side scripting disabled by default; re-enabling requires documented threat-model acceptance.
new_control_requirements.evidence: This CVE is the case the control names. Elasticsearch is the document datastore, dynamic scripting was on in the default configuration of every release before 1.2.0, and NVD's own summary attributes the flaw to 'the default configuration' rather than to any operator action. Elastic's remediation was to invert the default — from 1.2.0 scripting is off, and Elastic describes the Elasticsearch 1.5.2 shipped in Logstash 1.4.3 as one that 'by default disables the ability to run scripts'. The control is the vendor behaviour that closed it, stated as a requirement.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Elasticsearch 1.2.0 predates the 2022-03-25 KEV listing and its 2022-04-15 due date by years, so the clock here is about finding the stragglers rather than waiting on a vendor. The control's compensating-control branch matters on this product because a cluster upgrade is a rolling restart with shard reallocation: disabling dynamic scripting on the running nodes is deployable inside a four-hour window, and the version upgrade follows on a maintenance schedule.

CVE-2014-6287.name: Rejetto HTTP File Server (HFS) Remote Code Execution Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: A file server's macro parser finds macro markers with a regular expression that does not handle null bytes. Prefixing a marker with a null byte in the search parameter smuggles it past the filter, and because the macro language can write files and launch programs, an unauthenticated request becomes command execution as the server's user.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none — PR:N; the search endpoint is reached without presenting a credential, and CERT/CC VU#251276 records the flaw as remote, unauthenticated command execution.
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L; one GET request, no groom and no chain. CERT/CC's own note publishes a working example.
attack_vector.ai_factor: None. Disclosed on Bugtraq on 2014-09-11 with exploit code following four days later; the finding is manual inspection of a parser's regular expression.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Updating to HFS 2.3c and restarting the process; better, not running an unauthenticated file server on a workstation at all, enforced by application allowlisting that covers binaries run from user-writable paths.
prevention.adequacy: 2.3c is a real fix and trivially applied once a copy is found, which is the whole difficulty — HFS needs no installation, so the update cannot be pushed by any management console and the copy has to be located first. Allowlisting is the stronger control precisely because it does not require knowing the binary is there.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Alerting on the HFS process spawning any child process, and matching request logs for a null byte followed by a macro marker in the search parameter.
detection.adequacy: The process-spawn rule is the durable one: a file server has no legitimate child processes, so it holds regardless of which macro the attacker chooses. Request-log matching depends on HFS's own logs surviving on a host the attacker now controls, and the repeated launches from a single attempt mean one compromise can look like several.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treating the host as compromised at the privilege the HFS process held, removing the dropped script from the temporary directory, and rotating credentials that were used on or reachable from that machine.
response.adequacy: Updating to 2.3c closes the entry path and removes nothing already executed. Because the payload arrives as a script in a temporary directory and runs through a signed Windows interpreter, there is no unusual binary for signature-based tooling to find afterwards.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: The flaw-remediation process is intact and has no input for this product. CERT/CC records receiving no vendor statement, and version 2.3c was published as a download without a security bulletin, so an SI-2 programme consuming vendor advisories sees nothing for HFS at any point between the 2014 disclosure and the 2022-03-25 KEV listing, whatever its coverage of every vendor that does publish.

NIST-800-53-CM-7.gap: Least-functionality evidence is generated against installed software and enabled services, and those are the two lists an HFS process started from a user directory does not appear on. An estate can hold a well-evidenced CM-7 posture, produce a complete installed-programs report and a complete service inventory, and have neither document mention the unauthenticated file server listening on a workstation — the control is satisfied by the artefacts it defines, which do not reach this software.

NIS2-Art21-patch-management.gap: The measure is implemented and its coverage metric is computed over the managed inventory, which is exactly where these instances are absent. An HFS 2.3b binary left running after a one-off file transfer is not a patching failure in the process's own terms — it is invisible to it — so patch-compliance reporting can be complete and accurate while a CVSS 9.8 pre-auth path stays open on the estate.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: B4 is scoped to systems supporting essential functions, and HFS is ancillary software that supports nothing — which is precisely why it is out of scope and precisely why it is dangerous. Code execution on the workstation running it is a foothold inside the assessed boundary, so an accurate scoping decision under B4 produces an assessment that never examines the host the attacker actually enters through.

AU-Essential-8-App-Hardening.gap: Every measure in this control governs how deployed user applications handle content arriving from elsewhere. HFS is the opposite arrangement — it accepts requests from anyone who can reach it, and the vulnerable parser is its own macro engine — so an estate at a high maturity level has hardened the applications that consume content and applied nothing to the one that serves it.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: Vulnerability information for this CVE is abundant and high quality: a CERT/CC note carrying a working example, an EPSS score of 0.99323 at the 99.936th percentile as of 2026-08-17, and a KEV entry. A.8.8 still fails because its object is systems 'in use', and an unmanaged portable binary running on one workstation is not a system the organisation has recorded as in use — so exposure evaluation has nothing to evaluate.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: HFS 2.3c has been available since 2014 and CISA listed the CVE on 2022-03-25 with a 2022-04-15 due date, so the four-hour clock runs from the listing. On this product the 'documented compensating controls' branch is the one an operator can actually execute inside that window: locating every unmanaged HFS 2.3-series binary takes longer than four hours, whereas blocking its listening port and removing unsanctioned copies does not, and the EPSS score of 0.99323 makes the deferral cost concrete.

new_control_requirements.name: CVE-REGRESSION-WATCHER
new_control_requirements.description: Threat-intake pipelines must surface PoC announcements that reference historical CVE IDs (CVE-YYYY-NNN where YYYY <= current_year - 2) as candidate silent-regression cases. The historical-CVE-in-PoC-text class would have caught MiniPlasma's re-regression at T+0 — the original CVE-2020-17103 is cited in every news writeup but no advisory feed surfaces 'CVE-2020 references appearing in 2026 PoCs'.
new_control_requirements.evidence: HFS produces exactly the signal this control watches for. New standalone exploit code for a 2014 flaw kept being published years after 2.3c shipped: Exploit-DB 39161 on 2016-01-04 and 49125 on 2020-11-30, alongside a maintained Nuclei template still carrying the id. Since CERT/CC received no vendor statement and Rejetto publishes no advisory feed, that recurring PoC traffic is the available early-warning channel for this product, and it ran for years before the 2022-03-25 KEV listing.

CVE-2014-6324.name: Microsoft Kerberos Key Distribution Center (KDC) Privilege Escalation Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: The authorisation data inside a Kerberos ticket is protected by a signature the KDC must verify. Microsoft's KDC accepted a signature that carried no real keyed integrity, so any domain user could rewrite their own ticket to claim domain-administrator group membership and have the KDC honour it.
attack_vector.privileges_required: low — PR:L; Microsoft's stated requirement is 'valid domain credentials' held by a 'standard user account'. Local-only accounts cannot reach the component.
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L; no race and no memory corruption, only ticket construction, which public tooling performs automatically. The practical constraint is reaching a KDC that has not been patched.
attack_vector.ai_factor: None. Microsoft records the report as arriving 'through coordinated vulnerability disclosure' from outside the company, and the public exploit work that followed is credited to named individual researchers.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Applying MS14-068 / KB 3011780 to every domain controller acting as a KDC and rebooting each one, then verifying that no KDC anywhere in the domain was missed.
prevention.adequacy: This is the only prevention that exists — Microsoft states it 'has not identified any workarounds for this vulnerability', so there is nothing to fall back on for an unpatched DC. Its adequacy is all-or-nothing across the domain rather than proportional: one unpatched KDC leaves the domain fully exploitable no matter how many others were done.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Comparing the group memberships asserted in issued Kerberos tickets against the memberships Active Directory actually records, and alerting when an ordinary account begins exercising domain-administrator authority.
detection.adequacy: The directory-versus-ticket comparison is decisive because the two cannot legitimately disagree. It requires ticket-level telemetry to have been collected and retained before the attempt, which is a precondition rather than something that can be arranged afterwards; and privilege-use alerting on its own fires only once the attacker acts, which on a domain-administrator forgery is already past the point of containment.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treating a confirmed forgery as full domain compromise: rebuilding trust from the top, rotating the krbtgt account key twice so previously issued tickets cannot be revalidated, and reviewing every change made during the exposure window.
response.adequacy: Patching the KDC stops new forgeries and does not invalidate authority already obtained or persistence already established. Where an attacker held domain-administrator rights, no scoped remediation is credible — the recovery unit is the domain, not the affected host.

NIST-800-53-IA-2.gap: IA-2 evidence shows every domain user uniquely identified and strongly authenticated, and all of it is true during this attack. The attacker logs on as themselves with their own credentials; what is forged is the authorisation data the KDC returns afterwards, so the control operates entirely upstream of the defect and its assessment cannot distinguish an exploited domain from a healthy one.

NIST-800-53-AC-6.gap: An estate can demonstrate a rigorous least-privilege model — no standing administrative rights, tiered accounts, reviewed entitlements — and this flaw renders the whole model advisory. The privilege the attacker exercises is not one AC-6 ever granted or could revoke, because it is asserted in a forged PAC rather than held in the directory, so the control's effectiveness is unrelated to how well it is implemented.

NIS2-Art21-identity-management.gap: The identity-management measure produces exactly the artefacts it should: provisioning records, periodic access reviews, revocation procedures. None of them move during this attack, because no account is created, no membership is changed and no privileged credential is used. An entity can pass the review with complete documentation while any standard user in the domain can claim Domain Admins at will.

UK-CAF-B2.gap: B2 assessment rests on the organisation knowing who holds privileged access, evidenced from the directory. This flaw decouples that record from the privilege actually exercised, since authority is asserted in the ticket rather than granted in the directory. The assessor's evidence remains accurate about Active Directory and describes a control surface the attacker never touches.

AU-Essential-8-MFA.gap: MFA is genuinely effective at the step it governs and irrelevant to this one. The escalation begins after a successful authentication, and Microsoft's stated precondition is only that the attacker hold valid domain credentials for a standard user account — a condition an MFA-protected account satisfies. Maximum maturity on this control changes nothing about the outcome once any account exists.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: Patching operating systems is the correct remediation and the maturity model measures it in a way that misreports this CVE. Coverage is expressed as a proportion of the fleet patched within a window, whereas a domain with one unpatched KDC out of twenty is not 95 percent protected but wholly exploitable, so an organisation can meet its target maturity level and remain fully exposed.

ISO-27001-2022-A.5.15.gap: The access-control policy is defined from business requirements and implemented through Active Directory group membership, and both remain correct throughout. The failure is at the enforcement point: the KDC honours claimed membership over recorded membership, so the organisation's policy is properly documented, properly implemented and simply not what governs the access decision.

new_control_requirements.name: FLEET-CONTROL-PLANE-ADMIN-PRIVILEGE-TIER
new_control_requirements.description: Administrators of fleet-control-plane systems (MDM/UEM, EDR consoles, identity providers, container orchestrators, configuration management) must be classified as a distinct privilege tier above application admins, with: PAM-jumphost-only access, FIDO2 step-up per session, just-in-time elevation with approval workflow, separate identity from any other admin role, and dedicated PAW (privileged access workstation) hardware. Compliance frameworks must enumerate this tier explicitly rather than collapsing it into 'admin'.
new_control_requirements.evidence: A Windows domain controller acting as a KDC is the identity provider this control names, and MS14-068 shows what it means to treat that tier as ordinary: any standard domain account reaches domain-administrator authority over every domain-joined system, and Microsoft confirmed limited, targeted attacks were already under way when the bulletin published on 2014-11-18. The control's separation requirements are what keep an ordinary user account and the identity control plane from sharing a trust path in the first place.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: MS14-068 is the case where this control's compensating-control branch is unavailable by the vendor's own statement — Microsoft 'has not identified any workarounds' — so KB 3011780 and a reboot on every KDC is the entire mitigation set, against a KEV listing of 2022-03-25 with a 2022-04-15 due date. Verification has to be domain-wide rather than sampled, because a single unpatched Windows Server 2003 SP2 or 2008 SP2 domain controller keeps honouring the forged PAC for the whole domain.

CVE-2014-6332.name: Microsoft Windows Object Linking & Embedding (OLE) Automation Array Remote Code Execution Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: An operating-system automation library mishandles a size value when a script resizes an array, letting script read and write memory outside it. The public exploits use that to clear the flag that keeps the script engine in safe mode, turning a sandboxed page into a full scripting host running as the logged-on user.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none — PR:N; the attacker needs no account on the target, only for a page under their control to be rendered.
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L with UI:R; the corruption itself is deterministic and needs no groom or leak. The real constraint is Microsoft's: an attacker 'would have no way to force users to view the attacker-controlled content' and must rely on a link, a compromised site or a malicious advertisement.
attack_vector.ai_factor: None, and the attribution invites the confusion worth naming: the finder is IBM X-Force, a human security research organisation whose brand carries no AI claim, and neither Microsoft's bulletin nor the disclosure post describes any automated discovery.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Applying MS14-064 / update 3006226, rebooting, and relaunching browsers and every application that embeds the rendering engine. Microsoft identified no workaround for this CVE, so before the update the only lever was stopping untrusted content from being rendered at all.
prevention.adequacy: The update is a complete fix and its delivery has two failure modes worth planning for: a host that downloaded it but has not rebooted still runs the vulnerable library, and after the reboot a long-lived browser session started earlier keeps the old code mapped in its own process. Windows XP receives no fix at all, so for those units the terminal state is removal.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Alerting when a browser, or any application hosting the web-rendering control, spawns a child process — and extending that rule to the non-browser hosts of the same engine rather than to Internet Explorer alone.
detection.adequacy: Process-lineage alerting is the durable form because it keys on the outcome rather than on the exploit's script, which appeared in many variants across two years of published code. It fires after the sandbox has already been defeated, so it bounds dwell time rather than preventing execution, and it needs endpoint telemetry on ordinary user workstations.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treating the endpoint as compromised at the logged-on user's privilege: rotating that user's credentials and any secret reachable from their session, and reviewing what the account touched during the window.
response.adequacy: Patching removes the entry path and nothing installed through it. The scope of the credential rotation follows the account rather than the machine, so where the user held access to shared systems the response reaches those too — and Microsoft's least-privilege mitigating factor determines how far that goes.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: The remediation process ingests MS14-064 as a single item, and the bulletin carries two vulnerabilities whose exploitation status differed at publication: Microsoft had seen attacks against CVE-2014-6352 but none against CVE-2014-6332. Prioritisation driven by the bulletin rather than the CVE mis-sizes this flaw, and the workarounds an operator finds while reading it — the OLE packager Fix it, the EMET configuration — protect the other one.

NIST-800-53-AC-6.gap: Microsoft offers least privilege as the sole mitigating factor and words it as reduced impact, not prevention: users with fewer rights 'could be less impacted'. An estate running users as non-administrators is genuinely better off and still executes attacker code in the user's own context, with access to that user's data and sessions, so an AC-6 attestation cited as a compensating control claims more than the vendor did.

NIS2-Art21-patch-management.gap: Patch management is implemented per product, and this defect belongs to an operating-system library while the exposure belongs to every application that renders web content. An entity can evidence current patch levels for both its operating systems and its browsers and never ask the question that decides exposure — whether the host has taken update 3006226 and rebooted — because no product's version string answers it.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: B4 scoping follows the essential function, which concentrates assessment on servers and infrastructure. Microsoft places the risk elsewhere, on 'workstations or terminal servers' where Internet Explorer is used frequently, and a terminal server is the case where both scopes meet badly: it is in the essential-function estate and it renders untrusted content for many users at once, with one unpatched host exposing every session on it.

AU-Essential-8-App-Hardening.gap: The control's measures are specific — blocking web advertisements, Java from the internet, and named browser features — and the sink here is an operating-system automation library reachable from ordinary script, for which Microsoft records no disabling configuration. Advertisement blocking does remove one delivery route the bulletin names, so the control is not useless; it simply cannot close the path, and its maturity rating will not reflect that.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: Patch applications and patch operating systems are assessed independently, and the exploitable combination is a property of neither alone: a third-party browser or an HTML Compiler application reaching an unpatched OleAut32.dll. An estate can hit its target maturity level on both controls while no report anywhere pairs the embedding application with the library version it will call.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.7.gap: Malware protection is deployed, current and largely beside the point at the moment of compromise. The exploit is script in a page that a trusted process renders, and it defeats the sandbox by overwriting a safe-mode flag in memory, so nothing is written to disk for scanning until a later stage. The user-awareness half fares no better, since Microsoft names compromised legitimate sites and malicious advertisements as delivery routes where no judgement about the site is available to make.

new_control_requirements.name: BROWSER-MANAGED-UPDATE-NO-DEFERRAL
new_control_requirements.description: Enterprise update rings must not defer security-channel browser updates beyond 24h.
new_control_requirements.evidence: This CVE is the case that shows the deferral rule cannot be scoped to the browser's own update channel. The browser-reachable sink is OleAut32.dll and Microsoft shipped it as Windows update 3006226 on 2014-11-11, so the ring gating the fix is the operating-system ring, not a browser channel — an estate applying a no-deferral rule to browser updates alone leaves the exploitable code in place. The window is not theoretical: public exploit code appeared two days after the bulletin, and Microsoft identified no workaround to hold the gap.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Update 3006226 has been available since 2014-11-11 and CISA listed the CVE on 2022-03-25 with a 2022-04-15 due date, so the clock runs from the listing. Verification is the demanding part on this one: Microsoft names no workaround, so 'deployed' means the host took the update and rebooted, and the affected population is every supported Windows edition of the era plus any application embedding the rendering engine — with Windows XP units, which receive no fix, resolvable only by removal.

CVE-2015-0666.name: Cisco Prime Data Center Network Manager (DCNM) Directory Traversal Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: An unauthenticated caller sends a crafted pathname to the fmserver servlet on the DCNM web interface and receives the contents of a file outside the served tree, read with the privileges of the DCNM service account. On a fabric management server that account is SYSTEM or root, so the reachable material includes the credentials and configuration for every managed switch.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none - PR:N, and UI:N as well: no operator has to click anything and no DCNM account is needed at any point
attack_vector.complexity: low - AC:L; a single request with no race, no memory grooming and no chained bug. The one real constraint is network reachability of the DCNM web listener, which is why Cisco's statement that no workaround exists is the operative fact below 7.1(1).
attack_vector.ai_factor: None. Reported by Andrea Micalizzi through HP's Zero Day Initiative per the Cisco advisory; a human coordinated-disclosure finding with no automated-discovery claim anywhere in the record.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Upgrading to DCNM 7.1(1) or later; failing that, restricting the DCNM web listener so only operator jump hosts can reach it.
prevention.adequacy: The upgrade is complete prevention. Reachability restriction is not - it shrinks the population that can send the request but leaves the servlet exploitable to anything inside the permitted segment, and Cisco offers nothing configuration-side that changes the servlet's behaviour.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Alerting on traversal sequences in requests to the DCNM web tier, and on file-content responses to sessions that never authenticated.
detection.adequacy: Workable because the request is unauthenticated and structurally odd, but it depends on the DCNM web logs being shipped off the host and parsed; where that management application is not an onboarded log source, a read leaves no other artefact on the server to find.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treating every credential and key readable by the DCNM service account as disclosed for the exposure window, and rotating switch and SNMP credentials rather than closing the ticket on the upgrade.
response.adequacy: Rotation is the only response that reaches the actual loss, since the primitive is a read and the upgrade cannot un-read anything. Its limit is scope: without web-tier logs the exposure window is unbounded, so the rotation has to cover the whole period the interface was reachable.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: Flaw remediation is nominally satisfied by a patch programme that applies whatever the vendor channel offers, and for a DCNM instance left on 7.0(2) that channel has been quiet since the 7.1 train superseded it. Compliance is recorded against updates applied, not against the distance between the installed build and the first fixed release, so an asset that has been seven years past 7.1(1) reports the same green as one patched last week.

NIST-800-53-SC-7.gap: Boundary protection is implemented and evidenced at the edge of the management network, which is where this control is normally assessed. It is adequate against an external attacker and irrelevant to the one that matters here: any workstation, contractor laptop or compromised server already inside the management VLAN satisfies the only precondition this unauthenticated read has, and nothing in the SC-7 evidence pack distinguishes those hosts from the DCNM operators.

NIS2-Art21-vulnerability-handling.gap: The entity can show a vulnerability-handling process with intake, triage and remediation stages, and that process is fed by advisory publication events. This CVE's trigger was a seven-year-old advisory being amended in March 2022 to record attempted exploitation in the wild - a change to an existing document, which advisory-publication intake does not raise, so triage never happens and the KEV due date of 2022-04-15 passes against an unopened case.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: System security is claimed on the basis that managed software is kept supported and updated, and the DCNM host genuinely is maintained - on the fabric compatibility matrix. The gap is who decides: moving from 7.0(2) to 7.1(1) is a change with switch-interoperability risk, so it is scheduled against fabric availability, and the deferral is recorded as a change decision rather than as an accepted unauthenticated file-read exposure on the management plane.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: An estate can be at a defensible Essential Eight patch maturity for workstations and internet-facing services while this asset sits outside the population being measured, because DCNM is an internal management application and its placement in that scope is the operator's reading rather than an explicit clause. The consequence is that a defect with an EPSS score of 0.404 on 2026-08-17 and a 2022 KEV due date is governed by the change calendar of the network team.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: Technical vulnerability management exists and produces a register, but the register inherits the scanner's view and the CVSS ordering. A confidentiality-only 7.5 on an internal management server ranks below the code-execution findings above it, which is exactly the wrong ordering for an asset whose readable files are the administrative credentials for an entire switching fabric.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Cisco Prime DCNM's fixed release, 7.1(1), has been available since 2015, and the KEV listing on 2022-03-25 followed Cisco's own record of attempted exploitation in the wild in March 2022. A patch-availability clock alone would have fired seven years earlier and been absorbed by the fabric change calendar; tying the clock to the KEV listing puts a date on an asset whose upgrade decision otherwise belongs to interoperability planning, and the 2022-04-15 due date is the measurable version of it.

new_control_requirements.name: MITIGATION-ACTIVE-PATCH-PENDING-VERDICT-CLASS
new_control_requirements.description: Compliance verdicts must distinguish three states: (a) binary patch deployed (vulnerability eliminated), (b) vendor-mitigation rule active, no binary patch (residual risk: any defect in the mitigation rule reopens the vulnerability), (c) no mitigation, no patch (full exposure). Audit reports must surface (b) as a distinct compensating-control state with an associated time-bound action item, not as a 'patched per SLA' outcome.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Cisco's advisory for this CVE states plainly that there are no workarounds that mitigate the vulnerability, which means state (b) does not exist for Prime DCNM below 7.1(1) - an instance is either upgraded or fully exposed. Audits nonetheless close this finding by recording that DCNM is management-network only, which is a reachability statement being filed as a compensating control. Forcing the three-state verdict makes a 6.3(1)-to-7.1(0) instance appear as (c) with a dated action item rather than as risk-accepted.

CVE-2015-1187.name: D-Link and TRENDnet Multiple Devices Remote Code Execution Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: An unauthenticated HTTP POST to the ncc service's ping endpoint carries a shell command inside the ping_addr parameter. The handler hands that value to a shell, so the command runs on the router as the web service, and the published tooling uses that foothold to fetch, chmod and execute a binary on the device.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none - PR:N; the ncc service answers the diagnostic endpoint without the caller holding any device credential, which is the improper-authentication half NVD records as CWE-287
attack_vector.complexity: low - AC:L; a single POST with metacharacters, no memory corruption and no timing dependency. The real constraint is position rather than skill: the endpoint is LAN-side on a default configuration, so the attacker is either on the client network or reaching a unit whose remote management has been enabled.
attack_vector.ai_factor: None. Human firmware reverse engineering credited to Peter Adkins and Tiago Caetano Henriques, disclosed in March 2015; the weaponisation that followed was a hand-written Metasploit module, not tool-generated.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Flashing the fixed build named in SAP10052 for each D-Link model and confirming the reboot, and establishing per-model firmware status for the TRENDnet units before treating them as fixed.
prevention.adequacy: Complete where a fixed build exists and the unit reboots onto it. Where a model or revision has no fixed firmware, the only terminal state is replacement, because the endpoint cannot be turned off from the device's own configuration.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Watching for POSTs to /ping.ccp carrying shell metacharacters, and for outbound binary fetches originating from the router itself.
detection.adequacy: Partial at best. The request is visible only to something positioned between the client network and the router, and where no such device is deployed at the site there is nothing to observe it; the router itself keeps no log that survives the reboot the firmware update requires.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treating a suspected-exploited unit as compromised hardware: rebuild the configuration from a known-good baseline rather than carrying it into the new firmware, and rotate the administrative credential and anything else that transited the device.
response.adequacy: It is the only response that addresses command execution on the device, but it depends on knowing the unit was exposed, and without device telemetry that determination rests on the firmware version and the network position rather than on evidence.

NIST-800-53-CM-7.gap: Least functionality can be attested for these routers by listing the administrative services the operator enabled, and that list is honest and complete. It also omits the vulnerable component entirely, because ncc2 is not an option the operator can see or switch off - the assessment describes a configuration surface that does not contain the thing being exploited.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: The organisation runs flaw remediation and can evidence it for every asset its software distribution reaches. These units are not among them: firmware is fetched by hand per model and hardware revision, and the fixed builds have been available since March 2015 with no mechanism that notices a unit still on the vulnerable one. The control is met and the population it measures excludes the exposed devices.

NIS2-Art21-network-security.gap: Network security measures are in place and would ordinarily isolate a vulnerable service from the users who do not need it. Here the vulnerable service runs on the device that connects those users to everything, so there is no segment on the far side of it: at a single-router site, isolating the injectable endpoint means isolating the network from its own gateway, and the control has no adequate expression.

NIS2-Art21-incident-handling.gap: An incident-handling process exists and would be invoked, but its default remediation for a network device is a firmware update, which on this defect preserves whatever the attacker changed in the configuration and leaves credentials that transited the unit unrotated. The process treats the router as an asset to patch rather than as a host that ran attacker code.

UK-CAF-B5.gap: The CAF outcome is assessed against the network equipment the organisation manages, and that assessment can be entirely sound while these routers sit outside it, at the sites where the managed network ends. A device that is both the site's only gateway and an unauthenticated command-execution surface is therefore absent from the evidence, not judged inadequate in it.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: Patch maturity is measured from what the patch-management tooling reports, and router firmware produces no such report. The result is a maturity rating that is accurate for workstations and servers while a KEV-listed unauthenticated command injection, EPSS 0.829 on 2026-08-17, sits unpatched on the device every one of those workstations routes through.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.9.gap: Configuration management is satisfied by a documented baseline for each device type, and for these routers that baseline can only record the settings the administrative interface exposes. The injectable endpoint is not one of them, so a fully compliant configuration record and an exploitable device are the same device, and the only baseline item that touches the flaw - remote management off - governs reachability rather than exploitability.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: D-Link published fixed firmware for the affected DIR models in SAP10052 in March 2015, and a weaponised Metasploit module for the same defect has been public since that year; the KEV listing did not arrive until 2022-03-25, with a 2022-04-15 due date. On unmanaged hardware the clock is the only forcing function that exists, because nothing else in the estate notices a router seven years behind its fixed build - and the SLA has to be measured on the reboot, since a downloaded image that has not been booted leaves the vulnerable ncc service running.

new_control_requirements.name: PERIMETER-COMPROMISE-REBUILD-NOT-PATCH
new_control_requirements.description: Pre-rehearsed IR runbook for any perimeter device that suffers a pre-auth RCE CVE in active exploitation MUST default to config-exfil + rebuild + credential rotation, not patch-in-place. Patch-in-place leaves attacker-installed implants intact.
new_control_requirements.evidence: This is a pre-authentication command-execution defect on the device that terminates the site's internet connection, listed in KEV on 2022-03-25 and exploitable from a public Metasploit module. Flashing the fixed D-Link build closes the injection path and carries the existing configuration forward, so a unit that was already exploited keeps whatever DNS, port-forward or account change the attacker made. The runbook default has to be rebuild from a known-good configuration plus rotation of the administrative credential and anything else that transited the router.

CVE-2015-1427.name: Elasticsearch Groovy Scripting Engine Remote Code Execution Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: A single unauthenticated search request carries a Groovy script in script_fields. The script reaches java.lang.Runtime by reflection rather than naming it, which the sandbox does not inspect, and the resulting shell command runs as the Elasticsearch user with its output returned inside the search response.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none - PR:N; Elasticsearch 1.x ships with no authentication layer, so anything that can reach the HTTP API is already an authorised caller as far as the service is concerned
attack_vector.complexity: low - AC:L; one request, no groom, no offsets, and dynamic scripting enabled by default on every release before 1.4.3, so no configuration change is needed on the target either.
attack_vector.ai_factor: None. The public exploit is Darren Martyn's March 2015 Python script; the bypass is a reading of what the sandbox filter does and does not examine, and no automated-discovery claim exists in the record.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Upgrading to 1.4.3 or 1.3.8, with dynamic scripting disabled in the interim and the HTTP API bound away from untrusted networks.
prevention.adequacy: The upgrade fixes the sandbox. Disabling dynamic scripting is a genuine interim control because it removes the request path rather than filtering its contents, but it changes application behaviour for anything that legitimately submits scripts, and it does nothing for an embedded copy inside JBoss Fuse that the operator does not control.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Alerting on script_fields requests carrying Groovy, and on any child process spawned by the Elasticsearch JVM.
detection.adequacy: The process-spawn signal is high quality because a search node forking a shell is never legitimate. The request-side signal depends on the search API being logged with request bodies, and on that traffic not being TLS-terminated at the node itself.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treating a reachable vulnerable node as having executed attacker code: rotating credentials held in its configuration, reviewing the index data for tampering, and rebuilding the host rather than upgrading in place.
response.adequacy: Correct in scope and expensive in practice, since the primitive gives command execution and the upgrade removes nothing already dropped. Its weakness is the trigger: without process telemetry the decision rests on version and reachability rather than on evidence of execution.

NIST-800-53-CM-7.gap: Least functionality is implemented and evidenced through the services and ports enabled on each host, and an Elasticsearch node passes that review with one listener. The dangerous functionality is a default inside the application - dynamic Groovy scripting, on in every release before 1.4.3 - which the assessment never descends to, so the control is satisfied while a scripting engine remains reachable through the search API.

NIST-800-53-SI-10.gap: Information input validation is genuinely present here: submitted scripts are passed through a sandbox that inspects them before execution. It is inadequate because it validates the identifiers a script mentions rather than the operations it can reach, and reflection through class.forName resolves the forbidden class without mentioning it - an audit that confirms a validation mechanism exists cannot see that distinction.

NIS2-Art21-supply-chain.gap: Supply-chain measures are in place for the entity's direct suppliers, which is where the register is built. The vulnerable Elasticsearch engine reached some estates inside JBoss Fuse and A-MQ, and Red Hat fixed it only in the 6.3 R2 update of April 2017 - two years after 1.4.3 - so the entity's real remediation date was set by a supplier whose product name never mentions the vulnerable component.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: System security can be evidenced for this cluster by showing it runs on a protected network, which is exactly the deployment model Elasticsearch 1.x assumed since it shipped no authentication. That assumption is what the CVE breaks: the flaw needs only a well-formed search request, so every application server, batch job and analyst workstation inside the trusted zone holds a full remote-code-execution primitive against the node.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: Patch maturity is measured across the platform team's managed estate and can be strong there while a search cluster owned by an application team is not part of that population. The fixed builds have been available since 2015 and EPSS stands at 0.999 on 2026-08-17, so the gap is not timeliness against a difficult patch but visibility of an asset that the patch programme never enumerated.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.28.gap: Secure coding standards are documented and applied to code the organisation writes, which leaves this defect entirely outside their reach - the sandbox that failed is the supplier's. The transferable finding is one an A.8.28 programme scoped to first-party code does not reach: a filter that denies specific class names is not a security boundary in a runtime with reflection, and any in-house scripting feature built the same way fails the same way.

new_control_requirements.name: DATABASE-SERVER-SIDE-SCRIPTING-DEFAULT-DENY
new_control_requirements.description: In-memory and document datastores must ship with server-side scripting disabled by default; re-enabling requires documented threat-model acceptance.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Elasticsearch before 1.4.3 enabled dynamic Groovy scripting by default, which is why the Metasploit module describes the target as exploitable out of the box and why a single unauthenticated POST to _search reaches an execution path. Had scripting been off unless a deployment justified it, the sandbox bypass would have been reachable only on clusters that had accepted that risk deliberately, rather than on every 1.3 and 1.4 installation in existence.

new_control_requirements.name: TIER-3-DEPENDENCY-INVENTORY
new_control_requirements.description: Supply chain inventory must extend to tier-3 dependencies (dependencies of dependencies of direct dependencies). SBOM coverage for libsystemd-class transitive dependencies cannot be omitted under SR-3.
new_control_requirements.evidence: NVD records Red Hat JBoss Fuse against this CVE and RHSA-2017:0868 fixed it there in April 2017, two years after Elastic shipped 1.4.3. An estate that inventoried its Elasticsearch clusters and upgraded them was still exposed through a middleware product that embedded the same engine, and only a component-level inventory reaching below the purchased product name identifies that instance.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Elasticsearch 1.4.3 and 1.3.8 fixed this in 2015; the KEV listing arrived 2022-03-25 with a 2022-04-15 due date, against an id whose EPSS on 2026-08-17 is 0.999 at the 99.97th percentile. With a Metasploit module, a standalone shell script and a Nuclei template all public, the interval between finding a vulnerable node and executing on it is a single request, so the SLA has to be measured on each node's restart onto the fixed build rather than on package deployment.

CVE-2015-1770.name: Microsoft Office Uninitialized Memory Use Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: A crafted Office document drives Office 2013 into using an object before it is initialised, and the attacker controls what that uninitialised memory holds. Code then runs in the security context of the user who opened the file, with the ActiveX path that Microsoft's workaround disables - the osf.Sandbox control - as the route into the defective handling.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none - PR:N; the attacker needs no account on the target, and the code inherits whatever rights the opening user holds, so an administrative user turns a document into full host control
attack_vector.complexity: low - AC:L with UI:R; no memory disclosure or grooming step is described in the bulletin, but a person has to open the file, which makes delivery and provenance the real preconditions rather than exploit reliability.
attack_vector.ai_factor: None. MS15-059 records a coordinated disclosure with no finder named in the bulletin text, and there is no automated-discovery claim in the record.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Applying KB 3039782 and relaunching the Office applications; before that, disabling ActiveX controls in Office or the osf.Sandbox CLSID specifically, and keeping externally sourced documents in Protected View.
prevention.adequacy: The update is complete once the applications restart. The ActiveX workarounds are real but not free - they break documents that legitimately use those controls - and Protected View helps only where the untrusted-origin marking survived the delivery path.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Inspecting inbound OOXML packages for activeX parts referencing CLSID {CDDBCC7C-BE18-4A58-9CBF-D62A012272CE}, and alerting on Office processes spawning children.
detection.adequacy: The document-side check is precise, and Emerging Threats published exactly that logic, but it requires unpacking archives at the mail or web boundary and is defeated by encrypted containers. The process-spawn signal is generic and fires after execution has already happened.

response.what_would_have_worked: Retaining the original attachment for analysis and treating the opening user's session and credentials as compromised rather than only cleaning the endpoint.
response.adequacy: It matches the outcome, since code ran as the user with that user's tokens and network access. Its limit is the trigger: a downstream alert arrives after the fact, by which point the document may already have been deleted from the mailbox and the exposure window has to be inferred.

NIST-800-53-SI-3.gap: Malicious code protection is deployed on the mail path and the endpoint, and it will catch the second-stage payload if that payload is known. It has nothing to say about the first stage: the document is structurally valid OOXML whose only distinguishing feature is an ActiveX part referencing a specific CLSID, which is why detection for this CVE had to be written as a bespoke unpack-and-match script rather than as a signature.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: Flaw remediation is met the moment KB 3039782 shows as installed in the management console, and that is where the measurement stops. Office applications load their code at launch, so a machine that installed the update but has not had Word or Excel restarted is reported as remediated while still executing the vulnerable parser - the control has no state between deployed and effective.

NIS2-Art21-vulnerability-management.gap: Vulnerability management runs on a current inventory and a current scanner feed, both of which handle supported Office builds correctly. An Office 2013 SP1 machine surviving for a line-of-business reason is exactly the asset an inventory built from the supported estate can omit, and this CVE only reached the KEV catalogue on 2022-03-28, long after the 2015 fix, so the entity's process had no prompt to revisit it before the due date of 2022-04-18.

UK-CAF-C1.gap: Security monitoring is in place and would show the consequences of exploitation - a new process, an outbound connection - as endpoint telemetry. What it does not retain is the document that caused them: where the mail and web gateways record delivery metadata rather than the file body, C1 evidence exists for the effect and not for the cause, and establishing which other recipients received the same attachment has nothing to work from.

AU-Essential-8-App-Hardening.gap: User application hardening can be at a high maturity - browser plugins blocked, Office macros restricted to signed publishers - and none of it intersects this attack, which arrives as an ActiveX control inside a document rather than as a macro. Microsoft's own mitigation is to disable ActiveX in Office or to block one specific CLSID, and neither is part of the standard hardening set the maturity rating is measured against.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.7.gap: Protection against malware is satisfied with anti-malware on the gateway and the endpoint plus user awareness of suspicious attachments. Both are calibrated to files that look wrong; this one is a working document that opens as expected, so the user has nothing to notice and the scanner nothing to match, and the control's assurance rests on assumptions this defect does not meet.

new_control_requirements.name: ARCHIVE-CONTENT-TYPE-PROVENANCE
new_control_requirements.description: For this CVE the requirement is that Word's Protected View decision be taken from verified provenance of the file — established outside the document — rather than from metadata that travels with the document and that an attacker controls, and that the untrusted-origin marking survive whatever container the document is delivered in so the handler still sees it as externally sourced. The operator-side expression of the control: the mail gateway and file-share boundary apply and preserve the untrusted-origin marking themselves, so the sandbox decision does not depend on the application deriving it from attacker-supplied input. The distinguishing test: deliver an externally-sourced document through each ingress path and confirm it reaches Word marked untrusted, instead of confirming only that Protected View is enabled in policy.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Exploitation of this Office 2013 defect requires the user to open an attacker-supplied document, and on an estate that has not yet deployed KB 3039782 the ingress path is the only lever left - Microsoft's alternatives are disabling ActiveX in Office wholesale or blocking CLSID {CDDBCC7C-BE18-4A58-9CBF-D62A012272CE}, both of which break legitimate documents. A document that reaches the full parsing path with the untrusted-origin marking stripped by an archive or a file share gets the vulnerable handling at the user's own privilege.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Microsoft shipped KB 3039782 for Office 2013 SP1 on 2015-06-09 and CISA set the due date at 2022-04-18 after listing the CVE on 2022-03-28, so any host still exposed in 2022 was one the patch programme had lost track of rather than one waiting on a vendor. The SLA has to be closed against each install's build and an Office application restart, since the update is inert in an Office process that has not relaunched.

CVE-2015-2419.name: Microsoft Internet Explorer Memory Corruption Vulnerability (CVE-2015-2419)

attack_vector.description: A web page loaded in Internet Explorer 10 or 11 stringifies a deeply nested object with a replacer function, which frees a buffer while a pointer to it is still held and frees it again. The attacker reoccupies that memory with sprayed ArrayBuffers, corrupts an array object's virtual table, pivots the stack and executes a ROP chain as the browsing user.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none - PR:N; the attacker needs no account and no prior foothold, only that the target's browser fetches the page
attack_vector.complexity: low - AC:L with UI:R; the heap spray and per-build gadget offsets make it engineering-heavy to write once, and Check Point's analysis records the same code being reused across exploit kits, so the attacker running it needs no such capability.
attack_vector.ai_factor: None. MS15-065 marks it publicly disclosed before the fix without naming a finder; the analysis that documented the root cause was published by Check Point's researchers in February 2016.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Applying the MS15-065 cumulative update and restarting; on hosts that cannot be updated, removing Internet Explorer's access to untrusted content and accounting for applications that host its rendering engine.
prevention.adequacy: The update is complete prevention. Microsoft lists no workaround and no mitigating factor, so everything short of it is a restriction on where the browser is pointed rather than a change to the vulnerable engine.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Alerting on iexplore.exe spawning children or writing executables, and inspecting scripts for the nested-object plus stringify-plus-spray sequence.
detection.adequacy: The process-behaviour signal is reliable and late - it fires after code execution. Content inspection of the script is defeated by ordinary obfuscation of the same trigger sequence, so it is not a control to rely on alone.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treating the browsing user's credentials and session tokens as compromised and rebuilding the host, rather than removing a dropped file and closing the case.
response.adequacy: Proportionate to a drive-by that executes at user privilege with the user's tokens in memory. The limitation is scoping: the delivery is a page view, so establishing what else the same source served, and to whom, depends on proxy logs being retained for the period.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: Flaw remediation is fully met for managed Windows hosts, which took the MS15-065 cumulative update in July 2015 through the normal channel. The residual exposure lives in the assets deliberately excluded from that channel - kiosks, imaging and manufacturing consoles, machines pinned to a legacy internal application - and their exclusion is an exception approved elsewhere, so the SI-2 evidence stays clean while the vulnerable engine keeps running.

NIST-800-53-CM-7.gap: Least functionality is applied to services and installed software, and a browser classed as required software survives each such review. That framing is what leaves the exposure standing: on a host kept on Internet Explorer for one internal application, CM-7 has no mechanism to restrict the browser to that application, so the full JScript9 surface remains reachable from any page the user visits.

NIS2-Art21-patch-management.gap: Patch management is in place and demonstrably works, because the fix shipped in a cumulative update in 2015 and reached the managed estate. What it cannot express is the case this CVE actually represents in 2022: a browser that is no longer supported on hosts that cannot move, where the remediation is removing the software rather than updating it, and no patch metric reports a machine whose problem is that there is nothing left to install.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: System security is evidenced by keeping software supported and updated, and an organisation can show that for the bulk of its estate. The judgement it does not force is about the remainder: because this exploit circulated in exploit kits rather than in targeted tooling, an IE-dependent host is exposed by routine browsing, and B4 evidence does not distinguish that host from one where the browser is used for a single internal site.

AU-Essential-8-App-Hardening.gap: User application hardening can be at high maturity - web advertisements blocked, Java and Flash disabled, unnecessary browser features off - while this defect stays fully reachable, because the vulnerable code is the browser's own JSON handling rather than a plugin. The hardening that reaches it is not running Internet Explorer at all, which the control does not require.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: Technical vulnerability management processed MS15-065 on the schedule that severity assigns. That schedule is calibrated to advisory severity rather than to weaponisation speed, and the same exploit was circulating in exploit kits within months of the bulletin.

new_control_requirements.name: BROWSER-MANAGED-UPDATE-NO-DEFERRAL
new_control_requirements.description: Enterprise update rings must not defer security-channel browser updates beyond 24h.
new_control_requirements.evidence: This is a browser-engine defect fixed in the MS15-065 cumulative update of 2015-07-14 and found in the Rig and Angler exploit kits within months, per Check Point's February 2016 analysis. On that timeline a deferral ring measured in weeks hands attackers a window that commodity drive-by tooling is already inside, and for Internet Explorer the update is an operating-system update requiring a restart, so the ring has to be measured to the reboot rather than to package approval.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CISA listed this on 2022-03-28 with a 2022-04-18 due date, nearly seven years after the fix, which makes the clock a discovery mechanism for hosts the patch channel no longer reaches - the population where EPSS 0.447 on 2026-08-17 still describes live risk. Because Microsoft publishes no workaround for this CVE, the documented compensating-control branch of the SLA can only be a restriction on what the browser may reach, and that has to be recorded as such rather than as remediation.

CVE-2015-2426.name: Microsoft Windows Adobe Type Manager Library Remote Code Execution Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: A crafted OpenType font, embedded in a document or a web page, is parsed by atmfd.dll inside the Windows kernel and underflows a buffer. The corruption is in kernel memory, so the outcome is control of the host rather than of the rendering process - and the published exploit uses the same primitive as a local escalation injected into a sandboxed process to break out of it.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none - PR:N for the remote path described by MS15-078; the leaked exploit runs the same defect from inside an already-compromised process to reach kernel privilege
attack_vector.complexity: low - AC:L with UI:R; Microsoft assessed that exploit code could be created to exploit this consistently, and the public exploit ships a fixed malformed font rather than requiring per-target tuning.
attack_vector.ai_factor: None. The exploit was written by Eugene Ching of Qavar Security and became public through the Hacking Team archive; nothing in the record indicates automated discovery or automated exploit generation.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Applying KB 3079904, or KB 3074683 on Windows 10, and rebooting; before the update, disabling ATMFD by registry value or renaming atmfd.dll and restarting.
prevention.adequacy: The update is complete. The workaround is genuinely preventive rather than cosmetic, because it stops the driver loading at all, but Microsoft records that applications relying on embedded fonts may then not display properly, and it needs a restart of its own.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Alerting on a rendering process producing a SYSTEM-privileged child, and on kernel faults correlated with font-bearing content.
detection.adequacy: Weak by construction. The parse happens in the kernel on behalf of a legitimate process, so a successful exploit generates no file, no service and no new module - only failed attempts are noisy, and the published exploit ships a fixed, tested font blob rather than per-target tuning.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treating a host that reached kernel privilege as fully compromised - rebuild rather than clean, and rotate every credential that was present on it during the exposure window.
response.adequacy: The only defensible response to a kernel-level compromise, since nothing running on that host can be trusted to report its own state afterwards. The difficulty is establishing that it happened at all, given how little the exploit leaves behind.

NIST-800-53-CM-7.gap: Least functionality is assessed against installed applications, running services and open ports, and a standard Windows build passes each of those reviews. The component that matters is a kernel-mode font driver loaded by default, which no such review enumerates - even though Microsoft's own workaround is to disable it and the vendor notes Windows ships no OpenType fonts natively.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: Flaw remediation ran and applied MS15-078 when it was published out of band on 2015-07-20. What the control does not track is a bulletin changing after the fact: the 2015-07-29 rerelease added Windows 10 coverage under a different update, KB 3074683, so an organisation that processed the bulletin once shows a completed remediation while its Windows 10 hosts never received the fix.

NIS2-Art21-vulnerability-handling.gap: Vulnerability handling is implemented and works from advisories, which is a sound design for coordinated disclosure and the wrong shape for this event. Functional exploit code for this defect appeared in a third-party breach before any advisory existed, so for the days between the archive becoming public and the out-of-band bulletin the process had no artefact to act on and no state that describes exploit-public-patch-absent.

UK-CAF-C1.gap: Security monitoring can be comprehensively implemented and still be blind here, because the vulnerable code runs in the kernel at the request of a legitimate rendering process and a successful exploit produces no dropped file, no new service and no loaded module to alert on. The telemetry C1 is evidenced with describes what the attacker does after the escalation, never the escalation itself.

AU-Essential-8-App-Hardening.gap: User application hardening is measured on what the browser and Office are permitted to execute, and this attack does not need any of it - the font is data passed to a kernel component by whichever process renders the content. An estate can therefore hold a strong hardening maturity while the only effective measure, disabling the ATMFD driver, sits outside the control's scope entirely.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.9.gap: Configuration management is documented and applied to build baselines, which is precisely how the interim mitigation for this CVE can evaporate unnoticed: DisableATMFD set by hand in July 2015, or a renamed x-atmfd.dll, is host state that no baseline records. A later rebuild, image restore or hardware refresh silently returns the driver to service, and the configuration record shows no change because it never contained the item.

new_control_requirements.name: BUG-FAMILY-MITIGATION-PERSISTENCE
new_control_requirements.description: When a CVE patch lands, retain the pre-patch compensating controls (module blacklists, sysctl restrictions) until the patched code has soaked for a stated review period. Patches for one bug in a primitive class can introduce sibling bugs in the same class; the original compensating control may still apply to the sibling.
new_control_requirements.evidence: The interim mitigation for this CVE was to stop the ATMFD driver loading - DisableATMFD set to 1, or atmfd.dll renamed to x-atmfd.dll - and KB 3079904 fixed one parsing defect in that same driver on 2015-07-20. The driver kept parsing attacker-supplied OpenType fonts in kernel mode afterwards, so removing the workaround the moment the patch landed traded a control that covers the whole component for one that covers a single defect in it.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Working exploit code for this Windows font-driver defect was public in the Hacking Team archive before Microsoft shipped MS15-078 out of band on 2015-07-20, and CISA later set a 2022-04-18 due date against the same id. The SLA's compensating-control branch is what carries an estate through that pattern, because the DisableATMFD registry value can be pushed in minutes while KB 3079904 and its reboot are still being scheduled - and both halves have to be measured to the restart, since neither takes effect until the host reboots.

CVE-2015-3035.name: TP-Link Multiple Archer Devices Directory Traversal Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: One unauthenticated GET under /login/ carrying dot-dot segments walks out of the web root, and the router returns the requested file from its own filesystem. The value to an attacker is not the sample file the scanners use but the configuration and credential material that sits on the device alongside it.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none - PR:N and UI:N; the request precedes any login and needs no cookie, header or prior interaction with the device
attack_vector.complexity: low - AC:L; a single request with no encoding trickery required, which is why a verified detection template and a scanner module both implement it in a few lines. The one constraint is position: the web interface answers the client network by default, and the internet side only where remote administration was enabled.
attack_vector.ai_factor: None. Coordinated through SEC Consult Vulnerability Lab advisory 20150410-0 in April 2015; human embedded-firmware research with no automated-discovery claim in the record.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Flashing the dated build for the exact model and hardware revision and confirming the reboot; replacing any revision for which no fixed build exists.
prevention.adequacy: Complete where a fixed build exists for that revision. Disabling remote administration is not a substitute: it removes the internet-side path while leaving the flaw fully reachable by every client the router serves, which is the network the device exists for.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Matching requests to the device that begin /login/ and contain traversal segments, and alerting on 200 responses carrying file content.
detection.adequacy: Sound as a rule and hard to place, since the exchange happens between a client and its own gateway with nothing in between. The device's own log is the only witness and does not survive the firmware reboot.

response.what_would_have_worked: Rotating the router's administrative credential and any key or credential stored in its configuration, on the assumption that a reachable unit had its configuration read.
response.adequacy: It addresses the actual loss, because the primitive is a read and the firmware update cannot recall what was disclosed. Where one administrative password was reused across a fleet of these units, the rotation scope is the fleet rather than the device.

NIST-800-53-SC-7.gap: Boundary protection is implemented and, for once, is not the wrong control applied badly - it is the right control with nowhere to stand. The vulnerable interface belongs to the device that forms the boundary, and it must answer the client network to do its job, so an SC-7 assessment can be entirely correct while every client on the site retains an unauthenticated file-read primitive against its own gateway.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: Flaw remediation is met across the estate the patch tooling manages, and these routers are not in it. Their version is a date code readable only from the device's own web page and comparable only against a per-revision fixed build, so the control produces no measurement for them at all - the asset is not late on remediation, it is absent from the process.

NIS2-Art21-patch-management.gap: Patch-management measures are documented and applied, with cadences and exception handling that hold for servers and workstations. This asset class breaks the mechanism rather than the cadence: an operator must identify the exact hardware revision, download the matching image, flash it and reboot the site's gateway, and there is no channel through which the entity's process can perform or verify any of that remotely.

UK-CAF-B5.gap: Resilience is evidenced through redundancy and recovery planning for the managed network, and that evidence can be complete. Where a remote site runs a single gateway, any acceptance recorded for it was written against device failure rather than device compromise - and the same design makes remediation disruptive, since flashing the fixed build reboots the site's only path and a revision with no fixed build has to be swapped out entirely.

UK-CAF-C1.gap: Security monitoring is in place and collects from the sources the organisation controls, none of which observe a request made by a client to its own gateway. Whatever local log the router keeps does not survive the firmware-update reboot, so there is no telemetry from which to establish whether the traversal was ever used against a given unit - and the exposure window has to be assumed rather than measured.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: The estate can hold a defensible Essential Eight patch maturity while every one of these routers stays on a 2014 firmware build, because the maturity is computed from what the patching tooling reports and these devices report nothing. The fixed builds have existed since March 2015, so the shortfall is entirely one of enumeration rather than of remediation speed.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: Technical vulnerability management can be operating correctly and still be unable to answer whether a given unit is affected, because the answer depends on hardware revision as well as model - the fix arrives at 150310 for a TL-WR841N v9 and at 150317 for an Archer C5 v1.2. An asset register that records the model name alone cannot resolve that, so the finding stays open on paper or is closed without evidence.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
