For this CVE only two dispositions are real, because Cisco states no workaround exists: the appliance is at 5.8.0.32.9 or it is exposed. A register entry recording a compensating control during the wait for the maintenance window describes a state the product does not offer, and the handling process is judged on the existence of the entry rather than on whether the mitigation it names can exist.

NIS2-Art21-identity-management.gap: The identity-management measure governs how access rights are assigned and authenticated across the entity, and ACS is the machine that carries out those decisions for network device administration. A defect yielding root on that machine sits outside the measure's frame entirely: the attacker reads the TACACS+ and RADIUS shared secrets and can alter the authorisation policy without holding, requesting or being granted any identity. Complete conformance with the measure leaves this path exactly as open as non-conformance would.

UK-CAF-B2.gap: B2 asks how access to essential-service systems is granted, verified and revoked, and for a network estate every answer resolves to ACS. That makes ACS the asset whose compromise invalidates the whole B2 case rather than one system assessed within it, and the outcome carries no requirement that the enforcement point be remediated faster than what it protects. An organisation can evidence strong identity and access control end to end while the appliance implementing it runs a release Cisco scores 9.8 unauthenticated.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: Essential Eight patch maturity is demonstrated against operating systems and applications, and Cisco Secure ACS is delivered as an appliance image whose cumulative patches belong to neither population. The result is an accurate maturity rating that is silent on the AAA server: an organisation assessed at a high level for both patching strategies can be running ACS below 5.8.0.32.9, and no finding is generated because the asset class was never in the measured scope.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: A.8.8 requires vulnerability information to be obtained and evaluated for the systems in use, and the evaluation is the step that fails here. Cisco scores the same defect 9.8 below 5.8 Patch 7 and 8.8 at Patch 7 and 8, so the exposure an organisation actually holds cannot be read from a feed's headline severity — it requires comparing the installed patch level against the advisory's release table. A.8.8 audits the existence of the intake and evaluation process, not whether that per-release comparison was ever performed.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Cisco Secure ACS is the AAA control plane for network-device administration, and Cisco recorded attempted exploitation of this deserialization path in the wild in March 2022, weeks before CISA's 2022-03-25 KEV listing and 2022-04-15 due date. The control's 'documented compensating controls' branch is the operative one for ACS, because Cisco states there is no workaround: the only documentable interim measure is restricting reachability of the ACS web tier to the network-administration segment, and it must be recorded as such rather than as a substitute for the 5.8.0.32.9 cumulative patch. EPSS reads 0.18212 at the 96.96th percentile on 2026-08-17, which understates the case here — the appliance is internally reachable, not internet-exposed, so the exploitation probability the score models is not the exposure an operator holds.

new_control_requirements.name: MITIGATION-ACTIVE-PATCH-PENDING-VERDICT-CLASS
new_control_requirements.description: Compliance verdicts must distinguish three states: (a) binary patch deployed (vulnerability eliminated), (b) vendor-mitigation rule active, no binary patch (residual risk: any defect in the mitigation rule reopens the vulnerability), (c) no mitigation, no patch (full exposure). Audit reports must surface (b) as a distinct compensating-control state with an associated time-bound action item, not as a 'patched per SLA' outcome.
new_control_requirements.evidence: For Cisco Secure ACS this CVE has no state (b) at all: the advisory records no workaround, so an appliance below 5.8.0.32.9 is in state (c), full exposure, from the moment the March 2018 advisory published until the cumulative patch is applied. That distinction is the whole value of the control here. An audit report that lets the interim reachability restriction stand as a vendor mitigation records state (b) for an appliance that is in state (c), and the time-bound action item that the control forces is exactly what keeps the 2022-04-15 KEV due date attached to the appliance rather than dissolving into the next quarterly window.

CVE-2018-11138.name: Quest KACE System Management Appliance Remote Command Execution Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: An anonymous GET to the appliance's agent-download script carries a shell payload in the organisation-ID parameter, hidden behind a SQL comment character so the surrounding database query still succeeds. Commands run as the appliance's web-server user, and Core Security's disclosure shows privilege-management defects in the same appliance that carry that user to root — at which point the attacker owns the software-distribution channel for every managed device.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none — PR:N; the script is served to anonymous users by design so that unenrolled endpoints can fetch an agent, which is why no console account is ever involved
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L; Core Security notes agent versions are published on Quest's own site and the organisation ID defaults to 1, with both recoverable through a time-based SQL injection in the same parameter, so only the per-appliance serv hash is target-specific
attack_vector.ai_factor: Found by Leandro Barragan and Guido Leo of Core Security Consulting Services through manual review of the bundled web console. No automated discovery is described in CORE-2018-0004.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Applying Quest patch SEC2018_20180410 to reach 7.0.121307, 7.1.150, 7.2.103, 8.0.320 or 8.1.108, with the console restricted to the systems-management segment until the appliance restarts onto the fixed build.
prevention.adequacy: Closes the injection. It does not close the appliance's wider anonymous surface — the download script still answers unauthenticated callers by design — so reachability restriction remains worth keeping after the patch.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Web-tier logging on the appliance forwarded off-box, alerting on requests to /common/download_agent_installer.php whose orgid parameter contains shell metacharacters, and process-creation alerting for shells parented by the appliance's web-server user.
detection.adequacy: The request signature is well defined because the exploit is public, which makes this unusually tractable. The limit is that a vendor appliance carries no operator-installed endpoint agent, so process-level visibility depends on what the image forwards.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treating a reachable-and-unpatched appliance as a distribution-channel compromise: compare scripting, managed-install and agent-distribution content against a known-good copy, and rotate the credentials the appliance holds for endpoints and directory integrations.
response.adequacy: This is the step with lasting value, because the patch removes the write path and nothing written through it. It is also the step that scales badly — reviewing distribution content means auditing what the appliance has been handing every managed device.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: SI-2 will drive the KACE appliance to SEC2018_20180410 eventually, but it contains nothing that ranks the appliance ahead of the endpoints it serves. A remediation programme that places the management appliance in the same monthly tier as the managed estate patches the distribution channel last, which is precisely inverted for an asset that pushes software to every device — and the control reports compliant throughout, because the appliance was remediated within its assigned window.

NIST-800-53-AC-6.gap: Least privilege has no contact with this path. The attacker never authenticates to the KACE console, so the per-account privilege scoping that an AC-6 assessment examines is never consulted; the privilege that decides the outcome is the appliance's own web-server user, and Core Security's disclosure shows Sudo Server module defects in the same release carrying that user to root. An organisation with exemplary KACE role separation is exactly as exposed as one without it.

NIS2-Art21-supply-chain.gap: The supply-chain measure is discharged through supplier assessment and contractual security requirements, aimed at what the entity acquires from outside. KACE SMA is the internal hop after acquisition — the machine that stages and distributes software to managed devices — so root on it substitutes attacker content into the sanctioned delivery path without any supplier being compromised. A complete supplier-assurance file says nothing about the appliance in the middle.

NIS2-Art21-patch-management.gap: Article 21 asks for proportionate patch handling and does not say who patches the system that measures patching. Where an entity uses KACE SMA to evidence its own patch coverage and the appliance is running below 8.0.320 or its line's equivalent, the instrument generating the compliance evidence is the unremediated asset — and the measure contains nothing requiring that instrument to be assessed independently of the estate it reports on, so the circularity is never surfaced by conformance work.

UK-CAF-D1.gap: D1 asks for response and recovery plans covering the systems that support the essential service, and where those plans are written around server and endpoint compromise they do not reach this asset. A KACE compromise is neither of those things: the appliance holds integration credentials and can push content to every managed device, so recovery means auditing distribution content and rotating credentials across the estate rather than rebuilding one host. A D1 assessment finds a plan in place and no scenario that matches what this asset actually requires.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: Removing this weakness under B4 is a version comparison — is the appliance at 7.0.121307, 7.1.150, 7.2.103, 8.0.320 or 8.1.108 — and that is as cheap as maintenance gets. The failure is one of ownership: the appliance is run by the systems-management function whose remit is the managed estate, and where that function's maintenance regime covers the devices and not the appliance driving them, the B4 sample finds every managed endpoint inside scope and the box distributing to them outside it.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: The Essential Eight's two patching strategies address operating systems and applications, and a vendor-managed appliance image is neither, so KACE SMA falls outside the measured population by construction. The circularity makes it worse than a simple scoping gap: where the appliance is the tool producing the patch-maturity evidence, an organisation presents a high maturity rating generated by a machine that is itself running a build below 8.0.320.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: A.8.8 requires timely vulnerability information about systems in use, and this disclosure is a stress test of that requirement. Core Security published CORE-2018-0004 on 2018-05-31 in forced-release mode after, by its own account, being advised against distributing the findings; an intake process subscribed only to vendor advisories receives Quest's note about SEC2018_20180410 but never the technical description of the anonymous download-script path, which is the part that tells an operator what to hunt for.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: The Quest KACE System Management Appliance is the software-distribution channel for every device it manages, and the exploitation economics here are settled rather than speculative: a Metasploit module (modules/exploits/unix/http/quest_kace_systems_management_rce.rb) and Exploit-DB 44950 have both been public since June 2018, EPSS reads 0.91778 at the 99.808th percentile on 2026-08-17, and CISA's 2022-03-25 KEV listing carries the known-ransomware flag with a 2022-04-15 due date. Quest's patch SEC2018_20180410 has existed since 2018, so 'patch availability, whichever is later' resolved years before the KEV clock started — for this appliance the SLA runs from the listing, and the compensating-control branch means restricting the console to the systems-management segment while the appliance restarts onto 8.0.320 or its line's equivalent.

new_control_requirements.name: FLEET-COMPROMISE-IR-PLAYBOOK
new_control_requirements.description: Pre-rehearsed IR playbook for fleet-control-plane compromise including: MDM-pushed certificate revocation, device-trust-state invalidation, configuration-profile audit since the suspected compromise window, downstream device-quarantine criteria, and credential rotation for any account that authenticated through a compromised fleet device during the exposure period.
new_control_requirements.evidence: KACE SMA is a fleet control plane in exactly the sense this playbook addresses — it inventories and distributes software, scripts and patches to servers, PCs, Macs, Chromebooks, tablets, printers, storage and networking gear. The playbook's configuration-profile audit maps here onto the appliance's scripting, managed-install and agent-distribution content, which is what an attacker at root would alter and what Quest's patch SEC2018_20180410 does not revert; its credential-rotation step maps onto the endpoint and directory-integration credentials the appliance holds. CISA's KEV flag for known ransomware campaign use is the reason the playbook has to be pre-rehearsed rather than improvised: the ransomware value of this appliance is precisely its ability to push a payload to the managed estate through a sanctioned channel.

CVE-2018-1273.name: VMware Tanzu Spring Data Commons Property Binder Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: The property binder treats the name of an inbound request parameter as a property path and evaluates that path as a SpEL expression. Writing the expression into the parameter name — inside the bracketed index — hands the application an expression to evaluate, and the published payload uses it to reach java.lang.Runtime and execute a command inside the JVM.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none — PR:N against an unauthenticated Spring Data REST resource; Pivotal notes that authentication and authorization on the endpoints limits exposure to authorized users, which changes who can reach it rather than whether the binder is vulnerable
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L; one form-encoded POST, deterministic evaluation, no race and no groom. The variable is which of an application's Data REST resources are reachable unauthenticated
attack_vector.ai_factor: Disclosed by Philippe Arteau of GoSecure Inc. A named human researcher; the advisory describes no automated analysis.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Resolving spring-data-commons to 1.13.11 or 2.0.6, rebuilding every artifact that carries it, and redeploying so the running JVM loads the fixed binder.
prevention.adequacy: Complete where it is applied, but it depends on knowing the library is present. Where it arrives transitively, the hard part is the enumeration rather than the version bump.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Inspecting request parameter NAMES for expression syntax at the reverse proxy or WAF, and alerting on process creation by application-tier JVMs.
detection.adequacy: Parameter-name inspection is unusual — most request-validation rules examine values — so this is a rule an operator has to add deliberately. Process-creation alerting is the more reliable half, because a Spring web application that suddenly forks a shell is anomalous on its face.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treating an exposed service as executed-against rather than merely vulnerable: reviewing what the JVM's process tree and outbound connections did during the exposure window, and rotating any credential the application process could read.
response.adequacy: Bounded by retention. The payload leaves little on disk, so the evidence is process and network telemetry from the exposure period — and for a service that has been exposed since 2018, whether any of it survives is a question about that service's retention policy rather than about the investigation.

NIST-800-53-SR-3.gap: SR-3 assesses supply chain controls against the components an organisation believes it consumes, and that belief is formed from declared dependencies. spring-data-commons is not declared in most projects that ship it; it is resolved beneath Spring Data REST and the Spring Boot starters. The result is an inventory that is internally consistent, auditable and missing the library that carries the SpEL sink — the control is satisfied by a document whose omission is the finding.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: For a compiled-in library, flaw remediation is a rebuild and a redeploy rather than an installation, and SI-2 measures the timeliness of remediation actions rather than the currency of running artifacts. A pipeline that started resolving 2.0.6 in April 2018 evidences compliance, while a long-lived service last deployed before then keeps a JVM loaded with 2.0.5 in memory. The control has no field that distinguishes 'the build is fixed' from 'the running process is fixed'.

NIS2-Art21-supply-chain.gap: Article 21's supply-chain measure is built around relationships — direct suppliers, service providers, contractual security requirements — and there is no relationship here to assess. The vulnerable code is an open-source component the build system resolved, so an entity can hold complete supplier assurance files and still deploy an artifact whose property binder evaluates attacker-supplied SpEL. The measure's assessment surface and the actual exposure do not intersect.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: B4 expects known vulnerabilities in supporting systems to be identified and removed, and identification here is a build-system question: which deployed artifacts resolve spring-data-commons at 1.13.10 or 2.0.5. Where a CAF assessment is evidenced from host, platform and configuration records, none of them can answer it. The outcome is not tolerated by B4 so much as invisible to that class of evidence.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: Patch applications is evidenced from installed-software inventories and vendor update feeds, and a Java library packaged inside a WAR or fat JAR appears in neither — the host reports a JVM and an application name, not spring-data-commons 2.0.5. An organisation can therefore evidence a high maturity level for application patching while its services are still binding request parameters through the vulnerable property binder, with the assessment accurate about everything it was able to see.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: A.8.8 requires vulnerability information about systems in use to be obtained and evaluated, and Pivotal's 2018-04-10 advisory naming 1.13.11 and 2.0.6 is easy to obtain. Evaluation is where it stops: deciding whether the organisation is affected requires resolving the transitive dependency tree of every deployed artifact, and the control never names that step. An implementation that stops at intake receives the advisory, files it, and has no procedure that can answer whether it applies.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.28.gap: Secure coding governs the code an organisation writes, and nothing the application developer wrote is at fault here — a conventional Spring Data REST resource is exposed, and the binder underneath it evaluates the request parameter's name as an expression. No secure-coding standard, review checklist or static-analysis rule applied to the application's own source would have surfaced this, so a complete A.8.28 conformance file coexists with a service that accepts arbitrary SpEL from unauthenticated callers.

OWASP-Top-10-2021-A06.gap: This is squarely the vulnerable-and-outdated-components category, and it is also where the category's usual tooling fails. A dependency scanner reading declared manifests returns clean for an application that never names spring-data-commons, because the library is resolved beneath Spring Data REST or a Boot starter. Surfacing it requires scanning the resolved tree of the built artifact, and the clean declared-dependency scan is precisely what makes the application look unaffected.

new_control_requirements.name: TIER-3-DEPENDENCY-INVENTORY
new_control_requirements.description: Supply chain inventory must extend to tier-3 dependencies (dependencies of dependencies of direct dependencies). SBOM coverage for libsystemd-class transitive dependencies cannot be omitted under SR-3.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Spring Data Commons is the case this control describes in the Java ecosystem: an application declares Spring Boot or Spring Data REST, those resolve spring-data-commons, and the vulnerable property binder ships inside the artifact without appearing in any manifest a developer wrote. The versions that matter — 1.13.10 and earlier, and 2.0.0 through 2.0.5, against fixes at 1.13.11 and 2.0.6 published 2018-04-10 — can only be read from the resolved tree of the built artifact. With EPSS at 0.95649 (99.865th percentile, 2026-08-17), a KEV listing dated 2022-03-25 flagged for known ransomware use, and a maintained Nuclei template carrying the payload, an inventory that stops at declared dependencies is the difference between knowing the estate is exposed and being scanned for it.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Spring Data Commons 1.13.11 and 2.0.6 shipped on 2018-04-10, so by the time CISA listed this CVE on 2022-03-25 with a 2022-04-15 due date the 'whichever is later' term had resolved to the listing itself and the whole clock was remediation, not availability. The compensating-control branch is real for this library and has a stated limit: Pivotal's advisory records that authentication and authorization on the endpoints limits exposure to authorized users, which is a documentable interim measure and not a fix, so it must be recorded as compensating rather than closing. Verification for this CVE is the resolved dependency tree of the redeployed artifact plus a restarted JVM, because a rebuilt image that has not been rolled out leaves the vulnerable binder loaded in the running process.

CVE-2018-14839.name: LG N1A1 NAS Remote Command Execution Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: Two PHP scripts in the appliance's web application take a POST parameter and concatenate it into a sudo command line without a session check or any neutralisation. A semicolon in that parameter appends the attacker's command, and because the web user holds unrestricted passwordless sudo, the appended command runs as root on the machine holding the stored data.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none — PR:N; the researcher's method was specifically to find scripts that omit the session_manage.php validation the rest of the application performs, so no session or credential is involved
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L; a shell metacharacter in one parameter, and no privilege step afterwards because of the sudoers configuration. The only variable is whether the appliance's port 8000 is reachable
attack_vector.ai_factor: Independent researcher 0x616163, working on a device they owned: reproduce a known injection, grep the PHP directory for scripts taking POST parameters, filter for those omitting the session check, and test the ones feeding exec. Manual review throughout.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Retiring the appliance. No fixed firmware could be located, the last release dates to December 2011 with a dead download link, and the device's own update endpoint no longer answers — so the only measure that removes the exposure is taking the unit out of service and migrating the data.
prevention.adequacy: Complete, and with no fixed firmware locatable it is the only measure that removes the exposure. Its cost is a hardware replacement and a data migration; a KEV due date of 2022-04-15 against a device with no available update is a removal deadline whether or not it is read as one.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Network-side observation of who reaches TCP 8000 on the appliance, plus alerting on outbound connections initiated by the NAS itself.
detection.adequacy: Weak on its own. This is a closed consumer appliance with no operator-installed agent, so host telemetry is whatever the firmware happens to log locally — and an attacker with root through the sudoers entry can alter that. Network-side observation is the half that survives.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treating any exposed unit as fully compromised: the data it stores must be assumed read, and any credential stored on or transiting the appliance rotated, before or alongside decommissioning.
response.adequacy: There is no clean state to restore to, because there is no fixed firmware to restore onto. Response here is data-side rather than device-side, and it ends with the hardware being retired rather than returned to service.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: SI-2 is written as identify, report, correct — and for this device the correct step has no content. The researcher documents that firmware 3718.510 dates from June 2011, that the last N1A1 release was December 2011 with a dead download link, and that the appliance's update endpoint lgodd.lge.com no longer responds. An SI-2 implementation whose only disposition is 'apply the vendor fix' converts that into an open, indefinitely renewed risk acceptance, when the correction the situation actually calls for is retiring the hardware.

NIST-800-53-CM-7.gap: Least functionality is the control that maps most directly onto the defect — /system/sharedir.php looks, in the researcher's own reading, like a leftover development artifact — and it is the one an operator cannot exercise. CM-7 assessments of a closed appliance image examine which network services are enabled, not which endpoints inside a bundled web application answer without a session, and the vendor exposes no supported means to disable an individual PHP script. The control is nominally met at the service level and blind at the endpoint level.

NIST-800-53-SC-7.gap: SC-7 carries all the remaining leverage on this asset. Reaching TCP 8000 is equivalent to reaching root, because the web user holds 'www-data ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD: ALL', so the boundary around that port is the entire defence. Where the appliance sits on a general user segment and the SC-7 assessment is scoped to the external perimeter, the internal boundary that carries the whole defence is neither designed nor examined.

NIS2-Art21-patch-management.gap: Article 21's patch handling assumes a supplier issuing patches, and here there is none: no LG advisory for this CVE could be located, the last firmware predates the disclosure by nearly seven years, and the update channel the device uses is dead. An entity can run a fully conforming patch process and hold this appliance indefinitely, because the process has no terminal state for a product whose maintainer has stopped — only an open item that is re-accepted at each review.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: B4 expects known weaknesses to be removed through maintenance, and maintenance for the N1A1 does not exist. That leaves two available outcomes, and neither reduces risk: the appliance is scoped out as unmanaged storage, or it is carried as a standing exception with a compensating network control. The CAF outcome has no language for 'the only way to satisfy this is to remove the hardware', which is exactly what this device requires.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: The Essential Eight measures how quickly available patches are applied, and there are none to apply to a NAS whose firmware last changed in 2011. The strategy that would engage this risk is asset retirement, which sits outside the eight entirely, so an organisation's patch maturity rating is completely unaffected by whether this appliance is still serving files. The framework's measurement is accurate and its silence on the device is total.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: A.8.8 depends on obtaining vulnerability information about the systems in use, and for this device the only public source is an independent researcher's Medium write-up of 2018-08-02, tagged 'Exploit' by NVD. An intake process built on vendor advisory feeds and distribution security notices receives nothing whatever, because LG issued nothing that could be located — the control does not fail late here, it has no input at all until CISA's KEV listing on 2022-03-25 supplies one.

new_control_requirements.name: MITIGATION-ACTIVE-PATCH-PENDING-VERDICT-CLASS
new_control_requirements.description: Compliance verdicts must distinguish three states: (a) binary patch deployed (vulnerability eliminated), (b) vendor-mitigation rule active, no binary patch (residual risk: any defect in the mitigation rule reopens the vulnerability), (c) no mitigation, no patch (full exposure). Audit reports must surface (b) as a distinct compensating-control state with an associated time-bound action item, not as a 'patched per SLA' outcome.
new_control_requirements.evidence: The LG N1A1 is permanently in state (c) and no amount of scheduling moves it to (a): the researcher's write-up records firmware 3718.510 dating from June 2011, a last release in December 2011 whose download link is dead, and an update endpoint at lgodd.lge.com that no longer responds, and no LG advisory for this CVE could be located. Naming that state explicitly is what stops the appliance being carried on a report as 'patch pending' against a KEV due date of 2022-04-15 that no patch will ever satisfy. The network restriction on TCP 8000 that an operator can apply is state (b) at best, and the control's requirement that (b) carry a time-bound action item is what turns it into a decommissioning date rather than an indefinite compensating control on a device where reaching the web port reaches root.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: For the LG N1A1 the 'patch availability' term never resolves, so the clock starts at CISA's 2022-03-25 listing and the only branch of this control that can be satisfied is documented compensating controls. Applied honestly to this appliance that means one thing: blocking TCP 8000 from every untrusted segment and removing any internet port forward or UPnP mapping, documented as the mitigation and dated for removal of the hardware. The reason the documentation matters more than usual here is the sudoers entry the researcher published — 'www-data ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD: ALL' — which makes reachability of the web port equivalent to root, so the compensating control is load-bearing in full rather than a hardening measure layered over a patched device.

CVE-2018-6961.name: VMware SD-WAN Edge by VeloCloud Command Injection Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: An unauthenticated POST to the Edge's local web UI diagnostics endpoint carries shell command substitution inside the ping, traceroute or DNS-lookup target. The Edge builds its shell command from that value, the substitution executes as root, and the attacker owns the appliance terminating the branch's SD-WAN overlay.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none — PR:N; the published request sends an empty auth_token field and is answered, so the diagnostics path performs no authentication of its own
attack_vector.complexity: high — AC:H; not because the injection is hard but because the local web UI is disabled by default and VMware states it should not be enabled on untrusted networks, so exploitation depends on a configuration state the attacker cannot create
attack_vector.ai_factor: The public exploit is credited to ParagonSec of Critical Start on Exploit-DB 44959. VMSA-2018-0011.2 thanks 'Cory Mathews, Quentin Rhoads-Herrera, and Maggie Ligon of Critical Start and security researcher Brian Sullivan from Tevora for independently reporting this issue to us.' Nothing available indicates automated discovery.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Leaving the local web UI disabled, or disabling it where a turn-up or support session enabled it — this removes the path with no maintenance window — and separately moving Edge software to 3.1.2, preferring a release from which the component has been removed.
prevention.adequacy: The configuration step is complete and immediate, which makes it the better first move. It relies on knowing the current enabled state at every site, and on a large Edge fleet that readback is the work.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Alerting on POST requests to /scripts/ajaxPortal.lua carrying _cmd=run_diagnostic with shell substitution characters in the destination or name parameter, and on any Edge whose local web UI answers at all.
detection.adequacy: Unusually tractable because the request shape is published and narrow. Its limit is placement — the traffic is branch-local to the Edge, so a detection point in the data centre never sees it.

response.what_would_have_worked: For an Edge that had the local web UI reachable while below the fixed level, verifying its configuration and routing against the Orchestrator's intended state rather than accepting the on-device configuration as authoritative.
response.adequacy: Root on the Edge means the on-device state is attacker-influenced, so the Orchestrator's intended configuration is the only trustworthy reference. It does not cover anything the attacker read from traffic transiting the appliance.

NIST-800-53-CM-7.gap: CM-7 closes this completely and its evidence cannot show that it has. VMware ships the local web UI disabled, so an exposed Edge is one where the component was enabled after deployment, and that is per-device drift rather than a build-standard question. Where least-functionality evidence for the fleet is a golden configuration plus a sample, it cannot tell an operator which individual branch Edges currently have that optional management surface answering — which is the only question that decides exposure here.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: SI-2 will eventually drive the Edge fleet to 3.1.2, and every step of it costs a branch outage because upgrading the appliance drops the site's overlay tunnels. Meanwhile disabling the local web UI closes the identical path with no window at all. The control measures the timeliness of the expensive remedy and has no field for the free one, so an organisation can be behind on SI-2 while being fully protected, or current on it while an un-upgraded site sits exposed for another quarter.

NIST-800-53-SC-7.gap: SC-7 for an SD-WAN deployment is assessed against the segmentation and steering policy the Edge enforces, which is the wrong object. The published request needs a route to the Edge's own local web UI and an empty auth_token, so any branch-side host satisfies the precondition regardless of what the overlay policy says. VMware's warning that the component should not be enabled on untrusted networks is precisely a statement about the boundary around that management surface — and it is not the boundary an SC-7 sample of the overlay examines.

NIS2-Art21-network-security.gap: The network-security measure is evidenced through what the Edge does for the network: segmentation, encryption, traffic steering, resilience. This defect sits underneath all of that. A diagnostics endpoint on the appliance's own management surface executes a shell command as root, so the attacker becomes the device that implements the measure rather than an entity the measure constrains, and every artefact demonstrating conformance was produced by the compromised appliance.

NIS2-Art21-patch-management.gap: Because each Edge upgrade takes the site's tunnels down, proportionate patch handling for a branch fleet resolves to whatever maintenance-window cadence that site can absorb. The measure is met and the population stays partly unknown.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: B4 asks for secure configuration and maintenance, and configuration is the half that decides this CVE: an Edge with the local web UI disabled is not exposed at any software version. Where the CAF evidence for a distributed branch estate is a documented build standard plus sampling, it cannot separate an Edge whose optional management surface was turned on after deployment from one that never was, and an unrecorded post-deployment change is precisely what produces an exposed site.

AU-Essential-8-App-Hardening.gap: User application hardening measures the applications users run — browsers, Office, PDF readers, Java — and produces the same class of outcome this CVE needs: disable the function that is not required. But the function here is an optional management application bundled into a network appliance, which is outside the strategy's population entirely, so the hardening action that would close the path can never appear in an Essential Eight assessment however mature the organisation's rating is.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: Patching applications is evidenced against feeds for software the organisation installs on hosts it manages, and Edge software is an appliance image pushed through the SD-WAN Orchestrator. It is neither an operating system nor an installed application in the sense the strategy measures, so a branch fleet sitting below 3.1.2 generates no finding — the maturity rating is a true statement about a population that excludes the appliance terminating every branch's traffic.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.9.gap: A.8.9 is the control this CVE is really testing, because the whole question is whether the enabled state of an optional appliance component is established, documented and monitored across a distributed fleet. The published exploit only works where the local web UI was turned on, so drift monitoring is the mechanism that answers 'which of my sites are exposed'. An A.8.9 implementation with a documented baseline and no per-Edge drift detection satisfies the control and cannot produce that answer.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: A.8.8 requires vulnerability information to be obtained and evaluated, and evaluation is obstructed here by the state of the record itself. The CVE fixes the boundary at prior to 3.1.0 while Exploit-DB 44959 and the ProjectDiscovery template are both titled for below 3.1.2, and VMware's advisory is no longer served at its published URL after the migration to Broadcom's portal. An intake process that files the CVE without resolving that per-model discrepancy cannot say whether an Edge running 3.1.1 is remediated or exposed.

new_control_requirements.name: PERIMETER-DEVICE-ZERODAY-SLA-TIER
new_control_requirements.description: Compliance frameworks must define a distinct patch SLA tier for pre-auth RCE on perimeter-trust-boundary devices (firewalls, VPN concentrators, WAFs, edge load-balancers). Tier requirement: vendor-mitigation deployed within 4 hours of KEV listing OR isolation of the vulnerable interface; standard 14/30-day SLAs do not apply because the device IS the trust boundary.
new_control_requirements.evidence: The NSX SD-WAN Edge by VeloCloud is the branch trust boundary — it terminates the overlay and steers, encrypts and forwards the site's traffic — and this is an unauthenticated command-injection path landing as root on it, with an exploit public since 2018-07-02 (Exploit-DB 44959) and EPSS at 0.86252, the 99.716th percentile, on 2026-08-17. The control's second branch is what makes it usable on this fleet: isolating the vulnerable interface here means disabling the local web UI, which VMware ships disabled by default, so the four-hour path is a configuration change rather than an appliance upgrade and needs no site outage. That matters against the 2022-03-25 KEV listing and 2022-04-15 due date, because an Edge upgrade to 3.1.2 drops the branch's tunnels and cannot be driven at KEV speed across a large estate.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: VMware's fix for the NSX SD-WAN Edge predates the 2022-03-25 KEV listing by years, so the clock for this CVE runs entirely from the listing and its 2022-04-15 due date. What this Edge fleet needs from the control is its insistence on verified mitigation: verification cannot be the Orchestrator's recorded software version alone, because the NVD record's prior-to-3.1.0 boundary reads 3.1.0 and 3.1.1 as fixed where VMSA-2018-0011.1 places them among the affected. The verifiable state is whether each Edge's local web UI answers at all — which is also the documented compensating control the SLA accepts while upgrades are scheduled against branch maintenance windows.

CVE-2018-8405.name: Microsoft DirectX Graphics Kernel Privilege Escalation Vulnerability (CVE-2018-8405)

attack_vector.description: A user who can already run code on a Windows host calls into the DirectX Graphics Kernel driver in a way that makes it mishandle an object in kernel memory, and converts that into execution in an elevated context. It is a second-stage flaw: it turns a foothold into ownership of the machine.
attack_vector.privileges_required: low — PR:L; the attacker needs a working account on the host, no more. An unprivileged standard user is enough, and no administrative right is consulted anywhere on the path.
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L, AV:L, UI:N; entirely local, no user interaction, no documented race or information-leak precondition. The real constraint is obtaining the initial foothold, not triggering the driver.
attack_vector.ai_factor: None recorded. The CVE Program record carries an empty credits array and MSRC names no acknowledgement, so neither a human nor an automated discovery route is established for this id.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Taking the 2018-08-14 cumulative update for the branch and completing the reboot, on every host including Server Core instances and any machine rebuilt from an older image.
prevention.adequacy: Complete against the flaw and useless against the reason it persists. The update has existed since 2018; the hosts still carrying it are ones no patch cycle reaches, and BOD 22-01 assigns a date without giving an operator a way to find a machine restored from a pre-2018 backup.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Alerting on token-elevation transitions with no service or scheduled-task parent, and on dxgkrnl.sys bugchecks arriving outside a driver-change window.
detection.adequacy: Weak on its own. A successful exploit is quiet — no file dropped, no module loaded, no crash — so the reliable signal is the post-escalation action rather than the escalation, and the crash signal only fires on attempts that fail.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treating a host where this fired as fully compromised: rebuild rather than repair, and rotate every credential that was cached or used on it during the exposure window.
response.adequacy: Correct but late, and bounded by the KEV ransomware flag — if the escalation was the step before encryption, the response window has already closed by the time the alert is triaged.

NIST-800-53-AC-6.gap: An estate can hold a clean AC-6 assessment — every account scoped, no standing administrators — and remain exactly as exposed to this CVE as one with none, because the attacker exploits it from the ordinary user rights AC-6 grants. The control's evidence is the account model, and the account model is never consulted when a kernel-mode display driver mishandles an object.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: SI-2 remediation timeframes ran from the 2018-08-14 vendor release and were met years before CISA's 2022-03-28 listing, so the control was genuinely satisfied and the CVE still sits in KEV. What SI-2 does not model is regression: a host reimaged from a 2018 golden image or restored from an old backup re-acquires the vulnerable dxgkrnl.sys and reports as configuration-compliant, not as a remediation failure.

NIS2-Art21-patch-management.gap: The Article 21 evidence pack for an entity running this estate would show a maintenance process meeting its own deadlines in 2018 and a risk register carrying the Windows RT 8.1 and Server 2012 R2 residue as accepted exceptions. Those exceptions are where a KEV-listed escalation carrying a ransomware-use flag actually lives, and nothing in the article's process framing forces them back onto the remediation clock.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: B4 evidence is the build baseline and the patch ring, and both look correct here. The specific thing they do not measure is restart completion: this fix replaces a kernel-mode driver, so the update record and the running kernel diverge for as long as a host stays up, and a fleet with a long uptime tail carries the defect with a compliant-looking system-security attestation.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: The operating-system patching strategy measures a window from vendor release, and for a 2018-08-14 update that window closed on any estate still applying cumulative updates. It is directionless about backward drift — a machine reimaged from a stale image, restored from a 2018 backup, or delivered preloaded by a supplier — so a Windows 8.1 or Server 2012 R2 host that reacquires the vulnerable driver re-enters the affected population without re-entering the metric.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: A.8.8 is evidenced through scanner coverage and a remediation register, and a credentialed build-number scan is accurate here. The failure is prioritisation and scope: an EPSS score of 0.03444 at 2026-08-17 ranks this near the bottom of any risk-ordered register despite CISA's ransomware flag, and the scan reaches Server Core and Windows RT 8.1 instances only where the asset inventory it runs against enumerates them.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: This is the case where the control's 'whichever is later' clause carries the whole requirement. Microsoft shipped the DXGKRNL fix on 2018-08-14 and CISA listed CVE-2018-8405 on 2022-03-28 with knownRansomwareCampaignUse set to Known and a 2022-04-18 due date — so patch availability preceded the listing by more than three and a half years, and the clock that matters is the one the listing opened. An estate that took the 2018 update satisfies it; the hosts that do not are the ones no patch cycle reaches, and the control forces them to be enumerated against the KEV date rather than closed on the release date.

CVE-2018-8406.name: Microsoft DirectX Graphics Kernel Privilege Escalation Vulnerability (CVE-2018-8406)

attack_vector.description: An already-logged-on user runs a crafted application that makes the DirectX Graphics Kernel driver mishandle an object in kernel memory, and rides the resulting defect into an elevated context. It is the escalation step of a chain, not an entry point.
attack_vector.privileges_required: low — PR:L; Microsoft's own text sets the bar at 'log on to the system, and then run a specially crafted application', so any working account on the host qualifies.
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L, AV:L, UI:N; no remote reach, no victim action, and no documented timing or memory-layout precondition. The exploit's cost is entirely in getting the initial account.
attack_vector.ai_factor: Nothing recorded. The CVE Program credits array is empty and MSRC publishes no acknowledgement for this id, so no discovery route — human or tool-assisted — is established.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: One pass of the 2018-08-14 cumulative update across every Windows 10 branch and every Windows Server 2016 and Server 1709/1803 instance, with the reboot completed and the result recorded against all four identifiers from that release.
prevention.adequacy: The update itself is complete. What it does not do is enforce the enumeration: BOD 22-01 assigns a date per identifier, and an operator working id by id can close the calendar item while leaving Server Core instances outside the agent inventory untouched.

detection.what_would_have_worked: A rule for token elevation inside an interactive session with no legitimate elevation parent, correlated with dxgkrnl.sys bugchecks on the same host.
detection.adequacy: Partial. The correlation is what makes it usable — elevations alone are too common to alert on, and the driver bugcheck only appears when an attempt fails, so a clean exploit produces neither half on its own.

response.what_would_have_worked: Rebuilding any host where the escalation is suspected and rotating credentials that were present on it, rather than patching in place and closing the ticket.
response.adequacy: Sound in principle, and it costs a rebuild of whichever Windows 10 or Server 2016 host is implicated. Since the update remediates the code and removes nothing an attacker already installed, patch-and-close is the specific way this response fails.

NIST-800-53-SI-4.gap: SI-4 is satisfied by demonstrating that monitoring exists and is forwarded, and an estate can prove both while holding no rule that would fire on this path. The exploit writes no file, loads no module and creates no service; its only observable is a privilege transition that also describes every legitimate elevation on the host, so coverage without a tuned exclusion set is coverage of nothing here.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: The remediation register treats CVE-2018-8406 as one row among four from a single Microsoft release, and rows close independently. That structure lets an estate report substantial progress against the release while every affected host remains unrestarted and therefore unremediated against all four, because they share one update and one reboot rather than four.

NIS2-Art21-vulnerability-management.gap: An entity's Article 21 vulnerability-handling process consumed the 2018-08-14 advisory and closed it correctly. Nothing in the article requires that closure to be revisited when CISA reclassified the same flaw as actively exploited on 2022-03-28 with a ransomware-use flag, so a compliant process holds a closed finding against a live KEV entry and no clause makes the two meet.

UK-CAF-C1.gap: C1 is assessed on monitoring capability and coverage rather than on the specific detections in place. An organisation can evidence full log collection from its Windows Server 2016 fleet and pass, while the detection content that would surface a DXGKRNL escalation — a privilege transition with no legitimate elevation parent — has never been authored, because it is a tuning exercise the outcome does not name.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: The requirement quoted from the Essential Eight Maturity Model is patches "applied within one month of release" (ACSC, Maturity Level One), and this id's fix arrives inside the 2018-08-14 Windows package as a driver the running kernel keeps loaded until the host restarts. Where a Windows 10 1507-1803, Windows Server 2016 or Windows Server 1709/1803 host took that package inside the month and has stayed up since, the window is met and the loaded dxgkrnl.sys is still the pre-fix one — which is the population CISA's 2022-03-28 listing, due 2022-04-18 with ransomware use recorded, is aimed at.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.16.gap: A.8.16 requires monitoring for anomalous behaviour, and the anomaly here is indistinguishable from routine administration unless the legitimate elevation parents are excluded first. An auditor reviewing A.8.16 sees monitoring in place across the estate; the operator has no rule that separates a service-initiated elevation from one produced by a mishandled kernel object, so the control is met and the behaviour is invisible.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CISA listed CVE-2018-8406 on 2022-03-28 with a due date of 2022-04-18 and knownRansomwareCampaignUse set to Known, against a Microsoft fix released 2018-08-14. The control's value on this Windows 10 and Server 2016 population is that it starts a clock on the listing date for a defect the estate's own records had marked closed years earlier, and it requires verified mitigation — which for a kernel-mode display driver means the reboot completed, not the update downloaded.

CVE-2018-8414.name: Microsoft Windows Shell Remote Code Execution Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: An attacker sends a small XML file with a .SettingContent-ms extension, or embeds one in an Office document. It looks like a shortcut to a Windows settings page. When the recipient opens it, the shell reads the <DeepLink> element and runs whatever command line it contains, as that user.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none — PR:N; the attacker holds no account on the target and needs none. What they need instead is the recipient's click, and the impact scales with whatever rights that person happens to hold.
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L with UI:R; there is no memory corruption and no reliability variable, so opening the file executes the command deterministically. The constraint is delivery, and the extension was not on Office 2016's blocked-embedding list.
attack_vector.ai_factor: None. Matt Nelson found this by reading a Windows 10 file format and testing what its fields accepted; the 2018-06-11 SpecterOps post describes manual analysis with no automated discovery component.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Blocking the .SettingContent-ms extension at the mail gateway, on file shares and as an Office OLE embedded object type — available from 2018-06-11, nine weeks before the vendor fix, and independent of endpoint build.
prevention.adequacy: Effective, and available from 2018-06-11 — nine weeks ahead of the fix — but only to someone willing to block an unfamiliar Windows extension before there was a CVE to point at. BOD 22-01 arrived in 2022 and mandates the update rather than the extension block, so the action that would have helped in June 2018 is the one no framework asked for.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Alerting on explorer.exe spawning a shell or scripting host shortly after a file open, and on mshta.exe fetching content from a non-corporate host.
detection.adequacy: Usable, and noisy without tuning — explorer.exe legitimately launches shells. The mshta.exe egress signal is the sharper of the two, and it is specific to the downloader shape rather than to this CVE, so it also catches unrelated activity and misses payloads that avoid MSHTA.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treating a confirmed open as code execution at the user's privilege: isolate the workstation, review what that account could reach, and rotate its credentials.
response.adequacy: Appropriate, with an important limit — the command runs at the user's own rights, so on an account with local administrator the response scope is the machine, and where the user held broader access it is everything that account could reach.

NIST-800-53-SI-3.gap: Malicious-code protection assumes there is malicious code to identify. The delivered artefact is XML naming a command line, and the executing process is cmd.exe or mshta.exe started by the shell through a documented path, so a fully current anti-malware deployment has nothing anomalous to match on until the second-stage payload lands — by which point execution has already happened at the user's privilege.

NIST-800-53-CM-7.gap: CM-7 is the control that could have removed this before the CVE existed, and only in a form most assessments never take. Least-functionality evidence enumerates installed applications, running services and open ports; it does not enumerate shell file-type handlers, so an operating-system-supplied handler for a shortcut format no business process uses survives every review as part of the platform.

NIS2-Art21-vulnerability-handling.gap: The nine weeks between publication on 2018-06-11 and the fix on 2018-08-14 are the exposure, and they exist because MSRC assessed the report as below the servicing bar on 2018-06-04. Article 21 binds the entity running the systems, so its handling process — however compliant — had no vendor fix to consume and no clause requiring a compensating control while a public technique had no patch.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: System security assessed as build currency reaches this only from 2018-08-14, and the estate's real lever was earlier and elsewhere: whether a .SettingContent-ms file could arrive by mail or leave the web proxy at all. A B4 outcome evidenced through patch compliance is met on a fleet that still accepts the delivery vehicle for whatever the next unblocked shell handler turns out to be.

AU-Essential-8-App-Hardening.gap: User application hardening addresses browsers, Office macros, Flash, advertisements and Java. Nelson's post records the extension as absent from Office 2016's blocked-embedding list, so an Office configuration hardened against every one of those named categories still passes the object to the shell handler. The strategy hardens the application; the code runs one delegation past it.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.7.gap: A.8.7 combines anti-malware technology with awareness, and both are weakly placed here. There is no binary to sign, and the lure presents as a Windows settings shortcut rather than as an executable or a macro-bearing document, which is the shape awareness programmes train against. Full A.8.7 evidence coexists with a single click producing attacker-controlled command execution.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: The 'or documented compensating controls' clause is what this Windows Shell defect needs. Microsoft's record shows the flaw publicly disclosed and exploited before the 2018-08-14 fix, and CISA listed it on 2022-03-25 with a 2022-04-15 due date; blocking .SettingContent-ms at the mail gateway and as an Office OLE object type was deployable from Nelson's 2018-06-11 publication and required no endpoint change, which is exactly the mitigation an SLA written around patches alone would not have credited.

new_control_requirements.name: PROTECTION-MECHANISM-FAILURE-CLASS-REGRESSION
new_control_requirements.description: Detonation chambers, EDR rules, and AppLocker/WDAC policies covering protection-mechanism classes (MOTW, SmartScreen, AMSI, ASR, WDAC, Driver Block Rules) must include class-level regression testing executed on every patch deployment, not just one-off bypass-CVE remediation. The test battery for class-X must include all historic class-X bypass primitives — incomplete patches re-introduce risk that one-off testing does not detect.
new_control_requirements.evidence: This CVE is a protection-mechanism failure rather than a memory-safety bug: Nelson's 2018-06-11 post records that the .SettingContent-ms extension was not covered by Office 2016's OLE embedding blocklist and notes ASR rules did not appear to work on Office installed from the Windows Store. The Windows Shell fix of 2018-08-14 repaired one handler and left the blocklist question open, which is why the regression battery — detonating each historic shell and Office embedding bypass on every deployment — is what tells an operator whether the class is closed rather than whether this identifier is.

attack_vector.description: Any local process can ask Task Scheduler to set a security descriptor on a path under C:\Windows\Tasks. The service does the write with its own privileges instead of the caller's, so an unprivileged user hard-links a name in that directory to a protected file, asks for a permissive descriptor, and gets write access to the target. Overwriting a binary that a privileged scheduled task runs turns that into SYSTEM.
attack_vector.privileges_required: low — PR:L; the RPC method is reachable by any local process, so a standard user account with the ability to run code is the entire requirement.
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L, AV:L, UI:N; no race, no memory-layout dependency, no victim interaction. The only judgement involved is picking a target binary that something privileged will execute afterwards.
attack_vector.ai_factor: None. SandboxEscaper published the flaw and a working proof of concept directly, 0patch reverse-engineered the same drop, and neither account nor ESET's campaign report describes automated or AI-assisted discovery.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: The 2018-09-11 Windows update with the reboot completed; before that date, 0patch's 2018-08-31 micropatch on the covered builds, or removing privileged scheduled tasks pointing at binaries an unprivileged user could target.
prevention.adequacy: Complete once the update lands, and unavailable for the fifteen days that mattered. BOD 22-01 arrived three and a half years after the campaign, so it governs the residue rather than the event; the micropatch is what covered the gap, on 64-bit Windows 7, Server 2008, Server 2016, Server 1803 and Windows 10 1607/1709/1803.

detection.what_would_have_worked: File-integrity monitoring on binaries that privileged scheduled tasks execute, with alerting on DACL changes as well as content changes, plus hard-link creation under C:\Windows\Tasks.
detection.adequacy: The DACL-change half is the useful half. Content-only integrity monitoring produces a benign-looking result for an updater rewriting itself, which is exactly why ESET found PowerPool choosing GoogleUpdate.exe rather than a system binary.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treating a host with an unexplained DACL change on a task-executed binary as SYSTEM-compromised: rebuild, and rotate every credential exposed on it, since the exploit yields the highest local privilege.
response.adequacy: Correct and it must not stop at the patch. The September 2018 update repairs the impersonation and removes nothing PowerPool or a later actor wrote through the primitive, so a patched host with an unexamined replaced binary is still carrying the outcome.

NIST-800-53-AC-6.gap: Least privilege has no purchase on a service that stops consulting the caller's rights. 0patch's analysis pins the defect on Task Scheduler failing to impersonate during SetSecurityFile, which means the operation runs at the service's privilege whatever the calling account holds — an estate with zero standing administrators reaches SYSTEM by the same two steps as one with local admin handed out freely.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: SI-2's clock could not start until 2018-09-11, and by then ESET had already published a campaign report dated 2018-09-05. Flaw remediation as a control assumes the vendor fix leads the exploit; here the working exploit led by fifteen days, and the only interim fix was a third-party in-memory micropatch that an SI-2 programme scoped to vendor updates has no way to record as remediation.

NIS2-Art21-incident-handling.gap: The incident presents as routine software maintenance. ESET records the target as GoogleUpdate.exe, a binary whose whole job is to rewrite itself, so the artefacts an incident-handling process would collect — a changed file, a task running on schedule — carry no anomaly on their face. Compliance with the article establishes that a process exists; it does not supply the DACL-change rule that separates the updater from the attacker.

UK-CAF-D1.gap: Response and recovery planning is evidenced by tested plans, and this needed a branch a plan only has if it was written for it: a confirmed-exploited local escalation with a public proof of concept and no vendor patch for fifteen days. The decision that mattered on 2018-08-31 was whether to accept a third-party micropatch on production hosts — a change-control and risk-acceptance question, taken under time pressure, that a plan tested against outage and ransomware scenarios has no rehearsed answer for.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: The strategy's window opens at vendor release, so it was structurally silent from 2018-08-27, when the proof of concept was published, to 2018-09-11, when Microsoft shipped — the precise period ESET places the PowerPool campaign in. It also says nothing about the interim action available: enumerating which privileged scheduled tasks execute binaries reachable by an unprivileged user.

ISO-27001-2022-A.5.7.gap: Threat intelligence implemented as advisory-feed subscription would have delivered this on 2018-09-11. The actual signals were a repository drop on 2018-08-27, a reverse-engineering write-up on 2018-08-31 and a named-actor report on 2018-09-05, none of which are advisory feeds. An A.5.7 attestation can be entirely truthful and still describe an intake that arrives after the campaign it was meant to warn about.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Windows Task Scheduler is the asset and the timeline is the argument: SandboxEscaper published a working exploit on 2018-08-27, ESET identified PowerPool using it two days later, Microsoft shipped on 2018-09-11, and CISA listed the id on 2022-03-28 with knownRansomwareCampaignUse 'Known' and a 2022-04-18 due date. The control's three accepted mitigations map exactly onto what was available at each point — documented compensating controls in the first four days, 0patch's 2018-08-31 micropatch after that, and the vendor update from 2018-09-11.

new_control_requirements.name: MITIGATION-ACTIVE-PATCH-PENDING-VERDICT-CLASS
new_control_requirements.description: Compliance verdicts must distinguish three states: (a) binary patch deployed (vulnerability eliminated), (b) vendor-mitigation rule active, no binary patch (residual risk: any defect in the mitigation rule reopens the vulnerability), (c) no mitigation, no patch (full exposure). Audit reports must surface (b) as a distinct compensating-control state with an associated time-bound action item, not as a 'patched per SLA' outcome.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Between 2018-08-31 and 2018-09-11 a Windows estate running 0patch's micropatch was in state (b) against this Task Scheduler defect and had no way to say so: the micropatch inserts an RpcImpersonateClient call into a running process, so the on-disk binary and the reported patch level are both unchanged, and it covered 64-bit Windows 7, Server 2008, Server 2016, Server 1803 and Windows 10 1607, 1709 and 1803 — leaving Windows 8.1, RT 8.1, Server 2012 and Server 2012 R2 hosts in state (c) inside the same estate. Reporting both as a single figure hides which hosts ESET's PowerPool campaign could actually still take.

CVE-2019-0903.name: Microsoft GDI Remote Code Execution Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: An attacker crafts graphics content that makes the Windows Graphics Device Interface mishandle an object in memory, then gets it in front of a user — a website they are convinced to visit, or a document delivered through mail or a file share. Rendering it runs the attacker's code at that user's privilege.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none — PR:N; the attacker needs no account and no prior access to the target, only a route to put content in front of someone who has one.
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L with UI:R; NVD and Microsoft both record AC:L, but no root-cause analysis is public, so nothing establishes how reliable exploitation is in practice. The stated constraint is the user's action, not the trigger.
attack_vector.ai_factor: Unknown. The CVE Program record carries no credits and Microsoft publishes no acknowledgement, so neither a human researcher nor a fuzzing pipeline is established as the discovery route.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: The 2019-05-14 update with the reboot completed, plus constraining what content reaches the renderer on hosts that cannot take it — attachment filtering, web filtering, and isolated viewing of untrusted documents.
prevention.adequacy: Complete for the supported matrix and unavailable for part of it. The affected set includes Windows 7 SP1 and Server 2008, past end of extended support, where BOD 22-01's instruction to apply updates per vendor instructions terminates in replacement rather than a patch.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Alerting on a rendering or document process crashing or spawning a shell shortly after content is opened, and clustering Windows Error Reporting entries that name graphics modules.
detection.adequacy: Modest. Successful exploitation need not crash anything, so the crash signal captures failed attempts and unlucky ones; the process-lineage signal is the reliable half and it fires after code is already running.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treating a confirmed render as user-privilege code execution: isolate the workstation, enumerate what that account could reach, rotate its credentials, and check for persistence written in the same window.
response.adequacy: Right in shape, weak on scoping, because the public record gives no payload or campaign detail to hunt against — CISA's KEV listing is the only exploitation evidence, and it names no actor, no timeframe and no artefact.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: Flaw remediation works while fixes keep arriving. For the Windows 7 SP1 and Server 2008 SP2 and 2008 R2 SP1 hosts inside NVD's CPE set the supply has stopped, so an SI-2 programme records them as exceptions rather than as assets whose only remaining action is replacement. The control measures the speed of a process that, for those machines, has no further input.

NIST-800-53-SI-3.gap: The first stage is a graphics object crafted to corrupt memory inside a signed operating-system component, not a file with executable properties, so malicious-code protection has nothing to classify until a second stage lands. An estate can evidence current anti-malware on every endpoint in the 2019 matrix and still have no coverage of the moment the renderer is subverted.

NIS2-Art21-patch-management.gap: Consuming the 2019-05-14 release on schedule satisfies the maintenance requirement and leaves the end-of-support population outside the process entirely, carried as accepted risk. With an EPSS of 0.21713 at 2026-08-17 and a KEV listing from 2022-03-25, those acceptances describe an unauthenticated-delivery code-execution flaw that the article's process framing never returns to.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: B4 evidence comes from the managed estate's build baseline and update ring, and this CVE's matrix runs from Windows 7 SP1 and Server 2008 SP2 to Windows 10 1903 and Server 2019. Where that span crosses into machines outside the management plane — a supplier-owned appliance host, an instrument controller, a Server 2008 R2 box kept for one application — the B4 evidence is drawn from everything except the population that carries the residual exposure.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: The strategy presumes a vendor update exists to apply within a window. That holds for Windows 10 and Server 2016 or later and fails for the Windows 7 SP1 and Server 2008 hosts in the same CPE set, where the honest action is replacement. Reporting a compliant patch window across the supported population measures the part of the estate this CVE no longer threatens.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.9.gap: Configuration management is the control that could bound a client-side rendering flaw on an unpatchable host, by deciding what content reaches the renderer at all. Where A.8.9 evidence is baselines and change records for build state, an organisation holds a fully compliant configuration-management system that has never taken a decision about accepted attachment types or isolated document viewing — the two settings that matter on a Windows 7 SP1 or Server 2008 host with no fix available.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Microsoft released the GDI fix on 2019-05-14 and CISA listed CVE-2019-0903 on 2022-03-25 with a 2022-04-15 due date, so the clock that binds is the listing's. The clause that carries the weight on this Windows matrix is 'or documented compensating controls': the affected set includes Windows 7 SP1 and Server 2008 SP2 and 2008 R2 SP1, which are past end of extended support, and for those hosts the only mitigation an operator can deploy is constraining what content reaches the renderer — which the control accepts as a mitigation state rather than leaving them unrepresented.

CVE-2019-1003030.name: Jenkins Matrix Project Plugin Remote Code Execution Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: A user who can control what a Jenkins pipeline contains writes a Groovy script crafted so that the work happens during parsing, compilation and instantiation — before the sandbox that is supposed to constrain it is applied. The code then runs on the controller JVM, with the controller's access to credentials, agents and build output.
attack_vector.privileges_required: low — PR:L; the Jenkins advisory sets the bar at users able to control the contents of a pipeline, which on a controller with self-service jobs or repository-supplied Jenkinsfiles is an ordinary developer account rather than an administrator.
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L, AV:N, UI:N, and S:C because the escape crosses out of the sandbox's scope into the controller's. The bypass is structural rather than probabilistic, so there is no reliability variable.
attack_vector.ai_factor: None. The Jenkins advisory credits Georgy Noseevich (@webpentest) of SolidLab for both halves of SECURITY-1336; this is manual review of when a sandbox is applied relative to script compilation, with no automated discovery described.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Upgrading Pipeline: Groovy to 2.64 and Script Security to 1.54 in one pass and restarting the controller, plus withdrawing pipeline-authoring rights from accounts that do not need them.
prevention.adequacy: Effective and repeatedly incomplete in one specific way: the plugin upgrade is inert until the controller restarts, and a restart evicts running builds, so the deferral that follows is where a controller sits at 2.64 on paper and 2.63 in memory.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Alerting on the controller JVM spawning shell processes outside the agent path, and on controller-process reads of credentials.xml and the secrets directory.
detection.adequacy: Good coverage of the outcome, none of the bypass. The sandbox escape itself produces no log line — no script-approval request is generated because the approval mechanism is never reached — so the first evidence is whatever the attacker does with the controller.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treating a suspected escape as a build-system compromise: rotate every credential stored in Jenkins, review build artefacts produced during the window, and audit agent connections and job definitions for changes.
response.adequacy: Necessary and wide. Credentials are stored in Jenkins so builds can reach source control, registries and deployment targets, so the rotation scope is whatever this controller could authenticate to, and the artefact review has to cover everything it built while exposed.

NIST-800-53-AC-3.gap: Access enforcement evidence for Jenkins is the role-to-permission mapping, and that mapping is honoured exactly as designed here. The advisory places the bypass during parsing, compilation and script instantiation, which is upstream of the sandbox's enforcement point, so the control is satisfied and the enforcement mechanism it depends on never runs.

NIST-800-53-CM-7.gap: Least functionality on a build server is assessed against host services and packages, not the plugin inventory. A controller carrying workflow-cps 2.63 holds a code-execution engine because that is how Pipeline works, and CM-7 evidence has no line item that would prompt an operator to justify each installed plugin or to notice this one is two versions behind its fix.

NIS2-Art21-supply-chain.gap: The article's supply-chain requirement points outward at suppliers and service providers, while the asset at risk is the entity's own build controller — the CVSS S:C rating exists because the escape reaches it. An entity can hold complete supplier assurance documentation while a developer-level account rewrites the artefacts that assurance is about, because the build system is treated as internal infrastructure rather than as supply chain.

UK-CAF-B2.gap: Identity and access control evidence shows Jenkins users authenticated and authorised to defined roles, and the attacker is one of them — PR:L means every access decision on the path was made correctly. B2 has no outcome covering whether the mechanism that constrains an authorised principal inside a script actually holds, which is the only thing that failed.

AU-Essential-8-App-Hardening.gap: The strategy's subject is the software users browse and read documents with, so a Jenkins controller falls outside it entirely. Nothing in a user-application-hardening assessment causes workflow-cps 2.63 to be inventoried or causes the Groovy sandbox to be recognised as a hardening control whose version currency is worth measuring.

ISO-27001-2022-A.5.21.gap: ICT supply-chain management is normally scoped to contracted suppliers and their agreements, which leaves a community plugin ecosystem outside it. That framing is also how Red Hat OpenShift Container Platform 3.11 shipped the affected plugin, fixed by RHSA-2019:0739, to operators whose supplier assurance covered the platform vendor while the exposure arrived inside the image.

new_control_requirements.name: INCOMPLETE-PATCH-SEQUENCE-SEVERITY-MULTIPLIER
new_control_requirements.description: Vulnerability-management programs must apply a severity multiplier when a CVE is the Nth in an incomplete-patch sequence on the same primitive (third MOTW bypass, second AMSI bypass, etc.).
