Framework controls treating each CVE as discrete obscure the structural defect; the Nth CVE in a sequence implies that future bypasses on the same primitive are likely.
new_control_requirements.evidence: The Groovy sandbox is the primitive and this is one bypass in a run of them: the Jenkins advisory of 2019-03-06 issues SECURITY-1336 as two CVEs at once — CVE-2019-1003030 in Pipeline: Groovy 2.63 and CVE-2019-1003029 in Script Security 1.53 — and Metasploit's jenkins_metaprogramming module lists CVE-2019-1003000, 1003001, 1003002, 1003005 and 1003029 against the same family from the preceding advisory cycle. A programme scoring each on its own obscures the conclusion an operator needs: on a controller reachable by developer-level accounts, the sandbox is not a boundary to plan around.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Jenkins fixed this in Pipeline: Groovy 2.64 on 2019-03-06 and CISA listed it on 2022-03-25 with a 2022-04-15 due date, so the binding clock is the listing's. The word doing the work for this product is 'verified': a Jenkins plugin upgrade is inert until the controller process restarts, so the verification that satisfies the control is /pluginManager/api/json reporting workflow-cps at 2.64 or above on a restarted controller, not a completed download — and the same query must show Script Security at 1.54 or above for the other half of SECURITY-1336.

CVE-2019-10068.name: Kentico Xperience Deserialization of Untrusted Data Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: One HTTP POST to the Kentico content-staging service, carrying a SOAP body whose security headers are never validated, reaches a .NET deserialiser with attacker-controlled object input and executes code on the server. The published proof of concept uses that to write a web shell into the web root and then drive it with a query parameter.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none — PR:N; no account, no session and no prior foothold. The only requirement is being able to send an HTTP request to the site, which for a public-facing CMS is the entire internet.
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L, AV:N, UI:N; a single request with a known .NET gadget chain, no memory corruption and no timing element. The 2026-08-17 EPSS of 0.96254 at the 99.875th percentile reflects exactly that.
attack_vector.ai_factor: None. Manoj Cherukuri and Justin LeMay found it by examining how the staging web service handled SOAP authentication, published through Aon Cyber Labs on 2019-04-15; no automated or AI-assisted component is described.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Applying hotfix 12.0.15, 11.0.48 or 10.0.52 to the matching line, and — independent of the hotfix — blocking /CMSPages/Staging/ at the reverse proxy on any deployment that does not use content staging.
prevention.adequacy: The hotfix closes it and the reachability control is what an operator can deploy the same afternoon.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Alerting on any request to /CMSPages/Staging/SyncServer.asmx from outside the synchronisation source addresses, and on w3wp.exe spawning a shell process.
detection.adequacy: Strong here, because the endpoint has one legitimate caller set and everything else is anomalous by definition. The weakness is retention — the exploit is a single request, so a gateway that keeps only summary logs will not hold the evidence long enough to answer whether it was ever sent.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treating a confirmed request as code execution: hunt the web root and application directories for files written outside a deployment window, rotate the application-pool identity and any credentials in the CMS configuration, and rebuild rather than patch in place.
response.adequacy: This is the one the proof of concept makes non-optional — it drops x.aspx and invokes it, so a hotfix applied over an existing web shell produces a fully patched server that the attacker still controls.

NIST-800-53-SC-7.gap: Boundary protection evidence for a public CMS shows a firewall, a reverse proxy and often a WAF, all correctly deployed. None of them narrow the exposure, because the vulnerable path sits on the same host and port the site is meant to serve; closing it requires a path-level rule on /CMSPages/Staging/, which is a decision no boundary-protection assessment prompts anyone to make.

NIS2-Art21-network-security.gap: Network-security measures around the hosting environment address who can reach the server, and this attacker is meant to reach it — the site is public. What fails is inside the application: an endpoint that deserialises attacker-supplied .NET objects before checking the request's security headers. Segmentation evidence for a Kentico deployment is complete and reduces a single-request pre-auth path by nothing.

NIS2-Art21-incident-handling.gap: The incident-handling process will record the hotfix as the remediating action, which is where it goes wrong for this flaw. The published proof of concept writes x.aspx into the web root before doing anything else, so 12.0.15 removes the way in and leaves the way back; a handling process with no rebuild step closes a pre-auth code-execution finding over a live implant.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: System Security evidenced through CMS patch currency reaches this only from the hotfix onward, and says nothing about the endpoint's presence. Kentico installs the staging service regardless of whether content staging is configured, so a deployment that has never used it can hold a clean B4 assessment while answering /CMSPages/Staging/SyncServer.asmx to unauthenticated callers from the internet.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: The application patching strategy measures the window from release to application and presumes the package can be obtained.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.28.gap: Secure coding is the control this CVE is an instance of, and it binds whoever wrote the staging service rather than whoever runs it. An organisation deploying Kentico evidences A.8.28 across its own templates, widgets and integrations — all of which can be exemplary — while the sink that deserialises the attacker's gadget chain sits in vendor code the programme has no visibility into and no ability to review.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Kentico shipped hotfix 12.0.15 on 2019-03-22 and CISA listed CVE-2019-10068 on 2022-03-25 with a 2022-04-15 due date, so the binding clock is the listing's. The control's compensating-control branch is what makes it usable on this product: an operator who cannot reach the hotfix — 9.x has no fixed build in NVD's CPE set — can still satisfy it within the window by blocking /CMSPages/Staging/ at the reverse proxy, which removes the only precondition a pre-auth flaw with a 2026-08-17 EPSS of 0.96254 has.

new_control_requirements.name: PERIMETER-COMPROMISE-REBUILD-NOT-PATCH
new_control_requirements.description: Pre-rehearsed IR runbook for any perimeter device that suffers a pre-auth RCE CVE in active exploitation MUST default to config-exfil + rebuild + credential rotation, not patch-in-place. Patch-in-place leaves attacker-installed implants intact.
new_control_requirements.evidence: A public-facing Kentico instance is the internet-boundary asset this control's default applies to, and the exploit makes the point concretely: the proof of concept at github.com/cianananan/CVE-2019-10068-PoC writes x.aspx into the web root and drives it as /x.aspx?c=whoami, so a hotfix to 12.0.15 applied over it produces a fully patched server the attacker still owns. With CISA listing the id on 2022-03-25 and the exposure window running back to 2019, rebuild plus rotation of the application-pool identity and the credentials in the CMS configuration is the only action that reaches what the entry path already delivered.

CVE-2019-11043.name: PHP FastCGI Process Manager (FPM) Buffer Overflow Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: An encoded newline in the request URL underflows env_path_info in php-fpm's fpm_main.c, and a follow-on FCGI_PUTENV write past the buffer overwrites a FastCGI data-segment pointer, letting the attacker inject a PHP_VALUE ini directive and reach unauthenticated remote code execution.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none — PR:N; any web client can reach the PHP location on a vulnerable nginx config
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L; the public tool brute-forces the aligning query length, but the target must run the specific nginx fastcgi_split_path_info pattern
attack_vector.ai_factor: None. Found by a human at Real World CTF and weaponized by named researchers.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Upgrading PHP to 7.1.33/7.2.24/7.3.11 and restarting php-fpm, or adding try_files $uri =404 to remove the underflow reachability.
prevention.adequacy: The upgrade is complete only after the php-fpm master restarts; a package bump without the restart leaves forked workers exploitable.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Alerting on php-fpm worker SIGSEGVs and on FastCGI workers spawning shell children.
detection.adequacy: Crash telemetry catches the noisy brute-force stage but a tuned single-shot exploit can land without a visible crash.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treating a confirmed hit as web-server RCE: rebuild the host and rotate any credentials the PHP application held.
response.adequacy: Patching after exploitation removes the bug but not a web shell or cron implant already dropped through the RCE.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: SI-2 catalogues CVE-2019-11043 and pushes the PHP 7.1.33/7.2.24/7.3.11 package, but a version-based remediation check marks the host fixed while the running php-fpm master keeps vulnerable workers until it is restarted, so the control's own evidence overstates the closure.

NIST-800-53-CM-7.gap: CM-7 hardens services and ports but does not reach the FastCGI parameter wiring inside nginx; the anchored fastcgi_split_path_info + PATH_INFO + no-try_files combination that makes this CVE reachable survives a least-functionality review that only enumerates listening services.

NIS2-Art21-patch-management.gap: Article 21 obliges timely patching, yet its ordinary monthly cadence is far slower than the days-old public exploit for a 9.8 unauthenticated RCE at EPSS 0.994; NIS2 defines no expedited tier for internet-facing web-fabric RCE, so a compliant program can still be exposed for weeks.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: CAF B4 expects supported software and prompt fixes but conflates the nginx and PHP layers into a single maintenance target and never surfaces the process-restart requirement, so a green B4 maintenance outcome can coexist with php-fpm workers still executing the pre-patch binary.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: Essential Eight patch-application upgrades the PHP package on its 48-hour internet-facing clock, but its maturity evidence is package inventory; it does not verify the php-fpm restart or the nginx try_files mitigation, both of which govern whether CVE-2019-11043 is actually closed on the host.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: A.8.8 tracks the CVE and schedules the update but sets no requirement to validate the configuration precondition; an estate can close the technical-vulnerability record on the version bump while the exploitable anchored-split-path nginx location is still serving requests.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2019-11043 is a 9.8 unauthenticated PHP-FPM RCE (EPSS 0.994, percentile 0.999) added to KEV 2022-03-25 with known ransomware use; the ordinary patch window is far too slow and a KEV-tied 4-hour clock is the fitting requirement.

new_control_requirements.name: CONFIGURATION-SIDE-LIVE-PATCH-INVENTORY
new_control_requirements.description: For any web-fabric vulnerability with a configuration-side mitigation path: that path must be inventoried, tested, and deployable independent of the vendor-patch path. Operators cannot wait for nginx 1.30.1+ if a named-capture refactor mitigates immediately.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2019-11043 has exactly such a path: adding try_files $uri =404 or removing the anchored fastcgi_split_path_info in nginx removes the underflow reachability immediately, without waiting for the PHP 7.1.33/7.2.24/7.3.11 upgrade or the php-fpm master restart it requires.

CVE-2019-1253.name: Microsoft Windows AppX Deployment Server Privilege Escalation Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: A low-privileged user hard-links a Microsoft Edge settings.dat log to a chosen system file and forces AppXSvc's SYSTEM-context restore to rewrite that file's security descriptor, granting the user full control and enabling privilege escalation.
attack_vector.privileges_required: low — PR:L; an interactive standard-user session is the precondition
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L; a deterministic terminate/link/lock/restart sequence, no memory-corruption race
attack_vector.ai_factor: None. Disclosed and PoC'd by named human researchers.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: The September 2019 cumulative update on a serviced build, or migration off an out-of-servicing Windows 10 feature update.
prevention.adequacy: The fix closes AppXSvc's hard-link handling, but on out-of-servicing 1703-1903 builds only a feature-update move delivers it.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Alerting on AppXSvc modifying DACLs outside the AppData settings store and on hard links from settings.dat logs.
detection.adequacy: The link/lock sequence is observable, but only where endpoint tooling monitors reparse-point and DACL-change events.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treating a confirmed hit as SYSTEM-level LPE and rebuilding, given the ransomware association.
response.adequacy: A DACL-overwrite LPE can be a rung in a ransomware chain, so rotating credentials the host held is part of a complete response.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: SI-2 applies the September 2019 cumulative update, but on the out-of-servicing Windows 10 1703-1903 builds a version check can report 'no applicable update' instead of driving the feature-update migration that actually removes the AppXSvc hard-link path.

NIST-800-53-AC-6.gap: AC-6 least privilege scopes the foothold account, but the escalation comes from AppXSvc rewriting a target file's DACL as SYSTEM, so the flaw grants full control through a service and never relies on a privilege the AC-6-limited account already had.

NIS2-Art21-patch-management.gap: Article 21 would schedule the fix on a routine cadence, but CVE-2019-1253 is a KEV item with known ransomware use added 2022-03-15, and NIS2 defines no expedited tier for an actively-catalogued LPE that ransomware operators pair with initial access.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: CAF B4 expects supported, patched systems, but on an out-of-servicing Windows 10 build the maintenance obligation can only be met by a feature-update migration B4 does not spell out, so a 1803/1809 estate can look compliant while AppXSvc stays exploitable.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: Essential Eight patch-application checks that an OS patch is present within its window, but its evidence does not separate a serviced build that took the September 2019 fix from an out-of-servicing 1703-1903 build where none ships, so the maturity claim can be blind to CVE-2019-1253's real exposure.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: A.8.8 records the AppXSvc CVE and its September-2019 siblings (1215/1278/1303) but permits per-ticket closure.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2019-1253 is a Windows AppXSvc LPE (CVSS 7.8) added to KEV 2022-03-15 with known ransomware use and multiple public PoCs (Exploit-DB 47389, padovah4ck); the KEV clock forces the September 2019 cumulative update or a serviced-build move rather than a routine monthly window on an LPE ransomware operators chain.

CVE-2019-12989.name: Citrix SD-WAN and NetScaler SQL Injection Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: An unauthenticated request to the SD-WAN REST endpoint getpackagefile.cgi injects SQL into a concatenated query, which the public chain uses to forge a session token and bypass authentication on the appliance control plane.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none — PR:N; the endpoint answers before authentication
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L; a direct string-concatenation injection with no race or leak
attack_vector.ai_factor: None. Found by a Tenable researcher through manual REST-API analysis.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Upgrading to Citrix SD-WAN 10.2.3 / NetScaler SD-WAN 10.0.8, and restricting the management interface to a management network.
prevention.adequacy: The upgrade removes the SQLi, but a perimeter box exposed pre-patch may already have been auth-bypassed, so reachability restriction is the load-bearing interim control.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Alerting on unauthenticated hits to getpackagefile.cgi and on session-token files created without a login.
detection.adequacy: Detection depends on the appliance forwarding request-level logs off-box.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treating a confirmed hit as perimeter compromise: config exfil, rebuild from known-good image, rotate credentials the device held.
response.adequacy: Patch-in-place leaves any attacker-created accounts or implants intact, so rebuild is the safe response for a control-plane box.

NIST-800-53-SI-10.gap: SI-10 input validation is exactly the missing control in getpackagefile.cgi, but where an SI-10 attestation treats a purchased SD-WAN appliance's input handling as opaque, the Perl CGI concatenating unauthenticated input into SQL is never inspected and the control passes while the flaw remains.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: SI-2 drives the 10.2.3 / 10.0.8 upgrade, but where the reboot-required appliance firmware update waits on a quarterly window, that is far slower than a 9.8 pre-auth auth-bypass at EPSS 0.941 demands, and SI-2 defines no perimeter-specific expedited tier.

NIS2-Art21-network-security.gap: Article 21 network-security assumes the perimeter device enforces access, but CVE-2019-12989 makes the SD-WAN control plane forge a session for an unauthenticated caller, so the boundary appliance is itself the bypass and the obligation does not treat a control-plane device as a distinct, higher-risk asset.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: CAF B4 would schedule the SD-WAN upgrade as routine maintenance, not as a perimeter-trust-boundary emergency, so its standard cadence leaves an internet-reachable pre-auth SQLi and auth-bypass exposed between the 2022-03-25 KEV listing and the next appliance maintenance window.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: Essential Eight patch-application would cover an internet-facing service in 48 hours, but SD-WAN firmware falls outside the OS/application patch tooling the model assumes.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: A.8.8 would list the CVE, but where appliance firmware is outside the vulnerability-scan scope that feeds it, a Citrix/NetScaler SD-WAN unit on 10.2.2 is missing from the inventory that A.8.8 relies on to flag CVE-2019-12989 in the first place.

OWASP-Top-10-2021-A03.gap: A03 Injection names this class precisely, but an OWASP-aligned review examines first-party code, not a purchased appliance's bundled getpackagefile.cgi, so the concatenated SQL in the SD-WAN REST layer sits in a blind spot the A03 program never reaches.

new_control_requirements.name: PERIMETER-DEVICE-ZERODAY-SLA-TIER
new_control_requirements.description: Compliance frameworks must define a distinct patch SLA tier for pre-auth RCE on perimeter-trust-boundary devices (firewalls, VPN concentrators, WAFs, edge load-balancers). Tier requirement: vendor-mitigation deployed within 4 hours of KEV listing OR isolation of the vulnerable interface; standard 14/30-day SLAs do not apply because the device IS the trust boundary.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2019-12989 is a 9.8 pre-auth SQLi/auth-bypass on the Citrix/NetScaler SD-WAN control-plane appliance (EPSS 0.941, KEV 2022-03-25); as an edge-trust-boundary device its 10.2.3/10.0.8 upgrade or management-interface isolation belongs on the 4-hour tier, not a routine appliance window.

new_control_requirements.name: PERIMETER-COMPROMISE-REBUILD-NOT-PATCH
new_control_requirements.description: Pre-rehearsed IR runbook for any perimeter device that suffers a pre-auth RCE CVE in active exploitation MUST default to config-exfil + rebuild + credential rotation, not patch-in-place. Patch-in-place leaves attacker-installed implants intact.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2019-12989's auth-bypass lets an unauthenticated attacker forge an SD-WAN session and (chained with CVE-2019-12991) run root commands, so a Citrix/NetScaler SD-WAN unit reachable while unpatched must be rebuilt from a known-good image rather than upgraded in place.

CVE-2019-12991.name: Citrix SD-WAN and NetScaler Command Injection Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: An authenticated request to installpatch.cgi injects shell metacharacters through the installfile parameter to run commands as root on the SD-WAN appliance; the companion SQLi CVE-2019-12989 supplies the authentication, making the chain unauthenticated root command execution.
attack_vector.privileges_required: low — PR:L in isolation, but reduced to none when chained with CVE-2019-12989
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L; an unsanitized parameter reaching a shell, no additional constraint
attack_vector.ai_factor: None. Found by a Tenable researcher through manual analysis.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Upgrading to Citrix SD-WAN 10.2.3 / NetScaler SD-WAN 10.0.8 and restricting the management interface to a management network.
prevention.adequacy: The upgrade removes the injection, but a box exposed pre-patch may already have run attacker commands as root, so reachability restriction is the load-bearing interim control.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Alerting on the CGI service spawning root shells and on the getpackagefile-then-installpatch request sequence.
detection.adequacy: Detection requires the appliance to export process and request telemetry off-box.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treating a confirmed hit as root-level perimeter compromise: rebuild from known-good image and rotate every credential the device held.
response.adequacy: Root command execution can install persistence a scan will miss, so patch-in-place is not a safe response for this device.

NIST-800-53-SI-10.gap: SI-10 input validation is precisely what installpatch.cgi omits when it passes installfile to a shell, but an SI-10 attestation cannot reach inside a purchased SD-WAN appliance's CGI, so the missing neutralization escapes the control meant to detect it.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: SI-2 drives the 10.2.3 / 10.0.8 upgrade, and for a command injection reachable as unauthenticated root when chained (KEV 2022-03-25, EPSS 0.740) SI-2's routine cadence leaves a window of root exposure with no perimeter tier.

NIS2-Art21-patch-management.gap: Article 21 schedules the upgrade as an ordinary application patch and does not surface that CVE-2019-12991 collapses to unauthenticated root once paired with CVE-2019-12989, so the risk ranking a routine cadence assigns understates the chained impact on the perimeter.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: CAF B4 covers the upgrade as maintenance, but the installfile command-injection lives in vendor firmware B4 does not require the operator to assess, and its standard window is far slower than warranted for root command execution on a perimeter control-plane device.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: Essential Eight patch-application would target an internet-facing service quickly, but SD-WAN firmware is outside the OS/application tooling the model assumes.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.28.gap: A.8.28 secure-coding names the exact defect of concatenating request input into an OS command, but it governs the operator's own development, not the vendor's installpatch.cgi, so the unsanitized-parameter-to-shell code sits outside the scope A.8.28 can enforce.

new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2019-12991 is a root command injection on the Citrix/NetScaler SD-WAN appliance (CVSS 8.8, EPSS 0.740) added to KEV 2022-03-25 that becomes unauthenticated root when chained with CVE-2019-12989; the KEV clock forces the 10.2.3/10.0.8 upgrade or interface isolation rather than a routine appliance window.

Tier requirement: vendor-mitigation deployed within 4 hours of KEV listing OR isolation of the vulnerable interface; standard 14/30-day SLAs do not apply because the device IS the trust boundary.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Chained with CVE-2019-12989 this yields unauthenticated root command execution on the SD-WAN control-plane appliance, an edge-trust-boundary device, so its upgrade or management-interface isolation belongs on the 4-hour perimeter tier rather than a standard 14/30-day appliance SLA.

CVE-2019-1315.name: Microsoft Windows Error Reporting Manager Privilege Escalation Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: A low-privileged user uses an oplock, an NTFS junction on a WER ReportQueue subdirectory, and an \RPC Control symlink to make the SYSTEM-context wermgr.exe rename an attacker payload into a protected system location, escalating privilege.
attack_vector.privileges_required: low — PR:L; an interactive standard-user session is required
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L; the oplock makes the timing deterministic and the junction/symlink primitive is standard
attack_vector.ai_factor: None. Independently found by two named human researchers.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: The October 2019 cumulative update on serviced builds; migration off EoL Windows 7 / Server 2008/2012 lines.
prevention.adequacy: The fix corrects WER hard-link handling, but on the EoL builds in scope only migration delivers it.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Alerting on wermgr.exe writing into System32 and on junctions created on WER ReportQueue subfolders.
detection.adequacy: The reparse-point and symlink steps are observable, but only where endpoint tooling monitors object-manager and junction activity.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treating a confirmed hit as SYSTEM-level LPE and rebuilding, given the known ransomware association.
response.adequacy: An arbitrary-file-move LPE can seed persistence a scan misses, so rebuild and credential rotation complete the response.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: SI-2 applies the October 2019 fix on serviced builds, but CVE-2019-1315 also spans EoL Windows 7 / Server 2008/2012 lines where no current update ships, so a version check can read 'no applicable update' rather than driving the migration that closes the WER hard-link path there.

NIST-800-53-AC-6.gap: AC-6 bounds the foothold account, but wermgr.exe performs the file move as SYSTEM, so the escalation is delivered through a SYSTEM service and does not use any privilege the AC-6-scoped user legitimately holds, leaving least privilege on the account irrelevant to this path.

NIS2-Art21-vulnerability-handling.gap: Article 21 vulnerability-handling would track and fix the CVE, but for the EoL builds in scope the correct handling is retirement, and NIS2 does not force an end-of-life decision, so a KEV item with known ransomware use can persist as accepted risk on legacy Windows.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: CAF B4 expects supported systems, yet the affected span includes unsupported Windows 7 / Server 2008/2012; a B4 claim met via an ESU note or compensating control still leaves the WER arbitrary-file-move LPE present on those hosts.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: Essential Eight patch-application assumes a supported vendor channel, but no fix ships for the EoL builds among the affected set, so its two-week clock cannot apply and it credits no maturity for the migration CVE-2019-1315 needs on legacy Windows.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: A.8.8 would enumerate CVE-2019-1315 alongside the WER siblings CVE-2019-1339/1342, but it allows per-ticket closure and risk acceptance without a removal deadline.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2019-1315 is a WER arbitrary-file-move LPE (CVSS 7.8) added to KEV 2022-03-15 with known ransomware use and a public PoC (Mayter/CVE-2019-1315); the KEV clock forces the October 2019 update or, on EoL builds, migration/isolation rather than open-ended risk acceptance on an LPE ransomware operators chain.

attack_vector.description: From a LOCAL SERVICE identity (supplied by the paired CVE-2019-1405), the attacker rewrites the SYSTEM Update Orchestrator Service's binary path with sc config and starts it, running an arbitrary command as SYSTEM.
attack_vector.privileges_required: low — PR:L; a low-integrity foothold (LOCAL SERVICE) is the precondition
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L; deterministic service reconfiguration once the intermediate identity is held
attack_vector.ai_factor: None. Researched and published by NCC Group; no automated tooling in discovery.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: The October 2019 cumulative update on a serviced build, or migration off out-of-servicing Windows 10 1803-1903.
prevention.adequacy: The fix closes the UsoSvc reconfiguration path, but on out-of-servicing builds only a feature-update move delivers it.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Alerting on UsoSvc ImagePath changes and on the service launching a non-svchost binary as SYSTEM.
detection.adequacy: The sc config/start sequence is observable in service and registry telemetry, where that telemetry is collected off-host.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treating a confirmed hit as SYSTEM-level compromise in a likely ransomware chain: isolate, rebuild, rotate credentials.
response.adequacy: Because it is chained with initial-access flaws, a hit implies a broader intrusion, so single-host cleanup is insufficient.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: SI-2 applies the October 2019 fix, but the affected Windows 10 1803-1903 and Server 1803/1903 builds are out of servicing, so a version check can read 'no applicable update' rather than driving the serviced-build migration that closes the UsoSvc reconfiguration path.

NIST-800-53-AC-6.gap: AC-6 least privilege is the exact boundary the flaw defeats: a non-administrative LOCAL SERVICE identity reconfigures and starts the SYSTEM UsoSvc, so an attestation that all accounts are least-privileged passes while the service ACL still permits the escalation.

NIS2-Art21-patch-management.gap: Article 21 schedules the October 2019 fix on a routine cadence, but CVE-2019-1322 is the SYSTEM rung of the COMahawk chain and a KEV item with known ransomware use, and NIS2 defines no expedited tier for an actively-catalogued LPE that operators pair with initial access.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: CAF B4 would apply the update as maintenance, but on out-of-servicing Windows 10 builds the obligation can only be met by a feature-update migration B4 does not spell out, so a 1803/1809 estate can look compliant while UsoSvc stays reconfigurable to SYSTEM.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: Essential Eight patch-application verifies patch presence within its window but does not separate a serviced build that took the October 2019 fix from an out-of-servicing 1803-1903 build where none ships, so the maturity claim is blind to whether the UsoSvc path is actually closed.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: A.8.8 would list CVE-2019-1322 and the sibling elevations CVE-2019-1320/1340, but per-ticket closure obscures that this is a service-permission LPE, context the discrete record does not carry.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2019-1322 is the SYSTEM rung of the public COMahawk chain (CVSS 7.8) added to KEV 2022-03-15 with known ransomware use; the KEV clock forces the October 2019 update or, on out-of-servicing builds, a serviced-build move rather than a routine window on an LPE paired with initial access.

CVE-2019-1405.name: Microsoft Windows Universal Plug and Play (UPnP) Service Privilege Escalation Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: A standard user calls into the UPnP Device Host service's UPnPContainerManager COM objects and has the service create an in-process COM class on their behalf. The class runs with the service's LOCAL SERVICE token, so the caller gains code execution above their own privilege level without touching the account model, and a second flaw in the Update Orchestrator Service carries that to SYSTEM.
attack_vector.privileges_required: low - PR:L; any logged-on local account is sufficient, which on a shared workstation or session host is the ordinary state rather than an anomaly
attack_vector.complexity: low - AC:L; no race, no memory-corruption primitive and no information leak, only that the UPnP Device Host service is running, which NCC Group records as the Windows 10 default
attack_vector.ai_factor: None. NCC Group found and published this through manual COM-surface analysis; the write-up names Phillip Langlois and Edward Torkington and describes no automated or AI-assisted tooling.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Installing the Windows security update for CVE-2019-1405 and rebooting, or disabling the UPnP Device Host service on hosts with no UPnP hosting requirement - either removes the activation path entirely.
prevention.adequacy: Adequate where the reboot actually lands. The failure mode is a host that has taken the update but not restarted, which still runs the vulnerable upnphost image while every dashboard shows it as patched.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Process-lineage telemetry alerting on a scripting or shell process whose token is LOCAL SERVICE and whose ancestry runs through the UPnP Device Host service, correlated with a SYSTEM-context process appearing in the same user session.
detection.adequacy: Partial. The activation itself is an ordinary COM call and produces no crash, no driver load and no file-integrity change, so the only durable signal is the child process the attacker then runs - which they control and can keep quiet.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treating any host where the chain fired as a credential-exposure event: SYSTEM access means every secret cached on that machine, so rebuilding rather than cleaning, and rotating what the host held.
response.adequacy: Adequate as a containment step but expensive, and CISA's ransomware flag on this entry means the population that needs it is the population where an operator is already dealing with an intrusion rather than a single endpoint.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: SI-2 is satisfied by a documented flaw-remediation process, and a monthly Windows patch cycle is exactly that. What it does not reach is the gap between approving an update and the endpoint rebooting onto it, which for a service DLL like upnphost is the whole of the remediation; nor does it reprioritise a 7.8 local flaw when CISA later attaches a ransomware flag to it.

NIST-800-53-CM-7.gap: CM-7 least-functionality baselines enumerate installed software and listening ports. The UPnP Device Host service listens for local COM activations rather than on a port, and ships enabled, so it survives a baseline review that would have removed any equivalent third-party service - leaving the one component this CVE needs running on hosts that have no use for it.

NIS2-Art21-patch-management.gap: An entity can evidence Article 21 patch management with a monthly cycle and a compliance percentage. Neither shows whether the specific November 2019 update reached the multi-user hosts where a standard local account - the only precondition this flaw has - is a normal daily occurrence, and neither distinguishes downloaded from rebooted.

UK-CAF-B2.gap: B2 is assessed against the identity and privilege model, and that model is intact throughout this attack: the user authenticates as themselves and is granted exactly what they were assigned. The escalation happens inside a Windows service's COM activation, below anything B2 examines, so a clean B2 assessment says nothing about exposure here.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: The Essential Eight patch mitigations put internet-facing services first and this is a local-only privilege escalation, so it sits at the back of the queue by design. Read as an interpretation rather than a quotation, the timeframes run from vendor release - which was 2019 - and give an assessor no rule for a KEV listing that arrives three years later on an already-published fix.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: A.8.8 requires vulnerability information to be obtained and acted upon; the information was never scarce here, having been public since 2019 and re-issued by CISA in 2022. The control does not demand host-level verification of the acting-upon, so a management-console percentage satisfies the auditor while individual endpoints still load the pre-update image.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Microsoft's fix for the Windows UPnP Device Host flaw predates the KEV listing by well over two years - CISA added CVE-2019-1405 on 2022-03-15 with a 2022-04-05 due date and a known-ransomware-campaign flag, against a patch already shipped in 2019. The control's 'whichever is later' clause is the operative half here: patch availability was never the constraint, the KEV listing was the trigger, and the verified-mitigation requirement is what forces an operator to confirm the host rebooted onto the fixed upnphost rather than recording an approved update. The documented-compensating-control alternative maps directly onto disabling the UPnP Device Host service where the reboot cannot be taken.

attack_vector.description: An unauthenticated POST to Webmin's password_change.cgi puts shell metacharacters into the `old` parameter, which a Perl qx statement executes. miniserv runs as root, so the command runs as root. The qx statement was inserted into the source on a compromised build server, so the defect shipped in the release tarballs while the project's own source tree stayed clean.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none - PR:N; the password-expiry handler is reachable before authentication by design, which is what makes the injected qx statement a pre-auth path
attack_vector.complexity: low - AC:L; one HTTP request, no chaining. The real gate is configuration: default-reachable on 1.890, and on 1.900-1.920 only where expired-password changing is enabled
attack_vector.ai_factor: None. Ozkan Mustafa Akkus found it by inspecting the shipped CGI and released it at DEF CON 27; neither Webmin's incident page nor the Metasploit module describes any automated or AI-assisted analysis.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Comparing the release tarball against the project's version-control tree before deployment, which is the one check that surfaces a build-server substitution, plus keeping expired-password changing off on 1.900-1.920.
prevention.adequacy: The KEV clock only starts in 2022 and the substitution happened in 2018, so BOD 22-01 covers the tail rather than the exposure. The tarball comparison would have caught it at install time, but nothing required it.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Alerting on the Webmin miniserv process spawning a child process, which on a well-behaved management daemon is close to never, correlated with unauthenticated hits on /password_change.cgi.
detection.adequacy: Good signal but late - by the time miniserv spawns a child the command is already running as root. It bounds dwell time rather than preventing compromise.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treating an exposed instance as a root compromise of the management plane: rebuild the host from a known-good image and rotate every credential Webmin held or administered, rather than upgrading to 1.930 in place.
response.adequacy: Adequate and necessary, because upgrading to 1.930 removes the qx statement but removes nothing an attacker installed through it. Costly on estates where Webmin fronts many systems.

NIST-800-53-SR-11.gap: SR-11 component-authenticity evidence here consists of the right project, the right download page and the right version number, all of which were genuine. The substitution lived below that layer, in the build server that produced the tarball, with timestamps altered so a casual file inspection matched too. The control never asks for the comparison that would have shown the divergence.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: SI-2 drove operators toward newer Webmin releases across 2018 and 2019, which is precisely how an installation moved from an unaffected build into a backdoored one. A flaw-remediation control that treats newer as safer has no mechanism for a release that is worse than its predecessor, and no way to raise the question before 1.930.

NIS2-Art21-supply-chain.gap: Article 21 supply-chain measures are assessed against direct suppliers and service providers. A free administration package from an open project sits outside that relationship entirely, so a compliant entity's supplier list would not name Webmin, and the compromised build server that produced the artefact in April 2018 appears at no tier the assessment enumerates.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: On 1.900 through 1.920 the exposure turns on one authentication convenience setting, and B4 secure-configuration reviews of a management interface concentrate on listener exposure, account policy and TLS rather than on which optional handlers are reachable pre-authentication. On 1.890 the setting is irrelevant and B4 offers nothing at all.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: Every affected build was the current release when installed, so the patch-lag metric the mitigation produces reads green for the whole period between the July 2018 insertion and the August 2019 disclosure. The mitigation measures distance from the vendor's latest release, and here the vendor's latest release was the problem.

ISO-27001-2022-A.5.21.gap: A.5.21 evidence is questionnaires, contract clauses and supplier control reviews, none of which exist for a free download from a project's own site. The control also prescribes nothing that would surface a build artefact diverging from its published source, which was the only recoverable signal between April 2018 and August 2019.

new_control_requirements.name: REPRODUCIBLE-RELEASE-TARBALL-VERIFICATION
new_control_requirements.description: For any upstream OSS dependency in the boot or auth path: verify that the release tarball is bytewise-reproducible from the VCS tag. Binary test fixtures, generated artifacts, or build-time-generated files in the release tarball that do NOT appear in the VCS tag are a hard fail.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Webmin is squarely in the auth path - miniserv runs as root and password_change.cgi is one of its pre-authentication handlers - and the divergence between the release tarball and the project's source tree is the entire defect. Webmin's own account has the qx statement inserted on a development build server in April 2018 for 1.890 and again in July 2018 for the expired-password path, with timestamps manipulated and the compromised build directory later restored from backup onto a replacement server, so the substitution survived a server decommission and shipped through 1.920 until 1.930. A byte-level comparison of the distributed tarball against the tagged source is the one check that distinguishes those two artefacts, and it would have flagged 1.890 in 2018 rather than 2019.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Webmin 1.930 was available from 2019 and CISA listed CVE-2019-15107 on 2022-03-25 with a 2022-04-15 due date and a known-ransomware-campaign flag, so the KEV listing is the later of the two triggers and starts the clock. The documented-compensating-control branch has a real counterpart here that most CVEs lack: disabling expired-password changing under Webmin Configuration > Authentication makes the handler unreachable on 1.900 through 1.920 without an upgrade, though not on 1.890. Verified mitigation matters because the upgrade only takes effect once miniserv restarts.

CVE-2019-16920.name: D-Link Multiple Routers Command Injection Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: An unauthenticated POST to /apply_sec.cgi sets action=ping_test and embeds a newline in ping_ipaddr. Everything after the newline runs as a shell command with root privileges on the router, per CERT/CC's description of the flaw. The device that terminates the site's internet connection becomes the attacker's foothold, and there is no vendor firmware that removes the path.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none - PR:N; the CGI is exposed to unauthenticated users, which CERT/CC records as one of the two defects alongside the newline handling
attack_vector.complexity: low - AC:L; one HTTP request with an encoded newline. The only variable is whether the administration surface is reachable from the attacker's position, not the exploit itself
attack_vector.ai_factor: None. Fortinet's FortiGuard Labs found and coordinated it; the 'FortiGuard' name is a vendor research brand and implies nothing about automated discovery, and no source describes fuzzing or AI assistance.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Replacing the units. With no firmware fix, the only prevention that removes the flaw is taking the hardware out of service; short of that, disabling WAN-side administration removes internet reachability of the CGI.
prevention.adequacy: BOD 22-01's required action for an unfixable device is removal, which is honest but slow; disabling WAN administration is fast and partial, because every client on the served network still reaches the handler.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Watching for outbound connections from the router's own address to destinations outside DNS, NTP and ISP infrastructure, and for administration requests arriving on the WAN interface.
detection.adequacy: Weak in practice. These units are consumer and small-office hardware with little log retention and no forwarding path to a collector, so the detection has to be built on the network around the device rather than on the device.

response.what_would_have_worked: Replacing rather than resetting a unit believed to have been reached, and rotating the wireless keys and any credential that transited it.
response.adequacy: Adequate and the only honest option, because a factory reset restores firmware that is still vulnerable - the reset returns the device to the exploitable state rather than to a safe one.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: SI-2's correction step has no object here: CERT/CC records no available fix and the devices as unsupported. The control converts a public pre-auth root flaw into a standing open finding that is discharged by risk acceptance, and it prescribes no dated replacement obligation to close it, so the exposure can persist for as long as the hardware does.

NIST-800-53-SC-7.gap: The boundary-protection control is attested against an architecture in which the router enforces the perimeter. That is the same device a single unauthenticated POST turns into root-level attacker infrastructure, so SC-7 evidence describes the compromised asset as the control, and offers nothing on restricting which interface may reach the device's own administration surface.

NIS2-Art21-vulnerability-handling.gap: The handling and disclosure process ran correctly - CERT/CC published VU#766427 in October 2019 - and terminated in a vendor statement that the products are unsupported. Article 21 gives an in-scope entity no clock for the case where a correctly handled disclosure produces no fix, so the residual duty becomes replacement that nothing requires.

UK-CAF-B5.gap: B5 seeks resilience against disruption. The resilience measure B5 would drive - redundancy - adds a second device of the same unsupported generation, which increases the exposed count rather than reducing it.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: Patch lag is unmeasurable for firmware that will never be released, so the timeframe half of the mitigation scores a clean result by default. On my reading, the removal-of-unsupported-products requirement is the part that applies, and an assessment that reports only patch timeframes therefore certifies an estate carrying ten models with a published mass-exploitation script.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.22.gap: Network segregation is the only listed control with residual force, and its force is limited to bounding what a rooted router can reach next. It cannot remove the path, because the vulnerable handler is on the administration surface of the device serving the network, and every client on that network retains reachability to it by construction.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: Acquisition of vulnerability information has been satisfied since CERT/CC published in October 2019. The measure the control then asks for is the problem: with no firmware to apply, the appropriate measure is decommissioning, and A.8.8 accepts an evaluated-and-accepted disposition carrying no removal date, which is how a device with an EPSS of 0.99996 stays in service.

new_control_requirements.name: PERIMETER-DEVICE-ZERODAY-SLA-TIER
new_control_requirements.description: Compliance frameworks must define a distinct patch SLA tier for pre-auth RCE on perimeter-trust-boundary devices (firewalls, VPN concentrators, WAFs, edge load-balancers). Tier requirement: vendor-mitigation deployed within 4 hours of KEV listing OR isolation of the vulnerable interface; standard 14/30-day SLAs do not apply because the device IS the trust boundary.
new_control_requirements.evidence: These ten D-Link models are the trust boundary at the sites where they are deployed, and the flaw is exactly the class the tier exists for: unauthenticated POST to /apply_sec.cgi yielding root, per CERT/CC VU#766427. The control's disjunction is what makes it usable here - CERT/CC records no vendor fix and the devices as unsupported, so the vendor-mitigation branch is empty and isolation of the vulnerable interface is the only executable half, meaning WAN-side administration off and the served network treated as untrusted. A 14- or 30-day application-patch SLA is meaningless against a device with an EPSS of 0.99996 on 2026-08-17 and a public mass-exploitation script, which is the mismatch the tier is meant to correct.

new_control_requirements.name: PERIMETER-COMPROMISE-REBUILD-NOT-PATCH
new_control_requirements.description: Pre-rehearsed IR runbook for any perimeter device that suffers a pre-auth RCE CVE in active exploitation MUST default to config-exfil + rebuild + credential rotation, not patch-in-place. Patch-in-place leaves attacker-installed implants intact.
new_control_requirements.evidence: The patch-in-place option this runbook rejects does not even exist for a DIR-655, DIR-825 or DAP-1533 - CERT/CC records no fix - so the runbook's default becomes the only path: capture the configuration, replace the hardware, and rotate the wireless keys and any credential that transited the unit. The reset trap is sharper here than on a maintained product, because a factory reset restores firmware that still carries the /apply_sec.cgi injection, returning the device to the exploitable state rather than a clean one. With the KEV listing dated 2022-03-25 and a public single-target and mass-exploitation script available since 2019, an operator has to assume an internet-reachable unit was reached rather than prove it.

CVE-2019-2616.name: Oracle BI Publisher Unauthorized Access Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: An unauthenticated POST of XML to BI Publisher's report-template endpoint carries a document type declaration with an external identifier. The parser resolves it, so the reporting server fetches whatever the attacker names, from the reporting server's own network position. Oracle records the outcome as unauthorized read access to a subset of BI Publisher data plus unauthorized update, insert or delete access to some of it.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none - PR:N; Oracle's own text describes an unauthenticated attacker with network access via HTTP
attack_vector.complexity: low - AC:L; one request. The variable is not the exploit but the network position of the middleware host, which is what determines whether the resolved entity returns anything of value
attack_vector.ai_factor: None. The published exploit is credited to Vahagn Vardanyan on Exploit-DB and describes a hand-built XML payload; no source describes automated or AI-assisted discovery.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: The April 2019 Critical Patch Update applied to the BI Publisher component, plus denying the Fusion Middleware host outbound DNS and HTTP it does not need, which renders an external entity unresolvable.
prevention.adequacy: The patch is definitive but arrives on Oracle's quarterly calendar; the egress control works immediately and is the only lever between CPUs, though it does not stop entity references that resolve to local files.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Egress monitoring on the middleware tier - alerting when the BI Publisher host resolves or contacts a destination with no prior history, correlated with an inbound unauthenticated request to /xmlpserver/.
detection.adequacy: High fidelity where the telemetry exists, because a report server has a small and stable set of destinations. It sees the out-of-band variant that all three public artefacts use and misses a purely local-file entity that never leaves the host.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treating the middleware host's readable secrets - datasource credentials, keystores, connection configuration - as disclosed, and rotating them rather than closing on the patch record.
response.adequacy: Necessary because the patch removes the read primitive but not the value of anything already read. Scope is hard to bound, since an entity-resolution read leaves little trace in application logs.

NIST-800-53-SI-10.gap: SI-10 evidence is normally about the validity of application inputs - field types, lengths, ranges. The defect lives one layer below that, in whether the XML reader resolves an external identifier at all, on an endpoint that only ever needs report data. A conformant input-validation programme therefore passes while /xmlpserver/ turns a POST body into an outbound network request.

NIST-800-53-SC-7.gap: Boundary-protection evidence concentrates on inbound flows reaching the application tier. The half that decides this flaw's payoff is outbound: whether the Fusion Middleware host can resolve and reach http://attacker-host/. Middleware egress and its DNS path are rarely enumerated in an SC-7 package, so the control is attested while the callback the public exploit relies on still completes.

NIS2-Art21-vulnerability-management.gap: The article requires vulnerability handling and remediation planning, and a plan exists - but its timing is set by Oracle's quarterly Critical Patch Update rather than by the entity. With a working exploit published on 2019-04-19, the entity's own risk appetite does not shorten the interval, and the compensating-control phase that fills it has no prescribed evidence form under Article 21.

UK-CAF-C1.gap: C1 monitoring is normally evidenced from endpoint agents and perimeter devices. The signal this flaw generates is a middleware server making an unexpected outbound resolution, which sits outside that collection set, so a C1 assessment can be positive while the single highest-fidelity indicator of exploitation is never gathered.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: The mitigation's shorter timeframe is contingent on an exploit existing, and one was published four days before Oracle's April 2019 Critical Patch Update. On my reading of the mitigation that starts a fast clock at the moment the only fix is being released, which measures the operator's deployment speed and says nothing about the quarter-long intervals in which no Oracle fix is available at all.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.28.gap: Secure coding is assessed against code the organisation writes, and none of BI Publisher qualifies. The external-entity default sits in purchased Fusion Middleware, so an operator with an exemplary A.8.28 programme has no route through it to the parser handling unauthenticated XML on 11.1.1.9.0, 12.2.1.3.0 or 12.2.1.4.0.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Oracle's fix for BI Publisher 11.1.1.9.0, 12.2.1.3.0 and 12.2.1.4.0 shipped in the April 2019 Critical Patch Update and CISA listed CVE-2019-2616 on 2022-03-25 with a 2022-04-15 due date, so the KEV listing is the later trigger and sets the clock. The documented-compensating-control branch is what makes the control workable against a vendor on a quarterly patch calendar: restricting who can reach /xmlpserver/ and denying the Fusion Middleware host unnecessary outbound DNS and HTTP both land inside hours and both defeat the out-of-band callback the published exploit uses. Verified matters literally here - a Fusion Middleware patch is only in force once the managed server restarts, and an EPSS of 0.92183 on 2026-08-17 leaves little margin for an instance patched on disk but still running the old parser.

CVE-2019-6340.name: Drupal Core Remote Code Execution Vulnerability (CVE-2019-6340)

attack_vector.description: A request to an enabled Drupal web-services resource carries a serialised PHP object into a field type that does not sanitise non-form input. Drupal unserialises it, and with a gadget chain present in the deployed code that becomes arbitrary PHP execution in the web server's process - a full site takeover from an unauthenticated request.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none - PR:N; the REST resource answers without authentication, which is what makes this an internet-wide exposure rather than an authenticated abuse
attack_vector.complexity: high - AC:H; the request is trivial but two preconditions are not, namely an enabled web-services resource and a usable gadget chain in the installed code, which is why the public exploits ship alongside PHPGGC
attack_vector.ai_factor: None. Drupal's own security team reported it and the public proof of concept came from a named researcher; no source describes automated or AI-assisted discovery.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Upgrading to 8.5.11 or 8.6.10 within days of the 2019-02-20 advisory, or disabling the REST, JSON:API, Services and RESTful Web Services modules on sites that no longer use them.
prevention.adequacy: The upgrade is definitive. Disabling the modules is equally definitive and faster, whereas the method-blocking mitigation was retracted by the vendor within two days.

detection.what_would_have_worked: File-integrity monitoring on the document root and files directory, alerting on any PHP file appearing outside a deployment, plus alerting on the PHP process spawning a child.
detection.adequacy: This is the detection that still has value after the patch, because it finds what was written during the exposure window. It gives nothing at the moment of exploitation, since the triggering request is well-formed traffic to a legitimate endpoint.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treating any internet-reachable unpatched site that was live after 2019-02-25 as compromised: hunting for attacker-written files, and rotating the database and API credentials the web tier held.
response.adequacy: Necessary rather than optional given Drupal's own mass-exploitation report, and the piece an upgrade cannot do. Bounding scope is hard because the exploiting request looks like ordinary API traffic in access logs.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: A conformant flaw-remediation schedule with testing and change control cannot close a five-day gap, which is what Drupal's own record shows between the 2019-02-20 advisory and mass exploitation on 2019-02-25. SI-2 also stops at applying the fix and never asks whether the site was already exploited before it landed, so a clean remediation record coexists with an undiscovered webshell.

NIST-800-53-SI-10.gap: The request-method filter blocking POST, PATCH and PUT is exactly the kind of input restriction SI-10 rewards, and it was obsolete two days after the advisory when Drupal stated a GET-only REST resource is equally vulnerable. The control has no mechanism to invalidate a filter whose coverage assumption the vendor withdraws, so the evidence keeps reading as adequate.

NIS2-Art21-incident-handling.gap: The exploiting request is a well-formed call to a legitimate REST endpoint and its GET variant can be served from cache, so the handling process is asked to detect an incident with no anomalous method, status code or authentication failure. Article 21 also does not tell an entity that upgrading to 8.6.10 closes the entry point without evicting anything already placed through it.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: Exposure turns entirely on whether a web-services module is enabled. B4 configuration reviews of a CMS concentrate on permissions, admin accounts and update channels, so the one setting that decides whether this CVE applies is not the setting the review examines.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: This is the internet-facing category the mitigation's shortest timeframe targets, and even that timeframe is longer than the five days Drupal's own record shows before mass exploitation. Read as interpretation rather than quotation, a site can therefore be assessed compliant for internet-facing patching and still have been exploited inside the assessed window.

AU-Essential-8-Backup.gap: Backups are the recovery path once arbitrary PHP has run, but exploitation started within five days of disclosure, so an attacker-written file can propagate into every backup generation taken afterwards. Restoring from a post-2019-02-25 backup reinstates the implant with the content, and the mitigation prescribes no integrity comparison that would separate them.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.9.gap: Documented and reviewed configurations for a Drupal site normally cover theme, module list, caching and file permissions. An enabled REST or JSON:API resource is recorded as a functional choice rather than a security-relevant one, so the review completes successfully while leaving in place the single precondition without which this CVE is not exploitable at all.

OWASP-Top-10-2021-A06.gap: A06 asks for an inventory of components and their versions, and a version number is not a verdict here: 8.6.9 with every web-services module disabled is not exploitable, while 8.6.9 with JSON:API enabled is. An inventory-driven programme therefore raises findings on hardened sites and adds nothing beyond the version on exposed ones.

new_control_requirements.name: MITIGATION-ACTIVE-PATCH-PENDING-VERDICT-CLASS
new_control_requirements.description: Compliance verdicts must distinguish three states: (a) binary patch deployed (vulnerability eliminated), (b) vendor-mitigation rule active, no binary patch (residual risk: any defect in the mitigation rule reopens the vulnerability), (c) no mitigation, no patch (full exposure). Audit reports must surface (b) as a distinct compensating-control state with an associated time-bound action item, not as a 'patched per SLA' outcome.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Drupal SA-CORE-2019-003 produced a textbook instance of state (b) failing: the initial guidance let operators block POST, PATCH and PUT to web-services resources instead of upgrading, and the advisory's 2019-02-22 update then established that any enabled REST resource endpoint is vulnerable even if it only accepts GET requests. Every site whose compliance record said 'mitigated' on 2019-02-21 was in state (c) by 2019-02-22 with nothing in the record changing, and mass exploitation was being reported by 2019-02-25 per PSA-2019-02-22. Recording the method filter as a time-bound compensating control rather than a patch-equivalent outcome is what would have forced those sites back onto the upgrade to 8.5.11 or 8.6.10.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Drupal shipped 8.5.11 and 8.6.10 on 2019-02-20 and mass exploitation was reported five days later, so on this CVE the control's four-hour window is not conservatism - it is roughly the margin the defenders actually had, and CISA's 2022-03-25 KEV listing with a 2022-04-15 due date is the later trigger for anyone still unpatched. The documented-compensating-control branch has to be read carefully here, because the obvious one at the time was blocking POST, PATCH and PUT, which the vendor invalidated two days later; the compensating control that holds is disabling the REST, JSON:API, Services and RESTful Web Services modules. With EPSS at 0.92017 on 2026-08-17, a Drupal 8.6.9 site still exposing a web-services resource remains inside the population these exploits are written for.

attack_vector.description: An unauthenticated request to the SMA 100's handleWAFRedirect CGI carries a traversal path, and the appliance answers in a way that reveals whether the named file exists. The attacker learns the build, components and configuration artefacts present on a remote-access concentrator without holding any credential, which is targeting information rather than data theft.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none - PR:N; SonicWall's own text describes the traversal as unauthenticated, and the handler sits in front of the portal's authentication
attack_vector.complexity: low - AC:L; a single request per file tested, with the only precondition being network reachability of the appliance's web front end, which is its intended state
attack_vector.ai_factor: Unknown rather than none-with-evidence. No finder is named in the CVE record and the SonicWall PSIRT advisory did not render to a direct fetch, so no discovery method - manual, automated or otherwise - could be established.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Upgrading SMA 100 firmware past 9.0.0.3 and taking the appliance reboot; there is no setting that disables the handler, so the firmware is the only removal path.
prevention.adequacy: Definitive but availability-costly, since the reboot disconnects every remote user. Stopping at 9.0.0.4 also leaves the unit on a superseded firmware line, which is a fix rather than a supported position.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Forwarding SMA 100 web-access logs to a collector off the appliance and alerting on unauthenticated request bursts to one CGI with varying path arguments.
detection.adequacy: The signal is real because enumeration is repetitive, but it depends on log forwarding that was configured before the attempt. On an appliance with local-only logs and limited retention there is nothing to examine afterwards.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treating a confirmed enumeration burst as pre-attack reconnaissance against the concentrator and bringing forward the firmware window rather than closing the alert as scanning noise.
response.adequacy: Proportionate, and it is the response the primitive actually merits - nothing is exfiltrated, so there is no data-loss containment to run, only a reduced window before whatever the reconnaissance was selecting for.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: An impact-ranked remediation queue puts a file-existence oracle near the bottom, which is a defensible reading of SonicWall's description and the wrong operational answer. The control offers no way to weight a low-impact defect by the role of the asset it sits on, and here that asset is the appliance enforcing remote access for the whole estate.

NIST-800-53-SI-4.gap: SI-4 monitoring coverage is typically evidenced from host agents and network sensors, neither of which sees a CGI-level request pattern on a closed appliance. Since SonicWall provides no live-patch path, the interval before the reboot is exactly when this telemetry matters.

NIS2-Art21-network-security.gap: The network-security measures an entity evidences under Article 21 - segmentation, controlled ingress, restricted management planes - cannot be applied to an appliance whose purpose is answering unauthenticated connections from arbitrary user locations. The conformant architecture therefore designates this device as the intended exception, and the defect lives inside the exception.

UK-CAF-C1.gap: A positive C1 outcome rests on collecting and examining the right telemetry, and SMA 100 web logs are held locally with limited retention unless deliberately forwarded. The enumeration burst that would identify exploitation is only meaningful against that appliance's own baseline, so an estate monitoring servers and endpoints well can still have no visibility of the KEV-listed asset.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: The internet-facing timeframe applies cleanly, and the obstacle is not the clock but the outage: upgrading firmware reboots the concentrator and drops every remote session. On my reading the mitigation addresses deployment speed and not the availability trade-off, so a deferred upgrade is recorded as scheduled work rather than as continuing exposure.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.21.gap: A.8.21 evidence for a remote-access service covers authentication strength, encryption and access rules, all of which sit behind the portal login. The handleWAFRedirect handler answers before any of them is reached, so an appliance running 9.0.0.3 can satisfy every element of the review while exposing the flaw to the internet.

new_control_requirements.name: PERIMETER-DEVICE-ZERODAY-SLA-TIER
new_control_requirements.description: Compliance frameworks must define a distinct patch SLA tier for pre-auth RCE on perimeter-trust-boundary devices (firewalls, VPN concentrators, WAFs, edge load-balancers). Tier requirement: vendor-mitigation deployed within 4 hours of KEV listing OR isolation of the vulnerable interface; standard 14/30-day SLAs do not apply because the device IS the trust boundary.
new_control_requirements.evidence: The SMA 100 is the VPN concentrator this tier names, and the flaw is pre-authentication on the interface that faces the internet: SonicWall's record has an unauthenticated caller reaching handleWAFRedirect on firmware 9.0.0.3 and earlier. Applying the tier to this entry means the firmware upgrade past 9.0.0.3 runs on the clock CISA opened on 2022-03-28 with its 2022-04-18 due date, measured by the appliance's post-reboot firmware level rather than by a scheduled window, because there is no live-patch path and the reboot is the moment remediation takes effect. The tier's isolation alternative is where an operator has to be honest about the limits: a remote-access concentrator serving arbitrary user locations has almost no source-network restriction available, which is precisely why the standard 14- or 30-day application SLA is the wrong instrument.

new_control_requirements.name: FIREWALL-EGRESS-TELEMETRY-SEPARATE-TRUST-ZONE
new_control_requirements.description: Firewall and other perimeter-trust-boundary devices must forward syslog, threat logs, and authentication logs to a SIEM hosted in a separate trust zone (different management plane, different credentials, different authentication path). Telemetry stored on the compromised device is destroyed by the attacker; telemetry on a separate-trust-zone collector survives.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Everything an operator can learn about attempted exploitation of this handler is in the SMA 100's own web and access logs, which sit on the appliance with limited retention. The primitive is enumerative - one request per file tested - so the detectable artefact is a request burst against one CGI, and it only reads as a burst against that appliance's own baseline, which requires the log history to still exist when someone looks. Forwarding SMA 100 logs to a collector outside the appliance's management plane is what makes the 2022-03-28 KEV listing actionable retrospectively rather than only prospectively, since it lets an operator ask whether the unit was enumerated during the months it ran 9.0.0.3.

CVE-2020-1631.name: Juniper Junos OS Path Traversal Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: An unauthenticated request to the Junos HTTP/HTTPS service traverses out of its intended directory. Juniper records three outcomes: content injected into httpd.log and executed as the low-privileged httpd user, world-readable files read - including the device configuration from 19.3R1 - and J-Web session tokens obtained, which grants the attacker whatever access the logged-in user holds, up to J-Web administrator.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none - PR:N; the traversal is reached before authentication on the shared HTTP/HTTPS service
attack_vector.complexity: low for the request itself - AC:L; but the highest-impact outcome depends on an administrator being actively logged into J-Web at the time, which Juniper reflects as UI:R in its own 8.8 vector, and the configuration-read path is AC:H and needs 19.3R1 or above
attack_vector.ai_factor: Unknown rather than none-with-evidence. JSA11021 now resolves to a support portal that renders client-side, and the advisory text preserved in the CVE record carries no acknowledgement, so no discovery method could be established.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Disabling HTTP/HTTPS services on devices that do not need them, which Juniper states removes the exposure entirely and needs no reboot; otherwise upgrading to the fixed release for the device's train.
prevention.adequacy: The service-disable is complete and immediate but only available where J-Web, Web Authentication, Dynamic-VPN, web-redirect authentication and ZTP are all genuinely unused. The upgrade covers the rest and costs a reboot on a traffic-carrying platform.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Forwarding httpd.log off the device to a collector in a separate trust zone and matching Juniper's published patterns there, rather than grepping the copy on the router.
detection.adequacy: This is the only version of the detection the vendor has not already disclaimed. Juniper states a skilled attacker would remove the on-device entries, so an off-device copy is the difference between evidence and a clean-looking log.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treating an exposed J-Web device as a possible administrative compromise: comparing the running configuration against a known-good copy, rotating administrative credentials, and invalidating J-Web sessions.
response.adequacy: Proportionate to the session-token outcome, which yields the access of whoever was logged in. It is also the step an upgrade cannot substitute for, since the fixed release removes the traversal and nothing an attacker did through it.

NIST-800-53-CM-7.gap: A least-functionality baseline for Junos enumerates management protocols and typically records J-Web as an allowed convenience. The vulnerable component is the shared HTTP service that also backs Web Authentication, Dynamic-VPN, web-redirect authentication and ZTP, so a baseline that turned J-Web off and left one of those on has not disabled httpd and has not removed the flaw.

NIST-800-53-AU-9.gap: AU-9 protects audit records from unauthorised deletion, and Juniper's advisory says outright that a skilled attacker would likely remove the httpd.log entries and thereby eliminate any reliable signature that the device was attacked. The control is attested from on-device permissions and role separation, which is precisely the protection the vendor has told operators not to rely on here.

DORA-Art-9.gap: Article 9 asks a financial entity to protect and prevent by minimising ICT attack surface, and the minimisation available here is switching off one HTTP service. The article operates at the level of policy and asset class, not at the level of which service on an edge router is enabled, so a documented Junos hardening standard covering SSH and administrative accounts satisfies it while every J-Web-enabled device stays exposed.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: B4 secure-configuration reviews of network equipment concentrate on management access control, authentication and protocol hardening. The setting that decides exposure is simply whether the HTTP/HTTPS service is running, and checking the J-Web setting alone gives a false clean on any device where web-redirect authentication, Dynamic-VPN or ZTP keeps httpd alive.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: The internet-facing patch timeframe applies, and following it schedules a Junos upgrade with the reboot and traffic outage that entails. On my reading the mitigation makes no distinction between a workaround that removes the exposure immediately at no availability cost - disabling HTTP/HTTPS services - and a firmware upgrade, so the free mitigation is not the one an assessment steers toward.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.15.gap: Junos does generate the record A.8.15 wants, and Juniper publishes the exact patterns to match in httpd.log. The control does not require that record to be stored anywhere other than the device that produced it, which is the assumption the vendor's own warning about entry removal invalidates - a locally stored log satisfies A.8.15 and proves nothing after a competent attacker.

new_control_requirements.name: FIREWALL-EGRESS-TELEMETRY-SEPARATE-TRUST-ZONE
new_control_requirements.description: Firewall and other perimeter-trust-boundary devices must forward syslog, threat logs, and authentication logs to a SIEM hosted in a separate trust zone (different management plane, different credentials, different authentication path). Telemetry stored on the compromised device is destroyed by the attacker; telemetry on a separate-trust-zone collector survives.
