new_control_requirements.evidence: The RV320 and RV325 chain matches this control's trigger exactly, including the config-exfil step: the Metasploit module modules/exploits/linux/http/cisco_rv32x_rce.rb reads the device configuration through CVE-2019-1653 before injecting through CVE-2019-1652, so the credentials leave the device before the command runs. Cisco's PSIRT recorded active network scanning and public exploit code, and the outcome is arbitrary commands as root on the router's Linux shell. Firmware 1.4.2.22 closes the injection and removes nothing an attacker placed beforehand, so a unit exposed during the window needs its configuration rebuilt from a known-good baseline and every credential it held — administrative passwords, VPN pre-shared keys — rotated wherever they were reused.

CVE-2019-1297.name: Microsoft Excel Remote Code Execution Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: A crafted spreadsheet corrupts Excel's handling of an object in memory and the corrupted state becomes code execution as the user who opened it. The whole delivery cost falls on convincing that user to open the file, because Microsoft's FAQ states the Preview Pane is not an attack vector.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none — PR:N; the attacker needs no account on the target and the code runs at whatever privilege the opening user holds
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L; no race, groom or information leak appears anywhere in the record, and no public exploit exists to contradict that. The real constraint is UI:R, which makes provenance and Protected View the controls that matter rather than network position
attack_vector.ai_factor: None indicated. Microsoft's September 2019 CVRF acknowledges 'L4Nce working with Trend Micro's Zero Day Initiative', so the report came from an outside researcher through a broker; neither Microsoft nor NVD describes how the bug was found, and nothing points to automated or AI-assisted discovery.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Applying the September 2019 Office security update across every servicing channel in the affected list — Windows MSI, Click-to-Run and Mac — and confirming Excel was closed and relaunched afterwards.
prevention.adequacy: It eliminates the defect on every install it reaches. Its limits are coverage and timing: three consoles for six product families, and a vendor exploitability rating of less likely at release, which is the input any severity-driven schedule had to work from until the KEV listing arrived two and a half years later.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Alerting on EXCEL.EXE spawning a child process or opening a network connection shortly after a document was opened from a mail or download directory.
detection.adequacy: It is the strongest signal available, because the exploitation record for this id contains no published sample or artefact to write a file signature against. It fires after the parser has already run, so it bounds dwell time rather than preventing execution.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treating a workstation whose Excel crashed on an externally sourced spreadsheet during the exposure window as a possible failed exploitation attempt, preserving the document and examining the host rather than closing the ticket as an application fault.
response.adequacy: An exploit that has not been made reliable crashes the parser instead of executing, so a crash is a real observable for this class rather than a hypothetical one. The response depends on a user reporting a spreadsheet that would not open, and on the help desk routing that report to security rather than closing it as an application fault.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: Flaw remediation was performed on schedule against the vendor's severity input, and the vendor's input was Exploitation Less Likely for both the latest and older software releases on 2019-09-10. SI-2 contains no clause that reopens a scheduling decision when that assessment is later contradicted, and the contradiction here is CISA listing the CVE as exploited on 2022-03-03 — two and a half years after the decision was recorded as correct.

NIST-800-53-SI-3.gap: Anti-malware is deployed and inspecting the delivery path, and it inspects the wrong object. The malicious property is not content the scanner recognises but a structure that corrupts Excel's own memory handling, and no public sample exists for this id to build a signature from. The control passes a crafted spreadsheet that carries nothing known-bad straight into the vulnerable parser at the user's full privilege.

NIS2-Art21-patch-management.gap: Patch management is implemented and evidenced, and where that evidence comes from a single endpoint console it covers a single servicing model. The affected population is wider than any one console: six product families across MSI, Click-to-Run and Mac servicing, so a compliance figure of one hundred per cent describes the managed subset while Mac Office and per-user Click-to-Run installs of Excel 2016 or Office 365 ProPlus remain unpatched and uncounted.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: Secure maintenance was satisfied in 2019 and is not satisfiable now on the same hosts, because Microsoft's lifecycle record ends Office 2016 extended support in October 2025, and the other perpetual releases in the affected list each carry their own end date. B4 assesses supported-and-current as one state; it cannot record that a host is remediated for this specific id while being unpatched for every Office defect disclosed since its support ended, which is the actual position of an estate still on a perpetual build.

AU-Essential-8-App-Hardening.gap: Application hardening is implemented against the surface the control enumerates — macros, OLE, Flash, browser Java — and the exploit uses none of them. Opening a crafted file through Excel's ordinary parser is the vector, so top maturity on this control changes nothing about exploitability. The measure that would have applied, forcing externally sourced spreadsheets into Protected View, sits outside the control's own list.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: Patch Applications names Office and would have driven the update, and the window it applies is derived from the severity and exploit picture at release. At release Microsoft rated exploitation less likely and no public exploit existed — a state that still holds, since Exploit-DB, Metasploit and the ProjectDiscovery templates carry nothing for this id. The signal that would have accelerated it, the KEV listing, arrived on 2022-03-03, long after the scheduling decision it should have influenced.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.7.gap: Malware protection and awareness training are both in place and both address judgements the user can actually make about a file's origin and plausibility. Neither addresses the property that matters: the file's malicious character is a structure that corrupts Excel's memory handling, invisible in the rendered spreadsheet, and A.8.7 prescribes no technical boundary between the act of opening and the parser running at full user privilege.

new_control_requirements.name: DOWNLOAD-PROVENANCE-ENFORCEMENT
new_control_requirements.description: Exploitation here requires the victim to open an attacker-supplied Office document, so on an estate that has not yet reached the fixed build the delivery path is the only enforceable control. Require Mark-of-the-Web on every Office file arriving by mail, web download, or untrusted file share, and require MOTW-tagged documents to open in Protected View — an isolated, reduced-privilege render — instead of the full parsing path that carries the CWE-94 sink at the user's own process privilege. Provenance must survive the container: files extracted from an archive, mounted from an ISO or VHD, or renamed must inherit the tag rather than lose it, and 'Enable Editing' on externally sourced documents must be blocked by policy rather than left to the user. The distinguishing test: mail a MOTW-tagged spreadsheet nested inside a ZIP to a managed workstation, extract it, and confirm the extracted file still opens in Protected View — a user-application-hardening attestation that covers only macro and ActiveX/OLE settings still lets a provenance-stripped document reach the vulnerable parser with full user privileges.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Microsoft's FAQ for this Excel CVE settles that the delivery path is the whole exploitation cost: it states that exploitation requires a user to open a specially crafted file with an affected version of Excel and that the Preview Pane is not an attack vector. That makes Protected View the boundary that matters, and the control's spreadsheet-in-a-ZIP test is the right one for this defect because the affected population is wide — Excel 2010 SP2 through Excel 2016, Office 2016 and 2019 for Mac, Office 2019 and Office 365 ProPlus — and includes builds now past end of support where no further Office patch will arrive at all. The memory-handling defect itself is inside Excel; provenance enforcement is what keeps an untrusted file from reaching it at full user privilege.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: This Excel CVE is the case where a KEV-triggered clock corrects a vendor-severity-driven one. Microsoft published the fix on 2019-09-10 rating exploitation as less likely for both the latest and older software releases, which is the input a severity-driven schedule inherits; CISA listed the CVE as exploited on 2022-03-03 with a due date of 2022-03-17. Binding the SLA to the later of patch availability and KEV listing puts the clock on the 2022 date rather than leaving the 2019 assessment standing, and completion has to be measured per servicing channel — Windows MSI, Click-to-Run and Mac — because the affected list spans all three.

CVE-2018-8581.name: Microsoft Exchange Server Privilege Escalation Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: An EWS push subscription pointed at an attacker-controlled URL makes Exchange authenticate outbound as itself; the attacker relays that authentication back into EWS and then names any user's SID in a SOAP impersonation header, ending with delegate access to that user's mailbox. One ordinary mailbox account is the entire starting position.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none — PR:N per NVD; read against the published exploits this is optimistic, since both begin from credentials for a standard mailbox-holding account, so the real precondition is any single compromised or attacker-owned mailbox
attack_vector.complexity: high — AC:H; the listener, the outbound NTLM exchange and the relay have to line up inside one window, and the delegation change then takes about a minute to propagate before the attacker can use it, per the exploit's own README
attack_vector.ai_factor: None recorded. Microsoft's own acknowledgement is 'Anonymous working with Trend Micro's Zero Day Initiative', and ZDI's research team published the analysis on 2018-12-19, which both public exploit repositories cite; the work described is manual protocol analysis of the EWS subscription flow.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Deleting the DisableLoopbackCheck value under HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa on every Exchange server, which Microsoft states renders the vulnerability unexploitable and which needs no restart.
prevention.framework_requiring_it: CISA BOD 22-01 (KEV remediation, added 2022-03-03, due 2022-03-17, ransomware: Known)
prevention.adequacy: It closes this CVE completely and costs nothing operationally. Its weakness is that it leaves no version-shaped evidence: nothing in the Exchange build changes, so the remediation is invisible to a scanner and a restored baseline can undo it silently.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Alerting on outbound connections from an Exchange server to non-subscriber hosts, on NTLM authentication into EWS by the server's own machine account, and on delegate permissions appearing on high-value mailboxes.
detection.adequacy: The outbound-connection signal is specific, because a legitimate push subscription points at a known internal endpoint. The mailbox-permission signal is the weaker half: the exploit removes the delegation when it is done, so a periodic export is likely to sample either side of the change.

response.what_would_have_worked: For any estate exposed during the window, auditing delegate and folder permissions on administrative and executive mailboxes against a known-good baseline, and treating the contents of any mailbox that carried an unexplained delegate as read.
response.adequacy: It is the only response that addresses what the attacker actually took, which is mailbox content rather than a credential. It has a short useful life, because delegation changes are not retained indefinitely and the exploit's cleanup step removes the most visible artefact.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: Flaw remediation cannot be evidenced in its usual form, because Microsoft published no binary update for this CVE — the Security Update Guide entry of 2018-11-13 gives a registry-value deletion as the remediation and states no restart is needed. A programme that measures SI-2 compliance by installed Exchange build produces the identical reading on a remediated and an exposed server, so the control's own evidence cannot distinguish the two states.

NIST-800-53-CM-3.gap: Change control is in place and would govern the registry deletion correctly as a one-time change, which is exactly the shape that fails here. The remediation is a persistent absence rather than an applied artefact, so a baseline restore, an image rebuild or an application-compatibility change that re-adds DisableLoopbackCheck reopens the vulnerability with nothing in the Exchange build or the change record to signal it.

NIST-800-53-AC-6.gap: Least privilege is implemented across mailbox and administrative roles and is never consulted during the attack. The authenticating principal is the Exchange server itself, connecting out with CredentialCache.DefaultCredentials at NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM, and the impersonation is a SOAP header naming a SID rather than a privilege check on the attacker's account. The attestation passes on an estate where a standard user can reach a domain administrator's inbox.

NIS2-Art21-identity-management.gap: Identity and access management is assessed against how human accounts are provisioned, authenticated and reviewed, and the identity abused is the Exchange server's machine account. Both public exploits — WyAtu/CVE-2018-8581 and Ridter/Exchange2domain — begin with credentials for one ordinary mailbox and end with delegate rights on another, so a complete and correct user access review examines a population that plays no part in the escalation.

UK-CAF-B2.gap: Access is understood and controlled for accounts and groups, and mailbox delegation joins that picture only where the estate exports it alongside them. The exploit's own cleanup step removes the delegation after use, so the artefact a B2 assessment might catch exists only between the attacker adding it and removing it. A point-in-time permissions export is the wrong instrument for a right that is deliberately transient.

AU-Essential-8-MFA.gap: Multi-factor authentication can be at top maturity and contributes nothing, because no user logon occurs on this path. Exchange initiates the outbound connection and presents its own machine credential over NTLM; the attacker relays it and then names a SID in a SOAP header. Listing MFA as a mitigating control for this CVE is worse than listing nothing, since it records coverage where the mechanism guarantees none.

ISO-27001-2022-A.5.15.gap: Access-control rules are defined from business requirements and correctly permit Exchange to act on the mailboxes it hosts — that permission is the design, so a review finds nothing to change. The defect is that a relayed machine authentication lets an attacker exercise it, and the measures that would address that (Extended Protection for Authentication, blocking arbitrary outbound connections from Exchange, disabling unused EWS subscriptions) are not access-control rules over users and therefore fall outside A.5.15 entirely.

new_control_requirements.name: MITIGATION-ACTIVE-PATCH-PENDING-VERDICT-CLASS
new_control_requirements.description: Compliance verdicts must distinguish three states: (a) binary patch deployed (vulnerability eliminated), (b) vendor-mitigation rule active, no binary patch (residual risk: any defect in the mitigation rule reopens the vulnerability), (c) no mitigation, no patch (full exposure). Audit reports must surface (b) as a distinct compensating-control state with an associated time-bound action item, not as a 'patched per SLA' outcome.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Microsoft Exchange Server is the case where state (a) never becomes available. Microsoft's Security Update Guide entry of 2018-11-13 gives the remediation as deleting the DisableLoopbackCheck value under HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa, with no binary update and no restart, so every remediated Exchange 2010, 2013, 2016 and 2019 server sits permanently in state (b): a vendor mitigation is active, no patch exists, and any change that restores the value returns the server to full exposure with no build number moving. On a CVE that CISA lists as used in ransomware campaigns with a due date of 2022-03-17, an audit report that renders this as 'patched per SLA' has recorded the wrong state and dropped the recurring check the state requires.

new_control_requirements.name: OWA-PER-REQUEST-SIEM-INGESTION
new_control_requirements.description: Exchange OWA per-request access logs (not just authentication events) must be forwarded to an external SIEM with at least 90-day retention. Authentication-only logging misses XSS-stage telemetry — the malicious request flows over an already-authenticated session.
new_control_requirements.evidence: The same logging boundary fails on this CVE for a related reason: the decisive events are EWS requests rather than logons, so authentication-only telemetry records nothing useful. What has to be retained per request is the push-subscription call carrying an external NotificationURL, the inbound NTLM session whose principal is the Exchange machine account, and the SOAP impersonation header naming a SID that is not the caller's. Retention is the load-bearing part on this entry, because the public exploit at github.com/WyAtu/CVE-2018-8581 removes the delegation it added as a cleanup step — the mailbox permission is gone by the time anyone looks, and the request log is the only place the chain remains visible.

CVE-2018-8298.name: ChakraCore Scripting Engine Type Confusion Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: The ICU-backed Intl initializers in ChakraCore omit the already-initialized check their WinGlob counterparts perform, so script can initialize one object as both a NumberFormat and a DateTimeFormat and then read its internal slots under the wrong type. Four lines of ordinary JavaScript reach it; no plugin, macro or file download is involved.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none — PR:N; the attacker needs no account, only for the target to evaluate script from an origin the attacker controls
attack_vector.complexity: high — AC:H; the constraint is build-time rather than runtime. The ICU-backed initializers have to be the ones compiled in, which the proof of concept records as true for the Insider Preview builds it tested and not for WinGlob builds, and the operator cannot inspect that choice from outside
attack_vector.ai_factor: None recorded. Exploit-DB 45217 attributes the finding to Google Security Research via Project Zero issue 1582, and the write-up is manual source review that points at the ICU and WinGlob initializers in the repository.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Obtaining a product release rebuilt against ChakraCore 1.10.1 or later from every vendor whose software links the engine and evaluates untrusted script, and relaunching the hosting process.
prevention.adequacy: It eliminates the defect where a rebuilt release exists. The dependency is entirely on the embedding vendor: no operator can apply 1.10.1 to a statically linked engine, and with Microsoft's security updates for the 1.11 branch ended on 9th March 2021 there is no supplier commitment behind the engine's next defect.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Alerting on abnormal termination of a process that hosts a script engine when the fault lies inside Intl formatting rather than in the application's own code.
detection.adequacy: It is the most reliable signal available, because the public artefact is a crash proof of concept and any imperfect weaponization attempt produces the same crash. It says nothing about a working exploit, which by design does not terminate the process, and it requires crash telemetry attributable to the embedded engine rather than to the hosting application, which is a collection decision that has to have been taken before the disclosure.

response.what_would_have_worked: Enumerating every product in the estate that links ChakraCore and evaluates script from untrusted origins, and putting each on a dated decision — rebuilt release, or migration off the engine.
response.adequacy: It produces the inventory that every control on this entry is missing, and it is the only action that survives the engine's end of vendor support. It is slow, and it depends on vendors disclosing which engine their product embeds — what an SBOM would supply, and what cannot be established from outside the build.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: Flaw remediation is implemented and cannot execute on this defect, because the fixed level NVD gives — ChakraCore 1.10.1 — is not something an operator installs. Where the engine is statically linked, the remediation is the embedding vendor rebuilding and re-releasing, and the ChakraCore README records Microsoft's security updates for the 1.11 branch ending on 9th March 2021, so no supplier stands behind whatever comes next.

NIST-800-53-SR-3.gap: Supply-chain process runs against declared dependencies and a statically linked JavaScript engine is rarely declared. The project's final tagged release is v1.11.24 from 2020-12-09, so any product shipping at or below that carries the engine as the community left it. The assurance SR-3 asks a supplier to provide is, in this case, a README describing a community project rather than a maintenance commitment.

NIS2-Art21-vulnerability-management.gap: Vulnerability handling is in place and receives the disclosure, and the disclosure is not answerable at the operator's level. Exploitability turns on whether the embedding exposes Intl to untrusted script and whether the ICU-backed initializers rather than the WinGlob ones were compiled in — a source-level question the measure obliges nobody in the chain to answer, so the finding sits open with no determinable status.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: Configuration and maintenance are assessed on supported-and-current, a binary the situation does not fit. The AC:H in AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:R exists because the vulnerable ICU path must be the compiled one, which the proof of concept confirms for Microsoft Edge 42.17672.1000.0 and EdgeHTML 17.17672 and leaves open for every other embedding. B4 has no way to record a product as current while its exploitability depends on an unobservable build flag.

AU-Essential-8-App-Hardening.gap: Application hardening is applied to the surface the control names — plugins, ads, Java, OLE — and the exploit uses none of it. Four lines of standard JavaScript calling Intl.NumberFormat.apply, Intl.DateTimeFormat.apply and Intl.DateTimeFormat.prototype.formatToParts.apply reach the confused type, so the maturity level attained has no bearing on whether the trigger runs.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: Vulnerability information arrives in good time and in unusual detail — Exploit-DB 45217 names the file, the two initializer variants and the exact API sequence — and lands against an asset the register does not list. The record names ChakraCore; the register names applications, and nothing joins them, so an organisation that ships the engine inside a product cannot tell that this advisory concerns it.

CycloneDX-v1.6-SBOM.gap: A component inventory for a native application that embeds a script engine exists only where the vendor publishes one, and even then it answers half the question. An SBOM naming ChakraCore below 1.10.1 identifies the population to act on, which is genuine progress here, but the ICU-versus-WinGlob initializer choice is a build flag rather than a declared component, so the record establishes exposure candidates rather than exploitability.

new_control_requirements.name: TIER-3-DEPENDENCY-INVENTORY
new_control_requirements.description: Supply chain inventory must extend to tier-3 dependencies (dependencies of dependencies of direct dependencies). SBOM coverage for libsystemd-class transitive dependencies cannot be omitted under SR-3.
new_control_requirements.evidence: ChakraCore is the statically linked form of this problem. NVD scopes this CVE to the engine below 1.10.1 while the estate's asset register names applications, so an operator cannot tell which of its products the advisory concerns — and Exploit-DB 45217 supplies the vulnerable file path lib/Runtime/Library/InJavascript/Intl.js, which is only actionable by an organisation that already knows it ships that file. The inventory requirement outlives this CVE: the ChakraCore README records Microsoft's security updates for the 1.11 branch ending on 9th March 2021 and the project continuing as a community effort with v1.11.24 (2020-12-09) as its last tagged release, so knowing where the engine is embedded is the precondition for every future decision about it.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: For an embedded ChakraCore the SLA's compensating-control branch is the only branch available on the KEV clock, because the fix is a rebuilt product release from another vendor rather than an update the operator can deploy. Between the 2022-03-03 listing and its 2022-03-17 due date, the actionable measures are refusing untrusted script to the embedding product or withdrawing it from use — the same measures that remain necessary afterwards, since Microsoft's security updates for the ChakraCore 1.11 branch ended on 9th March 2021 and the engine will receive no further vendor fix for whatever is found next.

attack_vector.description: Sustained invalid SSH or Telnet login attempts arriving while an administrator modifies the login block-for configuration reach an attempt to free an area of memory that was never allocated, reloading the Cisco IOS device.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none — PR:N; the attacker supplies failed authentications only and never holds a credential
attack_vector.complexity: high — AC:H; the attacker controls the login attempts but not the concurrent administrative edit that the reload depends on, and no workaround exists
attack_vector.ai_factor: Attributed by the advisory to the resolution of Cisco TAC support cases. No tooling is named and nothing indicates AI-assisted discovery.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Reaching the first fixed release recorded against Cisco bug CSCuz60599 and reloading, combined in the interim with restricting SSH and Telnet management reachability so sustained invalid attempts cannot arrive from untrusted networks.
prevention.adequacy: The advisory publishes no workaround, so nothing short of the fixed release removes the defect. Management-plane reachability restriction reduces who can supply the attacker's half and is unavailable where the interface must remain broadly reachable.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Alerting on the %SYS-2-CHUNKBADREFCOUNT message naming the Secure Login process, which the advisory publishes as this defect's indicator of compromise, plus off-box collection of authentication and configuration-change events so the reload can be placed against a login-attempt burst and an administrative edit in one timeline.
detection.adequacy: The vendor-published error string classifies the event on its own and needs no correlation, but it has to be shipped off-box before the restart, because the on-box log buffer does not survive the reload. The authentication and change feeds add what the crashinfo does not carry — which edit was in flight and who was authenticating — and neither is remarkable alone.

response.what_would_have_worked: Retaining the crashinfo file the advisory says exploitation generates and taking it to Cisco TAC with show tech-support output, which is the vendor's own route to determining whether the device was compromised by exploitation, rather than attributing the reload to the change being faulty.
response.adequacy: Impact is availability only, so response restores the device and nothing more. Its value is that the advisory names an artefact and an adjudicator: the crashinfo file survives the restart, so the wrong conclusion — that the login block-for edit was itself bad — is refutable rather than merely suspected.

NIST-800-53-CM-3.gap: The approved change is the hazard. CM-3 evaluates whether an edit to login block-for is authorised and correctly specified, and on an affected IOS release the risk is entirely in when it is applied relative to inbound login attempts — a variable no approval workflow captures.

NIST-800-53-SI-4.gap: Where monitoring surfaces the failed-authentication burst and the operator responds by tuning login protection, that edit is the administrative action the advisory names as the exploitation condition on an affected IOS release. SI-4 built on authentication and traffic events also does not watch for %SYS-2-CHUNKBADREFCOUNT against the Secure Login process, which is the string cisco-sa-20180328-slogin publishes as the indicator and the only one that names the defect rather than describing a restart.

NIS2-Art21-availability.gap: Availability measures address capacity and continuity of service. The loss here originates in a maintenance action taken on the device while it was being probed, so the measures Article 21 asks for can all be in place and none of them stands between the administrator's edit and the reload.

UK-CAF-B5.gap: Network resilience is argued from redundancy and diverse paths, while the trigger here is a configuration change. Where that change is applied from one template to both members of a redundant pair, each takes the same edit and the failure correlates across the estate instead of being absorbed by the standby.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: Reporting against the fixed release for CSCuz60599 is correct and incomplete. It cannot record that no workaround exists, so an operator reading a patch dashboard has no way to see that the interim risk-acceptance line for this device is empty rather than merely unexercised.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: A.8.8 expects appropriate measures once a vulnerability is known. Between the 2022-03-03 KEV listing and the reload onto a fixed release there is no configuration change, no rule and no toggle to apply — only a constraint on when administrators touch login block-for, which the control has no field for.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CISA listed this Cisco IOS Login Block defect on 2022-03-03 with a 2022-03-17 due date, against a fix shipped 2018-03-28 under bug CSCuz60599. Cisco states that PSIRT 'became aware' of attempted exploitation in March 2022 but did not amend cisco-sa-20180328-slogin to say so until Version 1.1 on 2022-DEC-15, so for the nine months covering the KEV due date the listing was the only published signal an operator could act on — which is exactly the trigger this SLA keys on. Its NVD score is 5.9 and its EPSS 0.04967 (91.5th percentile). Because the advisory publishes no workaround for CSCuz60599, the SLA's compensating-control branch reduces to management-plane reachability restriction, which has to be recorded as such rather than as remediation.

new_control_requirements.name: FIREWALL-EGRESS-TELEMETRY-SEPARATE-TRUST-ZONE
new_control_requirements.description: Firewall and other perimeter-trust-boundary devices must forward syslog, threat logs, and authentication logs to a SIEM hosted in a separate trust zone (different management plane, different credentials, different authentication path). Telemetry stored on the compromised device is destroyed by the attacker; telemetry on a separate-trust-zone collector survives.
new_control_requirements.evidence: cisco-sa-20180328-slogin leaves two artefacts on the device itself — the %SYS-2-CHUNKBADREFCOUNT message against the Secure Login process, and the crashinfo file it says exploitation generates — and only the second survives the restart. The control names authentication logs specifically, which on a Cisco IOS device running an affected 15.4 train are the other half: the burst of invalid SSH or Telnet attempts, and the administrative edit to login block-for that the advisory names as the exploitation condition. Held off-box in a separate management plane, they arrive with the error string that the on-box buffer loses at reload, so a device below the first fixed release for CSCuz60599 yields a timeline rather than a bare crashinfo and a TAC case.

attack_vector.description: Where login quiet-mode access-class was configured before login block-for and the device has not reloaded since, Cisco IOS's login-block path frees memory that was never allocated. An unauthenticated remote attacker exercising that path reloads the device.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none — PR:N; the attacker exercises the login path itself and never needs valid credentials
attack_vector.complexity: high — AC:H; the vulnerable state depends on the order two commands were entered and on the absence of a reload since, none of which the attacker can observe or create
attack_vector.ai_factor: Found during the resolution of Cisco TAC support cases, per the advisory's Source section. No tooling is named and nothing indicates AI-assisted discovery.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Reaching the first fixed release recorded against Cisco bug CSCuy32360 and reloading; short of that, applying the advisory's ordering workaround and reloading so the device leaves the vulnerable state.
prevention.adequacy: Both routes end in a reload, because the vulnerable state does not clear while the device stays up. The workaround also has to be applied to the hardening template, or the next device built from it is created in the same state.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Off-box syslog carrying the %SEC_LOGIN-4-LOGIN_FAILED and %SEC_LOGIN-1-QUIET_MODE_ON pair the advisory publishes for CSCuy32360, plus configuration-change collection so the login quiet-mode access-class change and the later reload with no reload in between sit in one timeline.
detection.adequacy: The vendor publishes a specific paired message written at least twice immediately before the crash, so the event is identifiable from syslog alone where syslog is shipped off-box before the restart takes the local buffer. What the messages do not give is the device's exposure — the ordering of the two login commands and the absence of a reload since — which is why the configuration feed is needed alongside.

response.what_would_have_worked: On a repeat reload, checking the two login commands and the device's uptime against the change that introduced them, rather than replacing hardware.
response.adequacy: The impact is availability only, so response restores service and cannot reduce loss. It matters because the answer is a configuration-history question that a hardware-fault workflow will never ask.

NIST-800-53-CM-3.gap: Change control approves the content of a change, and both commands involved are hardening measures with an obvious security case. The defect is a property of their sequence on a device that has not reloaded since — something no change record expresses, and nothing an approval decision is asked to consider.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: Flaw remediation was satisfied when the fix for CSCuy32360 shipped in 2018. SI-2 has no state for a remediation that is a documented command ordering rather than a version, and no trigger for the 2022-03-03 KEV listing that changed the urgency without changing the fix.

NIS2-Art21-vulnerability-handling.gap: Handling a known vulnerability starts with determining applicability, and applicability here is a configuration-history fact. show running-config renders the end state and not the order it was reached in, so an entity following the obligation faithfully cannot answer the question the advisory poses.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: The hardening B4 encourages is what creates the precondition: login block-for with quiet-mode access-class is a brute-force defence, and where quiet-mode access-class is applied first the result is a device an unauthenticated attacker can reload. B4 has no way to record that one of its own recommendations carries this cost on affected IOS releases.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: The release number is a necessary input and not a sufficient one. On an affected train, whether the device is vulnerable depends on command ordering and reload history, so patch reporting can be simultaneously accurate and unable to tell the operator which devices are actually exposed.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.9.gap: On the reading above, A.8.9 acts on the configuration as it currently reads — establishing, documenting, implementing, monitoring and reviewing it. The vulnerable property is historical, so a conformant configuration-management programme produces a complete and accurate record that contains none of the information needed to scope this CVE.

new_control_requirements.name: MITIGATION-ACTIVE-PATCH-PENDING-VERDICT-CLASS
new_control_requirements.description: Compliance verdicts must distinguish three states: (a) binary patch deployed (vulnerability eliminated), (b) vendor-mitigation rule active, no binary patch (residual risk: any defect in the mitigation rule reopens the vulnerability), (c) no mitigation, no patch (full exposure). Audit reports must surface (b) as a distinct compensating-control state with an associated time-bound action item, not as a 'patched per SLA' outcome.
new_control_requirements.evidence: cisco-sa-20180328-slogin gives a real workaround for this defect — configure login block-for before login quiet-mode access-class, or reload after both are configured — which puts an unpatched Cisco IOS device squarely in the control's state (b). The residual risk the control warns about is concrete here: the ordering is a property of a hardening template, so the next switch built from an unamended template is created vulnerable again, and the mitigation silently lapses. Recording those devices as remediated against the 2022-03-17 KEV due date rather than as compensating-controlled with a time-bound upgrade is the specific misclassification the control exists to prevent.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CISA listed this Cisco IOS Login Block defect on 2022-03-03 with a 2022-03-17 due date, against a fix that shipped 2018-03-28 under bug CSCuy32360. Cisco states PSIRT 'became aware' of attempted exploitation in March 2022, but cisco-sa-20180328-slogin did not carry that finding until Version 1.1 on 2022-DEC-15 — so for the whole of the KEV remediation window the listing was the only published signal, which is the trigger this SLA keys on rather than the 5.9 NVD score or the 0.04967 EPSS (91.5th percentile). The documented-compensating-control branch is directly usable here because the vendor publishes an ordering workaround, and a queue ranked by score alone would not reach the advisory to find it.

CVE-2018-0175.name: Cisco IOS, XR, and XE Software Buffer Overflow Vulnerability (CVE-2018-0175)

attack_vector.description: An adjacent unauthenticated attacker plants format-string directives in LLDP message fields, which the subsystem stores and later hands to a formatting routine as a format string. The primitive fires when an authenticated operator runs the show command that renders the stored neighbour record, yielding a reload or code execution with elevated privileges.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none — PR:N; the LLDP message is accepted on any port where the feature is active, with no credential or session on the device
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L; the real constraint is UI:R, since the payload sits inert in the neighbour table until an operator runs the specific rendering show command
attack_vector.ai_factor: Attributed by the advisory to the resolution of a Cisco TAC support case. No tooling is named and nothing supports an AI-assisted-discovery reading.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Upgrading to the first fixed release for bug CSCvd73664 on the installed train and reloading, with LLDP disabled on ports facing untrusted endpoints while the upgrade is scheduled.
prevention.adequacy: The upgrade is complete only after the reload, and disabling LLDP on untrusted ports does not clear neighbour records already stored from before the change. Telling operators to avoid a show command is not a control — the advisory does not publish which command it is.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Off-box syslog with terminal-session accounting, so that a crash can be tied to the operator session and the command that immediately preceded it rather than to inbound traffic.
detection.adequacy: The reload clears the on-box buffer, so only what was already shipped survives. Command accounting also has to be enabled before the event, and it records the command without recording the neighbour data being rendered.

response.what_would_have_worked: Where the outcome may have been code execution rather than a reload, comparing the device's configuration against a known-good baseline and rotating credentials it held, before returning it to service.
response.adequacy: Depends on a baseline existing to compare against. Cisco's finding is of attempted exploitation and it names no actor, campaign or report, so the comparison is run without any indicator narrowing which devices to run it on — the cost scales with the number of switches carrying an affected image rather than with any evidence about them.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: The fix has existed since 2018-03-28, so SI-2 was satisfied years before the risk changed. The control cannot express a KEV listing on an already-patched, already-closed CVE, and it cannot express a vendor advisory amended long afterwards — cisco-sa-20180328-lldp reached Version 1.2 on 2022-DEC-15, nine months after the 2022-03-03 listing. Neither event moves anything in the flaw-remediation record.

NIST-800-53-CM-7.gap: CM-7 governs whether the service runs, not what the service retains. LLDP is kept for legitimate topology discovery, and keeping it means keeping a table of peer-supplied strings that this defect turns into a format string at render time — a residual the least-functionality decision never examined.

NIS2-Art21-network-security.gap: Network-security measures under Article 21 are framed around traffic and boundaries. Here the attacker's frame is accepted as ordinary link-local management traffic and does nothing; the exploitation event is an operator typing a show command later. No boundary control observes that gap between delivery and detonation.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: B4 evidence is compiled per CVE. cisco-sa-20180328-lldp carries two defects in the same subsystem — this format-string bug under CSCvd73664 and a buffer overflow under CSCvd73487 and CSCuo17183 — and remediating both as separate tickets produces complete evidence while leaving the subsystem's track record unexamined.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: Patch currency is a binary against the fixed release and takes no account of the UI:R condition that governs when this defect actually fires. Two devices on the same vulnerable image carry very different real exposure depending on how often operators run LLDP show commands on them, and the report shows neither.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.21.gap: Security of network services is assessed against what the service is for, and LLDP's purpose — advertising and collecting neighbour identity — is unobjectionable. The assessment has no mechanism for revisiting a service that has now produced two exploitable defects in one advisory, which is a code-quality signal rather than a functional one.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: The fix for Cisco bug CSCvd73664 shipped with cisco-sa-20180328-lldp on 2018-03-28; CISA listed the CVE on 2022-03-03 with a 2022-03-17 due date. Cisco amended that advisory to record attempted exploitation only at Version 1.2 on 2022-DEC-15, so an operator watching the vendor advisory alone had nothing new to act on across the whole KEV window. The SLA's 'whichever is later' clause is the operative half for a four-year-old fix: the clock runs from the listing, not from the 2018 patch date and not from the vendor's later amendment. EPSS of 0.03501 (88.2nd percentile) would not float this Cisco IOS LLDP defect to the top of a score-ranked queue on its own.

new_control_requirements.name: INCOMPLETE-PATCH-SEQUENCE-SEVERITY-MULTIPLIER
new_control_requirements.description: Vulnerability-management programs must apply a severity multiplier when a CVE is the Nth in an incomplete-patch sequence on the same primitive (third MOTW bypass, second AMSI bypass, etc.). Framework controls treating each CVE as discrete obscure the structural defect; the Nth CVE in a sequence implies that future bypasses on the same primitive are likely.
new_control_requirements.evidence: cisco-sa-20180328-lldp publishes two defects in Cisco's LLDP field handling on the same day — this format-string bug (CSCvd73664) and a buffer overflow (CSCvd73487 for IOS and IOS XE, CSCuo17183 for IOS XR) — and both were later listed by CISA on 2022-03-03. These are co-disclosed siblings rather than a sequence of incomplete patches, so the control's severity-multiplier arithmetic does not transfer literally. What does transfer is its second sentence: handling them as two discrete tickets produces complete remediation records and still leaves the estate with no assessment of an LLDP parser that yielded two exploitable primitives in one publication, on ports facing untrusted endpoints.

CVE-2018-0174.name: Cisco IOS Software and Cisco IOS XE Software Improper Input Validation Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: A crafted DHCPv4 packet reaches a Cisco IOS or IOS XE relay agent that encapsulates option 82 information from other relay agents; incomplete validation of that data reloads the device and drops DHCP and forwarding for the segments behind it.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none — PR:N; no credential is presented at any point in the path
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L; exposure is gated by four configuration conditions rather than by exploit difficulty, and the advisory publishes no workaround
attack_vector.ai_factor: Reported to Cisco by Tenable, credited in the advisory's Source section. No tooling is named and nothing indicates automated or AI-assisted discovery.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Upgrading to a release that is at or above the first fixed release for bug CSCuh91645 specifically — verified against that bug id rather than against the advisory bundle — and reloading.
prevention.adequacy: The reload is the outage the defect causes, so it needs a window. The verification has to be against CSCuh91645 rather than against the 2018-03-28 DHCP relay bundle, because the three advisories published that day carry three distinct bug ids — where a target release is chosen from one of the others, the device is upgraded and still below the first fixed release for this one.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Off-box syslog and reload accounting for every relay-configured router, so an unplanned restart is timestamped somewhere the restart cannot erase and can be compared with DHCPv4 activity.
detection.adequacy: This records that the device restarted and roughly when, not what was in the packet. It is enough to distinguish a pattern from a one-off and not enough to attribute the cause without crashinfo and a TAC case.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treating a second unexplained relay reload as a scoping question — check the four conditions in the advisory and the installed train against CSCuh91645 — rather than as a hardware replacement decision.
response.adequacy: Impact is availability only, so response restores service and nothing more. Its worth is that it stops a recurring outage being absorbed as an ageing-chassis problem when the answer is a release comparison.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: Where remediation records reference advisories rather than bug ids, three DHCP relay advisories published on 2018-03-28 collapse into one ticket while carrying three distinct bug ids. A release chosen to close one of them can sit below the first fixed release for CSCuh91645, and an SI-2 evidence trail of ticket plus version cannot reveal that.

NIST-800-53-CM-7.gap: The encapsulation policy for option 82 received from other relay agents is what puts a relay with nothing upstream of it into scope for no operational return. Where a least-functionality review of a network device examines management services rather than protocol feature settings, that condition survives a review which would have removed it on merit.

NIS2-Art21-patch-management.gap: The duty is met by having and following an update process. It says nothing about the specific tension this CVE creates, where applying the update means reloading the very relay whose reload is the impact, and the 2022-03-17 KEV due date has to win against a change-freeze calendar that the obligation does not mention.

UK-CAF-B5.gap: Where a relay's resilience is a redundant path or a second helper address and both units carry an image below the first fixed release for CSCuh91645, the two are not independent: the same crafted packet that reloads the primary reaches the secondary over that redundant path and meets identical option 82 handling. The design absorbs a chassis failure and not a software defect held in common, and B5 evidence records the redundancy without recording that it is duplicated exposure.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: Patch reporting keyed to the 2018-03-28 DHCP advisories can report the estate as remediated while devices remain below the first fixed release for CSCuh91645, because that bug id is tracked separately from the relay defects published alongside it.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: Timely vulnerability information and exposure evaluation both worked in 2018 and both were rendered stale in 2022 by two separate events landing on a four-year-old advisory: the 2022-03-03 KEV listing, and the amendment of cisco-sa-20180328-dhcpr3 to Version 1.1 on 2022-DEC-15. An intake process that watches new publications sees neither, and the nine months between them means the vendor channel could not have carried the warning inside the 2022-03-17 due date.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CISA listed this Cisco IOS and IOS XE DHCP relay defect on 2022-03-03 with a 2022-03-17 due date, four years after cisco-sa-20180328-dhcpr3 shipped the fix for bug CSCuh91645. Cisco states PSIRT 'became aware' of attempted exploitation in March 2022; the advisory itself did not say so until Version 1.1 on 2022-DEC-15, so the listing is the only thing that reached an operator inside the due date. EPSS reads 0.07658 (94.1st percentile). The SLA's mitigation branch is what makes it usable on a relay that cannot reload immediately: removing the encapsulation of option 82 information received from other DHCP relay agents drops one of the four criteria the advisory requires, and that state has to be documented rather than assumed.

new_control_requirements.name: INCOMPLETE-PATCH-SEQUENCE-SEVERITY-MULTIPLIER
new_control_requirements.description: Vulnerability-management programs must apply a severity multiplier when a CVE is the Nth in an incomplete-patch sequence on the same primitive (third MOTW bypass, second AMSI bypass, etc.). Framework controls treating each CVE as discrete obscure the structural defect; the Nth CVE in a sequence implies that future bypasses on the same primitive are likely.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Three advisories published on 2018-03-28 — cisco-sa-20180328-dhcpr1, -dhcpr2 and -dhcpr3 — address one primitive, the IOS and IOS XE handling of DHCP option 82 relay-agent information, under three bug ids: CSCvg62730, CSCvg62754 and this entry's CSCuh91645. They are co-disclosed rather than a chain of incomplete patches, so the control's multiplier arithmetic does not apply literally. The clause that does apply is the middle one: treating each as discrete is exactly how an operator upgrades against one bug id, records the DHCP relay finding as closed, and leaves the train below the first fixed release for the other two.

CVE-2018-0173.name: Cisco IOS and IOS XE Software Improper Input Validation Vulnerability (CVE-2018-0173)

attack_vector.description: An attacker's crafted DHCPv4 packet is forwarded by the relay to the DHCPv4 server; the server's DHCPOFFER carries encapsulated option 82 information back, and the relay's function for restoring that information validates it incompletely and reloads the device.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none — PR:N; the attacker needs no credential anywhere, only the ability to send a DHCPv4 packet the relay will forward
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L; the constraint is configuration rather than skill, and the round trip through a trusted server is what widens reachability rather than narrowing it
attack_vector.ai_factor: Reported to Cisco by Tenable per the advisory's Source section. No tooling is named, and nothing supports an automated- or AI-assisted-discovery reading.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Upgrading to the first fixed release for bug CSCvg62754 and reloading, with DHCPv4 reachability to the relay restricted to segments that legitimately need it while the window is arranged.
prevention.adequacy: The upgrade requires the same outage it prevents, so it must be scheduled. Restricting reachability bounds who can start the exchange but leaves every permitted client segment able to trigger it, and it is unavailable where the relay serves general user networks.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Checking the reload against the vendor's own indicator — a segmentation fault in the DHCPD Receive process, whose stack trace the advisory says a support organisation reviews to determine whether the device was compromised — and correlating relay reloads with DHCPv4 transaction records on both the client and server legs, using off-box collection so the correlation survives the reload.
detection.adequacy: The named process fault classifies the event: a restart attributable to DHCPD Receive is this defect rather than an unexplained crash, which is what the transaction correlation on its own could never establish, since the server sees a normal offer and the client leg a normal request. What neither gives is the packet — the advisory routes that question to the vendor's stack-trace review rather than answering it on the device.

response.what_would_have_worked: Preserving the device's crash state and taking the DHCPD Receive stack trace to a support organisation, as the advisory directs, and raising it against bug CSCvg62754 — so a recurring DHCP outage is classified as a KEV item with a 2022-03-17 due date rather than as flaky hardware.
response.adequacy: With C:N and I:N there is nothing to contain or eradicate, so response cannot reduce impact — its only product is a correct classification that moves the upgrade up the queue.

NIST-800-53-SC-7.gap: The exploit rides the relay-to-server conversation that boundary protection must permit for DHCP to function. SC-7 rules are written by direction and by host, and the malicious option 82 content arrives from the trusted server host in the trusted direction, so no rule that could be tightened would see it.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: Fixed software for bug CSCvg62754 has existed since 2018-03-28, so remediation timing was satisfied long before the risk changed. Nothing in SI-2 responds to a 2022-03-03 KEV listing on an already-patched CVE, which is the only event that occurred.

NIS2-Art21-business-continuity.gap: A continuity plan that restores the relay from a configuration backup restores the vulnerable state along with the service, since the same image and the same option 82 insertion configuration come back. Recovery-time objectives are met precisely while the exposure is unchanged.

UK-CAF-D1.gap: Response and recovery planning is shaped around compromise. This defect's outcome is availability only — C:N, I:N with a scope change — so the plan's containment and eradication branches have no work to do, and the branch that matters, preventing recurrence, is a patch decision rather than a response one.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: Patch currency against the first fixed release for CSCvg62754 is necessary and does not identify scope. Whether option 82 insertion is configured on the relay interface, and whether the DHCPv4 server supports option 82, are running-configuration and service facts that no patch inventory holds.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.16.gap: Where monitoring on this path watches interface state and DHCP pool health, the exploit presents as a normal-looking request on the client leg, a normal-looking offer on the server leg, and a device restart in between. The evidence that names the cause is not on that path at all: the advisory points at a segmentation fault in the DHCPD Receive process and at the stack trace behind it, which is collected by preserving crash state on the device rather than by monitoring the network the device sits in.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Fixed software for Cisco bug CSCvg62754 shipped with cisco-sa-20180328-dhcpr2 on 2018-03-28, and CISA listed this IOS and IOS XE DHCP relay-reply defect on 2022-03-03 with a 2022-03-17 due date while Cisco was recording attempted exploitation in the wild. EPSS reads 0.07658 (94.1st percentile). The SLA's value on this entry is that it forces the listing to start the clock on a CVE whose fix predates it by four years, and its compensating-control branch has a concrete form: restricting which client segments may send DHCPv4 to the relay while the reload is scheduled.

new_control_requirements.name: MITIGATION-ACTIVE-PATCH-PENDING-VERDICT-CLASS
new_control_requirements.description: Compliance verdicts must distinguish three states: (a) binary patch deployed (vulnerability eliminated), (b) vendor-mitigation rule active, no binary patch (residual risk: any defect in the mitigation rule reopens the vulnerability), (c) no mitigation, no patch (full exposure). Audit reports must surface (b) as a distinct compensating-control state with an associated time-bound action item, not as a 'patched per SLA' outcome.
new_control_requirements.evidence: cisco-sa-20180328-dhcpr2 states that no workarounds are available, so a Cisco IOS or IOS XE relay below the fixed release for CSCvg62754 is in state (c), not state (b) — full exposure with nothing standing in the way. The distinction has a concrete trap on this CVE: the reachability restriction an operator can apply while waiting for a maintenance window bounds who may send DHCPv4 to the relay and does not touch the defect, and because it looks like an action taken it invites recording as state (b). This control forces it into the compensating-control column with a time-bound action item instead of being counted as mitigation of a KEV item with a 2022-03-17 due date.

CVE-2018-0172.name: Cisco IOS and IOS XE Software Improper Input Validation Vulnerability (CVE-2018-0172)

attack_vector.description: A crafted DHCPv4 packet carries option 82 relay-agent information that a Cisco IOS or IOS XE relay agent copies without bounding it, overflowing the heap and reloading the device. The DHCP service, and everything else the relay forwards, goes down with it.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none — PR:N; the packet is processed by the relay agent with no authentication step anywhere in the path
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L; difficulty is not the constraint, configuration is: all four conditions in cisco-sa-20180328-dhcpr1 must hold, and no workaround exists for a device that meets them
attack_vector.ai_factor: Reported to Cisco by Tenable and credited in the advisory's Source section. No tooling is named and nothing indicates automated or AI-assisted discovery.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Upgrading to the first fixed release for bug CSCvg62730 and reloading, or — where the design permits — removing the option 82 encapsulation policy for packets received from other relay agents, which drops one of the four conditions the advisory requires.
prevention.adequacy: The upgrade needs a reload of a device whose reload is the impact being avoided, so it has to be scheduled rather than rushed. Removing the encapsulation policy is only available where no downstream relay depends on it, and it is a scope reduction rather than a fix.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Off-box syslog from the relay so the reload is recorded somewhere the reload cannot erase, correlated with DHCPv4 flow records on the relay path.
detection.adequacy: Flow records show a DHCPv4 packet, not its option 82 contents, so the correlation raises suspicion rather than confirming the cause. Both telemetry paths must be in place before the event; nothing is recoverable from the device afterwards.

response.what_would_have_worked: Retaining the crashinfo written at reload and opening it with Cisco TAC against bug CSCvg62730, so a repeat outage is classified rather than absorbed as instability.
response.adequacy: The impact is availability only — the vector carries C:N and I:N — so response cannot recover anything beyond service restoration. Its value is classification: it turns a recurring unexplained reload into a KEV item with a due date.

NIST-800-53-SI-10.gap: SI-10 is assessed against the organisation's applications and their input handling. The failing validation is Cisco's, inside an IOS relay agent parsing an option 82 sub-option, and no part of an SI-10 assessment reaches vendor firmware — the control is met on evidence drawn from an entirely different codebase.

NIST-800-53-SC-5.gap: SC-5 evidence is rate limits, thresholds and capacity headroom, all premised on denial of service arriving as volume. A single crafted DHCPv4 packet reloads the relay, so the traffic profile stays entirely normal and every threshold the control tests is left untouched.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: The fixed software has been available since 2018-03-28, so flaw remediation was satisfied years before the KEV listing on 2022-03-03. SI-2 has no mechanism that reacts to a vendor amending an existing advisory to add an exploitation finding, which is the only thing that changed.

NIS2-Art21-incident-handling.gap: The Article 21 incident-handling measure, and the Article 23 early warning that follows it, both depend on the event being recognised as an incident. A relay reload with its on-box log buffer wiped looks like a fault, so where the DHCP outage is handled as instability the incident-handling process is never entered at all.

UK-CAF-C1.gap: Where monitoring coverage of a distribution router consists of reachability and interface state, it records the reload faithfully and carries no information about cause. C1 can be well implemented on that basis and still leave an operator unable to distinguish this defect from a power interruption.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: Patch status is tracked per release, and release alone does not determine exposure here — the fourth condition in cisco-sa-20180328-dhcpr1, encapsulation of option 82 received from other relay agents, is a running-configuration property that no software inventory records.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.28.gap: Secure coding conformity covers software the organisation develops. The unbounded copy of peer-supplied option 82 data is in Cisco's firmware, which an operator can neither review nor rebuild, so A.8.28 can be fully satisfied while the defect stays in production.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Cisco shipped the fix for bug CSCvg62730 on 2018-03-28 and CISA listed this IOS and IOS XE DHCP relay heap overflow on 2022-03-03 with a 2022-03-17 due date. Cisco states PSIRT 'became aware' of attempted exploitation in March 2022, but cisco-sa-20180328-dhcpr1 was not amended to say so until Version 1.1 on 2022-DEC-15, so the listing was the only signal available inside the due date — which is the trigger this SLA keys on. Its EPSS is 0.07871, the 94.2nd percentile. The documented-compensating-control branch has a concrete form here: removing the option 82 encapsulation policy drops one of the four criteria the advisory requires, which is a defensible interim state while the reload is scheduled.

new_control_requirements.name: FIREWALL-EGRESS-TELEMETRY-SEPARATE-TRUST-ZONE
new_control_requirements.description: Firewall and other perimeter-trust-boundary devices must forward syslog, threat logs, and authentication logs to a SIEM hosted in a separate trust zone (different management plane, different credentials, different authentication path). Telemetry stored on the compromised device is destroyed by the attacker; telemetry on a separate-trust-zone collector survives.
new_control_requirements.evidence: The control's premise — that on-device telemetry does not survive the event — holds here for a mechanical reason rather than an adversarial one: the successful outcome of CVE-2018-0172 is a device reload, and an IOS relay agent's logging buffer is in memory. Whatever the router recorded about the crafted DHCPv4 packet is gone by the time an operator logs in to ask why DHCP failed. For a Cisco IOS or IOS XE aggregation router relaying for downstream relays, forwarding syslog to a collector outside its own failure domain is the difference between a KEV-listed defect with a 2022-03-17 due date being classified and being absorbed as unexplained instability.

CVE-2018-0167.name: Cisco IOS, XR, and XE Software Buffer Overflow Vulnerability (CVE-2018-0167)

attack_vector.description: A malformed LLDP data unit sent from the same Layer 2 segment drives the LLDP subsystem's error handling past a buffer, giving the sender either a device reload or arbitrary code execution with elevated privileges on IOS, IOS XE or IOS XR.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none — PR:N; the frame is parsed because the port is up and LLDP is active, with no session or credential involved
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L; the real constraint is AV:A adjacency, not exploit difficulty, and Cisco publishes no workaround that addresses the defect
attack_vector.ai_factor: Found during the resolution of a Cisco TAC support case per the advisory's Source section. No tooling is named and nothing indicates automated or AI-assisted discovery.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Upgrading to the first fixed release for the installed train and reloading — or, on IOS XR 4.1 through 5.0 where no on-train fix exists, migrating to 5.3.4 — with LLDP disabled on ports facing untrusted endpoints in the interim.
prevention.adequacy: The upgrade closes the parse path but requires a reload, so a device holding a fixed image it has not booted is still exposed. Disabling LLDP is a per-port reachability measure, not a fix, and it removes the topology data some operational tooling depends on.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Off-box syslog collection so that an LLDP-adjacent reload leaves evidence, plus retention of crashinfo from the affected chassis for correlation with port and VLAN activity.
detection.adequacy: A reload destroys the on-box logging buffer, so anything not already shipped off the device is gone. Detection also cannot distinguish a crash caused by this defect from an unrelated software fault without the crashinfo being read.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treating a device that may have executed code with elevated privileges as compromised: config export and comparison against a known-good baseline, image verification, and rotation of credentials that transited it, rather than closing on the upgrade.
response.adequacy: This is only actionable where a known-good configuration baseline exists to compare against. Cisco's wording is attempted exploitation and it names no actor, campaign or report, so nothing narrows which switches to examine — the comparison has to be run across every device that had LLDP active on a port facing untrusted endpoints during the exposure window, and it can only ever return a difference or no difference.

NIST-800-53-CM-7.gap: A CM-7 baseline records which services are permitted on a platform, not which are running on which port. LLDP survives the review as topology discovery, and Cisco's own statement that the feature's default state is platform- and release-dependent means an assessor cannot infer the answer from the baseline document at all.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: SI-2 is satisfied by reaching a fixed version, and for IOS XR 4.1 through 5.0 no fixed version exists to reach — the advisory's answer is migration to 5.3.4. The control has no state for a defect whose remediation is a train migration, so the chassis is either falsely compliant or permanently open depending on how the assessor rounds.

NIS2-Art21-vulnerability-management.gap: The obligation was met when the 2018-03-28 advisory was processed on publication, and nothing in it re-triggers on a vendor amendment four years later — cisco-sa-20180328-lldp reached Version 1.2 only on 2022-DEC-15. The priority signal in March 2022 came from CISA rather than from Cisco, and Article 21 as drafted does not require an entity to consume the KEV catalogue, so whether the entity saw it turns on a subscription the obligation never asks for.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: B4's system-security argument rests on the device running approved, current software. Where the vendor describes the outcome as arbitrary code execution with elevated privileges, that argument covers the freshly loaded image and not the startup configuration, the local account list or the contents of flash on a chassis that may have run attacker code before the upgrade.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: Where patch reporting for network hardware is keyed to platform and release, the grain is wrong twice over: it cannot show whether LLDP is active on the ports facing untrusted endpoints, and it cannot separate a train with a fixed release from an IOS XR 4.x train whose only path forward is a migration to 5.3.4.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.22.gap: Where a segregation attestation is built from the routed boundaries between user, server and management zones, it stops one layer above the one that matters. AV:A places the attacker on the access VLAN, inside that boundary by construction, so every host sharing the broadcast domain with the switch can send the LLDP frame the vulnerable parser reads — and the attestation is accurate about the routed design while saying nothing about the adjacency.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CISA listed this Cisco IOS / IOS XE / IOS XR LLDP defect on 2022-03-03 with a 2022-03-17 due date, four years after cisco-sa-20180328-lldp published a fix. Cisco states PSIRT 'became aware' of attempted exploitation in March 2022, but the advisory did not carry that finding until Version 1.2 on 2022-DEC-15 — so across the whole remediation window the KEV listing was the only published trigger, which is precisely what this SLA keys on rather than the 0.03376 EPSS (87.8th percentile). On IOS XR 4.1 through 5.0 the documented-compensating-control branch is the only branch available, since no fixed release exists on those trains and the advisory directs migration to 5.3.4.

new_control_requirements.name: PERIMETER-COMPROMISE-REBUILD-NOT-PATCH
new_control_requirements.description: Pre-rehearsed IR runbook for any perimeter device that suffers a pre-auth RCE CVE in active exploitation MUST default to config-exfil + rebuild + credential rotation, not patch-in-place. Patch-in-place leaves attacker-installed implants intact.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Cisco describes the outcome of CVE-2018-0167 as execution of arbitrary code with elevated privileges reachable by an unauthenticated adjacent attacker, and states that PSIRT 'became aware' of attempted exploitation in March 2022, published on the advisory at Version 1.2 on 2022-DEC-15 — the two conditions this runbook keys on. The half that binds here is the last sentence: an IOS or IOS XR image upgrade replaces the software carrying the LLDP parser and leaves the startup configuration, any local accounts and anything written to flash exactly as they were. A device that answered an LLDP frame from an untrusted access port during the exposure window needs its configuration compared against a known-good baseline and the credentials it holds rotated, not a version-number ticket closed. The device class differs from the firewalls and VPN concentrators the control names, but the reasoning transfers unchanged.

CVE-2018-0161.name: Cisco IOS Software Resource Management Errors Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: An SNMP GET for the Cisco flash MIB pins the main CPU on a Catalyst 2960-L or Digital Building 8P/8U until the SYS-3-CPUHOG watchdog restarts the switch. The request is a legitimate read; nothing about it is malformed.
attack_vector.privileges_required: low — PR:L in both NVD's and Cisco's vectors; the attacker needs a valid SNMPv2c community string or SNMPv3 user whose view reaches the Cisco flash MIB, which on a fleet sharing one read community is a single secret.
attack_vector.complexity: NVD records AC:H for 6.3, Cisco records AC:L for 7.7; neither states what additional condition NVD's AC:H reflects. The observable constraint is the credential and the switch family, not the packet.
attack_vector.ai_factor: Cisco attributes the find to handling customer service requests — vendor staff on a support case. No AI tooling is claimed and no AI-branded research arm appears in the attribution.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: An SNMPv2c/SNMPv3 view that excludes the Cisco flash MIB, applied estate-wide, plus an SNMP access list limiting queries to the monitoring collectors — both are in cisco-sa-20180328-snmp and neither needs a reload, unlike the image upgrade that actually fixes it.
prevention.adequacy: The view exclusion removes the reachable object; the ACL only narrows the source and still admits anything that can reach or spoof a permitted collector. Neither is the fix, and both must be documented as compensating rather than recorded as remediated.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Off-box syslog capturing the SYS-3-CPUHOG event and the process it names, correlated with the switch's reload, plus alerting on SNMP sources outside the collector set.
detection.adequacy: The switch's own logging buffer is volatile, so the evidence of what preceded the restart exists only if syslog already reached a collector before the reload. Detection here is post-hoc: it explains an outage, it does not prevent one.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treat a repeated CPUHOG reload on these families as a suspected exploitation attempt rather than a hardware fault, rotate the SNMP community or SNMPv3 credential, and bring the image upgrade forward into the next change window.
response.adequacy: Rotation matters only where the credential could have leaked; the flaw yields availability loss and no confidentiality or integrity impact, so there is no data-exposure response to run. The residual action is the reload.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: An estate can evidence SI-2 continuously from 2018-03-28 onward and still be running the vulnerable image in March 2022, because SI-2 measures that flaws are identified and remediated on a defined timescale without weighting a 6.3 availability-only finding above anything else in the queue. It also has no vocabulary for the cost of the remedy: on a 2960-L the fixed image is installed by reloading a switch that is carrying user ports, and that reload is a scheduling decision the control can only represent as an item still open.

NIST-800-53-CM-7.gap: CM-7 is satisfied by disabling unneeded services, and SNMP is a needed service on a monitored switch, so the control never reaches the question this CVE turns on: which objects the configured view exposes. A 2960-L with a documented, justified SNMP service and an unrestricted view passes a least-functionality review while still answering the single GET that reloads it.

NIS2-Art21-vulnerability-handling.gap: The Article 21(2)(e) vulnerability-handling measure is met in form — the advisory was ingested in 2018 and tracked — but form is what failed. A CVSS 6.3, availability-only entry affecting two access-switch families ranks behind every higher-scoring item in a severity-ordered queue, and nothing in the measure re-ranks it when the vendor later records attempted exploitation, which cisco-sa-20180328-snmp did in its 2022-12-15 revision for March 2022.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: A B4 assessment that compares running releases against advisory lists will mark this switch as a known outstanding patch and stop there.
