new_control_requirements.evidence: Cisco's impact statement for CVE-2017-6740 is arbitrary code execution with full control of the affected system, which on an IOS or IOS XE device includes its logging configuration and its local log buffer — so any record of the crafted SNMP request that stayed on the box is written by an attacker who owns the box. The control's separate-trust-zone requirement is what leaves an operator with evidence at all after an event Cisco states it has observed in the wild and CISA clocked on 2022-03-03. It matters specifically here because the collector is commonly reachable from the same management segment the SNMP request came from, which means a shared trust zone and a shared credential path rather than the separated one the control demands.

new_control_requirements.name: BUG-FAMILY-MITIGATION-PERSISTENCE
new_control_requirements.description: When a CVE patch lands, retain the pre-patch compensating controls (module blacklists, sysctl restrictions) until the patched code has soaked for a stated review period. Patches for one bug in a primitive class can introduce sibling bugs in the same class; the original compensating control may still apply to the sibling.
new_control_requirements.evidence: cisco-sa-20170629-snmp is a primitive class with nine CVE ids against it, and the compensating control — the snmp-server view exclusion — is a configuration statement that an upgrade gives an operator every reason to remove. The advisory itself shows why retention is the right default: revision 1.11 on 2025-07-30 added another MIB to that filter, eight years after the 2017-06-29 publication, so the exclusion set was still growing long after the fixed releases for CVE-2017-6740 had shipped. Keeping the view in place through and past the Software Checker upgrade costs nothing operationally and is the only state that covers the next MIB added to the list.

CVE-2017-6739.name: Cisco IOS and IOS XE Software SNMP Remote Code Execution Vulnerability (CVE-2017-6739)

attack_vector.description: One crafted SNMP packet, authorised by a read-only community string or SNMPv3 credentials, overflows a buffer in the Cisco IOS or IOS XE SNMP implementation while it is being parsed. The device either reloads or falls under the attacker's control, and the same request produces both outcomes depending on how precisely the corruption is steered.
attack_vector.privileges_required: low — PR:L; the read-only community string on v1 or v2c, or SNMPv3 user credentials. Read access is enough because the fault is in parsing, not in the operation requested.
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L; no leak, no race, no groom, and the affected MIBs are enabled by default with SNMP. Only traffic addressed to the device is usable, so the requirement is a route to its management address.
attack_vector.ai_factor: Cisco attributes the set to internal testing; no external researcher, no method described, no AI-assisted discovery claimed.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: The snmp-server view exclusion on every community string and SNMPv3 group from 2017-06-29 onward, with the Software Checker upgrade sequenced into the next change window rather than the next available one.
prevention.adequacy: The exclusion is the only measure that costs no availability, which is why it is the whole of the answer for a device that cannot take a reload soon. It expires the moment the configuration is rebuilt from an older template, and it does not remove the vulnerable code.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Treating an SNMP-process reload as a security event, retrieving crashinfo before it is overwritten, and correlating failover events with SNMP source addresses rather than with link state.
detection.adequacy: This catches the noisy outcome and misses the quiet one. A device that was taken rather than reloaded produces no crashinfo and no failover, and its own logs are then written by whoever holds it.

response.what_would_have_worked: For a reload with SNMP-process crashinfo from an unexpected source: rotating the community strings and SNMPv3 credentials that reached the device, and validating configuration and image against off-device copies before returning it to service.
response.adequacy: Returning a device to service after an unexplained reload is the default operational reflex and is the wrong one here, because the same request that reloaded it may have succeeded on an earlier attempt. Where the rotation scope is a shared string, it extends to every device that string reaches.

NIST-800-53-SC-5.gap: Denial-of-service protection is implemented as rate limiting, filtering and headroom, and a single authorised SNMP request presents none of the signatures those controls act on. Control-plane policing bounds an SNMP flood and does nothing about one packet the SNMP process is entitled to parse, so the only effective reduction is restricting who may send SNMP at all — a boundary control wearing an availability label.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: Flaw remediation and availability pull in opposite directions here, because the correction is the same reload the attack produces. Deferrals granted on availability grounds extend the window precisely where the impact is worst, and the evidence SI-2 needs is a per-device Cisco IOS Software Checker verdict, since cisco-sa-20170629-snmp publishes no fixed build to compare a version against.

NIS2-Art21-availability.gap: Redundancy, monitoring and recovery objectives are all satisfiable while this CVE stays open, and they respond to the symptom: a pair reloaded in turn by an attacker holding the community string fails over as designed. The measure cannot express that the availability impact is a by-product of a code-execution primitive, so demonstrating availability says nothing about whether the device is under someone else's control.

UK-CAF-B5.gap: Resilience is assessed and passes, and the resilient pair is reachable on identical terms because both members are polled by the same system with the same credential. Resilience turns the reload outcome into a failover and turns the code-execution outcome into nothing observable, so the question B5 would have to ask — whether the pair shares its SNMP credential and management reachability — is outside a normal resilience review.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: The strategies assume patch availability is the constraint, and for a network device the constraint is the change window, because applying the fix means reloading the device. On my reading nothing in the maturity model separates an asset class whose patch mechanism is an outage, which is how a device stays unfixed from the 2017-06-29 advisory through the 2022-03-24 KEV due date without the programme registering a failure.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.21.gap: SNMP management is treated as internal plumbing rather than a network service with agreed security requirements, so its actual properties go unstated: a cleartext shared secret on v1 and v2c, and a parser reachable on all three versions that can be driven to code execution. Writing those requirements down is what would turn the v3 migration and the OID view restriction into monitored controls instead of configuration preferences.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: For CVE-2017-6739 the four-hour clock cannot be met by patching — a Cisco IOS or IOS XE upgrade is a reload, and the fixed release has to be looked up per train in the Cisco IOS Software Checker before it can even be scheduled. The clause that makes the SLA achievable is documented compensating controls: the advisory's snmp-server view exclusion applies in seconds and without an outage, which is the only action available inside four hours of the 2022-03-03 KEV listing on a device that also carries an availability commitment. Recording the exclusion as the deployed mitigation, and the reload as a dated follow-on, is what stops the availability argument from converting into an indefinite deferral.

new_control_requirements.name: MITIGATION-ACTIVE-PATCH-PENDING-VERDICT-CLASS
new_control_requirements.description: Compliance verdicts must distinguish three states: (a) binary patch deployed (vulnerability eliminated), (b) vendor-mitigation rule active, no binary patch (residual risk: any defect in the mitigation rule reopens the vulnerability), (c) no mitigation, no patch (full exposure). Audit reports must surface (b) as a distinct compensating-control state with an associated time-bound action item, not as a 'patched per SLA' outcome.
new_control_requirements.evidence: An availability-framed programme reads a device that is up, failing over correctly and no longer reloading as remediated, and for CVE-2017-6739 that is state (b) and nothing more: the snmp-server view exclusion has suppressed the reachable OIDs while the vulnerable SNMP parsing code remains on a device that has never been reloaded onto a fixed release. The residual risk is concrete rather than theoretical — the exclusion list itself grew at advisory revision 1.11 on 2025-07-30 — and the time-bound action the control requires is the Software Checker upgrade with its reload, dated against the 2022-03-24 KEV due date rather than left to the next convenient window.

CVE-2017-6738.name: Cisco IOS and IOS XE Software SNMP Remote Code Execution Vulnerability (CVE-2017-6738)

attack_vector.description: A crafted SNMP request for an object in one of the advisory's MIBs overflows a buffer in the Cisco IOS or IOS XE SNMP subsystem during parsing. The attacker supplies a read-only community string or SNMPv3 credentials and sends one packet to the device; the device either falls under their control or reloads.
attack_vector.privileges_required: low — PR:L; per the advisory, knowledge of the read-only community string for SNMP v2c or earlier, or user credentials for SNMPv3.
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L; the affected MIBs are enabled by default with SNMP, all versions reach them, and no probing stage precedes the request. Only traffic addressed to the device can be used.
attack_vector.ai_factor: Found during internal testing at Cisco per the advisory's Source section; no method is described and no AI-assisted discovery is claimed.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Putting the snmp-server view exclusion into the device build template as well as onto live devices, as a change record in its own right, and scheduling the Software Checker upgrade as a separate software change.
prevention.adequacy: Template plus live device is the combination that lasts; either alone decays. The exclusion still leaves the vulnerable parsing code resident, and its OID list has needed maintenance since — a MIB was added at advisory revision 1.11 on 2025-07-30.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Configuration drift detection that includes the snmp-server view statements, and treating an SNMP-process reload on a process-network switch as a security event rather than only as a plant alarm.
detection.adequacy: Drift detection reliably catches the mitigation being lost, which is the failure mode most likely to occur, and catches nothing about exploitation. On a plant network the reload is consumed by the process-alarm path before any security queue sees it.

response.what_would_have_worked: Rebuilding the device configuration from a template known to postdate the advisory rather than restoring the last backup, and rotating the SNMP credentials that reached it.
response.adequacy: Restoring the last backup is the standard recovery action and it reinstates whatever configuration state existed before, including the absence of the exclusion. Where the process network cannot take a second outage, the rebuild competes with the upgrade for the same window.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: The control expects one remediation with one verification, and this CVE offers two partial ones — an immediate configuration exclusion that removes no code, and a reload-bearing upgrade that does. There is no state in SI-2 for the first, and the second cannot be verified against a published build number because the advisory names none, leaving a per-device Software Checker lookup as the only evidence.

NIST-800-53-CM-3.gap: Change control is in force and it applies to the workaround as much as to the upgrade, so the mitigation queues behind the same approvals as the fix it was meant to precede. Applied outside change control it leaves no record, which is what allows a template push or an RMA replacement to remove the exclusion later with nothing to flag the regression.

NIS2-Art21-vulnerability-handling.gap: Handling nine ids from one advisory forces a choice that the measure does not guide: nine near-identical assessments competing for one change window, or one merged record that closes on the first fixed release and never verifies this id. Either way the per-device question — is this train fixed, does this configuration exclude the listed OIDs — is the one the handling process does not produce.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: The device passes its hardening baseline, and the baseline predates the advisory, so it contains no snmp-server view excluding the ten OID subtrees. SNMPv3, ACL-restricted polling and the absence of default community strings are all genuine improvements that leave the vulnerable MIBs reachable, which makes the baseline's revision date the real control here.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: A device running the vendor workaround instead of the fixed release has no accurate representation in the model: counted unpatched it understates the position, counted informally handled it overstates it, and on my reading neither reading books the change window. Only removing the code satisfies the 2022-03-24 KEV due date, and the model does not distinguish that from applying a mitigation.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: The vulnerability record for this advisory was captured once and the advisory has moved since: revision 1.11 on 2025-07-30 added a MIB to the workaround filter, so a mitigation implemented from the original text is now short one exclusion. Reviews scheduled on the organisation's own cycle have no trigger that re-reads an advisory the process treats as closed.

IEC-62443-3-3.gap: Zone-and-conduit segmentation places the switch in a protected zone and then permits the monitoring conduit that carries the attack, and the authentication requirement is satisfied by SNMPv3 while the defect fires during parsing, before any permission check. The reload outcome is also more costly here than on corporate infrastructure, which is precisely why the upgrade window is hardest to obtain on the estate with the least tolerance for the alternative.

new_control_requirements.name: BUG-FAMILY-MITIGATION-PERSISTENCE
new_control_requirements.description: When a CVE patch lands, retain the pre-patch compensating controls (module blacklists, sysctl restrictions) until the patched code has soaked for a stated review period. Patches for one bug in a primitive class can introduce sibling bugs in the same class; the original compensating control may still apply to the sibling.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2017-6738 is one of nine ids against the Cisco IOS and IOS XE SNMP parsing primitive, so the sibling case the control describes is not a projection here — it is the advisory's own structure, and the advisory kept growing, with revision 1.11 on 2025-07-30 adding a further MIB to the workaround filter. Retaining the snmp-server view exclusion through and beyond the Software Checker upgrade costs nothing on a device that is already carrying it, and it is the state that covers the next MIB to join the list. The control also gives change management the reason it needs to keep the exclusion in the build template rather than removing it as obsolete once the fixed release is deployed.

new_control_requirements.name: INCOMPLETE-PATCH-SEQUENCE-SEVERITY-MULTIPLIER
new_control_requirements.description: Vulnerability-management programs must apply a severity multiplier when a CVE is the Nth in an incomplete-patch sequence on the same primitive (third MOTW bypass, second AMSI bypass, etc.). Framework controls treating each CVE as discrete obscure the structural defect; the Nth CVE in a sequence implies that future bypasses on the same primitive are likely.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Scored on its own, CVE-2017-6738 is an 8.8 with an EPSS of 0.1055 at the 95.411 percentile as of 2026-08-20, indistinguishable from any other high in the queue. The structural reading is different: nine CVE ids and eleven Cisco bug ids landed simultaneously against one SNMP parsing primitive in IOS and IOS XE, ten MIBs went into the workaround filter, and eight years later revision 1.11 added another. A multiplier applied on that basis is what moves the device upgrade ahead of unrelated 8.8s and what justifies keeping the exclusion permanently rather than treating the sequence as finished.

CVE-2017-6737.name: Cisco IOS and IOS XE Software SNMP Remote Code Execution Vulnerability (CVE-2017-6737)

attack_vector.description: A crafted SNMP packet sent to a Cisco IOS or IOS XE device overflows a buffer in the affected code area of the SNMP implementation, giving the sender arbitrary code execution with full control of the device or forcing a reload. The sender needs only the read-only community string or SNMPv3 credentials and a route to the device's own address.
attack_vector.privileges_required: low — PR:L; read-only SNMP access on v1 or v2c, or SNMPv3 user credentials, per the advisory's own exploitation requirements.
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L; one request, no preconditions beyond SNMP being enabled, and the affected MIBs enabled by default at that point. Reliable code execution rather than a reload remains image-specific.
attack_vector.ai_factor: Cisco internal testing per the advisory's Source section; no researcher named, no method described, no AI involvement claimed or evidenced.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: The snmp-server view exclusion applied on publication and the Software Checker upgrade taken soon after, so the device was never reachable and unpatched for the years between 2017-06-29 and the 2022-03-03 KEV listing.
prevention.adequacy: Fully effective before exposure and worth nothing after it. Once a device has been reachable and unpatched through a period in which the vendor states this id was exploited, prevention has become a response question and the upgrade alone does not answer it.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Collecting SNMP flow records at a network collector rather than relying on device logs, so the source addresses that reached UDP/161 are known independently of the device — and, after any unexplained reload, retrieving the crashinfo file Cisco's advisory names and submitting it to the Cisco Technical Assistance Center for review.
detection.adequacy: The flow records are the only contact-time signal that does not depend on the device's own logs, and they still show contact rather than exploitation; they also reach back no further than flow retention, which does not cover a 2017 advisory. The crashinfo sits on the other side of the event, is written on the exploited device, and is adjudicated by the vendor rather than by the estate.

response.what_would_have_worked: Comparing running configuration and image against an off-device baseline, rebuilding from that baseline rather than from the device's own backup, and rotating every community string and SNMPv3 credential that reached the device.
response.adequacy: The rebuild is the only step that removes attacker-written configuration, and it depends on a baseline that predates the exposure and that the device could not modify. Where one community string was configured across many devices, rotation scope follows the string rather than the device.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: Remediation closes when the fixed release is installed, and installing it over a device that was reachable and unpatched removes the code while preserving whatever the attacker wrote into the configuration. Nothing in SI-2 escalates a remediation into an investigation, so with EPSS at 0.42632 on 2026-08-20 and vendor-stated exploitation, the fastest-closing estates are the ones most likely to have upgraded straight over an incident.

NIST-800-53-SI-4.gap: The evidence SI-4 would provide comes from the device the exploit takes control of, and the triggering SNMP request is not logged by default with its source and requested OIDs. What does exist is retrospective and is not the programme's to read: Cisco's reload-plus-crashinfo indicator appears after exploitation and is submitted to the Cisco Technical Assistance Center for the verdict. A programme can evidence comprehensive monitoring on servers and endpoints and still hold no monitoring answer of its own for any router between the 2017-06-29 advisory and the 2022-03-24 KEV due date.

NIS2-Art21-incident-handling.gap: The procedures are complete and still cannot reach a verdict on their own. Cisco's indicator for this id is a reload plus a crashinfo file, and the advisory's instruction is to send that file to the Cisco Technical Assistance Center for the compromise determination — so the classification step the measure presumes the entity performs is held by a third party, while the awareness clocks that follow classification run against the entity. A reload alone is ambiguous; the crashinfo is what resolves it, and only Cisco is offered as the reader.

UK-CAF-D1.gap: Response and recovery plans for network devices are written for outages, and their standard steps — restore the configuration backup, swap the unit, bring the link up — carry an attacker's changes forward intact. What CVE-2017-6737 needs is absent from those plans: off-device baseline comparison, a decision not to reuse the running configuration, and credential rotation scoped to everything the community string reached.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: Maturity is measured from the point the patching process engages, so an estate that upgrades promptly today scores well while every device that sat reachable and unpatched from 2017 to the 2022-03-24 due date is closed on the patch record. On my reading the model has no concept of retrospective exposure, which is exactly the concept a vendor-confirmed exploited defect requires.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.16.gap: Network devices are monitored for availability and performance by the same SNMP polling this defect abuses, so the monitoring in place cannot separate a malicious request from a poll. Retention closes the question for good: an EPSS reading of 0.42632 on 2026-08-20 concerns a defect published on 2017-06-29, and no practical log retention covers that interval.

new_control_requirements.name: FIREWALL-EGRESS-TELEMETRY-SEPARATE-TRUST-ZONE
new_control_requirements.description: Firewall and other perimeter-trust-boundary devices must forward syslog, threat logs, and authentication logs to a SIEM hosted in a separate trust zone (different management plane, different credentials, different authentication path). Telemetry stored on the compromised device is destroyed by the attacker; telemetry on a separate-trust-zone collector survives.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Cisco states it has observed exploitation of CVE-2017-6737 and describes the impact as full control of the affected system, which on an IOS or IOS XE device includes the logging configuration and the local buffer — so the record of which source addresses reached UDP/161 is held by the device the attacker now controls. The vendor's own indicator does not cover that ground: the crashinfo file the advisory names is produced by the reload and is read by the Cisco Technical Assistance Center, and it answers whether the device was compromised rather than who reached it or when. Separating the collector's trust zone, credentials and authentication path from the device's own management plane is what makes those SNMP source addresses knowable independently of the router in question. On a device with an EPSS of 0.42632 as of 2026-08-20 and a KEV clock that opened 2022-03-03, that is the difference between a scoped rebuild and a guess.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: The gap between the 2017-06-29 Cisco advisory and the 2022-03-03 KEV listing for CVE-2017-6737 is the whole problem: by the time a federal clock started, devices had been reachable and unpatched for years against a defect the vendor states it has seen exploited, with EPSS reading 0.42632 at the 98.602 percentile on 2026-08-20. A four-hour SLA anchored on KEV listing forces the snmp-server view exclusion to be deployed as the documented compensating control immediately, and forces the Software Checker upgrade to be scheduled rather than queued behind the change backlog that produced the original delay.

new_control_requirements.name: FLEET-COMPROMISE-IR-PLAYBOOK
new_control_requirements.description: Pre-rehearsed IR playbook for fleet-control-plane compromise including: MDM-pushed certificate revocation, device-trust-state invalidation, configuration-profile audit since the suspected compromise window, downstream device-quarantine criteria, and credential rotation for any account that authenticated through a compromised fleet device during the exposure period.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Cisco's indicator for CVE-2017-6737 on Cisco IOS and IOS XE is a reload plus a crashinfo file that the advisory directs the operator to submit to the Cisco Technical Assistance Center, so the compromise verdict arrives on the vendor's turnaround and the entity's own actions have to be pre-committed rather than derived from it. Most of what this control names has a concrete referent on this defect: the suspected compromise window runs from the 2017-06-29 advisory to whenever the Cisco IOS Software Checker's fixed release was installed; the configuration-profile audit is a comparison of running configuration and image against a copy held off the device; the quarantine criterion is a router that was reachable on UDP/161 and unpatched across that window; and the credential rotation covers every community string and SNMPv3 user that reached it, which under one fleet-wide string is the whole fleet. The certificate-revocation and device-trust-state elements have no analogue on an SNMP path and do not apply here. Rehearsing the rest before the crashinfo is submitted is what gives the KEV clock that opened 2022-03-03 something the entity can act on while it waits.

CVE-2017-6736.name: Cisco IOS and IOS XE Software SNMP Remote Code Execution Vulnerability (CVE-2017-6736)

attack_vector.description: A crafted SNMP request against one of ten default-enabled MIBs overflows a buffer in the IOS SNMP subsystem and yields code execution on the router itself. The public exploit writes MIPS shellcode into memory, hands control back to the SNMP process, and uses the space to patch telnet and enable authentication so the operator's own management path becomes the attacker's.
attack_vector.privileges_required: low — PR:L; the attacker needs an SNMP credential, which for v1 and v2c is the read-only community string and for v3 is a user account. Read-only is enough; no write community and no device login is required.
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L; no race, groom or leak. The real constraints are network reachability to UDP/161 and matching the exploit to the platform, since the published code is built for a Cisco ISR 2811 on IOS 15.1(4)M12a.
attack_vector.ai_factor: None recorded. Cisco attributes the find to internal testing and the exploit to Artem Kondratenko; neither source describes automated analysis.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Applying the advisory's snmp-server view exclude list to every community string and SNMPv3 group on the day of publication, and restricting UDP/161 to the monitoring platform's addresses, then scheduling the reload onto a fixed release.
prevention.adequacy: The exclude list removes reachability to the vulnerable MIBs but leaves the parser in the image, so it holds only as long as nobody adds a community string without the view. Source restriction assumes the attacker is outside the permitted range, which does not hold once any host on the management segment is compromised.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Alerting on SNMP requests to the device from sources other than the monitoring platform, and on successful telnet or enable access that does not correspond to a known account, with the device's logs shipped off-box.
detection.adequacy: Detection here is weak by construction: the exploit returns control to the SNMP process so the device keeps working, and the example shellcode's purpose is to make an unauthorised login look like a normal one. The Snort rules Cisco publishes with the advisory are the strongest signal available, and they need SNMP traffic to traverse a sensor.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treating a device that answered SNMP from an untrusted source during the exposure window as compromised: pull the configuration for comparison against a known-good copy, rebuild rather than upgrade in place, and rotate community strings, local accounts and any credential that transited the device.
response.adequacy: The reload that installs a fixed image does clear the in-memory shellcode, which makes an upgrade look like a complete answer; it carries configuration and credentials forward, so anything the attacker changed on disk survives remediation.

NIST-800-53-CM-7.gap: The control is met by justifying SNMP as an operational requirement, and it stops there. It has no concept of a sub-surface inside an approved service, which is exactly what a MIB is — CISCO-BSTUN-MIB and CISCO-VOICE-DNIS-MIB answer on hardware with no BSTUN link and no voice dial peers because they came on with the protocol. Least functionality assessed at service granularity cannot see the ten objects that carry this flaw.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: Flaw remediation is satisfied by evidence that the running image is past the first fixed release for the train. Because Talos documents this CVE in use against ISR 2811s from at least 2019, the population that needs the control most is the population where the upgrade is a post-compromise action, and SI-2 produces the same clean attestation for a device that was exploited in 2018 as for one that never was.

NIS2-Art21-network-security.gap: An operator can evidence Article 21 with perimeter filtering, segmentation diagrams and a hardened edge while UDP/161 stays open across the whole management plane. The exploit needs only that reachability plus a read-only community string, so the measures that satisfy the obligation and the path that defeats it do not intersect.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: B4 assessments read software currency, and Cisco's answer to this advisory is split between a version and a configuration object. An estate can hold the snmp-server view exclude list on every device and still fail a version-led B4 review, or hold a fixed image on the routers and none on the switches and pass one — the outcome and the evidence are only loosely related here.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: Maturity Level One covers this device: ISM-1877 names "internet-facing network devices" and ISM-1695 names "non-internet-facing network devices", so an IOS router is inside the assessed population either way. What the mitigation does not do is rank it. Compressing the clock to 48 hours needs an internet-facing placement together with a vendor-critical rating or a working exploit, and a router whose SNMP agent faces only the management network fails the placement half even though Exploit-DB 43450 satisfies the exploit half. The KEV-listed RCE then sits on the same one-month window as a staff workstation's operating system.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.9.gap: Configuration management is met by a documented, version-controlled baseline that is monitored for drift. Since the exploitable state is the ordinary approved SNMP configuration, there is no drift to detect and the control reports health. It becomes useful only if the exclude view is written into the baseline, at which point drift detection starts guarding the mitigation instead of ignoring it.

new_control_requirements.name: PERIMETER-COMPROMISE-REBUILD-NOT-PATCH
new_control_requirements.description: Pre-rehearsed IR runbook for any perimeter device that suffers a pre-auth RCE CVE in active exploitation MUST default to config-exfil + rebuild + credential rotation, not patch-in-place. Patch-in-place leaves attacker-installed implants intact.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Cisco IOS and IOS XE routers exploited through this SNMP flaw are the case the runbook is for, with one honest qualification: the control's trigger says pre-auth, and this CVE is PR:L — the attacker needs a read-only community string first. Where they have one, the outcome is the same, and Talos' 2019-04-17 Sea Turtle report documents the actor using this CVE against ISR 2811s. The published exploit patches telnet and enable authentication in running memory, so a device that was exploited holds attacker-chosen configuration and credentials that an upgrade to a fixed release carries forward intact. Cisco PSIRT names CVE-2017-6736 among the vulnerabilities it is aware of being exploited, and CISA gave the estate three weeks — 2022-03-03 to 2022-03-24.

new_control_requirements.name: MITIGATION-ACTIVE-PATCH-PENDING-VERDICT-CLASS
new_control_requirements.description: Compliance verdicts must distinguish three states: (a) binary patch deployed (vulnerability eliminated), (b) vendor-mitigation rule active, no binary patch (residual risk: any defect in the mitigation rule reopens the vulnerability), (c) no mitigation, no patch (full exposure). Audit reports must surface (b) as a distinct compensating-control state with an associated time-bound action item, not as a 'patched per SLA' outcome.
new_control_requirements.evidence: cisco-sa-20170629-snmp offers exactly the middle state: an snmp-server view exclude list over the ten affected MIBs, bound to every community string and SNMPv3 group. It is a configuration mitigation, not a binary fix, and any later community string added without the view reopens the path with no change in reported patch level. A Cisco router sitting on that exclude list against an EPSS of 0.70559 (99.339th percentile, 2026-08-20) is materially different from one reloaded onto a fixed release, and a compliance report that records both as remediated has erased the difference.

CVE-2017-6663.name: Cisco IOS Software and Cisco IOS XE Software Denial-of-Service Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: An adjacent attacker captures Autonomic Networking traffic and replays it, resetting the Autonomic Control Plane channel and reloading the autonomic nodes of the device. Cisco states the underlying condition in the Autonomic Networking code is unknown, so the advisory establishes the delivery and the impact and stops there — no published source explains why the replay is accepted, and none records how far one capture goes.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none — PR:N; no credential and no user interaction. The gate is position rather than privilege: AV:A means the attacker must sit on an adjacent segment carrying autonomic traffic.
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L; capture and resend, no memory corruption to arrange. The real precondition is that the device is configured to use Autonomic Networking at all, which the advisory makes the scoping test.
attack_vector.ai_factor: None. Cisco credits Omar Eissa of ERNW, who disclosed it at Black Hat USA 2017; the advisory describes no tooling.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Removing Autonomic Networking from devices that do not require it, so `show running-config | include ^autonomic` returns nothing, and treating adjacency to autonomic-speaking segments as a controlled property rather than an incidental one.
prevention.adequacy: This is the only prevention available, and it is a feature withdrawal rather than a security control — it is unavailable to any site that genuinely uses Autonomic Networking, and for those sites Cisco has published neither a fix nor a workaround since 2017.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Alerting on autonomic node reloads and ACP channel resets that do not correlate with a change window, with device logs shipped to a collector that survives the reload.
detection.adequacy: Detection tells the operator the device was reloaded, which they would learn anyway, and gives them nothing to do about it while no fix exists. Its value is bounding the exposure window and distinguishing a replay from a hardware fault, not preventing the next reload.

response.what_would_have_worked: A standing decision, recorded before the event, on whether each autonomic-configured device keeps the feature — so the response to a reload is a configuration removal already agreed rather than a fresh architecture argument during an outage.
response.adequacy: Response cannot restore what is not broken: this is an availability defect with no confidentiality or integrity impact recorded in the CVSS vector, so there is no compromise to contain, only a reload to stop recurring.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: An SI-2 programme scanning for this CVE finds it, opens a remediation item, and can never close it — there is no fixed release to reach. The item ages, the exception is renewed, and the renewal review asks the same unanswerable question each cycle. Nothing in the control converts a permanently unfixable finding into the design decision it actually is.

NIST-800-53-CM-7.gap: Least functionality is the control that would have removed this exposure, and it is applied to network devices at the level of management services and unused ports. Autonomic Networking is neither: it is a provisioning-era infrastructure feature that leaves one line in the configuration and no listening service a port review would flag.

NIS2-Art21-vulnerability-handling.gap: The obligation is met by having a process that receives, triages and dispositions vulnerabilities. That process runs correctly here and produces no security outcome, because the disposition available — accept, or withdraw the feature — is not one a vulnerability-handling workflow is built to execute, and the flaw has carried a KEV due date of 2022-03-24 with no vendor artefact behind it ever since.

UK-CAF-B5.gap: Resilience evidence for a router pair is usually redundancy and failover testing. Both devices in such a pair are configured from the same template, so both accept the same replayed capture, and an attacker adjacent to both reloads both. The B5 outcome can be fully evidenced by a design that this defect defeats in a single step.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: There is no patch, no update and no vendor mitigation for this advisory, so the mitigation has no input. An organisation cannot fail this control on CVE-2017-6663 and cannot pass it either — the flaw is simply invisible to the assessment, which is a worse outcome than being marked non-compliant, because nothing surfaces for a risk committee to see.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: Technical vulnerability management is satisfied by identification, evaluation and action, and identification here is a single CLI command. The action, though, is removing a networking feature from production devices, which needs the network design owner's agreement and a change window — work that A.8.8 can record but has no authority to compel.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: This entry is the case where the control's third branch is the only one that exists. Cisco has released no software update and no workaround for cisco-sa-20170726-anidos since 2017-July-26, so on Cisco IOS and IOS XE devices configured for Autonomic Networking the documented compensating control — removing the autonomic configuration, verified by `show running-config | include ^autonomic` returning no output — is the whole of the available remediation. An SLA written as 'within 4 hours of patch availability' alone never starts on this CVE, and CISA's 2022-03-24 due date passed with nothing to install.

new_control_requirements.name: MITIGATION-ACTIVE-PATCH-PENDING-VERDICT-CLASS
new_control_requirements.description: Compliance verdicts must distinguish three states: (a) binary patch deployed (vulnerability eliminated), (b) vendor-mitigation rule active, no binary patch (residual risk: any defect in the mitigation rule reopens the vulnerability), (c) no mitigation, no patch (full exposure). Audit reports must surface (b) as a distinct compensating-control state with an associated time-bound action item, not as a 'patched per SLA' outcome.
new_control_requirements.evidence: A Cisco IOS or IOS XE device still configured for Autonomic Networking is in the control's third state and always will be: no binary patch exists and Cisco published no vendor mitigation rule either. Recording it as an open item pending a fix misrepresents it, because the pending fix is not coming — the advisory has carried one revision since 2017-July-26. The verdict an audit report needs to carry is that the exposure is permanent while the feature stays configured, which converts an ageing patch ticket into a decision about whether Autonomic Networking runs on that device at all.

CVE-2017-6627.name: Cisco IOS Software and Cisco IOS XE Software UDP Packet Processing Denial-of-Service Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: UDP sockets that IOS opens and never closes leave the device holding UDP packets sent to destination port 0 in its input interface queue. After 250 held packets the queue wedges and the interface stops taking traffic — an outage produced by a handful of datagrams rather than by volume.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none — PR:N; no credential, no session, no user interaction. The datagram must be addressed to the device's own interface rather than merely routed through it.
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L; a UDP packet with destination port 0 is trivially constructed and needs no protocol state. The only constraint is reachability of an interface address from wherever the attacker sits.
attack_vector.ai_factor: Unknown. The advisory carries no Source section and names no finder, so there is no attribution to characterise either way.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Applying Cisco's own workaround estate-wide on the day of publication — an ACL denying UDP destination port 0 on every interface, or an input hold queue above 250 — and scheduling the reload onto a fixed release from the four bug IDs.
prevention.adequacy: Both workarounds are per-interface, so their coverage is only as complete as the interface inventory; an interface added later without the ACL or the queue setting is exposed while the device as a whole still reads as mitigated.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Monitoring input queue occupancy per interface and alerting when it holds at its limit, plus counting hits on the deny udp any any eq 0 ACL entry so the attempt is visible before the wedge.
detection.adequacy: The ACL counter is the better signal because it fires before the interface is lost. Queue-occupancy monitoring depends on polling the device over a path the wedge may itself have removed, so it can arrive as absence of data rather than as an alert.

response.what_would_have_worked: A runbook that treats a silent interface with healthy CPU and memory as a candidate queue wedge, clears the queue to restore service, and applies the ACL before handing the device back.
response.adequacy: Recovery restores the interface and nothing prevents the next wedge, so the response is only useful when it ends with the workaround applied. There is no integrity or confidentiality impact to contain — the CVSS vector records C:N/I:N/A:H.

NIST-800-53-SC-5.gap: The control is typically evidenced with upstream scrubbing and rate limits sized for volumetric attacks. A queue that wedges at 250 packets is beneath every threshold such a design sets, so an organisation can hold a fully implemented SC-5 and lose an interface to traffic that its DoS protection never classifies as an attack.

NIST-800-53-SI-4.gap: Monitoring is nominally in place and the specific failure defeats it: the wedged interface is the one that would have carried the telemetry. The operator learns about the outage from users or from a reachability probe, not from the system monitoring capability the control describes, and the event arrives without the queue detail that would identify the cause.

NIS2-Art21-availability.gap: Availability measures are evidenced against unplanned failure rates, and this is a failure an unauthenticated attacker schedules. Redundancy helps only if the second path is not equally reachable — where both devices in a pair have interface addresses on the same untrusted segment, the same handful of packets wedges each in turn.

UK-CAF-C1.gap: Security monitoring is achieved for the estate as a whole, and this defect produces a condition monitoring handles poorly: an unexplained silence with no accompanying log. Distinguishing a wedged input queue from a physical fault requires the input-queue counters, which have to be collected from the device before it went quiet.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: The mitigation's population includes "non-internet-facing network devices" (ISM-1695), so a Cisco IOS router is assessed and draws a one-month window from the release of the fix. The two configuration workarounds Cisco offers — hold-queue 350 in, and an ACL denying UDP destination port 0 — satisfy the clause's "other vendor mitigations" wording as fully as the fixed image does, and both are applied per interface. The assessment produces a device-level verdict for a defect scoped per interface, so a device judged compliant can grow a new interface carrying neither workaround and change nothing the model measures.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.21.gap: The control is satisfied by identifying network services and their security features in agreements, which is done at the level of circuits, protocols and providers. The parameter that decides this outcome — how many packets an input queue will hold — sits below that level of description, so a complete A.8.21 record can coexist with every interface in the estate at the default depth.

new_control_requirements.name: MITIGATION-ACTIVE-PATCH-PENDING-VERDICT-CLASS
new_control_requirements.description: Compliance verdicts must distinguish three states: (a) binary patch deployed (vulnerability eliminated), (b) vendor-mitigation rule active, no binary patch (residual risk: any defect in the mitigation rule reopens the vulnerability), (c) no mitigation, no patch (full exposure). Audit reports must surface (b) as a distinct compensating-control state with an associated time-bound action item, not as a 'patched per SLA' outcome.
new_control_requirements.evidence: cisco-sa-20170906-ios-udp gives operators two configuration mitigations — an input hold queue above 250, and an ACL denying UDP destination port 0 — and Cisco still recommends upgrading to a fixed release, having recorded in December 2022 that PSIRT became aware of attempted exploitation in the wild in March 2022. Both mitigations are applied per interface, so a Cisco IOS 15.1/15.2/15.4 or IOS XE 3.14-3.18 device sits in the middle state with a residual-risk shape that one new interface reopens. Recording that device as remediated alongside one reloaded onto a fixed release loses exactly the distinction the estate needs to act on.

new_control_requirements.name: FIREWALL-EGRESS-TELEMETRY-SEPARATE-TRUST-ZONE
new_control_requirements.description: Firewall and other perimeter-trust-boundary devices must forward syslog, threat logs, and authentication logs to a SIEM hosted in a separate trust zone (different management plane, different credentials, different authentication path). Telemetry stored on the compromised device is destroyed by the attacker; telemetry on a separate-trust-zone collector survives.
new_control_requirements.evidence: The reason this control matters on a Cisco IOS queue wedge is different from the implant case it was written for, and stronger: the interface that stops passing traffic is also the interface the device would send its telemetry over, so the evidence is not destroyed but stranded. Forwarding syslog and interface counters over a management path that does not share the affected interface is what turns this event from an unexplained silence into an identifiable wedge, and it is the only way the deny udp any any eq 0 ACL counter Cisco's workaround creates ever reaches an analyst.

CVE-2017-12319.name: Cisco IOS XE Software Ethernet Virtual Private Network Border Gateway Protocol Denial-of-Service Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: A crafted BGP EVPN update — an Inclusive Multicast Ethernet Tag Route or a MAC/IP Advertisement Route — carries an IP address length the receiving IOS XE release miscalculates, because Cisco's implementation of the RFC 7432 draft changed between releases. The device reloads, or its BGP routing table is corrupted and the damage spreads with the routes.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none — PR:N in CVSS terms; there is no login. The functional requirement is different and larger: the update must arrive on a BGP session that is already established.
attack_vector.complexity: high — AC:H; the attacker needs a position on an established BGP session and an EVPN-configured target, and the advisory states plainly that a device not configured for EVPN is not vulnerable.
attack_vector.ai_factor: None. Cisco records the report as coming from a customer via a TAC case, which is production experience rather than tooling.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Upgrading every EVPN-configured IOS XE device to 16.3 or later, since no workaround exists, and restricting which peers may open a session carrying the EVPN address family so an untrusted party cannot present the update at all.
prevention.adequacy: Peer restriction bounds who can deliver the update but does nothing against a peer that is itself compromised, and the upgrade crosses a major IOS XE release boundary on a provider-edge device — real work, not a rollup.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Comparing the EVPN routing table against what peers actually advertised, and alerting on reloads that follow BGP update processing, with the comparison run from a collector rather than from the device itself.
detection.adequacy: Detection is the only defence that addresses the quieter outcome. A reload announces itself; a corrupted BGP table does not, and it will be read as a convergence problem unless something outside the device holds a reference copy of what should be there.

response.what_would_have_worked: Isolating the peer whose updates preceded the event, clearing and rebuilding the affected BGP sessions, and verifying the EVPN table against a known-good copy before returning the device to service.
response.adequacy: Clearing a session restores correct state on that device and cannot recall a corrupted route already advertised onward, so the response has to extend to every device that learned routes from the affected one during the window.

NIST-800-53-SI-10.gap: Input validation is implemented for application data crossing an untrusted boundary, and a BGP update from a configured peer is neither. The mismatch that carries this flaw is between two Cisco implementations of the same draft, so a validation rule derived from the specification would have passed both — the control cannot express 'validate against the version of the RFC the sender used'.

NIST-800-53-SC-7.gap: The BGP session is the boundary the control protects, so every SC-7 measure has already run to completion before the crafted update is parsed. Prefix filters and maximum-prefix limits, the standard evidence at a peering edge, inspect route content and volume and never look at the NLRI length field this defect miscalculates.

NIS2-Art21-network-security.gap: An operator can evidence Article 21 comprehensively for a fabric whose control plane carries this defect, because the measures they present govern zones and user traffic. Routing-table corruption is a control-plane integrity failure that surfaces as instability across the fabric, and there is no place in the usual evidence set where that risk is stated.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: The outcome is achievable and the timeline is where it fails. With no workaround available, the only compliant state is a major-release upgrade to IOS XE 16.3 or later on production provider-edge routers, and a B4 assessment that samples patch currency annually will not notice a three-week KEV window opening and closing in between.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: An IOS XE provider-edge router is inside the mitigation's stated population, and the version boundary could hardly be easier to assess — every release before IOS XE 16.3 that supports BGP EVPN is affected. What the mitigation cannot express is currency of obligation. Its windows are measured from the 2017-11-03 release of the fix, so a router still short of 16.3 in March 2022, when Cisco recorded attempted exploitation and CISA set a 2022-03-24 due date, produces a finding about a window that lapsed five years earlier rather than one that is live.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.21.gap: Network service records identify circuits, providers and service levels, and stop above the address families configured on each device. Because vulnerability here depends entirely on whether EVPN is configured, an A.8.21 record that is complete by its own terms still cannot answer which devices are in scope for this advisory.

new_control_requirements.name: MITIGATION-ACTIVE-PATCH-PENDING-VERDICT-CLASS
new_control_requirements.description: Compliance verdicts must distinguish three states: (a) binary patch deployed (vulnerability eliminated), (b) vendor-mitigation rule active, no binary patch (residual risk: any defect in the mitigation rule reopens the vulnerability), (c) no mitigation, no patch (full exposure). Audit reports must surface (b) as a distinct compensating-control state with an associated time-bound action item, not as a 'patched per SLA' outcome.
new_control_requirements.evidence: cisco-sa-20171103-bgp publishes no workaround, so on a Cisco IOS XE router the control's middle state does not exist: the device is either reloaded onto IOS XE 16.3 or later, or fully exposed. The state operators actually reach for is a fourth one the report has no column for — removing the EVPN configuration takes the device outside the advisory's stated conditions without touching the defect, and filing that beside an upgrade to 16.3 records a withdrawn service as a completed remediation. Cisco recorded attempted exploitation in March 2022 and CISA set a due date of 2022-03-24, so the distinction decides which routers still owe a reload.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: With no workaround published for cisco-sa-20171103-bgp, the compensating-control branch on this CVE has to be written before the listing rather than found after it — the only pre-agreed measure that bounds exposure is a peer policy limiting who can establish an EVPN-carrying session with an IOS XE device below 16.3. Cisco recorded attempted exploitation in the wild in March 2022, the same month CISA listed the CVE, so the interval between disclosure and pressure was the interval an operator had to already hold that policy.

CVE-2017-12240.name: Cisco IOS and IOS XE Software DHCP Remote Code Execution Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: A crafted DHCPv4 packet overflows a buffer in the DHCP relay subsystem of Cisco IOS and IOS XE, giving an unauthenticated attacker arbitrary code execution and full control of the router, or reloading it. The relay handles the packet before any identity exists in the exchange, which is why no credential is required.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none — PR:N; DHCP offers nothing for the relay to authenticate, so reaching it with a DHCPv4 datagram is the whole access requirement.
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L; no race and no groom. The precondition is deployment rather than difficulty: the device must be configured as a DHCP relay agent, and a relay is reachable from its client segment by design.
attack_vector.ai_factor: None. Cisco attributes the find to internal testing and describes no tooling; the exploitation attempts it later recorded are unattributed.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Reloading every relay-configured IOS and IOS XE device onto a fixed release, and removing ip helper-address from devices that were relaying only because a template put it there — the second reduces the affected population before the first has to reach it.
prevention.adequacy: With no workaround published, prevention is entirely the upgrade, and the upgrade takes client addressing down for everything behind the relay. There is no partial state: until the reload, the device runs the vulnerable code even if the image is already staged.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Watching for DHCPv4 messages that never complete a lease, for malformed giaddr or option 82 content arriving from client segments, and for configuration changes on relay devices, with logs held off the device.
detection.adequacy: Detection on a client VLAN is noisy by nature and a successful exploit produces full control of the device that would otherwise report it. The stronger signal is configuration drift observed from outside the router, not anything the router says about itself.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treating a suspected relay compromise as a device rebuild: capture the configuration for comparison, restore from a known-good baseline rather than upgrading in place, and rotate device credentials and any credential that transited it.
response.adequacy: The reload that installs the fix clears in-memory changes but carries the stored configuration forward, so an upgrade alone cannot distinguish a device that was exploited from one that was not — that judgement has to come from a baseline held elsewhere.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: Flaw remediation is evidenced from the tooling that knows about hosts, and a DHCP relay sits outside that tooling wherever network devices are inventoried separately. Where the device is tracked, the finding still has to wait for a network maintenance window, so a CVSS 9.8 item is governed by a change cadence set for link-affecting work rather than by its severity.

NIST-800-53-SC-7.gap: The control is fully implemented and structurally cannot help: a relay must accept DHCPv4 from the untrusted segment it serves, so the protocol carrying the overflow is the one boundary protection is required to let through. Restricting it would break addressing for every client behind the interface.

NIS2-Art21-patch-management.gap: The obligation is met by a documented patch cycle, and the cycle is the only defence available since Cisco published no workaround. A quarterly network-device window and a three-week KEV due date are not the same clock, and nothing in the Article 21 evidence surfaces the difference between them for a CVSS 9.8 unauthenticated RCE.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: The outcome is stated at the level of keeping systems secure and updated, and every practical obstacle here sits below that level: which devices carry ip helper-address, when a building's addressing can be interrupted, and whether the CMTS relays were included in scope at all after Cisco added them to the assessment in revision 1.1.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: A router or CMTS acting as a DHCP relay is inside the mitigation's population, so the Essential Eight does generate an obligation here — a one-month window from the release of the fixed IOS or IOS XE image, because the relay's attack surface faces client subnets rather than the internet. That is the same window a staff workstation's operating system draws, for a defect that hands an unauthenticated attacker on the served VLAN arbitrary code execution and full control of the very device that VLAN depends on for addressing.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: The control runs correctly on the assets it can see. Because scope here turns on a single configuration line rather than on a version, a vulnerability register can carry this CVE against the right release and still misidentify which devices are relaying — over-reporting devices that are not affected and missing relays the inventory never enumerated.

new_control_requirements.name: PERIMETER-COMPROMISE-REBUILD-NOT-PATCH
new_control_requirements.description: Pre-rehearsed IR runbook for any perimeter device that suffers a pre-auth RCE CVE in active exploitation MUST default to config-exfil + rebuild + credential rotation, not patch-in-place. Patch-in-place leaves attacker-installed implants intact.
new_control_requirements.evidence: This CVE meets the control's trigger exactly: pre-authentication remote code execution at CVSS 9.8 on Cisco IOS and IOS XE, with Cisco recording in December 2022 that PSIRT became aware of attempted exploitation in the wild in March 2022. A DHCP relay is a trust boundary in the same sense the control means — it accepts unauthenticated traffic from a client segment and holds full device privilege on the other side. Because the advisory publishes no workaround, the only action between the 2022-03-03 KEV listing and the reload is the runbook, and an upgrade applied to a relay that was already exploited carries its stored configuration and credentials across unchanged.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Fixed releases for cisco-sa-20170927-dhcp existed from 2017 and were extended in revision 1.2 on 2018-FEB-12, so on this CVE the control's clock starts at the KEV listing of 2022-03-03 — over four years of availability, with a due date of 2022-03-24. The compensating-control branch is narrow and worth naming in advance: removing ip helper-address from devices that relay only by template inheritance shrinks the population that has to make the four-hour window, which is the only way an estate of distribution-layer Cisco routers gets close to it.

CVE-2017-12238.name: Cisco Catalyst 6800 Series Switches VPLS Denial-of-Service Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: An adjacent attacker drives the creation of a large number of VPLS-generated MAC entries until the earl_ntfy_dm_thread process runs out of stack and the core-facing C6800-16P10G or C6800-16P10G-XL line card crashes. The chassis survives; the MPLS core link it carries does not.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none — PR:N; no credential is involved. What the attacker needs instead is adjacency to a segment whose traffic populates the VPLS MAC table.
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L for the action itself, generating MAC entries rather than crafting a packet. The binding constraint is the platform: Catalyst 6800, Supervisor Engine 6T, a specific pair of line cards, VPLS configured, and that card in the core-facing MPLS role.
attack_vector.ai_factor: None. Cisco found it while handling customer support requests, which is why the advisory carries a real crashinfo excerpt rather than a synthetic reproduction.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Upgrading affected Catalyst 6800 chassis to a fixed release, since no workaround exists, and limiting which adjacent segments can contribute MAC entries to the VPLS instance so the entry churn cannot be driven from an untrusted party.
prevention.adequacy: The upgrade requires a reload of a chassis carrying an MPLS core link, which is a scheduled event. Limiting adjacency helps only where the VPLS attachment circuits face a controllable population; on a service-provider handoff they face the customer by design.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Alerting on the %SYS-DFC1-6-STACKLOW line naming earl_ntfy_dm_thread, and baselining VPLS MAC entry growth so an abnormal rate is visible before the stack is exhausted.
detection.adequacy: The vendor gives defenders a precise, quotable signal here, and it is genuinely usable — provided chassis syslog reaches a collector at message granularity, because the crashinfo that confirms it is written on the card that just failed.

response.what_would_have_worked: Preserving the line-card crashinfo before recovering the card, comparing the earl_ntfy_dm_thread stack figures as the advisory describes, and treating a repeat crash on the same card as adversarial rather than as failing hardware.
response.adequacy: Response restores the link and prevents nothing, and its real value is diagnostic: without the crashinfo comparison, a card that crashes twice looks like a hardware fault and gets replaced, which resolves nothing and consumes a spare.

NIST-800-53-SI-4.gap: Monitoring is in place for the chassis and blind at the granularity that matters. A line-card process crash does not take the managed device offline, so the platform reports the switch as healthy while an MPLS core interface is gone, and the string that identifies the cause is only present if syslog is retained at message level.

NIST-800-53-SC-5.gap: The control's implementation is volumetric and the exhausted resource is a process stack, whose depletion the advisory records as 0/26000 in its STACKLOW message. No traffic threshold protects it, because the MAC entries consuming it are created by ordinary learning behaviour rather than by traffic an anomaly detector would classify as abusive.

NIS2-Art21-availability.gap: Redundancy is the standard availability evidence and it is the wrong shape here. Two identically configured C6800-16P10G cards on the same chassis share the defect, so failover moves the core-facing role onto hardware with the same crash condition, and the operator's continuity evidence overstates the independence of the paths.

UK-CAF-C1.gap: Security monitoring can be fully achieved without any of this advisory's evidence reaching a collector, because the crashinfo comparison it describes is performed on the device after the fact. C1 measures whether monitoring exists, not whether it captures the artefact that distinguishes an attack from a hardware fault on this specific platform.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: The mitigation covers the switch and measures the wrong thing about it. Its unit is the operating system version, while cisco-sa-20170927-vpls scopes exposure to a line-card part number, a supervisor engine, a VPLS configuration and a cabling role. An estate can hold a complete and accurate IOS currency record for every Catalyst 6800 it owns and still not know which of them meet the advisory's four simultaneous conditions — and Cisco has never revised that advisory from its 2017 statement that PSIRT is not aware of malicious use, so the assessment has no vendor signal pushing it to look.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.16.gap: Monitoring activities is satisfied by watching networks and systems for anomalous behaviour, and the anomaly here is a growth rate inside the MAC address table of one VPLS instance. Where MAC table growth on that instance is not baselined, the control's first observation of the anomaly is the crash it exists to anticipate.

new_control_requirements.name: FIREWALL-EGRESS-TELEMETRY-SEPARATE-TRUST-ZONE
new_control_requirements.description: Firewall and other perimeter-trust-boundary devices must forward syslog, threat logs, and authentication logs to a SIEM hosted in a separate trust zone (different management plane, different credentials, different authentication path). Telemetry stored on the compromised device is destroyed by the attacker; telemetry on a separate-trust-zone collector survives.
new_control_requirements.evidence: On this CVE the telemetry at risk is not deleted by an attacker but written to a component that has just crashed: the %SYS-DFC1-6-STACKLOW line naming earl_ntfy_dm_thread, and the crashinfo file on the C6800-16P10G card itself. Cisco publishes both as its Indicators of Compromise, and neither is useful to an operator whose Catalyst 6800 chassis forwards only interface up/down state. Forwarding chassis syslog at message granularity to a collector on a separate management path is what makes the vendor's own indicators actionable, and it is what separates a repeat exploitation from the failing-hardware diagnosis it otherwise resembles.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: This entry tests the control where the vendor and CISA disagree: cisco-sa-20170927-vpls has stood at revision 1.0 since 2017-September-27 stating that PSIRT is not aware of any public announcements or malicious use, while CISA listed the CVE on 2022-03-03 with a 2022-03-24 due date. An SLA keyed to KEV rather than to vendor exploitation language starts the clock anyway, which is the correct behaviour for an operator running a Catalyst 6800 with a C6800-16P10G card in the core-facing MPLS role, since no workaround exists and the only alternative to the upgrade is re-provisioning that role onto other hardware.

CVE-2017-12237.name: Cisco IOS and IOS XE Software Internet Key Exchange Denial-of-Service Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: IKEv2 packets sent to UDP 500, 848 or 4500 drive the Crypto IKEv2 process into sustained CPU consumption, CPUHOG tracebacks, or a device reload. Because IKEv2 comes on with ISAKMP, the exposed population is every device with ISAKMP enabled rather than every device running a VPN feature.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none — PR:N; the packets are processed before any negotiation completes, so no key, certificate or account is needed.
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L; the attacker sends packets over IPv4 or IPv6 and the device performs the expensive work. The precondition is only that one of the three UDP ports is open, which `show udp` answers directly.
attack_vector.ai_factor: None. Cisco found the defect while resolving a TAC support case, which is why the advisory publishes real CPU and traceback output rather than a synthetic example.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Applying crypto ikev2 limit queue sa-init on every ISAKMP-enabled device whose release supports it — Cisco calls this equivalent to upgrading to a fixed release — and disabling ISAKMP entirely on devices that terminate no tunnels, then scheduling the reload onto fixed software.
prevention.adequacy: The workaround is strong on Cisco's own account and depends on the running release supporting the command, so the estate splits into devices that can take it and devices that must wait for the reload. Disabling ISAKMP is complete where it applies and unavailable wherever a tunnel terminates.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Alerting on the Crypto IKEv2 process holding high CPU in `show proc cpu sorted`, and on CPUHOG tracebacks naming that process, with the alerts leaving the device before it reloads.
detection.adequacy: These are precise, vendor-published signals and they arrive during the attack rather than after it, which is what makes them usable against an availability defect at all. Their value collapses if syslog leaves the site over the VPN the same device terminates.

response.what_would_have_worked: Filtering the source of the IKEv2 traffic upstream where the peer set is known, applying the sa-init queue limit before returning the device to service, and treating repeated reloads of a head-end as adversarial rather than as an unstable image.
response.adequacy: Upstream filtering works only where legitimate peers are enumerable; a remote-access head-end accepts IKEv2 from anywhere its users are, so for that role there is no source list to filter down to.

NIST-800-53-SC-5.gap: DoS protection is implemented as bandwidth and rate control, and the resource this defect consumes is a single process's CPU on the device itself. Traffic that stays inside every rate limit still reloads the head-end, so the control is fully implemented against a bottleneck the attacker never touches.

NIST-800-53-CM-7.gap: The control is met by an inventory of enabled features, and Cisco states plainly that no IKEv2-specific feature needs to be configured for the device to be vulnerable. A least-functionality attestation can therefore be accurate, current and completely disconnected from the exposure, which is decided by whether UDP 500, 848 or 4500 answers.

NIS2-Art21-business-continuity.gap: Continuity plans are exercised against site loss and system failure, and this defect removes the remote-access and site-to-site connectivity that many such plans assume responders will use. The dependency is rarely written down, so the plan can be tested successfully every year without ever exercising the case where the VPN head-end is the thing that failed.

UK-CAF-B5.gap: Resilience is evidenced by a redundant head-end pair and a tested failover. Both members answer IKEv2 on the same ports from the same networks, so an attacker reaches the standby by the same route as the primary — the redundancy is real against hardware failure and absent against this.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: A VPN head-end running IOS or IOS XE is inside the mitigation's population, and it can satisfy the mitigation without the defect being fixed. The clause accepts "other vendor mitigations"; Cisco publishes one — `crypto ikev2 limit queue sa-init` — and states it is equivalent to performing an upgrade to a fixed release. A device carrying that line and a device reloaded onto fixed code produce the same maturity result, and only the second has the vulnerable IKEv2 packet-processing path out of the image.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.21.gap: The VPN service is documented under this control with its cryptographic and authentication requirements, and none of that record identifies devices where ISAKMP is enabled but no tunnel terminates. Those devices are in scope for the advisory and invisible to the control's own service inventory.

new_control_requirements.name: MITIGATION-ACTIVE-PATCH-PENDING-VERDICT-CLASS
new_control_requirements.description: Compliance verdicts must distinguish three states: (a) binary patch deployed (vulnerability eliminated), (b) vendor-mitigation rule active, no binary patch (residual risk: any defect in the mitigation rule reopens the vulnerability), (c) no mitigation, no patch (full exposure). Audit reports must surface (b) as a distinct compensating-control state with an associated time-bound action item, not as a 'patched per SLA' outcome.
new_control_requirements.evidence: cisco-sa-20170927-ike puts this control under direct pressure, because Cisco itself says the workaround is equivalent to performing an upgrade to a fixed release. That sentence invites an operator to record `crypto ikev2 limit queue sa-init` as remediation complete, when the device is still running unfixed code on a release between IOS 15.0-15.6 or IOS XE 3.5-16.5, and Cisco recorded attempted exploitation in the wild in March 2022. The command is also release-dependent, so an estate can hold it on some devices and not others while reporting a single state. The middle verdict class, with a dated action item for the reload, is what keeps that distinction visible.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: A four-hour clock is achievable on this CVE in a way it is not on the advisories with no workaround: the sa-init queue limit is a configuration line, deployable across an ISAKMP-enabled Cisco IOS and IOS XE estate without a maintenance window, which makes the KEV listing of 2022-03-03 actionable on the day rather than at the next outage. The verification step the SLA demands is available too — `show udp` confirms whether the device still answers on UDP 500, 848 or 4500, and the running configuration confirms whether the limit is in force.

CVE-2017-12235.name: Cisco IOS Software for Cisco Industrial Ethernet Switches PROFINET Denial-of-Service Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: A crafted PN-DCP Identify Request followed by ordinary ones drives an affected Cisco IOS switch into a reload. No code runs and no configuration changes; the loss is the switch itself, and with it every node attached to the cell it serves.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none - PR:N; the vector is CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:H and no credential, session or prior foothold is consumed. The attacker needs only to get PN-DCP Identify Requests to a switch that parses them.
attack_vector.complexity: low - AC:L; the real constraint is reachability of the PROFINET handler, and IOS 12.2(52)SE and later enable PROFINET by default on base and expansion-unit Ethernet ports, so the constraint is usually already satisfied.
attack_vector.ai_factor: Cisco's 2017 bundled advisory names no external reporter and no tooling, and attributes nothing to an AI-assisted process. No research arm with 'AI' in its brand name appears anywhere in the record, so there is no branding to disambiguate.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Upgrading each affected switch to the First Fixed release the Cisco IOS Software Checker returns for cisco-sa-20170927-profinet, scoped by running release rather than by model.
prevention.adequacy: It is the only thing that removes the defect, and it costs a reload - so on a switch serving a live cell the remediation itself imposes the outage the vulnerability threatens, only scheduled. Until that window arrives Cisco offers nothing: the advisory states there are no workarounds that address this vulnerability.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Off-box syslog with reload and crashinfo accounting per switch, so that a reload is recorded as a security-relevant event and correlated with PN-DCP traffic rather than logged as a maintenance blip.
detection.adequacy: Detection here is retrospective by construction - the device is already down when the evidence is generated, and the on-box buffer is destroyed by the reload it would have recorded. Its value is distinguishing a repeated exploit attempt from a hardware fault, not preventing the outage.

response.what_would_have_worked: A cell-level continuity procedure that treats a switch reload as an expected failure mode, with a decided answer for whether the process rides through a boot interval or halts safely.
