response.adequacy: This bounds the consequence rather than the exposure, and it is only useful if the answer was decided before the reload - the boot interval is not long enough to make the decision during.

NIST-800-82r3.gap: An OT risk assessment written against this guidance will show the switch inventoried, the advisory tracked and a compensating control recorded pending the maintenance window. The last of those three is fiction for this CVE: Cisco states there are no workarounds that address this vulnerability, so between the 2017 disclosure and an actual IOS image change the honest verdict is full exposure, and the guidance gives no vocabulary that forces that distinction onto the risk register.

NIS2-Art21-availability.gap: Availability obligations are met on paper by redundancy and continuity planning at the service tier, both of which sit above the access switch. Neither reaches a defect where an unauthenticated PN-DCP sequence reloads the device with EPSS at 0.07128 as of 2026-08-20, because the loss is the network element itself and everything the continuity plan relies on is reached through it.

UK-CAF-B5.gap: B5 evidence usually takes the form of a redundant topology diagram, which reads as adequate until you notice the shared exposure. Both members of a redundant pair running an affected IOS release with PROFINET default-enabled answer the same Identify Request sequence, so the failover target is as reloadable as the primary and the redundancy buys nothing against this particular input.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: The maturity rating is only as honest as the asset population it was computed over. Where patch evidence comes from an endpoint and server management console, an Industrial Ethernet switch running IOS between 12.2 and 15.6 never enters the denominator, so a high rating is produced without the vulnerable device having been assessed at all - and the KEV due date of 2022-03-24 passes without the asset appearing on any overdue list.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: A.8.8 is satisfied by a working intake process, and that process will duly ingest cisco-sa-20170927-profinet and mark a vendor fix as available. What it cannot produce from the advisory is a version number, because Cisco publishes none and defers to the IOS Software Checker for a per-train First Fixed result - so the control completes while every switch still lacks a named remediation target.

IEC-62443-3-3.gap: Zone-and-conduit design assumes hostile input is foreign to the automation zone and can be filtered at the conduit. PN-DCP Identify Requests are exactly the discovery traffic the zone exists to carry, so the conduit rules cannot distinguish the crafted request from the legitimate one, and any device already inside the cell - a compromised HMI, an engineering laptop, a contractor's tool - is on the permitted side of every boundary the standard would have you draw.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Cisco IOS on Industrial Ethernet switches carried this PN-DCP parser defect from the September 2017 advisory until each unit's individual image change, and CISA gave it a KEV clock of 2022-03-03 to 2022-03-24. The control's parenthetical matters more than its deadline here: of its three permitted mitigations, live patch does not exist for IOS and documented compensating controls do not exist either, because cisco-sa-20170927-profinet states there are no workarounds that address this vulnerability. That leaves the patch, and the patch is a reload - so on a switch running a live cell the SLA is a scheduling problem, and an estate that has not pre-agreed a reload window cannot meet it no matter how fast its intake is.

new_control_requirements.name: MITIGATION-ACTIVE-PATCH-PENDING-VERDICT-CLASS
new_control_requirements.description: Compliance verdicts must distinguish three states: (a) binary patch deployed (vulnerability eliminated), (b) vendor-mitigation rule active, no binary patch (residual risk: any defect in the mitigation rule reopens the vulnerability), (c) no mitigation, no patch (full exposure). Audit reports must surface (b) as a distinct compensating-control state with an associated time-bound action item, not as a 'patched per SLA' outcome.
new_control_requirements.evidence: This entry is the case where state (b) is not available at all. Cisco publishes no workaround for cisco-sa-20170927-profinet, so an Industrial Ethernet switch awaiting its reload window is in state (c) - full exposure - and any audit line describing it as mitigated pending maintenance has invented a middle state the vendor does not offer. The distinction is checkable per unit rather than per estate: `show profinet status` returning Enabled on an IOS release the Software Checker still lists as unfixed for this advisory is state (c), and Cisco treats Disabled, or a platform lacking the command, as not vulnerable.

CVE-2017-12234.name: Cisco IOS Software Common Industrial Protocol Request Denial-of-Service Vulnerability (CVE-2017-12234)

attack_vector.description: Crafted CIP packets sent to UDP 2222 or 44818 on a Cisco IOS device with CIP enabled are mis-parsed and reload the device. The reach is decided by one configuration line, because Cisco ships the CIP feature disabled.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none - PR:N; the vector is CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:H. No credential is presented and no session exists, but the attacker must be able to address the device directly, since Cisco states transiting packets cannot be used.
attack_vector.complexity: low - AC:L on the send side; the real constraint is configuration, not skill. Only a device where `cip enable` is configured parses the packets at all, which makes the exposed population a deliberate subset rather than the whole IOS estate.
attack_vector.ai_factor: Discovery sits inside Cisco's own process under bug ID CSCvc43709, with no external reporter, no tooling and no AI-branded research arm named in the advisory or in NVD's reference set.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Upgrading to the Cisco IOS Software Checker's First Fixed release for cisco-sa-20170927-cip, which resolves this defect and CSCuz95334 in the same image, on every device where `cip enable` is configured.
prevention.adequacy: It removes both CIP defects at once, which is efficient, and it costs a reload on a device that industrial peers depend on. Cisco offers no sanctioned interim measure - the advisory states there are no workarounds that address these vulnerabilities.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Inbound flow accounting on UDP 2222 and 44818 at the boundary of the segment holding CIP-enabled devices, so that traffic from a non-peer source is visible before a reload rather than inferred after one.
detection.adequacy: The ports are narrow and well documented by Cisco, which makes this cheap and specific. It sees the delivery attempt but does not stop it, and it is blind to an attempt sourced from a legitimate CIP peer inside the zone.

response.what_would_have_worked: An inbound ACL on UDP 2222 and 44818 to the device, restricted to the enumerated CIP peers, deployable ahead of the reload window.
response.adequacy: Cisco does not sanction this as a workaround and it must not be recorded as one. It narrows the sender population to the peer list and gives nothing against a compromised peer already on that list, which is why it is a holding measure rather than a remediation.

NIST-800-53-CM-7.gap: The control passes on the strength of a baseline that leaves CIP disabled, exactly as Cisco ships it, and that pass is honest for most of the estate. It is wrong precisely where it matters, because the vulnerable devices are the documented exceptions where an engineer enabled CIP for an operational reason - and a least-functionality review that audits the baseline rather than the exception register never returns to the small set of devices listening on UDP 2222 and 44818.

NIS2-Art21-network-security.gap: Segmentation evidence is genuinely relevant here, since Cisco confirms the parser is reachable only by device-destined IPv4 traffic to two named UDP ports. It is accepted at the wrong granularity: an estate that filters at the site edge satisfies the obligation while every CIP peer inside the plant retains a clear path to the defect, and the peers are precisely the hosts a plant intrusion lands on first.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: The B4 record for this device reads well - a supported Cisco platform, a non-default feature enabled against a documented requirement, change control applied. None of that reveals that the documented requirement is what puts the device inside cisco-sa-20170927-cip with a CWE-20 parser defect and a KEV due date of 2022-03-24 already behind it, because the principle asks whether the configuration is justified rather than what it exposes.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: Treating a Cisco IOS image as an operating system for the purposes of this mitigation is a reading rather than a quotation, and everything downstream depends on it. If the assessed population comes from a software-deployment console, the CIP-enabled IOS device is absent from the denominator, its unfixed release for cisco-sa-20170927-cip is never counted, and the resulting maturity rating describes an estate that does not include the exposed asset.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.9.gap: This is the control closest to the defect and it fails in the most ordinary way. `cip enable` is an authorised deviation from the baseline, correctly raised, approved and recorded - so A.8.9 evidence shows disciplined configuration management, while the register carries no link from that approved line to the advisory that makes the line dangerous, and nothing in the review cycle re-examines an old approval against a new disclosure.

IEC-62443-3-3.gap: Conduit restriction is the standard's answer and Cisco has specified the conduit precisely - IPv4, device-destined, UDP 2222 or 44818. That precision cuts both ways: those are the ports CIP needs to function, so the conduit cannot be closed without removing the capability, and every enumerated peer permitted through it holds the complete precondition for the reload.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CISA put this Cisco IOS CIP defect on the KEV clock on 2022-03-03 with a due date of 2022-03-24, roughly four and a half years after Cisco's September 2017 advisory - the exposure window was never bounded by patch availability. Of the control's three permitted mitigations, live patch does not exist for IOS and documented compensating controls do not either, since cisco-sa-20170927-cip states there are no workarounds that address these vulnerabilities. The one usable route is the Software Checker's First Fixed image and the reload it requires, and the population it must be driven across is not the IOS estate but the subset where `show running-config | include cip enable` returns `cip enable`.

new_control_requirements.name: INCOMPLETE-PATCH-SEQUENCE-SEVERITY-MULTIPLIER
new_control_requirements.description: Vulnerability-management programs must apply a severity multiplier when a CVE is the Nth in an incomplete-patch sequence on the same primitive (third MOTW bypass, second AMSI bypass, etc.). Framework controls treating each CVE as discrete obscure the structural defect; the Nth CVE in a sequence implies that future bypasses on the same primitive are likely.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Cisco disclosed two separate defects in the same Cisco IOS CIP parsing primitive in one advisory - CVE-2017-12234 as CSCvc43709 alongside CVE-2017-12233 as CSCuz95334 - and NVD's own text opens 'Multiple vulnerabilities in the implementation of the Common Industrial Protocol (CIP) feature'. Two distinct bug IDs against one parser reached through one pair of UDP ports is the structural signal this control exists to price: the finding is not that a packet crashed the device but that the CIP input path produced more than one way to do it. A programme that closes CSCvc43709 as a discrete ticket records a fix and carries forward the assumption that the parser is now sound.

CVE-2017-12233.name: Cisco IOS Software Common Industrial Protocol Request Denial-of-Service Vulnerability (CVE-2017-12233)

attack_vector.description: Crafted CIP packets to UDP 2222 or 44818 on a CIP-enabled Cisco IOS device are mis-parsed and reload it. This is the second of two separate defects Cisco disclosed against the same CIP parsing surface in one advisory.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none - PR:N; the vector is CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:H. Nothing is authenticated, but the packets must be addressed to the device, because Cisco excludes transiting traffic from the exploitation path.
attack_vector.complexity: low - AC:L; the constraint is finding a device with CIP configured, not building the packet. Cisco ships the feature off, so the vulnerable set is a deliberate subset of the IOS estate rather than its default state.
attack_vector.ai_factor: Cisco records the defect under its own bug ID CSCuz95334 with no external credit and no tooling named. Nothing in the advisory or NVD's references suggests automated discovery, and no AI-branded research group is involved for branding to be mistaken for evidence.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Moving every device with `cip enable` configured onto the Cisco IOS Software Checker's First Fixed release for cisco-sa-20170927-cip, and measuring completion by running image rather than by CVE identities closed.
prevention.adequacy: One image resolves both CIP defects, so the work is smaller than the finding count suggests - but it is a reload on a device industrial peers depend on, and Cisco states there are no workarounds that address these vulnerabilities, so there is no partial credit to take beforehand.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Off-box collection of reload and crashinfo records from every CIP-enabled device, so a reload is preserved as evidence rather than erased by the event that produced it.
detection.adequacy: This is the only way to tell a repeated exploitation attempt from an intermittent hardware fault after the fact, and it changes nothing about the outage. Its worth is entirely in the post-incident question of whether to expect another one.

response.what_would_have_worked: A pre-built inbound ACL limiting UDP 2222 and 44818 on each CIP-enabled device to its enumerated peers, ready to apply while the reload window is negotiated.
response.adequacy: It must be recorded as a holding measure and not as a vendor mitigation, because Cisco publishes none. It bounds the sender population to the peer list and offers nothing against a compromised peer inside it.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: SI-2 is nominally met by an intake-to-remediation pipeline that ingested the advisory and raised findings, and the pipeline's own unit of work is what defeats it. Two bug IDs behind one Cisco image mean the CVE-keyed record can reach a closed state through deduplication or acceptance on one identity while the device still runs the pre-fix release - and because the fixed version is not in the advisory, no ticket carries the value that would have caught the discrepancy.

NIS2-Art21-vulnerability-handling.gap: The handling obligation is discharged by demonstrating a process that receives, assesses and acts on disclosures, and this process will do all three. What it cannot do from cisco-sa-20170927-cip is produce a target version, because Cisco publishes none and defers to the Software Checker per running release - so the demonstrable output is two tickets against one bundled advisory, neither of which tells any device operator what image to install.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: B4 sampling is organised by system, and the population that matters here is defined by a configuration line rather than by a system class. A review that draws its sample across network devices by platform will land mostly on IOS units where CIP was never enabled and which are genuinely unaffected, so the evidence is sound and the conclusion is drawn about devices that do not carry the exposure.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: Beyond the interpretive question of whether an IOS image counts as an operating system for this mitigation - stated here as a reading, not a quotation - the counting unit distorts the result. Two CVE identities closed by one image mean a metric expressed in vulnerabilities remediated moves twice for a single device action, and an estate can show a rising figure while the number of devices actually running First Fixed has not changed.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.16.gap: Monitoring is covered by any reasonable logging arrangement, and this defect targets the monitoring itself: the reload that constitutes the impact also clears the device's in-memory log buffer. Unless reload and crashinfo records are shipped off-box before the event, A.8.16 is satisfied by an arrangement that is structurally incapable of retaining evidence of the one incident type this CVE produces.

IEC-62443-3-3.gap: A security-level assessment will credit the zone-and-conduit design, and Cisco's narrow port specification makes the conduit easy to define precisely. The credit overstates the protection because the same definition describes normal CIP operation - UDP 2222 and 44818 must reach the device from its peers - so every rule that could be written still permits the exact traffic that reloads it, from any peer an intruder reaches first.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CISA enrolled this Cisco IOS CIP defect on 2022-03-03 with a due date of 2022-03-24, against a Cisco advisory published in September 2017 - so the clock the control cares about is 'KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later', and the later of the two was the listing by more than four years. The mitigation menu is one item long: live patching does not exist for IOS and cisco-sa-20170927-cip states there are no workarounds that address these vulnerabilities, leaving the Software Checker's First Fixed image and its reload. Verification has to be the running release on each device with `cip enable` configured, because the CVE record can close without the image moving.

new_control_requirements.name: MITIGATION-ACTIVE-PATCH-PENDING-VERDICT-CLASS
new_control_requirements.description: Compliance verdicts must distinguish three states: (a) binary patch deployed (vulnerability eliminated), (b) vendor-mitigation rule active, no binary patch (residual risk: any defect in the mitigation rule reopens the vulnerability), (c) no mitigation, no patch (full exposure). Audit reports must surface (b) as a distinct compensating-control state with an associated time-bound action item, not as a 'patched per SLA' outcome.
new_control_requirements.evidence: A CIP-enabled Cisco IOS device awaiting its reload window is in state (c), not state (b): Cisco publishes no workaround for cisco-sa-20170927-cip, so there is no vendor-mitigation rule to be active. The trap specific to this entry is that an inbound ACL on UDP 2222 and 44818 looks exactly like state (b) on an audit line - it is operator-authored, it is real, and it narrows the sender population - while remaining an unsanctioned holding measure that a legitimate CIP peer walks straight through. Recording it as a compensating control converts full exposure into an apparently managed risk with no time-bound action attached.

CVE-2017-12232.name: Cisco IOS Software for Cisco Integrated Services Routers Denial-of-Service Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: A crafted Ethernet frame delivered on a segment directly attached to an ISR G2 is misclassified as the router's internal service-blade protocol and reloads the device. There is no feature to turn off, because the misclassified path is how the chassis talks to its own network modules.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none - PR:N; the vector is CVSS:3.1/AV:A/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:H. No credential is used, but AV:A means the sender must already occupy an adjacent position, which in practice is a host or port on an attached segment.
attack_vector.complexity: low - AC:L once adjacent; a single crafted frame with no groom, race or leak. The entire cost is obtaining the adjacency, which is why the CVSS base of 6.5 sits below the 7.5 carried by the AV:N defects Cisco disclosed alongside it, despite an identical availability impact.
attack_vector.ai_factor: Attributed to Cisco's own bug ID CSCvc03809 with no external credit. An internal-only chassis protocol is not a surface external tooling reaches, and neither Cisco nor NVD's references name automated or AI-assisted discovery.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Upgrading each ISR G2 to the Cisco IOS Software Checker's First Fixed release for cisco-sa-20170927-rbip-dos, and for units that can no longer reach a fixed release, replacing the platform rather than accepting the risk indefinitely.
prevention.adequacy: It is the only thing that removes the defect, and it takes the branch offline for the reload. Cisco states there are no workarounds that address this vulnerability, and because the vulnerable path is internal platform behaviour there is no configuration change that substitutes for the image.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Shipping reload and crashinfo records off the router to a collector on a different device, so that the event survives the reload that generates it, paired with port-level visibility on directly attached segments.
detection.adequacy: This is what makes the difference between an unexplained branch outage and a recognised exploitation attempt, and it prevents nothing. Its value is scoping: because the vector is AV:A, a confirmed attempt localises the adversary to an attached segment.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treating a repeated unexplained ISR G2 reload as an indicator that something adjacent is hostile, and investigating the attached segments rather than replacing the router as a hardware fault.
response.adequacy: The AV:A vector makes this inference sound and it is only available if the reload was captured off-box. It bounds where to look and does not shorten the outage.

NIST-800-53-SC-7.gap: An SC-7 attestation for a branch router is normally built from the untrusted-side boundary - ACLs on the WAN interface, a firewall posture, a segmentation diagram at the site edge. The frame in this defect never crosses that boundary; it originates on a segment already attached to the router. The control is genuinely implemented and simply not pointed at the interface the exploit uses, so an assessment can be both accurate and irrelevant to this CVE.

NIST-800-53-AU-9.gap: The control is met by restricting who may clear or modify audit records on the device, which addresses a deliberate adversary tampering with logs. Here the destruction is incidental and unavoidable: the reload that is the whole impact clears the in-memory buffer, so the record of the crafted frame is lost to the event itself. Nothing an AU-9 implementation does on the box changes that, and the control offers no prompt to move the records off it.

NIS2-Art21-business-continuity.gap: Continuity planning is covered and typically written on the assumption that connectivity survives to execute the plan. At a branch served by a single ISR G2 that assumption fails against this CVE, because one adjacent frame takes out the router and therefore the path to whatever the plan escalates to. The obligation is met by a document whose first step is unavailable in exactly the scenario this defect creates.

UK-CAF-C1.gap: Monitoring coverage for the router is claimed on the basis that it logs, and the claim is not usually tested against the specific incident the device is exposed to. Since the sole outcome of this CVE is a reload, and a reload clears the local buffer, coverage that terminates on the device produces no retained evidence - so C1 is satisfied by an arrangement that is blind precisely where this CVE is concerned.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: Two separate problems sit under one apparently-covered control. Whether the mitigation reaches a router's system image is an interpretation rather than a quoted requirement, and even granting it, the strategy speaks only in terms of applying vendor patches - which leaves an ISR G2 that can no longer be brought to a First Fixed release with no expressible status at all, so the honest answer of 'replace the platform' has nowhere to be recorded.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.15.gap: Logging is covered by any implementation that produces records, and the control text does not compel a decision about where they are retained. That omission is decisive for this defect: records that live only on the ISR G2 are erased by the reload, so an estate can hold a clean A.8.15 position and still be unable to say, after a branch outage, whether a crafted frame arrived or a power supply failed.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.22.gap: Segregation is covered, and it is normally designed to separate user populations from servers and from each other. This defect needs a different separation - untrusted hosts kept off the segments physically attached to the router - which a conventional A.8.22 design does not articulate. A network can therefore be well segregated by its own stated model while every user port on the branch LAN still supplies the adjacency the exploit requires.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CISA enrolled this ISR G2 defect on 2022-03-03 with a due date of 2022-03-24. The control's three-way mitigation menu collapses to one option: IOS has no live-patch path, and cisco-sa-20170927-rbip-dos states there are no workarounds that address this vulnerability, so only the Cisco IOS Software Checker's First Fixed image qualifies - and taking it reloads a branch router. The scoping instruction that matters is platform-level rather than feature-level: Cisco binds this advisory to ISR G2 and the vulnerable path is internal router-to-service-blade messaging, so the population is every ISR G2 on IOS 15.0 through 15.6 with no configuration line to narrow it by.

new_control_requirements.name: FIREWALL-EGRESS-TELEMETRY-SEPARATE-TRUST-ZONE
new_control_requirements.description: Firewall and other perimeter-trust-boundary devices must forward syslog, threat logs, and authentication logs to a SIEM hosted in a separate trust zone (different management plane, different credentials, different authentication path). Telemetry stored on the compromised device is destroyed by the attacker; telemetry on a separate-trust-zone collector survives.
new_control_requirements.evidence: The ISR G2 is the perimeter-trust-boundary device at its branch, and this CVE inverts the control's usual premise: the telemetry is not destroyed by an attacker deliberately clearing it but by the reload that is the entire impact, so off-box forwarding is the only way any record of the crafted frame survives. Because the vector is AV:A, that surviving record is also what tells an operator where to look - a confirmed attempt places the adversary on a segment directly attached to the router rather than somewhere on the internet. Cisco published nothing that would let a defender recognise the frame in flight, so the reload event itself is the primary evidence and it exists only if it was already leaving the device.

CVE-2017-12231.name: Cisco IOS Software Network Address Translation Denial-of-Service Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: A crafted H.323 RAS packet sent through a NAT'ing Cisco IOS router is mistranslated by the application layer gateway, and the router crashes and reloads. The packet transits the device rather than addressing it, and the ALG that mishandles it is on by default and invisible in the configuration.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none - PR:N; the vector is CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:H. No credential and no session are needed, and unlike a device-addressed attack the sender only has to be able to route a packet through the router, which is the router's purpose.
attack_vector.complexity: low - AC:L; a single crafted RAS packet with no groom, race or leak. The genuine constraint is nothing more than being on a path the router NATs, and Cisco's default enabling of the H.323 RAS ALG removes the configuration precondition entirely.
attack_vector.ai_factor: Held under Cisco's own bug ID CSCvc57217 with no external reporter credited and no tooling named by Cisco or NVD. No AI-branded research arm appears in the record, so there is no branding here to be mistaken for evidence of AI-assisted discovery.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Applying `no ip nat service ras` where H.323 RAS translation is not needed, immediately and without a reload, then upgrading to the Cisco IOS Software Checker's First Fixed release for cisco-sa-20170927-nat before re-enabling it.
prevention.adequacy: The workaround is vendor-sanctioned and takes effect on a running device, which is rare enough to be worth exploiting. It is not equivalent to the fix: it works by removing the H.323 RAS translation capability, so it is unavailable to any site that still depends on it, and the underlying defect remains in the image until it is replaced.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Alerting on H.323 RAS traffic transiting a router that has no H.323 endpoints or gatekeeper behind it, and shipping reload records off-box so the crash survives the reboot that causes it.
detection.adequacy: On a site with no H.323 deployment this is a high-signal, low-volume alert, because legitimate RAS traffic should not exist. On a site that genuinely runs H.323 the same alert has no discriminating power, since Cisco published no distinguishing feature of the malformed packet.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treating the workaround as a decision with a service consequence: confirming whether any H.323 endpoint or gatekeeper depends on RAS translation at that site before applying `no ip nat service ras`, so the mitigation is not reversed under pressure during an outage.
response.adequacy: This makes the mitigation durable rather than temporary, which matters because a mitigation removed to restore a service leaves the router exposed again with the audit record still reading as mitigated.

NIST-800-53-CM-3.gap: Change control is fully covered and structurally unable to see this. Every CM-3 artefact - the approved baseline, the change ticket, the post-change review - describes things that were configured, and the H.323 RAS ALG was never configured by anyone: Cisco enables it by default and states it does not appear in the running configuration. A device can pass every configuration review it will ever have while carrying the exposure, because the exposure is the absence of a line rather than the presence of one.

NIST-800-53-SC-5.gap: DoS protection is covered by rate limiting and resource controls sized for volumetric abuse, and this defect consumes no volume. One crafted H.323 RAS packet transiting the router produces a crash, so there is no rate at which the threshold fires before the impact lands, and setting one low enough to catch a single packet would drop the NAT'd traffic the router exists to forward. The control is well implemented against a failure model this CVE does not use.

NIS2-Art21-patch-management.gap: The obligation is met by evidence of prompt vendor-fix application, and this advisory makes that evidence ambiguous in a way that flatters the estate. Cisco publishes a workaround and no version number, so an operator who applies `no ip nat service ras` within hours has a strong, genuine, vendor-sanctioned response to show - while every router still runs an image the IOS Software Checker lists as unfixed for cisco-sa-20170927-nat, and the distinction between mitigated and patched is not one the reporting format forces.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: B4 evidence asks whether a configuration is secure and justified, and the two answers conflict here without the conflict ever surfacing. The vulnerable state is Cisco's default and is trivially justified as unmodified vendor configuration; the secure state requires removing H.323 RAS translation, which is a functional regression for any site using it. The assessment records a justified configuration and never has to state that the justification is what leaves the ALG reachable.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: Beyond the interpretive question of whether a router image is in scope of a mitigation written around operating systems, this CVE exposes a reporting hole. Cisco publishes two remediations of different kinds for cisco-sa-20170927-nat - the reload-free `no ip nat service ras` workaround, and a First Fixed image whose version the advisory leaves to the IOS Software Checker - and a maturity model expressed as patch application can represent only the second. A device carrying the workaround is neither unmitigated nor patched, and whichever of those two the assessment records, it states the device's position wrongly.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.9.gap: A.8.9 is met by baselining configurations and detecting drift from them, which presumes the baseline expresses the security-relevant state. It does not here: the H.323 RAS ALG is active by default and prints nothing, so the captured baseline is identical for an exposed router and a mitigated one until `no ip nat service ras` is added. Drift detection can only see a line appear or disappear, and the exposure is the permanent absence of a line nobody ever wrote.

new_control_requirements.name: MITIGATION-ACTIVE-PATCH-PENDING-VERDICT-CLASS
new_control_requirements.description: Compliance verdicts must distinguish three states: (a) binary patch deployed (vulnerability eliminated), (b) vendor-mitigation rule active, no binary patch (residual risk: any defect in the mitigation rule reopens the vulnerability), (c) no mitigation, no patch (full exposure). Audit reports must surface (b) as a distinct compensating-control state with an associated time-bound action item, not as a 'patched per SLA' outcome.
new_control_requirements.evidence: This Cisco IOS NAT defect produces a textbook state (b), and it is the state most likely to be misfiled as (a). Cisco supplies a real vendor mitigation - `no ip nat service ras`, applied in global configuration mode with no reload - and separately a fixed image whose version the advisory does not print, deferring it to the IOS Software Checker for cisco-sa-20170927-nat. A router carrying the workaround against the KEV due date of 2022-03-24 is mitigated, not patched, and the residual the control names is concrete rather than theoretical: the mitigation is a single configuration line that any operator restoring H.323 service can remove, at which point the device returns to full exposure with no new finding raised.

new_control_requirements.name: BUG-FAMILY-MITIGATION-PERSISTENCE
new_control_requirements.description: When a CVE patch lands, retain the pre-patch compensating controls (module blacklists, sysctl restrictions) until the patched code has soaked for a stated review period. Patches for one bug in a primitive class can introduce sibling bugs in the same class; the original compensating control may still apply to the sibling.
new_control_requirements.evidence: The compensating control for this CVE is `no ip nat service ras`, and the primitive it removes is the whole H.323 RAS application layer gateway - a payload-rewriting parser, which is the bug class most likely to yield siblings. The pull to reverse it is strong and specific: once a router reaches the First Fixed release for cisco-sa-20170927-nat, the line looks like leftover remediation debt and restores a working feature when deleted. Retaining it past the upgrade costs nothing at any site with no H.323 endpoint or gatekeeper behind the router, and it is the difference between a device that survives the next defect in the same ALG and one that has re-armed the parser. The exposure marker also inverts once it is kept: the presence of the line, not its absence, is what the configuration baseline can finally assert.

CVE-2017-11826.name: Microsoft Office Remote Code Execution Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: A crafted document corrupts memory in Word's OOXML parsing path; the corrupted object pointer is used in a virtual call and execution transfers to attacker-controlled heap data. Code runs as the user who opened the file. The same parsing surface exists in Microsoft's server-side rendering components, where no user opens anything.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none - PR:N with UI:R; the vector is CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:L/PR:N/UI:R/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H. The attacker holds no account and inherits whatever privilege the opening user has, which on a workstation is that user's full context rather than a constrained one.
attack_vector.complexity: low - AC:L; the exploit is deterministic rather than probabilistic, with the heap groomed by embedded ActiveX controls and ROP gadgets taken from msvbvm60.dll because that module was not ASLR-enabled. The binding constraint is UI:R, and the required action is opening a document.
attack_vector.ai_factor: Found by Qihoo 360 Core Security through analysis of malware already in circulation, per Tarlogic's write-up - human malware analysis, in 2017. No tooling is credited by Microsoft, NVD or the analysis, and no research group involved carries 'AI' in its brand name.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: The October 2017 Microsoft security update applied across the whole affected list - Word 2007 through 2016 and Office 2010 on the endpoint side, and SharePoint Server 2010, Office Web Apps Server 2010/2013, Word Automation Services and Office Online Server on the server side - with Word Viewer removed rather than patched.
prevention.adequacy: It closes the defect, and it did not exist during the period the flaw was actually used: Qihoo 360 found in-the-wild exploitation in the month before the 10 October 2017 patch. It also does not land where it is not applied - a patched desktop estate with an unpatched Office Online Server still parses the same content, and an already-running Word process keeps the vulnerable parser until it is relaunched.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Process-lineage monitoring for winword.exe and for the server-side rendering services spawning interpreters, script hosts or network-capable children, which catches the consequence of execution rather than the document.
detection.adequacy: This is the only layer that had a chance during the zero-day window, because it keys on what the payload does rather than on a known file. It fires after code has already run, so it bounds dwell time rather than preventing compromise, and it is only meaningful on the server tier if that tier is instrumented at all.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treating a confirmed open of a malicious document as a credential-exposure event for the opening user, since the payload executed at that user's privilege with access to whatever that account could reach.
response.adequacy: It scopes the response correctly and does nothing about the initial execution. Where the affected identity is a service account behind a rendering component rather than a person, the exposure scope is that service's reach rather than one desktop.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: The control is met and the metric is computed over the wrong denominator. Endpoint patch compliance for Word 2007 through 2016 is easy to evidence and will read well, while SharePoint Server 2010, Office Web Apps Server 2010 and 2013, Word Automation Services and Office Online Server sit on separate tracks owned by a different team. Both halves parse the same OOXML content, and only one half appears in the report an SI-2 assessment usually receives.

NIST-800-53-SI-3.gap: Anti-malware coverage is complete and was structurally irrelevant during the exposure that mattered. The flaw was used as a zero-day - Qihoo 360 found exploitation in the month before the 10 October 2017 patch - so no signature existed, and the sample's nested containers (RTF holding Word.Document.12 objects holding OOXML) are a deliberate obstacle to static inspection. The control becomes effective at precisely the point the vendor fix is also available.

NIS2-Art21-vulnerability-handling.gap: A functioning handling process satisfies the obligation, and the naming is what defeats it. Both the vendor title and the KEV record present this as a Microsoft Office issue, so the ticket routes to whoever owns Office, while the affected list reaches SharePoint, Office Web Apps Server, Word Automation Services and Office Online Server. The obligation is discharged against a product name rather than against the set of systems that actually parse the content.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: B4 is satisfied separately for endpoints and for infrastructure, and this CVE straddles the seam between them. The user-facing products are governed under endpoint hardening with UI:R offering apparent comfort; the rendering services parse identical documents as a service function with no user interaction and no UI:R protection at all. Neither assessment is wrong on its own terms, and nothing in the principle forces the question of whether the same parser was patched on both sides.

AU-Essential-8-App-Hardening.gap: Hardening is covered by the familiar Office configuration set - macro restriction, blocking OLE execution - and every one of those settings governs a decision point this exploit never reaches. Memory corruption occurs while the OOXML is parsed, before any enable-content prompt, and the ActiveX controls in the observed sample are heap-groom filler rather than an execution route. Reading the mitigation as covering this attack is an interpretation, and on that reading it is covered and ineffective.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.7.gap: The control is met by anti-malware plus awareness training, and awareness is the half that carries no weight here. UI:R implies a user action, but the action is opening a document rather than enabling a macro or dismissing a security warning, so there is no prompt at which training changes an outcome. On the server-side rendering components the human element is absent entirely, leaving A.8.7 resting on the signature-based half against what was a zero-day.

new_control_requirements.name: DOWNLOAD-PROVENANCE-ENFORCEMENT
new_control_requirements.description: Exploitation here requires the victim to open an attacker-supplied Office document, so on an estate that has not yet reached the fixed build the delivery path is the only enforceable control. Require Mark-of-the-Web on every Office file arriving by mail, web download, or untrusted file share, and require MOTW-tagged documents to open in Protected View — an isolated, reduced-privilege render — instead of the full parsing path that carries the CWE-94 sink at the user's own process privilege. Provenance must survive the container: files extracted from an archive, mounted from an ISO or VHD, or renamed must inherit the tag rather than lose it, and 'Enable Editing' on externally sourced documents must be blocked by policy rather than left to the user. The distinguishing test: mail a MOTW-tagged spreadsheet nested inside a ZIP to a managed workstation, extract it, and confirm the extracted file still opens in Protected View — a user-application-hardening attestation that covers only macro and ActiveX/OLE settings still lets a provenance-stripped document reach the vulnerable parser with full user privileges.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2017-11826 is CWE-119 rather than the CWE-94 sink the control's text describes, and the provenance argument transfers exactly because the failure is in parsing rather than in a feature the user enables. Qihoo 360 found this Microsoft Word flaw exploited in the wild in the month before the 10 October 2017 patch, and the container nesting in the analysed sample - an RTF carrying Word.Document.12 compound-document objects that hold the OOXML - is precisely the provenance-stripping shape the control's survive-the-container clause addresses. Protected View is the one measure that puts the corrupting parse in a reduced-privilege render instead of the opening user's own context, and it is the only thing that would have applied during the zero-day window when no patch and no signature existed. The control's caveat about macro and ActiveX/OLE attestations is literally the failure here: those settings govern decision points this exploit never reaches.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Microsoft published the fix on 10 October 2017 and CISA enrolled CVE-2017-11826 on 2022-03-03 with a 2022-03-24 due date, so the later of the two clocks is the KEV listing by more than four years - an interval in which EPSS reached 0.81454 at the 99.61st percentile as of 2026-08-20. What this control has to force for this particular CVE is the scope of 'deploy': the affected set includes SharePoint Server 2010, Office Web Apps Server 2010 and 2013, Word Automation Services and Office Online Server alongside Word 2007 through 2016, so verification must enumerate the server-side rendering tier by product rather than reporting endpoint patch coverage. Word Viewer, also affected and out of support, is verified by its absence rather than by a build number, and any Word process left running keeps the vulnerable parser loaded until it is relaunched.

CVE-2017-11292.name: Adobe Flash Player Type Confusion Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: A flaw in Flash Player's bytecode verification lets an untrusted value drive an array-index calculation, producing type confusion and from it arbitrary memory read and write, which the observed exploit used to run second-stage shellcode. It reached victims inside Office documents carrying an embedded ActiveX object, not through browsing.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none - PR:N with UI:R; the vector is CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:R/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H. The attacker holds no account and runs at the privilege of whoever opened the document.
attack_vector.complexity: low - AC:L; a verifier defect yields a direct read/write primitive rather than a pointer that needs grooming, so the path from trigger to shellcode is short. The binding constraint is the user action, and that action is opening a document rather than approving a plugin.
attack_vector.ai_factor: Reported by Anton Ivanov of Kaspersky Labs per Adobe's acknowledgement, from analysis of a live attack. No discovery tooling is named by Adobe or Kaspersky, and no organisation in the chain has 'AI' in its brand name, so there is no branding to disambiguate from genuine AI-assisted discovery.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Removing the Flash Player runtime from the estate rather than disabling it in browser policy, which is the only state that also closes the Office ActiveX delivery route and is what CISA's required action directs.
prevention.framework_requiring_it: CISA BOD 22-01 (KEV remediation, added 2022-03-03, due 2022-03-24; required action: the impacted product is end-of-life and should be disconnected if still in use)
prevention.adequacy: Removal is complete and final in a way patching is not, and it was not available as advice in 2017 when the flaw was actually used - Adobe's fixed build 27.0.0.170 was the answer then, and it was a zero-day, so during the attacks there was no build to reach. What removal does not do is address other software on the host: it ends this exposure and says nothing about the Office parser that carried the payload.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Alerting on an Office application instantiating the Flash ActiveX control, and on Flash-hosting processes spawning interpreters or network-capable children.
detection.adequacy: The first is a high-signal, low-volume indicator because loading Flash from a document is rare in normal work; the second fires only after code is already running. Against a targeted operator deploying commercial surveillance tooling, detection bounds dwell time rather than preventing the initial compromise.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treating a confirmed exploitation as a full-host compromise with a surveillance-implant payload - Kaspersky identifies FinSpy - rather than as a browser-plugin incident, and scoping credential rotation to everything the affected user could reach.
response.adequacy: It scopes the response to what the payload actually is. Where a host was exposed and its Flash runtime has since been removed, removal does not evict an implant installed beforehand, so the host belongs on the incident path rather than being closed on the uninstall record.

NIST-800-53-CM-7.gap: CM-7 is the control with the right answer and the wrong pass condition. An estate can evidence least functionality by disabling Flash in browser policy and score a clean result, while the runtime remains installed and reachable through the Office ActiveX path Kaspersky documented - a path that never consults browser configuration. The control does not force the distinction between a capability disabled at one entry point and a capability removed from the host.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: The control is met and its output is misleading in a specific, checkable way. A host at Flash Player 27.0.0.170 is genuinely patched against CVE-2017-11292 and simultaneously exposed to every Flash defect disclosed since Adobe stopped supporting the product on 31 December 2020, for which no fixed version exists or will. SI-2 closes findings by version comparison, so it reports this asset as remediated at the exact moment remediation stopped being possible.

NIS2-Art21-vulnerability-management.gap: The obligation is evidenced with a working scan-and-remediate cycle, and for this asset the cycle has no terminating step other than deletion. There is no advisory feed to monitor after end-of-life and no update channel to apply, so the process either loops indefinitely on an unfixable finding or accepts the risk - and the actual required action, removing software from production, belongs to change management rather than to the vulnerability-management workflow the obligation is demonstrated through.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: An organisation can present strong B4 evidence - patching cadence, configuration standards, supported platforms - across its estate while an unmaintainable runtime whose vendor ceased support on 31 December 2020 sits inside it. The principle expects systems to be maintained and provides no point at which unmaintainable becomes a failing state, so the conclusion that the software must be removed has to be reached on grounds the framework itself does not supply.

AU-Essential-8-App-Hardening.gap: Hardening against Flash in browsers is the canonical expression of this mitigation and it is aimed at the wrong door for these attacks. Kaspersky's account has the exploit arriving in a Microsoft Office document with an embedded ActiveX object, so a host whose browsers block Flash entirely still loads the runtime when the document opens. Whether the mitigation is read as reaching this path at all is an interpretation, and on the reading that it does, it is covered and bypassed.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: A.8.8 is judged on whether technical vulnerabilities are identified and managed, and the identification half has silently stopped for this component. With no advisories published since end-of-life, the register carries CVE-2017-11292 closed at 27.0.0.170 and nothing open, which reads as a well-managed asset. The clean register is an artefact of the vendor having stopped disclosing rather than of the software having stopped being vulnerable.

new_control_requirements.name: EOL-ASSET-DECOMMISSION
new_control_requirements.description: This entry is the case the control exists for, and both halves are documented here. patch_available is true — a fixed build carrying this JavaScriptCore fix exists — and the vector itself states that the impacted product could be end-of-life and/or end-of-service and that users should discontinue product utilization. Those facts together define the requirement: on a unit whose hardware can still take an Apple security update, reaching the fixed build is an interim state; on a unit that can no longer take one, the terminal state is removal or replacement, because that device is exposed not only to this code-execution flaw but to everything found in that engine since its last build. Scope to what the packet names — macOS, iOS, tvOS, Safari and watchOS — and inventory those. The packet ties the CWE-94 sink to JavaScriptCore in those products and gives no mapping into other vendors' browsers or other software that embeds a web engine, so treating every renderer in the estate as an instance of this CVE manufactures findings and replacement work against software no evidence implicates. In operational terms: enumerate every macOS, iOS, tvOS, watchOS and Safari install that renders untrusted web content, record for each whether its hardware can still receive a build carrying the fix, put those on the interim clock against the 2025-10-20 KEV listing, and put the rest on a dated replacement schedule — a risk acceptance with no removal date leaves a KEV-listed flaw with a public PoC and confirmed exploitation in service indefinitely. Precondition on the interim half: live_patch_available is false and the vendor patch typically requires a service restart or system reboot per the KEV requiredAction, so a device that downloaded the update but has not restarted still runs the vulnerable code and is not remediated. And because exploitation is confirmed and delivery is attacker-controlled web content, a device that rendered untrusted content while exposed belongs on the incident path rather than being closed on the patch record.
new_control_requirements.evidence: The control's structure fits this Adobe Flash Player entry with the vendor and engine changed and one difference that makes it stricter. Both halves hold: a fixed build exists - Adobe shipped 27.0.0.170 across every Flash Player line in APSB17-32 on 16 October 2017 - and CISA's required action states the impacted product is end-of-life and should be disconnected if still in use. The difference is that Flash Player has no interim half left for anyone. Where the control lets hardware that can still take an update sit at the fixed build as an interim state, Adobe stopped supporting Flash Player on 31 December 2020 and blocked Flash content from running on 12 January 2021, so every remaining install is in the terminal category regardless of the host it runs on, and removal is the only end state. Scope the inventory the way the control demands - to the products the record actually names: Flash Player Desktop Runtime on Windows, macOS and Linux, and the copies embedded in Google Chrome and in Microsoft Edge and Internet Explorer 11, which arrived through the browser's update channel and are missing from a standalone-installer inventory. Adobe AIR is a separate product line not covered by APSB17-32, and sweeping it in on the strength of a shared vendor name manufactures replacement work against software this record does not implicate. Because exploitation is confirmed - Kaspersky attributes it to BlackOasis delivering FinSpy - a host that opened untrusted Office documents while exposed belongs on the incident path rather than being closed on the uninstall record.

new_control_requirements.name: BROWSER-MANAGED-UPDATE-NO-DEFERRAL
new_control_requirements.description: Enterprise update rings must not defer security-channel browser updates beyond 24h.
new_control_requirements.evidence: For two of the four affected Flash Player lines the browser update channel was the remediation channel: APSB17-32 records that Flash Player installed with Google Chrome updates through Chrome, and that Flash Player with Microsoft Edge and Internet Explorer 11 on Windows 10 and 8.1 updates automatically with the browser. An update ring holding those browsers back also held back 27.0.0.170, and the Edge and Internet Explorer 11 line carried its own lower affected boundary of 27.0.0.130 and earlier - so an estate reasoning from the 27.0.0.159 figure quoted for the Desktop Runtime would have mis-scoped which browser hosts still needed the update. The control's deferral limit is the operative part here because this was a zero-day used in targeted attacks: Adobe states the exploit was being used in limited, targeted attacks against users running Windows, so the window between the 16 October 2017 publication and a ring's release was the window in which BlackOasis was still operating. The residual to hold onto: a browser that has taken an update keeps the previously loaded runtime until the process restarts.

attack_vector.description: A malformed EPS image inside an Office document drives the EPS import filter through a save/restore sequence that frees an array still referenced by a forall procedure. Reclaiming that memory hands the attacker read and write primitives inside the filter process, and a forged file object turns those primitives into code execution as the user who opened the document.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none — PR:N; the attacker needs no account on the target, only a document the victim opens or an image the victim inserts.
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L; the exploit is deterministic once the EPS is parsed. The real constraint is UI:R plus configuration: EPS rendering must be enabled, and Microsoft made disabled the default in April 2017.
attack_vector.ai_factor: Found by a vendor incident-response team examining live campaign traffic. Microsoft credits Genwei Jiang of FireEye, Inc. and Steven Hunter of MSRC; no AI-assisted discovery is claimed by any party in the record.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Disabling EPS image processing in Office, which removes the vulnerable filter from the path entirely, and applying KB3118310 / KB3172458 / KB3114375 once they shipped on 2017-05-09.
prevention.adequacy: The EPS disable is complete for this flaw and for its siblings in the same filter, but it is a configuration state that image reprocessing or a profile restore can silently reverse. The KBs are complete but only take effect after the Office processes and FLTLDR.EXE restart.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Process-lineage alerting on FLTLDR.EXE — a filter host that spawns a child or makes a network connection has already been subverted — plus crash telemetry for the same process during document opens.
detection.adequacy: This fires after the EPS has been parsed, so it bounds dwell time rather than preventing execution, and it depends on process-creation telemetry being collected from user workstations rather than servers.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treating any host that opened one of the documented lures as an implant investigation rather than a malware clean-up, since both documented campaigns dropped a persistent second stage.
response.adequacy: Response scoping depends on retaining mail and endpoint records back to March 2017 activity; where retention is shorter than the exposure window, the investigation cannot establish which users opened what.

NIST-800-53-CM-7.gap: An organisation can hold a complete CM-7 least-functionality baseline and still ship EPS rendering, because format import filters are not the kind of functionality these baselines enumerate — they list services, ports and installed applications. The control was satisfiable and satisfied while EPSIMP32.FLT sat in the path of every embedded image, and the disable that actually mattered arrived as a vendor default in April 2017 rather than as an operator decision.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: SI-2 is met by installing KB3118310, KB3172458 or KB3114375 on schedule, yet the campaigns FireEye documented ran at the end of March 2017 and the fix is dated 2017-05-09, so compliance covered none of the exposure. The control also counts an install as remediation, and this filter is only swapped once the Office processes restart, so a compliant SI-2 report can describe endpoints still loading the vulnerable EPSIMP32.FLT.

NIS2-Art21-patch-management.gap: Patch management as a measure had no artefact to deploy for roughly six weeks of live exploitation, and the mitigation that existed in that window was a configuration change to EPS handling that patch processes neither own nor evidence. An entity could report full patch-cadence compliance across the whole period, and the EPSS score of 0.7813 recorded at 2026-08-20 shows the underlying exploitation pressure long outlived the release date.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: A B4 system-security assessment of an Office estate examines application control, privilege and configuration management. It does not ask which document parsers can be invoked by untrusted content, so the EPS filter that carried this CVE and CVE-2017-0262 in the same period is outside the questions the outcome asks, and a positive assessment says nothing about whether the estate renders attacker-supplied PostScript.

AU-Essential-8-App-Hardening.gap: The strategy's subjects are browser content and Office OLE, and Essential Eight keeps macro restriction as a strategy of its own. The lures in both documented campaigns were plain .docx attachments containing an image — no macro, no OLE object, no browser involved — so neither strategy had anything to act on, and an estate assessed at high maturity on both is one where nothing in scope stands between the attachment and the filter that executed the attacker's PostScript.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.7.gap: Anti-malware controls under A.8.7 were being asked to recognise SHIRIME and NETWIRE deliveries that arrived through an exploit nobody had a signature for at the end of March 2017. The annex control requires malware protection, not constraint of the parser an untrusted image reaches, so it can be fully implemented while the exploit path itself is untouched, and its contribution is limited to catching the second stage after execution.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Microsoft Office 2010 SP2, 2013 SP1 and 2016 were exploited by two distinct actors from the end of March 2017 and the fixes are dated 2017-05-09, so the operative clause here is the one that accepts documented compensating controls: disabling EPS rendering was deployable throughout the exposure window, the KBs were not. CISA added the CVE on 2022-03-03 with a 2022-03-24 due date, and the EPSS score of 0.7813 at 2026-08-20 places it near the top of the distribution years after the fix.

new_control_requirements.name: ARCHIVE-CONTENT-TYPE-PROVENANCE
new_control_requirements.description: For this CVE the requirement is that Word's Protected View decision be taken from verified provenance of the file — established outside the document — rather than from metadata that travels with the document and that an attacker controls, and that the untrusted-origin marking survive whatever container the document is delivered in so the handler still sees it as externally sourced. The operator-side expression of the control: the mail gateway and file-share boundary apply and preserve the untrusted-origin marking themselves, so the sandbox decision does not depend on the application deriving it from attacker-supplied input. The distinguishing test: deliver an externally-sourced document through each ingress path and confirm it reaches Word marked untrusted, instead of confirming only that Protected View is enabled in policy.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Both documented CVE-2017-0261 campaigns delivered ordinary Word documents by mail — st07383.en17.docx for the Turla activity, Confirmation_letter.docx and variants for the NETWIRE activity — and between the end of March 2017 and the 2017-05-09 KBs the estate's only levers were how those externally sourced files were marked and handled on arrival. Provenance applied at the gateway rather than derived from the file is what makes that lever reliable for the next filter defect in the same suite.

CVE-2017-0001.name: Microsoft Graphics Device Interface (GDI) Privilege Escalation Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: An already-logged-on user runs a crafted application that manipulates GDI objects into a state the graphics subsystem mishandles, and the mishandling yields kernel-mode execution. Microsoft's fix description — correcting GDI object handling and preventing unintended user-mode privilege elevation — is the most specific public account of the defect; no root-cause analysis was ever published.
attack_vector.privileges_required: low — PR:L; the attacker needs an interactive local account of any kind, which on a shared or session-hosted machine is the ordinary condition rather than a compromise.
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L; no race, no groom and no information leak is described. The binding constraint is AV:L: the attacker must already be executing code on the host, so this is the second link of a chain.
attack_vector.ai_factor: Reported by Peter Hlavaty (@zer0mem) of KeenLab, Tencent — a human research team. No AI-assisted discovery is claimed anywhere in the record, and the acknowledgement names no tooling.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Installing the 2017-03-14 update for the SKU and rebooting, and for the SKUs now past support, moving the workload to a supported Windows release.
prevention.adequacy: Complete for the flaw, but it is a reboot-gated fix on kernel code, so the remediation is only real once the host restarts. On the majority of the affected SKUs the patch is no longer the honest answer, because those releases are out of support for everything found since.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Alerting on token elevation without a service or task lineage, correlated with execution of an unsigned binary by a non-administrative user in the preceding seconds.
detection.adequacy: There is no published exploit to derive a specific signature from, so detection here is generic escalation behaviour and will fire on unrelated tooling. It also needs process and token telemetry from workstations, which is where this class of flaw is used and where collection is thinnest.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treating a confirmed kernel-mode escalation on a host as a rebuild rather than a clean-up, because code that reached kernel context can neutralise the agent reporting on it.
response.adequacy: Sound as a policy, but it cannot be triggered by evidence specific to this CVE, since no artefact distinguishes this escalation from any other. It applies to the class, not to the identification.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: The KBs are enumerable per SKU and an SI-2 programme will deploy them, but the control's completion signal is installation and this fix is only in force after a reboot. That gap is widest on exactly the hosts where PR:L is easiest to satisfy — multi-user servers with long change windows. By the 2022-03-24 KEV due date most affected SKUs were out of support, so SI-2 was directing effort at a patch rather than at the operating-system upgrade the situation actually called for.

NIST-800-53-AC-6.gap: Least privilege is nominally met by removing local administrator rights, and it buys nothing against this flaw: exploitation requires only an ordinary interactive user and produces kernel-mode execution directly. The account model is never consulted on the exploit path, so an AC-6 assessment can be accurate, complete and entirely irrelevant to whether the host is exploitable.

NIS2-Art21-vulnerability-handling.gap: Handling processes are fed by vendor severity, public exploit availability and exploitation reporting. For this CVE Microsoft recorded Exploited:No and rated exploitation Less Likely in March 2017, no public exploit ever surfaced, and CISA's KEV addition came five years later on 2022-03-03 with no accompanying analysis. Every input the measure relies on pointed away from action for the whole interval, and at 0.03114 EPSS on 2026-08-20 they still do.

UK-CAF-B2.gap: B2 governs identity and access — who holds what, and how it is proven. This escalation starts from a legitimately authorised local session and crosses a boundary inside the graphics subsystem, so no part of the outcome's subject matter sits on the exploit path. An organisation can evidence strong identity assurance and privileged-access separation and still have every affected host one crafted application away from kernel-mode code.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: Patch operating systems is the correct strategy and the assessment fails on inventory rather than discipline. Windows Vista SP2, Server 2008 SP2 and R2 SP1, Windows 7 SP1, Windows 8.1, Server 2012, Windows 10 RTM and 1511 are all in the affected list and none can be made current by applying an update today, so a maturity rating measured on a fleet running them describes a remediation route that has closed.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: The technical-vulnerability register for this CVE has to reconcile twelve SKUs against ten KB identifiers, and the source most tooling normalises — the NVD description — names only eleven of them, leaving out Windows Server 2016 even though Microsoft ships KB4013429 for it under this CVE. A register built from that description is internally consistent and silently excludes a server population, which is precisely the failure A.8.8 is meant to prevent.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Windows GDI on Vista SP2 through Windows 10 1607 and Server 2016 had a vendor fix from 2017-03-14, and CISA listed the CVE on 2022-03-03 with a 2022-03-24 due date — a five-year interval in which Microsoft's own exploitability index said Exploited:No and no public exploit appeared. The clause that carries the weight for this entry is the whichever-is-later one: the KEV listing, not the patch date, is what should have driven the sweep, and on the affected SKUs now out of support the documented compensating control is migration off the release rather than an eight-year-old KB.

CVE-2016-8562.name: Siemens SIMATIC CP 1543-1 Improper Privilege Management Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: An attacker with network reach to udp/161 on the CP 1543-1 writes SNMP variables that the device documents as read-only and settable only from TIA Portal. The write degrades the communication processor or takes it out of service, cutting the S7-1500 station's Ethernet path and the firewall and VPN functions the CP provides for it.
attack_vector.privileges_required: low — PR:L; SNMP access to the device is needed, not an engineering account, which on a plant network with shared community strings is a low bar once the segment is reachable.
attack_vector.complexity: high — AC:H; Siemens states the write succeeds only under special conditions and does not publish what they are, which is what keeps the access complexity above Low rather than any groom or race the attacker has to perform.
attack_vector.ai_factor: Disclosed through ANSSI coordination with SOGETI, with a later scope correction from Artem Zinenko of Kaspersky. Human coordinated disclosure throughout; no AI-assisted discovery is claimed.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Updating both part numbers to firmware V2.0.28 or later, and in the interim restricting udp/161 on the CP to the engineering and network-management stations that have a reason to speak SNMP to it.
prevention.adequacy: The firmware update is complete for the flaw but needs a module reload that interrupts the station's Ethernet path, so it is gated on a production window. The SNMP restriction is available immediately and only bounds the attacker population: anything already inside the engineering segment still reaches the port.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Logging and alerting on SNMP SET operations to the CP from unexpected sources, and treating an unexplained CP restart or loss of the station's Ethernet path as a security event rather than only as a process fault.
detection.adequacy: Depends on SNMP traffic to control-system assets being visible to a collector at all. The signal this flaw produces is also weak on its own: a CP that has stopped passing traffic looks identical whether an SNMP SET took it down or a cable, power supply or switch port failed, so the outage alone does not distinguish an attack from a fault unless the SNMP write that preceded it was captured.

response.what_would_have_worked: Comparing the CP's running configuration against the TIA Portal project after any unexplained degradation, since the affected variables are documented as being configurable only from that project.
response.adequacy: This establishes that something wrote what it should not have; it does not restore availability and does not tell you who reached the port. It also depends on the project file being an authoritative, version-controlled baseline rather than a copy on an engineer's laptop.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: SI-2 will faithfully record that firmware V2.0.28 has been available since 2016-11-18 and remains undeployed, and the reason it remains undeployed is that the update reloads the module carrying the S7-1500 station's Ethernet path. The control has an exception mechanism for that and no mechanism for the interim risk, so a five-year-old open item looks like governed acceptance rather than a KEV-listed device on a live plant network.

NIST-800-53-SC-7.gap: Boundary protection is nominally satisfied because the CP 1543-1 is the boundary — it provides the firewall and VPN functions for the S7-1500 station. That framing is what makes it inadequate: an assessment that credits the device as a protection mechanism does not go on to ask what protects the device's own SNMP service on udp/161, so the control passes on the strength of the very asset that is exposed.

NIS2-Art21-availability.gap: Availability measures are designed against component failure and capacity loss, and this attack produces the same outcome from the configuration plane by writing variables the CP was documented to refuse. No redundancy or failover design treats the communication processor's own SNMP variables as a failure mode, so tested availability arrangements can be fully evidenced while a single write removes the station's network path.

UK-CAF-B5.gap: B5 asks whether networks and systems are designed to remain available under attack, and on this station the CP's firewall and VPN functions are the design being pointed at. The device providing the resilience is the device that fails, so the evidence and the exposure are the same object, and an assessment that reads the CP as a control rather than as an asset never examines the interface that is attacked.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: The patching strategies assume an update the operator can schedule. Firmware V2.0.28 on a CP 1543-1 reloads the module and interrupts the station, so the schedule belongs to production rather than to security. Where a site resolves that conflict by putting the OT cell outside the assessment scope, a measurable exposure becomes an unmeasured one and nothing about the device changes.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.22.gap: Segregation of networks is implementable here and is the interim posture: keep udp/161 on the CP reachable only from the engineering zone. Its limit is that the exploit precondition is network reach and nothing more, so every engineering workstation, jump host and contractor laptop inside the permitted zone satisfies it in full. The control shrinks the attacker population and leaves the path intact for anyone already in it.

IEC-62443-3-3.gap: Zone-and-conduit conformance is assessed on the traffic crossing the boundary and on the controls enforcing it. The CP's SNMP management service is neither process traffic nor an enforcement rule, so it can sit outside what the assessment examines while being the interface that accepts the write. A conformant architecture diagram and an exploitable conduit device are compatible states here.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Siemens shipped CP 1543-1 firmware V2.0.28 on 2016-11-18 and CISA listed the CVE on 2022-03-03 with a 2022-03-24 due date, so on this device the four-hour clock cannot be met by the firmware path — reloading the module drops the S7-1500 station's Ethernet link. The documented-compensating-control branch is the operative one: restricting udp/161 to the engineering segment is deployable inside the window, and it has to be recorded as an interim state with the firmware window dated, not as closure.

new_control_requirements.name: MITIGATION-ACTIVE-PATCH-PENDING-VERDICT-CLASS
new_control_requirements.description: Compliance verdicts must distinguish three states: (a) binary patch deployed (vulnerability eliminated), (b) vendor-mitigation rule active, no binary patch (residual risk: any defect in the mitigation rule reopens the vulnerability), (c) no mitigation, no patch (full exposure). Audit reports must surface (b) as a distinct compensating-control state with an associated time-bound action item, not as a 'patched per SLA' outcome.
new_control_requirements.evidence: A CP 1543-1 below V2.0.28 with udp/161 restricted to the engineering zone is exactly state (b), and it is where any such module stays for as long as the plant window that firmware V2.0.28 requires has not been scheduled — the reload drops the S7-1500 station's Ethernet path, so the window is a precondition of state (a). The residual risk is specific and namable: the restriction holds only against sources outside that zone, so a compromised engineering workstation reopens the path in full, and Siemens' 2020-02-10 advisory revision adding SIPLUS NET CP 1543-1 shows how easily the asset list behind such a rule drifts out of date.

attack_vector.description: Attacker-controlled Flash content drives the runtime into using memory it has already freed, and reclaiming that memory yields code execution in the hosting process.
