Adobe describes the class and not the object; the delivery paths are a crafted or compromised web page, a malicious advertisement, or a Flash ActiveX control embedded in a document that hosts the IE rendering engine.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none — PR:N; the attacker needs no account, only the ability to get content in front of the runtime.
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L; no precondition beyond rendering. UI:R is the only real constraint, and Adobe's own note narrows the observed use to limited, targeted attacks against Windows 7, 8.1 and 10 users rather than mass exploitation.
attack_vector.ai_factor: Reported by Neel Mehta and Billy Leonard of Google's Threat Analysis Group from observed in-the-wild activity. Human threat-intelligence discovery; no AI involvement is claimed by Adobe or Google.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Removing the Flash runtime from the estate. In October 2016 the equivalent action was reaching 23.0.0.205 or 11.2.202.643, but the flaw's KEV required action is to disconnect the product, and since 2020-12-31 removal is the only state that stays correct.
prevention.framework_requiring_it: CISA BOD 22-01 (KEV remediation, added 2022-03-03, due 2022-03-24; required action: the impacted product is end-of-life and should be disconnected if still in use)
prevention.adequacy: Removal is complete and permanent. What blocks it is content that still depends on the runtime, and the substitute reached for in that situation — blocking Flash in browsers — leaves installed code reachable through non-browser hosts.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Alerting on abnormal termination of a browser or plugin-host process followed by child-process creation or outbound connections, and inventorying every path the runtime is installed through rather than only the desktop version string.
detection.adequacy: Generic to browser exploitation rather than specific to this CVE, since no public artefact exists to signature. Against the limited, targeted use Adobe describes, the volume is low enough that a single crash may be the only signal available.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treating a suspected Flash exploitation on a targeted user as a foothold investigation with credential rotation, given that the reporting party found it in active espionage-grade activity.
response.adequacy: Sound but unbounded: with no published sample and no named campaign attribution in the vendor bulletins, scoping which users were in the targeting set is guesswork rather than evidence.

NIST-800-53-CM-7.gap: Least functionality points at the right answer — the runtime should not be present — but the baseline it is assessed against enumerates services and installed applications, and Flash arrived as a per-user desktop runtime, a Chrome bundle, a Windows component under KB3201860 and a separate Linux build. A CM-7 review that finds no Flash application installed can be accurate about the desktop runtime and wrong about three other delivery paths on the same machine.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: SI-2 was fully satisfiable in 2016 by moving to 23.0.0.205 or 11.2.202.643, and it remains satisfiable today in a way that misleads: an estate on the final Flash build reports zero outstanding vendor updates. That is true for CVE-2016-7855 and says nothing about the flaws found since Adobe stopped shipping fixes on 2020-12-31, and the control has no way to express the difference between current and abandoned.

NIS2-Art21-vulnerability-management.gap: The measure's cycle ends in remediation and verification, and neither exists for an end-of-life runtime, so the finding cannot be closed by the process that owns it. What the entity actually needs is a dated retirement decision for the component and for the content that depends on it — a lifecycle action the vulnerability-management measure neither triggers nor tracks, leaving a KEV-listed flaw with confirmed targeted exploitation permanently open.

UK-CAF-A1.gap: Retaining Flash past 2020-12-31 is a governance decision — accepting an unfixable dependency because some business content requires it — while the A1 outcome concerns governance structures — roles, policy, board-level oversight — rather than the register of specific accepted dependencies. The outcome can be assessed as achieved while no named owner holds the decision to keep a runtime whose vendor has confirmed targeted exploitation and shipped nothing since.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: The strategy that governs here is Patch applications, whose clause reads 'Office productivity suites, web browsers and their extensions, email clients, PDF software, Adobe Flash Player, and security products that are no longer supported by vendors are removed.' It has been unambiguous since Adobe's support end on 2020-12-31, and it names Adobe Flash Player once while the product is removed four different ways: uninstalling the 23.0.0.185 desktop runtime, taking a Google Chrome update, applying Windows servicing for the KB3201860 component across the products ADV160008 lists, and removing the 11.2.202.637 Linux build. Where the assessment produces one Flash verdict per host, three of those four removals go unevidenced and the runtime Adobe reported under targeted attack on 2016-10-26 stays loadable on a host recorded as compliant.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: The register that drives A.8.8 has to hold four separate version lines for one component: 23.0.0.185 for the desktop runtime and for Chrome, the same for Edge and IE11 serviced by a Windows KB, and 11.2.202.637 for Linux. Tooling that reports one Flash version per host collapses those into a single answer, and the resulting register is precise, consistent and incomplete.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: This is the case where the control's mitigation branch has to be read as removal: CISA's required action for CVE-2016-7855 is that the impacted product is end-of-life and should be disconnected if still in use, and Adobe stopped shipping Flash fixes on 2020-12-31, so no patch or live patch can satisfy the clock. Adobe reported the exploit in limited targeted attacks on 2016-10-26 and Microsoft's ADV160008 recorded Exploited:Yes the next day, which is why the four-hour standard is the right one to apply to the removal action rather than a routine deprecation timeline.

new_control_requirements.name: BROWSER-MANAGED-UPDATE-NO-DEFERRAL
new_control_requirements.description: Enterprise update rings must not defer security-channel browser updates beyond 24h.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Flash reached users through the browser on every channel this CVE affects — bundled in Google Chrome, serviced as a Windows component in Edge and Internet Explorer 11 under KB3201860, and as a plugin alongside the desktop runtime — so the browser update ring was the delivery mechanism for the 23.0.0.205 fix Adobe published on 2016-10-26, one day before Microsoft's own advisory recorded Exploited:Yes. A ring that defers browser updates defers the plugin fix with them, and the same ring is what removes the runtime from the estate now that no build is current.

CVE-2016-7262.name: Microsoft Office Security Feature Bypass Vulnerability (CVE-2016-7262)

attack_vector.description: The attacker sends a workbook and persuades the recipient to click a specific cell. Excel mishandles the input that cell carries, and instead of the handling the cell type should get, a command executes with the privileges of the user who clicked. The check that should have gated that launch is the security feature the CVE title names as bypassed.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none — PR:N; the attacker holds no account on the target and needs only to get a file in front of a user.
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L; there is no memory primitive to make reliable, which is why Microsoft rated exploitation More Likely on both the latest and older releases. The constraint is UI:R and it is specific: opening the file is not enough, the user has to click the crafted cell.
attack_vector.ai_factor: Reported by Iliyan Velikov of PwC UK through coordinated disclosure. Human research; the vendor record names no tooling and no automated discovery.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Applying the MS16-148 updates for every affected product — including Excel Viewer 2007 SP3 and the Office Compatibility Pack SP3, not only the Excel application — and relaunching Excel afterwards.
prevention.adequacy: Complete for the flaw. Its practical limit is inventory: two of the six patch targets are standalone products that Office-scoped tooling does not enumerate, and the fix is only live once the application restarts.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Alerting on EXCEL.EXE creating a child process, which no ordinary spreadsheet interaction requires, and correlating that with recent external file delivery to the same user.
detection.adequacy: This is a strong signal because the behaviour is rare, but it fires after the command has already run, so it bounds dwell time rather than preventing execution. Legitimate Office automation on some estates will produce the same lineage and has to be baselined out first.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treating a confirmed Excel child-process event as an execution incident on the user's context — rotating what that account could reach and reviewing what the command fetched — rather than as a blocked-file event.
response.adequacy: The command runs as the user, so scoping is bounded by that account's reach, which is knowable. What is not knowable from this CVE alone is what the command did, since nothing about the flaw constrains it.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: The programme deploys MS16-148 and reports remediation, but the bulletin has six patch targets and two of them — Excel Viewer 2007 SP3 under KB3128023 and the Office Compatibility Pack SP3 under KB3128022 — are separate installs that Office-scoped inventory does not see. Coverage measured against the Excel application is therefore accurate and incomplete, and the viewer left registered for spreadsheets is the one that opens the attacker's file.

NIST-800-53-SI-3.gap: Malicious code protection has nothing to match on. The delivered artefact is a genuine workbook whose cell content is mishandled by Excel, with no macro, no embedded binary and no packed payload, and the command that executes is chosen by the attacker rather than shipped in the file. The control is fully implementable and only engages after execution, on whatever that command pulls down next.

NIS2-Art21-patch-management.gap: Cadence compliance against the 2016-12-13 release is achievable and does not describe the residual state. The MS16-148 updates replace user-mode Office components, so an Excel process that has been open since before the install keeps running the vulnerable code, and the measure records installation rather than effect. On analyst workstations where Excel stays open for days, that difference is the whole exposure.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: A B4 assessment of this estate examines macro policy, application control, patch state and configuration hardening, and every one of those can be in the state the outcome expects while this path stays open — the exploit needs no macro, no additional executable and no configuration weakness, only a click on a crafted cell. The outcome does not ask whether a document element can reach a command launch, so its evidence has no bearing on the flaw.

AU-Essential-8-App-Hardening.gap: Inside Office this strategy reaches OLE; macro settings belong to a different Essential Eight strategy, and the rest of this one concerns browser content. The exploit touches none of them — Microsoft's account is a specially crafted document the user is convinced to open and then interact with by clicking a specific cell — so the estate can sit at the top maturity level with nothing in any of those scopes positioned between that click and the command that runs.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.7.gap: The annex control directs attention at the file arriving, and the file is an ordinary spreadsheet — the defect is in how Excel handles one of its cells, not in content that inspection could flag. Full implementation of malware protection therefore leaves the exploit path untouched and contributes only downstream, once the executed command starts doing something a detection engine can recognise.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Microsoft shipped the six MS16-148 updates for Excel 2007 through 2016, Excel Viewer 2007 SP3 and the Office Compatibility Pack SP3 on 2016-12-13, and CISA listed the CVE on 2022-03-03 with a 2022-03-24 due date. For this entry the clock has to be measured against completed relaunch of Excel on each host and against all six patch targets, not against the four that Office-scoped inventory enumerates; EPSS of 0.58204 at 2026-08-20 keeps it in the top percentile for predicted exploitation nearly a decade after the fix.

new_control_requirements.name: DOWNLOAD-PROVENANCE-ENFORCEMENT
new_control_requirements.description: Exploitation here requires the victim to open an attacker-supplied Office document, so on an estate that has not yet reached the fixed build the delivery path is the only enforceable control. Require Mark-of-the-Web on every Office file arriving by mail, web download, or untrusted file share, and require MOTW-tagged documents to open in Protected View — an isolated, reduced-privilege render — instead of the full parsing path that carries the CWE-94 sink at the user's own process privilege. Provenance must survive the container: files extracted from an archive, mounted from an ISO or VHD, or renamed must inherit the tag rather than lose it, and 'Enable Editing' on externally sourced documents must be blocked by policy rather than left to the user. The distinguishing test: mail a MOTW-tagged spreadsheet nested inside a ZIP to a managed workstation, extract it, and confirm the extracted file still opens in Protected View — a user-application-hardening attestation that covers only macro and ActiveX/OLE settings still lets a provenance-stripped document reach the vulnerable parser with full user privileges.
new_control_requirements.evidence: This CVE needs the victim to leave the read-only render and interact with the workbook — Microsoft's own account is that the attacker must convince the user to open the document file and interact with it by clicking on a specific cell — so whether an externally sourced spreadsheet reaches an editable Excel session is the whole of the operator-side lever before the MS16-148 updates land. The control's provenance-survives-the-container requirement is the load-bearing half for a spreadsheet delivered inside an archive, and its Enable Editing clause addresses the exact step the exploit depends on.

attack_vector.description: A crafted RTF file corrupts memory inside Office's RTF handling and the corruption is steered into executing code as the user who opened it. Delivery is a mail attachment or a download from a site hosting user-provided content, and because Word parses RTF by content, the extension the file carries has no bearing on whether it reaches the parser. The same parser sits behind Word Automation Services and Office Online Server, where documents are submitted rather than opened.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none — PR:N; the attacker needs no account, and on the server products no user is involved at all beyond submitting a document for conversion.
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L; Microsoft rated exploitation More Likely on the latest release and Exploitation Detected on older ones, and a weaponized sample from the campaign is public. UI:R applies to the desktop path only.
attack_vector.ai_factor: Reported by Austrian MilCERT, a national military CERT, from analysis of attacks already under way. Human incident-response discovery; no AI-assisted analysis is claimed anywhere in the record.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Applying all fourteen MS16-121 packages — including the SharePoint Word Automation Services, Office Web Apps and Office Online Server updates — and restarting Word on clients and the rendering service on the farms.
prevention.adequacy: Complete for the flaw, and it arrived after exploitation had already been detected, so it did nothing for the pre-2016-10-11 window. Its practical limit is that the server half of the affected list is owned by a different team from the Office client half.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Process-lineage alerting on WINWORD.EXE child processes and on abnormal termination of the SharePoint and Office Web Apps rendering processes, plus content-type inspection that treats RTF as RTF regardless of the extension it arrives under.
detection.adequacy: Effective on the client path and weak on the server path, where parsing untrusted documents is the service's purpose and produces no anomaly to key on. Before the sample was public there was also no signature to complement the behavioural view.

response.what_would_have_worked: Scoping an incident from the document rather than from the endpoint: identifying every recipient of the RTF and, on the server side, every document submitted for conversion during the exposure window.
response.adequacy: Feasible for mail delivery where gateway logs are retained. On the server side it depends on the farm's conversion audit trail holding enough detail, and reaching far enough back, to enumerate what was rendered; where it does not, server-side scoping is inference rather than evidence.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: A programme can deploy MS16-121 to every Office client and still be exposed, because five of the fourteen packages patch server products — Word Automation Services on SharePoint 2010 SP2 and 2013 SP1, Office Web Apps, Office Online Server 2016 — that render documents submitted by users. Endpoint-scoped SI-2 coverage reports complete against a bulletin whose most exposed half sits in the server estate, and Microsoft had already recorded Exploited:Yes when it shipped.

NIST-800-53-SI-3.gap: Malicious code protection was live and correctly configured while Austrian MilCERT was analysing attacks that Microsoft's index rated Exploitation Detected on older releases. Signatures follow samples, so the control's coverage of this RTF began after the exposure it was needed for; the sample published as 00bc76898f07f18122f386b890d79c9338d223a5b5c89213a4bbf1040bccfa28 is trivially detected now and was not when it mattered.

NIS2-Art21-incident-handling.gap: Incident handling is a process for responding to detected events, and the detection in this case happened at a national military CERT rather than at the targeted organisations. With exploitation confirmed by Microsoft before public disclosure, an entity running a mature handling process had no advisory, no CVE and no signature to trigger it, so the measure could be fully implemented and never engage during the window it was needed.

UK-CAF-C1.gap: The observables for this flaw are a Word process spawning a child on a workstation and a document-conversion service parsing a file it was built to parse. Neither appears in network flow, server or authentication telemetry, and the outcome does not require workstation process telemetry to be collected, so an organisation can demonstrate achieved monitoring and hold no data in which this attack would show up at all.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: Where Patch applications maturity is measured on the Windows Office client population, this bulletin extends past that population in two directions: Word for Mac 2011 and Word 2016 for Mac on a separate servicing channel, and five SharePoint and Office Web Apps packages that fall to whoever owns server patching. A high maturity score assessed on the clients describes roughly half of the fourteen affected patch targets.

AU-Essential-8-App-Hardening.gap: Inside Office the strategy governs OLE, macro settings sit under a separate Essential Eight strategy, and neither construct appears here — the artefact is an RTF that Word parses on content, so a hardening policy phrased around embedded objects and the file types a user sees does not describe what the parser accepts. An estate at full maturity has nothing configured that stands between the attachment and the vulnerable parser.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.16.gap: Monitoring activities depends on a baseline that separates normal from anomalous, and on the server half of this CVE the attack is indistinguishable from the workload: Word Automation Services and Office Online Server exist to render user-submitted documents. On the client half the discriminating data is WINWORD.EXE process lineage, which the annex control nowhere requires an organisation to collect, so it is achievable while holding neither signal.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Microsoft released MS16-121 on 2016-10-11 with its own exploitability index already recording Exploited:Yes for this CVE, so the patch-availability branch of this clock started against confirmed live attacks on Word and on the SharePoint and Office Online Server rendering products. CISA listed it on 2022-03-03 with a 2022-03-24 due date; measuring the SLA against all fourteen packages, and against the service restart on the farms rather than package installation, is what makes the verified-mitigation wording bite here.

new_control_requirements.name: ARCHIVE-CONTENT-TYPE-PROVENANCE
new_control_requirements.description: For this CVE the requirement is that Word's Protected View decision be taken from verified provenance of the file — established outside the document — rather than from metadata that travels with the document and that an attacker controls, and that the untrusted-origin marking survive whatever container the document is delivered in so the handler still sees it as externally sourced. The operator-side expression of the control: the mail gateway and file-share boundary apply and preserve the untrusted-origin marking themselves, so the sandbox decision does not depend on the application deriving it from attacker-supplied input. The distinguishing test: deliver an externally-sourced document through each ingress path and confirm it reaches Word marked untrusted, instead of confirming only that Protected View is enabled in policy.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Word decides how to handle this file from what arrives with it, and the file is an RTF that Word parses on content while presenting to the user as a .doc — so origin established at the gateway rather than derived from the document is the difference between a marked untrusted file and one that looks routine. With Microsoft recording Exploited:Yes at the 2016-10-11 release, provenance applied on ingress was the only lever an estate held before the fourteen MS16-121 packages landed, and it is the lever that still applies to the next defect in the same parser.

attack_vector.description: Two threads race the kernel's copy-on-write break: one asks for write access to a private read-only mapping through /proc/self/mem or ptrace, the other discards the mapping with madvise(MADV_DONTNEED). Retried at the wrong moment, the write lands on the page-cache page rather than on a private copy, giving an unprivileged process write access to files it can only read — /etc/passwd, a setuid binary, or the vDSO.
attack_vector.privileges_required: low — PR:L; any local execution context will do, including an unprivileged container workload or a compromised service account, and the scumjr variant needs no setuid binary on the host at all.
attack_vector.complexity: high — AC:H by CVSS because it is a race, but losing the race costs nothing: the published exploits loop until it lands. The practical constraint is having code execution on the host, not winning the window.
attack_vector.ai_factor: Found by Phil Oester from an exploit recovered out of live HTTP traffic on a compromised server. Human incident analysis, with the upstream fix authored by Linus Torvalds; no AI involvement in discovery or weaponisation is claimed anywhere.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Installing the fixed kernel and rebooting, or applying Red Hat's kpatch live patch on RHEL 7.2 and later, or loading the SystemTap mitigation on RHEL 5, 6 and 7 to cover the interval before the reboot.
prevention.adequacy: The kernel update is complete but reboot-gated. The kpatch route removes the reboot and is limited to RHEL 7.2 and later and to customers who open a support case; the SystemTap script needs manual reloading after every restart, so it fails silently on exactly the event that would otherwise have fixed the host.

detection.what_would_have_worked: File-integrity monitoring on setuid binaries and on /etc/passwd, and syscall-level telemetry for the madvise-plus-ptrace pattern the published exploits use.
detection.adequacy: Weak by construction: the project's own site states exploitation leaves no abnormal trace in the logs. File-integrity monitoring reads from disk, and the vDSO variant writes to memory only, so it produces no on-disk artefact for that method at all.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treating any confirmed exploitation as a host rebuild with credential rotation, since a process that reached root through this flaw could have modified any file the kernel had cached.
response.adequacy: Correct and expensive, and it depends on confirming exploitation in the first place, which the absence of log evidence makes unlikely. On a container host the rebuild scope is the host and every workload that shared it, not the container that escaped.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: The control is satisfied by installing the fixed kernel package, and installing it changes nothing until the host restarts — the running kernel is what is exploitable. Scanners that compare installed package versions will report an entire fleet remediated while every high-uptime host is still running pre-4.8.3 memory-management code, and SI-2 offers no state in which installed-but-not-running is distinguishable from remediated.

NIST-800-53-AC-6.gap: Least privilege is the natural answer to local escalation and this flaw ignores it entirely: PR:L is the whole requirement, and the primitive is a write to any file the process can read, which includes /etc/passwd and every setuid binary. Removing sudo, running services unprivileged and separating accounts are all worth doing and none of them changes whether this exploit succeeds, so an AC-6 attestation is honest and irrelevant here.

NIS2-Art21-business-continuity.gap: The continuity measure is what dictates when the reboot happens, and the better it is implemented — availability commitments, change freezes, staged restart schedules — the later the host stops running the vulnerable kernel. That inversion is the gap: continuity and remediation are pulling in opposite directions on this CVE, and neither measure owns the resulting interval or is required to report it as risk.

UK-CAF-C1.gap: Monitoring has almost nothing to work with here. The project's own site states that exploitation of this bug does not leave any trace of anything abnormal happening to the logs — no authentication event, no new binary, no crash — and the vDSO variant writes only to memory, so even file-integrity monitoring has no artefact for that method. C1 can be assessed as achieved on an estate where this exploit would produce no record at all.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: Patch operating systems is the right strategy and it measures package state rather than running state, so a host that has taken the kernel and not restarted scores as compliant while remaining exploitable. It also assumes an operating system the operator can update, which excludes the Android estate and every appliance — Cisco, Juniper, NetApp, Fortinet, Huawei, Arista, HPE, Palo Alto — where only the vendor image remediates.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: The vulnerability register for this CVE has to include distribution servers, container hosts and their workloads, Android devices and a long list of network appliances built on the same kernel, and a process driven by operating-system package inventory sees only the servers. That is how an A.8.8 assessment ends up accurate within its declared scope while the firewalls and storage controllers running the same defective mm/gup.c code are outside it.

new_control_requirements.name: LIVE-PATCH-CAPABILITY
new_control_requirements.description: For any system that processes production workloads and cannot tolerate unplanned reboots: live kernel patching capability (kpatch, livepatch, kGraft, or equivalent) must be deployed and tested quarterly.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Dirty COW is the case that shows why this has to exist before the disclosure rather than after it. The upstream fix in Linux 4.8.3 and the distribution backports under RHSA-2016:2098, USN-3104-1 and DSA-3696 all require a reboot to take effect, and the exploit was already in use in the wild before the 2016-10-19 disclosure. Red Hat's kpatch for RHEL 7.2 and later was available only through a support case, so where an estate holds no live-patching entitlement the live patch is unreachable on the day the race becomes public: opening the case is a precondition of the mitigation rather than part of it.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: For a Linux kernel flaw whose exploit was captured in live traffic before disclosure and which carries an EPSS of 0.83524 at 2026-08-20, the operative word in this control is verified: the mitigation is verified by the running kernel version on each host, not by the installed package, and the three routes that count — a rebooted fixed kernel, Red Hat's kpatch on RHEL 7.2 and later, or the SystemTap script — have to be recorded per host because they expire differently. CISA listed the CVE on 2022-03-03 with a 2022-03-24 due date, more than five years after Linux 4.8.3 shipped.

CVE-2016-4117.name: Adobe Flash Player Arbitrary Code Execution Vulnerability (CVE-2016-4117)

attack_vector.description: A crafted SWF makes Flash operate on an object through the wrong type in its DeleteRangeTimelineOperation path; the bad cast yields a pointer the runtime dereferences, and the published exploit rides that into code execution inside the plugin process. Delivery is a web page the victim visits.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none — PR:N in NVD's AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H vector; the attacker holds no account on the target and the plugin runs at whatever privilege the browser process holds.
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L; the stated precondition is only that a browser loads attacker-supplied Flash content. The real constraint is build coverage rather than access: the public module is written against 64-bit macOS with Flash 21.0.0.182.
attack_vector.ai_factor: None claimed. The finder credited on Exploit-DB 46339 is Genwei Jiang of FireEye, a human researcher at a vendor threat-research team; no AI-assisted discovery or weaponization is asserted in the module, the Exploit-DB entry or the NVD record.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Not having the Flash runtime resident. Removing the plugin, or refusing to load it, is the only measure that survives the product's end-of-life state, because every build after APSB16-15 stopped existing.
prevention.adequacy: Removal is complete for this CVE. Where a legacy application still requires the runtime and blocks removal, isolation of that host is the fallback, and isolation does nothing about the browsing the host itself performs.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Alerting on a browser or plugin-host process spawning a child, correlated with a SWF fetch from a third-party origin, would catch the published drive-by after the fact.
detection.adequacy: It fires after code is already running in the plugin process, and it depends on endpoint telemetry that records process ancestry — a workstation with logging limited to authentication events has nothing to correlate.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treating a host that rendered attacker-controlled Flash while exposed as compromised rather than as patched — removing the runtime and rebuilding the browsing profile rather than closing the item on a version bump.
response.adequacy: Removing the plugin ends the exposure but removes nothing an exploit already dropped; the IR decision has to be made per host that loaded untrusted content during the window.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: SI-2 is nominally met the moment APSB16-15 or flash-plugin 11.2.202.621 is deployed, and that is exactly the trap. The control's unit of closure is a version, and this CVE's unit of closure is an uninstall, because Flash Player was already end-of-life when CISA listed it on 2022-03-03 with a disconnection action. A flaw-remediation record showing the fixed build is a truthful record of a host that is still exposed to every Flash defect published after May 2016.

NIST-800-53-SC-44.gap: SC-44 is not met and would not have helped if it were. Detonation chambers inspect content crossing a boundary they control; the published exploit is a page load, so the SWF that carries the type confusion never enters a queue where a chamber could explode it. Naming a sandbox appliance in the control set for CVE-2016-4117 attributes coverage to a path the exploit does not take.

NIS2-Art21-patch-management.gap: An entity can show a working patch process, an inventory, and the applied APSB16-15 fix, and still be out of step with what the KEV record asks. The 2022-03-03 listing carries a required action of disconnecting the product, and a patch-management workflow has no state for that outcome — it records applied, deferred or not-applicable. Article 21 evidence built from that workflow will show a current Flash build where the actual obligation is that Flash is not installed.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: B4 evidence is usually a software baseline, and the baseline is where this CVE hides. The Flash runtime for CVE-2016-4117 reached hosts through at least four channels — the Adobe installer, browser-embedded builds, Red Hat's flash-plugin, and the Gentoo and openSUSE packages that carried GLSA-201606-08 and the May 2016 SUSE advisories. A B4 attestation drawn from one inventory source will report a clean estate while a distribution package below 11.2.202.621 sits on disk.

AU-Essential-8-App-Hardening.gap: Reading user application hardening as covering browser plugin content is an interpretation, and even under that reading the mitigation is asserted as policy while exploitation happens against resident code. The published module targets 64-bit macOS with Flash 21.0.0.182 under Safari and Firefox; because NVD scopes the flaw to the Flash build rather than to any browser, a hardening baseline written for a different browser family or platform can be fully satisfied without changing whether that runtime is loadable.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.9.gap: A configuration baseline for this class is buildable and is documented: MS16-050 publishes the ActiveX kill bit for CLSID {D27CDB6E-AE6D-11CF-96B8-444553540000} and the Group Policy switch that disables Flash in Internet Explorer. Both are Windows constructs, while NVD scopes CVE-2016-4117 to Flash Player 21.0.0.226 and earlier with no OS predicate and Adobe shipped that runtime on Windows, macOS and Linux. An A.8.9 baseline built only from those settings can be complete and enforced and still leave the macOS and Linux installations of the same vulnerable runtime untouched.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Adobe Flash Player carries CVSS 9.8 here with an EPSS of 0.94354 on 2026-08-20 — the 99.844th percentile of that publication — and a working Metasploit module has been public since the 2019 Exploit-DB 46339 import. CISA gave this entry a 21-day window (listed 2022-03-03, due 2022-03-24) for a product with no supported build, which means the only mitigation that can be verified inside any SLA is removal of the runtime. The control's 'documented compensating controls' branch is what an operator holding a legacy Flash application actually has to produce.

new_control_requirements.name: BROWSER-MANAGED-UPDATE-NO-DEFERRAL
new_control_requirements.description: Enterprise update rings must not defer security-channel browser updates beyond 24h.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Flash Player for CVE-2016-4117 was not only a standalone install: Adobe shipped browser-embedded builds, so where Flash arrived embedded in a browser its version was whatever that browser's update ring had delivered. An organization that defers browser security updates therefore defers the Flash fix without ever seeing a Flash item in its patch queue. The same ring is now the mechanism that removes the runtime, since browsers dropped Flash after its end-of-life — which makes update-ring currency the enforcement point for the disconnection CISA required on 2022-03-03.

CVE-2016-1019.name: Adobe Flash Player Arbitrary Code Execution Vulnerability (CVE-2016-1019)

attack_vector.description: Attacker-supplied Flash content corrupts memory inside the Flash runtime, killing the process or executing code in it. The defect class was never published by Adobe, NVD or MITRE, so what an operator has to work with is the reach — Flash Player at 21.0.0.197 and earlier plus the Adobe AIR runtime and SDK at 21.0.0.176 and earlier — rather than a code path.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none — PR:N in NVD's primary AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N vector. NVD also records a secondary AV:L/AC:L/PR:N/UI:R vector at 7.8, which models the same defect delivered as a local file the user opens.
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L; the runtime processes the hostile content as part of normal operation. The constraint that actually mattered was distribution: an exploit existed in the wild in April 2016 and no public exploit code exists today.
attack_vector.ai_factor: None claimed and none identifiable. The surviving public record names no finder at all; MITRE's reference list points at a FireEye post that no longer resolves, and nothing in the record asserts AI involvement in discovery or in exploit development.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Removing the Flash runtime, and separately inventorying and rebuilding Adobe AIR applications onto a current HARMAN AIR SDK — the two halves of this CVE need different actions and both are prevention.
prevention.adequacy: The Flash half is achievable and final. The AIR half depends on someone rebuilding each packaged application, which is an application-owner task rather than an endpoint task, and an estate with no AIR inventory cannot start it.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Alarming on repeated plugin-host crashes tied to one origin, since NVD records a crash as one of the two outcomes of this defect — a crash-loop is the cheapest visible symptom of a failed attempt.
detection.adequacy: It detects the failures, not the successes, and it requires crash telemetry from the workstation fleet. It gives nothing at all for the AIR delivery path, where there is no browser to report a plugin crash.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treating a compromise through this CVE as a ransomware precursor from the outset, given the KEV ransomware flag: isolate, check backup integrity, and rotate credentials the host held rather than closing on plugin removal.
response.adequacy: This is a triage posture, not a control. It assumes the intrusion is noticed, and the ransomware association is recorded by CISA at catalogue level rather than tied to a named campaign an IR team can pattern-match against.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: The control is met by any organization that applied APSB16-10 or shipped flash-plugin 11.2.202.616, and that is a partial answer to a CVE with two products in it. NVD scopes CVE-2016-1019 to the Adobe AIR Desktop Runtime and SDK at 21.0.0.176 and earlier as well, and AIR is maintained by HARMAN rather than dead, so its remediation is an upgrade that no Flash-branded flaw-remediation ticket will trigger. Two support states, one CVE id, one SI-2 record that describes only the half everyone thinks of first.

NIST-800-53-SI-3.gap: Where malicious-code protection is deployed and current, it is the control an assessor is likely to cite against a KEV entry carrying a ransomware flag, and it sits downstream of this defect. The corruption happens inside a signed Adobe runtime while it parses content it is built to parse, so there is no file, no boundary crossing and no unusual process for SI-3 to judge until attacker code is already executing in the plugin.

NIS2-Art21-vulnerability-management.gap: Article 21 vulnerability management done well over browsers still under-scopes this CVE. The Adobe AIR runtime is embedded in packaged desktop applications, so it appears in an inventory as the application's name and not as a runtime version, and a register keyed on browser plugins will show CVE-2016-1019 closed while AIR 21.0.0.176 or earlier is installed under whatever names the packaged applications carry. The failure is inventory granularity rather than process discipline.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: B4 can be assessed as met against a patch date that does not describe the estate. Adobe's fix reached Red Hat as RHSA-2016:0610 on 2016-04-08 and reached Internet Explorer and Edge only with MS16-050 on 2016-04-12, so hosts of different types were protected on different days for the same CVE. An assessment recording a single vendor-release date as the point of protection overstates coverage for whichever channel lagged, and here that was the Internet Explorer and Edge builds, which NVD scopes as Flash Player products distinct from the Linux runtime Red Hat fixed four days earlier.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: Patch application is straightforwardly satisfiable for this CVE and still produces a misleading result. The Flash Player component's correct end state is removal, because the product is end-of-life and CISA's action against the 2022-03-03 listing is disconnection; the Adobe AIR component's correct end state is a current HARMAN build. A maturity assessment that expresses both as a percentage of applications patched will count a host with Flash Player 11.2.202.616 installed as compliant when the requirement was that it not be there.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.7.gap: A.8.7 is the natural control to cite for an entry CISA marks as used in ransomware campaigns, and it does not touch the initial access. The exploit arrives as Flash content processed by a trusted runtime, so A.8.7 has nothing to inspect until a second stage lands, and by then the attacker already holds execution inside the plugin process. Citing A.8.7 as coverage for CVE-2016-1019 describes the response to the payload, not the defence against the flaw.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Adobe Flash Player and the Adobe AIR runtime are both in scope for this CVE, and CISA listed it on 2022-03-03 with a 2022-03-24 due date and a ransomware flag. The 'whichever is later' clause is the operative half: Adobe's fix landed in April 2016 (RHSA-2016:0610, flash-plugin 11.2.202.616, 2016-04-08; MS16-050 for Internet Explorer and Edge, 2016-04-12), so the clock the control starts is the KEV listing, and the verified mitigation it demands must be stated separately for the end-of-life Flash Player half and the HARMAN-maintained AIR half.

new_control_requirements.name: BROWSER-MANAGED-UPDATE-NO-DEFERRAL
new_control_requirements.description: Enterprise update rings must not defer security-channel browser updates beyond 24h.
new_control_requirements.evidence: NVD scopes CVE-2016-1019 to distinct Flash Player builds for Chrome, Edge and Internet Explorer, which means those hosts' exposure was governed by the browser update ring rather than by any Flash-branded patch item. Microsoft delivered the fix for Internet Explorer and Edge as MS16-050 (KB 3154132) on 2016-04-12, four days after the Linux downstream, so an organization deferring browser-channel updates was extending an exposure it had no ticket for. The same rings are what carry the removal of Flash after its end-of-life.

CVE-2016-0099.name: Microsoft Windows Secondary Logon Service Privilege Escalation Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: An already-logged-on user starts a process through the Secondary Logon service, keeps the thread handle the service failed to sanitize, and races a token swap onto that thread until a launched process inherits SYSTEM. No credential is guessed and no authentication is defeated; a privilege boundary inside a Windows service fails.
attack_vector.privileges_required: low — PR:L with AV:L in NVD's AV:L/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H vector, and Microsoft states the attacker 'would first have to log on to the system'. On a session or terminal server, that precondition is the machine's normal state rather than an anomaly.
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L; the race is cheap to retry, which is what keeps complexity low despite the timing dependency. The published exploit's real constraint is the host having two or more CPU cores and PowerShell 2.0 or later available.
attack_vector.ai_factor: None. Discovery is credited to James Forshaw, with the technique documented in a Project Zero post on exploiting a leaked thread handle and the PowerShell exploit written by Ruben Boonen; every step in that chain is human research published under a named handle.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Installing MS16-032 and restarting the host. Microsoft published no workaround and no mitigating factor for this CVE, so the update is the only measure that closes it.
prevention.adequacy: Complete once the restart is taken, and worth nothing before it. On a session host — where this flaw's precondition of an already-logged-on user is the machine's normal state — taking that restart evicts the logged-on users, so the restart and the exposure are in direct tension.

detection.what_would_have_worked: A rule keyed on the exploit's own shape: repeated CreateProcessWithLogonW invocations from a non-administrative session, thread handles duplicated and suspended, followed by a SYSTEM process whose parent is a user process.
detection.adequacy: It needs process-and-API telemetry already being collected and shipped off-host. The individual API calls are legitimate; only the burst and the resulting token transition distinguish the exploit.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treating any host where the escalation succeeded as SYSTEM-compromised — credential material cached on it rotated, local accounts audited for additions, and the machine rebuilt rather than patched in place.
response.adequacy: Correct but late, and scoped by what the attacker did next. Microsoft's own description notes that SYSTEM lets an attacker 'create new accounts with full user rights', so the account audit has to extend to the domain the host authenticated against, not just the host.

NIST-800-53-AC-6.gap: Least privilege can be implemented perfectly and is still useless here. The exploit's entry condition is a valid low-privilege logon, and its exit condition is a SYSTEM token obtained from a service, so no account was ever over-privileged and no privilege was ever abused — a boundary inside seclogon failed. The control's evidence and this CVE's exploit path do not intersect, which is why an AC-6 attestation for a host running the unpatched service is accurate and meaningless.

NIST-800-53-SI-4.gap: Where monitoring is deployed, it is not by default looking for this. The exploit produces no crash, loads no driver, changes no file and drops no binary — its whole footprint is a loop of ordinary process-creation and handle-duplication calls from a legitimate user session, delivered as PowerShell. SI-4 coverage assessed on the presence of an endpoint agent will read as adequate without ever establishing that a rule on that agent matches this sequence.

NIS2-Art21-patch-management.gap: The patch has existed since 2016-03-08 and any reasonable Article 21 process applied it long ago, so this control looks closed. The residue is the pending-restart state: MS16-032 replaces Secondary Logon service code, and a host that installed KB 3139914 or the Windows 10 cumulative without rebooting is still running the vulnerable service while the console shows compliant. Article 21 evidence has to be measured on the running build, not on deployment status, or it certifies the wrong thing.

UK-CAF-B2.gap: B2 is likely to be well evidenced — reviewed privileged groups, controlled access, strong authentication — and it never comes into play. The escalation happens entirely inside an authenticated session the user was entitled to open, and the SYSTEM token is produced by the service rather than granted by an access decision. An assessor reading B2 as coverage for CVE-2016-0099 records a control that the exploit path routes around by construction.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: The operating-system patching mitigation applies cleanly and mis-ranks the item. Microsoft rated MS16-032 Important rather than Critical, and a patch programme sequenced on vendor severity will place a SYSTEM escalation behind remote-code-execution fixes — even though CISA marks this CVE as used in ransomware campaigns, where a local escalation is the step that converts a foothold into estate-wide impact. The mitigation is met at every maturity level while the ordering it produces is wrong for this flaw's actual role.

ISO-27001-2022-A.5.7.gap: Threat intelligence is marked not covered here because for this CVE it is the only channel that would have carried the change, and a vendor-advisory subscription does not supply it. Microsoft's 2016-03-08 bulletin recorded the flaw as neither publicly disclosed nor exploited, so the vendor feed said one thing on the day of the fix and never revised it. What changed the risk was researcher publication — the Project Zero write-up, then Exploit-DB 39719 on 2016-04-21 — and an intelligence function reading only advisory feeds registers neither.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.16.gap: Monitoring activities exist as a control, and the distinguishing signal here is a pairing — a burst of logon-service process creations from a non-administrative session, then a SYSTEM process parented to a user process — rather than either event on its own. Because the widely mirrored exploit is PowerShell, there may be no new binary on disk at all — the artefact is a script block, visible only where script-block logging is enabled and retained — so A.8.16 evidence built around file and binary events has no input for this.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Windows Secondary Logon here has no compensating-control branch to fall back on: MS16-032 states Microsoft identified no mitigating factors and no workarounds, so the 'verified mitigation' the control demands can only be the update plus the restart. CISA listed the CVE on 2022-03-03 with a 2022-03-24 due date and a ransomware flag, and public PowerShell exploit code has existed since Exploit-DB 39719 on 2016-04-21 — which makes verification against each host's running build, rather than against the management console's deployment state, the load-bearing part of the control for this entry.

new_control_requirements.name: RESEARCHER-HANDLE-ACTIVITY-TRACKER
new_control_requirements.description: When a researcher handle is named in any catalog entry's discovery_attribution_note or poc_description, their public code-platform activity (GitHub events or a GitLab activity feed) must be polled by the threat-intake pipeline. The handle becomes a known signal source after a single catalog-grade drop and warrants prioritized surfacing of subsequent drops.
new_control_requirements.evidence: This CVE is the pattern the control describes. Microsoft's MS16-032 bulletin of 2016-03-08 recorded CVE-2016-0099 as not publicly disclosed and not exploited, and no revision followed; the risk changed when named researchers published — James Forshaw's Project Zero write-up on the leaked thread handle, then Ruben Boonen (b33f / @FuzzySec) releasing the PowerShell exploit as Exploit-DB 39719 on 2016-04-21, later folded into Metasploit as ms16_032_secondary_logon_handle_privesc with both handles among its authors. Polling those handles surfaces the change on the day it happens; the vendor feed never carries it.

CVE-2015-7645.name: Adobe Flash Player Arbitrary Code Execution Vulnerability (CVE-2015-7645)

attack_vector.description: A crafted SWF overrides IExternalizable.writeExternal with a non-function value; Flash's serializer resolves the override without confirming it is a method binding, casts it and calls it, and execution leaves the ActionScript vtable. The result is memory corruption reachable purely by getting Flash to serialize the attacker's object.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none — PR:N in NVD's AV:L/AC:L/PR:N/UI:R/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H vector; the attacker holds no account, and the code runs at the privilege of the process hosting the plugin.
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L, with UI:R capturing the delivery assumption that a user opens the content. The public artefact is a crash-level proof of concept, so the real work in weaponizing it is heap control the PoC does not provide.
attack_vector.ai_factor: None on either half. Trend Micro is credited by NVD's reference list with finding it in use; Google Project Zero published the root cause and PoC as issue 547. Neither is an AI-branded programme and neither claims automated discovery.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Not having the Flash runtime present. Once it is present, both maintained lines have to be tracked, because 18.x and 19.x carried the defect at the same time under different version numbers.
prevention.adequacy: Removal closes it outright. Version tracking as a substitute is where estates went wrong on this CVE, because a fix verified against 19.0.0.207 says nothing about a host held on 18.0.0.252 for compatibility.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Recording which users received Flash content from third-party origins, so that a targeted delivery to a small role-defined group is visible as a pattern rather than as isolated browsing.
detection.adequacy: Only useful if the proxy or DNS records are retained long enough for a pattern across weeks to emerge, and it identifies targeting rather than exploitation — a delivered SWF looks the same whether or not the type confusion succeeded.

response.what_would_have_worked: Scoping the response by target set rather than by alert count: identifying who else in the same role received similar content, and treating those users' hosts and credentials as in scope even without an alert.
response.adequacy: It depends on knowing the campaign's targeting logic, and for this CVE the report that described it is no longer retrievable — an organization relying on the public link today has the attribution without the detail needed to act on it.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: Flaw remediation is satisfiable and was satisfied in October 2015, and it still leaves two failure modes. The first is line coverage: NVD scopes this CVE to 18.0.0.160 through 18.0.0.252 and to 19.0.0.185 and 19.0.0.207 simultaneously, so a single remediation target under-describes the estate. The second is that the whole exercise is now superseded — CISA's action against the 2022-03-03 listing is to disconnect an end-of-life product, and no version satisfies that.

NIST-800-53-SC-44.gap: Detonation is marked not covered because a chamber sits on file and mail boundaries rather than on browser-delivered content, and for this CVE it would have limited value even where it did. The trigger is a serializer resolving an overridden writeExternal, which only happens when a real Flash runtime of a matching version renders the file; a chamber that lacks that runtime, or runs a different Flash build, records the sample as benign and passes it through with a clean verdict.

NIS2-Art21-incident-handling.gap: Incident handling exists and is exercised, and its classification logic is the problem. A Flash exploitation event scored on technical impact reads as one workstation with a contained plugin process, which routes it to routine handling. The reference NVD carries for CVE-2015-7645 names a campaign, and campaign-driven intrusion needs the scope question — who else in this role was approached — that impact-based triage never asks.

UK-CAF-D1.gap: Response and recovery plans exist and are typically written for availability events and for mass exploitation. Neither shape fits this CVE: the public record describes a zero-day used against a defined target set, and the report that described that set is now unreachable behind a dead link in NVD's reference list. A D1 plan with no targeted-intrusion branch offers procedures calibrated for a different kind of event entirely.

AU-Essential-8-App-Hardening.gap: User application hardening read as covering browser plugin content is the applicable mitigation, and that reading is an interpretation of the mitigation rather than its stated text. Even granting it, the mitigation is asserted as configuration while exposure is a property of which of two parallel Flash lines is resident, so a hardening baseline can be fully implemented on a host deliberately pinned to 18.0.0.252 for a legacy application and leave that host exploitable.

ISO-27001-2022-A.5.7.gap: Where a threat-intelligence function exists, its stored output decays in the way this entry demonstrates. The campaign attribution that justifies prioritizing CVE-2015-7645 above other 2015 Flash flaws now exists only as a report title in NVD's reference list, with the report itself gone. A function that files links rather than extracting and storing the finding ends up holding a citation nobody can open, which is indistinguishable from having no intelligence at review time.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Adobe Flash Player carried this defect across two maintained lines at once — 18.0.0.160 through 18.0.0.252 and 19.0.0.185 / 19.0.0.207 — and Adobe covered it with advisory APSA15-05 and bulletin APSB15-27, with the fix reaching Red Hat as flash-plugin 11.2.202.540 on 2015-10-16. CISA listed the CVE on 2022-03-03 with a 2022-03-24 due date and a required action of disconnecting the end-of-life product, so the 'verified mitigation' this control demands is the absence of the runtime, verified per host, and not a build number on either line.

new_control_requirements.name: NATION-STATE-INITIAL-ACCESS-IR-ESCALATION
new_control_requirements.description: IR runbooks must include an explicit nation-state-initial-access escalation path triggered by APT28/APT29/Lazarus/Volt-Typhoon/etc. attribution on a confirmed exploit chain. Standard malware-infection IR under-escalates nation-state activity by treating it as commodity threat.
new_control_requirements.evidence: The first reference NVD carries for CVE-2015-7645 is Trend Micro's report titled 'New Adobe Flash Zero-Day Used in Pawn Storm Campaign' — a specific tracked campaign rather than commodity exploit-kit activity, attached to a Flash zero-day Adobe covered with APSA15-05 and APSB15-27 in October 2015. That named-campaign attribution is the class distinction this control exists to force; this entry asserts no state attribution beyond the campaign name the reference carries, which is itself the point — NVD now marks that reference as broken, so an IR team reaching for the source at escalation time finds a title and nothing behind it.

attack_vector.description: Crafted Flash content overrides valueOf, frees the ByteArray backing buffer from inside that override, and lets the class keep operating through the stale pointer. The attacker reallocates the freed memory with chosen content and gains read and write inside the plugin process, ending in code execution.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none — PR:N in NVD's AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H vector; the code runs at the privilege of whatever process hosts the runtime, which CERT/CC notes can be an Office process as well as a browser.
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L, and genuinely so: the allocation timing is driven from ActionScript rather than raced against the runtime, which is why exploitation was reliable enough to ship inside a commercial intrusion product.
attack_vector.ai_factor: None. CERT/CC credits the discovery to Hacking Team, a human offensive-tooling vendor; the exploit became public through the breach of that company's archive rather than through any automated discovery pipeline.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Not having the runtime present. Where it had to be present, CERT/CC's own interim list — click-to-play, EMET restricting Flash inside Office and Internet Explorer — was the only prevention available during the days when exploit code existed and the fix did not.
prevention.adequacy: Uninstalling is complete. The interim measures are partial by construction: click-to-play still permits a user to click, and the EMET rule covers Office and Internet Explorer rather than every process that can load the control.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Watching for the Flash control being instantiated by a process that has no reason to render Flash — an Office application in particular, which CERT/CC names as a delivery path for this CVE.
detection.adequacy: It catches the delivery shape rather than the exploit, and it only works where module-load telemetry from Office processes is already being collected; without that, the Office path CERT/CC names produces no record at all.

response.what_would_have_worked: Scoping any suspected exploitation as an intrusion-tooling event rather than as commodity malware, given that the exploit reached the public inside a commercial intrusion product's archive and was adopted immediately by unrelated operators.
response.adequacy: It sets the right posture and identifies nothing on its own. Because the exploit was public and widely reused within days, the payload it delivered on any given host says more about who used it than the exploit does.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: Flaw remediation is fully met by any organization that reached 18.0.0.203 or flash-plugin 11.2.202.481, and the control's clock started in the wrong place. Working exploit code was public on 2015-07-05 and fixed downstream packages landed on 2015-07-08, so SI-2's timeframe — however aggressive — began after the period of maximum exposure had already ended. A control measured from patch availability cannot describe a defect that was weaponized before it was disclosed.

NIST-800-53-CM-7.gap: Least functionality is usually implemented for this class as a browser plugin policy, and CERT/CC's note for CVE-2015-5119 makes clear that is half the surface: it names Office documents alongside Flash content and recommends EMET specifically to stop the Flash control loading in Office and Internet Explorer. A CM-7 baseline that disabled the browser plugin passes review while leaving the documented Office path intact.

NIS2-Art21-vulnerability-handling.gap: Vulnerability handling as an Article 21 measure presumes a disclosure channel between finder and vendor that this CVE never had. CERT/CC credits the discovery to Hacking Team and records that the proof of concept became public with the July 2015 breach of that company, so the first notification any entity received was a third-party archive rather than a vendor advisory. A procedure that begins at advisory intake is structurally a day behind for this class of event.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: System security under B4 is normally evidenced against a supported-version baseline, and this CVE affected two supported lines simultaneously: 13.0.0.182 to 13.0.0.296 on extended support and 14.0.0.125 to 18.0.0.194 on the current line. An organization that had deliberately standardized on the extended-support branch for stability holds a defensible B4 position and the same defect, under version numbers a baseline written for the 18.x range does not recognize.

AU-Essential-8-App-Hardening.gap: Treating user application hardening as the mitigation for browser plugin content is an interpretation of the mitigation rather than a quotation of it, and even so it is scoped to the browser as usually implemented. What this CVE actually needed during its exposure window was EMET restricting the Flash control inside Office and Internet Explorer — a separate product with its own deployment — so an estate at a high maturity rating on browser hardening still had the Office path open.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: A.8.8 is an Annex A control any certified organization has to address, and the process built to it is written for a patch tempo this CVE did not respect. The gap between public exploit code on 2015-07-05 and downstream fixed packages on 2015-07-08 is the whole risk, and during it the available responses were configuration changes, not updates. An A.8.8 process whose only defined action is applying a vendor patch has no state to occupy while the exploit is public and the patch is not.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Adobe Flash Player's ByteArray use-after-free is the case the control's 'documented compensating controls' branch exists for. CERT/CC VU#561288 dates public exploit code to 2015-07-05 and the fix reached Red Hat as flash-plugin 11.2.202.481 on 2015-07-08, with the same CERT/CC note publishing the interim measures — click-to-play, EMET restricting Flash in Office and Internet Explorer, uninstall — that were the only deployable mitigation in between. With EPSS at 0.99344 on 2026-08-20 and CISA's 2022-03-03 listing carrying a disconnection action, the verified mitigation today is the runtime's absence.

new_control_requirements.name: BROWSER-MANAGED-UPDATE-NO-DEFERRAL
new_control_requirements.description: Enterprise update rings must not defer security-channel browser updates beyond 24h.
new_control_requirements.evidence: For CVE-2015-5119 the Flash runtime's version on a large share of hosts was whatever the browser channel had delivered, and the Metasploit module targets exactly that population — Internet Explorer 11 and Firefox 38.0.5 or later with Flash up to 18.0.0.194. With a fixed build available on 2015-07-08 and exploit code public since 2015-07-05, every day of update-ring deferral extended an exposure the organization had no Flash-branded patch ticket for.

CVE-2015-4902.name: Oracle Java SE Integrity Check Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: A malicious page makes jp2launcher.exe fetch an init.jnlp whose progress-class names javax.naming.InitialContext rather than a DownloadServiceListener implementation. The JRE instantiates it unchecked, and the constructor resolves an attacker-controlled rmi:// provider URL through RegistryContextFactory, pulling and running Go.class from the attacker's server — Java code executing with no click-to-play prompt.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none — PR:N in NVD's AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:L/A:N vector. No account and no interaction are required, which is why the base score is 5.3 despite the narrow impact.
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L in NVD's vector, though Red Hat scored the same flaw AV:N/AC:M at 4.3 under CVSS 2.0. The real constraint is what the flaw is worth alone: with C:N and A:N it buys a step, not an outcome.
attack_vector.ai_factor: None. Trend Micro found the flaw and privately disclosed it to Oracle, which credited Trend Micro in the October 2015 Critical Patch Update; the finder's 2015-10-19 write-up describes human analysis of a live campaign and asserts no AI involvement in discovery or in exploit development.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Removing the browser deployment path for Java. The flaw is in the subcomponent that handles remotely delivered content, so an estate that does not permit that content is not exposed even on an unpatched runtime.
prevention.adequacy: It closes the surface but is not the required action: CISA asks for vendor updates here, and Java SE is a supported line where updating is available. Removing the deployment path is the answer for hosts pinned to an old JRE by an application.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Alerting where remotely delivered Java runs on a workstation without the deployment prompt an operator would expect, since a subverted deployment decision is visible as a missing gate rather than as a crash.
detection.adequacy: The published mechanism is specific enough to alert on — a JNLP whose progress-class names javax.naming.InitialContext, or jp2launcher.exe opening an rmi:// connection to an external host. What is missing is an obtainable exploit sample to validate a rule against, and a missing click-to-play prompt is only anomalous where the baseline behaviour was recorded first.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treating exploitation of this CVE as evidence of a chain rather than as an incident in itself, and hunting for the second-stage flaw the removed barrier was meant to enable — in the campaign the finder documented, that was the Java zero-day CVE-2015-2590.
response.adequacy: There is concrete material to key on: the 2015-10-19 write-up names the Pawn Storm campaign, its NATO and White House targeting, the paired CVE-2015-2590, and the SHA1 of the JNLP that initiated the exploit. What it does not cover is any later reuse of the same bypass, so the hunt still has to be scoped by the host's own activity as well.

NIST-800-53-CM-7.gap: Least functionality expressed as a decision about whether Java is installed is too coarse for this CVE. The defect is in the Deployment subcomponent, so the runtime can stay for a pinned application while its remote-delivery path goes — a distinction a control expressed as one inventory line per product cannot record. The control that would have closed the exposure is available and is not the one being attested.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: Flaw remediation is met and is mis-sequenced. At CVSS 5.3 from NVD and 4.3 from Red Hat, with impact capped at partial integrity, this CVE sorts near the bottom of any severity-ordered queue built from the October 2015 Critical Patch Update. CISA's decision to list it as known-exploited seven years later is the correction, and an SI-2 process driven by CVSS alone will never generate it — a low-impact flaw that removes a barrier is worth more to an attacker than its score.

NIS2-Art21-vulnerability-handling.gap: Vulnerability handling is in place and the vendor record it rests on is thinner than the item needs. Oracle's October 2015 Critical Patch Update page still serves: NVD's cpuoct2015-2367953 link redirects to oracle.com/security-alerts/cpuoct2015.html and returns the matrix row for CVE-2015-4902 — Java SE, Deployment, remotely exploitable without authentication, CVSS 2.0 base 5.0, affecting 6u101, 7u85 and 8u60. Nothing in that row says the flaw is a click-to-play bypass or that it ran beside CVE-2015-2590 against the targets the finder named, so an entity triaging from vendor data alone sees a 5.0 partial-integrity issue and never sees why CISA listed it on 2022-03-03.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: B4 is assessed against an inventory, and an inventory recorded at product-family granularity cannot answer this CVE's question. NVD scopes it to three exact builds — 6u101, 7u85 and 8u60 — rather than to version ranges, so a record showing 'JRE 8' on a host is compatible with both affected and unaffected. The attestation is not wrong; it is being drawn from data that does not contain the answer.

AU-Essential-8-App-Hardening.gap: User application hardening is the mitigation most directly aimed at Java arriving from the internet, which is exactly this flaw's surface, and it is attested as configuration state. The gap is that this CVE is a failure of the deployment layer's own access decision, so a browser policy can be correctly set and correctly reported while the layer it delegates to reaches the wrong verdict. Hardening evidence describes intent, not the behaviour of the component that was defective.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: The technical-vulnerability register exists and under-resolves the estate. Java SE reached Red Hat systems through nine errata spanning Enterprise Linux 5, 6 and 7 plus Satellite 5.6 and 5.7, and SUSE systems through a further set covering three Enterprise Linux generations and two openSUSE releases. A register holding one Java entry per host cannot map that fan-out, so partial application across a mixed estate closes the register entry while some platforms stay unpatched.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Oracle Java SE is the case where a KEV listing has to override the score. CVSS is 5.3 from NVD and 4.3 from Red Hat, EPSS is 0.13354 on 2026-08-20, and no obtainable exploit code exists — every automated prioritization signal points down, while the flaw was in fact the click-to-play bypass paired with the Java zero-day CVE-2015-2590 in the Pawn Storm attacks the finder documented, and CISA placed it in KEV on 2022-03-03 with a 2022-03-24 due date and a required action of applying vendor updates. The control's value here is that it keys on the listing rather than on severity, and its compensating-control branch is what a host pinned to 8u60 by an application actually needs.

new_control_requirements.name: PROTECTION-MECHANISM-FAILURE-CLASS-REGRESSION
new_control_requirements.description: Detonation chambers, EDR rules, and AppLocker/WDAC policies covering protection-mechanism classes (MOTW, SmartScreen, AMSI, ASR, WDAC, Driver Block Rules) must include class-level regression testing executed on every patch deployment, not just one-off bypass-CVE remediation. The test battery for class-X must include all historic class-X bypass primitives — incomplete patches re-introduce risk that one-off testing does not detect.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Java SE's Deployment subcomponent is a protection-mechanism class in exactly the sense this control describes: click-to-play exists to make the user approve remotely delivered Java, and CVE-2015-4902 is that gate being walked around — the JRE accepts javax.naming.InitialContext where a DownloadServiceListener implementation is required, and the attacker's class loads and runs with no prompt. Because the mechanism's whole job is to hold a boundary, remediating one bypass tells an operator nothing about the next, and the affected builds (6u101, 7u85, 8u60) show the class carried across three concurrently maintained Java lines.

CVE-2015-3043.name: Adobe Flash Player Memory Corruption Vulnerability (CVE-2015-3043)

attack_vector.description: An FLV carrying oversized Nellymoser-encoded audio is decoded into an undersized buffer and the decoder writes past its end. Delivery is a page that serves the HTML, the SWF and the FLV together, so a visit is the whole precondition and the out-of-bounds write lands as code execution in the plugin process.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none — PR:N in NVD's AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H vector; the attacker holds no account and the code runs at the browser process's privilege.
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L; the overflow is reached by the decoder handling attacker-sized input during normal operation, and the exploit's tested range covers Internet Explorer and Firefox on Windows as well as Linux.
attack_vector.ai_factor: None identifiable. The flaw surfaced through in-the-wild exploitation with no finder named in NVD, MITRE or the Red Hat errata; the analyses the exploit module cites are human write-ups, and no AI involvement is claimed in discovery or weaponization.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Removing the Flash runtime. Patching to APSB15-06 was the contemporaneous answer and an incomplete one, because the same decoder failed again under CVE-2015-3113 within two months.
prevention.adequacy: Removal is complete. The patch route required tracking two bulletins — APSB15-06 and APSB15-14 — as one defect, and nothing in either bulletin's own CVE list tells an operator to join them.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Alerting where a single third-party origin serves a SWF and an FLV in the same page load, which is the delivery shape the public exploit produces.
detection.adequacy: It keys on a content pattern that legitimate Flash video also produces, so it generates false positives wherever Flash video is genuinely in use, and it needs proxy logging that records content type rather than destination alone.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treating a hit on this decoder as a component decision rather than a patch decision: two CVEs on the same primitive within two months is the point at which the answer is removing Flash from the estate.
response.adequacy: It is a programme-level response and gives nothing to the host already exploited; that host needs the same handling as any plugin-process compromise, since the fix removes the flaw and not what was dropped through it.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: Flaw remediation is met by anyone who deployed APSB15-06 or flash-plugin 11.2.202.457, and the control has no way to express that the fix was incomplete. CVE-2015-3113 landed two months later on the same Nellymoser root cause, and the Metasploit module that exploits this CVE exploits that one too — so the identical exploit code kept working against hosts whose SI-2 record for CVE-2015-3043 read closed and accurate.
