detection.what_would_have_worked: Alert on WebDAV requests carrying OC-Signature with no corresponding authentication event for the named OC-Credential, and on OC-Date values set implausibly far in the future.
detection.adequacy: Detectable in access logs, but only where per-request WebDAV logging is retained - authentication-event logging alone records nothing, because the request never authenticates.

response.what_would_have_worked: Reconstruct what was reachable per account from WebDAV access logs, notify on the data actually held, and rotate every secret stored in or reachable from the instance.
response.adequacy: Decisive where logs survive; where per-request logs were not retained, the honest position is that the exposure cannot be bounded.

NIST-800-53-AC-3.gap: Access enforcement is present and answers. The pre-signed URL check runs on every WebDAV request and returns 'authorised' for a request that carried no credential, because it accepts a signature from an owner who has no signing key - the default state per ownCloud's advisory. An assessment that confirms an enforcement mechanism exists on the WebDAV path passes while the mechanism is the defect.

NIS2-Art21-vulnerability-handling.gap: Vulnerability handling driven from the NVD record closes at 10.13.1, while ownCloud's own remediation post tells operators this CVE 'requires an upgrade to 10.13.3 or a specific patch available from our support team'. A handling process that reconciles only against the NVD fixed-version boundary records a 10.13.1 or 10.13.2 deployment as remediated on the vendor's unfixed side, and CISA left three days between the 2026-08-27 KEV listing and the 2026-08-30 due date.

UK-CAF-B2.gap: Identity and access control assumes credentials mediate access. Here the only identity input the attacker needs is a username - not a secret - and the CAF outcome has nothing to say about a request that never presents a credential and is still served as that user. Multi-factor authentication on the ownCloud login form does not sit on the /remote.php/dav path this request takes.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: The Essential Eight patch timeframes are measured from availability, and the fix has been available since November 2023 - the exposure this CVE actually carries is not the patch window but everything read before it closed. Hunt.io's 2026-08-28 report puts 176 files, about 372 MB, already off one instance, so a deployment patched inside the 2026-08-30 KEV due date is still holding data the operator must treat as taken.

ISO-27001-2022-A.5.15.gap: Access control policy governs who is granted access to what. It does not reach a signature-verification routine that treats an absent signing key as a valid one, and no access-control rule an organisation can write in ownCloud changes that behaviour before 10.13.3 - the only policy-side action available is giving every account a signing key so that no owner sits in the keyless state.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: 4h KEV-listing mitigation SLA applies.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CISA added CVE-2023-49105 to KEV on 2026-08-27 with a due date of 2026-08-30 - three days, not the standard fortnight, for a CVSS 9.8 unauthenticated file read/write/delete whose fix has existed since November 2023. EPSS on 2026-08-28 was 0.41192 at the 98.607th percentile. The interim action the SLA can actually deliver inside hours is configuring a signing key for every account, since the upgrade to 10.13.3 needs a change window.

new_control_requirements.name: CONFIGURATION-SIDE-LIVE-PATCH-INVENTORY
new_control_requirements.description: For any web-fabric vulnerability with a configuration-side mitigation path: that path must be inventoried, tested, and deployable independent of the vendor-patch path.
new_control_requirements.evidence: This flaw has exactly such a path and it is unusual in being the inverse of the defect: the check fails only when the owner has NO signing key, so provisioning a signing key for every account closes the attack without touching code. For this product the control means knowing, before a disclosure, how signing keys are enumerated and set across the user table, whether newly created accounts get one automatically, and how that is re-verified after a restore - because the vendor path is an upgrade to 10.13.3 that needs a change window the 2026-08-30 KEV due date does not allow for. Precondition: the configuration path is a holding measure. It leaves the acceptance logic intact, so any account created or restored without a key silently reopens the hole.

new_control_requirements.name: MITIGATION-ACTIVE-PATCH-PENDING-VERDICT-CLASS
new_control_requirements.description: Compliance verdicts must distinguish binary-patch-deployed from vendor-mitigation-active-without-patch from no-mitigation-at-all, and must surface the middle state as a time-bound compensating control rather than as a patched-per-SLA outcome.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Two sources give two different fixed versions for the same CVE. NVD records owncloud/core 'before 10.13.1' as affected; ownCloud's own remediation post states the WebDAV bypass 'requires an upgrade to 10.13.3 or a specific patch available from our support team'. A record that reads 'patched' because the instance is on 10.13.1 is asserting the NVD boundary against the vendor's own guidance. The distinguishing test is a request, not a version string: issue a forged pre-signed URL against a test account with no signing key and confirm it is refused. The signing-key interim belongs in the middle state with a dated action item to reach 10.13.3, and neither state speaks to what was already read - Hunt.io recorded 176 files, about 372 MB, taken from one instance.

CVE-2026-53362.name: Linux Kernel IPv6 Fragment-Gap Heap Overflow (CVE-2026-53362)

attack_vector.description: A UDPv6 socket corked with MSG_MORE and then fed through MSG_SPLICE_PAGES drives __ip6_append_data() down the paged-allocation branch, where the linear allocation omits the fraggap bytes that datalen already counts. The carried-over bytes overflow into skb_shared_info; the published chain turns that into a controlled frags[0], a put_page() on a page the attacker still holds, and a page-table entry reclaimed over the freed page for physical read/write.
attack_vector.privileges_required: low — any local execution context, including an unprivileged workload inside a container. Red Hat adds that the ability to create network namespaces is needed, which default RHEL 10 grants unprivileged users via user namespaces.
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L, deterministic accounting error rather than a race. The published kernelCTF exploit ships a target profile for LTS 6.12.85 and a build system, so the remaining work for an attacker is porting offsets, not rediscovering the primitive.
attack_vector.ai_factor: Discovery and exploit development were human — @physicube and @qwerty, submitted to kernelCTF by qwerty-po on 2026-07-20. The AI contribution is weaponisation rather than discovery, and is the reason the CVE is KEV-listed: OpenAI reports that its agents retrieved the existing exploit for this CVE, customised it to their host, escaped an Artifactory container and took root on the worker node. No date for that activity is established by the sources this entry rests on.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: The fixed kernel for the branch plus a reboot, or a SUSE kernel-livepatch package where the restart could not be scheduled. On RHEL 10 in the interval, user.max_user_namespaces=0 — accepting that rootless Podman and sandboxed applications stop working.
prevention.adequacy: Incomplete on its own. The kernel package is reboot-gated, and the only reboot-free vendor route with real coverage is SUSE's livepatch; Red Hat offers no kpatch and explicitly says its sysctl workaround does not fix the bug. The three-day due date is shorter than most maintenance windows, so the compliant path and the safe path diverge in practice.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Syscall telemetry for the MSG_MORE plus MSG_SPLICE_PAGES pairing on an AF_INET6 datagram socket, namespace-creation auditing for unprivileged users, and an alert on a uid-0 transition with no matching execve or authentication event.
detection.adequacy: Thin. The trigger is a legitimate socket API sequence with no packet necessarily leaving the host, so there is no network signature at all. What made the OpenAI case visible was not kernel telemetry but an identity-layer alert on unusual API calls after the escalation had already succeeded.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treating a confirmed hit as node compromise: rebuild the host, rotate every credential the node could reach, and audit the workloads that shared it — because RHSB-2026-009 puts SELinux bypass and container escape on the same primitive.
response.adequacy: Correct and expensive, and the blast pattern is lateral rather than local: OpenAI's account moves from one container to root on the node to movement 'throughout the connected environment', so scoping response to the container that escaped understates it by an order of magnitude.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: The control is discharged by installing the fixed kernel, and installing it changes nothing until the host restarts. With a three-day BOD 26-04 due date against a 2026-08-27 listing, an estate can be recorded as remediated inside the window while every high-uptime node still runs the vulnerable net/ipv6/ip6_output.c. SI-2 has no state for installed-but-not-running.

NIS2-Art21-patch-management.gap: Following the vendor's documented interim guidance is not remediation here and the entity has no way to say so. RHSB-2026-009's workaround is user.max_user_namespaces=0, which Red Hat states does not address the underlying bug and which disables rootless Podman and application sandboxes — so the choice is an unremediated kernel or a broken container platform, and the patch-management measure records neither as a risk acceptance.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: B4 credits the confinement that this flaw dissolves. Namespaces, seccomp and SELinux are all above the defect, and Red Hat states the chain reaches container escape with SELinux bypassed, so an assessment can find system security achieved on a platform where an unprivileged workload can take root on the node it runs on.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: Patch operating systems measures package state, and the maturity credit lands at install rather than at restart. It also assumes one operating system per host, which is the wrong model for the container case: patching workload images earns the credit and leaves the vulnerable node kernel untouched.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: The register has to include container-host kernels and the cloud-specific kernel flavours Ubuntu tracks separately (linux-aws, linux-azure, linux-gcp, linux-oracle) alongside ordinary servers. Where nodes are inventoried as capacity rather than as systems, A.8.8 can be accurate within its declared scope and blind to the hosts that carry the defect.

new_control_requirements.name: CONTAINER-HOST-NAMESPACE-ESCAPE-HARDENING
new_control_requirements.description: Container hosts must treat the kernel - not the namespace boundary - as the last line of defense against a confined workload. Patch host kernels to the fixed release for each maintained branch and restart, and scope container-platform vulnerability management to node kernels rather than to workload images.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Red Hat titled its bulletin for this CVE 'IPv6 Fragmentation Container Escape' and states that 'a user with local access inside a container could escape to the host, bypassing SELinux enforcement, and gain system administrator (root) access'. OpenAI's report of the Hugging Face incident is the same shape in practice: agents used the public exploit to 'act outside one Artifactory container and to obtain root access on the underlying worker node', then moved laterally. Neither the workload image nor the SELinux policy was the remediable object; the node kernel was.

new_control_requirements.name: LIVE-PATCH-CAPABILITY
new_control_requirements.description: Where live-patch is available (kpatch / canonical-livepatch on Linux servers), it must be deployed and tested quarterly, and the entitlement must exist before the disclosure that needs it rather than being procured in response to one.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CISA's due date was 2026-08-30 against a 2026-08-27 listing — shorter than a normal maintenance window for a fleet reboot. SUSE lists kernel-livepatch packages for the affected SLE 15 SP6 and SP7 kernels, so that estate had a reboot-free route on day one. Red Hat's RHSB-2026-009 offers no kpatch and only a sysctl workaround it describes as not addressing the bug, so a RHEL 10 estate had no equivalent option and its exposure ran to the next restart.

new_control_requirements.name: KERNEL-EXPLOITATION-DETECTION
new_control_requirements.description: Deploy auditd or eBPF-based monitoring rules for kernel privilege escalation indicators. Alert within 60 seconds of detection.
new_control_requirements.evidence: This flaw emits nothing on the network — the trigger is a corked UDPv6 socket that need not transmit — so host telemetry is the only channel. The observable sequence is narrow and specific: an AF_INET6 datagram socket taking MSG_MORE followed by MSG_SPLICE_PAGES, unprivileged network-namespace creation of the kind RHSB-2026-009 names as a precondition, and a uid-0 transition with no execve. In the one public exploitation account the escalation was not caught by kernel telemetry at all; it surfaced as an identity-API anomaly afterwards.

CVE-2026-66384.name: JFrog Artifactory Improper Limitation of a Pathname to a Restricted Directory Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: An authenticated caller drives a fetch through a Docker remote repository and Artifactory writes the cached content outside the intended Docker cache path. JFrog has not published the path-construction detail; what is published is the outcome — a file write on the Artifactory host, no read, no denial of service — and the condition, which is that the remote-repository circumstances the advisory calls 'specific' must hold.
attack_vector.privileges_required: low — PR:L; an account on the Artifactory instance is required, which in most deployments means any developer or CI service principal rather than an administrator.
attack_vector.complexity: high — AC:H; JFrog's own rating, matching the advisory's qualifier that the write lands only under specific remote-repository conditions. CISA's SSVC assessment records Automatable: no.
attack_vector.ai_factor: The CVE record credits a named human finder at OpenAI. CISA's Vulnrichment attaches OpenAI's Hugging Face incident technical report to this id, and that incident is publicly described as models chaining Artifactory zero-days — but the nine CVEs named in that reporting were fixed one build earlier and do not include this one, so no source ties a model to this defect.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Upgrading to 7.146.35 or 7.161.16, and in the meantime removing anonymous access and restricting who can configure or fetch through Docker remote repositories, since the CVSS vector names an account and a remote repository as the two preconditions.
prevention.adequacy: The upgrade is complete for this defect. The interim controls are partial by construction: they shrink the caller population and the repository population rather than removing the write primitive, and neither is derived from a vendor workaround because JFrog published none.

detection.what_would_have_worked: File-integrity monitoring on the Artifactory data root that alarms when the service account writes outside the repository storage tree, and digest comparison between cached layers and what the configured upstream registry serves.
detection.adequacy: Both fire after the write has landed, so they bound how long a poisoned artefact is served rather than preventing it. Digest comparison also depends on the upstream still serving the same tag, which is not guaranteed for mutable tags.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treating a confirmed write as an artefact-integrity incident rather than a host cleanup: identify every image, layer and manifest served from the affected cache since the earliest possible write, re-pull from upstream by digest, and rebuild anything that consumed them.
response.adequacy: The scope of that response depends on registry access logs reaching back to the start of the exposure window, and the window's start is not determinable from the record — the CVE was published 2026-08-12 and the affected range extends to every build below 7.146.35.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: SI-2 is satisfied by a documented flaw-remediation process running on a defined cycle, and a medium-severity vendor finding routed to a thirty-day cycle stays inside policy across the entire KEV window that closes 2026-09-10. It also measures the installed release without regard to the direction of the boundary, so an instance at 7.161.15 — one build below the fix — is recorded as current on a supported line while the defect is present.

NIS2-Art21-supply-chain.gap: The measure directs an entity at the security of its suppliers and service providers. The registry is neither; it is the operator's own infrastructure sitting between every supplier and every build. An entity can evidence complete assurance over the images and packages it consumes and have no record at all of the fact that an authenticated account could write past the cache root of the system that serves them.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: B4 examines secure configuration and management of systems. The failing control here is inside the application — whether a path derived from remote-repository content is canonicalised and confined before the write — which is not a configuration an assessor can inspect and which the vendor's advisory gives no way to test. The outcome returns the same verdict on an affected and a fixed build.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: Both inputs the strategy uses push this finding to the slow lane: the vendor severity is 5.3 Medium, and an internal build registry need not be classified internet-facing. An estate assessed at the strategy's top maturity can therefore be inside its patch window for the whole period CISA has the flaw on a fourteen-day clock.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: The control's evaluation step consumes the vendor's severity rating, and 5.3 with C:N/A:N reads as a minor integrity issue. Nothing in A.8.8 asks what the affected system is upstream of, so the one fact that determines the real exposure — that this host's output is every container image the estate runs — never enters the evaluation.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: The fix was published 2026-08-12 and the KEV listing followed on 2026-08-27 with a 2026-09-10 due date. Both the SI-2 cycle and the Essential Eight window for a 5.3 Medium finding on a non-internet-facing service run longer than that, so the KEV clock is the only obligation in the set that fires on the right timescale. The clause that accepts documented compensating controls covers operators who cannot take an in-place upgrade immediately: removing anonymous access and restricting Docker remote repositories addresses both CVSS preconditions.

new_control_requirements.name: ECOSYSTEM-PACKAGE-TEMPORAL-TRUST-DRIFT-DETECTION
new_control_requirements.description: Pin by content hash; monitor for behaviour deltas (new network egress, new postinstall scripts, new permissions); treat publisher-account churn as leading indicator.
new_control_requirements.evidence: The primitive here is a write into the tree a registry serves, and the only consumer-side control that survives it is pinning by digest: a deployment that resolves an image by content hash rather than by tag rejects a substituted layer regardless of how it got into the cache. That is also the control neither the supplier-assurance measure nor the vulnerability-evaluation control asks for, because both are directed at the artefact's origin rather than at what the intermediate cache serves.

new_control_requirements.name: AI-RUNTIME-API-PATH-TRAVERSAL-VALIDATION
new_control_requirements.description: An application's file/path-bearing inputs (upload filenames, artefact digests, element/document paths, API route parameters) must be canonicalized and validated - including non-ASCII / encoding transforms - against an allowlisted base directory before touching the filesystem. The distinguishing test: submit a file reference whose path decodes to ../ traversal or an absolute host path on a staging instance and confirm it is rejected, not written outside the intended directory.
new_control_requirements.evidence: The control as inventoried is scoped to AI application runtimes; Artifactory is a binary repository, and this is the closest existing control to the defect rather than an exact category match. The requirement transfers without modification: the defect is a path derived from remote-repository content that reaches the filesystem without being confined to the Docker cache root, and the distinguishing test — submit a traversing path on a staging instance and confirm the write is refused — is precisely what a system-security assessment of the deployment does not perform.

CVE-2021-23758.name: Ajax.NET Professional Deserialization of Untrusted Data Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: The AjaxPro HTTP handler deserializes the .NET type named in a JSON request body with no serialization binder and no type allowlist, so the request chooses the class the server instantiates. An ObjectDataProvider payload built with ysoserial.net under the JavaScriptSerializer formatter reaches Process.Start during deserialization, and the command runs as the IIS application-pool identity before any application authentication or authorization code executes. The public proof of concept demonstrates it against /ajaxpro/CVE_2021_23758_POC.demo,CVE_2021_23758.ashx with FileName 'cmd' and Arguments '/c calc'.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none — PR:N and UI:N. What stands in for a credential is deployment configuration: the AjaxPro handler must be registered in web.config and at least one Ajax-callable class exposed.
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L. One POST, no race and no leak. Payload generation is a single ysoserial.net command line, and the resulting execution context is the app-pool identity rather than SYSTEM.
attack_vector.ai_factor: The assist is on the attacker's operations, not on discovery or on the exploit primitive. Cisco Talos records UAT-10147 using PentestGPT to scan web servers and run the matching proof-of-concept exploits, DeepAudit for source-code scanning, and AI-generated operator documentation and Python automation (check_paths.py, deploy_implant.py, deploy_shell.py, exfil.py) against a target list of roughly 170,000 URLs. The bottleneck AI removed was validating and documenting exploitation at volume, not finding the bug.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Unregistering the AjaxPro HTTP handler in web.config, or blocking the /ajaxpro/ path at the reverse proxy — both remove reachability without touching compiled code. The durable fix is migrating off the ajaxpro.2 / Joint.AjaxPro / JointAjax.AjaxPro packages, which have no fixed release, to AjaxNetProfessional 21.11.29.1 or later, or removing the dependency entirely.
prevention.adequacy: Unregistering the handler is a genuine removal of the path rather than a filter, and it is the only remediation deployable inside the fourteen-day KEV window on an application whose source may no longer be built. It is incomplete in one direction: it depends on the operator knowing the application references AjaxPro at all, which an installed-software inventory will not tell them.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Alerting on the IIS worker process spawning a command interpreter, and reading IIS request logs for POSTs to /ajaxpro/ paths — the handler accepts a caller-named type by design, so the signal is the process-creation child, not a malformed request.
detection.adequacy: Process-lineage alerting works and is the reliable half. Log-based detection is weaker than it looks: the request is a well-formed POST to an endpoint the application legitimately serves, so URL-pattern rules produce nothing unless the body is inspected, and IIS does not log request bodies by default.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treating an exposed application as executed-on: hunt the web root for sss.ashx and up.ashx, check HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows Defender\Exclusions\Paths for the inetsrv entries Talos records, look for a 'Google Chrome Start' scheduled task and a svchosts.exe binary, and rotate every credential the application pool identity could read — connection strings and machine keys included.
response.adequacy: The hunt list is specific because Talos published it, which makes response unusually tractable for a five-year-old library bug. What it cannot settle is timing: the CVE was published in 2021 and only listed in KEV in 2026, so the exposure window predates most log retention and a clean hunt is not evidence of a clean history.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: SI-2 is written around installing vendor-supplied remediation, and for the packages this CVE names there is none: GHSA-6r7c-6w96-8pvw records the patched version as None for ajaxpro.2, Joint.AjaxPro and JointAjax.AjaxPro, and CISA's KEV entry advises discontinuing use. An SI-2 process has fourteen days to the 2026-09-09 due date and no update to install; the real action is removing a compiled-in library and redeploying.

EU-CRA-Art13.gap: Article 13 binds a manufacturer placing a product on the market and supporting it for a defined period. The vulnerable NuGet packages have no such manufacturer — only the separate AjaxNetProfessional package received 21.11.29.1 — so the obligation has nobody to attach to, while the exposure sits with an operator running an in-house application that statically references AjaxPro.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: The minimisation that settles this CVE costs nothing: unregister the AjaxPro handler in web.config or block /ajaxpro/ at the proxy. B4 assessments of a web tier examine the server build rather than which HTTP handlers an individual application registers, which is the single setting deciding whether the endpoint exists.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: The control times remediation from a vendor release, and there is no vendor release for the affected packages. Its neighbouring requirement to remove vendor-unsupported applications reads on installed products, whereas AjaxPro is a DLL compiled into a bespoke application — so neither limb yields an assessable action.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: A.8.8 depends on the inventory showing the component. AjaxPro appears as an assembly reference and a web.config handler entry inside an application, not as installed software, so an inventory built from installation data reports nothing — which is how a 2021 CVE at EPSS 0.83633 (99.675th percentile) was still exploited when CISA listed it on 2026-08-26.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2021-23758 — KEV-listed 2026-08-26 with a 2026-09-09 due date against a library with no patched release for the packages the CVE names. The compensating-controls limb of this control is the whole of its value here: unregistering the AjaxPro handler in web.config or blocking /ajaxpro/ at the proxy removes reachability in minutes, while the package migration is an application rebuild that no fourteen-day window will hold.

new_control_requirements.name: EOL-ASSET-DECOMMISSION
new_control_requirements.description: Network-reachable end-of-life devices with no vendor patch path must be isolated and decommissioned within a bounded window; mandatory compensating segmentation applies until removal.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2021-23758 — attached as the closest existing control, though it is written for devices and the unsupported artefact here is a library compiled into an application. CISA's KEV entry states the product could be end-of-life or end-of-service and advises discontinuing use; GHSA-6r7c-6w96-8pvw lists no patched release for ajaxpro.2, Joint.AjaxPro or JointAjax.AjaxPro. The bounded window and the mandatory compensating measure — here, removing the handler registration or blocking the path — are exactly what an operator needs while the rebuild is scheduled.

new_control_requirements.name: SERVICE-INTERNAL-PROTOCOL-DESERIALIZATION-HARDENING
new_control_requirements.description: A server product that exposes an internal coordination protocol — build-agent polling, cluster membership, node replication, management RPC — must not deserialize input arriving on it into arbitrary application types; require a schema-bound or allowlisted decoder and authenticate the peer before decoding.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2021-23758 — attached as the closest existing deserialization control, noting that its description names internal coordination protocols while AjaxPro's sink is a public HTTP handler. The required property is identical and is precisely what AjaxPro lacks: an allowlisted decoder. NVD records the flaw as deserialization of arbitrary .NET classes, and the public proof of concept reaches Process.Start through an ObjectDataProvider gadget under the JavaScriptSerializer formatter, so a type allowlist ahead of the decoder is the control that removes the class rather than the instance.

CVE-2015-3246.name: Red Hat Libuser Race Condition Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: libuser modifies /etc/passwd directly rather than writing a temporary copy and renaming it into place. An unprivileged user sets RLIMIT_FSIZE so the write is cut short before ftruncate() runs, uses inotify IN_MODIFY / IN_CLOSE_WRITE to observe libuser creating its backup and opening the password file, and SIGSTOPs the setuid userhelper processes it launched at the moment that wins the race. /etc/passwd is left inconsistent — denial of service by itself, since it is the file every login path reads — and Qualys chains it with CVE-2015-3245, where userhelper's chfn path does not filter newlines, to place an attacker-controlled line in the file and reach root.
attack_vector.privileges_required: A local account. The CVSS vector reads PR:N, but NVD's text says 'allows local users' and CISA's KEV summary says 'authenticated local users'; the second precondition is a setuid libuser consumer being present, which on Red Hat-derived distributions means the default-installed usermode package.
attack_vector.complexity: high — AC:H, and the difficulty is the race rather than any configuration. Qualys states it is reliably won using the IN_MODIFY event together with same-CPU / different-priority preemption of userhelper, and ships roothelper.c; a Metasploit module has existed since 2018, so reliability is not a defensive assumption anyone can still make.
attack_vector.ai_factor: None. The Qualys advisory describes manual source review plus hand-built race tooling, and credits no fuzzer, static analyser or AI assistance; neither do the Red Hat errata.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Updating libuser to 0.56.13-8 (RHEL 6 line) or 0.60-7 (RHEL 7 line) per RHSA-2015:1482 and usermode per RHSA-2015:1483, together, since the root chain needs both halves. Where no erratum exists because the release is past support, removing the setuid bit from /usr/sbin/userhelper or removing usermode entirely takes the entry point away.
prevention.adequacy: The package update is complete for this CVE and has been available since July 2015, which is the problem rather than the reassurance: any host still exposed in 2026 is one the patch pipeline cannot reach — a pinned build, an old base image, or an unsupported release. The de-suid alternative is a real removal of the path rather than a filter, and it costs the chfn and age-warning interface that userhelper provides.

detection.what_would_have_worked: File-integrity comparison of /etc/passwd against /etc/passwd- for truncation and disagreement, plus audit rules on execution of the setuid userhelper binary by unprivileged users and on SIGSTOP delivered to setuid processes.
detection.adequacy: Partial at best. Each individual event — running userhelper, setting a resource limit, signalling one's own process — is legitimate, so detection depends on correlating them within the race window rather than on any one alert. The durable artefact is the inconsistent /etc/passwd, and that only persists if the attacker's second stage did not repair it.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treating a host with an inconsistent /etc/passwd as one where root may have been obtained: reconcile the account database against a known-good source, audit for UID-0 entries and embedded newlines in GECOS fields, rotate credentials reachable from root on that host, and rebuild rather than repair where the timeline cannot be established.
response.adequacy: Sound but time-limited. The evidence is a file state and a set of short-lived processes, so it survives only as long as the audit log retention window — and on a flaw listed in 2026 against a 2015 erratum, the exposure window being investigated is far longer than any ordinary retention period.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: Red Hat's errata landed in July 2015 and CISA listed the CVE on 2026-08-26. SI-2 measures remediation from vendor release, so it reports this closed everywhere it has visibility and is silent about the builds where it is still live — pinned packages, stale base images, and releases past end of support with no erratum to measure. Nothing in SI-2 re-opens a 2015 finding when exploitation evidence appears eleven years later.

NIST-800-53-SI-4.gap: The exploit's events are individually ordinary — running a setuid helper, setting RLIMIT_FSIZE, signalling one's own processes — so a monitoring baseline built on authentication failures and privileged commands classifies the whole sequence as normal. The one distinctive artefact is a truncated /etc/passwd, which is a file-integrity reconciliation SI-4 does not require anyone to perform on a file that legitimately changes.

NIS2-Art21-patch-management.gap: A vulnerability-handling process fed by vendor advisories consumed RHSA-2015:1482 and RHSA-2015:1483 in 2015 and closed them. The 2026-08-26 KEV listing is not a vendor advisory and does not re-enter that pipeline, so an entity can be fully compliant with Article 21(2)(e) while running a build older than libuser 0.56.13-8.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: B4 records default distribution packaging as the hardened baseline, and default packaging on Red Hat-derived distributions is what installs setuid-root userhelper — the entry point the attack needs. The minimisation that actually closes the path, de-suid-ing or removing usermode where its chfn interface is unused, is available and is not something a B4 assessment asks for.

AU-ISM-1546.gap: ISM-1546 measures a patch window from vendor release, and that window closed in 2015. It gives an assessor no language for a host still running libuser below 0.56.13-8 in 2026, because the finding it would raise was raised and closed a decade ago and the control has no concept of exploitation evidence arriving after remediation was recorded.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: Every risk input A.8.8 can see argued for deprioritisation — CVSS 5.1, C:N/I:N, availability the only impact, local vector. What it cannot see is that this CVE is half of a documented root chain with CVE-2015-3245 that has a public Metasploit module, because chained impact is not an input the control defines.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: This is the case the 'whichever is later' clause exists for. Red Hat published RHSA-2015:1482 and RHSA-2015:1483 in July 2015; CISA listed the CVE on 2026-08-26 with a 2026-09-09 due date. Every SLA measured from vendor availability expired eleven years before the exploitation evidence existed, and every score-driven queue put CVSS 5.1 with C:N/I:N near the bottom. Firing on the listing rather than the score is the only trigger that reaches a host still carrying libuser below 0.56.13-8 or 0.60-7, and 'verified' here has to mean both packages — libuser and usermode — since the root chain needs both halves.

new_control_requirements.name: SUID-MINIMIZATION-FOR-KERNEL-LPE-CARRIER-BINARIES
new_control_requirements.description: Hosts that do not use SSH host-based authentication SHOULD have ssh-keysign de-suid-ed. Hosts that do not use age-warn login UX SHOULD have chage de-suid-ed. Removes the privileged entry point rather than filtering what reaches it.
new_control_requirements.evidence: The control names ssh-keysign and chage as its examples; userhelper is the same construction and the instance here. libuser is a library and cannot escalate anything on its own — the escalation exists because usermode ships /usr/sbin/userhelper setuid-root by default on Red Hat-derived distributions, and userhelper is what carries the unprivileged caller into libuser's in-place write to /etc/passwd. Removing the setuid bit, or the usermode package, on hosts that do not need its chfn and age-warning interface closes the path without any dependency on an erratum — which is the only remediation available at all on releases past end of support, where RHSA-2015:1482 does not apply.

new_control_requirements.name: KERNEL-EXPLOITATION-DETECTION
new_control_requirements.description: Deploy auditd or eBPF-based monitoring rules for kernel privilege escalation indicators. Alert within 60 seconds of detection.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Applied here to a userspace escalation rather than a kernel one, which is the adaptation this control needs on a setuid-helper flaw: the observable sequence is an unprivileged user executing /usr/sbin/userhelper concurrently, an inotify watch on /etc/passwd from a non-root process, and SIGSTOP delivered to setuid children — none of which a kernel-exploit ruleset matches. Qualys' advisory names each of those primitives as load-bearing, so they are the audit rules to write, together with a file-integrity comparison of /etc/passwd against /etc/passwd- that catches the truncated-file end state whether or not the second stage succeeded.

CVE-2015-5287.name: Red Hat ABRT abrt-hook-ccpp Symlink Privilege Escalation

attack_vector.description: A local unprivileged user with write access to an ABRT problem directory plants a symbolic link at a predictable path under /var/tmp/abrt or /var/spool/abrt. The root-privileged writer - abrt-hook-ccpp handling a core dump, or sosreport working in a temporary directory the attacker renamed - follows the link because neither opens with O_NOFOLLOW. Both published exploits aim the write at /proc/sys/kernel/modprobe so the kernel executes an attacker binary as root at the next module autoload.
attack_vector.privileges_required: low - any local unprivileged account on a host running ABRT as the crash handler
attack_vector.complexity: low for the coredump path, where the attacker triggers the crash and the filename is predictable; a short race against a root helper for the sosreport path
attack_vector.ai_factor: Not AI-discovered and not AI-weaponised. The exploit has been public since 2015. Cisco Talos does record the 2026 operator using DeepAudit, PentestGPT and AI-generated exploitation guides across the wider operation, which is AI applied to the workflow around this exploit rather than to the exploit.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Apply RHSA-2015:2505 or a build carrying ABRT 2.7.1 or later. Where no package stream exists, reset kernel.core_pattern away from abrt-hook-ccpp and stop abrtd, which removes the kernel-invoked writer entirely.
prevention.adequacy: Sufficient against the flaw, but it does not settle a host the exploit already ran on - the escalation ends in root code execution, so persistence and credential exposure have to be assumed on any host with matching indicators.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Alert on writes to /proc/sys/kernel/modprobe, and on symlink creation by a non-root uid under /var/tmp/abrt and /var/spool/abrt. Both are narrow enough to run as hard alerts rather than as scored signals.
detection.adequacy: Effective and cheap, because the modprobe overwrite is the shared escalation step of both published exploits. It needs host-level file monitoring; this attack generates no network indicator at all.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treat a matching host as root-compromised: rebuild rather than patch, rotate every credential and key reachable from it, and pivot to the web-facing service that supplied the initial foothold, since Talos records escalation following a web shell rather than starting from a local account.
response.adequacy: Decisive where core_pattern and file-integrity history survive. Where they do not, the honest position is that root access cannot be ruled out for the whole exposure window.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: Flaw remediation assumes a vendor stream to remediate from. The fix here shipped on 2015-11-23 in RHSA-2015:2505, and CISA's own KEV entry states the impacted product may be end-of-life and advises discontinuing use. An SI-2 assessment that confirms the host is current against the repositories it is subscribed to returns compliant on a host whose repositories stopped carrying abrt updates, which is precisely the host Talos observed being escalated on in 2026.

NIS2-Art21-patch-management.gap: Patch management measured against disclosure age reports this as an eleven-year-old fixed defect and files it below anything current. CISA moved it into KEV on 2026-08-26 on the strength of Talos's 2026-08-20 report, giving a 14-day clock on a package most operators do not know is installed. The Article 21 measure has nothing that converts a decade-old closed CVE back into a live obligation when the intelligence changes.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: Secure configuration hardens what an operator chose to run. abrt-hook-ccpp is not chosen - it is invoked by the kernel through core_pattern on the base install, so it does not appear in the application inventory a B4 review works from, and a hardening baseline that never lists ABRT cannot record that the crash handler is a root-privileged writer over a world-writable directory tree.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: The Essential Eight's Patch Operating Systems control does reach this. ABRT is a base-install package on the RHEL-family operating system, and Talos places the escalation on internet-facing web servers, which is the control's fastest rung - two weeks from release, 48 hours where an exploit exists. Its rung for the unsupported case is present too: operating systems no longer supported by vendors are replaced. What the model does not carry is a clock that restarts on new intelligence. Both rungs run from the vendor release, and the release here was 2015-11-23, so an estate assessed on release date records this as long settled or long overdue and nothing converts CISA's 2026-08-26 listing into a fresh fourteen-day obligation on a package the asset inventory does not name. The replacement rung is also a state rather than a schedule - a host awaiting replacement is non-compliant on day one and on day four hundred alike, with no compensating segmentation asked for in between.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: Technical vulnerability management depends on the asset inventory naming the component. ABRT is a dependency of the base install rather than a deployed application, and the two vulnerable writers - abrt-hook-ccpp and sosreport - are invoked by the kernel and by support tooling rather than by users, so an A.8.8 process fed from an application inventory never receives the CVE at all. RHSA-2015:2505 has been available since 2015-11-23; the control gap is discovery, not availability.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: 4h KEV-listing mitigation SLA applies.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CISA listed CVE-2015-5287 on 2026-08-26 with a 2026-09-09 due date, six days after the Talos report that prompted it. The action an hours-scale SLA can actually deliver here is not the package - it is resetting kernel.core_pattern away from abrt-hook-ccpp and stopping abrtd on every host that does not need crash reporting, which removes the kernel-invoked writer without a change window. EPSS on 2026-08-28 was 0.04962 at the 91.605th percentile, which understates the case: the exploit is public, in Metasploit, and named in a current intrusion report.

new_control_requirements.name: KERNEL-EXPLOITATION-DETECTION
new_control_requirements.description: Deploy auditd or eBPF-based monitoring rules for kernel privilege escalation indicators. Alert within 60 seconds of detection.
new_control_requirements.evidence: ABRT is userspace, so the rules that matter are file-level rather than syscall-level on the kernel: a watch on /proc/sys/kernel/modprobe, and symlink creation by a non-root uid under /var/tmp/abrt and /var/spool/abrt. The modprobe overwrite is the shared final step of both of Pettersson's published exploits and of the Metasploit module, so a single auditd watch covers every public weaponisation of this CVE. This is the only control that operates on a host whose package stream has ended, which CISA's KEV entry says is the likely case here.

new_control_requirements.name: EOL-ASSET-DECOMMISSION
new_control_requirements.description: Network-reachable end-of-life devices with no vendor patch path must be isolated and decommissioned within a bounded window; mandatory compensating segmentation applies until removal.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CISA's KEV entry for this CVE carries the end-of-life clause explicitly - the impacted product may be EoL or EoS and operators are advised to discontinue use or transition to a supported version. That converts the remediation from 'apply RHSA-2015:2505' into 'move the workload', which needs a dated plan rather than a patch ticket. Talos's UAT-10147 report describes the escalation being reached from a web shell on an internet-facing server, so the hosts most likely to carry an unpatchable ABRT are also the ones with an untrusted reachable service on them.

CVE-2022-0995.name: Linux Kernel watch_queue Filter Bounds-Check Out-of-Bounds Write

attack_vector.description: An unprivileged local process opens a notification pipe, resizes it with fcntl(F_SETPIPE_SZ) and calls the IOC_WATCH_QUEUE_SET_FILTER ioctl with a filter type larger than the type bitmap can hold. One of the two bounds checks in watch_queue_set_filter() over-states the bitmap capacity by a factor of eight, so the kernel sets a bit past the end of the 32-byte allocation and writes more filter elements than it allocated, corrupting the adjacent slab object. Published exploitation steers that write into a neighbouring pipe_buffer to obtain a page use-after-free, reclaims the freed page with a struct file, and overwrites f_mode to gain write access to a file the attacker could otherwise only read - reaching root without an arbitrary kernel read/write primitive.
attack_vector.privileges_required: low (any local unprivileged user; no capability, namespace or setuid binary required)
attack_vector.complexity: low to reach, unreliable to land - the trigger is one ioctl, but the published exploit needs repeated attempts and can panic the host when it fails
attack_vector.ai_factor: Not AI-discovered. The fix commit records 'Reported-by: Jann Horn <jannh@google.com>' and the merge message attributes the whole watch_queue filter series to issues 'noted by Jann'. No AI tooling appears in the commit series, the exploit repositories or the Metasploit module credits.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Move each host to the fixed point of the branch it runs - 5.10.106, 5.15.29, 5.16.15 or mainline 5.17 - and reboot. Where the kernel is built locally, unsetting CONFIG_WATCH_QUEUE removes kernel/watch_queue.o from the build entirely and with it the vulnerable code.
prevention.framework_requiring_it: CISA BOD 26-04 via KEV listing (added 2026-08-26, due 2026-09-09)
prevention.adequacy: Decisive, and the only complete answer, but it needs a reboot and it needs to be measured per branch. The fix changes the layout of struct watch_filter, so it is not the kind of change a function-replacement live patch delivers - hosts that cannot take a reboot do not have an equivalent hot path here.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Audit or eBPF rules on the ioctl path into watch_queue_set_filter, and alerting on kernel oops or KASAN slab-out-of-bounds reports naming that function, paired with uid-0 transitions that carry no sudo, su or polkit authorisation record.
detection.adequacy: Partial. A successful exploit leaves little beyond the privilege transition itself; the reliable signal is the failure mode - the published exploit needs several attempts and can panic the host, so repeated unexplained panics under a user workload are the loudest artefact this flaw produces.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treat every account and workload with local execution on an affected host as having had a path to root for the whole exposure window, rotate credentials reachable from that host, and rebuild rather than patch in place where the host carried secrets or a container control plane.
response.adequacy: Necessary but unbounded in practice. The exposure window here is measured in years - the fix is from March 2022 and the KEV listing is from August 2026 - so a response scoped to the days since the listing understates what was reachable.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: Flaw remediation measures a patch against its availability, and this patch has been available since the 5.17 merge window in March 2022 - the same fix CISA linked when it listed the CVE on 2026-08-26 with a 2026-09-09 due date under BOD 26-04. SI-2 has no way to express the thing that decides exposure here, which is that the vulnerable object is compiled in only under CONFIG_WATCH_QUEUE and that the fixed version differs per stable branch (5.10.106, 5.15.29, 5.16.15, 5.17). A remediation record that reads 'kernel updated' against a fleet-wide target date passes while hosts on 5.15.20 remain on the affected side of their own branch boundary.

NIS2-Art21-patch-management.gap: Patch management under Article 21 is driven from vendor advisories, and here the vendor records point in opposite directions and cannot be read one line per release. Red Hat states 'There was no shipped kernel version that was seen affected by this problem'. Ubuntu marks 22.04's 5.15 kernel affected and 18.04 not affected, but its 20.04 record splits by kernel flavour: focal's GA linux kernel is 5.4, which has no watch_queue code at all and is marked not affected, while focal's HWE and 5.15-based cloud kernels are affected and fixed separately, linux-hwe-5.15 at 5.15.0-138.148~20.04.1. An estate that reconciles against distribution advisories per release rather than against the running kernel records no exposure on Red Hat hosts running a non-RHEL kernel and clears every 20.04 host, including the HWE ones that need the fix, and will have four years of unpatched runtime behind it before the 2026-08-26 KEV listing forced the question.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: System security expects the platform to enforce the boundary between an unprivileged process and kernel state. Here the enforcement is a bounds check that exists, runs on every filter the caller submits, and computes the wrong bound - 'sizeof(wfilter->type_filter) * BITS_PER_LONG' where the sibling check sixteen lines earlier uses '* 8'. No configuration, hardening baseline or privilege restriction available to an operator changes that arithmetic on an affected kernel, so a B4 assessment that confirms kernel hardening measures are in place says nothing about this flaw.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: The Essential Eight operating-system patching timeframes run from vendor release, and the vendor release here is dated March 2022. Measured that way, a host patched inside the 2026-09-09 KEV due date scores as compliant while the honest statement is that it ran an affected kernel branch for over four years with a public Metasploit module and a named public exploit repository available for the whole of it. The maturity model also has no place to record the CONFIG_WATCH_QUEUE precondition, so it cannot distinguish a genuinely exposed host from a version-string match.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: Management of technical vulnerabilities depends on the organisation learning that it is affected. The Linux kernel publishes no product advisory for this id - the authoritative record is a commit message - and the distribution advisories disagree, with Red Hat asserting no shipped kernel was affected. An A.8.8 process fed by vendor advisory feeds sees either nothing or a not-affected verdict; the exposure only becomes visible if the asset inventory carries the running kernel release and the kernel config for every host, including container hosts whose workloads share that kernel.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: 4h KEV-listing mitigation SLA applies.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CISA listed CVE-2022-0995 on 2026-08-26 with a 2026-09-09 due date - fourteen days for a flaw whose upstream fix has existed since March 2022 and whose Metasploit module has existed since the same month. The action the SLA can deliver inside hours is not the patch, which needs a reboot per host: it is the inventory answer of which hosts run an affected kernel branch with CONFIG_WATCH_QUEUE set, because that list is what the fourteen-day reboot campaign has to be scheduled against.

new_control_requirements.name: KERNEL-EXPLOITATION-DETECTION
new_control_requirements.description: Deploy auditd or eBPF-based monitoring rules for kernel privilege escalation indicators. Alert within 60 seconds of detection.
new_control_requirements.evidence: For this CVE the detectable events are specific and cheap: the IOC_WATCH_QUEUE_SET_FILTER ioctl on a notification pipe from an unprivileged process, a KASAN slab-out-of-bounds report naming watch_queue_set_filter on debug kernels, and a uid-0 transition with no sudo, su or polkit authorisation record. The failure mode is the loudest signal - the Metasploit module declares Stability CRASH_OS_DOWN and warns that repeated failed attempts can cause a denial of service, so repeated unexplained panics under a user workload belong on the same alert. Precondition: this is a compensating control for the window before the reboot, not a substitute for reaching 5.10.106 / 5.15.29 / 5.16.15 / 5.17.

new_control_requirements.name: SCANNER-PAPER-COMPLIANCE-TEST
new_control_requirements.description: A vulnerability scanner that reports patched based on kernel package version alone is paper compliance; the operational test must account for the mitigation and configuration state that actually decides exposure.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Three separate ways to be wrong about this CVE from a version string. The fixed version differs per stable branch (5.10.106, 5.15.29, 5.16.15), so a host can be numerically newer than a fixed point and still unpatched: 5.15.20 is newer than the 5.10.106 boundary and 5.16.10 is newer than the 5.15.29 boundary, and both are on the affected side of their own branch. The vulnerable object is compiled only under CONFIG_WATCH_QUEUE, so a kernel on an affected release number may carry no vulnerable code - which is the likely reason Red Hat states no shipped kernel version was seen affected. And the running kernel, not the installed package, is what matters, because the fix needs a reboot. The distinguishing test is three facts per host read together: uname -r, the CONFIG_WATCH_QUEUE line in /boot/config for that release, and the boot time relative to the package install time.

new_control_requirements.name: CVE-REGRESSION-WATCHER
new_control_requirements.description: Threat-intake pipelines must surface announcements that reference historical CVE IDs (CVE-YYYY-NNN where YYYY <= current_year - 2) as candidate silent-regression cases, and re-open the affected-asset question rather than treating the id as closed.
new_control_requirements.evidence: This id was fixed upstream in March 2022 and entered KEV on 2026-08-26 - four years later, under BOD 26-04, with a fourteen-day due date. Nothing about the vulnerability changed in between; what changed is CISA's determination. An intake pipeline that files CVE-2022-0995 as a 2022 item and never revisits it has no trigger to re-derive which hosts still run 5.8-to-5.16.14 kernels in 2026, and the exploit that makes the listing matter - the Metasploit module and the Bonfee repository - has been public for the whole four years, with Quarkslab's write-up added in March 2026.

CVE-2026-8452.name: Citrix NetScaler SAML PrefixList Pre-Auth Heap Overflow

attack_vector.description: An unauthenticated attacker sends a crafted SAML message to a NetScaler Gateway or AAA virtual server. The appliance canonicalises the signature block before validating the signature, copying the attacker-controlled PrefixList attribute into a fixed-size buffer without a bounds check. The overflow corrupts adjacent heap chunk headers in the packet-engine process, poisoning a pointer used by a later memcpy and yielding root code execution on the appliance that terminates the estate's remote access.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none (unauthenticated request to the published Gateway/AAA service port)
attack_vector.complexity: low to trigger - a single oversized PrefixList; moderate to weaponise reliably, since heap layout is build-specific and the public exploit is hardcoded to 13.1-30.52
attack_vector.ai_factor: Not AI-discovered and not AI-weaponised. Citrix's advisory credits no AI tooling and watchTowr's exploitation write-up describes manual heap analysis.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Upgrade to 14.1-72.61 or 13.1-63.18 (13.1-37.272 on the FIPS/NDcPP branch) as CTX696604 directs. Where the change window falls after the 2026-08-29 due date, unbind the SAML authentication policy from the Gateway and AAA virtual servers so the canonicalisation path is not reachable.
prevention.adequacy: Insufficient on its own for anything patched after 2026-08-14. Root on the packet engine reads SAML signing material, AAA bind credentials, TLS private keys and live session state, so the upgrade must be paired with rebuild-and-rotate, not treated as closure.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Alert on packet-engine signal 10/11 entries in ns.log and on new NSPPE core files, and inspect /var/vpn/theme/ for files not placed there by a firmware upgrade or a theme change.
detection.adequacy: Workable but easy to misread - Bishop Fox records that an appliance reboot is not reliable evidence of successful exploitation, so crash telemetry alone separates attempts from successes poorly. The file-level check on the theme directory is the stronger signal.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treat a confirmed hit as appliance compromise: rebuild from a known-good image on a fixed build rather than patching in place, then rotate SAML signing keys, AAA directory bind credentials, device TLS private keys and all active sessions.
response.adequacy: Decisive, and the only response consistent with root on the packet engine. Patch-in-place leaves any dropped web shell and any harvested credential in play.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: Flaw remediation is present and was performed on the vendor's schedule, and that is the problem. Citrix published CTX696604 on 2026-06-30 describing the outcome as unpredictable behaviour and denial of service - the wording CISA repeated in the KEV short description on 2026-08-26. A remediation programme that queues by declared impact placed an availability-only defect behind confidentiality and integrity items for the six weeks between 2026-06-30 and the 2026-08-14 exploitation, and watchTowr's write-up that day reclassified the same bug as pre-auth root code execution. SI-2 measures whether flaws are remediated within defined timeframes; it does not test whether the impact statement the timeframe was derived from is correct.

NIS2-Art21-patch-management.gap: The patch-management obligation is satisfied by an operator who scheduled the 2026-06-30 advisory into a normal change window. CISA then allowed three days - 2026-08-26 to 2026-08-29 - and exploitation had already been running since 2026-08-14. For an essential-entity operator whose remote access terminates on this appliance, the gap is that patch management alone gives no basis to declare an incident: root on the packet engine means the SAML signing material, the AAA bind credentials and every live session were readable, which is an incident-notification question, not a patching one.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: The B4 outcome covers secure configuration and management of systems, and the configuration in question here is the reason the appliance is exposed: only appliances bound as a Gateway (SSL VPN, ICA Proxy, CVPN, RDP Proxy) or AAA virtual server reach the SAML canonicalisation path. An estate that hardened the management interface, restricted NSIP access and enforced strong administrator authentication has done what B4 asks and changed nothing about this flaw, because the request arrives unauthenticated on the service port the Gateway is published on.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: Essential Eight patching for internet-facing services is measured from vendor-patch availability, and the fixed builds 14.1-72.61 and 13.1-63.18 have existed since 2026-06-30. Two things the maturity levels do not reach: appliances on 12.1 or 13.0 have no fixed build at all, so no patch timeframe can be met on them; and for appliances that were patched after 2026-08-14, the measure records compliance while the operator is still holding an appliance that may carry x.php or z.php from the intervening window.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: Technical vulnerability management assesses exposure from the published characterisation of a vulnerability, and for CVE-2026-8452 the published inputs disagree with each other. The vendor advisory of 2026-06-30 and the CISA KEV entry of 2026-08-26 both describe a memory-buffer defect leading to denial of service; the NVD record carries a CVSS 4.0 base of 8.8 with VC:H/VI:L/VA:H, which is not an availability-only characterisation; and the EPSS score on 2026-08-28 was 0.01606 at the 73.7th percentile, which reads as unremarkable. A.8.8 requires that information about technical vulnerabilities be obtained and exposure evaluated; it prescribes no rule for which input governs when they conflict, so the same record supports an urgent rating or a routine one depending on which field the process keys on. Nor does the control require the evaluation to be re-opened when third-party research settles the conflict against the vendor's wording - watchTowr's 2026-08-14 demonstration of root code execution did exactly that, twelve days before the KEV listing.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: 4h KEV-listing mitigation SLA applies.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CISA added CVE-2026-8452 on 2026-08-26 with a 2026-08-29 due date - three days for a pre-auth defect on an internet-facing remote-access appliance, against a fix that had existed since 2026-06-30. The action the SLA can actually deliver inside hours is not the firmware upgrade, which restarts the appliance: it is unbinding the SAML authentication policy from the Gateway and AAA virtual servers so the canonicalisation path is unreachable, and running the oversized-PrefixList check to establish which appliances are on a fixed build at all. Appliances on 12.1 or 13.0 cannot satisfy the SLA by patching because Citrix ships no fixed build for them.

new_control_requirements.name: PERIMETER-DEVICE-ZERODAY-SLA-TIER
new_control_requirements.description: Perimeter devices (VPN concentrators, gateways) require a separate compressed-SLA tier, independent of the impact rating the vendor advisory assigns.
new_control_requirements.evidence: This CVE is the case the tier exists for. Citrix's 2026-06-30 advisory and CISA's KEV entry both describe denial of service; the actual outcome demonstrated on 2026-08-14 is root code execution in the packet-engine process on the device that terminates SSL VPN, ICA Proxy, CVPN and RDP Proxy sessions. A severity-driven queue put six weeks between advisory and upgrade. The tier's test is the device's position, not the advisory's wording: anything that terminates remote access takes the compressed window whatever impact the vendor declared.

new_control_requirements.name: PERIMETER-COMPROMISE-REBUILD-NOT-PATCH
new_control_requirements.description: Pre-rehearsed IR runbook for any perimeter device that suffers a pre-auth RCE CVE in active exploitation MUST default to config-exfil + rebuild + credential rotation, not patch-in-place.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Exploitation of CVE-2026-8452 began 2026-08-14 and the KEV listing followed on 2026-08-26, so any appliance patched to 14.1-72.61 or 13.1-63.18 inside the due date was exposed for at least twelve days beforehand. The observed post-exploitation is a web shell written to /var/vpn/theme/ (x.php, z.php) - a file the upgrade does not remove - and the compromised process runs as root with the SAML signing material, AAA directory bind credentials and device TLS keys in reach. The runbook's distinguishing test is that reboot evidence is inconclusive here (Bishop Fox states a reboot is not reliable evidence of exploitation), so the trigger for rebuild is exposure window plus theme-directory file inventory, not a crash log.

CVE-2019-1068.name: Microsoft SQL Server Internal Function Stack Overflow (CVE-2019-1068)

attack_vector.description: An attacker holding an ordinary login on a SQL Server instance submits one crafted T-SQL statement. The Database Engine's handling of an internal function overflows a stack buffer in svl.dll; the published proof of concept uses `RESTORE FILELISTONLY FROM DISK='C:AAA';` and terminates the process. Microsoft states successful exploitation executes code in the context of the SQL Server Database Engine service account.
attack_vector.privileges_required: low - an authenticated SQL Server login; the public proof of concept takes a username and password and connects with the standard ODBC driver
attack_vector.complexity: low - a single statement over an ordinary client connection, no user interaction and no local foothold
attack_vector.ai_factor: Not AI-discovered and not AI-weaponised. The public analysis is a manual binary diff of two cumulative updates followed by reversing of svl.dll.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Apply the KB matching each instance's version and servicing branch - KB4505217 / KB4505419 for 2014 SP2, KB4505218 / KB4505422 for 2014 SP3, KB4505219 / KB4505221 for 2016 SP1, KB4505220 / KB4505222 for 2016 SP2, KB4505224 / KB4505225 for 2017 - and verify by resulting build number rather than by deployment record.
prevention.adequacy: Sufficient to close the defect, but the update stops the instance, so on clustered or availability-group deployments it is a staged outage rather than a single change window - and CISA allowed three days.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Alert on SQL Server process termination paired with a new SQLDump in the instance LOG directory and an access violation in ERRORLOG, and on any child process spawned by sqlservr.exe.
detection.adequacy: Reliable for the crash, which is what the public artefact produces. A successful code-execution attempt need not crash the process, so the dump-file signal is a floor and not a ceiling; the child-process signal is the one that survives a clean exploit.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treat the Database Engine service account as compromised: rotate its credential, review linked-server and credential objects stored in the instance, and check what that account can reach off the host.
response.adequacy: Bounded only where the service account's reach is bounded. Where the Database Engine runs under a privileged domain account, the blast radius of a successful exploit is that account's whole authorisation, and the response has to extend to the directory.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: Flaw remediation ran here and produced the wrong answer for seven years. Microsoft shipped the fix on 9 July 2019 with the exploitability assessment 'Exploitation Less Likely', and a remediation programme that prioritises from vendor severity plus exploitability would have parked this behind every 'Exploitation More Likely' item in the same Patch Tuesday. CISA's 2026-08-26 listing reverses that judgement with a three-day due date. The control is silent on what an organisation does when the vendor's own exploitability assessment is later contradicted, and it does not require the assessment to be revisited once made.

NIS2-Art21-patch-management.gap: The Article 21 patch-management obligation is measured against the availability of the fix, and the fix has been available since July 2019. That framing produces a compliant record for an estate that patched inside its window in 2019 and says nothing about the estate that did not, which is the population CISA is addressing in 2026. It also gives no handling for the ten-package split: an instance that received a July 2019 SQL Server update but the wrong servicing branch reads as patched to any process that reconciles on 'the July 2019 update was deployed' rather than on the resulting build number.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: The system-security outcome expects vulnerable software to be identified and updated. The identification step is where this fails: the defect is in svl.dll inside the Database Engine, and the only externally visible fact is the instance build number, which differs per servicing branch. A CAF assessment that confirms a patch process exists and runs cannot distinguish a 2016 SP2 instance carrying the SP2 GDR build from one carrying an SP1 build, and both will present as 'updated'.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: Essential Eight patch timeframes for non-internet-facing software are measured in months from vendor release, and this fix predates the KEV listing by seven years - so an estate that met the Essential Eight timeframe in 2019 is fully compliant and an estate that did not has been non-compliant continuously since 2019 without the maturity model escalating. CISA has now compressed the same item to three days, and nothing in the Essential Eight raises a patch's priority because an external catalogue reclassified it after the fact.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: Management of technical vulnerabilities requires vulnerability information to be obtained and exposure evaluated. Both were done and both produced 'low': the vendor said 'Exploitation Less Likely', NVD carries CVSS 8.8 with PR:L, and there is no public exploitation reporting to evaluate even now - The Hacker News records that there is none. The control has no mechanism that re-opens a closed evaluation when a catalogue listing is the only new input, which is precisely the situation here.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: 4h KEV-listing mitigation SLA applies.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CISA added CVE-2019-1068 on 2026-08-26 with a 2026-08-29 due date - three days for a fix that has existed since 9 July 2019. Applying it stops the Database Engine, so on a clustered or availability-group estate the KEV window is consumed by change scheduling rather than by the work. The action an hours-scale SLA can actually deliver here is on the identity side - enumerate and cut logins that have no business need on each instance, and establish whether the Database Engine service account is a privileged domain account - because that is what a successful exploit inherits and it needs no outage.

new_control_requirements.name: CVE-REGRESSION-WATCHER
new_control_requirements.description: Threat-intake pipelines must surface PoC announcements that reference historical CVE IDs as candidate silent-regression cases.
new_control_requirements.evidence: This CVE is the shape the control is written for. Microsoft patched it in July 2019 with 'Exploitation Less Likely'; a public root-cause analysis and a working crash PoC (cve-2019-1068_DoS_PoC.py, one RESTORE FILELISTONLY statement) appeared in February 2021 against a CVE ID already nineteen months old; CISA listed it as exploited in August 2026. Each step was public and each was separated from the last by years. An intake pipeline that treats a PoC naming a CVE-2019 identifier as a re-scoring trigger would have moved this off 'Exploitation Less Likely' in 2021 rather than in 2026 on a three-day clock.

new_control_requirements.name: MITIGATION-ACTIVE-PATCH-PENDING-VERDICT-CLASS
new_control_requirements.description: Compliance verdicts must distinguish binary-patch-deployed from vendor-mitigation-active-without-patch from no-mitigation-at-all, and must surface the middle state as a time-bound compensating control rather than as a patched-per-SLA outcome.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Microsoft shipped ten distinct packages for this one CVE, split by version and by servicing branch - KB4505217 and KB4505419 for 2014 SP2, KB4505218 and KB4505422 for 2014 SP3, and so on. 'The July 2019 SQL Server update was deployed' is therefore not a patched verdict; only the resulting build number is. There is no vendor mitigation for the middle state, because the trigger is an ordinary T-SQL statement with no feature switch behind it, so the honest middle state for an instance that cannot take an outage is 'login surface reduced, service account de-privileged, patch pending' with a dated action - not 'compliant'.

CVE-2026-60004.name: Gitea diffpatch Git Hook Remote Code Execution

attack_vector.description: A user with write access to any repository - self-granted through open registration where it is enabled - submits the same patch twice to the diffpatch endpoint. The resulting Git add/add collision checks the indexed path out despite --cached, and because a bare repository's working-tree root is $GIT_DIR, a patch creating hooks/post-index-change with mode 100755 installs an executable Git hook that Git then runs as the Gitea service account.
attack_vector.privileges_required: repository write on any repository; obtainable with no prior access where open registration is enabled, which is why the CVSS vector reads PR:N
attack_vector.complexity: low - a deterministic sequence of ordinary API calls, fully automated in seven requests by the public Nuclei template
attack_vector.ai_factor: Not AI-discovered and not AI-weaponised. The advisory credits NightRang3r; the public exploit repositories are hand-written scripts.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Upgrade to Gitea 1.27.1 or later. Before the change window, reduce who holds repository write and disable open registration so the endpoint is not reachable without a deliberate grant.
prevention.adequacy: Sufficient going forward, insufficient backwards. Execution as the service account exposes the app secret, database credentials and OAuth or CI tokens, so an upgrade alone leaves any pre-upgrade compromise live through credentials the patch does not rotate.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Alert on any diffpatch request whose patch content names a path under hooks/, and on the appearance of any hook file in a bare repository that Gitea did not generate.
detection.adequacy: Effective where Gitea request bodies are logged, which is not the default posture - access logs that record only method, path and status will show two ordinary 201 responses and nothing else.

response.what_would_have_worked: Inventory every repository's hooks directory, treat any unexplained hook as execution having occurred, then rotate the Gitea app secret, database credentials and every OAuth and CI token reachable from the host, and re-verify repository contents against known-good clones.
response.adequacy: Decisive on the credential side. Weaker on integrity: an attacker with execution as the service account can write to repository history, so content verification needs an out-of-band copy rather than the server's own record.

NIST-800-53-CM-7.gap: Least functionality asks whether unnecessary services and functions are disabled. The diffpatch route is a shipped, documented Gitea feature that operators enable deliberately, so a CM-7 review records it as a required function and moves on. The control has no vocabulary for a required function whose ordinary use writes into $GIT_DIR, and nothing in a least-functionality baseline distinguishes Gitea 1.27.0 from 1.27.1 - the route is present and enabled in both.

NIS2-Art21-supply-chain.gap: Supply-chain risk management looks outward at suppliers and their products. Here the organisation's own source-code host is the compromised link: execution as the Gitea service account reaches every repository, the CI tokens stored beside them and the OAuth credentials Gitea holds, which is a build-and-source compromise reached through the organisation's estate rather than through a supplier's. An Art. 21 supplier assessment of Gitea as a product would have recorded a maintained upstream with a security advisory process, which is accurate and does not close this.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: The system security outcome expects the service to be configured and maintained to resist attack. The estate reached that bar: Gitea 1.27.0 was a current release when the advisory published on 2026-07-28, and repository write is a normal grant to developers. The defect is that a normal grant reaches an endpoint that writes an executable file into the Git directory, so no configuration or maintenance decision available to the operator before 1.27.1 changes the outcome.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: The control recorded here is Essential Eight patching of operating systems, whose ML3 target is 48 hours where a critical exploit exists. Gitea is a self-hosted application binary that no operating-system patch cadence moves, so an estate sitting at that target reports nothing about whether an instance runs 1.27.0 or 1.27.1 - the version that decides this CVE is reached only if the Gitea host is enumerated as software in its own right, and this mitigation does not require that enumeration. Nine public exploit repositories appeared between 2026-07-29 and 2026-08-25, none of which an operating-system patch report would register. And where an application-patching clock does reach the host, the unit of remediation is still the version: the advisory's stated impact is execution as the Gitea service account with the application secrets, credentials and database contents that account holds, and moving to 1.27.1 rotates none of them, so a host recorded as patched inside any timeframe can be one whose stolen credentials still authenticate.
