response.what_would_have_worked: Treating a confirmed hit as user-context code execution on the endpoint: capture the browser's process tree and network history, rotate the user's credentials and any session tokens the browser held, and rebuild rather than clean, since the second stage is unconstrained by anything the browser bug itself did.
response.adequacy: Adequate if the sequence is recognised, and recognition is the weak link — the compromise starts with an ordinary browsing session and leaves no authentication event to alert on. On Windows XP hosts the response also has no patched end state to return to.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: The remediation clock starts at the 2013-10-08 vendor release, and exploitation ran from 2013-09-18. SI-2 is structurally blind to the interval in which the flaw was actually dangerous, and it prescribes nothing for an organisation that has no patch to apply during it.

NIS2-Art21-patch-management.gap: MS13-080 is a cumulative Internet Explorer update fixing nine issues, and the obligation consumes it as one release. There is no way inside Article 21(2)(e) to express that two of the nine were already under targeted attack, this CVE among them, so the entity cannot justify an out-of-band window for the exploited pair against the other seven.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: B4 treats the OS-bundled browser as platform rather than as an optional component with its own attack surface. A host where Internet Explorer is present, unused and still reachable by a user assesses as hardened while carrying a vulnerable mshtml.dll and a working delivery path.

AU-Essential-8-App-Hardening.gap: The browser is the control's primary target, and its measures work by removing content classes the browser processes — the Java and Flash legacy surface among them. This exploit is plain script driving onpropertychange on a document object, core HTML and script handling that a working browser cannot disable, so every enumerated content restriction can be in force and the use-after-free in mshtml.dll is untouched. The gap is not that the control misses browsers; it is that it names no measure reaching a memory-safety defect inside the engine it hardens.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: Between 2013-09-18 and 2013-10-08 there was no CVE, no advisory and no vendor acknowledgement to prioritise, because the finding was deliberately held back. Then on release day a public Metasploit module changed the risk profile inside a single day — faster than the reassessment cycle A.8.8 describes.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: MS13-080 shipped on 2013-10-08 and CISA listed the CVE on 2022-03-03 with a 2022-03-24 due date. By 2022 the operative question is not whether the October 2013 cumulative was applied but whether any host still runs an mshtml.dll predating it — which on Windows XP and Server 2003 estates is the normal state, since their update channel closed on 2014-04-08. The control's 'documented compensating controls' branch is what carries those hosts: on a platform with no supported update, the verified mitigation is removing user reachability to Internet Explorer or removing the host, and it has to be written down as such rather than left as an overdue patch ticket.

new_control_requirements.name: EOL-ASSET-DECOMMISSION
new_control_requirements.description: Network-reachable end-of-life devices with no vendor patch path must be isolated and decommissioned within a bounded window; mandatory compensating segmentation applies until removal.
new_control_requirements.evidence: The exploited configuration was Internet Explorer 8 on Windows XP, and Windows XP support ended on 2014-04-08 — months after MS13-080. For every such host the terminal state is removal, not patching: KB2879017 is the last fix that will ever exist for that platform, and any later Internet Explorer flaw has no fix at all. Treating those hosts as an overdue patch queue misstates the remediation; the control's isolate-then-decommission framing is the only one that describes an accurate end state, and browser reachability is what the interim segmentation has to cut.

CVE-2013-3346.name: Adobe Reader ToolButton Use-After-Free Sandbox-Chained Document Exploit

attack_vector.description: A PDF whose document JavaScript nests ToolButton objects and frees a parent from inside a child's cEnable callback, then uses the stale reference. The script also grooms the heap, builds the ROP chain and stages the shellcode, so opening the document is the only user action required. On sandboxed Reader builds the observed sample chained CVE-2013-5065, a Windows XP and Server 2003 NDPROXY kernel flaw, to escape the sandbox.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none - the code runs as the user who opens the document
attack_vector.complexity: low against the versions Metasploit records as tested; the JavaScript grooming makes the free deterministic rather than racy
attack_vector.ai_factor: None. Disclosed and weaponised in 2013, with the Metasploit module public from 2013-08-08. No AI tooling is credited in discovery or in the in-the-wild sample FireEye analysed.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Apply APSB13-15 - Reader and Acrobat 9.5.5, 10.1.7 or 11.0.03. Where the update lags, disable document JavaScript in Reader, which removes the only trigger path the public exploit uses.
prevention.adequacy: Sufficient against this CVE. It does not address the second half of the observed chain: on Windows XP and Server 2003 the CVE-2013-5065 escape remains available to any other Reader-level bug.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Alert on AcroRd32.exe spawning a child process or writing an executable, and inspect PDF JavaScript for nested ToolButton objects freed from a cEnable callback.
detection.adequacy: Process-lineage detection is reliable; content inspection is weaker, because the exploit is assembled at runtime in script rather than present as a recognisable blob in the file.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treat a hit as user-context compromise, and on Windows XP or Server 2003 as kernel-level compromise given the documented escape; rebuild rather than clean, and rotate what the user could reach.
response.adequacy: Adequate where process lineage was recorded. Where only anti-malware verdicts exist, the exposure cannot be bounded - the chain's own design put its code beneath the agent.

NIST-800-53-SI-3.gap: Malicious code protection is positioned to catch the payload, and in the sample FireEye analysed there is almost no payload to catch until the end: the heap grooming, the ROP chain and the shellcode are all constructed in JavaScript inside the PDF at runtime, with only the final stage arriving as a separate executable. A signature-driven SI-3 control inspecting the document at delivery has a script to read, not a shellcode blob, and the exploit had been public in Metasploit since 2013-08-08 by the time the November campaign ran.

NIS2-Art21-patch-management.gap: Adobe fixed this in APSB13-15 in May 2013 and FireEye found it in use in November 2013, so the compromised population is defined by a six-month gap on a client-side application update, not by a missing patch. Article 21's patch measure sets no separate expectation for document readers, which are updated on user-visible schedules and are the exact class the attacker chose to target.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: Secure configuration for Reader has one lever that matters here - disabling document JavaScript - and it is not a lever a B4 baseline usually pulls, because it breaks form workflows. A configuration review that confirms Reader is deployed with vendor-recommended settings leaves the scripting surface that carries the entire exploit switched on.

AU-Essential-8-App-Hardening.gap: User application hardening does cover PDF software, but only from Maturity Level Two - Maturity Level One is browser scope, so an organisation working to the model's entry rung carries no PDF requirement at all while this exploit arrives in a PDF. At Maturity Level Two the rung that bites is a process-lineage block: PDF software is blocked from creating child processes, which stops the second-stage executable FireEye records as the only non-script component of the chain. It does not reach the exploit itself - the use-after-free, the heap grooming and the ROP chain all run inside the reader process - so an ML2-compliant host still takes code execution in the user's context and loses only the last step. The one action that removes the primitive outright, disabling document JavaScript, is not a rung of its own; the model reaches it only through the general requirement that ACSC or vendor hardening guidance for PDF software is implemented, whose content is set by the guidance document rather than by the assessment.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.7.gap: Protection against malware is assessed on the presence and currency of anti-malware controls. The in-the-wild sample defeats that framing rather than evading a particular product: FireEye records the exploit executing entirely from document script, and the accompanying CVE-2013-5065 kernel flaw put the attacker's code below the level any endpoint agent of that era ran at. An A.8.7 verdict of compliant is available on a host that this chain compromises end to end.

new_control_requirements.name: CONFIGURATION-SIDE-LIVE-PATCH-INVENTORY
new_control_requirements.description: For any web-fabric vulnerability with a configuration-side mitigation path: that path must be inventoried, tested, and deployable independent of the vendor-patch path.
new_control_requirements.evidence: This CVE has such a path and it is a switch, not a workaround: FireEye's analysis records the exploit as implemented entirely in document JavaScript, so disabling JavaScript in Reader and Acrobat removes the only trigger the public weaponisations use. For this product the control means knowing in advance which business processes depend on PDF forms and scripting, having the registry or Reader-policy setting staged for fleet push, and having tested that the setting survives a Reader update. Precondition: this is a holding measure. It disables a feature rather than repairing the use-after-free, and it is drawn from a researcher's description of the sample rather than from an Adobe-published workaround.

new_control_requirements.name: DOWNLOAD-PROVENANCE-ENFORCEMENT
new_control_requirements.description: Enforce Mark-of-the-Web / content-provenance on all internet-sourced files and block execution of provenance-stripped shortcuts, installers, and script hosts regardless of a reputation verdict.
new_control_requirements.evidence: The delivery step for this chain is a PDF that arrives from outside and is opened locally. Provenance marking is what lets the reader open the file in its restricted mode and what lets an endpoint policy refuse the second-stage executable FireEye records as the only non-script component - the part of the chain where a provenance decision is still available. The control is stated as reputation-independent for the reason this sample demonstrates: there is no recognisable malicious blob in the document to form a reputation about, because the exploit is assembled at runtime in script.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: 4h KEV-listing mitigation SLA applies.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CISA listed this on 2022-03-03 with a 2022-03-24 due date, nine years after Adobe's May 2013 fix - the KEV clock here is a sweep for installs that never took APSB13-15, not a response to a new disclosure. EPSS on 2026-08-28 was 0.78581 at the 99.567th percentile, which is what a fully public, Metasploit-packaged document exploit looks like a decade on. The hours-scale action available before the update lands is the JavaScript switch, not the patch.

CVE-2013-1675.name: Firefox DOMSVGZoomEvent Uninitialized Member Memory Disclosure

attack_vector.description: A crafted web page reads the previousScale and newScale properties of an SVGZoomEvent. The nsDOMSVGZoomEvent constructor never initialises the backing members mPreviousScale and mNewScale, so each read returns four bytes of whatever the browser heap last held there. Repeating the read harvests uninitialised process memory - the bug report notes the exposure includes material such as passwords and cookies - with no crash, no console error and no write primitive.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none (remote web content; the user need only visit the page)
attack_vector.complexity: low - a standard DOM property read, no heap grooming and no crash risk, limited only by how much memory the attacker can accumulate two floats at a time
attack_vector.ai_factor: Not AI-discovered. MFSA 2013-47 credits Mozilla community member Ms2ger, who filed bug 866825 with an HTML reproducer; no tooling of any kind is credited.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Update to Firefox 21.0 or later, or ESR 17.0.6 or later, and restart the application. For hosts pinned to an affected build with no supported successor on that branch, removal or isolation rather than patching.
prevention.adequacy: Complete as a fix, and it has been available since May 2013. Inadequate as an answer to the 2022 KEV listing on any host still running an affected build, because the branch those hosts are on has had no vendor release for nine years - there the required action is decommissioning, which the update process does not perform.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Browser version inventory across the estate, including embedded Gecko builds inside internal applications, and comparison of running process versions against installed package versions to catch updates that landed without a restart.
detection.adequacy: This is the only detection that works. The exploitation itself produces no crash, no error and no distinctive log line - it is a legitimate property read on a legitimate object - so hunting for the behaviour after the fact is speculative and hunting for the vulnerable build is not.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treat anything the browser process held during the exposure - session cookies, saved credentials, page content from authenticated sessions - as potentially read, and rotate session material for users of affected builds.
response.adequacy: Honest but unbounded. The leak is untargeted: the attacker takes whatever the allocator left behind, so there is no way to say from the browser side what was recovered. Where the affected build has been in use for years, the only defensible scope statement is that the exposure cannot be bounded.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: Flaw remediation timelines start from the fix, and this fix shipped on 2013-05-14. When CISA listed the id on 2022-03-03 with a 2022-03-24 due date, no SI-2 action could satisfy it in the ordinary sense: the fixed versions the advisory names, Firefox 21 and ESR 17.0.6, had themselves been unsupported for nine years. An SI-2 record that closes the item by asserting the browser is current is answering a different question from the one the KEV listing asked, which is whether any affected build is still present anywhere in the estate.

NIS2-Art21-patch-management.gap: Article 21 patch management assumes an update channel exists to be kept current. For an ESR 17 build there is no such channel - Mozilla stopped servicing that branch in 2013 - so the control has nothing to apply and no way to express the state the estate is actually in. The compliant action for a host stuck on an affected build is removal, which patch management is not the process that authorises.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: System security expects the platform to keep untrusted content away from process memory. The flaw here is not a boundary that failed under attack but a constructor that never ran: two float members declared and left with whatever the allocator last wrote, then exposed to script through a standard DOM property. Sandboxing, site isolation and content restrictions all remain intact while the leak proceeds, because the read is a legitimate property access on a legitimate event object.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: Essential Eight application patching names web browsers explicitly and measures from vendor release, so an estate that took Firefox 21 in May 2013 scored compliant then and scores compliant now. Neither state addresses what the 2022-03-03 KEV listing is actually asking about, which is a build that never took the update - and for those hosts the Essential Eight timeframe cannot start, because the vendor has published no release for their branch since 2013.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: Technical vulnerability management depends on the vulnerability being visible in the inventory. MFSA 2013-47 is nine years older than the KEV listing that made it urgent, and an A.8.8 process driven by current vendor advisory feeds will never surface it again - the advisory is not new, the vendor has said everything it intends to say, and only a query against installed browser builds across the estate finds the affected hosts.

new_control_requirements.name: BROWSER-MANAGED-UPDATE-NO-DEFERRAL
new_control_requirements.description: Enterprise update rings must not defer security-channel browser updates beyond 24h.
new_control_requirements.evidence: MFSA 2013-47 shipped in Firefox 21 and ESR 17.0.6 on 2013-05-14 and the id entered KEV on 2022-03-03. The hosts that made that listing meaningful are the ones whose update ring never delivered the 2013 release at all - and for a browser the deferral compounds, because the ESR branch an estate is pinned to eventually stops receiving releases entirely. For this CVE the control has a second half that the ring alone does not deliver: the update must be followed by an application restart, since the running process keeps the vulnerable constructor until it exits.

new_control_requirements.name: EOL-ASSET-DECOMMISSION
new_control_requirements.description: Network-reachable end-of-life software and devices with no vendor patch path must be isolated and decommissioned within a bounded window; mandatory compensating segmentation applies until removal.
new_control_requirements.evidence: The remediation MFSA 2013-47 names - Firefox 21, ESR 17.0.6 - was itself unsupported by the time CISA listed this id on 2022-03-03 with a 2022-03-24 due date. On a host still running an affected build there is no update to apply, so patching cannot discharge the KEV obligation and removal is the only terminal state. The same applies to any embedded Gecko or XULRunner build vendored inside an internal application, which carries the flaw without appearing in the browser inventory at all.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: 4h KEV-listing mitigation SLA applies.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CISA listed CVE-2013-1675 on 2022-03-03 with a 2022-03-24 due date, nine years after Mozilla fixed it. The action available inside hours is not a patch deployment - most of the estate took that in 2013 - but an inventory query: which hosts still run Firefox below 21.0 or an ESR 17.x below 17.0.6, and which internal applications embed a Gecko build that no browser inventory covers. That list is what the three-week due date has to be worked against, and it is the only output the SLA can produce quickly here.

attack_vector.description: A crafted HTML page frees a CGenericElement object while the Document retains a reference, then reoccupies the freed allocation with attacker-controlled data before the renderer dereferences it again. Delivery in the observed campaign was a watering hole: nuclear-content pages on the United States Department of Labor website were injected to pull the exploit from dol.ns01.us, after fingerprinting each visitor's antivirus and browser plug-ins. Code executes in the current user's context inside Internet Explorer.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none for the attacker; the victim must load the page in Internet Explorer 8
attack_vector.complexity: low - a single crafted page, and the watering-hole placement removes the need to lure the target anywhere unfamiliar
attack_vector.ai_factor: None. Found in the wild in April 2013 and reported by Daniel Caselden of FireEye; no AI tooling is credited in the bulletin.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Before 2013-05-14, the Fix it 'CVE-2013-1347 MSHTML Shim Workaround' from Security Advisory 2847140, or setting the Internet and Local intranet zones to High to block Active Scripting; EMET configured for Internet Explorer also mitigated. After 2013-05-14, update 2847204 (MS13-038). Today, removing Internet Explorer 8 from the estate.
prevention.adequacy: The update is complete for this CVE. It is not sufficient as a security position, because every operating system MS13-038 covers is now out of support and the host has no path for anything found since.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Watch for Internet Explorer crashing or spawning child processes on a normally-trusted site, and for workstations resolving dynamic-DNS names immediately after browsing a first-party site.
detection.adequacy: Weak against this campaign as run. The delivery domain imitated a Microsoft update host and the injection sat on a government site the targets were expected to visit, so neither reputation nor destination anomaly separates it cleanly.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treat any workstation that loaded the injected pages in the exposure window as compromised at user-context level, and inventory which hosts still carry Internet Explorer 8 at all.
response.adequacy: Adequate for scoping, but the inventory answer is the durable one - a host still running Internet Explorer 8 in 2026 needs a removal date, not an incident record.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: Flaw remediation had nothing to remediate for the period that mattered. The Department of Labor injection was live in late April 2013 with dol.ns01.us first sighted on 2013-04-30, and MS13-038 did not publish until 2013-05-14 - the vulnerability was a zero-day, publicly disclosed before the fix, and Microsoft states in the bulletin that it was aware of attacks through Internet Explorer 8 at issue time. The only SI-2-shaped action available in that fortnight was Microsoft's Fix it shim from Advisory 2847140, which SI-2 does not describe or require, and which most flaw-remediation processes have no channel to deploy.

NIS2-Art21-patch-management.gap: Patch management measured against MS13-038 declares the estate clean once update 2847204 is installed. The exposure this CVE actually carries for an operator today is not the missing patch but the presence of Internet Explorer 8 at all: every operating system in the MS13-038 affected list is out of support, so a host still running it has no patch path for anything found after its lifecycle ended. A patch-management process that reconciles against a 2013 KB reports full compliance on a host that cannot be patched again.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: B4 covers secure configuration, and the configuration levers that would have blocked this are documented in the bulletin itself - Internet Explorer Enhanced Security Configuration (which is why servers rated Moderate rather than Critical), zone settings raised to High, Active Scripting disabled, and EMET installed and configured for Internet Explorer. None of these are default on a Windows 7 workstation, which is precisely the population the Department of Labor watering hole reached, and B4 does not distinguish a browser configuration that happens to be the default from one that was deliberately hardened.

AU-Essential-8-App-Hardening.gap: User application hardening is the Essential Eight measure aimed at web browsers, and it is aimed at the wrong layer for this flaw. Its measures - blocking Flash, Java and web advertisements in the browser - remove plug-in and ad-network delivery. CVE-2013-1347 is a use-after-free in the browser's own object model reached from ordinary HTML rendering, injected directly into first-party pages on dol.gov that the target intended to visit, so nothing the hardening measure blocks is in the path. Configuring Internet Explorer to block ActiveX and Active Scripting, which MS13-038 lists as a workaround, would have helped and is not what the measure asks for.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: Technical vulnerability management assumes a supplier fix to consume. For the fortnight between the injection appearing on dol.gov and MS13-038, none existed - the vulnerability was publicly disclosed and under attack with only an interim shim available. A.8.8 also gives no basis for the decision an operator actually faces on this CVE now: Internet Explorer 8 is not a vulnerable version awaiting an update, it is a terminal one, and the control's vocabulary of assessment and patching does not contain the word for removal.

new_control_requirements.name: EOL-ASSET-DECOMMISSION
new_control_requirements.description: Network-reachable end-of-life software and devices with no vendor patch path must be isolated and decommissioned within a bounded window; mandatory compensating segmentation applies until removal.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Every operating system in the MS13-038 affected list - Windows XP SP3, XP x64 SP2, Server 2003 SP2, Vista SP2, Server 2008 SP2, Windows 7 SP1, Server 2008 R2 SP1 - is out of support, and Internet Explorer 8 is out of support with them. Installing update 2847204 closes CVE-2013-1347 and leaves the host with no path for anything found afterwards, which is why CISA's 2022-03-03 KEV listing of a 2013 browser bug is a decommissioning signal rather than a patching one. For this CVE the control means: the browser inventory, not the patch inventory, is the compliance artefact, and a host carrying Internet Explorer 8 needs a removal date.

new_control_requirements.name: BROWSER-MANAGED-UPDATE-NO-DEFERRAL
new_control_requirements.description: Enterprise update rings must not defer security-channel browser updates beyond 24h.
new_control_requirements.evidence: MS13-038 was a standalone out-of-band-shaped update rather than the monthly cumulative Internet Explorer rollup, and Microsoft's own guidance in the bulletin is that MS13-037 - the May 2013 cumulative - must also be installed to avoid compatibility problems. A deferral ring that batches browser updates with the monthly rollup therefore both delays the fix and creates a reason to hold it back for compatibility testing, on a bug Microsoft had already confirmed was under attack in Internet Explorer 8. The distinguishing test is whether the browser has its own update lane that can carry a single-CVE update without waiting for the OS ring.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: 4h KEV-listing mitigation SLA applies.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CISA added CVE-2013-1347 to KEV on 2022-03-03 with a 2022-03-24 due date, nine years after MS13-038 shipped, and EPSS on 2026-08-28 stands at 0.77889 - the 99.549th percentile - because a Metasploit module (exploit/windows/browser/ie/cgenericelement_uaf, Exploit-DB 25294) has been public since 2013-05-03. The action the SLA delivers inside hours here is not patching: it is establishing whether any host in the estate still runs Internet Explorer 8, and disabling Active Scripting in the Internet and Local intranet zones on the ones that do, per the workaround MS13-038 documents, until they can be removed.

CVE-2013-0641.name: Adobe Reader and Acrobat Crafted-PDF Buffer Overflow (CVE-2013-0641)

attack_vector.description: A spear-phishing message delivers a PDF posing as a Turkish visa application form. Opening it in an affected Reader or Acrobat overflows a buffer; in the observed chain this CVE is paired with CVE-2013-0640, one bug executing code inside the Reader process and the other escaping Protected Mode, after which a DLL disguised as a language-bar add-in is dropped, persisted through the registry, and used to fetch further payloads.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none beyond the rights of the user who opens the document
attack_vector.complexity: low for the attacker once the document is opened - the PDF fingerprints the Reader version, selects shellcode and runs a ROP chain against ASLR and DEP without further interaction
attack_vector.ai_factor: Not AI-discovered and not AI-weaponised; this predates AI-assisted exploit development entirely.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Update to 11.0.02, 10.1.6 or 9.5.4 per branch (APSB13-07, 2013-02-20). In the seven days before that existed, the only available control was Adobe's own interim guidance: enable Protected View for all files and push it by Group Policy.
prevention.adequacy: The update closes the defect. The interim control does not cover the 9.x and X installations the same advisory lists as affected, because Protected View is an XI setting - so for part of the estate there was no interim control at all.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Alert on a Reader or Acrobat process writing an executable or DLL, on any process running outside the sandbox that descends from one, and on registry persistence written in the minutes after a document open.
detection.adequacy: This is the detection that survives the exploit, because it watches behaviour rather than file content - and the file content was deliberately built to defeat signatures. Signature detection for this CVE existed only after samples were captured.

response.what_would_have_worked: On a host that opened one of these documents, audit add-in registration and autorun keys rather than trusting an update to remediate, and treat the user's credentials and anything the account could reach as exposed.
response.adequacy: Necessary, because the chain persists outside the application: patching Reader on a host that already ran the payload changes nothing about the DLL that is already registered.

NIST-800-53-SI-3.gap: Malicious code protection is present and the signature approach is exactly what this exploit was built to defeat. The JavaScript inside the PDF was assembled by string manipulation specifically to avoid detection, and it fingerprinted the installed Reader version to select shellcode - so the file on disk differs per target. Adobe's advisory of 2013-02-13 confirms exploitation was already under way, meaning every host in the exposure window met the control and was still reachable. A signature for Exploit:Win32/CVE-2013-0641 exists only because samples were captured after the fact.

NIS2-Art21-patch-management.gap: The window that matters here is 2013-02-13 to 2013-02-20 - Adobe acknowledged in-the-wild exploitation a week before it had an update to ship. A patch-management obligation measured from the availability of a fix has nothing to say about that week, and the only action available in it was the Protected View configuration change, which Adobe published in the advisory rather than in an update and which does not exist in the 9.x and X installations the same advisory lists as affected.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: The system-security outcome assumes a vulnerable component can be identified and updated. Reader and Acrobat here span three separately-versioned branches whose fixed versions are 9.5.4, 10.1.6 and 11.0.02, and the affected version 11.0.01 sorts above the fixed version 10.1.6. An assessment that confirms an estate runs 'the current Reader' does not establish which branch each install is on, and the branch is what determines whether the host is fixed.

AU-Essential-8-App-Hardening.gap: User application hardening is the Essential Eight strategy that speaks to this document class, and its published measures for PDF readers do not include the one control Adobe actually recommended for this CVE - Protected View for all files, pushed by Group Policy. Worse, the hardening step most estates would count on here is the Reader sandbox itself, and this chain is the case that broke it: Kaspersky confirmed the escape on a fully patched 64-bit Windows 7 host running Reader 11.0.1, so 'Protected Mode is on' was true and irrelevant at the same time.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: Management of technical vulnerabilities depends on vulnerability information reaching the organisation and exposure being evaluated. Both happened on 2013-02-13 through APSA13-02, and the evaluation had no fix to act on for seven days. The control does not require an organisation to hold a pre-tested configuration-side mitigation for its document readers, and Protected View - the only lever available in that week - is a setting that has to be found, tested against document workflows and pushed, which is not a same-day exercise if it has never been rehearsed.

new_control_requirements.name: CONFIGURATION-SIDE-LIVE-PATCH-INVENTORY
new_control_requirements.description: For any web-fabric vulnerability with a configuration-side mitigation path: that path must be inventoried, tested, and deployable independent of the vendor-patch path.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Adobe published APSA13-02 on 2013-02-13 naming Protected View as the interim mitigation and did not ship the fix until 2013-02-20. For that week the configuration path was the only defence, and it is Group-Policy deployable - so an organisation that had already tested Protected View against its document workflows could act on day one, and one that had not spent the week deciding. The control's precondition matters here and must be recorded with it: Protected View is a Reader and Acrobat XI setting, so it does not exist on the 9.x and X installations the same advisory lists as affected. Inventorying the mitigation therefore also means knowing which fraction of the estate the mitigation cannot cover.

new_control_requirements.name: PROTECTION-MECHANISM-FAILURE-CLASS-REGRESSION
new_control_requirements.description: Detonation chambers, EDR rules, and AppLocker/WDAC policies covering protection-mechanism classes must include class-level coverage rather than per-instance signatures.
new_control_requirements.evidence: This chain is the first publicly confirmed escape of Adobe Reader Protected Mode, verified by Kaspersky on a fully patched 64-bit Windows 7 host running Reader 11.0.1. Every control that assumed a document exploit stays inside the sandbox was defeated at once, and the file-side control was defeated deliberately - the embedded JavaScript was assembled by string manipulation to evade static detection and branched on the installed Reader version so no two samples matched. The class-level rule that survives is behavioural: a Reader or Acrobat process writing a DLL, a descendant process running outside the sandbox, registry persistence written in the minutes after a document open.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: 4h KEV-listing mitigation SLA applies.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CISA listed this on 2022-03-03 with a 2022-03-24 due date - nine years after Adobe shipped 9.5.4, 10.1.6 and 11.0.02, which means the population the listing addresses is estates still carrying an unpatched or unsupported Reader branch. For those, an hours-scale response is not an update: it is enabling Protected View where the branch supports it, and identifying the 9.x and X installs where it does not so they can be removed rather than mitigated.

CVE-2013-0640.name: Adobe Reader AcroForm Sandbox-Escaping Memory Corruption

attack_vector.description: A spearphishing attachment - a PDF themed on human-rights seminars or Ukrainian foreign policy - corrupts memory in Adobe Reader's AcroForm component on open. The in-the-wild exploit carried its own DEP and ASLR bypass and escaped the Reader X and XI sandbox, dropping a roughly 20 KB assembler downloader that fetched a backdoor and resolved its C2 through Twitter and Google Search when its primary servers in Panama and Turkey were unreachable.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none - the victim need only open the attachment
attack_vector.complexity: low for the operator, high for the exploit author: reliable code execution plus a sandbox escape across Reader 9, 10 and 11
attack_vector.ai_factor: Not AI-discovered and not AI-weaponised; the campaign predates operational AI-assisted exploit development by roughly a decade.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Update Reader and Acrobat to 9.5.4, 10.1.6 or 11.0.02. Before those shipped, the CERT/CC set in VU#422807: Protected View on Reader XI and Acrobat XI for Windows, Acrobat JavaScript disabled, EMET deployed, DEP and ASLR confirmed on.
prevention.adequacy: The update is decisive; the mitigations are not. Kaspersky records the exploit as bypassing the sandbox across Reader 9, 10 and 11, so the containment layer the mitigations reinforce is the layer the exploit was built to defeat.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Alert on AcroRd32.exe spawning children, writing executables or making outbound connections, and on hosts resolving C2 by parsing Twitter or Google Search results.
detection.adequacy: Process-lineage detection is the reliable half. The dead-drop resolver traffic is genuinely hard: it is TLS to two of the most-visited domains on the internet, and separating it from user browsing needs content or timing analysis rather than destination reputation.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treat the opening user's context as compromised rather than the application: rebuild the host, rotate that user's credentials and tokens, and review what they could reach during the exposure window.
response.adequacy: Correct in scope, but bounded by retention - the campaign ran through February 2013 with victims across 23 countries, and reconstructing what a backdoor read requires logs most estates of that period did not keep.

NIST-800-53-SI-3.gap: Malicious code protection is the control that is supposed to catch a weaponised document, and it is the control the campaign was built against. The delivered artefact was a PDF whose lures were legitimate-looking human-rights and foreign-policy material, and the payload was a roughly 20 KB assembler downloader - Kaspersky's point about its size and hand-written assembler is that it presented almost no signature surface. SI-3 assessed as implemented, signatures current, is exactly the state 59 victims in 23 countries were in.

NIS2-Art21-vulnerability-handling.gap: Vulnerability handling starts when a fix exists, and here the exploitation preceded the advisory: NVD dates in-the-wild use to February 2013 and Adobe's APSA13-02 was published in response to it. A handling process cannot compress a window it is not yet aware of, so the measure that mattered was the pre-patch mitigation set in CERT/CC VU#422807, which sits outside what an Art. 21 vulnerability-handling procedure is scoped to trigger.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: The system security outcome expects software to be maintained and configured to resist attack. Reader XI running with the sandbox enabled was the maintained, correctly configured state, and the campaign's exploit was built specifically to bypass it - Kaspersky records the exploit working against Reader 9, 10 and 11 and bypassing the sandbox. An outcome-based assessment reads the containment layer as present and functioning, which is true and does not describe what happened.

AU-Essential-8-App-Hardening.gap: Application hardening for this product means Protected View, disabled JavaScript and EMET - the CERT/CC mitigation set. Two things limit it. Enabling Protected View and disabling JavaScript degrades the interactive PDF forms AcroForm exists to render, so the hardening competes with the business function; and the hardening was only actionable once VU#422807 published, which is after the February 2013 exploitation NVD records. The measure is real but arrives after the window it would have covered.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.7.gap: Protection against malware is the control that owns 'a user opened an attachment'. It is satisfied by anti-malware coverage plus user awareness, and both were defeated here by construction: the lure documents were topical and plausible, the exploit needed no macro or scripting prompt the user could decline, and the backdoor was a hand-written assembler binary sized to avoid detection. A conformity assessment finds the control implemented; the control's implementation is not what failed, its premise is.

new_control_requirements.name: PROTECTION-MECHANISM-FAILURE-CLASS-REGRESSION
new_control_requirements.description: Detonation chambers, EDR rules, and AppLocker/WDAC policies covering protection-mechanism classes (MOTW, SmartScreen, AMSI, ASR, WDAC, Driver Block Rules) must include class-level coverage rather than per-bypass signatures.
new_control_requirements.evidence: The Adobe Reader sandbox belongs to the same class this control governs - a containment mechanism the estate treats as a compensating control. Kaspersky records the in-the-wild exploit as working against Reader 9, 10 and 11 and bypassing the sandbox, so the mechanism's presence was not protection. The class-level requirement for this product is a detection that fires on the renderer process behaving outside its broker-mediated set, independent of which document format or CVE achieved the escape, plus an explicit register entry recording that Protected View is a delay rather than a boundary.

new_control_requirements.name: EMBEDDED-MEDIA-PARSER-LIBRARY-INVENTORY-AND-PATCH-PARITY
new_control_requirements.description: An organization must inventory every place a high-risk embedded media-parsing library (FreeType, image/codec/font/document parsers) is statically or dynamically bundled, including copies shipped inside other products.
new_control_requirements.evidence: AcroForm is the document-parsing component this control's class describes, and the CVE is an out-of-bounds write inside it reached by opening a file. The inventory obligation for this flaw is not just the Reader and Acrobat installs an asset register already lists: it is every product that embeds a PDF renderer for preview or print, since those inherit the parser without inheriting the patch cadence of the branch boundaries 9.5.4, 10.1.6 and 11.0.02.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: 4h KEV-listing mitigation SLA applies.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CISA added this CVE to KEV on 2022-03-03 with a 2022-03-24 due date - nine years after the February 2013 exploitation NVD records and long after every affected branch reached end of support. The SLA is therefore not a patch clock here but a discovery clock: four hours to answer whether any host still runs Reader or Acrobat at 9.5.3, 10.1.5 or 11.0.01 or earlier, since the fixed versions are themselves unsupported and the real action is migration rather than an update. EPSS on 2026-08-28 stood at 0.86979, the 99.737th percentile.

attack_vector.description: A remote attacker logs in to the ColdFusion RDS component using the empty password it ships with, and reuses that session against the ColdFusion Administrator web interface, which accepts it despite the Administrator password being different. Administrative access follows, and from there arbitrary CFML execution: the public implementation schedules a task that fetches a .cfm command-runner into the CFIDE webroot and invokes it.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none - unauthenticated HTTP to the ColdFusion instance; the only precondition is that the RDS password is empty
attack_vector.complexity: low - two HTTP exchanges, no user interaction, implemented as a GreatRanking Metasploit module with Windows and Linux targets
attack_vector.ai_factor: Not AI-discovered and not AI-weaponised; a 2012-2013 manual finding with a hand-written module.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Set an RDS password or disable RDS, and apply the APSB13-03 hotfix for the exact release; restrict /CFIDE/administrator, /CFIDE/adminapi and /CFIDE/componentutils to an administrative source range.
prevention.adequacy: Setting the RDS password closes this exact path immediately and without an outage, which is more than the hotfix can claim on a change-controlled estate. Neither is a durable answer: ColdFusion 9.x and 10 are both end-of-life, so the supported state is migration.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Alert on RDS logins with an empty password, on Administrator sessions with no preceding Administrator authentication, and on scheduled tasks that fetch a remote URL and publish a file into the CFIDE webroot.
detection.adequacy: Good for the published exploitation chain, which is noisy by construction - it writes a file into the webroot and then calls it. An attacker who stops at administrative access and reads configuration rather than dropping a file produces only the session anomaly, which is why the missing-Administrator-login signal is the one that matters.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treat the instance as administratively compromised: inventory the CFIDE webroot and the scheduler for artefacts, rotate every credential stored in the ColdFusion configuration including datasource passwords, and check what the ColdFusion service account can reach off the host.
response.adequacy: Bounded by what the Administrator console can read, which on a typical deployment includes datasource credentials for every database the application uses. The hotfix does not remove a web shell already written, so version remediation alone leaves the access in place.

NIST-800-53-IA-2.gap: Identification and authentication is enforced on the ColdFusion Administrator, and that enforcement is correct and irrelevant. The credential that mattered belongs to a different component - RDS - which authenticates on an empty default password and then hands out a session the Administrator accepts. IA-2 governs authenticating users to the system; it does not require an inventory of every component that can mint a session the management interface will honour, which is precisely the object here. An IA-2 assessment that verifies the Administrator password is set and strong records a pass on a fully exploitable installation.

NIS2-Art21-identity-management.gap: The Article 21 identity and access-management obligation is satisfied by having credential policy and access control in place, and this installation has both. What defeats it is that the vulnerable credential is a development-time default on a component that is not thought of as an identity surface at all - Adobe's own remedy, per the hotfix and the advisory's interim guidance, is to set the RDS password, meaning the fix is to stop using the default. The control gives no handling for a shipped-empty credential on a secondary component whose only function in production is to be unused.

UK-CAF-B2.gap: The identity and access-control outcome expects access to be granted only to authenticated and authorised parties. Two things break here that a B2 assessment does not test. First, the authorisation decision is transitive: an RDS session is accepted as an Administrator session, so authenticating against the weaker of two doors admits you through the stronger. Second, the exploitable state is a configuration default rather than a granted access, so a review of accounts, roles and privileges finds nothing wrong - there is no account to review, only an empty password on a component nobody enumerated.

AU-ISM-1546.gap: The ISM requirement that users are authenticated before being granted access to a system and its resources was met, and the attacker authenticated - to RDS, with the empty password the product shipped. The control does not distinguish between authenticating and authenticating against something worth authenticating against, and it has no requirement that a session issued by one component be scoped to that component rather than accepted by another. That transitivity, not the strength of any password, is the defect.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: Management of technical vulnerabilities requires exposure to be evaluated and acted on, and here the evaluation has been correct and unactionable for over a decade. Adobe hotfixed this on 2013-01-15; ColdFusion 9.x went end-of-life on 2014-12-31 and ColdFusion 10 on 2017-05-16. For any installation still carrying this CVE, the control's remedy - obtain the vendor fix - has been unavailable since 2017, and the control offers no state between 'patched' and 'accept the risk' for software whose vendor has stopped shipping fixes entirely.

new_control_requirements.name: OT-DEFAULT-CREDENTIAL-ELIMINATION
new_control_requirements.description: No internet-reachable device or service may ship or run with a vendor-default or blank administrative credential; enforce mandatory credential rotation at commissioning and verify it on a schedule.
new_control_requirements.evidence: The exploitable state of this CVE is literally a blank credential: NVD's description is 'logging in to the RDS component using the default empty password'. Adobe's own interim guidance for unsupported installations is to set that password. The catalogued control is written for internet-reachable OT devices, so this is a scope stretch to an application server's secondary authentication component - attached because no narrower control in the catalogue covers a blank vendor default, and because the check it demands (verify no component authenticates on an empty password) is the exact test that separates an exploitable ColdFusion instance from a safe one at any patch level.

new_control_requirements.name: ENTERPRISE-ERP-MANAGEMENT-FUNCTION-AUTHENTICATION
new_control_requirements.description: An enterprise platform must authenticate every management-plane and environment-management function before it can act, on every request path rather than on the primary one.
new_control_requirements.evidence: The ColdFusion Administrator authenticates callers correctly on its own login path and accepts an RDS-minted session on another. That is the failure this control names: authentication proven on the path the assessor tests and absent on the path the attacker uses. The catalogued wording is scoped to ERP platforms (PeopleSoft, E-Business Suite, SAP); the stretch to an application server's administration console is deliberate, because the structural fault - one management plane, two entry points, one of them unauthenticated - is identical.

new_control_requirements.name: EOL-ASSET-DECOMMISSION
new_control_requirements.description: Network-reachable end-of-life products with no vendor patch path must be isolated and decommissioned within a bounded window; mandatory compensating segmentation applies until removal.
new_control_requirements.evidence: ColdFusion 9.x has had no vendor patch path since 2014-12-31 and ColdFusion 10 since 2017-05-16, yet CISA's 2022-03-03 KEV listing directs 'Apply updates per vendor instructions' for a product line whose vendor stopped issuing them years earlier. For any instance still carrying this CVE, the only honest remediation states are segmentation with a dated removal or migration to a supported release - which is what this control requires and what a patch-availability-based verdict cannot express.

CVE-2012-4681.name: Oracle Java SE Runtime Environment (JRE) Arbitrary Code Execution Vulnerability (CVE-2012-4681)

attack_vector.description: A browser with the Java plugin enabled loads a crafted applet. The applet reaches restricted classes such as sun.awt.SunToolkit through com.sun.beans.finder.ClassFinder.findClass, leveraging an exception from forName, then uses reflection with a trusted immediate caller to reach getField and modify private fields - manipulating AccessControlContext to disable the SecurityManager. The applet then runs as fully trusted code with the browser user's privileges. NVD records the in-the-wild samples as Gondzz.class and Gondvv.class, August 2012.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none on the target - the attacker needs only to serve content the browser loads
attack_vector.complexity: low - a pure-Java logic bug with no memory corruption, so exploitation is deterministic with no ASLR or DEP to defeat, and the same applet works across browsers and operating systems because the defect is in the runtime
attack_vector.ai_factor: Not AI-discovered and not AI-weaponised. No AI tooling is credited in any source consulted, and the flaw surfaced through analysis of samples already in use in the wild.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Disable or remove the Java browser plugin. Applet execution is the only path to this defect, so removing it closes this CVE and every other applet-sandbox bypass at once - which is the direction Oracle itself took, deprecating the plugin at Java 9 and removing it from the JDK at Java 11.
prevention.framework_requiring_it: AU Essential Eight user application hardening (blocking Java from the internet in web browsers); CISA BOD 22-01 for the KEV listing added 2022-03-03, due 2022-03-24
prevention.adequacy: Sufficient and durable, and it is the action that still applies. Patching above 7u6 was sufficient in 2012 but is not a durable answer now, because the Java 7 line has no supported fix left to move to.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Alert on the Java runtime process spawning a child process after a browser navigation, and on JAR retrieval from hosts outside the applet allowlist.
detection.adequacy: The child-process signal is sound and technique-independent - a sandboxed applet has no legitimate reason to create a process. It is also late: by the time it fires, the SecurityManager is already disabled and code is running as the user.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treat the endpoint as compromised at user privilege: rotate the user's credentials and any tokens cached on the host, and check what that account reaches, since the exploit inherits it exactly.
response.adequacy: Bounded by the user account's own authorisation, which on a 2012-era desktop estate frequently included local administrator - and where it does, the response extends past the endpoint to everything that account can reach.

NIST-800-53-CM-7.gap: Least functionality is the control that closes this, and it did not because CM-7 operates on whether a function is needed rather than on which part of it is needed. The Java browser plugin was not an optional extra in 2012 - it was a default-enabled component of a runtime that line-of-business applications required. CM-7 asks that unnecessary functions be disabled and provides a documented-exception route for the ones that are not, so an exception written for the runtime carries its browser plugin along with it. Nothing in CM-7 distinguishes 'the JRE is required' from 'the JRE's browser plugin is required', which is the distinction that decides exposure here, and the one Oracle itself eventually settled by deprecating the plugin at Java 9 and removing it from the JDK at Java 11.

NIS2-Art21-patch-management.gap: The Article 21 patch-management obligation is keyed to fix availability, and the fix has been available since 2012. For an estate that patched on schedule then, the obligation produces a clean record and says nothing further. For an estate still exposed in 2026 it produces a finding that has been open continuously for fourteen years without the obligation escalating, because there is no mechanism in it that treats duration as severity. It is also silent on the case that actually applies now: the Java 7 line has no supported fix to apply, so 'apply the vendor's patch' has no target and the obligation cannot express the answer, which is removal.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: The system-security outcome expects vulnerable software to be identified and updated, and identification fails here for a reason a CAF assessment will not surface: the property that determines exposure is not the JRE version but whether the browser plugin is enabled. A host at 7u6 with no plugin is not exposed; a host at 7u6 with a plugin is fully exposed; both present identically to an inventory that records installed software versions. The outcome asks whether vulnerable software is updated and gets a version number back, when the question that decides the risk is a configuration one.

AU-Essential-8-App-Hardening.gap: User application hardening is the Essential Eight control aimed directly at this - blocking Java from the internet in web browsers is one of its named requirements - and it is the right control, which makes the gap a maturity-model one rather than an absence. The requirement is expressed as a browser configuration state, and it carries no obligation to verify that state per host against the JRE actually installed, nor to re-verify after a browser or runtime update re-registers the plugin. An organisation can hold the control at a documented maturity level while individual endpoints have the plugin back, and nothing in the model surfaces the drift.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: Management of technical vulnerabilities requires vulnerability information to be obtained and exposure evaluated. Both ran here and the evaluation input was as strong as this control ever receives - NVD's own description names the in-the-wild sample classes, Gondzz.class and Gondvv.class, and dates the attacks to August 2012. The gap is on the other side: A.8.8 has no clause that converts a repeatedly-exploited component into a removal decision. Fourteen years of the same control cycle re-evaluating the same finding produces fourteen compliant evaluations of an exposure whose correct disposition was to delete the plugin, which is what the platform vendor itself did - deprecating it at Java 9 and removing it from the JDK at Java 11.

new_control_requirements.name: CONFIGURATION-SIDE-LIVE-PATCH-INVENTORY
new_control_requirements.description: For any vulnerability with a configuration-side mitigation path, that path must be inventoried, tested and deployable independently of the vendor-patch path, so that operators are not dependent on a patch cycle to remove reachability.
new_control_requirements.evidence: The configuration-side path here is stronger than the patch and outlives it. This defect is reachable only through applet execution, so disabling the Java browser plugin closes CVE-2012-4681 and every other applet-sandbox bypass, on every host, without a version change - whereas patching above 7u6 closed one defect on a line that has since run out of fixes entirely. The plugin state is also what actually determines exposure: two hosts at identical JRE versions differ completely depending on it, which is why the mitigation has to be inventoried per host rather than assumed from a policy document.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: 4h KEV-listing mitigation SLA applies.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CISA added CVE-2012-4681 on 2022-03-03 with a 2022-03-24 due date, nearly ten years after the fix shipped and after NVD had already recorded in-the-wild exploitation in the CVE description itself. An hours-scale SLA is deliverable here precisely because the mitigation is a configuration push rather than a runtime upgrade: disabling the browser plugin needs no package deployment, no reboot and no application regression testing against a new JRE build.

new_control_requirements.name: EOL-ASSET-DECOMMISSION
new_control_requirements.description: A network-reachable component with no vendor patch path must be isolated and decommissioned within a bounded window, with mandatory compensating segmentation or disablement applying until removal completes.
new_control_requirements.evidence: This control is written in the catalogue for end-of-life devices and is attached here as the closest existing control for the same terminal state in software, which is where CVE-2012-4681 now sits: the Java 7 line is long past public updates, so there is no version above 7u6 that an operator can move to and stay supported. Oracle deprecated the browser plugin at Java 9 and removed it from the JDK at Java 11, which means the reachable surface does not exist on a current runtime - so the bounded window here is a migration window off Java 7 with the plugin disabled as the compensating control in the interim, not a patch window.

CVE-2012-1856.name: Microsoft Office MSCOMCTL.OCX TabStrip ActiveX Remote Code Execution Vulnerability (CVE-2012-1856)

attack_vector.description: A crafted document — Microsoft's workarounds point at RTF — or a web page instantiates the TabStrip ActiveX control in MSCOMCTL.OCX and corrupts the system state, executing code as the logged-on user. The interesting property is not the corruption but the binary: MSCOMCTL.OCX is the shared Windows Common Controls OCX, so the affected population is defined by whichever of Office, SQL Server, Commerce Server, Host Integration Server, Visual FoxPro or the VB6 Runtime happens to be installed, each with its own MS12-060 package.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none — PR:N, but UI:R. No account is needed; a user must open the document or view the page. Code then runs with that user's rights, not SYSTEM.
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L, with no race and no memory-disclosure prerequisite. The real difficulty is on the defender's side: establishing whether a given host still carries a pre-MS12-060 MSCOMCTL.OCX under a product nobody thinks of as patchable.
attack_vector.ai_factor: None. A 2012 disclosure found through in-the-wild targeted attacks; no AI-assisted discovery or weaponisation is claimed by any source.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Installing MS12-060 for every affected product present on the host, so the replaced MSCOMCTL.OCX is the only copy on disk. Short of that, the kill bit for CLSID {1EFB6596-857C-11D1-B16A-00C0F0283628} plus the Office RTF FileOpenBlock policy and 'Disable all controls without notifications' in ActiveX Settings.
prevention.adequacy: The binary replacement is complete. The workarounds are not, and the bulletin is honest about the split: the kill bit covers Internet Explorer instantiation only, and the document vector is closed by the RTF block and the ActiveX setting, each of which costs functionality. An estate that applied the kill bit alone mitigated the vector the observed attacks did not use.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Inventorying MSCOMCTL.OCX by file version rather than by installed application, and alerting on an Office or VB6 process spawning a command interpreter after a document open.
detection.adequacy: The file-version sweep is the reliable half and it answers the question the software inventory cannot. The behavioural half is generic: an Office process spawning cmd.exe is an indicator for a large family of document-borne execution, so it will not attribute a hit to this CVE. Nothing available here detects the corruption itself, and Microsoft published no detection guidance beyond the update and the workarounds.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treating a hit as user-context execution: audit what the affected user account could reach, and complete the MS12-060 rollout across every product on the host rather than the one that opened the file.
response.adequacy: Proportionate — code ran as the logged-on user, not SYSTEM, so the containment boundary is that user's access rather than the machine. The weakness is timing: by the 2022 KEV listing, the affected products were long out of support, so 'complete the rollout' can mean sourcing a 2012 update package for Commerce Server 2002 or the VB6 Runtime, which is a procurement problem rather than a patching one.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: The fix has existed since 2012-08-14 and CISA still listed the CVE in March 2022. SI-2 measures remediation of identified flaws, and the identification step fails here because MS12-060 spans six product families with separate packages — a host can be fully patched for Office and still carry the vulnerable MSCOMCTL.OCX under SQL Server 2005 or the VB6 Runtime.

AU-Essential-8-App-Hardening.gap: The Essential Eight application-hardening control lands directly on this vector by requiring ActiveX to be blocked in Office, which is unusually good coverage. It stops at Office, PDF, Java, Flash and the browser, so the same shared OCX remains instantiable through Visual FoxPro, the VB6 Runtime and the SQL Server client tools, which the control does not reach.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: Evaluating exposure requires knowing which hosts carry a pre-MS12-060 MSCOMCTL.OCX, and an asset inventory records installed applications rather than shared library file versions. A.8.8 can therefore be executed correctly and still return the wrong answer for this CVE.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: MS12-060 shipped on 2012-08-14 and CISA listed the CVE on 2022-03-03 with a due date of 2022-03-24 — nine and a half years in which the patch existed and estates carried the flaw. This control fires on the listing rather than on a score, which matters here because EPSS reads 0.72225 at the 99.407th percentile: high enough to be prioritised, but the CVE has been available to prioritise for over a decade. 'Verified' on this product cannot mean 'MS12-060 installed'; it has to mean the MSCOMCTL.OCX file version on disk is the post-update build, because the update is per-product and the binary is shared.

new_control_requirements.name: MITIGATION-ACTIVE-PATCH-PENDING-VERDICT-CLASS
new_control_requirements.description: Compliance verdicts must distinguish three states: (a) binary patch deployed, so the vulnerability is eliminated; (b) a vendor-mitigation rule is active with no binary patch, leaving the residual risk that any defect or gap in the mitigation reopens the flaw; (c) neither.
new_control_requirements.evidence: MS12-060 is the textbook case for this distinction because it ships both states in one update: it sets the Internet Explorer kill bit for CLSID {1EFB6596-857C-11D1-B16A-00C0F0283628} and separately replaces MSCOMCTL.OCX. The kill bit is state (b) and covers the browser vector only; Microsoft's own workaround list adds the RTF FileOpenBlock policy and 'Disable all controls without notifications' precisely because the kill bit does not close the crafted-document path, which is the one the limited targeted attacks used. A verdict that records 'mitigated' without naming which of the two mechanisms is in place cannot tell an operator whether the observed attack vector is closed.

CVE-2012-1723.name: Oracle Java HotSpot Bytecode Verifier Type Confusion Sandbox Escape

attack_vector.description: A crafted class exploits an invalid optimization of GETFIELD/PUTFIELD/GETSTATIC/PUTSTATIC in the HotSpot bytecode verifier, which performs insufficient type checks and allows a field to be read back as a type it was not written as. The resulting type confusion forges a reference, disables the security manager and escapes the applet sandbox into user-context execution. Delivery in the documented campaigns is a hostile applet served from a compromised website.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none on the target - the applet arrives through the browser and executes as the logged-on user
attack_vector.complexity: low - deterministic type confusion with no memory grooming, published as an Excellent-ranked exploit module a month after the fix
attack_vector.ai_factor: Not AI-discovered and not AI-weaponised; the exploit and the Epic Turla loader documented by Kaspersky are hand-written.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Install the Oracle June 2012 Critical Patch Update on every runtime, including application-bundled JREs, and disable the Java browser plugin on hosts that do not need it.
prevention.adequacy: Sufficient where the inventory is complete, which is the weak point: four separate branch boundaries and bundled runtimes mean a host can be patched and still carry a vulnerable copy. Removing the plugin closes the observed delivery path but not the defect.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Alert on java.exe or javaw.exe spawning a child process, and treat any Exploit.Java.CVE-2012-1723 family detection as a confirmed exploitation attempt rather than a blocked-file event.
detection.adequacy: Partial. Kaspersky's own naming shows four distinct sample variants plus a generic heuristic, so signature coverage trails each recompilation; the process-lineage rule is the durable half because it keys on the consequence rather than the sample.

response.what_would_have_worked: On a confirmed detection, treat the workstation as compromised at user level: rotate the user's credentials and any token cached on the host, hunt for injection into explorer.exe, and check whether the site that served the applet is used by other staff - Kaspersky records these as targeted watering holes rather than opportunistic ones.
response.adequacy: Adequate for the host, insufficient for the campaign. The watering hole stays live after one victim is remediated, so a response that ends at reimaging leaves every other visitor to that site exposed.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: Flaw remediation asks that flaws be identified, reported and corrected. On this CVE the identification half fails on inventory rather than on process: the affected component is the Hotspot verifier inside a JRE, and the branch boundaries are four separate lines (7u4, 6u32, 5u35, 1.4.2_37), so a host can carry a patched desktop JRE and a second runtime bundled inside an application that SI-2 never enumerated. Correcting the managed runtime and closing the ticket is a compliant outcome that leaves the exploit working against the copy nobody listed.

NIST-800-53-SI-3.gap: Malicious code protection is signature-and-reputation driven, and Kaspersky's own detection names for this CVE - Exploit.Java.CVE-2012-1723.eh, .ou, .ov, .ow - are per-variant, with a separate HEUR: generic added alongside them. That enumeration is the shape of the problem: the operators recompiled the applet in, as the report puts it, various configurations, so SI-3 coverage was retrospective for each new variant while the underlying verifier defect stayed identical.

NIS2-Art21-patch-management.gap: Art. 21 measures resolve here to installing the June 2012 Oracle CPU. The gap is not the timeframe but the asset boundary: an Art. 21 patch-management measure is written against the entity's network and information systems, and the exploited component is a browser plugin whose delivery path is a third-party website the entity does not operate - Kaspersky records the Epic Turla operators compromising sites of interest to their victims. Nothing in the patch measure reaches the compromised intermediary, so the entity's exposure ends only when its own runtime is updated.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: The system security outcome expects services to be configured and maintained to resist attack. An estate on a supported, currently-patched Java branch met that until the June 2012 CPU published, and had no configuration lever that would have refused the crafted class - the verifier is the mechanism that was supposed to make untrusted classes safe. The only pre-patch measure that works, removing the browser plugin, is a functionality decision rather than a maintenance one.

UK-CAF-D1.gap: Response and recovery planning is written around incidents the organisation detects on its own systems. This intrusion arrives as a browser visiting a legitimate site, and the recovered artefact is an applet in the Java deployment cache, not an alert from a service the organisation runs. Kaspersky's report attributes the delivery network to the Epic Turla operators; a response plan that classifies a Java exploit detection as commodity malware and reimages the host will close the ticket without ever reaching the credential and lateral-movement questions that attribution demands.

AU-Essential-8-App-Hardening.gap: Application hardening is the Essential Eight control that names this exact class - blocking Java from the internet in web browsers is one of its stated requirements, and applying it would have removed the delivery path Kaspersky documents. Two things limit it here. It is scoped to the browser, so a vulnerable runtime invoked outside the browser is untouched; and the Essential Eight maturity model that states the requirement postdates the June 2012 disclosure, so no organisation was measured against it during the period the exploit was being served.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: Management of technical vulnerabilities requires vulnerability information to be obtained and acted on. Acting on it means replacing the runtime on every host that carries one, and A.8.8 offers no interim measure for the window before that: the vendor documents no workaround for the verifier defect, and the lever that does work - removing the Java browser plugin - is an availability decision about an application capability that an A.8.8 process is not scoped to take.

new_control_requirements.name: PROTECTION-MECHANISM-FAILURE-CLASS-REGRESSION
new_control_requirements.description: Detonation chambers, EDR rules and application-control policies covering protection-mechanism classes must include class-level regression testing executed on every patch deployment, not one-off remediation of the individual bypass CVE. The test battery for a class must include all historic bypass primitives for that class, because incomplete patches re-introduce risk that one-off testing does not detect.
new_control_requirements.evidence: The control is written for Windows protection mechanisms (MOTW, SmartScreen, AMSI, application control); the class it names - a security boundary defeated by a bypass primitive - is exactly the JRE applet sandbox here, and this CVE is a sandbox escape rather than a memory-corruption bug. The regression discipline is the load-bearing part for this entry because Kaspersky recovered the exploit in, in its wording, various configurations, with four distinct sample variants named. The operational test: after any Java update, re-run the stored class of sandbox-escape samples against the deployed runtime and confirm the security manager is not disabled, rather than confirming only that the version string moved past 7u4 / 6u32 / 5u35 / 1.4.2_37.

new_control_requirements.name: NATION-STATE-INITIAL-ACCESS-IR-ESCALATION
new_control_requirements.description: IR runbooks must include an explicit escalation path triggered by named threat-actor attribution on a confirmed exploit chain. Standard malware-infection IR under-escalates targeted activity by treating it as a commodity threat.
new_control_requirements.evidence: This CVE has published attribution: Kaspersky GReAT's 'The Epic Turla Operation' (2014-08-07) names watering-hole attacks using CVE-2012-1723 as an initial-access method for that operation, publishes the sample detection names, and describes a loader that injected the Epic backdoor into explorer.exe. The trigger condition for this entry is therefore concrete rather than hypothetical: an Exploit.Java.CVE-2012-1723 detection on a workstation is a candidate for that escalation path, and the questions it opens - which site served the applet, who else in the organisation visits it, what credentials the logged-on user held - are precisely the ones a reimage-and-close response never asks.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CISA listed this on 2022-03-03 with a 2022-03-24 due date - a three-week window for a flaw whose vendor fix had existed since June 2012, whose exploit module had been public since 2012-07-11 as Exploit-DB 19717, and which CISA itself flags as known to be used in ransomware campaigns; EPSS on 2026-08-28 was 0.93688 at the 99.837th percentile. A four-hour clock on a CVE this old is not a patch clock, because any host still affected has missed a decade of updates: the deliverable is disabling the Java browser plugin and enumerating every bundled runtime, with the version upgrade scheduled behind that.

CVE-2012-1535.name: Adobe Flash Player Kern Table Integer Overflow (CVE-2012-1535)

attack_vector.description: A crafted SWF carrying an embedded OpenType font declares a kern table with version 0x10000 and an nTables value of 0x10000000 or higher. The size calculation overflows, the undersized allocation is overrun, and heap corruption becomes code execution as the user. In the observed attacks the SWF was embedded in a Word document, reaching the ActiveX build of Flash Player through Office rather than through a browsed page.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none, but the victim must open the document or page carrying the SWF
attack_vector.complexity: low - deterministic parser arithmetic, with public ROP chains for three specific Flash builds within three days of the bulletin
attack_vector.ai_factor: Not AI-assisted. Found in the wild in 2012; no AI tooling is credited in any source consulted.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: At the time, updating to Flash Player 11.3.300.271 (Windows, Mac OS X) or 11.2.202.238 (Linux) per APSB12-18. Now, uninstalling the runtime, since Adobe ended support on 2020-12-31 and began blocking Flash content on 2021-01-12.
prevention.adequacy: Updating was adequate in 2012 and is not an option now - the only terminal state for a surviving installation is removal, which a patch-oriented process will not produce on its own.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Alert on Office applications spawning child processes after a document open, and on Flash Player faults during font handling.
detection.adequacy: Behavioural only. Adobe describes limited targeted attacks, so volume-based detection would not have fired; the parent-child process signal is the reliable one.

response.what_would_have_worked: Remove the runtime from the affected host, then investigate the second stage rather than the exploit - execution runs as the user, so credential and session exposure follows.
response.adequacy: Removal is decisive for the exposure; it says nothing about what already executed, which is why the response has to reach the payload.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: Flaw remediation has no destination for this CVE any more. The version that fixes it, 11.3.300.271, belongs to a runtime Adobe stopped supporting on 2020-12-31 and began actively blocking on 2021-01-12, so an SI-2 process that tracks 'apply the vendor update' has nothing to apply - the only terminal state is removal of the runtime, which SI-2 does not itself require.

NIS2-Art21-patch-management.gap: Patch management assumes the supplier is still shipping. Here the supplier withdrew the product: a NIS2-aligned process that records Flash Player as fully patched at 11.3.300.271 is recording a true statement about this CVE and a false one about the asset, because every Flash defect disclosed after end of life has no fix at all. The obligation this CVE actually creates is an inventory and removal action, not a patch action.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: Secure system configuration and maintenance treats an application as a maintainable component. The CAF outcome does not distinguish a component that is current from one whose vendor has withdrawn it, so a host running Flash Player 11.3.300.271 evidences 'patched to the latest available version' indefinitely while carrying an unsupported runtime that parses attacker-supplied fonts out of Word attachments.
