attack_vector.ai_factor: Not AI-discovered and not AI-weaponised. The public exploit is a short hand-written Python script.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Set load_examples=False and confirm example_trigger_target_dag is gone from the DAG list - NVD states a deployment with examples disabled is not vulnerable - then upgrade to Airflow 1.10.11 or later and close the Experimental REST API's default auth backend.
prevention.adequacy: Effective and unusually cheap, because the vulnerable code is optional sample content rather than platform logic. It is insufficient backwards: execution as the worker or scheduler account exposes the connection store and the Fernet key, so neither the setting change nor the upgrade undoes a prior compromise without credential rotation.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Alert on any DAG run of example_trigger_target_dag, on DAG runs created through the Experimental REST API, and on the airflow account spawning shell commands that no task definition accounts for.
detection.adequacy: Strong for this CVE specifically, because the DAG name is a fixed, meaningless-in-production string that makes for a precise signal. Weaker as a class defence - an attacker who reaches DAG authoring after the first execution runs code under a legitimate DAG name, and the same alert then says nothing.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treat every credential in the connection store as burned: rotate the connections and the Fernet key, review DAG files and the metadata database for definitions no deployment produced, and audit the downstream systems those connections reach for activity in the exposure window.
response.adequacy: The credential half is decisive and is the part most often skipped. Integrity is harder: an attacker with execution can modify DAG code that then runs on schedule, so verification needs an out-of-band comparison against the source repository rather than a review of what the scheduler currently holds.

NIST-800-53-CM-7.gap: Least functionality asks that unnecessary functions be disabled, and this CVE is the clearest possible case for it: the vulnerable code is a shipped example DAG that no production deployment needs, and NVD states that disabling examples makes the deployment not vulnerable. The gap is in the default and in the verification. Example DAGs load unless load_examples is set to False, so a CM-7 baseline that does not name this specific setting leaves the function enabled by inaction rather than by decision; and because an already-imported DAG persists in the metadata database after the setting changes, a CM-7 check that reads the configuration file records the function as disabled while example_trigger_target_dag is still triggerable.

NIST-800-53-AC-6.gap: Least privilege is doubly bypassed here. On the front side, the vendor's own description says any authenticated user reaches the injection, so an AC-6 model that grants ordinary users the minimum Airflow role still grants them command execution; on the back side, the command runs as the worker or scheduler account, which holds every credential the platform orchestrates, so the privilege that matters is the service account's rather than the user's. AC-6 has no expression that separates 'a user who may trigger a DAG' from 'a user who may run shell commands as the orchestration service account', because on an affected version those are the same permission.

NIS2-Art21-patch-management.gap: Art. 21 measures resolve to moving to 1.10.11. What Art. 21 does not carry is the second half of the remediation this flaw needs: the execution account can read Airflow's connection store and the Fernet key protecting it, so an upgrade that leaves those credentials in place leaves any pre-upgrade compromise live through credentials the patch does not rotate. A patch-management measure that records 1.10.11 as deployed states something true and incomplete, and the article provides no obligation that reaches the credential rotation.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: The system security outcome expects services to be configured and maintained to resist attack. An estate could be maintained correctly on Airflow 1.10.10 - a supported release at the time - and be fully exposed, because the vulnerable artefact is content the vendor ships and enables by default. The configuration decision that would have saved it, load_examples=False, is presented in the documentation as a convenience setting about sample content rather than as a security control, so a B4 assessment reviewing the deployment against vendor guidance would not have flagged it.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: The Essential Eight patch-applications control runs its timeframes from vendor release and is scoped to internet-facing services and named application classes. Airflow's webserver is frequently an internal service rather than an internet-facing one, so the shortest timeframe may not attach at all; and the unit the control tracks is the deployed application version, while the exposure here is a combination of that version and two configuration settings - load_examples and the Experimental API auth backend - that no patch-timeframe assessment inspects.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.9.gap: Configuration management requires that configurations, including security configurations, be established, documented, implemented, monitored and reviewed. That is exactly the control that would have caught this, and its weakness here is the monitoring clause: the two settings that decide exposure are load_examples and the Experimental API auth backend, both of which have permissive defaults, and A.8.9 baselines are typically derived from vendor hardening guidance rather than from an enumeration of which defaults reach a shell. Monitoring the setting is also insufficient without monitoring its effect, since an already-imported example DAG survives the setting change.

new_control_requirements.name: AI-APP-BUILDER-EXECUTION-ENDPOINT-AUTH-AND-SANDBOX
new_control_requirements.description: A workflow or agent builder platform must authenticate every endpoint that can reach a code-execution path, must never run request-supplied content through a dynamic-evaluation or shell path with host privileges, and must be placed behind authenticated access control and never exposed to untrusted networks. The distinguishing test is to send an unauthenticated request to each build, validate and run endpoint on a staging instance with a payload attempting a non-workflow action, and confirm it is refused before any code runs.
new_control_requirements.evidence: The control names visual LLM and workflow builders including n8n-class platforms; Airflow is the same shape - a workflow platform whose by-design function is executing operator-authored code, reached over an HTTP API. Both halves of the control fail on an affected deployment: the Experimental REST API's default auth backend permits unauthenticated calls (the paired CVE-2020-13927), and the shipped example_trigger_target_dag interpolates a request-supplied conf field straight into a shell command as the worker or scheduler account. The distinguishing test maps directly: POST to /api/experimental/dags/example_trigger_target_dag/dag_runs on a staging instance with a conf message carrying a shell metacharacter and confirm it is refused - which requires both the auth backend closed and the example DAGs gone.

new_control_requirements.name: AI-ML-DEVELOPER-TOOLING-INVENTORY
new_control_requirements.description: Organizations using AI/ML systems must maintain a separate inventory of developer-tooling control planes (notebook servers, experiment trackers, model registries, vector-DB admin UIs, agent frameworks) recording each exposed network endpoint, the authentication mechanism per endpoint, the blast radius reachable from that tool, and a patch SLA tier distinct from generic application patching.
new_control_requirements.evidence: An Airflow deployment is a pipeline control plane of exactly the class this control enumerates, and this CVE shows why the per-endpoint authentication column and the blast-radius column both matter. The endpoint column would record that /api/experimental/ answers under a permissive default auth backend, which is what turns an authenticated-user flaw into an unauthenticated one. The blast-radius column for this host is not the DAG metadata but the connection store and the Fernet key that protects it, because the injected command runs as the worker or scheduler account - so the systems reachable from Airflow are the ones to list against it, and they are the ones that need credential rotation after any exposure window.

new_control_requirements.name: CISA-KEV-RESPONSE-SLA
new_control_requirements.description: For any CVE listed in CISA KEV: deploy verified mitigation (patch, live patch, or documented compensating controls) within 4 hours of KEV listing or patch availability, whichever is later.
new_control_requirements.evidence: CISA listed this on 2022-01-18 with a 2022-07-18 due date - six months for a flaw whose fix shipped in 1.10.11 in July 2020, whose Metasploit module carries a 2020-07-14 disclosure date, and whose EPSS on 2026-08-28 was 0.99189 at the 99.932nd percentile, the highest in this set. This is one of the rare entries where a four-hour clock is genuinely achievable end to end: setting load_examples=False and restarting the scheduler removes the vulnerable code entirely per NVD's own statement, so the compensating control and the remediation coincide, with the 1.10.11 upgrade and the credential rotation scheduled behind it.

CVE-2020-13927.name: Apache Airflow Experimental API Default Allow-All Authentication

attack_vector.description: An unauthenticated caller reaches Airflow's Experimental REST API, which the shipped `[api] auth_backend` default allowed through without authentication, and uses it to trigger DAG runs. A DAG is Python the scheduler and workers execute, so the API is a code-execution surface; the public chain pairs it with the CVE-2020-11978 example-DAG command injection for unauthenticated RCE against Airflow 1.10.10, landing next to the connection credentials Airflow holds for every system its pipelines touch.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none (unauthenticated HTTP request to the Airflow webserver)
attack_vector.complexity: trivial - a single request; the API answers because that was the shipped default, so there is no exploit to develop
attack_vector.ai_factor: Not AI-related. The project changed its own default and documented the change; no AI tooling is involved in discovery or exploitation.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Set `[api] auth_backend = airflow.api.auth.backend.deny_all` in airflow.cfg and restart the webserver, per the project's 1.10.11 Updating guide, and remove the bundled example DAGs from production. Upgrading past 1.10.11 alone does not do this for an existing install.
prevention.adequacy: Sufficient and easily mis-evidenced: the check that matters is the running configuration value, not the version string a scanner reports.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Alert on unauthenticated /api/experimental/ requests returning 200, and on DAG runs created with no corresponding webserver session.
detection.adequacy: Reliable, because a legitimate caller on a correctly configured instance cannot produce that response at all.

response.what_would_have_worked: Rotate every credential stored in Airflow connections, audit the DAGs folder for additions and modifications, and review worker egress for the exposure window.
response.adequacy: Decisive, and the part most often skipped - the flaw's real value to an attacker is the connection store, not the orchestrator itself.

NIST-800-53-IA-2.gap: Identification and authentication is assessed per system, and the Experimental API is a second, separate entry point on a system whose primary web interface does authenticate. An assessor who confirms that Airflow's UI enforces login has evidenced IA-2 truthfully and has not touched /api/experimental, where the shipped `[api] auth_backend` default answered every caller - the control does not require the authentication mechanism to be proven complete across every request path the service exposes.

NIS2-Art21-vulnerability-management.gap: Vulnerability management resolved against version numbers gets the wrong answer here, and the vendor says so: the project's own guidance is that 1.10.11 'fixes it for new installs but existing users need to change their config'. A scanner reporting Airflow 1.10.11 or later marks the finding closed while an upgraded instance carrying its original airflow.cfg still serves the Experimental API unauthenticated.

UK-CAF-B2.gap: Identity and access control assumes a service has an access-control decision point that policy can be applied to. Before the configuration change there is none on this path - the shipped backend's decision is to allow - so there is no policy an operator can write, no role to scope and no credential to strengthen. The CAF outcome is satisfiable in every respect that does not touch the Experimental API's own configuration line.

AU-Essential-8-MFA.gap: Multi-factor authentication is the Essential Eight mitigation for exactly this asset class - an internet-reachable service holding privileged access to other systems - and it has nothing to attach to. The Experimental API accepts requests with no authentication step at all, so there is no first factor for a second factor to strengthen, and an Essential Eight assessment scoring MFA on the Airflow web UI records maturity on the interface that was never the exposure.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.9.gap: Configuration management is the control that matches this defect exactly, and the gap is what it takes as the configuration baseline. The vulnerable value is the vendor's own shipped default, so a baseline derived from the product's out-of-the-box state encodes the vulnerability as the standard - and the corrected state is not a version but a specific line, `[api] auth_backend = airflow.api.auth.backend.deny_all`, which has to be asserted and then re-verified after every upgrade that might reintroduce an older config.

new_control_requirements.name: AI-ML-DEVELOPER-TOOLING-INVENTORY
new_control_requirements.description: Organizations must maintain a separate inventory of developer-tooling and pipeline control planes with, per entry: exposed network endpoints, the authentication mechanism on each endpoint, blast-radius mapping of what data and production systems are reachable from the tool, and a patch SLA tier separate from generic application patching.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Airflow is the data-pipeline control plane the control describes, and this CVE turns each clause into a concrete question. Exposed endpoints: the webserver UI and /api/experimental are two distinct surfaces on one port. Authentication mechanism per endpoint: the UI authenticates while the Experimental API's shipped `[api] auth_backend` default did not, which is precisely why a per-system authentication verdict is the wrong granularity. Blast radius: an Airflow DAG is executed Python, and Airflow connections hold the credentials for the databases, cloud accounts and SaaS APIs its pipelines touch, so unauthenticated API access reaches those credentials - the reason Intezer's October 2021 survey of exposed instances recovered AWS, PayPal and Slack credentials. Separate SLA tier: CISA listed this on 2022-01-18 with EPSS reaching 0.99778 on 2026-08-28, which is not a cadence a generic application-patching tier serves.

new_control_requirements.name: MITIGATION-ACTIVE-PATCH-PENDING-VERDICT-CLASS
new_control_requirements.description: Compliance verdicts must distinguish binary-patch-deployed from vendor-mitigation-active-without-patch from no-mitigation-at-all, and must surface the middle state as a time-bound compensating control rather than as a patched-per-SLA outcome.
new_control_requirements.evidence: This CVE inverts the control's own ordering, and the vendor states the inversion: the 1.10.11 change 'fixes it for new installs but existing users need to change their config'. So the version upgrade is not state (a) at all for an existing deployment - the configuration edit is, and an instance on 1.10.11 or later with an unmodified airflow.cfg is in state (c), full exposure, while every version-based record calls it patched. The distinguishing test is a request rather than a version string: issue an unauthenticated GET to /api/experimental/latest_runs and confirm refusal, the same probe the public detection template sends. Precondition: neither verdict speaks to what was already read - the credentials in Airflow connections stay valid until rotated.

new_control_requirements.name: CONFIGURATION-SIDE-LIVE-PATCH-INVENTORY
new_control_requirements.description: For any web-fabric vulnerability with a configuration-side mitigation path: that path must be inventoried, tested, and deployable independent of the vendor-patch path.
new_control_requirements.evidence: Here the configuration-side path is not the fallback - it is the remediation. There is no code defect to fix: the vulnerable value is a shipped default, so the operator action is setting `[api] auth_backend = airflow.api.auth.backend.deny_all` and restarting the webserver, deployable immediately and entirely independent of any upgrade. For this product the control means knowing in advance where airflow.cfg lives in each deployment, how the value survives a container rebuild or a config-management run, and whether the bundled example DAGs the public exploit chain uses are present. Precondition: the setting is durable only if it is owned by configuration management - an upgrade or a redeploy that restores an older airflow.cfg silently reopens the API, and nothing in the version string records that.

CVE-2021-22017.name: VMware vCenter rhttpproxy URI Normalization Bypass (CVE-2021-22017)

attack_vector.description: rhttpproxy on vCenter port 443 decides which internal endpoint a request may reach, and normalises `..;/` path segments differently from the backend it forwards to. A request that starts at a permitted prefix therefore lands somewhere it should not — in the published template, on the CVE-2021-22005 analytics upload endpoint.
attack_vector.privileges_required: none — unauthenticated network access to the one port vCenter must expose.
attack_vector.complexity: low, and compositional. A single request tests it, with a 201-and-empty-body success condition. On its own the impact is access-control bypass; the code execution comes from whatever endpoint the bypass restores reach to.
attack_vector.ai_factor: None claimed or observed. VMSA-2021-0020 records that the issues were privately reported to VMware.

prevention.what_would_have_worked: Upgrading to vCenter 6.7 U3o or 6.5 U3q, or Cloud Foundation 3.10.2.2 via KB85719. There was no alternative — VMware records no workaround for this CVE.
prevention.adequacy: Adequate and reboot-gated, and the sequencing trap is that the same advisory offered a workaround for the critical companion CVE. An estate that applied KB85717 and deferred the appliance restart satisfied the urgent-looking item and left this one open.

detection.what_would_have_worked: Alerting on request paths containing `..;/` at the vCenter perimeter and in rhttpproxy access logs, and on requests resolving to analytics endpoints from an external source.
detection.adequacy: Straightforward once the token is known — the published nuclei template makes the exact request shape available to defenders as much as to attackers — but it requires rhttpproxy access logs to be forwarded off the appliance, which on most estates they are not.

response.what_would_have_worked: Treating a confirmed bypass as reachability to whatever it fronted: on 6.7 that means checking the CVE-2021-22005 upload path and the vCenter file system for what the chain would have left, not just closing the proxy finding.
response.adequacy: Correct and unlikely to be scoped that way, because the CVE that triggers the response is the low-severity one and the evidence to gather belongs to the high-severity one it was chained with.

NIST-800-53-SC-7.gap: The boundary is rhttpproxy and the defect is in rhttpproxy's own path normalisation, so the control is enforced by the component that fails. An assessment can verify the proxy exists, is configured, and restricts internal endpoints, and gather no evidence that bears on whether `..;/` resolves the same way on both sides of it.

NIS2-Art21-network-security.gap: Reachability here is a property of one URI parser rather than of the network. VMware published no workaround, port 443 is the port vCenter must expose, and the bypass rides legitimate management connections — so between the 2021-09-21 advisory and the appliance reboot there is no network-layer measure available.

UK-CAF-B4.gap: Assessed per system, each half of the observed attack looks tolerable: a low-impact proxy bypass and a critical upload flaw with a published mitigation. GreyNoise observed them chained, and no per-system assessment produces the finding that the mitigation on one is defeated by the other.

AU-Essential-8-Patch.gap: Severity-ordered patching takes CVE-2021-22005 at 9.8 before this at 5.3, and the critical one had a workaround (KB85717) while this one had none. The compliant queue therefore closes the flaw with an alternative first and leaves the flaw with no alternative open, which is the exact residue the observed chain runs through.

ISO-27001-2022-A.8.22.gap: Segregation of networks assumes a network boundary to inspect, and this boundary is a string comparison inside a single process on a single port. There is no VLAN, ACL or firewall rule that carries the separation between the external and internal vCenter namespaces, so the control has nothing to assess.

new_control_requirements.name: HYPERVISOR-VM-ESCAPE-TENANCY-ASSUMPTION
new_control_requirements.description: Treat the virtualisation control plane as a distinct trust tier: management interfaces reachable only from an operator network, and every endpoint behind the management proxy treated as externally reachable for threat-modelling purposes rather than as internal.
new_control_requirements.evidence: VMware's own description of the impact is 'internal endpoints being accessed', which means the internal/external split on this appliance is maintained by rhttpproxy's URI normalisation and by nothing else. With no workaround published and port 443 mandatory, restricting who can open a connection to vCenter at all was the only control available between the 2021-09-21 advisory and the appliance reboot to 6.7 U3o or 6.5 U3q.

new_control_requirements.name: MITIGATION-ACTIVE-PATCH-PENDING-VERDICT-CLASS
new_control_requirements.description: Compliance verdicts must distinguish three states: (a) binary patch deployed and the vulnerability eliminated, (b) a vendor mitigation active with no binary patch, and (c) neither — with the residual risk of (b) stated, including any other unpatched flaw that could defeat the mitigation.
new_control_requirements.evidence: VMSA-2021-0020 offered KB85717 as a mitigation for CVE-2021-22005 and no workaround at all for CVE-2021-22017. An appliance in state (b) on the critical flaw and state (c) on the bypass is the configuration GreyNoise observed being chained, and a verdict that records the mitigated critical as handled describes the estate as safer than it is. The residual-risk statement for (b) has to name what would defeat the mitigation.
